# Best final year projects for CSE: choosing one, building it, and writing the report
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-final-year-projects-cse/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best final year projects for CSE solve a real problem for real users, use current technology sensibly, and are deployed, measured and well documented. In 2026, strong options include RAG assistants over real documents, document AI, speech tools for local languages, and privacy-preserving vision apps. My own projects, from KrishGyan, which won Changethon 2025, to five production AI apps in 2026, taught me what makes projects stand out, so this page covers ideas, choosing, building, documentation, length, black books, resumes, and why buying projects backfires.

## What are the best final year projects for CSE?

Strong projects combine a real user, a working deployment and measurable results. AI-focused ideas stand out today, but a well-built web or systems project with real users beats a shallow AI demo.

Ideas with depth:

- A RAG assistant that answers questions from your college's handbooks with page citations.
- Document AI that extracts and validates fields from forms or invoices.
- Speech-to-text and question answering in Hindi or another Indian language.
- Browser-based face attendance with liveness checks, storing embeddings, never images.
- A fine-tuned small model for a domain task, with base versus tuned evaluation.
- A coordination platform for a social problem, like surplus food redistribution.

Each mirrors work I have shipped or seen win hackathons.

## How do I choose a final year project in computer science?

Choose at the overlap of three things: a problem you care about, skills relevant to the job you want, and data or users you can actually access. Then check scope: can your team build a working version in the time available?

Questions to ask:

- Who exactly is the user, and can you talk to them?
- Is data available legally, or can you collect it?
- Does it show skills employers in your target role want?
- Can you demo one complete flow end to end?
- What can you measure: accuracy, time saved, users?

Avoid copying popular project titles from lists; examiners and interviewers have seen them many times. A specific twist, such as a local language or a real organisation's data, makes ordinary ideas distinctive.

## What is the best AI for a final year project?

Use the AI that fits your problem: open models from Hugging Face for fine-tuning and offline use, hosted model APIs for language and vision features, and AI coding assistants to learn and speed up development. "Best" means appropriate, measured and explained.

For a project's AI component, prefer approaches you can evaluate: a RAG system with a test set, a classifier with accuracy metrics, or a fine-tuned model compared against its base. Examiners value understanding over novelty. As a development aid, AI assistants help you learn frameworks and debug faster, but write and understand your code yourself, because you must explain every part in your viva and interviews.

## How do I make a final year project step by step?

Define the problem and users, research existing solutions, design the system, build a minimal working version early, test with real users, iterate, then document and prepare the demo. Keep weekly milestones.

A practical sequence:

- Weeks 1 to 2: problem statement, user interviews, literature review.
- Weeks 3 to 4: requirements, architecture and data plan.
- Weeks 5 to 8: minimum working version, deployed.
- Weeks 9 to 12: features, testing and evaluation with real users.
- Weeks 13 to 14: polish, documentation and demo video.
- Final weeks: report, presentation rehearsal and viva preparation.

Use Git from day one, divide work by components, and hold short weekly check-ins with your guide.

## How do I make final year project documentation?

Follow your university's template, and write as you build rather than at the end. A typical report includes an abstract, introduction, literature review, requirements, system design, implementation, testing and results, conclusion, future work and references.

Tips for strong documentation:

- Include architecture, data flow and database diagrams.
- Explain why you made key design decisions, not just what you built.
- Show results with tables and charts: accuracy, response times, user feedback.
- Add screenshots of the working system.
- Cite sources properly with a reference manager such as Zotero.
- Keep a changelog during development to make writing easier.

Write the abstract last, once you know your actual results.

## How many pages should a final year project report be?

Most final year project reports run between 40 and 80 pages, including diagrams, screenshots, code excerpts and appendices, but your university or department guidelines decide. Some specify exact page ranges, fonts, margins and line spacing.

Quality matters more than length: examiners prefer a clear, well-structured 50 pages over 120 pages padded with copied theory. Put long code listings and raw data in appendices or a linked repository. Check formatting rules early, such as font size, spacing and margins, since these change page counts significantly. Ask your guide for an example of a well-graded report from previous years.

## How many words should a final year project report be?

Typical reports are about 10,000 to 15,000 words for the main body, excluding references, appendices and code, though requirements vary widely by university and programme. Always follow the official guideline, which may specify a range.

Distribute words sensibly: about 10 percent introduction, 15 to 20 percent literature review, 25 to 30 percent design and implementation, 20 percent testing and results, and the rest for discussion and conclusion. Avoid filling word counts with generic textbook explanations; examiners want your problem, your decisions and your evidence. Use precise language and let diagrams carry structural information.

## How do I make a black book for a final year project with AI?

The "black book" is the bound final project report used in some Indian universities. AI tools can help you outline chapters, improve grammar, summarise papers you have read, create diagram drafts and check formatting, but the content, results and analysis must be your own.

A responsible workflow:

- Write your own draft of each chapter from your project notes.
- Use AI to suggest structure and improve clarity, then review every change.
- Generate diagram drafts, then correct them to match your actual system.
- Verify every fact and citation; AI can invent references.
- Check your institution's policy on AI use and declare it if required.
- Run a plagiarism check before submission.

## Should I include my final year project on my resume?

Yes, especially as a fresher. Include it under projects with a one-line description, your specific role, the stack, and measurable results, plus links to the live demo and code.

A strong entry: "Built a RAG assistant answering questions from 300 pages of college handbooks with page citations; 85 percent answer accuracy on a 50-question test set; Next.js, FastAPI, PostgreSQL." Recruiters will ask about it, so be ready to explain architecture, trade-offs and what you would improve. If the project was team work, state your part clearly. A deployed, well-documented project can carry a fresher's resume.

## Where can I buy final year projects?

You should not buy final year projects. Submitting purchased work is academic misconduct that can lead to failing or degree cancellation, and you will struggle in the viva and in interviews when asked to explain code you did not write.

Bought projects are also usually generic, reused across many students and easy for examiners to recognise. If you are short on time or skills, choose a smaller scope, ask your guide for help, use open-source libraries legitimately with attribution, learn from tutorials and adapt them to your problem, and ask seniors or mentors for reviews. A modest project you built and understand is worth far more than an impressive one you cannot defend.

# Best free AI coding assistants for developers and students: GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini Code Assist compared
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-free-ai-coding-assistants-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are the best free AI coding assistants right now?

**For inline autocomplete inside an editor, GitHub Copilot's free tier is the most widely usable, with a real monthly request allowance rather than a short trial [1]. For agentic coding, changes that span multiple files, run commands, and verify their own work, Claude Code is what I reach for daily on real codebases [2]. Cursor bundles both styles into one editor with a capable free tier [3]. Codeium, now Windsurf, offers unlimited autocomplete free with a smaller agentic allowance [4]. Students should check the GitHub Student Developer Pack before paying for any of these [2].**


I run production work through several of these depending on the task, and the honest answer to "which is best" is that autocomplete tools and agentic tools solve different problems and most serious developers end up using one of each.

> Autocomplete finishes your sentence. An agentic coding tool reads the paragraph, understands the chapter, and rewrites the section. Know which job you actually need done.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the difference between autocomplete and agentic coding tools?

**Autocomplete tools, GitHub Copilot's classic mode, Codeium, suggest the next few lines as you type, based on the surrounding code and your comment. Agentic coding tools, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor's agent mode, take a task description, read the relevant files across your repository themselves, make multi-file edits, run tests or commands, and iterate until the task is done or it needs your input. The first speeds up typing; the second does a chunk of the engineering work itself.**



## Is GitHub Copilot actually free?

**Yes, with a real free tier for individuals: a monthly allowance of completions and chat requests, not a time-limited trial, alongside paid tiers for higher limits and more model choice [1]. Students, teachers and open-source maintainers can often qualify for free access to paid tiers through GitHub's education and open-source programmes; check the GitHub Student Developer Pack, which also bundles other developer tools, before assuming any of this costs money [2].**



## What is Claude Code, and is there a free way to use it?

**Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: it runs in your terminal or editor, reads your actual repository, makes changes, runs commands, and works through engineering tasks end to end rather than only chatting [2]. It is usage-based rather than a flat free product, billed through the same API access as Claude generally, so cost scales with how much you use it; check current plans directly, since pricing structures change. For students exploring it, starting with small, well-scoped tasks keeps usage, and cost, predictable while you learn what it is good at.**


## What about Cursor, Windsurf and other AI-native editors?

**Cursor is a fork of VS Code with both autocomplete and agentic editing built in, with a usable free tier and paid tiers for heavier use and stronger models [3]. Codeium, rebranded Windsurf, historically offered unlimited free autocomplete with a separate, smaller free allowance for its agentic "Cascade" feature [4]. Both are worth trying because they are full editors, not just a plugin, which changes the experience meaningfully compared with bolting an assistant onto an editor you already use.**



## What is Gemini Code Assist, and are there open-source alternatives?

**Gemini Code Assist is Google's coding assistant, with a free tier for individual developers and integration into Google's own cloud and Android tooling [5]. For a fully open, self-hostable option, Continue.dev lets you plug in any model, including a local one through Ollama, with no vendor billing at all beyond whatever compute you provide yourself [8]. This is the right choice when privacy or cost predictability matters more than having the newest closed model.**


## How do I choose without paying for something a free tier already covers?

**Start with GitHub Copilot's free tier for everyday autocomplete, since it is genuinely free and widely supported. Add one agentic tool for real implementation tasks, Claude Code or Cursor's agent mode, and use it deliberately on scoped tasks rather than leaving it running unsupervised on your whole codebase. Reassess every few months, since free tiers, limits and the strongest model at each tier change on a timescale of months, not years, and the tool that was worth paying for six months ago may now have a free tier that covers the same use.**




## What mistakes do students make picking a coding assistant?

**Paying for a tool before checking student eligibility for free or discounted access. Treating an agentic tool's first draft as final without reviewing the diff the way you would a colleague's pull request. Using only autocomplete and never trying an agentic tool on a real multi-file task, missing what the category can actually do. Switching tools every week chasing whichever launched most recently, instead of learning one well enough to use it fast.**



## Where should I start?

**Turn on GitHub Copilot's free tier today, and this week give one agentic tool a single well-scoped task, add a feature to a small project, and review its diff line by line before merging.** For a workshop on using AI coding assistants well, autocomplete and agentic, without losing code quality, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Best Gemini prompts: photo prompts for couples, girls and boys, plus Jio, courses, fixes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-gemini-prompts/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best Gemini prompts are specific: they tell Gemini who to act as, what you want, the context, any constraints, and the exact format of the answer, and photo prompts add style, setting, lighting and what must stay unchanged. Trending photo prompts for portraits and couples are popular in India, so they are covered here with privacy tips. I write prompts for AI products daily, so this page covers general and photo prompt examples, the Jio Gemini offer, Gemini courses, freezing fixes and parallel API requests.

## What are the best Gemini prompts?

The best prompts include five parts: a role, a clear goal, relevant context, constraints, and the output format. "Explain photosynthesis" becomes "You are a biology tutor. Explain photosynthesis to a Class 10 student in five bullet points with one everyday example, then ask me one quiz question."

High-value prompt patterns:

- "Summarise this document in 7 bullets for a busy manager, with deadlines highlighted."
- "Act as an interviewer for a fresher data analyst role; ask one question at a time."
- "Rewrite this email to be polite and concise, under 120 words."
- "Compare these two laptops for coding in a table with a recommendation."
- "Create a 4-week study plan for DBMS with daily 1-hour sessions."

## What are some example Gemini prompts?

Examples for everyday use: "Plan a three-day trip itinerary on a student budget with travel times", "Explain this error message and how to fix it", "Turn my meeting notes into action items with owners", and "Give me ten project ideas using RAG for college students".

For learning: "Teach me recursion with three examples from easy to hard, then test me." For writing: "Give me three headline options for this blog post in a professional tone." For coding: "Write a Python function that validates Indian phone numbers, with tests." Follow up to refine: ask for shorter answers, different tone, more examples or sources.

## What are the best Gemini photo prompts for girls?

Popular photo-editing prompts transform a portrait into styles such as a vintage film look, a traditional saree portrait with golden-hour lighting, a professional studio headshot, or an artistic illustration. Always ask Gemini to keep the face and identity unchanged.

Example prompts:

- "Turn this into a retro 1990s film-style portrait with warm tones and soft grain; keep my face exactly the same."
- "Create a studio portrait in a red saree with soft golden lighting and a plain backdrop; preserve facial features."
- "Make a professional LinkedIn headshot with a neutral grey background and natural lighting."

Upload only your own photos, avoid sharing images of others without consent, and remember edited images carry AI watermarks.

## What are the best Gemini photo prompts for boys?

Popular prompts for boys include cinematic portraits, streetwear fashion shoots, sports-poster styles, superhero-style illustrations and professional headshots, with instructions to keep the face and identity unchanged.

Examples:

- "Create a cinematic portrait at night in a city street with neon reflections; keep my face identical."
- "Make a sports magazine cover style photo in a cricket jersey with stadium lights."
- "Turn this into a clean professional headshot with a navy background and soft light."
- "Create a 3D cartoon figurine version of me on a desk display."

Refine with follow-ups such as lighting, outfit colour or background, one change at a time.

## What are the best Gemini photo prompts for men?

For men, effective prompts often target professional images, such as executive headshots and speaker portraits, plus stylised looks like vintage film, formal wedding portraits or outdoor adventure scenes, always preserving facial features.

Examples:

- "Professional speaker portrait on a stage with soft spotlight and a blurred audience; same face and hairstyle."
- "Executive headshot in a dark suit, light grey background, natural expression."
- "Vintage black-and-white portrait with dramatic side lighting."

For professional use, such as LinkedIn or company profiles, choose natural results over heavy stylisation, and consider whether AI-edited photos are appropriate in your context.

## What are the best Gemini photo prompts for couples?

Couple prompts often create romantic or festive portraits: golden-hour beach scenes, traditional wedding-style portraits, vintage film photos, or illustrated keepsakes, using a photo of both people and asking Gemini to keep both faces unchanged.

Examples:

- "Turn this into a golden-hour portrait on a beach with soft warm light; keep both faces identical."
- "Create a traditional Indian wedding-style portrait with marigold decorations."
- "Make a vintage 1970s film photograph look with warm tones."
- "Create a watercolour illustration of us for an anniversary card."

Get your partner's consent before uploading, and avoid uploading intimate photos to any AI service.

## Which Gemini plan is free with Jio?

Reliance Jio and Google have offered eligible Jio users access to Google's AI Pro plan, which includes advanced Gemini features, for a limited period through partnership offers. Eligibility, duration and activation steps depend on the current offer terms.

Check the MyJio app or Jio's official website for the latest offer, eligible plans and age criteria, and activate it through official channels only. Beware of messages or websites claiming free Gemini access that ask for payments or passwords; they may be scams. Google also offers student promotions in some periods, worth checking on Google's official pages.

## Is there a Gemini AI course?

Yes. Google offers free learning paths on Google Cloud Skills Boost and Google's AI learning pages covering Gemini, prompting and building with the Gemini API, and Kaggle has hosted Google's generative AI intensive courses with codelabs.

A learning path: start with prompting basics and everyday Gemini use; then try Google AI Studio to experiment with models; then build a small app with the Gemini API, such as a document question-answering tool; and finally learn evaluation and safety. Courses help, but building one real project teaches the most.

## Why does Gemini freeze up?

Gemini can freeze because of very long conversations, large uploads, heavy modes like Deep Research or image generation, slow networks, outdated apps or browsers, low device memory, or temporary service problems.

Fixes:

- Start a new chat when one gets long.
- Upload smaller files or fewer pages.
- Update the app and browser; clear cache.
- Close other heavy apps and tabs.
- Switch networks or try mobile data.
- Try the web version if the app freezes, or vice versa.

If it freezes for everyone at once, wait; service issues are usually resolved quickly.

## How do I send parallel requests to the Gemini API?

Use asynchronous code to send several requests concurrently, for example with Python's asyncio and the Gemini SDK's async client, limiting concurrency with a semaphore so you stay within rate limits, and retrying 429 errors with exponential backoff.

```python
import asyncio
from google import genai
client = genai.Client()
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)
async def ask(prompt):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.aio.models.generate_content(model="gemini-2.5-flash", contents=prompt)
        return r.text
results = asyncio.run(asyncio.gather(*[ask(p) for p in ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3"]]))
```

For large offline jobs, use batch processing instead, which is cheaper and avoids rate-limit pressure.

# Best machine learning courses, free and paid, and what learning AI means
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-machine-learning-courses/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best machine learning course for most beginners is Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Specialization from DeepLearning.AI and Stanford; the best free alternatives are Google's Machine Learning Crash Course, fast.ai's Practical Deep Learning for Coders and Kaggle Learn's short courses. Machine learning itself is the branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data rather than following fixed rules. This page compares the courses, including YouTube and Udemy options and those learners recommend most, then explains what machine learning, learning models and "learning AI" mean, with examples.

## What is the best machine learning course?

For a structured start, Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Specialization is the most widely recommended: clear explanations, Python labs and a gentle path from regression to neural networks. You can audit much of it for free.

How the top options differ:

- **Machine Learning Specialization**: theory with intuition, good for complete beginners.
- **Google's Machine Learning Crash Course**: free, practical, with interactive exercises.
- **fast.ai Practical Deep Learning**: free, top-down, building working models from lesson one; best if you can already code.
- **Kaggle Learn**: free micro-courses on Python, pandas, ML and deep learning, with notebooks in the browser.

Pick one, finish it, then build a project. Switching between courses is the most common way beginners stall.

## What is the best free AI learning course?

Google's Machine Learning Crash Course, fast.ai, Kaggle Learn, Elements of AI and Hugging Face's courses are excellent and free. NPTEL offers free courses from IIT and IISc faculty, with optional paid certification exams.

Choose by goal:

- **Understand AI without coding**: Elements of AI.
- **Learn ML with Python**: Google's crash course or Kaggle Learn.
- **Build deep learning models**: fast.ai.
- **Work with large language models**: Hugging Face's LLM course.
- **Academic depth with an Indian certificate**: NPTEL machine learning courses.

Free courses are enough to reach a job-ready level. Certificates help a little on a CV; a deployed project helps much more.

## What is a free AI course for beginners?

Elements of AI is the gentlest free start if you have no coding background. If you can code a little, Kaggle Learn's Python, Intro to Machine Learning and Intro to Deep Learning courses are short, practical and free.

A beginner path that works in about three months of steady evenings:

- Python basics and pandas with Kaggle Learn.
- Core ML concepts with Google's crash course.
- One classic project: predict house prices or classify messages as spam.
- Deep learning basics with fast.ai's first lessons.
- One GenAI project: a small assistant over your own notes using an LLM API.

Spend at least half your time building, not watching. Explaining what you built to a friend is a good test of understanding.

## What is the best machine learning course on YouTube?

Strong free YouTube choices include Stanford's CS229 lectures for theory, Andrej Karpathy's Neural Networks: Zero to Hero for building neural networks from scratch, 3Blue1Brown's neural network series for intuition, StatQuest for clear explanations of algorithms, and MIT's Introduction to Deep Learning.

Use them for different needs:

- **Intuition**: 3Blue1Brown and StatQuest.
- **Theory and maths**: Stanford CS229.
- **Building from scratch in code**: Karpathy's series.
- **Modern deep learning overview**: MIT's course.

YouTube's weakness is structure: it is easy to watch passively and never practise. Code along with every video, pause to predict what comes next, and turn each series into a notebook of your own.

## What is the best machine learning course on Udemy?

Udemy has popular machine learning courses, such as long "A to Z" style courses covering many algorithms with Python. Quality varies, so judge a course by its update date, curriculum, instructor background and reviews that mention projects.

Before buying, check:

- **Last updated**: older than two years can mean outdated libraries.
- **Curriculum**: covers data preparation, evaluation and at least one end-to-end project.
- **Instructor**: practical industry or teaching experience.
- **Preview lectures**: watch two to see if the teaching style suits you.

Udemy courses are good for broad, hands-on coverage; for depth, pair them with a stronger free course. Udemy often runs discounts, so never pay full price in a hurry.

## Which machine learning courses do learners recommend most?

The courses learners recommend most consistently in forums and communities are Andrew Ng's courses, fast.ai, Stanford CS229, Karpathy's Zero to Hero series and the book Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras and TensorFlow.

The common advice that comes with those recommendations is more useful than any single course: learn enough Python and maths to follow along, finish one course instead of starting five, do Kaggle competitions or projects to apply what you learned, and read code from good repositories. Recommendations shift as new courses appear, especially for LLMs and GenAI, where Hugging Face's course and providers' own documentation are often more current than general ML courses.

## Why is machine learning considered AI?

Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence. AI is the broad goal of building systems that perform tasks needing intelligence; machine learning is the approach of reaching that goal by learning from data rather than hand-coding every rule.

Early AI relied heavily on rules written by experts, such as chess heuristics or medical decision trees. Machine learning flipped that: show a system many examples, and it finds the patterns itself. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses large neural networks, and today's large language models are deep learning models trained on huge text datasets. So the hierarchy is AI, then machine learning, then deep learning, then generative models such as LLMs.

## What are AI learning models?

An AI learning model is the result of training: a mathematical function with parameters, adjusted on example data, that maps new inputs to outputs, such as an email to "spam" or "not spam", or a prompt to a written answer.

Common types:

- **Linear and logistic regression**: simple, fast, interpretable.
- **Decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting**: strong on tabular data.
- **Neural networks**: for images, audio and text.
- **Transformers**: the architecture behind large language models.

Models are trained with supervised learning (labelled examples), unsupervised learning (finding structure without labels) or reinforcement learning (learning from rewards). A model is only as good as its data and evaluation, so test it on data it has never seen.

## What does learning AI mean?

"Learning AI" can mean two things: a person studying artificial intelligence, or a system that learns from data. For students, it means building skills in programming, maths, machine learning and, increasingly, building products with AI models.

For a career in GenAI engineering, learning AI today means:

- Python and software engineering basics.
- Enough maths: linear algebra, probability and calculus intuition.
- Machine learning fundamentals and evaluation.
- Working with LLM APIs: prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use and fine-tuning with methods like LoRA.
- Shipping: APIs, deployment, monitoring and cost.

I learned by building: five production AI applications, including a RAG platform and a fine-tuning studio. Projects force you to learn what courses skip.

## What are examples of AI that learns?

Everyday examples include spam filters that learn from emails marked as spam, recommendation systems on YouTube and Netflix, voice assistants that recognise speech, face unlock on phones, fraud detection in banking, and chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini.

Each one learns from data: spam filters from labelled emails, recommendations from what users watch and skip, speech recognition from thousands of hours of transcribed audio, and language models from vast amounts of text. Some keep learning after deployment as new data arrives and models are retrained. Good student projects copy these patterns at small scale: a spam classifier, a movie recommender, a speech-to-text note-taker or a question-answering bot over your college handbook.

# Which Ollama model is best for coding? Local, agentic, tools, reasoning and embeddings
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-ollama-model-for-coding/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best Ollama model for coding is usually the largest coding-specialised model your hardware runs comfortably: the Qwen Coder family is a common first choice, with Devstral, DeepSeek Coder and general models such as gpt-oss as strong alternatives. Benchmarks change monthly, so test two or three on your own code. I run local models for private document work alongside cloud APIs, so this page covers coding, agentic and cloud models, tool support, reasoning, image generation, embeddings, reranking, and training models for Ollama.

## Which Ollama model is best for coding?

Coding-specialised models, especially the Qwen Coder series, are widely regarded as the best open coding models on Ollama, with Devstral, DeepSeek Coder and Codestral as other strong options. General models such as gpt-oss and Qwen also code well.

Size matters: a 7 to 8 billion parameter coder runs on a laptop GPU with 8 GB of VRAM when quantised, handling autocomplete and small functions; 14 to 32 billion models need 16 to 24 GB but reason much better about larger code. Compare models on tasks from your real projects: writing a function, fixing a bug and explaining unfamiliar code. Community comparisons, such as Reddit threads, are useful starting points, but your stack and languages decide.

## What is the best local Ollama model for coding?

Locally, choose by VRAM: on 8 GB, a 7B coder in 4-bit; on 12 to 16 GB, a 14B model; on 24 GB or more, a 30B-class coder such as a larger Qwen Coder variant. Apple silicon Macs with unified memory can run larger models with enough RAM.

Practical tips:

- Use the instruct versions for chat and the base or FIM-capable versions for autocomplete.
- Increase the context length setting for multi-file work, if memory allows.
- Pair Ollama with editor extensions such as Continue for in-editor use.
- Keep a smaller model for fast completions and a larger one for chat.

Local models keep code private, which matters for client or proprietary work.

## What is the best Ollama model for agentic coding?

Agentic coding needs models trained for tool use, instruction following and long context, so they can read files, run commands and edit code over many steps. Models built for this, such as Devstral and newer Qwen Coder releases, are the best local candidates.

Even strong open models are less reliable at long agent loops than frontier cloud models, so keep tasks small, provide good project instructions, and review every change. Run agents with tools such as Cline, Continue or OpenHands configured to use Ollama. Increase the context window, since agents accumulate long histories. Test on your repository with a handful of realistic tasks before trusting a model for bigger changes.

## What is the best Ollama cloud model for coding?

Ollama offers cloud models that run large open models on Ollama's servers through the same interface, letting you use models too big for your machine, such as very large Qwen Coder or gpt-oss variants, for coding tasks.

Cloud models trade privacy for capability: code is sent to Ollama's servers, so review their data policy before using them with sensitive code. They are useful when local hardware cannot run strong models, or for occasional heavy tasks. Check the Ollama library for models marked as cloud, their limits and pricing, and compare results with local models and other providers on the same tasks.

## Which Ollama models support tools?

Models tagged "tools" in the Ollama library support function calling, including recent Llama, Qwen, Mistral, gpt-oss and other families. You pass tool definitions with the chat request, and the model returns tool calls with arguments for your code to execute.

```python
import ollama
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_order_status",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}}}}}]
resp = ollama.chat(model="qwen3", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 4521?"}], tools=tools)
print(resp.message.tool_calls)
```

Validate tool arguments before executing them, and test reliability, since smaller models sometimes call tools incorrectly.

## Which Ollama model is best for reasoning?

Reasoning-tuned models, such as DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, Qwen models with thinking modes, and gpt-oss with adjustable reasoning effort, perform best on maths, logic and multi-step problems. They think step by step before answering, which takes longer.

Choose the largest reasoning model that runs at acceptable speed. For quick questions, disable or reduce thinking to save time. Reasoning models help with debugging complex code, planning and analysis, but can overthink simple tasks. Evaluate on problems from your domain with known answers, because reasoning benchmarks do not always reflect practical usefulness.

## Which Ollama model is best for image generation?

Ollama is designed mainly for language models and vision models that understand images, such as LLaVA, Gemma and Qwen vision variants, rather than for generating images. For image generation, use tools such as ComfyUI or Automatic1111 with Stable Diffusion or Flux models.

Vision models in Ollama can describe photos, read text in screenshots and answer questions about diagrams, useful for document and accessibility tools. For generation workflows, ComfyUI with GGUF-quantised models runs well on consumer GPUs. Check Ollama's release notes for any newer multimodal capabilities, since the project evolves quickly.

## What is the best embeddings model on Ollama?

Popular Ollama embedding models include nomic-embed-text, mxbai-embed-large, bge-m3 for multilingual use, and newer options such as Qwen3 Embedding and EmbeddingGemma. The best choice depends on language, document type and speed needs.

For English RAG, start with nomic-embed-text or mxbai-embed-large; for Hindi and other languages, try bge-m3 or a multilingual Qwen embedding. Evaluate retrieval recall on your own questions before deciding. Use the same model for indexing and queries, record the model name with your index, and re-embed everything if you switch. Local embeddings keep private documents on your machine.

## What is the best reranking model for Ollama?

Ollama does not provide a dedicated reranking endpoint, so most people run rerankers, such as BGE rerankers or other cross-encoders, through Sentence Transformers, a separate inference server, or a framework integration, alongside Ollama for generation.

A typical local RAG stack: Ollama for embeddings and the chat model, a vector store for retrieval, and a cross-encoder reranker in Python to reorder the top 20 to 50 candidates before generation. Some people prompt an LLM to score relevance as a workaround, but dedicated rerankers are faster and more consistent. RAG.NextUpgrad's reranking step after fusion is where much of its answer quality comes from.

## How do I train an Ollama model?

Ollama runs models but does not train them. Fine-tune a base model elsewhere with tools such as Unsloth or Hugging Face TRL using LoRA or QLoRA, merge or export it to GGUF format, then create an Ollama model from it with a Modelfile.

Steps:

- Fine-tune with QLoRA on your instruction data, as FineTune Studio does.
- Merge the adapter into the base model or export it.
- Convert to GGUF and quantise with llama.cpp tools, or export directly with Unsloth.
- Write a Modelfile with `FROM ./model.gguf`, the chat template and parameters.
- Run `ollama create mymodel -f Modelfile`, then test it.

Compare the tuned model against the base on held-out prompts before relying on it.

# Best open source LLMs now: examples, coding, function calling, embeddings, rerankers

Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Open-weight language models now rival proprietary ones on many tasks, and a full open-source stack exists around them: embedding models, rerankers, vector databases and observability tools. I use open models in practice, with Groq-hosted Llama in DocuLens AI and QLoRA fine-tuning in FineTune Studio, so this page covers the current best open LLMs, examples, Hugging Face picks, function calling, coding, rerankers, embeddings, vector search, observability, and open weight versus open source. What is the current best open source LLM? Leading open-weight models in 2026 come from the DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and gpt-oss families, with large mixture-of-experts models approaching frontier proprietary performance on many benchmarks. Rankings shift almost monthly as new releases arrive. Also asked as: best open source llm huggingface · best open source llm models for coding · open weight vs open source llm The best choice depends on hardware and task. Very large models such as DeepSeek's latest releases, Kimi K2 and the biggest Qwen3 models need multi-GPU servers or hosted providers. gpt-oss-120b runs on a single high-memory GPU, while mid-size models serve laptops and smaller servers. Licences vary from MIT and Apache 2.0 to custom terms. Check LMArena and task-specific leaderboards, then test shortlisted models on your own prompts before deciding. What are examples of open source LLM models? Examples include Meta's Llama family, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek's V3 and R1, Mistral's models, Google's Gemma, Microsoft's Phi, OpenAI's gpt-oss, Moonshot's Kimi K2, Zhipu's GLM, and fully open research models such as AI2's OLMo. Most are open-weight rather than fully open source: weights are downloadable, but training data and full training code are not. OLMo and similar projects release data, code and checkpoints, enabling full reproducibility. Sizes range from under one billion parameters for phones to hundreds of billions for servers. Many come in base, instruct, reasoning and coding variants. Community fine-tunes and quantizations on Hugging Face multiply the options further, so check provenance before using derivatives. What is the best open source LLM on Hugging Face? On Hugging Face, the most downloaded and trending open models include the Qwen3, Llama, Gemma, gpt-oss, DeepSeek and Mistral families, each with instruct and quantized versions. The best one depends on your size limits and task. Use the Hub's filters for task, parameter size, licence and library, then sort by trending or downloads. Read model cards for benchmarks, context length, languages and intended use. Prefer official organisations or trusted quantizers for GGUF and other formats. Hugging Face's Inference Providers let you test large models without hosting them. Once you shortlist candidates, compare them on your own evaluation set, measuring quality, speed and memory on your target hardware. What is the best open source LLM for function calling? Strong open models for function calling include Qwen3, gpt-oss, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5 and later GLM releases, and recent Llama and Mistral models. The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard compares models on tool-use accuracy across many scenarios. Also asked as: best function calling open source llm Reliable function calling needs correct JSON arguments, choosing the right tool, knowing when not to call tools and handling multi-step sequences. Serving matters too: use inference engines such as vLLM or Ollama with each model's correct chat template and tool parser, or tool calls will fail. Smaller models handle single, well-described tools well but struggle with long agent chains. Validate arguments against schemas and test on your actual tools before production. What are the best open source LLMs for coding? Leading open coding models include Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek's latest models, Kimi K2, GLM's recent releases, Mistral's Devstral and gpt-oss. Large versions approach proprietary models on benchmarks such as SWE-bench, while smaller variants run locally. For editor autocomplete, small models such as Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B or 7B respond quickly. For agentic coding, models trained on software engineering tasks, like Devstral and Qwen3-Coder, handle tool use and multi-file edits better. Running the largest models needs serious hardware or hosted APIs from inference providers. Test on your own repositories with tools such as Aider, Cline or OpenHands, measuring correctness and how much human review each change needs. What are the best open source reranking models? Strong open rerankers include BAAI's bge-reranker-v2-m3, mixedbread's mxbai-rerank models, Jina's rerankers, Qwen3-Reranker and ColBERT-style late-interaction models. They reorder retrieved passages by relevance, improving RAG answer quality. Rerankers use cross-encoders that read the query and each passage together, which is more accurate but slower than embedding similarity, so apply them to the top twenty to one hundred candidates from first-stage retrieval. RAG.NextUpgrad reranks after merging dense and BM25 results with reciprocal rank fusion. Multilingual rerankers matter for Indian languages and mixed-language text. Check licences, since some models restrict commercial use, and measure latency on your hardware. Start without a reranker, then add one and measure the gain. What are the best open source text embedding models? Strong open embedding models include BGE-M3, Qwen3 Embedding, multilingual E5, Nomic Embed, GTE models and Google's EmbeddingGemma. The MTEB leaderboard compares them across retrieval, clustering and classification tasks. Also asked as: best text embedding models open source Choose by language coverage, maximum input length, dimension size, speed and licence. BGE-M3 supports dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval in one model, useful for hybrid search. Smaller models such as EmbeddingGemma suit on-device use. Some popular embedding models carry non-commercial licences, so verify terms before shipping. Benchmark rankings rarely match your domain exactly, so build a small set of real queries with known relevant documents and measure recall for each candidate. Re-embed your corpus whenever you switch models. What are the best open source vector search databases? Popular open-source options include Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Chroma, LanceDB, OpenSearch and Vespa, plus pgvector for PostgreSQL and libraries such as FAISS for in-memory search. Qdrant and Weaviate offer strong filtering and hybrid search, Milvus targets very large deployments, Chroma and LanceDB suit local development and embedded use, and OpenSearch and Vespa combine full-text and vector search at scale. pgvector keeps vectors beside relational data with no extra service. FAISS is a library rather than a database, ideal for experiments. Choose by scale, filtering needs, operations and your team's existing stack, then benchmark on your data. Measure recall and latency with realistic filters, not just raw speed. What is the best open source LLM observability tool? Popular open-source LLM observability tools include Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, OpenLLMetry, Helicone, Opik and MLflow's tracing features. They record prompts, responses, latency, token usage, costs and evaluation scores for every model call. Observability helps debug wrong answers, find slow or expensive steps and track quality over time. Most tools support OpenTelemetry and integrate with LangChain, LlamaIndex and provider SDKs. Self-hosting keeps sensitive prompts and data inside your infrastructure. Combine tracing with evaluation datasets, so every prompt or model change is measured before release. For RAG, log retrieved passages alongside answers, since many failures come from retrieval rather than generation. Start simple: even basic logs of inputs and outputs reveal most problems early. What is the difference between open weight and open source LLMs? Open-weight models release downloadable weights you can run and fine-tune, often under custom licences, but not their training data or full code. Fully open-source models also release training data, code and details under open licences, enabling reproduction. The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition requires enough information about training data, plus code and weights under open terms. Most popular models, including Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek, are open-weight; projects such as OLMo aim for full openness. For most builders, open weights provide what matters day to day: local deployment, privacy and fine-tuning. For research, auditing and reproducibility, fully open models are more valuable. Always read the licence before commercial use.

# Best OpenCV tutorial: where to start, GitHub, Java, PDF, and OpenCV vs Pillow or PyTorch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-opencv-tutorial/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best OpenCV tutorial for most people is the official OpenCV-Python tutorial series on docs.opencv.org, combined with small hands-on projects: reading images, filtering, edge detection, contours, face detection and webcam processing. Official samples on GitHub fill gaps, and courses help if you like structure. I use OpenCV around the vision and OCR work in FaceVision and DocuLens AI, so this page covers tutorials for beginners, GitHub, Java and PDFs, and how OpenCV differs from Pillow, PyTorch, deep learning and computer vision.

## What is the best OpenCV tutorial?

The official OpenCV-Python tutorials are the best free starting point: they cover core operations, image processing, feature detection, video analysis, camera calibration, machine learning and deep learning modules, with code you can run immediately.

Complement them with a project-based course or book if you prefer guided learning, and with the computer vision theory in Stanford's CS231n notes when you reach deep learning. Community recommendations, such as those on Reddit, often point to the same combination: official docs for reference, one structured course, and lots of practice on your own images. Avoid tutorials using OpenCV 2 or 3 syntax without checking for updates. Whatever you choose, type the code yourself rather than copying it, change parameters to see what happens, and keep a notebook of small experiments; that habit turns tutorials into real skill.

## What is a good OpenCV tutorial for beginners?

Start with Python and the official tutorials' "Gui Features" and "Core Operations" sections, then image processing. Practise each concept on your own photos and webcam feed.

A beginner sequence:

- Install with `pip install opencv-python` and read, show and save an image.
- Convert colour spaces, resize, crop and rotate.
- Apply blur, thresholding and edge detection.
- Find and draw contours to detect shapes.
- Capture webcam video and process frames in real time.
- Run a pretrained face detector.

Then build a mini project, such as a document scanner that finds a page and flattens it, which uses most of these skills together. A second good project is a webcam app that counts fingers or detects motion, which teaches real-time processing and performance basics.

## What is the OpenCV tutorial and where can I find it?

The OpenCV tutorial is the official set of guides in the OpenCV documentation, organised by language and topic. Find it at docs.opencv.org, choose your version such as 4.x, and open the Tutorials section for C++, Python, Java or JavaScript.

Other reliable places: the samples folder in the OpenCV GitHub repository, the OpenCV website's courses and blog, and university course materials. Third-party sites such as GeeksforGeeks and W3Schools-style tutorials can help with quick examples but vary in depth and accuracy. Prefer sources that state which OpenCV version they use, and test code yourself.

## Where can I find OpenCV tutorials on GitHub?

The OpenCV repository's `samples` folder contains official examples in Python, C++, Java and other languages, and the `opencv_contrib` repository includes samples for extra modules. Community repositories collect projects and notebooks too.

Useful approaches: browse `samples/python` for runnable scripts on topics like optical flow, feature matching and video; search GitHub for "opencv tutorial" or "opencv projects" filtered by recent updates and stars; and study complete projects such as document scanners, lane detection and face recognition apps. Check licences before reusing code, and prefer repositories with clear READMEs and recent commits.

## Is there an OpenCV tutorial for Java?

Yes. OpenCV provides official Java bindings and tutorials covering setup, building with Maven or Gradle, and basic image processing. Android developers also use OpenCV's Android SDK, which builds on the Java API.

Setup is the main hurdle: you need the OpenCV Java library and native libraries for your platform, then load them with `System.loadLibrary(Core.NATIVE_LIBRARY_NAME)`. After that, the API mirrors C++, with classes such as `Mat` and `Imgproc`. For Android, consider whether Google's ML Kit covers your need more simply. For desktop Java, the official tutorial and the Java samples in the repository are the best references.

## Is there an OpenCV tutorial PDF?

The official documentation is web-based, and older versions offered downloadable PDF references. You can save tutorial pages as PDFs from your browser, and some books and university course notes are available as PDFs.

Web documentation is better for learning because it matches your version and includes working links. If you need offline access, download the documentation build for your version, or save the specific tutorials you are using. Be cautious with free PDFs of paid books shared on unofficial sites; they may be pirated or outdated. Books from reputable publishers remain good structured resources, and many include downloadable code you can run alongside the chapters.

## What is the difference between Pillow and OpenCV?

Pillow is a Python imaging library for basic tasks: opening, resizing, cropping, converting formats, drawing and simple filters. OpenCV is a full computer vision library with advanced image processing, video, feature detection, geometry, camera calibration and deep learning inference.

Choose Pillow for simple image manipulation in web apps and scripts; choose OpenCV for vision tasks, real-time video and performance-heavy processing. One common gotcha: OpenCV loads images in BGR colour order, while Pillow uses RGB, so convert when passing images between them. Many projects use both, Pillow for I/O with web frameworks and OpenCV for processing.

## What is the difference between PyTorch and OpenCV?

PyTorch is a deep learning framework for building and training neural networks. OpenCV is a computer vision library for processing images and video, which can also run trained models through its DNN module.

They work together: OpenCV reads camera frames, resizes and normalises them, PyTorch runs a model, then OpenCV draws results such as boxes and labels. For training, use PyTorch; for deployment on lightweight systems, you can export a PyTorch model to ONNX and run it with OpenCV or ONNX Runtime. FaceVision follows a similar idea in the browser, running ONNX models with ONNX Runtime Web.

## What is the difference between OpenCV and deep learning?

OpenCV is a software library; deep learning is a method of building models with many-layered neural networks. OpenCV includes many classical algorithms that involve no learning, plus tools to run deep learning models.

Classical OpenCV techniques, like thresholding, edge detection and contour analysis, work well for controlled conditions and need no training data. Deep learning handles complex, variable scenes, such as recognising objects in cluttered photos, but needs data and compute. Modern pipelines combine them: OpenCV for preprocessing and geometry, deep learning for recognition.

## What is the difference between OpenCV and computer vision?

Computer vision is the scientific field of enabling computers to understand images and video. OpenCV is an open-source library that implements many computer vision algorithms, making the field practical for developers.

Computer vision includes theory, research and many tools beyond OpenCV, such as deep learning frameworks, specialised libraries and cloud vision services. OpenCV is one of the most widely used tools in the field, but knowing OpenCV is not the same as understanding computer vision. Learn the concepts, like image formation, filtering, features and neural networks, alongside the library. Courses such as Stanford's CS231n teach the deep learning side, while classic textbooks cover geometry and image processing foundations that OpenCV functions implement.

# Best portfolio websites for developers: hosting, designs, project ideas and templates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-portfolio-websites-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best portfolio website for a developer is usually your own site on your own domain, hosted free on GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify, showing three to five strong projects with live demos, code links and short case studies. Platforms like GitHub and LinkedIn support it but do not replace it. My own site, [pranjulrathour.scult.in](https://pranjulrathour.scult.in), runs on Next.js with project, invite and hire pages, so this page covers hosting, GitHub, frontend, backend and software developer portfolios, project ideas, designs, templates and examples.

## What are the best portfolio websites for developers?

The strongest option is a personal website you control, linked from GitHub, LinkedIn and your resume. It lets you present projects your way, rank in search for your name, and give recruiters one link that tells your story.

Supporting platforms help too: GitHub shows code and activity, LinkedIn reaches recruiters, Dribbble or Behance suit design-heavy front-end developers, and Devpost records hackathon projects. Use them as evidence pointing back to your site. Whatever you choose, keep it current; a portfolio last updated three years ago signals inactivity more than it showcases skill. Add a short update every time you finish a meaningful project, give a talk or win an event, so the site keeps reflecting your current level rather than where you were when you built it.

## What are the best sites to host a developer portfolio?

GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages all host portfolios free, with HTTPS and custom domains. GitHub Pages suits static sites from a repository; Vercel suits Next.js; Netlify and Cloudflare Pages suit most static site generators.

Choosing:

- **Plain HTML or a static generator**: GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages.
- **Next.js with server features**: Vercel.
- **Forms and simple serverless functions**: Netlify.

Buy a domain with your name; it costs little and looks professional. Avoid site builders that lock content in or add their branding, because developers are judged partly on how they build their own site. Whichever host you pick, connect it to your repository so every push redeploys automatically, and add basic analytics to see which projects visitors actually open.

## What are the best GitHub-based portfolios for developers?

A strong GitHub portfolio has a profile README introducing you, pinned repositories for your best projects, each with a clear README, screenshots, live demo links and setup instructions, plus consistent commit history. GitHub Pages can host the portfolio site itself.

Make each pinned repository self-explanatory: what it does, why you built it, the stack, architecture, and results. Recruiters skim, so screenshots and a demo link in the first lines matter. Clean up abandoned forks and tutorial repositories, or move them off your pinned list. A profile README with a short bio and links to your site, writing and talks ties everything together.

## What makes the best portfolio website for frontend developers?

Frontend portfolios should demonstrate the skills they claim: fast loading, responsive layouts, accessibility, polished interactions and attention to detail. The site itself is a sample of your work, so its quality is part of your evaluation.

Include projects showing component design, state management, animations used with restraint, performance optimisation and accessibility fixes. Link live demos, since frontend work is best judged interactively. Mention metrics such as performance scores or load times where relevant. Avoid heavy animations that slow the first screen; recruiters often open portfolios on phones between meetings, so mobile performance matters most.

## What makes the best portfolio website for software developers?

Software developer portfolios should show breadth and engineering judgement: well-structured projects, tests, documentation, deployment and clear explanations of trade-offs. Case studies matter more than visuals.

For each project, explain the problem, architecture, key decisions, challenges and outcomes, with a diagram where helpful. Show different strengths: one full-stack app, one systems or tooling project, one contribution to open source, for example. Link code with readable READMEs. Writing, such as technical blog posts about problems you solved, signals communication skills that employers value highly.

## What are the best portfolio projects for back-end developers?

Back-end projects should show APIs, data modelling, authentication, performance and reliability. Strong examples include a REST or GraphQL API with auth and rate limiting, a background job system, a real-time service with WebSockets, and a RAG or search service with evaluation.

Ideas with depth:

- A multi-tenant API with role-based access, tests and documentation.
- An event-driven system with queues, retries and idempotency.
- A search service combining keyword and vector search.
- A file-processing pipeline with OCR and status tracking.
- Load testing results showing how you optimised performance.

Provide API docs, a simple front end or Postman collection to try it, and deployment with Docker.

## What are good portfolio project ideas for web developers?

Good ideas solve real problems for real people: a booking system for a local business, a dashboard for a college club, a tool you personally use, or a clone of a popular app with a meaningful improvement. Real users make projects far more convincing.

More ideas:

- An AI study assistant over your course notes with citations.
- An expense splitter with authentication and offline support.
- A job application tracker with reminders.
- A community event site with registrations and QR check-in.
- A browser extension that solves a daily annoyance.

Ship each with a live link, a case study, and something measurable, such as users or time saved.

## What are the best portfolio designs for developers?

The best designs are simple, fast and readable, with a clear first screen that says who you are and what you build, followed quickly by projects. Typography, spacing and consistent colours matter more than effects.

Design principles: one strong accent colour, readable font sizes, plenty of whitespace, clear navigation, project cards with images and one-line summaries, and obvious contact links. Dark and light themes are nice but optional. Avoid long loading animations, autoplaying sounds and novelty navigation that hides content. Test with a friend: if they cannot tell what you do within ten seconds, simplify. Then check the page on a phone and with a slow connection, because many first visits happen there.

## Where can I get a developer portfolio website template?

Good templates are available in Vercel's template gallery, Astro's themes directory, Netlify and GitHub Pages themes, and open-source repositories tagged "portfolio". Pick one built with a framework you know so you can customise it.

After choosing, replace placeholder text, adjust colours and fonts to make it distinct, remove sections you do not need, and check performance and accessibility. Read the licence. Templates are a starting point; your projects, writing and explanations make the portfolio effective. Keep the site's code on GitHub too, since recruiters may look at how you built it.

## What are the best portfolio examples for web developers?

Curated collections, such as the widely shared GitHub list of developer portfolios, design galleries, and personal sites of engineers you admire, are good sources of examples. Study structure and content, not just visuals.

As you browse, note how strong portfolios introduce the person in one line, show three to five projects with outcomes, include writing or talks, and make contact easy. Notice what you skip as a visitor; your recruiters will skip the same things. Combine ideas from several examples, then build your own version rather than copying any one site. Revisit your favourite examples every few months as your work grows.

# Text embedding models: how they are trained, uses, best for RAG and Ollama, OpenAI facts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/best-text-embedding-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Text embedding models turn sentences and documents into vectors so software can compare meaning, powering semantic search, RAG, clustering and classification. They are trained mostly with contrastive learning on huge sets of related text pairs. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense embeddings with BM25, so this page explains how embedding models are trained, what they are used for, strong choices for 2026, RAG and Ollama, whether OpenAI's models are open source or multilingual, which similarity metric to use, and joint text-image embeddings.

## How are text embedding models trained?

Most start from a pretrained transformer, then train with contrastive learning: pairs of related texts, such as a question and its answer, are pulled together in vector space, while unrelated texts in the same batch are pushed apart.

Training usually has stages: weakly supervised pretraining on hundreds of millions of naturally paired texts, such as titles and bodies or questions and answers, then fine-tuning on high-quality labelled datasets for retrieval, similarity and classification, often with hard negatives that look relevant but are not. Recent models are built from decoder LLMs and trained on synthetic data generated by larger models. Techniques such as Matryoshka learning let embeddings be shortened without retraining.

## What are text embedding models used for?

They are used for semantic search, retrieval for RAG, recommendation, clustering similar documents, classification with simple models on top, duplicate detection, anomaly detection and measuring text similarity in evaluation.

In RAG, embeddings let a system find passages that answer a question even when the wording differs. In support systems, they route tickets by topic and find similar past issues. In analytics, clustering embeddings of customer feedback reveals themes without manual labels. Embeddings also power memory for agents, storing and retrieving past interactions. Because they are cheap to compute compared with generation, embeddings are often the first, most scalable step in AI pipelines.

## What are the best text embedding models in 2026?

Strong options include Qwen3-Embedding and other leaders on the MTEB leaderboard, Google's gemini-embedding-001, OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large, Cohere Embed, Voyage AI models, and open models such as BGE-M3, multilingual E5, Jina embeddings, Nomic Embed and EmbeddingGemma.

Rankings change often, so check the MTEB leaderboard for current results by task and language, then test two or three candidates on your own data. Consider dimension size and storage, maximum input length, multilingual needs, licence, latency and whether you need local hosting. A smaller model well matched to your domain can beat a larger general model. Re-evaluate yearly, since switching requires re-embedding your corpus.

## What are the best text embedding models for RAG?

Choose models trained for retrieval, which handle queries and documents separately or accept instructions. Hosted options include OpenAI text-embedding-3, Voyage, Cohere and Gemini embeddings; open options include BGE-M3, E5, Qwen3-Embedding, Nomic and Jina models.

For RAG, retrieval benchmarks such as BEIR and the retrieval tasks in MTEB matter more than average scores. Test with your own questions and known relevant passages, measuring recall at k. Multilingual corpora need multilingual models such as BGE-M3 or Qwen3-Embedding. Pair any embedding model with BM25 for hybrid search and a reranker, since those often improve quality more than switching embedding models. Also check the maximum input length against your chunk size.

## What are the best text embedding models on Ollama?

Popular Ollama embedding models include nomic-embed-text, mxbai-embed-large, bge-m3, snowflake-arctic-embed, all-minilm and embeddinggemma, plus newer options such as Qwen3 embedding models. Pull one and call Ollama's embeddings endpoint.

Choose by needs: all-minilm is tiny and fast for prototypes; nomic-embed-text and mxbai-embed-large are strong general English choices; bge-m3 handles many languages and long inputs; embeddinggemma offers good quality in a small size. With LangChain or LlamaIndex, use their Ollama embedding classes, and make sure documents and queries use the same model. Local embeddings keep data private and avoid API costs, which suits sensitive RAG systems. Benchmark speed on your hardware, since large models slow indexing.

## Is text-embedding-3-large open source?

No. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large and text-embedding-3-small are proprietary models available only through OpenAI's API and Azure OpenAI. Their weights are not released, so you cannot run them locally or fine-tune them.

If you need open weights, for privacy, offline use or fine-tuning, choose open embedding models such as BGE-M3, E5, Qwen3-Embedding, Nomic Embed, Jina embeddings or EmbeddingGemma, checking each licence for commercial terms. Using the API means sending text to OpenAI, so review data policies for sensitive content. Vectors from text-embedding-3 models are tied to that service: if you switch to an open model later, you must re-embed your documents.

## Are text-embedding-3 models multilingual?

Yes. Both text-embedding-3-large and text-embedding-3-small support many languages. OpenAI reported large gains on the multilingual MIRACL benchmark, with the large model scoring about 54.9 and the small model about 44.0.

Quality varies by language: widely used languages perform well, while lower-resource languages, including some Indic languages, may be weaker. Cross-lingual retrieval, such as an English query finding a Hindi passage, often works but should be tested. For multilingual RAG, compare text-embedding-3-large with open multilingual models like BGE-M3 and Qwen3-Embedding on your languages. Keep language metadata on chunks, so you can filter results and report recall per language.

## Is text-embedding-ada-002 multilingual?

Partly. ada-002 handles many languages, but its multilingual retrieval quality is much weaker than OpenAI's newer models: OpenAI reported about 31.4 on MIRACL for ada-002, compared with 44.0 and 54.9 for text-embedding-3-small and large.

For English-heavy applications, ada-002 still works, but for any multilingual or cross-lingual system, migrating improves results substantially. Migration means re-embedding all documents with the new model and rebuilding your index, because vectors from different models are incompatible. Run a comparison on your own queries before switching production traffic. If your users write in several languages, include examples of each in your evaluation set, since averages hide weak languages.

## Which metric should you use for semantic similarity with text embeddings?

Use cosine similarity by default, or dot product when embeddings are normalised, since they then rank identically. Most sentence embedding models are trained and evaluated with cosine similarity, and their documentation states the intended metric.

Some models are trained for dot product without normalisation, where vector length carries meaning, so cosine would discard useful information; follow the model card. Euclidean distance gives the same ranking as cosine for normalised vectors. Whatever you choose, use the same metric in your vector index and evaluation. For decisions such as duplicate detection, calibrate thresholds on labelled pairs from your own data, since raw similarity values differ between models.

## Can you create a single embedding for both text and an image?

Yes. Multimodal embedding models such as CLIP and SigLIP map text and images into a shared space, and some newer models accept interleaved text and image input to produce one combined embedding for a pair, such as a product photo with its description.

Options: use a model that natively embeds mixed inputs, as offered by some commercial multimodal embedding APIs; or embed text and image separately with a shared-space model like CLIP and combine the vectors by averaging or concatenation, then normalise. Concatenation preserves both signals but doubles dimensions. Evaluate on your retrieval task, since the right weighting between text and image depends on whether users search mainly by words or by visual similarity.
