# BM25 explained: Best Matching 25 meaning, origin, formula, TF-IDF, BM25F, SPLADE, BM42
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/bm25-explained-formula-vs-tfidf/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

BM25, short for Best Matching 25, is the ranking function behind most keyword search engines, including Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. It scores documents by query term frequency, term rarity and document length. I use BM25 alongside dense vectors in RAG.NextUpgrad, merging both with reciprocal rank fusion before reranking, so this page covers what BM25 means, its name and origin, how it is calculated, and how it compares with TF-IDF, BM25F, SPLADE and BM42, plus determinism and probabilities. What does BM25, Best Matching 25, mean? BM25 stands for Best Matching 25, a ranking function that estimates how relevant a document is to a keyword query. It rewards documents containing rare query terms, with diminishing returns for repeated terms and adjustments for document length. Also asked as: bm25 best matching 25 It is often called Okapi BM25, after the Okapi information retrieval system at City University London where it was developed. BM25 needs no training: it works from term statistics in your index, which makes it fast, explainable and strong on exact names, codes and rare words. It remains a standard baseline in search research and a key component of hybrid retrieval, where it complements dense embeddings that capture meaning but miss exact matches. Why is BM25 called BM25? BM stands for Best Matching, and 25 refers to the version number: it was the 25th in a series of weighting functions the Okapi team developed and tested, after earlier variants such as BM11 and BM15. BM11 and BM15 handled document length differently, and BM25 combined their ideas with a tunable parameter, b, that controls length normalisation. It performed best in experiments at the Text REtrieval Conference, TREC, and became the standard. Later variants, such as BM25F for documents with fields and BM25+ for very long documents, kept the name. The number has no other meaning, which surprises many people who expect it to describe the formula. When was BM25 created? BM25 was developed by Stephen Robertson, Karen Spärck Jones and colleagues at City University London, and presented in the Okapi team's experiments at TREC-3 in 1994. It built on probabilistic retrieval research from the 1970s. Spärck Jones introduced inverse document frequency in 1972, and Robertson and Spärck Jones formalised probabilistic relevance weighting in 1976. BM25 added practical handling of term frequency and document length on top of that foundation. Despite its age, it remains hard to beat on many keyword search tasks, and Lucene adopted it as the default similarity in version 6, which made it the default in Elasticsearch and Solr as well. How is BM25 calculated? For each query term, BM25 multiplies the term's inverse document frequency by a saturated term frequency, then sums over all query terms. Saturation uses the parameter k1, and document length normalisation uses the parameter b. In words: the score equals the sum, over query terms, of IDF times term frequency times k1 plus 1, divided by term frequency plus k1 times one minus b plus b times document length over average document length. Typical values are k1 between 1.2 and 2.0 and b equal to 0.75. For example, a rare term appearing three times in a short document scores higher than a common term appearing ten times in a long one. Libraries such as rank_bm25 in Python implement this in a few lines. How is BM25 different from TF-IDF? BM25 refines TF-IDF in two ways: term frequency saturates, so repeating a word many times adds less and less, and document length is normalised, so long documents do not win simply by containing more words. Also asked as: how is bm25 different from tfidf Classic TF-IDF grows linearly with term frequency, which rewards keyword stuffing and long documents. BM25's k1 parameter controls how quickly frequency saturates, and its b parameter controls how strongly length is penalised. BM25 also uses a probabilistic form of inverse document frequency. In practice, BM25 ranks noticeably better than plain TF-IDF on most search tasks, which is why it replaced TF-IDF as the default in Lucene-based search engines. Both remain useful as features in machine learning models. What is the difference between BM25 and BM25F? BM25F extends BM25 to documents with multiple fields, such as title, headings and body. It weights each field differently, combining term frequencies across fields before applying saturation, so a match in the title can count more than one in the body. Also asked as: bm25 vs bm25f Simply summing separate BM25 scores per field overcounts terms that appear in several fields, which BM25F avoids. It suits web pages, product catalogues and structured documents. Elasticsearch approximates this with the combined_fields query, which treats multiple fields as one with per-field boosts. Tune field weights using real queries and relevance judgements. For RAG over documents with titles and sections, field-aware scoring often improves retrieval of the right chunk. BM25 vs SPLADE: which is better? SPLADE usually retrieves better than BM25 on benchmarks because it learns term weights and adds related terms through expansion, capturing some meaning. BM25 needs no model, runs faster, works on any language with tokenisation and is easier to debug. SPLADE requires running a transformer model over every document at indexing time and over queries at search time, adding infrastructure and latency. It may also perform worse on domains or languages its model was not trained on, where BM25 stays robust. A practical approach starts with BM25 plus dense vectors in a hybrid setup, then tests SPLADE if retrieval quality still falls short. Evaluate both on your own queries, measuring recall at the depth your reranker uses. BM25 vs BM42: what is the difference? BM42 is a sparse retrieval method proposed by Qdrant in 2024. It keeps BM25's inverse document frequency but replaces term frequency with attention weights from a small transformer model, aiming to work better for the short text chunks common in RAG. The idea is that in short chunks, term frequency is usually one, so BM25's frequency component adds little, while attention weights indicate how important each word is to the chunk's meaning. After community review, Qdrant revised its initial benchmark claims, and results suggest BM42 is not a clear winner over BM25 or SPLADE in general. Treat it as an experimental option: test it on your data alongside BM25 before switching production retrieval. Is BM25 deterministic? Yes. Given the same index, tokenisation, parameters and query, BM25 always produces the same scores and ranking. Apparent differences usually come from index changes, tie-breaking or distributed search statistics. In Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, each shard computes inverse document frequency from its own documents by default, so scores can differ slightly between shards or after updates; the dfs_query_then_fetch search type uses global statistics instead. Deleted documents still affect statistics until segments merge. Equal scores may return in different orders unless you add a tie-breaker, such as document ID. These properties make BM25 easy to test and debug compared with neural retrieval. Can a BM25 score be a probability? No. A BM25 score is an unbounded relevance score that depends on the query and collection, not a probability between 0 and 1. It comes from a probabilistic model, but the final score only ranks documents within a query. Also asked as: can bm25 be a probability Scores are not comparable across queries: a long query with rare terms produces higher scores than a short common one. To combine BM25 with other signals, normalise scores with min-max scaling, calibrate them into probabilities with logistic regression on labelled data, or use rank-based fusion. Reciprocal rank fusion ignores raw scores entirely and merges ranks, which is why RAG.NextUpgrad uses it to combine BM25 with dense vector results before reranking.

# What is a BM25 score? Ranking, calculation, negatives, normalisation, indexes, and cosine
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/bm25-score-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A BM25 score measures how well a document matches a keyword query: for each query term, it multiplies the term's rarity across the collection, its inverse document frequency, by how often the term appears in the document, with diminishing returns and an adjustment for document length, then sums across terms. Higher scores mean better matches for that query. BM25 is the keyword half of hybrid retrieval in RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers ranking and scores, calculating them, negative scores, normalisation, indexes, Gensim, cosine similarity and legitimacy.

## What is BM25 ranking?

BM25 ranking orders documents by their BM25 score for a query, from most to least relevant. It is the default ranking function in Lucene-based search engines such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, and a standard first-stage retriever in RAG systems.

It improves on simple term counting in two ways: repeated occurrences of a word add less and less, so keyword stuffing does not dominate, and long documents are penalised relative to the average length, so short focused documents can rank well. Tuning parameters k1 and b control these effects. BM25 ranks only documents containing at least one query term, which makes it fast and precise for exact words.

## What is a BM25 score?

A BM25 score is a number expressing a document's relevance to a specific query within a specific collection. It is relative: a score of 12 means nothing on its own, only that the document ranks above one scoring 8 for the same query.

Scores depend on the collection's statistics, such as how many documents contain each term and the average document length, so scores from different indexes or queries are not comparable. They are not probabilities and can exceed any fixed range. This is why combining BM25 with vector similarity requires either normalisation or rank-based fusion rather than adding raw scores.

## How do I calculate a BM25 score?

For each query term, compute IDF, then multiply by f times k1 plus one, divided by f plus k1 times one minus b plus b times document length over average length, where f is the term's frequency in the document. Sum over query terms.

Worked example with k1 of 1.2 and b of 0.75: a term appears in 10 of 1,000 documents, giving IDF of about log of 990.5 over 10.5, plus one in Lucene's variant, roughly 4.56. If it appears 3 times in a document of average length, the term-frequency part is 3 times 2.2 over 3 plus 1.2, about 1.57. The contribution is about 7.2. Repeat for each term and add.

## Can a BM25 score be negative?

With the classic Robertson IDF formula, yes: terms appearing in more than half of the documents get negative IDF, which can make scores negative. Many implementations, including Lucene, use a variant that adds one inside the logarithm, keeping IDF and scores non-negative.

Negative contributions mean a very common term counts slightly against a document, which is rarely useful. If your library produces negative scores, check its IDF formula; you can clip IDF at zero, use the Lucene variant, or remove stop words that appear everywhere. When fusing with other retrievers by rank, the sign of raw scores does not matter.

## How do I normalise BM25 scores?

Normalise per query, since scores vary by query: min-max scaling maps the top result to 1 and the lowest retrieved to 0, or divide by the maximum score. Alternatively, avoid score normalisation entirely by fusing result lists with reciprocal rank fusion.

Min-max normalisation is sensitive to outliers and the number of results retrieved, and normalised scores still differ in meaning across queries. Reciprocal rank fusion, which sums one over a constant plus each document's rank in each list, is simpler and robust, which is why many hybrid search systems, including RAG.NextUpgrad, use it. If you need weighted combinations, tune weights on an evaluation set.

## How does a BM25 index work?

A BM25 index is an inverted index: for each term, it stores the list of documents containing it, with term frequencies, plus document lengths and collection statistics. At query time, the engine reads only the lists for query terms and scores those documents.

Building the index involves tokenising, normalising and possibly stemming text, then recording postings. Search engines compress postings and use skipping and early termination to score millions of documents quickly. Elasticsearch has used BM25 as its default similarity since version 5. Updates add new postings; deletions are marked and cleaned up during segment merges.

## Does BM25 use an inverted index?

Yes, in practice. BM25 is a scoring formula, and inverted indexes are the data structure that makes computing it fast at scale, by looking up only documents that contain the query terms rather than scanning every document.

Small experiments, such as the rank_bm25 Python library, compute scores by iterating over all documents in memory, which works for thousands of documents but not millions. For production, use search engines or databases with inverted indexes, such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Lucene-based tools, or Postgres extensions offering BM25. Learned sparse retrieval models also use inverted indexes.

## How do I use Gensim BM25 ranking in Python?

Older Gensim versions had a BM25 module in its summarisation package, removed in Gensim 4. Recent Gensim releases include BM25 model classes in its models package for building sparse BM25 representations. Many developers simply use the `rank_bm25` library instead.

With rank_bm25: tokenise documents into word lists, build `BM25Okapi(tokenised_docs)`, then call `get_scores` or `get_top_n` with a tokenised query. Keep tokenisation identical for documents and queries. For larger datasets, move to a search engine. If you follow an old tutorial importing `gensim.summarization.bm25`, it will fail on current Gensim; check your version's documentation.

## What is the difference between BM25 and cosine similarity?

BM25 scores lexical matches between a query and documents using term statistics, rewarding exact shared words. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, typically embeddings that capture meaning, so it matches paraphrases without shared words.

BM25 excels at exact names, codes and rare terms; cosine similarity over embeddings excels at synonyms and concepts. Cosine can also be applied to TF-IDF vectors, a lexical approach, but in modern RAG it usually means semantic embeddings. Combining both in hybrid search, then reranking with a cross-encoder, gives the most robust retrieval, which is why it is standard in production RAG.

## Is BM25 legit?

As an algorithm, yes: BM25 is a well-established, peer-reviewed ranking function from information retrieval research, used for decades in major search engines and still a strong baseline that neural methods must beat. It is legitimate and widely trusted.

If you are asking about a shop or product that happens to use the name BM25, that is unrelated to the algorithm; check independent reviews, company details, return policies and payment protections before buying, as with any online store. Community discussions are useful for experiences, but verify claims through multiple sources.

# What is DevTools in Chrome? Opening it on Mac, Safari, Edge, mobile, React DevTools, MCP
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/browser-devtools-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Chrome DevTools is the set of developer tools built into the Chrome browser for inspecting HTML and CSS, debugging JavaScript, viewing network requests, measuring performance and testing mobile layouts. Every web developer uses it daily. I build web apps with Next.js and FastAPI, so this page explains what DevTools is, how to open it and the console in Chrome, Mac, Safari and Edge, debugging on phones and iPads, React DevTools, and the Chrome DevTools MCP server for AI agents.

## What is DevTools in Chrome?

Chrome DevTools is a suite of web development tools built into Chrome. Panels include Elements for HTML and CSS, Console for logs and JavaScript, Sources for debugging, Network for requests, Performance and Lighthouse for speed, and Application for storage.

You can edit styles live, set breakpoints, inspect API responses, simulate slow networks, emulate mobile devices, audit accessibility and performance, and view cookies, local storage and service workers. Changes made in DevTools are temporary, affecting only your browser session, so they are safe for experiments. Learning DevTools well is one of the fastest ways to debug front-end problems, since it shows exactly what the browser receives and how it renders.

## How do you open DevTools in Chrome?

Press F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows and Linux, or Cmd+Option+I on Mac. You can also right-click any element and choose Inspect, or open the Chrome menu, then More tools, then Developer tools.

Ctrl+Shift+C, or Cmd+Shift+C on Mac, opens DevTools in element-picking mode, so you can click any part of the page to inspect it. Dock DevTools to the side, bottom or a separate window from its menu. If DevTools will not open, check whether your organisation has disabled it through policy on managed devices. On school or work Chromebooks, administrators often restrict access, and only they can change it.

## Where is the DevTools console?

The Console is a tab in DevTools. Open it directly with Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows and Linux or Cmd+Option+J on Mac in Chrome, or open DevTools and click the Console tab. Press Escape to show a console drawer in other panels.

The console shows logs, warnings and errors from the page, and lets you run JavaScript in the page's context, such as inspecting variables or testing functions. Filter messages by level or text, and keep logs across page reloads with the preserve log option. Errors include file names and line numbers you can click to open in Sources. Be careful pasting code from strangers into the console, since it can steal session data.

## How do you open DevTools on a Mac?

In Chrome, Edge or Firefox on Mac, press Cmd+Option+I to open developer tools, or Cmd+Option+J in Chrome to open the console directly. You can also right-click an element and choose Inspect.

In Safari, first enable developer features in Settings, Advanced, by checking the option to show features for web developers, then use Cmd+Option+I to open the Web Inspector and Cmd+Option+C for the console. On newer Mac keyboards, Option may be labelled with a symbol only. If shortcuts conflict with other apps, use the browser menu instead. Developers often keep a Chromium browser and Safari both available to test rendering differences.

## How do you open DevTools in Safari?

Open Safari Settings, go to Advanced, and enable the option to show features for web developers, which adds the Develop menu. Then open Web Inspector with Cmd+Option+I or by right-clicking and choosing Inspect Element.

Web Inspector includes Elements, Console, Sources, Network, Timelines and Storage tabs, similar to Chrome DevTools. The Develop menu also lets you disable caches, simulate different user agents, test responsive designs and connect to iPhones and iPads for remote debugging. Testing in Safari matters because WebKit renders some CSS and handles some APIs differently from Chromium, and WebKit powers all iOS browsers, so some bugs appear only there.

## Where is DevTools in Edge?

In Microsoft Edge, press F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows, or Cmd+Option+I on Mac. You can also open the menu, choose More tools, then Developer tools, or right-click and select Inspect.

Edge DevTools is based on Chromium, so it closely matches Chrome's panels, with some additions such as 3D View for inspecting layers and Edge-specific tools for accessibility and issues. If F12 opens a prompt the first time, choose to open DevTools and optionally remember the choice. Organisations can disable DevTools on managed devices through policy. Skills transfer directly between Chrome and Edge, so learning one teaches you both. Edge also integrates DevTools with Visual Studio Code through an extension.

## Can you open DevTools on a mobile phone?

Not directly in most mobile browsers, but you can debug mobile pages from a computer. For Android, enable USB debugging, connect the phone, and open chrome://inspect in desktop Chrome. For iPhone, use Safari's Develop menu on a Mac.

Remote debugging gives full DevTools for the phone's page: inspect elements, view console errors, check network requests and profile performance on real hardware. For quick checks without a computer, tools such as Eruda or vConsole can be injected into a page to show an on-screen console. Desktop DevTools device emulation also simulates screen sizes and touch, but real-device testing catches issues emulation misses, such as performance and browser-specific bugs.

## Can you open DevTools on an iPad?

Safari on iPad has no built-in DevTools panel. Enable Web Inspector in the iPad's Settings, under Safari, Advanced, then connect the iPad to a Mac and inspect its pages from Safari's Develop menu.

Without a Mac, options are limited: injected on-page consoles like Eruda, bookmarklets that show console output, or apps that offer basic web inspection. Since all iPad browsers use WebKit, debugging in Safari on a Mac covers Chrome and other browsers on iPad too. Test layouts with desktop responsive modes first, then verify on the real device. For web apps, logging errors to a remote service also helps diagnose problems users hit on iPads.

## What are React DevTools?

React Developer Tools is a browser extension for Chrome, Firefox and Edge that adds Components and Profiler tabs to DevTools, letting you inspect the React component tree, props, state and hooks, and measure rendering performance.

With the Components tab, select a component to see its props and state, edit values live, and find which component rendered a DOM element. The Profiler records renders, showing which components re-rendered, why, and how long they took, which helps fix slow interfaces. A standalone version works for React Native and other environments. It is essential for debugging Next.js and React apps, alongside the browser's own Network and Console panels.

## What is the Chrome DevTools MCP server?

Chrome DevTools MCP is a Model Context Protocol server, released by the Chrome team in 2025, that lets AI coding agents control and inspect a live Chrome browser: open pages, read console errors, inspect network requests and record performance traces.

It closes a gap for coding assistants, which previously wrote front-end code without seeing how it ran. With the server connected to tools such as Claude Code, Cursor or Gemini CLI, an agent can reproduce a bug, check errors, verify a fix and measure performance metrics like largest contentful paint. Use it with test accounts and non-sensitive data, since the agent can see whatever the browser loads.

# How to build AI agents: first agent, code, architecture, workflows, skills and projects
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/build-ai-agent-code-architecture/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

An AI agent is a program in which a language model decides which tools to call, in what order, to reach a goal. Building one takes a model API, a few well-designed tools and a loop, plus guardrails and evaluation. I build AI products such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, so this page covers what agents are and how to build one, a developer's first agent, example code, architecture, workflows, projects, skills, context graphs, ChatGPT agent and VS Code extensions. What are AI agents, and how do you build one? AI agents are systems where a language model plans and takes actions with tools, such as search, databases or APIs, to complete a goal. To build one, choose a model, define tools with clear schemas, write instructions, and run a loop that executes tool calls. Also asked as: what are ai agents and how to build one Start with a narrow, valuable task where success is easy to check, such as answering questions from your documentation with citations. Give the agent only the tools it needs, with descriptive names and parameter docs. Add step limits, error handling and logging from the start. Then build a small evaluation set of realistic tasks and measure completion rates before expanding scope. Frameworks help later, but understanding the basic loop first makes debugging far easier. How do you build your first AI agent as a developer? Pick one provider SDK, write two tool functions with JSON schemas, and implement the loop: send the goal and tools, execute any requested tool, append the result and repeat until the model returns a final answer or hits a step limit. Also asked as: how to build your first ai agent: a practical guide for developers A good first project is a research helper with a web search tool and a page-reading tool, which must return an answer with source links. Print every model message and tool call so you can see the reasoning path. Then add a test set of ten questions and track how many it answers correctly. Once that works, port it to a framework such as LangGraph or an agent SDK to compare what the framework handles for you. What does example AI agent code look like? Typical agent code has four parts: tool functions, such as get_weather or search_docs; tool schemas describing names, purposes and parameters; a messages list holding the conversation; and a while loop that calls the model and executes tool requests. Inside the loop, the code checks whether the model's response contains a tool call. If so, it looks up the function by name, validates the arguments, runs it with error handling, and appends the result as a tool message. If not, the response is the final answer and the loop ends. A counter enforces a maximum number of steps. Official examples in the Anthropic and OpenAI SDK documentation show this pattern in Python and TypeScript. What does an example AI agent architecture include? A production agent architecture includes the model, a tool layer with permissions, an orchestrator running the loop, short-term memory for the current task, long-term memory or retrieval for knowledge, guardrails, human approval steps and observability through traces and metrics. Common patterns include a single ReAct agent for focused tasks; a router that sends requests to specialised agents; and an orchestrator that splits work among worker agents and merges results. Tools often connect through the Model Context Protocol. Retrieval follows the same principles as RAG.NextUpgrad: hybrid search, reranking and citations. Store state in a database so runs can resume after failures, and keep secrets out of prompts by handling credentials in the tool layer. What is an example AI agent workflow? A support agent workflow: classify the incoming ticket, retrieve relevant help articles, look up the customer's order with a tool, draft a reply grounded in those sources, check it against policy, request human approval for refunds, then send and log the outcome. Each step has clear inputs, outputs and failure handling. Classification routes simple questions to automatic replies and complex ones to humans. Retrieval with citations prevents invented policies. Policy checks catch replies that promise things the business cannot deliver. Logging every step lets the team review mistakes and improve prompts or tools. Many successful agents look like this: mostly structured workflow, with the model making focused decisions at specific points rather than controlling everything. What is a good example AI agent project? Good portfolio projects include a research agent that writes cited reports, a GitHub issue triage agent that labels and summarises issues, a meeting assistant that turns transcripts into tasks, and a document agent that answers questions over uploaded PDFs. Choose a project with real users, even classmates or a club, and measurable success, such as correct labels or accepted answers. A document agent can build on OCR, as in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, which uses Mistral OCR and document-scoped RAG with page citations. Include an evaluation report, a demo video and a README explaining design choices, failure cases and guardrails. Projects that show judgement about limits impress more than flashy demos without testing. What is an example AI agent skill? Agent Skills, introduced by Anthropic in 2025 and later published as an open format, are folders containing a SKILL.md file with a name, description and instructions, plus optional scripts and reference files that an agent loads only when relevant. For example, a report-formatting skill might describe the company's document structure, include a template file and a script that checks headings, with a description saying when to use it. The agent sees only skill names and descriptions until a task matches, then reads the full instructions, which keeps context small. Skills package repeatable expertise, such as brand guidelines, data analysis procedures or code review checklists, so agents apply them consistently across tasks and teams. Why do AI agents need context graphs? Context graphs, or knowledge graphs, give agents structured knowledge about entities and their relationships, such as customers, orders, products and policies, so agents can reason across connected facts instead of searching disconnected text chunks. Also asked as: why ai agents need context graphs (and how to build one with aws Plain vector search finds similar passages but struggles with questions requiring multiple hops, such as which customers bought products affected by a recall. A graph stores these relationships explicitly, and agents can query it through tools. On AWS, teams often use Amazon Neptune for graph storage alongside vector search, combining both in GraphRAG patterns. Building one involves extracting entities and relations from data, defining a schema, keeping it updated and exposing safe query tools to the agent. What is an example of ChatGPT agent? ChatGPT agent mode lets ChatGPT complete multi-step tasks using a virtual browser, terminal and connectors, such as researching competitors and building a slide deck, comparing products across websites, or compiling information into a spreadsheet. Also asked as: example chatgpt agent For example, you might ask it to find three venues matching your requirements, compare reviews and availability, and summarise options in a table. It works step by step, showing progress, asks for confirmation before consequential actions, such as purchases or submitting forms, and hands control to you for logins or CAPTCHAs. Results still need checking, since it can misread pages. Availability and limits depend on your plan, so check OpenAI's help centre. What are the best VS Code AI agent extensions? Popular VS Code agent extensions include GitHub Copilot with agent mode, the Claude Code extension, OpenAI's Codex extension, Gemini Code Assist, and open-source agents such as Cline, Roo Code, Continue and Kilo Code. They differ in model choice, pricing approach, autonomy and how they show changes. Copilot integrates tightly with GitHub and VS Code features. Open-source agents such as Cline let you bring your own API keys or local models through Ollama. Look for clear diffs, approval prompts before running terminal commands, checkpoint or undo support, and Model Context Protocol support for connecting tools. Try two on a real task in your repository before settling on one.

Also asked as: how to start a public speaking speech Avoid weak openings such as apologising, long thank-you lists or reading your title slide. For a student audience, a story about a common struggle, such as not knowing where to start in tech, works well. Keep the first thirty seconds rehearsed until automatic, since that steadies nerves. Make eye contact, smile, and pause after your hook to let it land. A strong opening builds trust for everything that follows.

# Can anyone join a hackathon? No coding, no experience, after college, AI events, pitching
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-anyone-join-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Most hackathons are open to anyone who meets their eligibility rules: students, professionals, designers and beginners, often with no coding experience required. Student-only and college-specific events are the main exceptions. I have competed in 10+ hackathons and pitched winning projects such as KrishGyan at Changethon 2025, so this page covers who can join, joining without coding, experience or college, finding AI hackathons, and how to pitch, including at Smart India Hackathon, with examples.

## Can anyone join a hackathon?

Usually yes, within each event's eligibility rules. Open hackathons welcome students, professionals and hobbyists; student hackathons require enrolment in a college; some corporate or government events have age, nationality or institution requirements.

Check the rules page for age limits, team size, location restrictions and whether employees of sponsors may compete. Online hackathons widen access, since you can join from anywhere with internet. Many events also welcome non-coders such as designers, product thinkers and domain experts, because strong teams need more than programmers. If you are unsure whether you qualify, email the organisers; they generally prefer more participants and will clarify quickly.

## Can you join a hackathon without coding?

Yes. Teams need designers for interfaces and slides, researchers who understand users and the problem, presenters who pitch well, and people who manage time and scope. Many hackathons explicitly welcome non-technical participants.

Contribute by interviewing potential users, writing the problem statement, designing screens in Figma, preparing the pitch deck, testing the product and making the demo video. No-code tools such as Bubble, Glide or automation platforms also let non-programmers build working prototypes, and AI assistants can help with simple scripts. Some events have design or ideathon tracks where code is optional. Learning basic coding over time widens your role, but you can make a real impact from day one.

## Can you join a hackathon with no experience?

Yes. Beginner-friendly hackathons, including many MLH and college events, offer workshops, mentors and starter kits, and some have prizes for the best beginner team. Everyone starts with a first hackathon.

Prepare a little: learn basic Git, set up your laptop, and try building a tiny project beforehand. At the event, join a team with at least one experienced member, take a clear role, ask mentors for help early, and focus on learning rather than winning. Keep the project small so you finish. After the event, write down what you learned and publish the project. By your third hackathon, you will contribute far more confidently.

## Can you join a hackathon after college?

Yes. Many hackathons are open to working professionals and graduates, including corporate challenges, open innovation events, Web3 and AI hackathons, and online global competitions. Only student-specific events require current enrolment.

Graduates often find hackathons useful for career switches, building portfolio projects, meeting startup founders and testing business ideas. Check rules carefully: some events limit participation to people under a certain age or within a few years of graduation. Professional hackathons may involve harder problem statements and stronger competition, but also bigger opportunities, such as investor interest or job offers. Employers sometimes run internal hackathons too, which are a good way to work with new colleagues.

## Can you join a hackathon without being in college?

Yes. Open hackathons accept self-taught developers, freelancers, professionals, career changers and, in some cases, school students. Student hackathons that require a college ID are the main ones you cannot join without enrolment.

Look for open events on Devpost, Devfolio, Unstop and community platforms, plus company and government challenges that list eligibility as open to all. School students should check age limits and may need guardian consent. Without a college network, find teammates through event Discord servers and team formation sessions, which are common at the start of hackathons. Self-taught builders often do well because they are used to learning quickly and shipping independently.

## Where can you join an AI hackathon?

Find AI hackathons on Devpost, Devfolio, Unstop, MLH, lu.ma event listings, Kaggle competitions, and the event pages of AI companies, cloud providers and developer communities, which frequently host online and in-person AI events.

Many AI companies and cloud providers run hackathons with credits for their APIs, and college tech fests across India include AI tracks. Follow AI developer communities and newsletters, since announcements spread there first. Kaggle offers long-running data and model competitions, which differ from weekend build events but sharpen ML skills. Choose events whose tracks match your interests, such as agents, RAG or vision, and prepare a reusable starter project to save setup time.

## What is a hackathon pitch?

A hackathon pitch is a short presentation, usually two to five minutes, where a team explains the problem, demonstrates its solution and convinces judges of its impact and feasibility, often followed by a few minutes of questions.

Unlike startup pitches, hackathon pitches centre on the working demo and what was built during the event. Judges score innovation, technical execution, design, impact and presentation, so the pitch must make each visible quickly. A strong pitch has a sharp problem statement, a live demo of the core flow, a brief explanation of how it works, and a clear next step. A pitch deck, if used, is usually five to seven slides.

## How do you give a pitch at a hackathon?

Open with the problem and who suffers from it in one or two sentences, show the live demo immediately, explain the technology briefly, state the impact and next steps, and finish on time. Practise at least twice with a timer.

Assign roles: one speaker, one demo driver, and others ready for technical questions. Prepare a backup recording in case the live demo fails. Use real examples, such as an actual user scenario, instead of abstract claims. Avoid spending time on team introductions or long architecture slides. When judges ask questions, answer honestly, including what is mocked or unfinished, since credibility matters. Keep the demo at the centre so judges see value in seconds.

## How do you pitch at Smart India Hackathon?

SIH evaluations focus on your understanding of the problem statement, feasibility, innovation and impact for the organisation that posed it. Pitch by restating the problem in the ministry's or company's terms, demonstrating your prototype, and showing how it can be deployed.

Prepare for rounds: the idea submission presentation in the official template, then evaluation by experts at the grand finale, often with mentoring rounds in between. Show research on the problem owner's context, a working prototype, data or validation from users, a deployment plan and cost-conscious design. Expect detailed questions on scalability, security and integration with existing systems. Practise answering in simple, confident language, and keep your demo running reliably on your own devices.

## What are some hackathon pitch examples?

A strong example opening: "Farmers lose crops because expert advice arrives too late and in the wrong language. KrishGyan gives farmers advice over WhatsApp in their own voice and language. Let us show you a farmer asking about a leaf disease."

Then demo the core flow, explain the technology in two sentences, mention validation or impact, and close with next steps, such as piloting with a farmer group. Another useful structure: the problem in numbers, a user story, the live demo, how it works, what we built this weekend, and what comes next. Watch winning demo videos on Devpost to study pacing. Write your pitch as a script, cut it to fit the time, then rehearse until it sounds natural.

# Can ChatGPT edit videos? What it can and cannot do with video
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-chatgpt-edit-videos/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


ChatGPT cannot open a video file and cut, trim or colour-grade it the way an editor such as DaVinci Resolve or CapCut does. What it can do is plan and script videos, write captions and titles, edit photos, write code that assembles simple clips, and, through OpenAI's separate video model Sora, generate short video from text or images. This page sorts what works from what does not for making, editing and analysing video, how Claude compares, and which free tools sit alongside ChatGPT.

## Can ChatGPT edit videos?

No, not directly. ChatGPT is not a video editor: it cannot trim your footage on a timeline, add transitions or export a finished edit of the clip you upload.

It helps with everything around the edit. Give it your script or transcript and it will suggest where to cut, write an edit decision list with timestamps, draft on-screen text and captions, and propose B-roll ideas. It can also write commands for tools that do edit, for example an `ffmpeg` command that trims a clip from 00:01:10 to 00:02:30 or burns subtitles into a video, which you then run on your own machine. For real editing, pair it with an editor: DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro or CapCut, several of which have their own AI features such as automatic captions and silence removal.

## Can ChatGPT make videos?

ChatGPT on its own produces text and images, not finished videos. Video generation comes from Sora, OpenAI's video model, which is offered alongside ChatGPT on eligible plans and in supported countries.

Inside ChatGPT you can still produce the parts of a video: a script, a shot list, voice-over text, thumbnails and images for each scene. With its code tool it can sometimes assemble a very simple clip, such as a slideshow, by writing and running Python, but that is a workaround, not a video feature. For a talking explainer, the dependable workflow is ChatGPT for the script, a screen or camera recording by you, and an editor for the cut. Generated footage is best for short illustrative shots, not for a full lecture or product demo.

## Does ChatGPT generate videos?

Not by itself. OpenAI's text-to-video model Sora generates short videos from a prompt or an image, and it is available through its own app and website for eligible users.

Sora produces short clips with sound from a description such as "a time-lapse of a college campus at dawn". Results are impressive for mood and motion but can still get hands, text on screen and physics wrong, so plan to generate several takes and pick the best. Availability, clip length and limits depend on plan and region and have changed since launch, so check OpenAI's Sora page for the current details. Label AI-generated footage clearly when you publish it; platforms increasingly require this.

## Can ChatGPT make videos from photos?

Not as a built-in feature, but it can write the command that does it. A slideshow from photos is one `ffmpeg` command, and image-to-video models such as Sora can animate a still photo.

For a simple slideshow, name your photos in order and run:

```bash
ffmpeg -framerate 1/3 -i img%03d.jpg -c:v libx264 -r 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p slideshow.mp4
```

That shows each image for three seconds and writes an MP4 that plays everywhere. Ask ChatGPT to add a fade between images or a music track and it will extend the command. If you want the photo itself to move, a camera push or a person turning their head, that is image-to-video generation, which needs a video model such as Sora rather than the chat.

## Can ChatGPT edit photos?

Yes. ChatGPT can generate images and edit an uploaded photo from a text instruction: change the background, alter the style, remove an object, or combine elements from several images.

Upload the photo and describe the change precisely, for example "replace the background with a plain light grey studio backdrop, keep the person unchanged". Edits regenerate the image, so faces and small text can shift slightly; check details before using the result in anything official. For pixel-exact work, such as a passport-style photo or brand assets, use a real editor like Photoshop, GIMP or Canva. Never use AI edits to misrepresent a real person or a document, and keep the original file.

## Can ChatGPT analyse videos?

Only in limited ways. The dependable method is to give ChatGPT a transcript and a few key frames as images. It reads those well, while full-length video understanding is stronger in models built for it, such as Gemini.

For a lecture or meeting, generate a transcript with a speech-to-text tool, then ask ChatGPT for a summary, chapter timestamps or quiz questions. I built live speech-to-text into my OCR & Speech Workspace for exactly this reason: once speech is text, every search and summary tool works on it. For visual questions, export frames at the moments that matter and upload them as images. In the mobile app, voice mode with the camera can look at what you show it live, which helps for quick visual questions.

## Can you send ChatGPT videos?

You can attach some files, but a video upload is not the same as video understanding. What ChatGPT can do with an attached video depends on the tools available in your plan, and long clips are rarely handled well.

In practice, ChatGPT may be able to process a short file with its code tool, for example extracting frames or metadata with Python, then look at those frames. It will not reliably watch a long video and answer about every scene. Sending a link to a YouTube video does not help either: unless browsing can read a transcript, it sees the page, not the footage. Send the transcript plus key frames instead, and say exactly what you need from them.

## Can Claude AI edit videos?

No. Claude works with text, images and documents such as PDFs, not video files, so it cannot cut or render video. Like ChatGPT, it is useful for scripts, transcripts, captions and the code that drives editing tools.

Claude is strong at turning a rough transcript into a tight script, writing subtitles in SRT format, and producing `ffmpeg` or Python commands for repetitive edits such as batch trimming or adding a watermark. Developers also use it to write programmatic video code, for example a Remotion project where each scene is a React component rendered to MP4. Analyse footage the same way as with ChatGPT: a transcript plus selected frames as images.

## Can ChatGPT edit videos for YouTube?

It cannot cut your YouTube video, but it can do most of the work around it: script, hook, title, description, chapter timestamps, tags, thumbnail concepts and a pinned comment.

A workflow that saves hours:

- Write the script with ChatGPT, then read it aloud and rewrite anything you would not say.
- Record, edit in your editor, and export a transcript with timestamps.
- Ask ChatGPT for chapters from the transcript, three title options and a description that opens with the main point.
- Generate thumbnail ideas, then design the final thumbnail yourself so your face and text stay sharp.

Watch retention, not the assistant's opinion, to judge what works.

## What are free AI tools like ChatGPT?

Google Gemini, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Perplexity, Meta AI, DeepSeek and Mistral's Le Chat are general AI assistants with free tiers. All of them chat, write and explain code, and most read images and documents.

Each has a strength. Gemini fits into Gmail, Docs and Android and handles video input well. Claude is careful with long documents and code. Copilot is built into Windows, Edge and Microsoft 365. Perplexity answers with sources from a live web search. Free tiers come with usage limits and sometimes older models, and the limits change often. Pick two, run the same real task, such as summarising your lecture notes, in both, and keep the one whose answer you would actually use.

# Can Claude AI generate images? Editing images, videos, PPT files, and the free model
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-claude-generate-images/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Claude does not generate photographic or painted images the way dedicated image models do. It can, however, create visuals through code: SVG illustrations, diagrams, charts, interactive web pages and slide decks, and it can read and analyse images you upload. I build AI products across several model providers, so this page explains Claude's image abilities, image editing, video, PowerPoint files, the free model, what Claude specialises in, its name and origin, and which apps to use for image generation instead.

## Can Claude AI generate images?

Not natively in the sense of photos or artwork from a text prompt. Claude generates text and code, which can produce visuals: SVG graphics, Mermaid and other diagrams, charts with code, HTML and CSS designs, and visual artifacts you can view directly in the app.

So for a logo concept as an SVG, a flowchart, an infographic layout or a data chart, Claude works well. For a realistic photo, a painting or a product shot, use an image generation model. Claude can still help there by writing detailed prompts for image tools, describing composition, lighting, style and constraints, which often improves results from those tools. A useful workflow is to brainstorm concepts with Claude, ask it for three detailed prompts per concept, then generate and compare the images in a dedicated tool.

## Can Claude AI make images like diagrams and graphics?

Yes, through code-based visuals. Ask for an SVG icon, an architecture diagram in Mermaid, a chart from your data, or a styled HTML poster, and Claude produces it as an artifact you can preview, refine and download.

Examples that work well:

- "Draw an SVG diagram of a RAG pipeline with labelled boxes and arrows."
- "Create a bar chart of these monthly sign-ups."
- "Design a simple event poster as an HTML page."
- "Make a flowchart of our college admission process."

Iterate with follow-ups such as "make the colours match our brand" or "add a legend". These visuals are editable code, which is an advantage over flat images.

## Can Claude AI edit images?

Claude can understand images, describing them, reading text in them, analysing charts and screenshots, but it does not repaint pixels like an image editor. It can edit images indirectly by writing code, for example Python with Pillow or OpenCV, to crop, resize, annotate or adjust them.

In environments with code execution, Claude can run that code on an uploaded image and return the edited file. This suits batch operations, such as resizing hundreds of photos, adding watermarks or converting formats. For creative edits, like removing objects or changing backgrounds realistically, use AI image editors such as those in Gemini, ChatGPT, Adobe Firefly or Photoshop's generative tools.

## Can Claude AI generate videos?

No, Claude does not generate video footage. It can help with video work by writing scripts, storyboards, shot lists, captions and subtitles, and by writing code that creates animations or edits videos with tools such as ffmpeg.

For example, Claude can produce an HTML and CSS animation, code for programmatic video libraries, or a Python script that cuts clips, adds captions and assembles a vertical reel, which you then run. For AI-generated footage, use dedicated video models such as Google's Veo or OpenAI's Sora, with Claude helping plan the content. For explainer videos, a common pipeline is Claude writing the script and on-screen text, a voice tool recording narration, and an editor or script assembling clips, captions and music.

## Can Claude AI generate PPT files?

Yes. Claude can create PowerPoint presentations, as well as Word documents, Excel spreadsheets and PDFs, through its file creation features in the Claude apps, producing downloadable files rather than only text.

Give it the content, audience, number of slides and style: "Create a 10-slide deck for first-year students on starting with AI, with one idea per slide and speaker notes." Review and refine in follow-ups, then download and polish in PowerPoint or Google Slides. Claude can also turn documents or meeting notes into slide outlines. Check facts and figures before presenting. For branded decks, upload your template or describe your colours and fonts so the output needs less manual cleanup.

## Which Claude AI model is free?

The free Claude plan gives access to a capable current Claude model, usually from the Sonnet line, with daily usage limits. Paid plans add higher limits, access to the most powerful models such as Opus, and extra features.

Which exact model is free changes as Anthropic releases new versions, so check the model selector in the app or the plans page. For light use, such as studying, writing help and small coding tasks, the free plan is often enough. If you regularly hit limits or need the strongest model for complex work, a paid plan or the API may be worth it. Developers using the API choose models explicitly and pay per token, which suits apps rather than personal chat.

## What does Claude AI specialise in?

Claude is a general-purpose assistant, but it is especially known for coding, including agentic coding with Claude Code, working with long documents, careful writing and editing, analysis and reasoning, and following detailed instructions.

Common uses include drafting and editing reports, summarising research papers and contracts, analysing data files, building prototypes as artifacts, writing and reviewing code, and creating documents and slides. Anthropic emphasises safety and reliability in its training. Like any model, Claude can make mistakes, so verify important facts and test code before relying on it.

## Why is Claude AI named Claude?

Anthropic has not given one official, detailed explanation, but the name is widely reported as a nod to Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory. The company has also described wanting a friendly, human-sounding name rather than a technical acronym.

Shannon's work on information and communication underpins modern computing and, indirectly, language models, which predict text by modelling information. A human name also signals the conversational, assistant-like experience Anthropic aimed for. The name causes occasional search confusion with other Claudes, such as a character in the game Fire Emblem: Three Houses.

## Where was Claude AI developed?

Claude was developed by Anthropic, an AI safety and research company founded in 2021 and headquartered in the United States, with teams in several countries. It is trained on Anthropic's infrastructure with cloud partners.

Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI researchers, including Dario and Daniela Amodei. Claude is available globally through Anthropic's apps and API, and through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Vertex AI and Microsoft's platforms. Availability of specific features and plans varies by country, so check Anthropic's supported regions list.

## Which AI app can generate images?

Popular image generation apps include ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, Ideogram, Leonardo and Canva's AI tools, plus open models such as Stable Diffusion and Flux that you can run locally.

Choose by need: ChatGPT and Gemini for conversational creation and editing; Midjourney for artistic quality; Adobe Firefly for commercially safer content within Adobe workflows; Ideogram for images with readable text; local models for control and privacy. Read each tool's terms on commercial use, and never create misleading images of real people.

# Can Copilot create images? Editing photos, timing, PPT, Excel, Power BI, agents and Gemini
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-copilot-create-images/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, Microsoft Copilot can create images: describe what you want, and it generates pictures using image models from OpenAI and Microsoft, which you can refine, restyle and download. Microsoft 365 Copilot also creates PowerPoint decks, builds Excel tables and formulas, and helps make Power BI reports, while Copilot Studio builds agents. I build AI products across several providers, so this page covers Copilot images and where they come from, editing, timing, Office features, Power BI, agents, and Gemini's image generation.

## Can Copilot create images?

Yes. In the Copilot app, on the web, in Windows and in Microsoft Edge, you can ask Copilot to create an image from a description, such as "a watercolour of students coding at night", and it returns generated images you can refine with follow-up prompts.

For better results, describe the subject, setting, style, lighting, composition and aspect ratio, and say what to avoid. Microsoft Designer, integrated with Copilot, adds design templates for social posts and invitations. Usage limits and speed depend on your account and plan. Generated images follow Microsoft's content policies, so requests involving real people, violence or copyrighted characters may be refused. Students often use it for presentation visuals, event posters and project mock-ups, saving time compared with searching stock image sites.

## Where do Copilot images come from?

Copilot images are generated by AI image models, including models from OpenAI and Microsoft's own image models, not copied from the internet. The models learned visual patterns during training and create new images from your prompt.

Microsoft adds provenance information, such as content credentials, to indicate images are AI-generated. Because models learned from large datasets, outputs can sometimes resemble existing styles, so avoid prompts imitating specific living artists or brands for commercial use. Check Microsoft's terms for how you may use generated images, especially in business or published materials.

## Can Copilot edit images?

Yes. Copilot can modify images it created, and you can upload images and ask for changes such as changing the style, background, colours or adding elements, within content policies. Microsoft Designer and Photos apps provide further AI editing tools like background removal and generative erase.

Editing works best with specific instructions: "keep the person and pose, change the background to a library, warm lighting". Results may alter details you wanted to keep, so iterate step by step. For precise professional edits, combine AI tools with traditional editors. Only edit images you have rights to, and do not create misleading edits of real people.

## Can Copilot create images from photos?

Yes, you can upload a photo and ask Copilot to create a new image based on it, for example restyling it as an illustration or using it as a reference for composition. Results are new generations, not exact edits, so details may change.

Uses include turning product photos into stylised marketing images, creating cartoon versions of scenes, or generating variations of a design. Privacy matters: avoid uploading photos of other people without consent, and remember content policies may limit edits of identifiable faces. For accurate product photos, real photography or careful editing remains more reliable than generation.

## How long does Copilot take to generate images?

Usually from a few seconds to under a minute per request. Time depends on demand, the model used, image complexity and your account's priority; during busy periods it can take longer or hit usage limits.

If generation stalls, refresh, simplify the prompt or try again later. Paid plans may offer faster or more generations. For many images, generating one at a time with refinements tends to give better results than asking for many at once. Developers needing image generation in apps typically use image APIs from providers directly, with their own rate limits.

## Can Copilot create a PPT?

Yes. Copilot in PowerPoint, part of Microsoft 365 Copilot, can create a presentation from a prompt or from a Word document, generating slides with titles, text, images and speaker notes, and can summarise or restyle existing decks.

Give it structure: audience, purpose, number of slides and key points, or a source document. Use your organisation's template for consistent branding. Review every slide for accuracy and add your own examples and data. The free Copilot app can draft outlines and content you paste into PowerPoint, but direct deck creation inside PowerPoint requires a qualifying Microsoft 365 plan.

## Can Copilot create Excel sheets?

Copilot in Excel can create formulas, add calculated columns, build PivotTables and charts, highlight data and explain results from your instructions, working best with data formatted as tables. It can also help build spreadsheets from descriptions in newer versions.

Example prompts: "Add a column calculating profit margin", "Show total sales by region as a chart", "Highlight overdue invoices". Check formulas on a few rows, since AI can misinterpret columns. For complex models, ask Copilot to explain each formula so you understand and can maintain the workbook. Requires a qualifying Microsoft 365 plan and files saved in OneDrive or SharePoint. Without it, you can paste sample data into the free Copilot chat and ask for formulas to copy into Excel yourself.

## Can Copilot create a Power BI dashboard?

Yes, Copilot in Power BI can suggest and create report pages from prompts, summarise data, write DAX measures and answer questions about your data, depending on your organisation's capacity and licensing.

Prompts like "Create a page showing sales trends by region and top products" generate visuals you can refine. Copilot works best with a clean, well-named data model; unclear column names and missing relationships produce poor results. Review generated measures and visuals for correctness before sharing dashboards. Admins must enable Copilot features in Power BI or Fabric settings.

## Can I create AI agents in Microsoft Copilot?

Yes. Use the agent builder in Microsoft 365 Copilot for simple agents grounded in your files and sites, or Copilot Studio for more advanced agents with custom topics, actions, connectors, triggers and publishing to Teams, websites and other channels.

Start with a narrow agent, such as an HR policy assistant using SharePoint documents. Test with real questions, refine instructions, and add actions, such as creating tickets, only with appropriate permissions. Organisations should govern agents with admin controls, data policies and monitoring. Licensing affects which features are available. Measure whether the agent answers correctly on a test set of real questions before rolling it out widely, and review conversation logs in the first weeks.

## Will Gemini create images?

Yes. Google's Gemini app creates and edits images from text prompts and uploaded photos using Google's image models, and Gemini models are available to developers for image generation through Google's APIs.

Gemini is especially good at conversational editing: upload a photo and describe changes step by step while keeping other details consistent. Generated images include SynthID watermarks marking them as AI-made. Usage limits depend on your plan. As with any image tool, respect consent and copyright, and avoid misleading images of real people.

# Can Gemini transcribe audio? Files, M4A, video, and ChatGPT or Copilot
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-gemini-transcribe-audio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, Gemini can transcribe audio. Its models accept audio as input, so you can upload a recording in the Gemini app or send it through the Gemini API and ask for a transcript, with timestamps, speaker labels, a summary or a translation. It can also transcribe the audio track of a video. This page covers files and formats including M4A, video, how ChatGPT and Copilot handle transcription, how Gemini compares with GPT, which Gemini model to use for images, where Gemini is available, and practical examples.

## Can Gemini transcribe audio?

Yes. Upload a recording or record directly, then ask Gemini to transcribe it. Because Gemini understands the content, you can ask for more than a transcript: clean it up, label speakers, summarise, list action items or translate.

A good prompt: "Transcribe this recording verbatim with timestamps every minute and label speakers as Speaker 1 and Speaker 2. Then give a five-bullet summary." Check names, numbers and technical terms, the most common errors in any transcription. For very long recordings, the API handles large files better than the app, and dedicated speech-to-text services offer features such as guaranteed verbatim output and streaming. I built live speech-to-text into my OCR & Speech Workspace for this reason: transcripts turn speech into something you can search and summarise.

## Can Gemini transcribe audio files?

Yes. In the Gemini app, attach the audio file and ask for a transcript. Through the Gemini API, upload the file with the Files API and pass it with your prompt. Common formats such as MP3, WAV, AAC, FLAC and OGG are supported.

Using the API from Python:

```python
from google import genai
client = genai.Client()
audio = client.files.upload(file="lecture.mp3")
resp = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=["Transcribe this lecture with timestamps.", audio])
print(resp.text)
```

There are limits on file size and total audio length per request; the audio documentation lists them. Split very long recordings into parts and combine the transcripts.

## Can Gemini transcribe M4A audio?

M4A files contain AAC audio, which Gemini generally handles, but uploads of the M4A container itself sometimes fail depending on where you upload. If that happens, convert the file to MP3 or WAV, which work reliably.

Convert with one ffmpeg command:

```bash
ffmpeg -i recording.m4a -ac 1 -ar 16000 recording.mp3
```

That also reduces the file to mono at 16 kHz, which is plenty for speech and makes uploads faster. Phone voice memos are often M4A, so this is a common fix. If you do not use the command line, many free audio converters do the same thing; avoid uploading private recordings to unknown converter websites.

## Can Gemini transcribe audio from a video?

Yes. Gemini accepts video files and YouTube links in many cases, and can transcribe the speech, describe what is shown, and give timestamps. You can also extract the audio and send only that, which is faster and uses less of your limits.

To extract audio:

```bash
ffmpeg -i talk.mp4 -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 talk.mp3
```

Then ask for a transcript or chapter list. When you need both speech and visuals, such as a lecture where slides matter, send the video and ask Gemini to note slide titles alongside the transcript. For YouTube videos with captions, those captions may already be a good starting transcript.

## Can ChatGPT transcribe audio?

Yes, in several ways. ChatGPT transcribes your voice input when you dictate, voice mode understands speech in conversation, and uploaded audio can be transcribed depending on the tools and limits of your plan. OpenAI's API offers dedicated transcription models.

For reliable transcripts of files, developers use OpenAI's speech-to-text API or the open-source Whisper model, which runs locally for free. In the ChatGPT app, short recordings work best; long meetings are better handled by a transcription tool, with ChatGPT then summarising the transcript. As with Gemini, check names and numbers. Do not upload recordings of other people without their consent.

## Will Copilot transcribe audio?

Microsoft's tools transcribe audio, though not always through the Copilot chat itself. Teams transcribes meetings live, Word's Transcribe feature turns uploaded recordings into text with speakers and timestamps, and Copilot can then summarise those transcripts.

In Word for the web, use Dictate, then Transcribe, upload an audio file, and insert the transcript into your document. In Teams meetings, turn on transcription, and Copilot can answer questions about the meeting and create a recap. For other cases, generate a transcript with one of these tools or with Whisper, then paste it into Copilot for summaries and action items. Availability depends on your Microsoft 365 plan and organisation settings.

## Gemini vs GPT: which is better?

Gemini and OpenAI's GPT models are close in overall quality, and leadership changes with each release. Gemini is strong on long, multimodal inputs such as audio and video and is built into Google's apps; GPT models power ChatGPT's broad ecosystem.

For transcription and media work, Gemini's native audio and video input is an advantage. For writing, coding and general assistance, both are excellent, and the better choice depends on your tasks and tools. Developers should compare cost, speed, rate limits and features such as structured outputs for their own workload. Run the same five real tasks on both and keep the one whose answers need less fixing.

## Which Gemini version is best for image generation?

Use Google's Gemini image models, the family nicknamed Nano Banana, for creating and editing images in conversation, and Google's Imagen models for high-quality text-to-image generation through the API. The newest versions are usually the best.

Gemini's image models are good at editing existing photos with instructions, keeping a character consistent across images, and combining several images. Imagen focuses on generating high-quality images from text. In the Gemini app, image creation picks a model for you; in the API and AI Studio you choose. Check the image generation documentation for current model names, and label AI-generated images when they could be mistaken for real photos.

## Where is Gemini available?

Gemini is available in most countries and in many languages, on the web, Android and iOS, and inside Google Workspace. Availability of some features, such as image generation, Gemini Live or specific integrations, varies by country, age and account type.

In India, Gemini supports English and several Indian languages and is widely available on Android, where it is replacing Google Assistant on many phones. Some regions have limited or no access because of local regulation or Google's rollout decisions. Google's Gemini help centre lists supported countries and languages. Work and school accounts depend on the administrator enabling Gemini. If a feature is missing, check your account type, age settings and app version before assuming it is unavailable.

## What are some examples of using Gemini AI?

People use Gemini to summarise long documents and videos, transcribe and summarise recordings, plan study schedules and trips, draft emails and reports, explain code, generate and edit images, and research topics with cited sources.

Examples to try:

- "Transcribe this voice note and turn it into a to-do list with deadlines."
- "Summarise this YouTube lecture into revision notes with timestamps."
- "Here is my project report; point out unclear sections and missing evidence."
- "Plan a one-week revision schedule for these five subjects."
- "Explain this error and the fix, step by step."
- "Edit this photo to a plain white background for my resume."

Check facts and names in every output before relying on it.

# Can GPT generate images and videos? GPT-4o, gpt-oss, coding models and GPT disks
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/can-gpt-generate-images/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, GPT can generate images: ChatGPT creates and edits images with OpenAI's native image generation, which arrived with GPT-4o and is available through the API's image models. GPT chat models do not generate video; OpenAI's Sora does. The open-weight gpt-oss models are text-only. This page covers image generation and free access, gpt-oss, video, the best GPT model for coding and why teams sometimes choose GPT-4.1 over Claude or the reverse, how GPT works in brief, what to do when GPT is down, and the unrelated "GPT disks" in Windows.

## Can GPT generate images?

Yes. ChatGPT can generate images from text descriptions and edit uploaded images, using OpenAI's native image generation. Developers access the same capability through OpenAI's image models in the API.

Describe the subject, style, composition, lighting and any text you want in the image, then refine with follow-ups such as "make the background plain white" or "add more space at the top for a title". The model handles text inside images and consistent edits much better than earlier image generators, though it can still misspell or alter small details. Respect copyright and people's likeness, and label AI images when they could be mistaken for real photographs.

## Can ChatGPT generate images for free?

Yes, within limits. Free ChatGPT users can generate a limited number of images per day, and paid plans raise those limits. During busy periods, free limits may be reduced.

To get the most from a free allowance, write one detailed prompt instead of many vague attempts, and edit an image with targeted follow-ups rather than regenerating from scratch. Other free options include Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Designer, which also offer image generation with daily limits. Check each service's current limits, since they change frequently, and review terms for commercial use of generated images.

## Can GPT-4o generate images?

Yes. GPT-4o introduced native image generation in ChatGPT in 2025, meaning the model can create images directly as part of a conversation, using context from the chat and uploaded images, rather than handing off to a separate older image model.

That integration is why ChatGPT can follow detailed instructions, keep a character consistent across images, and edit specific parts of an uploaded picture. Newer OpenAI models and dedicated image models continue this capability, so the exact model behind image generation in ChatGPT may change over time. In the API, use the current image generation models listed in OpenAI's documentation.

## Can gpt-oss generate images?

No. OpenAI's gpt-oss models are open-weight language models for text: reasoning, coding, tool use and writing. They do not generate images and do not take images as input.

If you want local image generation, use open image models such as Stable Diffusion-family models through tools designed for image generation, on a capable GPU. You can combine them with gpt-oss: let the language model write detailed prompts, then pass them to an image model. For hosted image generation, use ChatGPT or OpenAI's image API, or other providers' image models.

## Can GPT generate videos?

GPT chat models do not generate videos. OpenAI's Sora is the video generation model, available through its own app and website for eligible users and regions. ChatGPT can write scripts, storyboards and Sora prompts.

A workflow: plan the video in ChatGPT, generate short clips in Sora from detailed shot prompts, then edit them together with narration and captions in a video editor. ChatGPT can also produce simple slideshow-style videos by writing and running code, but that is not true video generation. Generated videos carry watermarks and provenance signals; label them when publishing.

## Which GPT model is best for coding?

Use OpenAI's newest coding-tuned or reasoning models for serious programming, such as the Codex models built for agentic coding, and faster smaller models for quick completions. The best choice changes with each release, so check OpenAI's models page.

More important than the model is the tool: Codex, GitHub Copilot or another agent that reads your repository, runs tests and iterates will outperform pasting code into chat. For a fair comparison, give two or three models the same real task in your own codebase, such as adding an endpoint with tests, and compare how much you had to fix. Keep a project instruction file with build and test commands so any agent works well.

## Why choose GPT-4.1 and not Claude?

Teams choose between GPT-4.1 and Claude models based on their own tests, cost, speed, context length, instruction following and which tools they use. GPT-4.1 has been a common default in some coding tools for its speed and instruction following, while Claude models are widely chosen for agentic coding and long, careful work.

There is no universal winner. A tool may pick a default model for cost, latency or availability reasons, and you can often switch models in the picker. Model generations move fast, so a comparison from a few months ago may not hold. Run your own evaluation: the same tasks, the same prompts, and a clear score for correctness and edits required.

## How does GPT work?

GPT is a transformer language model that generates text by predicting the next token over and over, based on everything before it. It learned language, facts and patterns from large-scale pre-training, then was tuned to follow instructions and be helpful.

Each word piece of your prompt becomes a vector; attention layers relate every token to every other, building context; the final layer gives probabilities for the next token, one is chosen, and the process repeats. ChatGPT adds tools around the model, such as search, code execution and image generation, plus memory and safety systems. Because it predicts plausible text, it can be wrong while sounding confident, so verify important facts.

## Why is GPT down?

When ChatGPT or the OpenAI API is not working, first check OpenAI's status page for incidents. If it shows no problems, the cause is usually local: network issues, browser extensions, an expired login, rate limits or very long conversations.

Steps to try:

- Check status.openai.com for outages or degraded performance.
- Refresh, sign out and back in, or try another browser or the app.
- Start a new conversation if one chat is stuck.
- Disable VPNs or extensions that interfere.
- For the API, check error codes: rate limits and server errors need retries with backoff.

For apps that depend on the API, build a fallback to another provider so outages do not stop your users.

## What are GPT disks?

In computer storage, a GPT disk uses the GUID Partition Table, a modern partitioning scheme that replaced the older MBR scheme. It has nothing to do with OpenAI's GPT models.

GPT partitioning supports very large disks and many partitions, stores redundant partition tables for resilience, and is required for booting Windows in UEFI mode. In Windows Disk Management, you will see disks labelled GPT or MBR. Converting between them usually requires deleting partitions or using specific tools, so back up data first. If you searched for OpenAI's GPT, the rest of this page covers the AI models.
