# What is the chunking method? Memory, English language chunks, NLP, and division
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/chunking-method-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The chunking method means grouping individual pieces of information into larger, meaningful units, chunks, so they are easier to remember, understand and use. Psychology uses it to explain memory, language teachers use it for fluent speaking, maths teachers use it for division, and AI engineers use it to split documents for retrieval. I work with document chunking in RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers chunking in memory, its origin and examples, why it works, English language chunks, chunking versus tokenization in AI, and chunking division.

## What is the chunking method?

The chunking method is a strategy of breaking information into small, meaningful groups, or combining small items into bigger units, so the mind processes fewer, richer pieces. A phone number remembered as 98765 43210 is easier than ten separate digits.

It appears across fields: as a memory technique for studying, as a way to learn phrases in a new language, as a teaching approach that presents content in digestible segments, as a maths method for long division, and as a data-processing step in AI that splits long documents into retrievable passages. The common idea is organising information into units that match how it will be stored or used.

## What is chunking information?

Chunking information means organising content into meaningful groups based on patterns, categories or relationships, so that each group can be remembered or processed as a single unit. Experts chunk naturally: a chess master sees familiar board patterns, not individual pieces.

In learning and design, chunking means presenting content in short sections with clear headings, lists and summaries, rather than long undivided text. Web pages, lessons and manuals all benefit. In study, you chunk by grouping related facts, creating acronyms and linking new ideas to familiar frameworks. The better you understand a subject, the larger and more useful your chunks become.

## Who came up with chunking information?

Psychologist George A. Miller popularised chunking in his 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", which argued short-term memory holds a limited number of items, and that grouping information into chunks expands what we can hold.

Later research, including work on chess expertise by William Chase and Herbert Simon in the 1970s, showed how experts build large chunks from experience. Researchers such as Nelson Cowan later suggested a typical working memory capacity closer to about four chunks. The concept remains central in cognitive psychology, education and the design of interfaces and learning materials.

## What are examples of chunking information?

Familiar examples include remembering phone numbers in groups, splitting card numbers into blocks of four, memorising the colours of the rainbow as an acronym, grouping a shopping list by aisle, and learning a speech as a few key sections rather than every sentence.

Study examples: grouping chemistry elements by family, learning historical events by period, summarising each chapter into three key points, and turning formulas into a single linked concept map. Designers chunk by breaking forms into steps and articles into sections with headings. Programmers chunk by organising code into functions and modules with clear names, which makes systems easier to reason about.

## Why is chunking important for a good memory?

Working memory can hold only a few items at once. Chunking packs more information into each item, so you remember more with the same capacity. Meaningful chunks also link to long-term memory, making recall and understanding easier.

Chunking turns isolated facts into structured knowledge: a group of related ideas is remembered as one concept connected to others, which supports retrieval later. It reduces mental overload during problem solving and learning. To use it, look for patterns, categories and stories in what you learn, summarise in your own words, and practise recalling chunks rather than rereading. Spaced repetition of chunks strengthens long-term memory.

## What is chunking in English?

In English language learning, chunking means learning and using common multi-word phrases, chunks, as single units: "How's it going?", "on the other hand", "I was wondering if", "make a decision". Fluent speakers rely heavily on such ready-made phrases.

This idea is central to the lexical approach, associated with linguist Michael Lewis in the 1990s, which argued language is largely made of prefabricated chunks rather than single words combined by grammar rules. Learning chunks improves fluency, because you retrieve whole phrases instead of building every sentence word by word, and accuracy, because chunks include correct grammar and word partnerships, called collocations.

## What are examples of chunking in English?

Examples of English chunks include collocations such as "heavy rain", "take a photo" and "strong coffee"; fixed expressions such as "by the way" and "as far as I know"; sentence starters such as "Would you mind..." and "The thing is..."; and phrasal verbs such as "look forward to".

Practical ways to learn them:

- Notice chunks in what you read and hear, and note them as whole phrases.
- Learn words with their common partners, not alone.
- Practise speaking with sentence frames you can complete.
- Shadow native speakers, repeating phrases with their rhythm.
- Group chunks by situation, such as meetings, interviews or travel.

## What is chunking in communicative English?

In communicative English teaching, chunking means teaching useful phrases for real situations, such as greeting, requesting, agreeing and disagreeing, so learners can communicate fluently sooner. It also refers to speaking in thought groups, pausing between meaningful chunks for clarity.

For example, learners practise chunks like "Could you please...", "I'd like to add that..." and "Let me check and get back to you" in role-plays. In speaking, chunking the sentence "When I joined college / I didn't know anyone / so I joined the coding club" into thought groups makes speech clearer and easier to follow. This helps in interviews, presentations and group discussions.

## What is the difference between chunking and tokenization?

In AI, tokenization splits text into tokens, small units like words or word pieces, that a language model processes. Chunking splits documents into larger passages, often hundreds of tokens, for indexing and retrieval in systems like RAG. In classic NLP, chunking also means grouping words into phrases, such as noun phrases.

They work at different levels: a 500-token chunk contains 500 tokens. Tokenization is fixed by the model's tokenizer; chunking is a design choice you make based on document structure and retrieval quality. In RAG.NextUpgrad, chunk sizes are measured in tokens so they fit the embedding model's limits, which is where the two concepts meet in practice.

## How do I do the chunking method of division?

The chunking method divides by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of the divisor, such as 10 or 5 times it, from the number, then adding up how many times you subtracted. It builds understanding before formal long division.

Example, 156 divided by 12:

- 10 × 12 = 120; 156 minus 120 leaves 36. Count 10.
- 3 × 12 = 36; 36 minus 36 leaves 0. Count 3.
- Total: 10 + 3 = 13, so 156 ÷ 12 = 13.

If something is left that is smaller than the divisor, it is the remainder. Students can use whatever multiples they find easy, which makes the method flexible and confidence-building.

# CI/CD with GitHub Actions: what it is, setup steps, Android, popular actions, vs GitLab
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ci-cd-github-actions-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation platform, and it is widely used for CI/CD: automatically testing code on every push or pull request, then building and deploying it. Workflows live as YAML files in your repository. I ship products with Python, FastAPI, Next.js and Docker, so this page explains CI/CD with GitHub Actions, whether GitHub counts as a CI/CD tool, setting up and implementing pipelines, Android builds, popular actions, comparisons with GitLab, CircleCI and Jenkins, and speeding workflows up.

## What is CI/CD with GitHub Actions?

CI, continuous integration, automatically builds and tests code whenever changes are pushed. CD, continuous delivery or deployment, automatically releases tested code to staging or production. GitHub Actions runs both through workflows defined in YAML files in your repository.

A workflow is triggered by events such as push, pull_request or a schedule, and contains jobs that run on GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners. Each job runs steps: shell commands or reusable actions from the Marketplace, such as checking out code or setting up Python. Results appear on pull requests as status checks, so broken code can be blocked from merging. Deployment jobs can target clouds, container registries or platforms like Vercel.

## Is GitHub a CI/CD tool?

GitHub itself is a code hosting and collaboration platform, but it includes GitHub Actions, a full CI/CD and automation service. So yes, you can run complete CI/CD pipelines on GitHub without a separate tool.

Before Actions launched in 2019, teams paired GitHub with external services such as Travis CI, CircleCI or Jenkins. Now many projects use Actions alone, benefiting from tight integration with pull requests, issues, packages and security features. Public repositories get generous free usage on GitHub-hosted runners, while private repositories have included minutes depending on the plan. External CI tools remain useful for complex enterprise pipelines or existing investments, and they integrate with GitHub through webhooks and status checks.

## How do you set up a CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions?

Create a file such as .github/workflows/ci.yml with a name, triggers like push and pull_request, and a job that checks out the code, sets up your language runtime, installs dependencies, and runs linting and tests.

For a Python project: use actions/checkout, then actions/setup-python with your version, run pip install with your requirements, then run pytest. Commit the file, and GitHub runs it on the next push. Add a deploy job that depends on the test job through needs, runs only on the main branch, and uses secrets stored in repository settings for credentials. Protect the main branch so pull requests must pass checks before merging.

## How do you build a CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions in four simple steps?

Step one: add a workflow file triggered by pushes and pull requests. Two: add a test job that installs dependencies and runs tests. Three: add a build job producing an artifact or Docker image. Four: add a deploy job gated on main.

Connect the jobs with needs, so deployment runs only after tests and builds pass. Store credentials as encrypted secrets, or better, use OpenID Connect to obtain short-lived cloud credentials without long-lived keys. Use environments, such as staging and production, with required reviewers for production releases. Finally, add notifications and status badges. These four steps give you a pipeline that catches bugs before merge and deploys consistently, which you can refine over time with caching and matrices.

## How do you implement continuous deployment with GitHub Actions?

After CI passes, add deployment jobs that publish your application: push a Docker image to a registry and update your server or cluster, deploy to a platform like Vercel or Render, or upload build artifacts to cloud storage.

Use GitHub environments to separate staging and production, each with its own secrets and protection rules, such as manual approval. Trigger production deploys on tags or releases for controlled versioning. Add health checks after deployment and roll back automatically if they fail. Keep deployment steps idempotent so reruns are safe. For containers, tag images with the commit SHA, which makes rollbacks and debugging straightforward. Log deployments so teams know exactly which version is live.

## How do you set up CI/CD for Android using GitHub Actions?

Use actions/setup-java with the required JDK, cache Gradle dependencies, then run Gradle tasks such as ./gradlew lint test assembleRelease on an Ubuntu runner. Upload the APK or AAB as a workflow artifact.

For signed releases, store the keystore as a base64-encoded secret, decode it during the workflow, and pass passwords through secrets to Gradle. Run instrumented tests with an Android emulator action on supported runners, which takes longer, so limit them to main branch builds. Automate publishing to Google Play with the Gradle Play Publisher plugin or Fastlane, using a service account key stored as a secret. Start with unit tests and debug builds, then add signing and publishing.

## What GitHub Actions do people commonly use?

Common actions include actions/checkout for code, actions/setup-node, setup-python and setup-java for runtimes, actions/cache for dependencies, actions/upload-artifact and download-artifact, and docker/build-push-action for container images.

Teams also use github/codeql-action for security scanning, Dependabot for dependency updates, official cloud credential actions with OpenID Connect, Pages actions for static site deployment, and release automation actions such as release-please. Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA rather than a tag, since tags can be moved, which reduces supply chain risk. Review an action's permissions and popularity before adopting it, and set minimal workflow permissions. Prefer official and verified publishers where available.

## What is the difference between GitLab CI/CD and GitHub Actions?

Both define pipelines in YAML stored in the repository. GitLab CI/CD is built into GitLab with stages and jobs in a single .gitlab-ci.yml file, while GitHub Actions uses multiple workflow files and a large marketplace of reusable actions.

GitLab offers an integrated DevOps platform with a built-in container registry, security scanning, environments and strong self-managed options, popular in enterprises hosting their own GitLab. GitHub Actions excels in ecosystem size, community actions and integration with GitHub's pull request workflow and open-source community. Runner models are similar: hosted runners plus self-hosted ones. Choose based on where your code lives; migrating CI between them is manageable, since concepts map closely, but rarely worth it alone.

## What can GitHub Actions do that CircleCI or Jenkins cannot?

Its main advantage is native integration with GitHub: workflows can trigger on almost any repository event, such as issues, comments, labels, releases or pull request reviews, not just code pushes, and they can automate repository management as well as CI/CD.

Examples: label issues automatically, welcome first-time contributors, publish releases when tags are created, update documentation sites, or run checks when a comment says retest. The marketplace offers thousands of reusable actions, and setup requires no separate server, unlike Jenkins. CircleCI and Jenkins still shine in some areas, such as advanced caching, complex enterprise pipelines or fully self-controlled infrastructure. For projects living on GitHub, Actions usually offers the simplest complete solution.

## How do you automate and speed up CI/CD with GitHub Actions?

Cache dependencies, run independent jobs in parallel, use matrix builds for multiple versions only where needed, skip workflows for documentation-only changes with path filters, and cancel outdated runs with concurrency groups.

More techniques: split slow test suites across parallel jobs; build Docker images with layer caching; reuse common steps through reusable workflows or composite actions; run expensive end-to-end tests on main or nightly schedules instead of every pull request; and fail fast on linting before heavier jobs. Monitor workflow durations to find bottlenecks. Faster pipelines matter because developers merge more confidently and context-switch less when feedback arrives within minutes.

# How Claude agents work: skills, projects, Excel, limits, billing, credits, autonomy
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-agents-skills-projects-billing/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Claude can work as an agent in Claude Code, Cowork and apps built with the Claude Agent SDK, and features such as Skills and Projects shape how it handles repeated work. Usage limits, billing and credits determine how much you can do. I build AI products with several providers, such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers Claude agents, Skills, Projects, Excel, limits, billing, API credits, whether agents show their work, autonomy and a step-by-step agent flow. How do Claude agents work? Claude agents run a loop: gather context, take actions with tools, check results and repeat. In Claude Code, tools include reading and editing files, running commands and searching; the Claude Agent SDK lets developers build similar agents for other tasks. Permissions control which actions need approval, and hooks let developers run checks before or after tool use. Subagents can handle parallel subtasks with separate context, returning summaries to the main agent. Project instructions in CLAUDE.md files give persistent guidance. Cowork brings this loop to non-coding work in the desktop app. Verification is part of the design: agents run tests, check outputs or ask for review before considering a task complete. How do Claude Skills work? Skills are folders containing a SKILL.md file with a name, description and instructions, plus optional scripts and resources. Claude sees only each skill's name and description until a task matches, then loads the full instructions and files it needs. Also asked as: how do claude ai skills work This progressive loading keeps context small while giving Claude specialised know-how, such as creating Word documents, following brand guidelines or running a data analysis procedure. Skills can include scripts that Claude executes in a code environment. They work across the Claude apps, Claude Code and the API, where enabled. Clear descriptions help Claude pick the right skill. Anthropic provides built-in skills for common file types, and you can write your own or share them across teams. How do Claude Projects work? A Project is a workspace in the Claude apps with its own knowledge files and custom instructions. Every chat inside the project can use that knowledge and follow those instructions, so you do not re-upload context each time. Also asked as: how do claude ai projects work Upload documents such as reports, code or guidelines to project knowledge, and write instructions describing tone, format or goals. For large knowledge bases, Claude retrieves relevant parts rather than reading everything at once. On Team and Enterprise plans, projects can be shared with colleagues, making them useful for shared workflows such as client accounts or course materials. Keep project knowledge current and remove outdated files to avoid conflicting answers. How does Claude work in Excel? Claude can analyse spreadsheets you upload, create and edit Excel files with formulas and charts through its file creation feature, and Anthropic has introduced a Claude add-in for Excel for some plans that works directly inside workbooks. Also asked as: how does claude ai work in excel Typical uses include cleaning data, building summary tables, writing formulas, explaining complex workbooks, creating financial models and generating charts. Ask Claude to explain each formula it adds, and verify calculations on sample rows, since errors in spreadsheets spread quickly. Keep a copy of the original file before edits. For sensitive financial data, check your organisation's policies before uploading. Availability of the add-in and file features depends on your plan, so check Anthropic's current documentation. How do Claude usage limits work? Claude usage limits cap how much you can use within rolling time windows, with some plans also having weekly limits. Usage depends on message length, attachments, conversation length, model choice and features such as Research or Claude Code. Also asked as: how do claude limits work Higher plans provide substantially more usage, and Claude Code shares limits with the apps on the same subscription. When you approach a limit, Claude shows when it resets. To stretch usage, start fresh chats, attach only relevant files, use Projects for shared context and pick lighter models for simple tasks. The API uses separate rate limits based on your organisation's usage tier, measured in requests and tokens per minute. How does Claude AI billing work? Claude app subscriptions, such as Pro and Max, bill monthly or annually through the website or mobile app stores. Team plans bill per seat, Enterprise plans use contracts, and the API bills separately for tokens used, paid through credits in the developer console. Also asked as: how do claude ai credits work Subscriptions and API billing are independent: a subscription does not include API usage, and API credits do not unlock app features. Manage app billing under Settings, Billing, or through your app store for mobile purchases. Some plans offer options to continue beyond usage limits with additional paid usage. Review invoices regularly, and for teams, assign seats only to active users. Check Anthropic's pricing page for current plans and terms. How do Claude API credits work? Claude API usage is paid from prepaid credits in Anthropic's developer console. You buy credits, and each API request deducts the cost of its input and output tokens, with optional automatic reloading when the balance runs low. Without credits, API requests fail with billing errors, so set up reload thresholds for production applications. Usage dashboards show spending by model and workspace, helping control costs. Some startup, research and education programmes provide promotional credits. Check the console's billing terms for details such as credit expiry and invoicing options. Reduce spending with prompt caching, the Batch API for asynchronous work and smaller models for simple tasks. Do AI agents show their work? Well-designed agents do. They display plans, the tools they call, intermediate results and reasoning summaries, so people can follow and correct them. Coding agents show diffs and command outputs, and browser agents show what they click and type. Transparency builds trust and catches mistakes before they cause harm. Behind the interface, traces record every model call and tool action for debugging and audits. Not all products expose this detail, and some agents summarise rather than showing every step. When choosing agent tools, prefer ones that show their work and ask for approval on important actions. When building agents, log everything and make plans visible to users. How do AI agents work autonomously? Agents work autonomously by running a loop without step-by-step human input: they receive a goal, decide the next action, execute tools, evaluate results and continue until success criteria are met, a limit is reached or they need help. Also asked as: how ai agents work diagram Autonomy can be triggered by schedules, events such as new emails, or user requests. Good designs bound autonomy with step and spending limits, permissions and approval gates for risky actions. Agents maintain state so they can resume after interruptions. Full autonomy suits low-risk, checkable tasks; high-stakes tasks keep humans in the loop. Measuring success rates on realistic tasks shows how much autonomy an agent can safely be given. What does an AI agent workflow diagram look like? A typical diagram flows from the user's goal into an orchestrator, which calls the language model. The model either returns a final answer or requests a tool; the tool runs, its result returns to the model, and the loop repeats until done. Side boxes show memory and retrieval feeding context into each model call, guardrails checking actions before execution, human approval gates for risky steps, and logging capturing every step for review. Multi-agent diagrams add an orchestrator agent delegating to worker agents. Drawing your agent's diagram before building clarifies which steps are deterministic code and which need model judgement, and where failures could occur. Share the diagram with teammates to align on behaviour.

# Why is Claude AI down? Who owns Claude, when it launched, plans, apps and skills
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-ai-down-plans-apps/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


When Claude AI seems down, the cause is usually a service incident, heavy demand, a usage limit on your plan, or a local network or browser problem. Check Anthropic's status page first; if it shows no incident, the problem is likely on your side. I build AI products that call several model providers, with automatic fallback when one fails, so this page covers outages, Claude's launch and ownership, its model family, safety, plans, apps, skills, video, and Claude inside Cursor.

## Why is Claude AI down?

Claude can be unavailable because of an outage or degraded performance on Anthropic's side, very high demand, reaching your plan's usage limit, or problems with your connection, browser extensions or VPN. Error messages often indicate which.

What to do:

- Check Anthropic's status page for incidents on the app or API.
- If it says limit reached, wait for the reset time or check your plan.
- Refresh, log out and back in, or try another browser or the app.
- Disable extensions or VPN temporarily.
- For API users, retry with exponential backoff on overload errors.

For products that depend on an AI model, design for outages: RAG.NextUpgrad falls back across multiple model providers, so users still get answers when one provider has an incident.

## When was Claude AI launched?

Anthropic introduced Claude in March 2023, initially to business partners and through its API. The consumer chat app at claude.ai opened to the public in July 2023 alongside Claude 2.

Since then, Anthropic has released several generations, including the Claude 3 family in 2024, which introduced the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus sizes, then Claude 4 and newer models. Each generation improved reasoning, coding, context length and tool use. Release dates and model names change often, so check Anthropic's announcements for the latest models.

## Who does Claude AI belong to?

Claude belongs to Anthropic, an AI safety and research company founded in 2021 by Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei and colleagues, several of whom previously worked at OpenAI. Anthropic develops, trains and operates Claude.

Anthropic is a privately held public benefit corporation, with major investments from technology companies including Amazon and Google. Claude is available through Anthropic's own apps and API, and through cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI and Microsoft's offerings. Anthropic is known for research on AI safety, interpretability and its "Constitutional AI" approach to training models with written principles.

## How many Claude AI models are there?

Claude is a family of models rather than one. Each generation typically comes in sizes such as Haiku, the fastest and cheapest, Sonnet, the balanced workhorse, and Opus, the most capable, with newer generations adding further options.

In the apps, you can choose among current models; through the API, developers select a model by its ID. Older models are retired over time on a published schedule. Which to use depends on the task: small, fast models for classification and simple chat; larger ones for complex reasoning, coding and long documents. Test the models on your own tasks, because the best choice varies by use case and cost constraints.

## Is Claude AI safe to use?

Claude is generally safe for everyday use: Anthropic applies safety training, usage policies and security controls. As with any AI service, avoid sharing sensitive personal data, verify important outputs, and review your privacy settings.

Practical safety tips:

- Do not paste passwords, ID numbers or confidential client data into consumer chats.
- Check privacy settings, including whether your chats may be used to improve models.
- Use Team or Enterprise plans for business data, which offer stronger data controls.
- Verify facts, code and legal or medical information before acting.
- Be cautious when giving any AI agent access to accounts or the ability to take actions.

## What are the Claude AI plans?

Claude offers a free plan with limited usage, Pro and Max plans for individuals who need more usage and features, and Team and Enterprise plans for organisations, with admin controls and data protections. Developers pay separately for API usage by tokens.

Paid plans add higher usage limits, access to more models and features, and tools such as Claude Code for software development. Plan names, limits and features change, so check the official pricing page for current details in your country. Whether Pro is worth it depends on how often you hit free limits and whether you need its extra features; try the free plan for a week with your real tasks first.

## Does Claude AI have an app?

Yes. Claude is available on the web at claude.ai, as desktop apps for macOS and Windows, and as mobile apps for iOS and Android. Developers also use Claude Code in the terminal and IDEs, and the API.

Install the desktop app from Anthropic's official download page and the mobile apps from the App Store or Google Play, avoiding look-alike apps from other publishers. Your conversations and projects sync across devices when you sign in with the same account. The desktop app adds features such as connecting local tools and files, depending on settings and plan.

## What are Claude AI skills?

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude can load when relevant to a task, such as creating spreadsheets, following a company's brand guidelines, or running a team's review checklist. Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in 2025.

Claude reads only a short description of each skill until it needs one, then loads the full instructions, which keeps context efficient. Skills work across Claude's apps, Claude Code and the API. Organisations can create custom skills to package their own workflows and share them with teams. As with any extension, use skills from trusted sources, since they can contain code that runs in Claude's environment.

## Can Claude AI make videos?

Claude does not generate video files directly the way dedicated video models do. It can write video scripts, storyboards, shot lists and captions, analyse images and documents, and write code that produces animations or edits video.

For example, Claude can write HTML and CSS or JavaScript animations, code for animation libraries, or Python scripts using ffmpeg to cut and assemble clips, which you then run to produce videos. For AI-generated footage, use dedicated video generation tools and let Claude help plan prompts and scripts. Capabilities evolve, so check Anthropic's announcements for new media features.

## Does Cursor AI use Claude?

Yes. Cursor, the AI code editor, lets users choose among models from several providers, and Claude models are among the options and widely used for coding in it. Cursor also has its own models for some features.

Model availability in Cursor depends on your Cursor plan and settings, and Cursor's documentation lists the current models. Many developers pick Claude for complex coding tasks, refactoring and agent mode, while using faster models for quick edits. Anthropic also offers its own coding tool, Claude Code, which runs in the terminal and integrates with editors such as VS Code and JetBrains IDEs.

# Claude AI: slow replies, rate limits, sources, Turnitin, the real app and business uses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-ai-slow-rate-limits-uses/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Claude is Anthropic's AI assistant, available on the web, desktop and mobile apps, in Claude Code and through the API. Most frustrations, such as slow replies, rate exceeded messages or incomplete answers, come from demand, usage limits and long tasks. I build AI apps with multi-provider fallback, such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers Claude's delays and errors, where it gets information, Turnitin and watermarks, the real Claude, meeting minutes, email automation and business uses. Why is Claude AI taking longer than usual? Claude takes longer than usual when demand is high, when the conversation or attached files are very long, when extended thinking is on, or when it is running tools such as web search, research or code execution. Long contexts take more time to process on every message, so starting a new chat with a short summary often speeds things up. Research and agentic tasks deliberately take minutes as Claude searches and reads many sources. If everything is slow, check Anthropic's status page for incidents, try refreshing, and test another network or the desktop app. For developers, streaming responses improves perceived speed, and fallback to another model or provider keeps apps responsive during incidents, as RAG.NextUpgrad does. Why does Claude AI say rate exceeded? Rate exceeded means you have sent more requests or used more capacity than your plan or API tier allows in a time window. In the Claude apps, usage limits reset after a set period; in the API, limits apply per minute. Claude app usage depends on message length, attachments, conversation length and model choice, so long chats with large files use limits faster. Paid plans offer higher limits, and the app shows when access resets. For the API, rate limits cover requests and tokens per minute, and they rise with usage tier; handle 429 errors with exponential backoff and retries. Reduce usage by starting fresh chats, trimming attachments, choosing lighter models for simple tasks and using prompt caching for repeated context. Why does Claude AI say response incomplete? An incomplete response usually means generation stopped early: the reply hit the maximum output length, the connection dropped, a usage limit was reached mid-answer, or a temporary server error interrupted it. In the apps, ask Claude to continue from where it stopped, or retry the message. For very long outputs, such as full documents or large code files, split the task into parts or ask for one section at a time. Check your connection and Anthropic's status page if it happens repeatedly. In the API, check the stop reason: max_tokens means you should raise the limit or continue the response, while errors call for retries with backoff and clear logging. Where does Claude AI take its information from? Claude's built-in knowledge comes from training on a large dataset, including public web data and licensed data, up to a knowledge cutoff date. It can also use information you provide, web search results and connected tools. Also asked as: where claude ai take the informations from Anthropic's documentation describes its training data sources and how consumer chats may be used for training depending on account settings. Beyond training, Claude reads files you upload, project knowledge, and content from connectors such as Google Drive when you enable them. With web search on, it cites live sources, which you should open and verify. Without search, it may not know recent events, and like any language model it can state outdated or incorrect facts confidently. Can Claude AI be detected by Turnitin? Turnitin's AI writing detection is designed to flag text likely generated by large language models, which can include Claude. Detection is probabilistic: it can miss AI text and can wrongly flag human writing. Turnitin reports an estimated share of AI-generated content for instructors, who should treat it as one signal rather than proof. Heavily edited or mixed text is harder to classify, while short texts give less reliable scores. The safest approach is to follow your institution's AI policy: use Claude for brainstorming, explanations and feedback where allowed, write your own work, and disclose AI assistance when required. Keeping drafts and version history helps show your writing process if questions arise. How does a Claude AI watermark work? Anthropic has not publicly documented a watermarking scheme for Claude's text outputs. Unlike Google's SynthID Text, there is no published method for verifying Claude-generated text through hidden statistical marks. Also asked as: how claude ai watermark works Text watermarking generally works by subtly biasing word choices during generation, so a detector with the key can spot the pattern statistically. Such watermarks weaken when text is paraphrased, translated or edited. Without a watermark, detection tools rely on classifiers that estimate how machine-like text appears, which is less reliable. Claude focuses on text and code rather than image generation, so image provenance labels rarely apply. For transparency, disclose AI assistance directly rather than relying on technical marks. Which Claude AI is the real one? The real Claude is made by Anthropic and available at claude.ai, in the official Claude apps for iOS, Android, Windows and macOS published by Anthropic, in Claude Code, and through Anthropic's API. Claude models are also offered legitimately through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI and Microsoft's platforms, and inside products such as GitHub Copilot and Notion. # How the Claude API works: keys, pricing basics, tokens, Pro, PDFs, MCP and Cursor
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-api-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Claude API lets developers send messages to Anthropic's Claude models from their own code: you choose a model, provide a system prompt and conversation messages, optionally define tools, and receive Claude's reply, paying per token processed. It powers chatbots, document analysis, coding tools and agents. I build AI products with multiple providers and fallbacks, so this page covers how the API works, keys, payment, rates and tokens, Pro versus API, data use, PDFs, MCP, and using your key in Cursor.

## How does the Claude API work?

You send an HTTPS request to the Messages endpoint with your API key, a model name, a maximum output length, an optional system prompt and a list of messages. Claude returns a response containing content blocks, such as text or tool calls, plus token usage.

```python
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in two sentences."}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

The API is stateless: send the conversation history with each request. Features include streaming, tool use, vision, PDF input, prompt caching, batch processing and extended thinking. Check the documentation for current model names.

## How do I find my Claude API key?

Sign in to the Anthropic Console, open the API keys section, and create a new key. Copy it immediately, because it is shown only once, and store it in an environment variable or a secrets manager.

If you lose a key, create a new one and delete the old one. Use separate keys for development and production, and for different applications, so you can revoke one without breaking others. Never commit keys to git, paste them into front-end code, or share them in screenshots. If a key leaks, revoke it in the Console right away and check usage for unexpected activity.

## Is the Claude API paid?

Yes. The Claude API is billed by usage: you pay for input and output tokens, with prices varying by model. New accounts may receive limited free credits for testing depending on current offers, and you add credits or set up billing to continue.

Costs depend on model choice, prompt length, output length and volume. Reduce them by choosing smaller models for simple tasks, keeping prompts concise, using prompt caching for repeated context, using the batch API for non-urgent jobs, and limiting maximum output tokens. Set spending limits and alerts in the Console. Check Anthropic's pricing page for current rates.

## What are the Claude API rates and limits?

"Rates" can mean prices or rate limits. Prices are charged per million input and output tokens per model, with larger models costing more. Rate limits cap requests and tokens per minute, and they increase as your account moves up usage tiers.

When you exceed a rate limit, the API returns a 429 error with headers indicating when to retry. Handle it with exponential backoff, spread requests over time, and batch work where possible. Higher tiers come with sustained usage and payment history. For high-volume production, contact Anthropic or use cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud, which have their own quotas.

## What is a token in the Claude API?

A token is a chunk of text, often part of a word, that the model processes. Billing, context limits and rate limits are all measured in tokens: input tokens for everything you send, and output tokens for what Claude generates.

As a rough guide, one English token is about three to four characters, so a page of text might be several hundred tokens; other languages and code tokenise differently. The API returns exact usage with each response, and a token-counting endpoint estimates costs before sending. Long conversations grow input tokens every turn, since history is resent, which is why summarising or trimming history saves money.

## Can I use the Claude API with a Pro subscription?

No, the API is billed separately. A Claude Pro subscription covers the Claude apps, not API usage, so you need API credits or billing in the Anthropic Console for developer access.

Some Anthropic tools can use your subscription instead of API billing; for example, Claude Code can be used with Pro or Max plans, within their usage limits. For building your own applications, though, the API with its own billing is required. Keep personal subscription use and application API use separate, which also helps track costs per project.

## Does the Claude API train on your data?

According to Anthropic's commercial terms, data sent through the API is not used to train its models by default. Anthropic retains API data for a limited period for safety and abuse monitoring, with options such as zero data retention for eligible enterprise customers.

Always review the current terms and privacy documentation, since policies can change, and consumer apps have different settings from the API. For sensitive data, minimise what you send, redact personal information where possible, and check compliance needs such as data residency. Cloud platforms offering Claude, such as Amazon Bedrock, also have their own data handling terms.

## Can the Claude API read PDFs?

Yes. You can send PDFs directly as document content blocks, either base64-encoded or by URL or file reference, and Claude reads both the text and visual elements such as charts and tables on each page, then answers questions or extracts data.

PDF limits apply on size and page count per request, and each page uses tokens for both text and images. For large document collections, a RAG pipeline that retrieves relevant pages is more efficient than sending entire PDFs every time. Enable citations to have Claude point to the passages it used, which is how document question answering stays verifiable.

## Can the Claude API use MCP?

Yes. The API's MCP connector lets you specify remote MCP servers in a request, so Claude can call their tools directly, and the Claude Agent SDK and Claude apps support MCP servers too. You can also convert MCP tools into standard tool definitions in your own code.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data sources, such as GitHub, databases or internal services. Only connect trusted servers, scope their permissions narrowly, and review which tools Claude can call, because tool results can contain malicious instructions in prompt-injection attacks.

## Can I use my Claude API key in Cursor?

Yes. Cursor's settings let you add your own Anthropic API key so requests to Claude models are billed to your Anthropic account instead of Cursor's included usage, subject to Cursor's current options for custom keys.

Using your own key can be useful for higher limits or cost tracking, but some Cursor features may only work with its built-in models. Keep the key secure, monitor usage in the Anthropic Console, and remove it if you stop using it. Similar options exist in other tools, such as Continue and Cline, which let you choose Claude models with your own API key.

# What is a Claude API key, and how do you get and set up the Claude API?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-api-key-setup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A Claude API key is a secret token that lets your own code call Claude models through Anthropic's API; requests made with it are billed to your developer account. You create keys in the Claude Console, store them in an environment variable, and use them with Anthropic's SDKs or plain HTTP. This page covers getting a key, the Console and developer platform, the docs, how the API differs from the claude.ai app, how a request works, setting it up in Python, using Claude in VS Code, and whether the API supports skills.

## What is a Claude API key?

A Claude API key is a long secret string, beginning with `sk-ant-`, that authenticates requests to Anthropic's API. Anyone who has your key can make requests that are charged to your account, so it must be kept private.

Keys belong to a workspace in your organisation in the Claude Console, so you can create separate keys for development and production, set spending limits per workspace, and revoke a key instantly if it leaks. A key is not your claude.ai login and does not give access to your chat history. Common leaks happen when keys are pasted into front-end JavaScript, committed to a public GitHub repository or shared in screenshots. Keep keys in environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate any key you suspect has been exposed.

## How do I get a Claude AI API key?

Sign up in the Claude Console, set up billing for your organisation, then open the API keys page and create a key. Copy it immediately; the Console shows the full key only once.

The steps:

- Sign in to the Console with your email or Google account.
- Add billing details and purchase credits or set up payment, as the Console prompts.
- Go to API keys and choose "Create key", giving it a clear name such as "college-project-dev".
- Copy the key into a password manager or your project's `.env` file.

A claude.ai Pro or Max subscription does not include API credits; the two are billed separately. Students should set a low spending limit while learning, so a bug in a loop cannot run up a large bill.

## Where is the Claude API Console?

The Claude Console, previously called the Anthropic Console, is Anthropic's web dashboard for developers, linked from the Claude developer documentation. It is where you create keys, manage billing, test prompts and see usage.

Inside the Console you will find a Workbench for trying prompts and model settings before writing code, a prompt generator and improver, usage and cost dashboards, rate-limit information for your tier, and organisation settings for inviting teammates and creating workspaces. It is separate from claude.ai, even though you can use the same email for both. If a link or tutorial points to an old address, start from Anthropic's documentation site and follow the link to the Console from there.

## What is the Claude API platform?

The Claude Developer Platform is Anthropic's set of services for building with Claude: the API itself, the Console, SDKs, documentation and features such as tool use, batch processing, prompt caching, files and agent tooling.

Building blocks you will meet:

- **Messages API**: the core request for a model response.
- **Tool use**: let Claude call your functions and APIs.
- **Message Batches**: process large jobs asynchronously at lower cost.
- **Prompt caching**: reuse long, repeated context cheaply and quickly.
- **Files API** and PDF support: reuse uploaded documents.
- **Agent SDK and MCP**: build agents and connect tools in a standard way.

Claude models are also available through cloud providers such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI, which suits teams already on those clouds.

## Where are the Claude API docs?

Anthropic's developer documentation covers getting started, every API endpoint, the SDKs, model details, pricing, rate limits and guides on prompting, tool use, retrieval and agents. It is linked from anthropic.com and the Console.

Read these first: the quickstart, the Messages API reference, the models overview for current model names, the guide to tool use, and the prompt engineering guide. The docs include runnable examples in Python and TypeScript, and an API reference with every parameter. When a blog post or video disagrees with the docs, trust the docs; model names and parameters change, and older tutorials go stale quickly.

## What is the difference between Claude AI and the Claude API?

Claude AI usually means claude.ai, the chat product for people, with a free tier and subscriptions. The Claude API is the developer interface for building Claude into your own software, paid per token used.

The chat app gives you a ready interface, conversation history, projects, file uploads and apps on every device. The API gives you only the model: you send messages and get responses, and you build the interface, storage and logic yourself. Subscriptions and API credits are billed separately; a Pro plan does not cover API usage. Use claude.ai to learn, write and think; use the API when you want Claude inside a website, bot, app or automated workflow.

## How does the Claude API work?

Your code sends an HTTPS request to the Messages endpoint with your API key, a model name, a maximum number of output tokens and a list of messages. Claude returns a response containing content blocks, a stop reason and token usage.

Key ideas:

- **Stateless**: the API does not remember earlier calls; send the conversation history you want it to consider each time.
- **System prompt**: sets the role, rules and context for the whole conversation.
- **Tokens**: you pay for input and output tokens, and limits apply per minute.
- **Streaming**: receive the response as it is generated for a responsive UI.
- **Tools**: describe functions with JSON schemas; Claude replies with a tool call, you run it and send the result back.

Errors come back with clear types, such as rate limits and temporary overload, which you handle with retries.

## How do I set up the Claude API?

Install the SDK, set your key as an environment variable, and make a first request. In Python, that is three steps and about ten lines.

```bash
pip install anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."     # on Windows PowerShell: $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
```

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=400,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Give me three RAG project ideas for students."}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)
```

For projects, keep the key in a `.env` file loaded at startup and add `.env` to `.gitignore`. Check the models overview for the current model names.

## How do I use the Claude API in VS Code?

The simplest route is Claude Code's VS Code extension, which brings Claude's coding agent into the editor. Alternatively, coding extensions that support multiple providers let you paste an Anthropic API key and choose a Claude model.

With Claude Code, you install it, sign in with your Claude account or use an API key, and work with it in the editor: it reads your project, proposes edits shown as diffs and runs commands with your approval. Third-party extensions such as open-source coding assistants also accept Anthropic keys and bill usage to your API account. Whichever you use, set a spending limit in the Console, keep the key out of your settings files that get committed, and review every change before accepting it.

## Can the Claude API use skills?

Yes. Agent Skills, packaged folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads when relevant, can be used through the Claude API together with its code execution tool, as well as in Claude Code and the Claude apps.

Anthropic provides some prebuilt skills, for example for working with document formats, and you can upload custom skills for your organisation, such as your report template or data-cleaning procedure. Claude sees a short description of each available skill and loads the full contents only when a task needs it, which keeps context small. Because this feature is newer and its request format may change, follow the current skills guide in the API documentation for the exact parameters, and test custom skills on small tasks first.

You can also access Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud Vertex AI, billed through those cloud accounts. Also asked as: where to buy claude api credits Cloud marketplaces suit organisations with existing cloud commitments or procurement processes, while the console suits individuals and startups. Start with a small purchase while prototyping. Set up automatic reload for production apps to avoid outages from empty balances, and configure spending alerts. Avoid third-party resellers offering discounted Claude credits or shared keys, which may violate terms, expose your data or stop working without notice. Keep invoices organised for accounting and reimbursement. Is the OpenAI API cheaper than Claude? It depends on which models you compare and how you use them. Both providers offer tiers from small, inexpensive models to premium frontier models, and per-token rates change often. Compare equivalent tiers on your actual workload. Also asked as: is openai api cheaper than claude Total cost depends on tokens per request, output length, caching, batch discounts and how many retries or tool calls each task needs. A model that costs more per token but solves tasks in fewer attempts can be cheaper overall. Measure cost per successful task on a representative sample. Many teams use several providers, routing simple requests to cheaper models, as RAG.NextUpgrad's multi-provider fallback design allows. Check both pricing pages for current rates. What does Claude API stand for? API stands for Application Programming Interface: a defined way for software to communicate with another service. The Claude API lets your programs send messages to Claude models and receive responses over the internet. Instead of chatting in an app, your code sends structured requests containing a model name, instructions and messages, and receives Claude's reply as data. This lets developers build Claude into websites, mobile apps, internal tools and agents. The API also exposes features such as tool use, vision, file handling, prompt caching and batch processing. Anthropic's SDKs wrap the API in convenient libraries for popular programming languages. Learning one API pattern makes other AI APIs easy to adopt.

# Claude API vs Claude AI and Claude Code, 529 errors, keys, Gemini, Vertex, Azure OpenAI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-api-vs-apps-gemini-azure/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Model providers offer the same models through different products: chat apps with subscriptions, developer APIs billed per token, coding tools and enterprise cloud versions. Mixing them up causes confusing errors and bills. I build apps with multi-provider fallback, such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers the Claude API versus the Claude apps and Claude Code, API keys in Claude Desktop, 529 and key errors, the Gemini API, AI Studio, Vertex AI and Google keys, and OpenAI versus Azure OpenAI. What is the difference between the Claude API and Claude AI? Claude AI usually means the Claude apps at claude.ai, desktop and mobile, used through Free or paid subscription plans. The Claude API gives developers programmatic access to Claude models, billed separately per token through Anthropic's developer console. Also asked as: difference between claude api and claude ai A Pro or Max subscription does not include API credits, and API usage does not unlock app features. The apps provide a ready interface with projects, artifacts, connectors and memory, while the API lets you build your own applications, control prompts and parameters, and integrate Claude into products. Developers often use both: the app for daily work and the API for building. Each has separate usage limits, billing and data terms, so review both. Can you use your Claude API key in Claude Desktop? No. Claude Desktop signs in with your claude.ai account and uses your subscription, not API keys. API keys work with the Anthropic SDKs, direct API calls, Claude Code and third-party applications that accept your own key. Also asked as: can i use my claude api key in claude desktop If you want a desktop chat interface billed through your API account, some third-party clients let you enter an Anthropic API key, though you should review their security before trusting them with it. Claude Code can authenticate either with your subscription login or with an API key from an environment variable. Keep API keys secret, store them in environment variables or secret managers, and rotate them immediately if exposed. What is the difference between the Claude API and Claude Code? The Claude API is raw access to Claude models for any application you build. Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool, built on those models, that reads your codebase, edits files and runs commands in your terminal, IDE, desktop or browser. Also asked as: difference between claude api and claude code Claude Code handles the agent loop, tools, permissions and context management for software tasks, so you do not have to build them. It can bill through a Claude subscription or through API usage. The API suits building your own products, including custom agents with the Claude Agent SDK, which exposes the same agent framework that powers Claude Code. Choose Claude Code for development work and the API for shipping features to users. Why are you getting 529 errors from the Claude API? A 529 error means overloaded: Anthropic's API is temporarily experiencing high demand across users. It is not caused by your account or code, unlike a 429 error, which means you exceeded your own rate limits. Also asked as: why am i getting 529 errors from claude api Handle 529 errors with automatic retries using exponential backoff and jitter; the official SDKs retry some errors automatically, and you can raise the retry count. Check Anthropic's status page during persistent errors. For production reliability, add fallback to another Claude model or another provider, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with multi-provider fallback. Avoid hammering the API with immediate retries, which worsens congestion. Log error rates so you can see patterns over time. Why does a Claude API call fail even with a key? Common causes include sending the key in the wrong header, which should be x-api-key; a missing anthropic-version header; a revoked or mistyped key; no credits or billing set up; a wrong model name; or calling the wrong endpoint. Also asked as: why fail to call claude api even with the eky Read the error type in the response: authentication errors point to the key, permission errors to workspace or model access, not found errors to the model name or URL, and invalid request errors to malformed parameters. Using the official SDK avoids most header mistakes. Check that your environment variable is loaded in the process making the call. Keys from Anthropic's console do not work on Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI, which use cloud credentials. What is the difference between the Gemini API and Vertex AI? Both serve Google's Gemini models. The Gemini Developer API, used with Google AI Studio keys, is simpler and has a free tier, suiting prototypes and smaller apps. Vertex AI is Google Cloud's enterprise platform, adding IAM, private networking, data residency and service agreements. Also asked as: difference between gemini api and vertex ai Vertex AI also integrates with other Google Cloud services, such as BigQuery, model tuning, evaluation tools and access to third-party models. Authentication differs: the Developer API uses API keys, while Vertex AI uses Google Cloud service accounts and credentials. The Google Gen AI SDK supports both, so code can move between them with configuration changes. Start with the Developer API, and migrate to Vertex AI when compliance or scale requires it. What is the difference between Google AI Studio and the Gemini API? Google AI Studio is a web interface for experimenting with Gemini models, testing prompts, adjusting settings and getting API keys. The Gemini API is the programmatic interface your code calls to use those models in applications. Also asked as: difference between google ai studio and gemini api In AI Studio, you can try multimodal prompts, structured outputs, function calling and system instructions, then view equivalent code in Python or JavaScript. It also shows usage and manages keys and projects. Once a prompt works, move it into your application using the API and SDK. Think of AI Studio as the workshop and the API as the production line. Both use the same underlying models and project quotas. What is the difference between a Google API key and a Gemini API key? A Gemini API key is a Google Cloud API key enabled for the Generative Language API, usually created through Google AI Studio. A general Google API key might be enabled for other services, such as Maps or YouTube. Also asked as: difference between google api key and gemini api key Technically, both are Google Cloud API keys, and one key can be enabled for several APIs, but best practice is separate, restricted keys for each service and environment. Restrict each key to specific APIs and, for browser keys, to specific websites. Gemini keys should stay on servers, since they grant access to your quota and billing. If a key is exposed publicly, delete it and create a new one immediately. What is the difference between the OpenAI API and the Azure OpenAI API? Both offer OpenAI models. The OpenAI API is run by OpenAI directly. Azure OpenAI runs the same models on Microsoft Azure, adding enterprise security, regional deployment, private networking, Azure identity integration, content filtering and Microsoft's compliance commitments. Also asked as: difference between openai api and azure openai api With Azure, you create deployments of specific models in chosen regions and call them by deployment name, using Azure endpoints and authentication. New models sometimes reach the OpenAI API before Azure. Organisations already using Azure often prefer it for governance, billing consolidation and data residency. The official OpenAI SDKs support both with configuration changes. Compare model availability, regional options and quotas for your needs before choosing one. What is the difference between the Gemini API and Google AI? Google AI is Google's umbrella for its artificial intelligence research, products and developer tools, including Gemini models, Gemma open models, Google AI Studio and research from Google DeepMind. The Gemini API is one specific developer product within it. Also asked as: difference between gemini api and google ai Google AI for Developers is the documentation hub covering the Gemini API, Gemma, on-device AI with LiteRT and other tools. Consumer products such as the Gemini app and AI features in Search and Workspace also fall under Google's AI efforts but are separate from the API. When reading guides, check whether they refer to the consumer app, the developer API or Vertex AI, since features, limits and terms differ.

# What is the Claude app, the Claude SDK and API, and can Claude apply to jobs?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/claude-app-sdk-api-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Claude app is Anthropic's assistant on the web at claude.ai, on desktop for macOS and Windows, and on iOS and Android; Claude Code is its coding tool for the terminal and IDEs. Developers reach the same models through the Claude API, usually with Anthropic's official SDKs. This page covers the apps and where your data lives, the API and SDKs and how they differ, what the "overloaded" error means, how to connect Apify's scrapers to Claude, whether that is free, and whether Claude can apply to jobs for you.

## What is the Claude app?

The Claude app is Anthropic's AI assistant, available in a browser at claude.ai and as desktop and mobile apps. You chat with it, upload files and images, create documents and small apps in a side panel, and connect it to tools.

All versions share one account, so conversations and projects appear everywhere you sign in. The desktop app adds conveniences such as a quick-launch shortcut and connecting local tools through the Model Context Protocol. The mobile app is good for voice and quick questions. Claude Code is a separate tool for developers that works directly on code in your terminal or IDE. The same family of Claude models powers all of them, with plans that set your usage limits.

## What are the Claude apps?

The official Claude apps are the web app at claude.ai, desktop apps for macOS and Windows, mobile apps for iOS and Android, and Claude Code for the terminal and IDEs such as VS Code and JetBrains. All are published by Anthropic.

Each suits a different job:

- **Web and desktop**: writing, research, analysing documents and spreadsheets, projects with shared files.
- **Mobile**: voice conversations, photos of notes or whiteboards, quick questions.
- **Claude Code**: reading a codebase, editing files, running tests and commands.

Inside the chat apps, "artifacts" are small documents or apps Claude creates that you can preview, edit and share. Be careful with third-party apps that use the Claude name: unless the publisher is Anthropic or a known IDE vendor, avoid entering your credentials.

## Does the Claude app keep all data locally?

No. The Claude apps store your conversations in your Anthropic account on Anthropic's servers, so they sync across devices. The desktop app is a client, not an offline model; nothing runs fully on your computer.

What stays local depends on what you connect: files on your computer that you expose through a local MCP server are read on your machine and only the parts Claude uses are sent with the conversation. Anthropic's privacy settings let you control whether your chats may be used to improve models, and you can delete conversations. Check the privacy settings once and choose deliberately. If you need data to stay entirely on your own hardware, you need a local open-weight model, not Claude.

## What are the Claude APIs?

The Claude API is Anthropic's HTTP interface for using Claude models in your own software. The core is the Messages API: you send a list of messages and settings, and get Claude's reply, with options for streaming, tool use, images, PDFs and structured outputs.

Around it are supporting APIs: token counting, the Message Batches API for large asynchronous jobs at lower cost, a Files API for reusing uploaded documents, and features such as prompt caching to cut cost on repeated context. You authenticate with an API key from the Anthropic Console and pay per token used, separately from any chat subscription. The API is what you use to build a chatbot into a college project, add document Q&A to an app, or run an agent on a server.

## What is the Claude SDK?

The Claude SDKs are Anthropic's official client libraries for calling the API from code, available for Python, TypeScript and several other languages. There is also the Claude Agent SDK, for building agents on the same foundations as Claude Code.

A minimal Python example:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain BM25 in two sentences."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Install it with `pip install anthropic`. Check the model overview in the docs for the current model names, since new versions replace old ones regularly.

## What is the difference between the Claude API and SDK?

The API is the service: HTTP endpoints that accept requests and return Claude's responses. An SDK is a library in your programming language that calls those endpoints for you, handling authentication, retries, streaming and typed responses.

You can call the API directly with any HTTP client, which is useful for languages without an SDK or for quick tests with `curl`. In practice, the SDK saves effort and prevents mistakes: it retries temporary errors automatically, parses streaming events correctly, and gives editor autocompletion for parameters. Both reach the same models with the same limits and prices. Use the SDK for real projects and raw HTTP only when you have a reason.

## What does "Claude API is overloaded" mean?

It means Anthropic's servers are temporarily under heavy load and could not process your request. The API returns an `overloaded_error`, with HTTP status 529, and the right response is to wait briefly and retry.

It is not a problem with your key, code or account, and it is different from a rate-limit error, which means you exceeded your own limits. Handle it with retries using exponential backoff and a little randomness, so many clients do not retry at the same instant. The official SDKs already retry such errors a couple of times by default, and you can raise the retry count. In production, also add a fallback, such as a smaller model or a different provider, so users see a slower answer rather than an error. RAG.NextUpgrad uses multi-provider fallback for exactly this reason.

## How do I connect Apify to Claude?

Apify provides an MCP server that exposes its scrapers, called Actors, as tools. Add the Apify MCP server to Claude, through the connectors settings or the desktop app's MCP configuration, with your Apify API token, and Claude can run Actors and read their results.

Once connected, you can ask Claude, for example, to collect the titles and links of recent posts from a public page using a suitable Actor, then summarise them. Keep three things in mind: scrape only public data you are allowed to collect and respect each site's terms; store your Apify token like a password; and limit which Actors are exposed so Claude cannot run expensive jobs by accident. Apify's documentation has current setup instructions for its MCP server.

## Is Apify for Claude free?

Connecting Apify to Claude through its MCP server does not need a special paid add-on, but running Apify Actors uses your Apify account's platform usage. Apify has a free plan with a monthly usage allowance, and heavier use needs a paid plan.

Your Claude plan applies on the Claude side as usual. Costs depend on the Actors you run, how many pages they process and how often; some Actors are maintained by third parties and have their own pricing. Start with small test runs and check usage in the Apify console before scheduling anything recurring. Apify's pricing page lists the current free allowance and plans.

## Can Claude apply to jobs for me?

Claude can do most of the work around applying: tailoring your resume to each job description, drafting cover letters and referral messages, and preparing you for interviews. You should still submit applications yourself.

Agent tools that control a browser can technically fill in forms, but automated applications on LinkedIn, Indeed and similar sites can break their terms of service and get accounts restricted. Mass-applying also produces poor matches that recruiters ignore. A better use of Claude: "Here is the job description and my resume. List the gaps, rewrite my project bullets using only facts from my resume, and draft a 100-word note to an engineer at the company." Then read, edit and send it yourself. Quality and a referral beat volume.
