# Context windows explained: Claude Code, Codex, memory, tokens and largest models
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/context-window-claude-code-codex-tokens/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can consider at once, including instructions, conversation history, files and its own reply. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex fill it quickly. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad that retrieve only relevant passages to stay within context, so this page covers checking and clearing context in Claude Code, what happens when it fills, the largest windows, memory, tokens, input and output, and why size matters. How do you check the context window in Claude Code? Run the /context command inside a Claude Code session. It shows how much of the context window is used and breaks usage down by category, such as the system prompt, tools, MCP tools, memory files and messages, plus remaining free space. Also asked as: how to check context window in claude code Claude Code also warns you as the conversation approaches the limit, showing the percentage left before automatic compaction, and a custom status line can display usage continuously. Checking /context helps you spot hidden costs: many connected MCP servers can consume a large share of context with tool definitions before you type anything, and large CLAUDE.md files load in every session. Disable unused MCP servers, trim memory files, and read files selectively rather than whole directories. The /cost command reports token usage for the session. How does the context window work in Claude Code? Every request Claude Code sends includes the system prompt, tool definitions, CLAUDE.md memory files and the whole conversation so far, including file contents and command outputs. All of it, plus Claude's reply, must fit within the model's context window. Also asked as: how does context window work in claude code As you work, tool results such as file reads, search results and test logs accumulate quickly, so long sessions fill the window. When usage nears the limit, Claude Code automatically compacts the conversation, summarising earlier turns to free space while keeping key decisions. Subagents run in their own separate context windows and return only summaries, which keeps the main session lean. Prompt caching reduces the cost of resending the stable prefix on every turn. The window size depends on the model, commonly 200,000 tokens, with larger options on some models. How do you clear the context window in Claude Code? Use /clear to wipe the conversation and start fresh in the same session, or /compact to replace the history with a summary while keeping important details. You can pass instructions to /compact, such as telling it what to keep. Also asked as: how to clear context window in claude code Clear context when you switch to an unrelated task, since leftover history wastes tokens and can confuse the model. Compact when you want to continue the same task but the window is filling. Before clearing, ask Claude to write important decisions or next steps into a file, such as a notes file or CLAUDE.md, so they survive the reset. Starting a new session in the terminal also gives a fresh context. Regular clearing keeps responses faster, cheaper and more focused, especially in long coding sessions with many file reads. What happens when the context window is full in Claude? In Claude Code, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary so you can continue. On the API, a request whose input exceeds the window is rejected with an error, and output stops early if it runs out of room. Also asked as: what happens when context window is full claude In the Claude apps, very long conversations may be summarised automatically or you may be asked to start a new chat, depending on features and plan. Compaction keeps the gist but loses details, such as exact code snippets or early instructions, so restate critical requirements afterwards. Developers using the API can manage context themselves by trimming old turns, summarising history, using retrieval, or using context editing and compaction features where available. Starting fresh with a short summary often works better than pushing a degraded conversation forward. What happens when the context window is full in Codex? OpenAI's Codex CLI shows how much context remains and, as the limit approaches, compacts the conversation by summarising earlier turns. You can trigger this yourself with the /compact command, or start a fresh conversation with /new. Also asked as: what happens when context window is full codex Without compaction, requests would fail once the conversation exceeded the model's window. After compaction, details from early in the session may be lost, so keep important plans in files such as AGENTS.md, which Codex reads for project instructions. Long tool outputs, such as test logs and large file reads, fill context fastest, so ask for targeted reads and summaries. When switching tasks, start a new conversation rather than carrying irrelevant history. The same habits apply to Claude Code and other coding agents, since they all share the same underlying limit. Which model has the largest context window? Among widely available models, Meta's Llama 4 Scout advertises a window of up to 10 million tokens, while Google's Gemini models, OpenAI's GPT-4.1 and some Claude models offer around one million tokens. Limits change often, so check current documentation. Advertised size is not the same as usable quality. Models often recall facts less reliably from the middle of long contexts, a pattern documented in the Lost in the Middle study by Liu and colleagues, and cost and latency grow with input length. Long contexts suit whole-codebase analysis, long documents and video, while retrieval remains cheaper and more precise for large knowledge bases. Test your own task at the lengths you need before relying on a huge window. For many applications, a well-built RAG pipeline with a smaller window beats stuffing everything into one prompt. What is the difference between a context window and memory? The context window is the text the model sees in a single request, and it is gone afterwards. Memory is information stored outside the model, such as saved facts, files or databases, and selectively loaded back into context when needed. Also asked as: difference between context window and memory Models have no persistent memory between requests on their own; every call starts from what is in the context window. Applications create the effect of memory by storing facts and inserting them into later prompts. ChatGPT's and Claude's memory features save preferences and past details, while Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md files at the start of each session. Retrieval systems act as long-term memory for documents. Memory is persistent but must be retrieved; context is immediate but limited and temporary. Good assistants combine both, loading only the memories relevant to the current task. What is the difference between a context window and tokens? Tokens are the units of text a model processes, roughly three quarters of an English word on average. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can handle in one request, covering prompt and response together. Also asked as: difference between context window and tokens So tokens measure amount, and the context window is the capacity. A 200,000 token window holds roughly a long book's worth of English text, though code, numbers and many non-English languages use more tokens per word. Providers bill per token, separately for input and output, so filling a large window costs more. Count tokens with each provider's tokenizer or token counting endpoint before sending large inputs, and remember that images, PDFs and tool definitions also consume tokens. Tracking token counts per request is the simplest way to understand both cost and context pressure. Does the context window include input and output? Yes. The context window covers the input, meaning system prompt, conversation, documents and tool definitions, plus the output the model generates. Input tokens and the maximum output you request must fit together within the window. Also asked as: does context window include input and output Models also have a separate maximum output limit, usually much smaller than the context window. For reasoning models, thinking tokens count as output and occupy the window during generation, although providers may strip earlier reasoning from later turns. If input is close to the limit, the model has little room to answer and may stop mid-response. Leave headroom by trimming inputs, retrieving only relevant passages and setting sensible maximum output values. Check each provider's documentation, since accounting rules for thinking, images and cached tokens differ between them. Why is context window size important in LLMs? Context size decides how much information a model can use at once: longer documents, bigger codebases, longer conversations and more examples. Too small a window forces truncation or retrieval; a larger one enables whole-document reasoning. Size is not everything. Larger contexts cost more, add latency and can reduce accuracy when relevant facts are buried among irrelevant ones. Good systems use context deliberately: retrieve the most relevant passages, keep instructions clear and near the start or end, and remove stale history. RAG.NextUpgrad, for example, combines hybrid retrieval, reranking and a confidence gate so only strong evidence reaches the prompt. Evaluate quality at realistic lengths, since a model that handles long context well on benchmarks may still struggle with your specific data.

# What is a context window in AI? How it works, limits, resets, and how long 128K or 1M is
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/context-window-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can take into account at once: your instructions, the conversation so far, any documents, and the response it generates. Long context windows, from hundreds of thousands to a million tokens, let models read whole reports, books or codebases in one go. Context management is central to RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page explains how context windows work, their limits, why they matter, resets in Claude, and what different sizes hold.

## What is a long context window in AI?

A long context window is a model's ability to handle very large inputs, commonly 128,000 tokens and above, with some models supporting around a million tokens. That is enough to include long contracts, multiple research papers or substantial codebases in a single request.

Long context enables tasks such as summarising whole books, answering questions across many documents, analysing large logs and reviewing code across files. It does not mean the model uses every part equally well: research found models can miss information placed in the middle of long inputs. For large knowledge bases, retrieval still helps by selecting the most relevant parts. A good rule: use long context when the task genuinely needs the whole document, and retrieval when only a few passages matter.

## How does a context window work?

Text is split into tokens, pieces of words, and the model processes all tokens in its window together using attention, which lets each token consider the others. Everything outside the window is invisible to the model for that request.

In chat apps, the window holds the system prompt, conversation history, uploaded content and the new answer. As conversations grow, older parts may be summarised, truncated or dropped to stay within the limit. Each request is processed fresh: the model has no memory beyond what is placed in the window, plus any separate memory features that add saved information to the context.

## What is a context window limit?

The context window limit is the maximum number of tokens a model accepts per request, combining input and output. Exceeding it causes errors in APIs, or truncation and summarisation in chat apps. Output usually has its own, smaller maximum.

Limits vary by model and plan, from a few thousand tokens in older models to hundreds of thousands or a million in recent ones. Practical limits are often lower than technical ones because of cost, latency and quality. In applications, budget tokens deliberately: system prompt, retrieved chunks, conversation history and space for the answer, trimming whichever matters least.

## What is the input context window?

The input context is the portion of the window filled by what you send: system instructions, conversation history, documents, retrieved passages and the current question. The remaining space is available for the model's output.

Input tokens are typically cheaper than output tokens in API pricing, but large inputs still add cost and latency, especially when resent with every turn. Prompt caching reduces cost for repeated, stable input such as long system prompts or documents. Designing inputs carefully, putting the most important instructions and content clearly, improves both quality and cost.

## Why is the context window limited?

Context windows are limited because the attention computation and the memory for storing intermediate values grow with input length, increasing compute cost, GPU memory needs and latency. Models also need training on long sequences to use them well.

Engineering advances, such as efficient attention kernels, better memory management and training techniques, have extended windows dramatically. But longer context still costs more per request and can reduce precision on details. That is why many systems combine moderate context with retrieval: select relevant passages rather than sending everything.

## Why does the context window matter?

It determines how much information a model can use at once: long documents, extended conversations, many retrieved passages or large codebases. Too small a window forces aggressive trimming, losing details; a large window enables richer tasks but costs more.

For developers, context shapes architecture: whether to send whole documents or retrieve chunks, how to manage chat history, and how agents keep track of long tasks. For users, it explains why long chats start "forgetting" early details. Good context management, keeping what matters and dropping what does not, often improves results more than a bigger window. Agents in particular need careful context handling, since tool outputs accumulate quickly over many steps.

## Is the context window per chat?

Yes. Each conversation has its own context; starting a new chat begins with an empty window, apart from system instructions and any saved memory or project files the app adds. Within a chat, the window holds as much of the conversation as fits.

Features such as projects, custom instructions and memory carry selected information across chats by inserting it into each new context. Through APIs, applications decide exactly what context to send each time. If a chat becomes long and unfocused, starting a new one with a short summary of key points usually gives better answers.

## When does the context window reset in Claude?

In the Claude apps, each new conversation starts with a fresh context window. Within long conversations, the app manages context as it grows, and you may be prompted to start a new chat. In Claude Code, long sessions are automatically compacted, summarising earlier history to free space, and you can clear or compact manually.

Practical tips: start new chats for new topics, use projects to keep shared files and instructions available across chats, and in Claude Code use project memory files such as CLAUDE.md for durable instructions. Similar mechanisms exist in other tools, such as automatic summarisation in coding agents.

## How long is a 128K context window?

A 128K context window holds about 128,000 tokens, roughly 96,000 English words using the common estimate of about three-quarters of a word per token, equivalent to a few hundred pages of text, such as a long novel or a large technical report.

For comparison, 32K tokens is about 24,000 words, roughly a long article series or a short book section, and 200K tokens is about 150,000 words. Code and non-English text use tokens differently, often more tokens per word for Indian languages, so actual capacity varies. Use a tokenizer tool to measure your own documents.

## How long is a 1M context window?

A one million token context window holds roughly 750,000 English words, the equivalent of several long novels, thousands of pages of documents, or a large codebase, in a single request.

Such windows enable tasks like analysing entire code repositories, many hours of transcripts or large document collections at once. Requests this large are slower and more expensive, and models may not use all details equally well. For repeated questions over the same large corpus, retrieval or caching usually beats sending a million tokens each time.

# When Copilot becomes autopilot: roadmaps, best Copilot prompts, and Copilot courses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-autopilot-prompts-courses/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


"When Copilot becomes autopilot" describes the move from AI assistants that help when you ask, to agents that take actions on their own when triggered, such as processing new invoices or summarising tickets every morning, within limits set by people. Microsoft's Copilot products now span both. This page explains that shift, where to follow the Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio roadmaps, the best prompts for Copilot in general, Excel, Outlook and meeting notes, and Microsoft's courses, certificates and a Copilot Studio tutorial.

## What does it mean when Copilot becomes autopilot?

It means moving from a copilot, an assistant that suggests and drafts while you stay in control, to an autopilot-style agent that carries out tasks by itself when an event or schedule triggers it, such as handling routine requests without someone starting a chat.

In Microsoft's ecosystem, Copilot Studio supports autonomous agents with triggers, and Microsoft 365 Copilot includes agents that perform multi-step work. Autonomy needs safeguards: narrow scope, limited permissions, human approval for consequential actions, logging and monitoring. Even in aviation, autopilot works under a pilot's supervision; good AI automation follows the same principle, with people reviewing outcomes and handling exceptions.

## Where is the Microsoft 365 Copilot roadmap?

The Microsoft 365 roadmap website lists upcoming and rolling-out features; filter by the Microsoft 365 Copilot product to see planned, in-development and launched items with target dates. Release notes on Microsoft Learn describe what has already shipped.

Admins use the roadmap to prepare training and change management before features reach users. Treat target dates as estimates, since rollouts happen in stages by region and release channel. For a quick view of recent changes, the "What's new" pages in Microsoft Learn's Copilot documentation are more reliable than news articles, which may describe previews or announcements that changed before release.

## Where is the Copilot Studio roadmap?

Copilot Studio's upcoming features appear on the Microsoft 365 roadmap and in Power Platform release planning, while its documentation's "What's new" page lists recent releases. Microsoft also announces major changes at its developer and partner events.

When building agents, check the roadmap before starting a custom solution, because a planned built-in feature might replace your workaround. Preview features may change or have limits, so avoid relying on them for critical production agents. Subscribe to official release notes or check them monthly if your organisation depends on Copilot Studio.

## What are the best Copilot prompts?

The best Copilot prompts include four elements: the goal, the context, the source to use, and what you expect the output to look like. For example: "Summarise the decisions from the project sync meeting yesterday and the client's follow-up email, as five bullet points with owners and deadlines."

General prompt patterns that work:

- "Draft [document] for [audience] using [file], in [tone], under [length]."
- "Compare [A] and [B] from [sources] in a table with [columns]."
- "What did [person] ask me for in the last [period]? List with links."
- "Turn [document] into a [number]-slide presentation outline."

Microsoft's Copilot Prompt Gallery offers ready-made prompts to adapt and save.

## What are the best Copilot prompts for Excel?

Good Excel prompts are specific about columns, calculations and outputs, and assume the data is formatted as a table. For example: "Add a column that calculates profit margin as (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue, formatted as a percentage."

More examples:

- "Which three products had the largest month-on-month drop in sales?"
- "Highlight rows where the due date is past and status is not Paid."
- "Create a PivotTable of total sales by region and quarter."
- "Show a line chart of monthly signups for the last 12 months."
- "Explain this formula in plain words and suggest a simpler version."

Check any formulas Copilot inserts on a few rows by hand before trusting the totals.

## What are the best Copilot prompts for Outlook?

Outlook prompts work best when they state the recipient, purpose, tone and length. For example: "Reply to Priya accepting the Tuesday meeting, ask for the agenda in advance, keep it to three sentences, friendly but formal."

More examples:

- "Summarise this thread and list the open questions directed at me."
- "Draft a follow-up to the vendor asking for the revised quote by Friday."
- "Rewrite my draft to be more concise and polite."
- "What are the action items from emails with the project team this week?"
- "Draft a meeting invite from this thread with a short agenda."

Read every draft before sending; Copilot can add details that were never agreed.

## What are the best Copilot prompts for meeting notes?

In Teams meetings with transcription on, ask Copilot for structured notes: decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions. For example: "Summarise this meeting as decisions, action items with owners and deadlines, and unresolved questions."

More examples:

- "What did I miss in the last ten minutes?"
- "List the main arguments for and against the proposal discussed."
- "Draft a follow-up email to attendees with decisions and next steps."
- "Which questions were asked but not answered?"
- "Summarise what [person] said about the budget."

Review notes before sharing, because summaries can merge points or drop important qualifications.

## Is there a Microsoft Copilot course?

Yes. Microsoft Learn offers free training paths for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot, covering how to use Copilot in each app, prompt techniques, and building agents. Partner training and online learning platforms offer additional courses.

A practical learning plan: complete the Microsoft Learn path for the Copilot you use, practise with the Prompt Gallery, then apply it to five real tasks from your work or studies. For Copilot Studio, follow a guided module and build a small agent. Microsoft also runs virtual training events; check Microsoft Learn's events pages for current sessions.

## Is there a Copilot course certificate?

Microsoft Learn modules give badges and trophies for completion, which are not formal certifications. Formal credentials come from Microsoft certification exams and Microsoft Applied Skills, which include assessments related to Copilot and AI solutions.

Check the Microsoft Learn credentials catalogue for current options related to Copilot, such as credentials for building agents or AI solutions. Third-party course certificates show completion but carry less weight with employers than Microsoft credentials or, better still, a demonstrable project such as a working Copilot Studio agent with documented results. Add verified credentials to LinkedIn with their links.

## Is there a Copilot Studio tutorial?

Yes. Microsoft Learn has Copilot Studio tutorials and quickstarts. A good first project is a narrow agent, such as an FAQ assistant for a department, built from real documents and tested with real questions.

A first build:

- Open Copilot Studio and create an agent with a clear description and instructions.
- Add knowledge: a SharePoint site or uploaded policy documents.
- Write starter prompts users can click.
- Test with twenty real questions, including tricky ones, and refine instructions.
- Add one action, such as creating a ticket through a connector.
- Publish to Teams for a small pilot group and review conversations weekly.

Keep scope narrow; reliable small agents earn trust for bigger ones.

# What is Copilot CLI, and why is Copilot not showing in Outlook?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-cli-and-outlook/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot CLI is GitHub Copilot's coding agent for the command line: you run it in a project folder, describe a task, and it reads code, edits files and runs commands with your approval. Separately, if Copilot is not showing in Outlook, the cause is nearly always the licence, the signed-in account, an outdated Outlook version or an admin policy. This page covers the CLI, how to fix Copilot missing from new and classic Outlook, what Copilot does in Outlook including scheduling, what Copilot skills are, and a short tutorial for Copilot's agents.

## What is Copilot CLI?

GitHub Copilot CLI is a terminal application that brings GitHub Copilot's agent to the command line. It can explain a codebase, write and edit files, run shell commands and work with GitHub, asking for permission before it acts.

You install it with npm and start it inside a repository:

```bash
npm install -g @github/copilot
cd my-project
copilot
```

Sign in with a GitHub account that has Copilot access, then type a request such as "find why the login test fails and fix it". It shows the commands and edits it wants to make, and you approve or reject each one. It can connect to extra tools through MCP servers. Treat it like any agent: small tasks, review the diff, run the tests, commit often.

## Does Copilot have a CLI?

Yes. GitHub Copilot has a CLI, the Copilot CLI agent, and Copilot features are also available in terminals inside VS Code and other editors. Microsoft 365 Copilot does not have a general-purpose command line for end users.

Before the current Copilot CLI, GitHub offered an extension for the GitHub CLI, `gh copilot`, that suggested and explained shell commands. The newer Copilot CLI is a full agent that can change files and run multi-step tasks. If you prefer a terminal workflow, other coding agents work similarly: OpenAI's Codex CLI and Anthropic's Claude Code. All of them follow the same safety habits: run them in a project under version control, read every command before approving it, and never let them handle secrets.

## Why is Copilot not showing in Outlook?

Usually because the account you are signed into does not have a Copilot licence, Outlook is out of date, or your organisation has not enabled Copilot. Personal Outlook.com accounts and work accounts also show Copilot differently.

Check in this order:

- **Licence**: your work or school account needs Microsoft 365 Copilot for the full in-Outlook features; Copilot Chat may be all you have.
- **Account**: make sure Outlook is signed in with the licensed account, not a personal one.
- **Version**: update Outlook; new features reach current builds first.
- **Admin policy**: admins can turn Copilot features off or roll them out in stages.
- **Restart**: sign out of Office, sign in again and restart Outlook after a new licence is assigned.

If colleagues with the same licence see it and you do not, ask IT to check your licence assignment.

## Why is Copilot not showing in classic Outlook?

Classic Outlook for Windows shows Copilot only on recent versions of Microsoft 365 Apps. If you are on an older build or a slow update channel, Copilot features may be missing even with a valid licence.

Go to File, then Office Account, then Update Options, and choose Update Now. Check which update channel you are on; organisations on a semi-annual channel get features months later than those on the current channel. Copilot features have generally appeared in the new Outlook and Outlook on the web first. If your organisation allows it, try the new Outlook toggle or Outlook on the web: if Copilot appears there, the problem is your classic Outlook build, not your licence.

## Why is the Copilot icon not showing in Outlook?

If you have the licence and an up-to-date Outlook but no icon, the button is often hidden by the ribbon layout or not pinned. Copilot can also appear in different places depending on whether you are reading or writing an email.

Try these:

- Switch between the simplified and classic ribbon, or use the "more options" menu on the ribbon, where overflow buttons hide.
- Look inside a message: summary options appear at the top of a thread, and drafting options appear in the compose window.
- In the new Outlook and on the web, check the app bar for the Copilot icon and pin it.
- Use "Customise ribbon" to add the Copilot button back if it was removed.

If the icon still does not appear, the feature is probably not enabled for your account yet.

## How does Copilot work in Outlook?

Copilot in Outlook uses a large language model to summarise email threads, draft replies and new emails from a short instruction, and coach you on tone and clarity. With a full licence it can also use context from your other work content.

When you open a long thread, the summary gives the key points, decisions and open questions. To draft, type an instruction such as "politely decline, suggest next Tuesday instead" and adjust the length and tone. Coaching reviews your own draft for tone, reader sentiment and clarity. Copilot works within your permissions, so it only uses mail and files your account can already open. Read every draft before sending: it can state a date, figure or commitment that nobody agreed to.

## How does Copilot simplify scheduling in Outlook?

Copilot can turn an email thread into a meeting: it suggests times based on attendees' availability, drafts the invitation with an agenda drawn from the thread, and saves you switching to the calendar.

From a thread, use the scheduling option, review the proposed attendees and times, then edit the agenda Copilot drafted before sending. It can also help you prepare by summarising the related emails and files before the meeting. Availability depends on everyone's calendars being shared within your organisation, so external guests may still need a manual poll. Exact options vary by Outlook version and licence, and Microsoft adds scheduling features over time, so check what your version shows.

## Is there a tutorial for Copilot in Outlook?

Yes. Microsoft's support and training pages have step-by-step guides, and the fastest way to learn is to use Copilot on your own inbox for a week with one feature a day.

A practical sequence:

- **Day 1**: summarise your longest thread and check the summary against the emails.
- **Day 2**: draft a reply from a one-line instruction, then edit it into your own voice.
- **Day 3**: write a draft yourself and use coaching to improve it.
- **Day 4**: ask Copilot to find what a colleague asked you for last week.
- **Day 5**: schedule a meeting from a thread and review the agenda it proposes.

Write instructions with the goal, the audience and the tone, for example "reply to my professor, formal, confirm the submission date".

## What are Copilot skills?

Skills are packaged capabilities that an AI agent can load when a task needs them: instructions, examples and sometimes scripts for a specific job, such as running your project's tests or following your design system. GitHub Copilot's agents support them.

A skill usually lives as a folder with a short description file that says what it does and when to use it, plus any supporting files. The agent reads only the descriptions up front and loads a skill's full contents when a request matches, which keeps the context small and focused. That is different from tools, which are functions the agent can call, and from MCP servers, which connect it to outside systems. Good skills are narrow, clearly described and tested, like good functions. In Microsoft 365, "skills" is also used loosely for the actions an agent built in Copilot Studio can perform.

## Is there a tutorial for the Copilot agent?

Yes. The quickest start is agent mode in VS Code: open Copilot Chat, switch to agent mode, and give it a small, testable task. On GitHub, you can also assign an issue to Copilot and review the pull request it opens.

A first session in VS Code:

- Open a repository with tests and start Copilot Chat in agent mode.
- Add a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file with build commands and coding rules.
- Ask: "Add input validation to the signup endpoint, write tests, run them and fix failures."
- Review each edit and terminal command before approving.
- Read the final diff and run the tests yourself.

For the GitHub coding agent, write the issue like a ticket for a new teammate: goal, files involved, acceptance criteria. Then review its pull request as carefully as any human's.

# Will Copilot share my data? Where Copilot data goes, and connectors
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-data-privacy/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Whether Copilot shares your data depends on which Copilot you use. Microsoft 365 Copilot for work and school keeps your prompts and responses inside your organisation's Microsoft 365 environment, respects existing permissions, and does not use them to train the foundation models. Consumer Copilot for personal accounts and GitHub Copilot have their own privacy settings. This page explains the Copilot app, what is saved and where, whether OpenAI sees your data, how GitHub Copilot handles code, what connectors are, and which Copilot fits which job, with agent examples.

## What is the Copilot app?

There are two main Copilot apps. The Microsoft 365 Copilot app, formerly the Microsoft 365 or Office app, is the hub for work files, Copilot Chat and agents. The Microsoft Copilot app is the consumer assistant for personal accounts on Windows, the web and phones.

The Microsoft 365 Copilot app opens your recent Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, gives you Copilot Chat grounded in the web and, with a licence, in your work data, and lists agents your organisation provides. The consumer Copilot app is a general assistant like ChatGPT: chat, voice, image generation and web answers. GitHub Copilot, by contrast, lives inside code editors, not in a standalone app. If you are unsure which you have, check the account shown in the corner: a work account means the Microsoft 365 version.

## Will Copilot share my data?

Microsoft 365 Copilot does not share your work data outside your organisation's tenant, and only shows you content you already have permission to open. Consumer Copilot processes your data under Microsoft's privacy statement, with settings that control some uses.

For work accounts, Microsoft's commitments include: prompts, responses and data accessed through Microsoft Graph are not used to train the foundation models; data stays within the Microsoft 365 service boundary; and existing security, compliance and data residency commitments apply. For personal accounts, review Copilot's privacy settings, which include controls over personalisation and whether your conversations may be used to improve models. In both cases, do not paste passwords, identity numbers or other people's private data into a prompt.

## Does Copilot save your data?

Yes, in most cases. Consumer Copilot keeps your conversation history until you delete it. Microsoft 365 Copilot stores interactions within your organisation's environment so they can be governed by retention and compliance policies.

On a personal account, you can delete individual conversations or your whole history from Copilot's settings or your Microsoft privacy dashboard. On a work account, your organisation decides how long Copilot interactions are kept, in the same way it decides for email and Teams chats, and deleting a chat from your view may not delete the organisation's record. Files you upload to Copilot Chat on a work account are typically stored in your OneDrive. Assume what you type into any assistant may be kept and reviewed.

## Where is Copilot data stored?

Microsoft 365 Copilot data is stored in Microsoft's cloud within your organisation's Microsoft 365 tenant, under the same data residency commitments as the rest of your Microsoft 365 data. Consumer Copilot data is stored in Microsoft's cloud under its consumer privacy terms.

For organisations, that means Copilot interaction data sits with your mailbox and other Microsoft 365 content, and is covered by tools such as retention policies, audit logs and eDiscovery. Organisations in the EU also have Microsoft's EU Data Boundary commitments. Generated files and uploads usually land in OneDrive or SharePoint, inside the same tenant. If your college or company has specific data residency needs, the Microsoft Learn page on Copilot privacy and the admin centre are the authoritative sources.

## Does Copilot share data with OpenAI?

Microsoft states that Microsoft 365 Copilot uses OpenAI models hosted in Microsoft's Azure cloud, not OpenAI's own services, so your prompts and work data are not sent to OpenAI and are not used to train OpenAI's models.

The distinction is between the model and the service. OpenAI builds the GPT models; Microsoft runs copies of them in its own data centres through the Azure OpenAI Service and its Copilot infrastructure. OpenAI does not receive the data flowing through Microsoft's deployment. The same separation applies to the consumer Copilot app, which runs on Microsoft's infrastructure under Microsoft's privacy statement. Microsoft has also added models from other providers in some features, and its documentation notes where data handling differs, so check those notes if your organisation enables them.

## Does GitHub Copilot share your data?

GitHub Copilot sends the code context around your cursor and your chat prompts to GitHub's service to generate suggestions. For business and enterprise plans, GitHub states that this data is not used to train its models. Individual plans have settings controlling such use.

On Copilot Business and Enterprise, organisation admins control policies such as which models are allowed and whether suggestions matching public code are blocked. On individual plans, check your GitHub Copilot settings for options about data use for product improvement and choose deliberately. Practical rules for any plan: keep secrets out of source files and prompts, add sensitive files to content exclusions where available, and follow your employer's policy on AI tools. The details per plan are in GitHub's Copilot documentation and trust centre.

## What are Copilot connectors?

Copilot connectors, previously called Microsoft Graph connectors, bring content from systems outside Microsoft 365, such as ServiceNow, Jira, Confluence, Salesforce, file shares or websites, into the index that Microsoft 365 Copilot searches.

Without connectors, Copilot only knows your Microsoft 365 content: mail, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive. With a connector, an employee can ask "what is the status of the onboarding tickets for the new interns?" and get an answer that draws on items in the ticketing system, with links back to them. Microsoft provides prebuilt connectors for many popular services, and developers can build custom ones for internal databases. Admins set them up, so as a user you will see their results appear in Copilot answers and Microsoft Search.

## How do Copilot connectors work?

A connector crawls an external system, converts its items into a standard schema with their text, properties and access permissions, and loads them into the Microsoft Graph index. Copilot then retrieves from that index at question time.

The important detail is access control: each item carries an access list, so a user only sees results for items they could open in the original system. Connectors refresh on a schedule, with full crawls and faster incremental crawls, so recent changes appear after a short delay. This is retrieval-augmented generation at company scale: the same pattern I built in RAG.NextUpgrad, where retrieval quality decides answer quality. Clean titles, good metadata and correct permissions in the source system make connectors far more useful.

## Which Copilot is right for me?

Pick by the work you do. Microsoft 365 Copilot for documents, email and meetings at work, consumer Copilot for personal questions and creativity, GitHub Copilot for writing code, and Copilot Studio for building your own agents.

A quick guide:

- **Student or personal use**: the free consumer Copilot, or Copilot Chat through your college account.
- **Office worker**: Microsoft 365 Copilot if your organisation licenses it; Copilot Chat otherwise.
- **Developer**: GitHub Copilot in your editor and on GitHub.
- **Team that needs a custom assistant**: Copilot Studio or Agent Builder.

Microsoft Learn publishes a comparison of the Copilot offerings that is kept up to date; use it to check current features before buying anything.

## What are some examples of Copilot agents?

Copilot agents include Microsoft's built-in research and data analysis agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot, meeting and project agents in Teams, GitHub Copilot's coding agent, and custom agents organisations build with Copilot Studio.

Examples of custom agents that work well:

- An HR policy agent that answers leave and travel questions from the policy documents, with citations.
- An IT helpdesk agent that answers common questions and creates a ticket when it cannot.
- A sales assistant that summarises an account from CRM records through a connector.
- A college admissions agent that answers questions from the prospectus and fee notices.
- A coding agent that picks up small GitHub issues and opens pull requests for review.

The best agents have a narrow job, trusted knowledge sources, a clear handover to a person, and logs you review every week.

# Copilot vs Claude and Gemini vs Claude: the differences and when to use each
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-gemini-vs-claude/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot is Microsoft's AI assistant, built into Windows, Edge and Microsoft 365, running mostly on OpenAI models and, in some features, Anthropic's Claude. Claude is Anthropic's assistant and model family, used through claude.ai, Claude Code and an API. Gemini is Google's assistant and model family. All three are capable; they differ mainly in integration, strengths and limits. This page explains how Copilot and Claude relate, when to use each, how Claude compares with GitHub Copilot for coding, how Gemini and Claude differ, and how ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini compare in 2026.

## What are Copilot and Claude?

Copilot is Microsoft's brand of AI assistants: the consumer Copilot app, Microsoft 365 Copilot for work, and GitHub Copilot for code. Claude is a family of AI models made by Anthropic, available in the Claude apps, in Claude Code for software development, and through the Claude API.

Copilot is defined by where it lives: inside Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams, Windows and code editors, with access to your work context. Claude is defined by the models: strong at reasoning, long documents, writing and coding, with its own apps and tools. Both are used by students and companies, often side by side. Your choice depends on whether you want an assistant inside the tools you already use, or a strong standalone assistant and coding agent.

## Are Copilot and Claude the same?

No. They are different products from different companies: Copilot from Microsoft, Claude from Anthropic. They do overlap, because Microsoft has added Claude models as options in parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio, and GitHub Copilot lets you choose Claude models.

So "using Claude in Copilot" is possible in some places: for example, picking a Claude model in GitHub Copilot's model picker or in certain Microsoft 365 Copilot features where your organisation enables it. In those cases, Microsoft's product, permissions and data handling apply, with a Claude model doing the generation. Using Claude directly through claude.ai or Claude Code gives you Anthropic's own features, such as Projects, artifacts and Claude Code's agent tooling.

## What is the difference between Copilot and Claude?

The biggest difference is integration versus depth. Copilot is woven into Microsoft's apps and sees your work context; Claude is a standalone assistant and API known for long-context understanding, careful writing and strong coding.

Practical differences:

- **Context**: Microsoft 365 Copilot can search your organisation's mail, files and meetings; Claude works from what you give it or connect through integrations.
- **Coding**: GitHub Copilot plugs into editors; Claude Code is an agent that works across your repository from the terminal or IDE.
- **Documents**: Claude handles very long documents in one go; Copilot is strongest on documents already in Microsoft 365.
- **Data**: each follows its own company's privacy terms and enterprise controls.

Many people use Copilot at work and Claude for deep reading, writing and coding.

## When should I use Copilot vs Claude?

Use Copilot when your task involves Microsoft 365 content, such as summarising a Teams meeting, drafting from your Outlook mail or analysing an Excel sheet, or when your organisation requires it. Use Claude for long documents, careful writing, complex reasoning and serious coding work.

Examples:

- "What did the client ask for in last week's meetings?": Copilot.
- "Turn this Word report into slides": Copilot in PowerPoint.
- "Read these three long PDFs and compare their methods": Claude.
- "Refactor this module and fix the failing tests": Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot's agent.
- "Help me write my project report clearly": either; Claude is often preferred for prose.

For company data, use the tool your organisation approves.

## How does Claude compare to Copilot for coding?

GitHub Copilot is an assistant built into editors and GitHub, with completions, chat, agent mode and a coding agent for issues, and a choice of models including Claude. Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool that reads your repository, edits files and runs commands from the terminal or IDE.

Choose GitHub Copilot if your team lives on GitHub, wants inline completions in VS Code, Visual Studio or JetBrains, and needs enterprise policies. Choose Claude Code for long, multi-step changes across a codebase, where its agent loop and project memory file shine. Many developers use both: Copilot completions while typing, Claude Code for larger tasks. The fair test is one real task in your own repository with each, judged on how much you had to fix.

## Gemini vs Claude: which is better?

Neither is better at everything. Gemini is strong at multimodal input, including video and long audio, very long context and integration with Google's apps; Claude is strong at careful writing, following detailed instructions, long documents and coding.

For students: Gemini fits naturally if you use Google Docs, Gmail, YouTube lectures and Android, and Google has run free plan offers for students. Claude is excellent for reading and writing long reports, explaining code, and agentic coding with Claude Code. Both have free tiers. Run the same three tasks in both, such as summarising a paper, explaining a bug and drafting an email, and keep the one that needs less fixing.

## What is the difference between Gemini and Claude?

Gemini is made by Google and built into Google Search, Workspace and Android; Claude is made by Anthropic and offered through its own apps, Claude Code and its API, as well as through cloud platforms. The models differ in strengths and in how each company approaches safety and features.

Notable differences:

- **Media**: Gemini natively handles video and audio input and generates images and video; Claude works with text, images and documents.
- **Ecosystem**: Gemini connects to Gmail, Drive, Maps and YouTube; Claude connects through integrations and MCP.
- **Coding tools**: Google has Gemini CLI and Antigravity; Anthropic has Claude Code.
- **Safety approach**: Anthropic is known for its Constitutional AI training and safety research; Google DeepMind has its own frameworks.

Both offer free and paid plans and developer APIs.

## When should I use Gemini vs Claude?

Use Gemini when your work involves Google Workspace, YouTube videos, audio or video files, or you want image and video generation. Use Claude for long documents, structured writing, detailed analysis and coding with Claude Code.

A simple split many developers use:

- Summarise a YouTube lecture or analyse a video: Gemini.
- Draft inside Google Docs or Gmail: Gemini.
- Compare long PDFs or write a detailed report: Claude.
- Make multi-file code changes with tests: Claude Code.
- Quick everyday questions: whichever you have open.

For an app you are building, test both APIs on your own data, and design your code so switching models is a configuration change, as I did with multi-provider fallback in RAG.NextUpgrad.

## How does Gemini compare to Claude for long documents?

Both handle long documents well. Gemini offers very large context windows and handles mixed media, such as a PDF with images, or a long recording; Claude is known for careful reading, accurate quoting and following detailed instructions across long inputs.

Practical tips for either: ask for answers with page or section references so you can check them; ask specific questions rather than "summarise everything"; and for very large collections, use retrieval, such as NotebookLM for Gemini or Projects in Claude, instead of pasting everything at once. Long-context models can still miss details in the middle of huge inputs, so verify anything important against the source.

## ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini in 2026: which is best?

In 2026 the three are close in overall quality, and each new model release shifts the lead on specific tasks. The best choice depends on your tasks, your tools and which one gives you better answers in your own tests.

A practical summary: ChatGPT is the broad all-rounder with a large ecosystem; Claude is strong for writing, long documents and coding agents; Gemini is strong for multimodal work and Google integration. Free tiers of all three are enough for most students. Rather than trusting rankings, spend twenty minutes running five of your real tasks in each. Many people end up using two: one for daily work and one for coding or deep analysis.

# How to use Copilot in PowerPoint, why it is missing, and how many Copilots exist
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-in-powerpoint-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To use Copilot in PowerPoint, open PowerPoint with a Microsoft 365 account that includes Copilot, select Copilot on the Home tab, and type what you want, such as a new deck from a prompt or from a Word document, a summary, or speaker notes. I build AI products and pitch them, so this page covers using Copilot in PowerPoint, finding it, fixing it when it is missing, creating decks, timing, prompts, and how many Copilot products and users exist.

## How do you use Copilot in PowerPoint?

Open PowerPoint signed in with an account that has Copilot, select the Copilot button on the Home tab, and type a request in the pane. You can create a presentation, add slides, summarise a deck, organise content or draft speaker notes.

Example prompts: "Create a presentation about our hackathon project for judges, with problem, solution, demo and roadmap slides", or "Summarise this presentation in five bullet points". To build from a document, ask Copilot to create a presentation from a file and reference it, such as a Word document or PDF stored in OneDrive. After Copilot generates slides, edit the text, replace generic images, and check every fact, because the first draft is a starting point, not a finished deck.

## Where is Copilot in PowerPoint?

The Copilot button sits on the Home tab of the ribbon, usually at the right end, in PowerPoint for Windows, Mac and the web. Selecting it opens the Copilot pane on the right side of the window.

In newer versions, Copilot can also appear as an icon on the slide or in a new blank presentation, offering to create a deck. On mobile apps, look for the Copilot icon in the toolbar. If your ribbon is customised or collapsed, the button may be hidden, so reset the ribbon or expand it. If you still cannot see it, your account may not have Copilot access or your app may need an update, as explained in the next answer.

## Why is Copilot not showing in PowerPoint?

The usual causes are an account without a Copilot licence or plan, signing in with the wrong account, an outdated version of Microsoft 365, connected experiences turned off in privacy settings, or an administrator disabling Copilot.

Fixes: confirm your plan includes Copilot, and in work accounts ask your admin to assign a licence; sign out and sign in with the licensed account; update Office through File, Account, Update Options; enable connected experiences in File, Options, Trust Center, Privacy Options; and restart PowerPoint. Some features need the file saved in OneDrive or SharePoint. After a new licence is assigned, it can take some time to appear, so restart again later if needed.

## Can Copilot create a PowerPoint presentation?

Yes. Copilot can create a full draft presentation from a prompt or from a document, generating a title slide, section slides, bullet text, images and speaker notes, often using your organisation's template if one is set.

Quality depends on your input. A detailed prompt with audience, purpose, key points and slide count works better than a single topic word. Creating from a well-structured Word document usually gives the most accurate deck, because Copilot follows the document's headings and content. Expect to rewrite headlines, cut filler, fix image choices and verify facts. Copilot is strongest for first drafts and restructuring, while storytelling, data accuracy and final design still need your judgement.

## How long does Copilot take to create a PowerPoint?

Usually under a minute for a draft deck of several slides, depending on the length of your prompt or source document, the number of slides and service load. Long documents and many slides take longer.

The real time cost is editing: plan 15 to 60 minutes to turn a generated draft into a deck you would present, checking facts, tightening wording, adjusting layouts and adding your own data and visuals. If generation stalls, check your connection, try a shorter prompt or smaller document, and retry later, since busy periods can slow responses. For important presentations, generate early, so you have time to rehearse after editing.

## How does Copilot assist in PowerPoint presentations?

Copilot drafts new decks, adds slides on a topic, summarises long presentations, answers questions about a deck's content, reorganises slides into sections, rewrites text to be shorter or clearer, generates images, and writes speaker notes.

It is especially useful for turning documents into slides, creating summaries for colleagues who missed a meeting, and preparing notes for rehearsal. It can also help translate or adapt a deck for a different audience. It is weaker at precise data visualisation, complex custom layouts and judgement about what matters most to your audience. Treat it as a fast assistant: you remain the editor responsible for accuracy, story and design consistency.

## What is a good Copilot PowerPoint tutorial?

Practise this five-step workflow: write a clear prompt, generate a draft, review the outline, refine with follow-up prompts, then edit manually. Microsoft's support pages include official step-by-step guides with screenshots for each feature.

A sample session: prompt "Create a 10-slide presentation for first-year students on how to start with AI projects, friendly tone, include a roadmap slide"; then ask "Make slide 3 shorter", "Add a slide comparing Python and JavaScript for beginners", and "Write speaker notes for every slide". Finally, apply your template with Designer, replace stock images with real screenshots, and rehearse with Speaker Coach. Save useful prompts so you can reuse them for future decks.

## How many Copilot products are there?

Microsoft uses the Copilot name across dozens of products, so there is no single fixed count. Major ones include Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Copilot Studio, Security Copilot, Copilot in Windows and Edge, and Copilots in Dynamics 365 and Power Platform.

They share branding but differ in purpose, plans and data access: Microsoft Copilot is the consumer assistant; Microsoft 365 Copilot works inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams with your work data; GitHub Copilot helps developers write code; Copilot Studio lets organisations build custom agents; and Security Copilot assists security teams. When reading about Copilot, check which product is meant, since features and availability differ widely between them.

## How many Copilot users are there?

Microsoft reported in 2025 that its family of Copilot apps had passed 100 million monthly active users, and GitHub Copilot had passed 20 million all-time users. Figures change quickly, so check Microsoft's latest earnings materials.

These totals combine many products and include both consumer and business use, so they do not tell you how many people use Copilot in PowerPoint specifically. Adoption inside organisations varies: some deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot to all staff, others to small pilot groups. For decisions about your own team, measure usage and time saved in your pilot, since published totals say little about whether the tool fits your workflows.

## How many Copilot uses do you get in a day?

It depends on your plan, and limits change over time. Free Microsoft Copilot has usage limits during busy periods, consumer Microsoft 365 plans include a monthly allowance of AI credits for Copilot in Office apps, and business licences follow fair-use limits.

If you hit a limit, you will see a message in the Copilot pane; wait for the reset or upgrade your plan. Heavy tasks, such as creating whole presentations or generating images, may use more of your allowance than simple questions. For accurate current limits, check your account page and Microsoft's plan comparison, since Microsoft has revised its consumer and business Copilot plans several times. Plan important work so you are not blocked near deadlines.

# How to use Copilot in Word, why it is missing, and writing copilot-instructions.md files
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-in-word-and-instructions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To use Copilot in Word, open a document in a Word version with Copilot enabled and select the Copilot icon on the Home ribbon or in the margin; then ask it to draft, rewrite, summarise or answer questions about the document. It needs a Microsoft 365 plan that includes Copilot and the right account sign-in. Developers searching "Copilot instructions" mean something else: instruction files that guide GitHub Copilot in code repositories. I use both, so this page covers Copilot in Word and how to write instruction files for coding assistants.

## How do I use Copilot in Word?

Open Word, start a new document or open an existing one, and select Copilot. For a new document, describe what you want, such as "Draft a two-page project proposal for a campus recycling app", optionally referencing files. For existing text, select it and ask Copilot to rewrite, shorten or change tone.

Useful actions:

- Draft from a prompt or from referenced files.
- Rewrite selected paragraphs in a different tone.
- Summarise a long document into key points.
- Ask questions about the document, such as deadlines mentioned.
- Convert text into a table.

Always review drafts for accuracy, since Copilot can invent details.

## How does Copilot work in Word?

Copilot in Word sends your prompt, plus relevant document content and, with permission, content from referenced files in your Microsoft 365 account, to large language models running in Microsoft's cloud, then inserts or displays the generated text for you to keep, edit or discard.

For organisations, Microsoft 365 Copilot respects existing permissions: it only uses files the signed-in user can access, and enterprise data protections apply under work accounts. Copilot does not automatically change your document; you choose what to insert. Version history lets you restore previous text if an edit goes wrong. For academic work, check your institution's rules on AI assistance and disclose its use where required.

## Can I use Copilot in Word?

You can if you have a Microsoft 365 plan that includes Copilot, either a personal or family subscription where Copilot is offered, or a work or school account with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, and you use a supported version of Word.

Availability varies by plan, region and account type, and features differ between consumer and business versions. Students should check whether their institution's licence includes Copilot. Without access, you can still use the free Copilot app or other AI assistants to draft text, then paste it into Word, though without direct document integration.

## Where do I find Copilot in Word?

In supported versions, the Copilot button appears on the Home tab of the ribbon, and a Copilot icon may appear in the margin next to your text or when you start a new document. Selecting text often shows a Copilot option for rewriting.

If you open Word for the web, Copilot appears in similar places. On mobile versions, availability is more limited. If you see no Copilot button at all, the cause is usually licensing, the wrong signed-in account, an outdated Word version, or settings, covered in the next section.

## Why is Copilot not showing in Word?

Common reasons: your account lacks a Copilot-enabled plan or licence, Word is signed in with a different account, Word is outdated or on a channel without Copilot yet, connected experiences are disabled in privacy settings, or your organisation's administrator has turned Copilot off.

Fixes:

- Check your licence in your Microsoft account or with your IT admin.
- Sign out and back in with the licensed account.
- Update Word through File, Account, Update Options.
- Enable connected experiences in privacy settings.
- Restart Word and refresh your licence.
- Save files to OneDrive or SharePoint where required.

## What does Copilot in Word focus on?

Copilot in Word focuses on writing tasks: drafting new content, rewriting and editing for tone and length, summarising documents, answering questions about content, and turning text into structured formats such as tables, using your organisation's files as context when permitted.

It is strongest for first drafts, reworking existing text and digesting long documents. It is weaker at precise facts not in your files, specialised formatting and nuanced arguments, where your judgement matters. Treat it as a fast assistant: you remain responsible for accuracy, citations and final quality, especially in academic and professional documents.

## Where do I put copilot-instructions.md?

For GitHub Copilot in a repository, create the file `.github/copilot-instructions.md` at the repository root. Copilot Chat and agent features in supported editors and on GitHub automatically include its contents as context for requests in that repository.

VS Code also supports additional instruction files, such as `.instructions.md` files that apply to specific file patterns, and settings for personal instructions. Keep the main file concise: describe the stack, coding conventions, testing commands and things to avoid. Commit it to the repository so the whole team shares the same guidance.

## What is an example of Copilot instructions?

A good instructions file is short and specific about how your project works and what good code looks like.

```markdown
# Project instructions
- Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind, PostgreSQL via Prisma.
- Use server components by default; client components only for interactivity.
- Validate all API input with Zod; never trust client data.
- Write tests with Vitest for new utilities; run `npm test` before finishing.
- Never commit secrets; read config from environment variables.
```

Add project-specific rules as you notice repeated mistakes, and remove outdated ones. Keep the file under a page or two; very long instruction files dilute the important rules and cost context on every request.

## What is an example of Copilot agent instructions?

Agent instructions add guidance on how to work, not just how code should look: how to plan, which commands to run, how to verify changes, and what needs approval. Many tools also read shared files such as AGENTS.md.

Example rules:

- Before changing code, read related files and summarise the plan.
- Make small, focused changes; one feature per pull request.
- Run lint and tests after edits and fix failures before finishing.
- Do not modify database migrations or CI configuration without asking.
- Explain any new dependency and why it is needed.

Clear agent rules reduce wasted iterations and risky changes.

## Why does Claude ignore my instructions, and how does CLAUDE.md help?

AI assistants, including Claude, may ignore instructions that are buried in long conversations, contradictory, vague, or stated once early in a session. Over long sessions, earlier instructions compete with newer context. CLAUDE.md files give Claude Code persistent project instructions it loads at the start of each session.

To make instructions stick: keep CLAUDE.md concise and specific, explain the reason behind important rules, remove contradictions, put critical rules near the top, and update the file when you notice repeated mistakes. Start fresh sessions for new tasks rather than continuing very long ones. The same principles apply to copilot-instructions.md and other assistants' instruction files.

# Fix 'language model unavailable' in VS Code Copilot, and which Copilot model is best
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-language-model-unavailable/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The "language model unavailable" message in VS Code's GitHub Copilot means the extension cannot use the selected AI model right now, usually because of a sign-in or subscription problem, an outdated VS Code or Copilot Chat extension, network or proxy blocking, an organisation policy, an exhausted quota, or a GitHub service incident. Updating, re-signing in and switching models fixes most cases. I use AI coding assistants daily, so this page explains each cause, step-by-step fixes, and which Copilot models suit coding and documentation.

## What does "language model unavailable" mean in VS Copilot?

It means Copilot in VS Code tried to send your request to a language model and could not, because the model is not accessible to your account, client or network at that moment. The editor still works; Copilot's AI features do not respond until the issue is resolved.

The message is generic, covering several underlying problems: authentication failures, unsupported client versions, models not enabled for your plan or organisation, rate limits, connectivity issues and outages. The Copilot output logs in VS Code usually reveal the specific reason, which tells you which fix to apply rather than trying everything blindly.

## Why is the Copilot language model unavailable in VS Code?

The most common causes are an outdated VS Code or Copilot extension, an expired sign-in, an inactive Copilot subscription or trial, network restrictions such as corporate proxies or firewalls, and organisation policies that disable certain models.

Other causes include reaching your plan's premium request limit for a particular model, selecting a model that is in preview or not available in your plan, and temporary GitHub incidents. If Copilot worked yesterday and fails today without changes on your side, check GitHub's status page first. If it fails only on one network, suspect the proxy or firewall. College and office networks sometimes block the domains Copilot uses, so testing on a mobile hotspot is a quick way to confirm a network cause.

## How do I read the "language model unavailable" error details?

Open VS Code's Output panel, choose "GitHub Copilot Chat" or "GitHub Copilot" from the dropdown, and look for error lines around the time of the failure. Messages often mention authentication, quota, policy, network or model errors with status codes.

Status codes help: 401 or 403 suggest authentication or policy problems; 429 indicates rate limits; 5xx codes point to service issues; and connection or certificate errors suggest network or proxy problems. Copy relevant log lines, without tokens, when asking for help in GitHub Community discussions or reporting issues, since they speed up diagnosis.

## Why does GitHub Copilot say the language model is unavailable?

From GitHub's side, the model may be unavailable because your account lacks an active Copilot plan, your organisation has not enabled that model, the model requires a higher plan, or your premium requests for the period are used up.

Check your Copilot settings on github.com: subscription status, which models are enabled, and usage. Students and teachers may have free access through GitHub Education, which must be verified and renewed. Organisation members should ask administrators whether policies allow the model. Switching to a model included in your plan often restores Copilot immediately. If you recently changed GitHub accounts, make sure VS Code is signed in with the account that actually holds the Copilot licence.

## Why is the Copilot Chat language model unavailable?

Copilot Chat often fails when the Copilot Chat extension version does not match your VS Code version, since the extension depends on recent VS Code APIs. Updating VS Code and both Copilot extensions to their latest versions resolves many chat failures.

Also check that chat is enabled in your settings and organisation policy, that you are signed in with the correct GitHub account in VS Code's accounts menu, and that conflicting extensions are not interfering. Reloading the window with the "Developer: Reload Window" command clears transient extension problems. Insiders builds sometimes need the pre-release Copilot Chat extension.

## Why is a Copilot language model not available in the model picker?

A model may be missing or greyed out because your plan does not include it, your organisation disabled it, it is not supported in your client version, or it was retired or renamed. Model availability changes as GitHub adds and removes models.

Update VS Code and extensions to see current models, check GitHub's documentation listing supported models by plan and client, and ask administrators about policies. If a preferred model disappears, choose a comparable alternative. Some models require opting in through settings on github.com before they appear in the editor. After enabling one, reload VS Code so the model list refreshes.

## How do I fix "Copilot language model unavailable"?

Work through these steps in order, testing after each:

- Check GitHub Status for Copilot incidents.
- Update VS Code and the GitHub Copilot and Copilot Chat extensions.
- Sign out of GitHub in VS Code and sign back in.
- Confirm your Copilot subscription and model settings on github.com.
- Select a different model in the chat model picker.
- Reload the VS Code window.
- Check proxy settings, certificates and firewall rules on your network.
- Read the Copilot output logs for specific errors.

If nothing works, try another network or a fresh VS Code profile to isolate configuration problems, then contact GitHub Support with logs.

## Which Copilot model is best?

There is no single best model; GitHub Copilot offers models from several providers, such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, each with strengths. The best choice depends on the task, your plan's included models and premium request budget.

General guidance: use faster, included models for quick completions and simple questions; use stronger reasoning models for complex refactoring, debugging and agent mode tasks; and compare models on your own codebase for a week. Model line-ups change frequently, so check GitHub's model documentation and changelog for current options and their premium request costs.

## Which Copilot model is best for coding?

For complex coding and agent mode, developers often prefer the strongest available reasoning and coding models, with Claude Sonnet-class and recent GPT models popular choices; for quick edits and completions, faster models work well and save premium requests.

Test with real tasks: implement a feature, fix a bug with a failing test, and refactor a module, then compare correctness, diff quality and how much you had to fix. Results vary by language and framework. Provide good context with instruction files and open relevant files, which improves any model's output more than switching models does.

## Which Copilot model is best for documentation?

For documentation, such as READMEs, docstrings, API docs and explanations, fast models that write clearly are usually enough, and reasoning-heavy models add little. For documenting complex architecture, a stronger model that reads more context helps.

Give clear instructions: audience, format, tone and examples of good documentation from your project. Ask Copilot to document one module at a time and to flag anything it is unsure about. Always review generated documentation for accuracy, since models can describe behaviour the code does not actually have, which is worse than no documentation.
