# Copilot Notebooks and Copilot premium requests, explained
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-notebooks-premium-requests/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot Notebooks are workspaces in Microsoft 365 Copilot where you gather the files, pages, meeting notes and links for one project, so Copilot answers questions and drafts content using that collection as its main source. They are also arriving in OneNote. "Copilot premium" is a looser phrase: it can mean Microsoft's higher consumer plans with more Copilot capability, or the premium requests that GitHub Copilot counts when you use its most capable models. This page explains notebooks, when to use them, and what premium plans and premium requests include, cost you in usage, and when they reset.

## What are Copilot Notebooks?

Copilot Notebooks are project spaces in Microsoft 365 Copilot. You add references, such as Word files, PDFs, Copilot Pages, meeting notes and links, and Copilot uses that set as context for every question and draft in the notebook.

Think of a notebook as a focused folder with a built-in assistant. Instead of searching all your mail and files, Copilot prioritises the material you chose, which makes answers more relevant and easier to check. Notebooks keep your Copilot responses and notes together, so you can come back to a project days later without rebuilding the context. They are similar in spirit to Google's NotebookLM, but they live inside Microsoft 365 and follow your organisation's permissions and compliance settings.

## How do Copilot Notebooks work?

You create a notebook, add references, then chat with Copilot inside it. Copilot retrieves relevant passages from those references, answers with citations to them, and can save useful responses as pages in the notebook.

Under the hood this is retrieval-augmented generation scoped to a chosen set of documents, the same principle I used in the OCR & Speech Workspace, where chat is limited to one document and answers cite page numbers. Scoping improves accuracy because Copilot has fewer irrelevant files to confuse it. References stay where they are stored, in OneDrive or SharePoint, and permissions still apply, so sharing a notebook does not give others access to files they could not already open. Keep references current: if you update a file, check that the notebook points to the right version.

## When should I use Copilot Notebooks?

Use a notebook when you work on the same body of material over days or weeks and keep asking questions about it: a course module, a research project, a client engagement, a product launch or exam revision.

Good fits:

- A semester course: lecture slides, notes and past papers in one notebook for revision questions.
- A thesis or report: sources, drafts and supervisor feedback together.
- A client project: proposal, meeting notes and requirements, so drafts stay consistent.
- Interview preparation: job description, company documents and your notes.

For a one-off question, plain Copilot Chat is quicker. For anything where you need answers from exactly your chosen files, and to see where each answer came from, a notebook is the better tool.

## What are Copilot Notebooks in OneNote?

Microsoft has been bringing Copilot Notebooks into OneNote, so the AI project space sits alongside your handwritten and typed notes. You can gather pages and files for a topic and ask Copilot questions grounded in them.

This suits students who already keep class notes in OneNote: your notes become part of the material Copilot can use when you ask for a summary, a list of key definitions or practice questions. It also keeps the familiar OneNote structure of sections and pages. Availability depends on your Microsoft 365 plan, licence and OneNote version, and features roll out in stages, so update OneNote and check whether the Copilot notebook option appears for your account.

## How do Copilot Notebooks work in OneNote?

In OneNote, you create or open a Copilot notebook, add the pages and files you want it to use, and ask Copilot questions in the Copilot pane. Answers draw on that material and point back to the pages they used.

A practical study workflow: create a notebook for one subject, add your lecture notes and the syllabus, then ask for a one-page summary per unit, a list of terms with definitions, and ten practice questions. Check every answer against your notes, because summaries can drop a condition or merge two ideas. Use Copilot to find gaps, for example "which topics in the syllabus have no notes yet?". Keep personal or sensitive notes out of shared notebooks, since anyone with access can query them.

## What is Copilot premium?

"Copilot premium" has no single meaning. For Microsoft's consumer Copilot, it refers to the paid plans that include more Copilot capability across apps. For GitHub Copilot, it usually refers to premium requests, the metered allowance for the most capable models and features.

On the Microsoft side, the free Copilot app covers everyday chat, while paid Microsoft 365 consumer plans add Copilot inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook with higher limits; Microsoft has renamed and restructured these plans more than once. On the GitHub side, every paid Copilot plan includes a monthly number of premium requests, and you can pay for more. Before buying anything, confirm which product the page you are reading is about, because the names overlap.

## What does Copilot premium include?

On Microsoft's paid consumer plans, it typically includes Copilot in the Microsoft 365 desktop and web apps, higher usage limits, priority access to newer features and image creation. On GitHub, premium requests unlock the most capable models, agent mode and the coding agent at higher volumes.

Because both sides change often, rely on the current plan pages rather than lists in older articles. A sensible check before paying: list the three tasks you would use it for each week, try them on the free tier first, and see whether limits or missing features actually block you. Students often find that the free consumer Copilot, Copilot Chat through a college account, and GitHub Copilot's free tier or student benefits cover most needs.

## What is the difference between Copilot basic and premium?

The basic, free tiers give general chat and limited use of advanced features. Premium tiers add Copilot inside the Office apps or more powerful coding features, higher limits and earlier access to new models and tools.

In GitHub Copilot, the practical difference is which models and features you can use and how often: base models are included for routine completions and chat, while premium models and agent features draw on the premium request allowance. In Microsoft's consumer Copilot, the difference is mainly whether Copilot works inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook and how much you can use it. Neither tier changes the need to check outputs; premium means more capability and volume, not guaranteed accuracy.

## What are Copilot premium requests?

Premium requests are GitHub Copilot's unit for metering use of its more capable models and features. Each chat message, agent step or coding agent session that uses a premium model consumes one or more requests from your monthly allowance.

Models have multipliers: a lightweight model may count as a fraction of a request or be free on paid plans, while the most capable models count as several requests per message. Your plan includes a monthly allowance, and organisations can set a budget for paid overage. You can see your usage in your GitHub settings, and in the editor the model picker shows which models are premium. To stretch the allowance, use an included model for routine edits and save premium models for hard debugging and design.

## When do Copilot premium requests reset?

GitHub Copilot's premium request allowance resets at the start of each monthly billing cycle; GitHub's documentation states the exact reset time. Unused requests do not roll over.

If you run out before the reset, Copilot falls back to included models, or you can enable paid overage if your plan or organisation allows it. Check the usage page in your GitHub settings to see how many you have used and when the counter resets. For organisations, admins can view usage per user and set spending limits. Because GitHub has adjusted allowances and multipliers since premium requests were introduced, check the current billing documentation instead of numbers quoted in forums.

# Copilot vs Copilot Pro, Copilot+ laptops, and can Copilot make videos?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-pro-laptops-and-video/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Free Microsoft Copilot gives you chat, web answers with citations, voice and image creation. Microsoft's paid consumer plans, which started as Copilot Pro and have since been folded into Microsoft 365 consumer subscriptions, add Copilot inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, higher limits and earlier access to new features. Copilot does not edit videos itself, though Microsoft offers AI video tools elsewhere. On laptops, "Copilot" means the Copilot key and app, and Copilot+ PCs are Windows laptops with a fast neural processing unit for on-device AI. This page covers each point and how to choose a laptop.

## Copilot vs Copilot Pro: what is the difference?

Free Copilot is the general assistant on the web, in Windows and on phones. Copilot Pro was Microsoft's paid consumer upgrade, adding Copilot in the Microsoft 365 apps, priority access at busy times and higher limits; Microsoft has since moved these benefits into its Microsoft 365 consumer plans.

In practice, the free version is enough for questions, writing help, summaries and images. The paid tier matters if you want Copilot working inside your Word documents, Excel sheets, PowerPoint decks and Outlook mail with a personal account, or you hit usage limits often. Work and school accounts are different again: they use Microsoft 365 Copilot or Copilot Chat under the organisation's licence. Because Microsoft renames and rebundles consumer plans, check the current plan comparison before buying.

## Which Copilot Pro features are free?

Many former Pro-only features are now in free Copilot: access to strong models, web-grounded answers, voice conversations, image creation within limits, and vision features that understand images you share.

What generally remains paid on consumer plans is Copilot inside the Microsoft 365 desktop and web apps with a personal account, higher usage limits for heavy features, and early access to experiments. Free use also has daily limits on things like image creation and the most advanced modes. If you are a student with a college Microsoft 365 account, check whether your institution provides Copilot Chat or Microsoft 365 Copilot, which may give you more than any consumer plan. Microsoft's plan pages list the current split.

## Is there a tutorial for Copilot Pro?

Yes. Microsoft's support pages have guides for Copilot in each Microsoft 365 app, and the quickest way to learn is to try one task a day in the app you already use.

A five-day plan:

- **Word**: turn rough notes into a structured report, then ask for a shorter version for a different reader.
- **PowerPoint**: create a draft deck from that Word file and fix the design yourself.
- **Excel**: format a dataset as a table and ask three specific questions about it.
- **Outlook**: summarise a long thread and draft a reply from a one-line instruction.
- **Copilot app**: plan a week of study with deadlines, then ask it to make a checklist.

Write prompts with the goal, the audience, the source material and the format you want.

## Does Copilot make videos?

Not in the chat itself. Copilot creates text and images, but it does not edit or render videos. Microsoft offers AI video generation separately, and its Clipchamp editor is where you assemble a finished video.

Copilot is still useful for video work: it can write a script, a shot list, captions and a title and description, and generate images for scenes or thumbnails. You then record and edit in Clipchamp, which is built into Windows, or another editor. For explainer videos, a script from Copilot plus your own voice-over and screen recording usually beats generated footage. Check what is current, because Microsoft has been adding video features to its creative tools.

## Can Copilot create AI videos?

Microsoft has offered AI video generation through separate tools rather than the main Copilot chat, including a video creator in the Bing mobile app built on OpenAI's Sora model. Availability depends on region and the tool's current status.

Generated clips are short and best used as B-roll or illustrations, not as a full video. Write a specific prompt: subject, setting, camera movement, lighting and style, for example "slow aerial shot over green rice fields at sunrise, cinematic". Generate several versions and pick the best. Then edit the clips together with narration and text in Clipchamp. Label AI-generated footage when you publish it, and never generate videos of real people without their consent.

## Can Copilot make videos from photos?

Not directly in Copilot chat. To turn photos into a video, use Clipchamp or the Photos app's video tools on Windows, which assemble images with transitions, music and text, or ask Copilot to write an `ffmpeg` command that builds a slideshow.

In Clipchamp, import your photos, drag them onto the timeline, set how long each shows, add transitions, music and captions, then export. If you want the photos to move, for example a slow zoom or pan, use Clipchamp's motion effects. For command-line users, ask Copilot "write an ffmpeg command that turns img001.jpg to img030.jpg into a video showing each image for three seconds", run it, and check the result. Image-to-video AI models can animate a single photo, but they live in separate tools.

## Can Copilot watch or work with videos?

Copilot in Microsoft Edge can summarise and answer questions about some online videos, typically by using their transcripts. It does not reliably analyse the visual content of every frame of a long video.

For YouTube videos with captions, open the video in Edge, open Copilot in the sidebar and ask for a summary or key points with timestamps. For your own recordings, generate a transcript first, for example with Word's Transcribe or Teams for meetings, then give the transcript to Copilot. For visual questions, take screenshots of the moments that matter and share those as images. Copilot cannot record video for you; for screen recordings use the Windows Snipping Tool or Clipchamp.

## What is Copilot in a laptop?

On a Windows laptop, Copilot is the built-in AI assistant you open from the taskbar or the Copilot key on newer keyboards. On Copilot+ PCs, extra AI features run on the laptop's own neural processing unit instead of the cloud.

Every recent Windows 11 laptop can run the Copilot app, which uses Microsoft's cloud models. Copilot+ PCs add on-device features, such as improved Windows Studio camera effects, live captions with translation, image tools in Photos and Paint, and search that understands natural language, with availability varying by region. The Copilot key simply launches the assistant. If you mainly use Copilot for chat and writing, any decent Windows laptop works; the Copilot+ label matters for the on-device features.

## What is the best Copilot+ laptop?

The best Copilot+ laptop is the one that fits your work, budget and comfort. Copilot+ models come from Microsoft Surface, Dell, HP, Lenovo, ASUS, Acer and Samsung, with Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Intel Core Ultra or AMD Ryzen AI processors.

Choose by use:

- **Long battery life and light weight**: Snapdragon-based models are strong, but check that the apps you need run well on Arm.
- **Development and compatibility**: Intel or AMD models run every Windows app natively, including older tools.
- **Light gaming or GPU work**: look for models with a discrete graphics card.

Read reviews that test battery life, heat and keyboard quality, and try the keyboard and screen in a shop if you can.

## What should I look for in a Copilot AI laptop?

Look for a Copilot+ certified processor with a capable neural processing unit, at least 16 GB of RAM, a fast SSD of 512 GB or more if you code or edit media, a good screen and long battery life.

Microsoft's Copilot+ PC requirements include an NPU of at least 40 trillion operations per second, 16 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage, so certified laptops meet a baseline. For students in computer science, 16 GB is the practical minimum and 32 GB is comfortable for Docker, virtual machines and local AI models. The NPU helps Windows AI features but does not replace a GPU for training models; for serious machine learning work, use cloud GPUs or Google Colab. Check ports, warranty and service centres near you before buying.

# Where is the Copilot Prompt Gallery? Prompt length, system prompts and prompt engineers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-prompt-gallery-and-prompt-length/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Copilot Prompt Gallery is Microsoft's collection of ready-made prompts for Microsoft 365 Copilot, organised by app, task and role, which you can open from the Copilot app or on the web, try and save. This page explains where to find it and why prompting matters so much for Copilot, then answers practical questions about length: how long a prompt, a system prompt, Claude's own system prompt and a creative writing prompt should be. It ends with how long it takes to learn prompt engineering and what prompt engineers do, including in India.

## Where is the Copilot Prompt Gallery?

The Copilot Prompt Gallery is available in the Microsoft 365 Copilot app and on the web, and you can also open it from Copilot inside apps such as Word, Teams and Outlook, often through a "view prompts" option. It was previously called Copilot Lab.

In the gallery you can filter prompts by app, such as Excel or Teams, by task, such as summarise or create, and by role. You can save your favourite prompts and, in many organisations, share prompts with colleagues. Using it is a fast way to learn what Copilot can do: try a prompt as written, then adapt it with your own files and goals. Availability depends on your licence and organisation settings.

## Why is prompt engineering important for Copilot?

Copilot answers from your organisation's content, so a good prompt tells it what you want, which content to use and what form the answer should take. Vague prompts make Copilot search broadly and guess.

Microsoft's guidance on Copilot prompts centres on four elements: the goal, the context, the source to use, and your expectations for the answer. For example, "Summarise the decisions from yesterday's project sync meeting and the follow-up email from the client, as five bullet points with owners" works far better than "what happened yesterday?". Referencing specific files, people or meetings directly improves grounding. Good prompts also reduce errors, because Copilot has less room to fill gaps with assumptions.

## How long should a prompt be?

As long as needed to be clear, and no longer. A simple question can be one line; a complex task may need a few paragraphs with context, constraints, examples and the output format. Clarity matters more than length.

Rules of thumb:

- Include the goal, audience, constraints and format.
- Add the material to work on, such as a document or data, which can be long.
- Use examples when format matters.
- Remove repeated or contradictory instructions.
- Put the most important instruction clearly, not buried in the middle.

Models accept very long inputs, but a long prompt full of loosely related text can dilute what matters. If a prompt keeps growing, split the task into steps.

## How long is too long for a system prompt?

There is no fixed limit, since modern models accept long system prompts, but a system prompt is too long when instructions start contradicting each other, important rules get lost among details, or performance on your test cases stops improving as you add more.

Signs to trim: the model ignores some rules, behaviour changes unpredictably when you add instructions, or most lines cover rare edge cases. Better structure helps: clear sections for role, rules, tools and output format; examples only where they change behaviour; and moving reference material into retrieval or attached documents rather than the system prompt. Measure with an evaluation set when you add or remove instructions, rather than guessing.

## How long is Claude's system prompt?

Anthropic publishes the system prompts used in its Claude apps in its documentation's release notes. They are long, detailed documents covering behaviour, formatting, tool use and safety, and they change as new models and features are released.

These published prompts apply to Claude's own apps, such as claude.ai and the mobile apps, not to the Claude API, where developers write their own system prompts. Reading them is a useful lesson in how a production assistant is specified: clear sections, explicit guidance on edge cases, and descriptions of available tools. They also explain why the same model can behave somewhat differently in the app and through the API.

## How long is a writing prompt?

A creative writing prompt is usually short, a sentence or two, sometimes a single line or image, designed to spark ideas rather than specify the piece. Prompts for school or exams may add requirements such as word count, form or audience.

When you give a writing task to an AI model, a longer brief usually works better than a short spark: describe the genre, audience, tone, length, point of view and anything to avoid, and include an example of the style you like. For your own practice, short prompts are best, because they leave room for your ideas. If you are learning to write, use AI for feedback on your drafts rather than for producing the piece.

## How long is a prompt engineering course?

Short courses take one to a few hours, such as free courses on prompting for developers. Broader courses that include building applications with LLMs, retrieval and evaluation take several weeks part-time.

Course length matters less than practice. A practical path: a few hours on an official prompting guide and a short course, then two to four weeks building one small application, such as a document Q&A bot or an extraction tool, with a test set to measure improvements. Look for recently updated courses, because techniques change as models improve, and prefer ones that include structured outputs and evaluation, not just prompt templates.

## How long does it take to master prompt engineering?

The basics take days. Being genuinely skilled, able to design prompts for real applications, measure them, and handle edge cases, takes months of building and evaluating, and it keeps evolving as models change.

What mastery looks like in practice: you can write clear specifications, choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning, design structured outputs, write tool descriptions for agents, build evaluation sets, and diagnose failures from logs. Those skills come from shipping projects. Keep a log of prompts, results and changes for each project; reviewing what worked and why builds judgement faster than reading prompt lists.

## What are prompt engineers?

Prompt engineers design, test and refine the instructions, examples and context that make AI models produce reliable results for specific tasks, often inside products. Today the work is usually part of broader roles such as AI engineer, GenAI developer or conversation designer.

Day to day, they write system prompts and tool descriptions, build test sets, run evaluations, analyse failures, and collaborate with domain experts and engineers. In companies building AI products, the skill matters, but standalone "prompt engineer" titles are less common than at first, because the work blends into AI engineering. Students should pair prompting skills with programming, retrieval and evaluation to be employable.

## How many prompt engineers are there in India?

There is no reliable public count, because prompt engineering is rarely a separate job title and is usually part of roles such as AI engineer, data scientist or GenAI developer. Job platforms show many listings mentioning prompt engineering as a skill.

What is clear is that demand for people who can build with generative AI is growing in India across startups, IT services firms and product companies. For students, the useful question is not how many prompt engineers exist, but which skills employers ask for: Python, LLM APIs, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation, deployment and communication. Build a project that demonstrates those, and you will match far more roles than a "prompt engineer" title alone.

# Copilot vs GitHub Copilot: the difference, model updates and limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-vs-github-copilot/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot share a name but do different jobs. Microsoft Copilot is a general AI assistant for questions, writing and Office work; GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant inside VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs and GitHub itself. This page explains the difference, how new models such as Anthropic's Claude Fable reach Copilot, why Copilot is sometimes wrong, what to do when it seems broken, its usage limits and history, where Copilot Studio agents live, and how GitHub Copilot compares with Cursor, Windsurf and Antigravity.

## Copilot vs GitHub Copilot: what is the difference?

Microsoft Copilot is a general assistant for questions, writing, images and Microsoft 365 work. GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant: completions as you type, chat about your code, and agents that edit files and open pull requests.

They use different accounts and plans. Microsoft Copilot signs in with a Microsoft account or a work account; GitHub Copilot signs in with a GitHub account, and GitHub offers a free tier plus paid individual and organisation plans. Their context is different too. Microsoft Copilot sees the web and, for work accounts, your Microsoft 365 files. GitHub Copilot sees your open files, your repository and, on GitHub, issues and pull requests. If your question is about code, use GitHub Copilot or another coding tool, because a general assistant does not see your project.

## Will Copilot get Fable?

Possibly, but only GitHub can say. GitHub Copilot already offers a model picker with models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and new models are added through announcements on the GitHub changelog.

Claude Fable is Anthropic's newest and most capable generally available model tier, above Opus. Whether and when a model appears in Copilot depends on agreements between GitHub and the model provider, and new models often arrive first for some plans or in preview. The reliable way to know is to watch the GitHub changelog and open the model picker in Copilot Chat in your editor. Organisation admins may also have to enable a new model in Copilot policies before members can select it. Microsoft Copilot, the consumer assistant, does not let you pick a model in the same way.

## Will Copilot get better?

Yes, in the sense that the models and features improve with each update, as they have since launch. It will not stop needing review: better models make fewer mistakes, not zero.

Most improvements come from three places: stronger underlying models, better retrieval of the right context, such as indexing your whole repository, and agent features that let Copilot check its own work by running tests or builds. You can improve results today without waiting. Keep files and functions small and clearly named, add a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file with your project's conventions, give precise requests, and include the error message or failing test when you ask for a fix.

## Is Copilot ever wrong?

Yes. Copilot can state wrong facts confidently, cite sources that do not say what it claims, and suggest code that compiles but has bugs or security problems. That is a property of language models, not a fault in your setup.

Habits that catch most errors:

- Open the citations behind any factual claim you plan to reuse.
- Run the code and its tests; never merge a suggestion you have not executed.
- Ask "what could be wrong with this?" for an independent check.
- Be extra careful with dates, numbers, API names and library versions, which models often get wrong.

In my own RAG work the fix for confident errors was a confidence gate that refuses to answer on weak evidence. As a user, your version of that gate is checking before you trust.

## What is wrong with Copilot today?

If Copilot stops responding or gives errors suddenly, check the service status first: GitHub Status for GitHub Copilot and the Microsoft 365 service health or status page for Microsoft Copilot.

If the status pages are green, work through the usual causes. Sign out and in again, because expired sessions are common. Update the editor extension, since old versions break when the service changes. Check whether you hit a usage limit for the month or for a premium model. On a work or college network, a proxy or firewall may block the Copilot endpoints; try another network to confirm. In an organisation, an admin policy may have disabled a feature or model. Finally, check the extension's output log in VS Code, which usually names the real error.

## How many Copilot responses do I get?

It depends on the product and plan. Free tiers include a monthly allowance of completions and chat requests, paid plans raise it, and the most capable models count against a separate allowance of premium requests.

GitHub publishes the current allowances for each plan in its documentation, and your usage is visible in your GitHub settings. Microsoft Copilot has its own limits per conversation and per day that vary by account type and have changed several times. Quoting numbers here would date quickly, so check the plan page for the current figures. If you keep hitting limits, use a smaller model for routine edits and save the premium model for hard problems, and keep conversations focused, because one long rambling chat burns requests faster.

## Do Copilot conversations get deleted?

Not automatically in most cases. Consumer Copilot keeps your conversation history until you delete it, and work accounts store Copilot interactions under the organisation's retention policies, which admins control.

In the consumer Copilot app you can delete individual conversations or clear your history in settings. In Microsoft 365, Copilot interactions are kept in the organisation's own environment and can be retained or deleted by compliance policies, so deleting a chat from view may not remove the record your employer keeps. GitHub Copilot Chat in an editor keeps session history locally in the editor, and GitHub documents what prompt and suggestion data it retains for each plan. Never paste passwords or private keys into any assistant.

## Where do Copilot Studio agents get stored?

Copilot Studio agents are stored in a Microsoft Power Platform environment, inside that environment's Dataverse database, together with their topics, knowledge settings and connections.

That has practical effects. You choose the environment when you create the agent, and its region decides where the agent's data lives. Agents move between development, test and production environments as solutions, the same way as other Power Platform components, which is how teams version and deploy them. Knowledge files you upload are stored with the agent, while connected sources such as SharePoint sites stay where they are and are searched at question time. Access to the agent follows the environment's security roles, so plan who can edit it before you build.

## Can you vibe code with GitHub Copilot?

Yes. Agent mode in VS Code and other editors lets you describe a feature in plain language while Copilot plans the change, edits several files, runs commands and fixes its own errors, which is vibe coding in practice.

It works best for prototypes, hackathon builds and internal tools. To keep the result maintainable, start each task with a short spec, ask for tests alongside the feature, review every diff before accepting it and commit after each working step. Keep secrets in environment variables, not in prompts or code. If a session goes in circles, stop, revert to the last good commit and restate the task in smaller pieces. You should be able to explain every file in the project, because judges and interviewers will ask.

## GitHub Copilot vs Cursor vs Windsurf vs Antigravity: which should you use?

All four are AI coding environments with chat, multi-file edits and agents. GitHub Copilot plugs into existing editors and GitHub; Cursor and Windsurf are AI-first editors built on VS Code; Antigravity is Google's agent-first development environment.

How they differ in practice:

- **GitHub Copilot**: best if your team lives on GitHub and wants enterprise controls, issue-to-pull-request agents and support for VS Code, Visual Studio and JetBrains.
- **Cursor**: a polished AI-native editor with strong codebase-wide context and fast multi-file edits.
- **Windsurf**: an AI-native editor with an agent called Cascade; now owned by Cognition.
- **Antigravity**: built around agents that plan and run tasks across the editor, terminal and browser, with Gemini models.

Pick by trying one real task, such as adding an endpoint with tests, in each.

# How to create a personal website: GitHub Pages, builders, design and examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/create-personal-website/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A personal website is a site about you: who you are, what you do, your projects or writing, and how to reach you. For students and developers it works as a portfolio, resume and blog in one, and it is the one online profile you fully control. You can create one for free on GitHub Pages or Vercel if you code, or with a website builder if you do not. My own portfolio at pranjulrathour.scult.in and this answers site, hosted on GitHub Pages, are examples. This page covers creating one, GitHub Pages, a tech blog, examples, design, builders and who should build it.

## What is a personal website?

A personal website is a website that represents an individual rather than a company: typically a homepage with a short introduction, an about page, a portfolio or projects section, a blog or writing, and contact details.

It serves different purposes: a portfolio for job seekers and freelancers, a home for writing and talks, a hub linking all your profiles, or a place to share hobbies. Unlike social media profiles, you control the design, content and data, and it stays even if platforms change. For anyone in tech, a well-made personal site signals initiative and gives recruiters and clients a fuller picture than a resume.

## How do I create a personal website?

Decide the purpose and pages, choose how to build it, write the content, design simply, publish on a host, and connect a domain if you want one. Content first, design second.

Steps:

- **Purpose**: job hunting, freelancing, writing or all three.
- **Pages**: home, about, projects, blog, contact.
- **Build**: code it with HTML and CSS or a framework such as Next.js, or use a builder.
- **Host**: GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify for code; the builder's hosting otherwise.
- **Domain**: optional but professional, usually your name.
- **Basics**: page titles, descriptions, a favicon, fast images, mobile check.

Launch a simple version in a weekend, then improve it over time.

## How do I create a personal website on GitHub?

Use GitHub Pages: create a repository named `yourusername.github.io`, add an `index.html` or a static site, push it, and GitHub serves it at `https://yourusername.github.io`. It is free for public repositories.

Options:

- **Plain HTML and CSS**: fastest to start, full control.
- **Static site generators**: Jekyll is built into GitHub Pages; others such as Astro or Hugo build with GitHub Actions.
- **React or Next.js static export**: build and deploy with Actions.

You can add a custom domain in the repository settings and enable HTTPS. GitHub Pages serves static files only, so forms and dynamic features need third-party services or a separate backend. This answers site is a static site published to GitHub Pages by pushing generated HTML.

## How do I create a tech blog website?

Choose a platform that lets you own your content and domain, write in Markdown, and publish easily: a static site generator on GitHub Pages or Vercel, a Next.js blog, or a hosted blogging platform that supports custom domains.

What makes a tech blog work:

- One clear topic area, such as web development or GenAI.
- Articles that solve specific problems, with code and screenshots.
- Good titles that match what people search for.
- Fast pages, readable fonts and code highlighting.
- An RSS feed and links from your social profiles.

Consistency matters more than volume: one useful article a fortnight for a year builds an audience and a strong portfolio. You can cross-post to developer communities while keeping your own site as the canonical home.

## What are some personal website examples?

Good personal websites share traits: a clear headline about what the person does, a few highlighted projects with outcomes, a short story, writing or talks, and easy contact. Developer portfolios, designer portfolios, researcher homepages and writer sites all follow this pattern.

Elements worth copying from strong examples:

- A one-line positioning statement at the top.
- Project cards with a problem, approach, result and links.
- An about section with personality and a photo.
- A list of articles, talks or publications.
- Clear contact options and social links.

Look at sites of developers and creators you admire, note what you remember after thirty seconds, and apply that to yours.

## What is the best personal website design?

The best design is simple, fast and readable: generous white space, one or two fonts, a limited colour palette, clear navigation, and content that leads with your best work. Personality should come from writing and work, not heavy effects.

Design principles:

- Mobile-first layout; most visitors are on phones.
- Strong contrast and readable font sizes.
- Fast loading: optimised images, minimal scripts.
- Consistent spacing and alignment.
- Accessible: alt text, keyboard navigation, semantic headings.

A personal site is also a test of your judgement; a clean, fast site impresses more than a flashy slow one.

## How do I design a personal website?

Start with content and structure, sketch a simple layout, pick a font pair and a small colour palette, design for mobile first, then refine spacing and hierarchy. Use a design system or component library to stay consistent.

A practical process:

- List sections and write the content.
- Sketch the homepage on paper: headline, intro, projects, contact.
- Choose fonts from Google Fonts and two or three colours.
- Build with a simple CSS framework or utility classes.
- Test on a phone, a laptop and a slow connection.
- Ask two friends what they remember after a quick look.

Iterate on content more than visuals; visitors come for substance.

## What is the best website builder for a personal website?

For non-developers, popular builders such as Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Webflow, Carrd and WordPress.com make it easy to create a good-looking site without code. Developers often prefer building their own with static hosting.

Choose by need:

- **One-page simple site**: a minimal one-page builder.
- **Designer portfolio**: a design-focused builder with strong templates.
- **Blog-heavy site**: a blogging platform or WordPress.
- **Full control and learning**: code it and host on GitHub Pages or Vercel.

Check costs for custom domains and removing branding, export options in case you move later, and performance on mobile.

## What is the best personal blog website design?

A great blog design prioritises reading: a comfortable text width, large readable font, good line spacing, clear headings, code highlighting for technical posts, and a simple list of posts with dates and topics.

Useful features:

- A short author bio on each post.
- Table of contents for long articles.
- Related posts at the end.
- Tags or categories for browsing.
- RSS feed and newsletter option.
- Fast loading and dark mode support.

Avoid pop-ups, auto-playing media and cluttered sidebars. The best blog designs feel invisible: readers notice the ideas, not the layout.

## Who can create a website for personal use?

Anyone can. Developers can build it themselves, which doubles as a portfolio project; non-developers can use website builders; and people who want a custom site without the effort can hire a freelance web developer or designer.

If you hire someone, be clear about pages, content, design references, budget, timeline and who owns the domain and hosting accounts; always keep ownership in your name. If you are a student learning web development, building your own site is one of the best projects you can do: it teaches HTML, CSS, deployment, domains and performance, and it shows employers what you can make.

# What is a CRM for agencies? Best CRMs for marketing, creative, AI and small agencies
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/crm-for-agencies/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An agency CRM is customer relationship management software used by agencies, such as marketing, creative, AI, travel or real estate agencies, to track leads, clients, deals, projects and conversations in one place, so nothing falls through the cracks between first contact and delivery. I lead engineering at SCULT INDIA, an AI-first studio, and designed SCULT Studio CRM, our internal platform, so this page explains agency CRMs, what agencies use, the best options by agency type, and travel and real estate requirements.

## What is a CRM for an agency?

For an agency, a CRM is the system that manages the client lifecycle: capturing leads from forms and referrals, tracking deals through stages, storing contacts and communication history, sending proposals, and handing won clients over to delivery and account management.

Agency CRMs often connect to email, calendars, proposal tools, invoicing and project management. The goal is visibility: who is in the pipeline, what was promised, which deals need follow-up and which clients are at risk. Without a CRM, agencies rely on scattered spreadsheets and inboxes, which breaks down as the team and client list grow. A good CRM also protects the agency when people leave, because client history stays in the system rather than in one person's inbox.

## What CRM do agencies use?

Many agencies use HubSpot, Zoho CRM, Pipedrive, Salesforce or monday CRM, while creative studios often use all-in-one tools for proposals, contracts and invoices. Some agencies build their own platform when their workflow is unusual.

At SCULT INDIA, we built SCULT Studio CRM, an internal platform designed around how our 14-member team handles client work, from enquiries to delivery. Building your own makes sense only when off-the-shelf tools genuinely do not fit and you have engineering capacity; for most agencies, configuring an existing CRM is faster and cheaper. Whatever you choose, adoption by the team matters more than features. Building our own platform also meant owning maintenance, security and updates, a commitment worth weighing honestly before choosing that route.

## What is the best CRM for a marketing agency?

HubSpot is a common choice for marketing agencies because it combines CRM with marketing tools, email, forms, landing pages and reporting, and has a free starting tier. Zoho CRM, Pipedrive and Salesforce are strong alternatives depending on size and budget.

Choose based on needs: HubSpot for inbound marketing and integrated tools; Pipedrive for a simple, visual sales pipeline; Zoho for affordability and a broad suite, popular in India; Salesforce for large agencies needing deep customisation. Check integrations with ad platforms, email tools and reporting dashboards you already use, and run a trial with real deals before committing.

## What is the best free CRM for a digital marketing agency?

HubSpot's free CRM is the most popular free option, with contacts, deals, pipelines, email tracking and forms for unlimited users within its limits. Zoho CRM's free edition and Bitrix24's free plan are other options for small teams.

Free tiers are great for starting, but check limits on contacts, automation, reporting and integrations, which often push growing agencies to paid plans. Export your data regularly, and choose a tool you could grow into, since migrating CRMs later is painful. Even a free CRM used consistently beats an expensive one nobody updates. Set a weekly pipeline review so data stays current.

## What is the best CRM for an AI agency?

AI agencies benefit from CRMs with strong pipelines, proposal tracking and APIs for automation, such as HubSpot, Pipedrive or Attio-style flexible CRMs, plus integrations with tools such as n8n or Zapier to automate lead handling with AI.

AI agencies often use their own skills on their CRM: automatically enriching leads, summarising calls, drafting proposals and scoring opportunities with language models, while keeping humans in control of client communication. Make sure client data handling is clear, especially if you send CRM data to AI services; check data processing terms and avoid sending sensitive information unnecessarily.

## What is the best CRM for a small agency?

Small agencies do best with simple, affordable CRMs that the whole team will actually use: HubSpot's free or starter tiers, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, or a well-structured Notion or Airtable setup for very small teams.

Priorities for small agencies: quick setup, a clear deal pipeline, email integration, reminders for follow-ups, and basic reporting. Avoid complex enterprise tools that take months to configure. Define your pipeline stages, required fields and who updates what, because process matters more than software. Review the setup every few months as the agency grows, and remove fields nobody fills in, since clutter discourages updates.

## What is the best CRM for a design agency?

Design agencies often prefer tools that combine client management with proposals, contracts, invoicing and project tracking, such as HoneyBook, Dubsado or Bonsai, or a general CRM such as HubSpot or Pipedrive paired with project tools like Notion or Asana.

Key features: attractive proposals with packages, e-signatures, payment schedules, client portals for sharing files and approvals, and scheduling for discovery calls. Check whether the tool supports your country's invoicing and tax needs, since some popular creative tools focus on specific markets. A smooth client experience from proposal to delivery is part of a design agency's brand.

## What is the best CRM for a creative agency?

Creative agencies, covering branding, video, content and design, benefit from CRMs that link sales with project delivery: HubSpot or Pipedrive for pipelines, monday CRM or similar for combined CRM and project management, and all-in-one tools for proposals and billing.

Look for: visual pipelines, time and resource tracking, retainers and recurring billing, client communication history, and integration with file sharing. Creative work involves many revisions, so tracking scope and approvals in the CRM or linked project tool protects margins. Choose tools your producers and account managers like using, since they update them daily.

## What CRM features does a travel agency need?

Travel agencies need CRM features for managing traveller profiles and preferences, enquiries and quotes, itineraries, bookings and supplier details, payment tracking, document storage such as passports and visas, and automated reminders before trips.

Also valuable: integration with booking systems, WhatsApp and email communication, lead capture from websites and social media, follow-ups for repeat trips and reviews, and reporting on sales by destination or agent. Because travel data includes identity documents, strong security and access control are essential, and local data protection laws apply.

## What is the best CRM for a real estate agency?

Real estate agencies need CRMs that manage property listings, buyer and seller leads, site visits, follow-ups and deal stages. Options include general CRMs such as Zoho CRM, HubSpot and Salesforce configured for property, and real estate-specific CRMs with listing and portal integrations.

Key features: automatic lead capture from property portals and ads, matching buyers to listings, scheduling site visits, WhatsApp and call integration, reminders for follow-ups, and team assignment. Fast follow-up is crucial in real estate, so automation that routes leads to agents immediately is worth prioritising. Test with your actual lead sources before choosing, and check how easily agents can update records from their phones, since much real estate work happens away from a desk.

# What is Cursor AI code editor? Install, use, VS Code, and vs Copilot and Windsurf
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/cursor-ai-code-editor-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Cursor is an AI-first code editor built as a fork of VS Code: it looks and works like VS Code, but adds deeply integrated AI features, such as multi-line autocomplete, chat that understands your whole codebase, inline edits and an agent that can change many files and run commands. This page covers what it is, installing it on any system including Ubuntu, how it relates to VS Code, a beginner tutorial and everyday use, changing themes, how it compares with GitHub Copilot and Windsurf, and what to make of big productivity claims.

## What is the Cursor AI code editor?

Cursor is a desktop code editor from Anysphere that integrates AI throughout the editing experience. Because it is built on VS Code's open-source core, most VS Code extensions, themes and shortcuts work, so the switch feels familiar.

Its main features: Tab, which predicts multi-line edits as you type; inline edit, which changes selected code from a natural-language instruction; chat that can reference files, symbols, docs and the whole codebase; and an agent mode that plans and makes multi-file changes, runs terminal commands and fixes errors. You can choose among several AI models. Project rules files let you set coding standards the AI should follow.

## How do I install the Cursor AI code editor?

Download the installer for Windows, macOS or Linux from cursor.com, run it, sign in or create an account, and choose whether to import your VS Code settings and extensions during setup.

After installing, open a project folder and let Cursor index the codebase, which improves the context available to chat and the agent. Review privacy settings, especially for company code: Cursor has a privacy mode that limits how code is stored. Free and paid plans differ in usage allowances and model access; check the current pricing page. Keep the editor updated, since features change quickly.

## How do I install Cursor on Ubuntu?

Download the Linux build from cursor.com, which is offered as a package or AppImage, then install the package with your package manager or make the AppImage executable and run it. Create a desktop entry if you want it in your applications menu.

For an AppImage, the usual steps are: download it, run `chmod +x` on the file, then launch it; some systems need the FUSE library installed for AppImages. If a package format is offered for your distribution, installing it handles menu entries and updates more neatly. Check Cursor's documentation for the current Linux instructions, as packaging options have changed over time.

## How do I use Cursor AI in VS Code?

You cannot install Cursor inside VS Code; Cursor is a separate editor based on VS Code. Instead, install Cursor and import your VS Code extensions, settings and keybindings, so it feels like VS Code with AI built in.

If you prefer staying in VS Code, use AI extensions there instead, such as GitHub Copilot or other assistants. Some developers keep both editors: VS Code for certain workflows and Cursor for AI-heavy work. Projects open the same way in both, since they share the same file-based workspace model. Make sure your Git setup, formatters and linters are configured in whichever editor you use.

## Is there a Cursor tutorial for beginners?

Yes. Cursor's documentation has getting-started guides, and a good beginner path is to practise each core feature on a small project for a day.

A beginner plan:

- **Day 1**: open a small project, accept and reject Tab suggestions while writing a function.
- **Day 2**: select code and use inline edit, such as "add input validation and error handling".
- **Day 3**: ask chat questions with file references, such as "how does auth work in this project?".
- **Day 4**: use the agent for a small feature with tests, reviewing each change.
- **Day 5**: add a project rules file with your conventions and test commands.

Commit after each successful step so you can roll back easily.

## How do I use the Cursor AI code editor day to day?

Use Tab for routine typing, inline edit for targeted changes, chat for understanding and planning, and the agent for multi-file tasks. Keep a project rules file updated and review every diff.

Useful habits:

- Reference specific files and symbols in chat instead of asking about the whole repository vaguely.
- Ask for a plan before large agent tasks, then approve step by step.
- Paste exact error messages and test output when asking for fixes.
- Choose faster models for simple edits and stronger ones for hard problems.
- Exclude large folders such as `node_modules` and data from indexing.

Treat AI suggestions like a teammate's pull request: understand them before merging.

## How do I change the theme in Cursor?

Open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P, search for "Color Theme", and choose a theme. Install more themes from the extensions panel, just as in VS Code.

Because Cursor is based on VS Code, theme extensions and settings work the same way: you can set themes, fonts, font size and icon themes in settings, or edit the settings JSON directly. If you imported VS Code settings during setup, your existing theme may already be applied. For long coding sessions, choose a theme with good contrast and a readable monospaced font.

## Cursor vs GitHub Copilot: which is better?

Both are strong. Cursor is a whole editor designed around AI, with deep codebase context and smooth multi-file editing. GitHub Copilot is an assistant that works inside editors you may already use, such as VS Code, Visual Studio and JetBrains IDEs, with strong GitHub integration and a coding agent for issues.

Choose Cursor if you want the most integrated AI editing experience and are happy to switch editors. Choose Copilot if your team relies on a specific IDE, GitHub workflows and enterprise policies. Both offer agent modes and multiple models, and both improve quickly. Run the same real task, such as adding an endpoint with tests, in each and compare how much you had to fix.

## Cursor vs Windsurf: which should I use?

Cursor and Windsurf are both AI-native editors built on VS Code foundations, with chat, autocomplete and agents that make multi-file changes. Differences are in agent behaviour, context handling, model options, pricing and team features, and both change frequently.

Windsurf's agent, called Cascade, emphasises continuing context across steps; Cursor emphasises fast edits and a rich set of interaction modes. Many developers try both on their own project for a few days. Compare reliability on your stack, how well each follows project rules, speed, and cost at your usage level. Whichever you choose, the habits that matter most are the same: small tasks, clear context, review and tests.

## Can Cursor really make you code much faster?

Cursor can make some work much faster, such as boilerplate, refactors, tests and unfamiliar APIs, but headline percentages like "259% faster" describe individual experiences, not guaranteed results. Overall gains depend on the task, your skill and how carefully you review.

Speed comes from good context, such as a clear rules file, focused requests and existing tests, and from knowing when not to use AI. Time can also be lost: debugging plausible but wrong code, or untangling large changes made without review. Measure your own results: track how long similar tasks take with and without AI over a few weeks. The developers who gain most use AI for drafts and spend saved time on design, testing and review.

# Data analyst vs machine learning engineer vs AI engineer: what each job actually does, the skill overlap, and which path fits you
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/data-analyst-vs-ai-ml-engineer-career-path/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is the difference between a data analyst, an ML engineer, and an AI engineer?

**A data analyst answers business questions using data that already exists: what happened, why, and what it suggests, delivered as a dashboard, a report, or a recommendation. A machine learning engineer builds, trains and ships predictive models: forecasting, classification, recommendation, and takes ownership of getting a model into production and monitored. An AI engineer, increasingly synonymous with GenAI engineer, builds products on top of models, often via API rather than training from scratch, RAG systems, agents, AI features inside a larger application. The tools overlap heavily; the deliverable at the end of the day is what actually differs.**


I get this question constantly from BCA and B.Tech students choosing a direction, because all three paths are taught with overlapping tools in the same few semesters, and the job titles in the market are inconsistent enough to add to the confusion [4].

> Three different jobs can share the same first two years of learning and diverge completely in year three. Know which deliverable you actually want to own before you specialise.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What does a data analyst actually do day to day?

**Pulls data with SQL, cleans and shapes it in Python or a spreadsheet tool, builds dashboards in something like Power BI or Tableau, and answers specific business questions, why did signups drop last month, which channel drives the most retained users. The core skill is turning a vague business question into a precise data question and a clear answer a non-technical stakeholder can act on. Little to no model training; the value is in analysis and communication, not in building systems.**


## What does a machine learning engineer actually do day to day?

**Prepares and validates training data, trains and evaluates models, builds the pipeline that retrains and serves a model in production, and monitors it for drift once it is live. Deep Python, a real understanding of the modelling techniques being used, and increasingly MLOps skills, versioning, deployment, monitoring, because a model that works once in a notebook and a model that keeps working in production under changing data are different achievements entirely.**




## What does an AI or GenAI engineer actually do day to day?

**Builds features on top of existing models rather than training them from scratch in most cases: RAG systems, agents, document extraction pipelines, evaluation suites, and the production code, APIs, validation, logging, that turns a model call into a reliable product feature [5]. The skill that separates this role from a hobbyist prompt-writer is the same discipline an ML engineer applies to a trained model, applied instead to a system built around calls to someone else's model: measured evaluation, validated outputs, monitored production behaviour.**


## Where do the skills overlap, and where do they diverge?

**SQL and Python are near-universal across all three. Statistics and basic modelling concepts show up everywhere, though depth differs sharply. The divergence starts at "what happens with the result": a data analyst's output is a decision someone else acts on; an ML engineer's output is a model running in a pipeline they own; an AI engineer's output is a feature end users touch directly, often without ever training a model themselves. Knowing which of those three endings you actually want to be responsible for is the real decision, more than any specific tool choice.**



## How do I get my first role in each path?

**For a data analyst role: two or three real analyses of public or personal datasets, written up as a decision a stakeholder could act on, not just a chart. For an ML engineer role: one model you trained, evaluated honestly, and deployed, with monitoring, not just a notebook with a good accuracy number. For an AI engineer role: one shipped product using a model, RAG, an agent, an extraction pipeline, with measured evaluation and real users or a realistic test set [6][7]. Each portfolio proves the specific deliverable that role actually owns.**



## Can I move between these paths later?

**Yes, and it is common. A data analyst who learns to train and deploy models moves toward ML engineering. An ML engineer who starts building API-driven product features moves toward AI engineering. The underlying skills, data handling, statistics, evaluation discipline, Python, compound across all three rather than being wasted if you switch. Pick the path that matches what you want to build right now, and treat the switch as a realistic option later rather than a wall.**



## Interview questions across these three paths

**Every one of these roles gets asked "walk me through a project", and the strongest answer matches the role: a data analyst should describe the decision their analysis drove; an ML engineer should describe how they evaluated and monitored their model; an AI engineer should describe how they measured whether their shipped feature actually worked. Confusing which deliverable you are being asked about is the most common way a strong candidate gives a weak answer.**



## Where should I start?

**Write one sentence for each path: the decision, the model, or the feature you would want to be responsible for. Whichever sentence excites you most is the direction to build your next project toward.** For a career session that helps students choose between data, ML and AI engineering paths honestly, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate: exam, prep, and the GenAI role
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/databricks-generative-ai-engineer-associate/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate is a certification that tests whether you can design, build, deploy and govern LLM-powered applications on the Databricks platform, especially retrieval-augmented generation with Vector Search, model serving and evaluation. It suits engineers working in Databricks-based companies. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page explains the certification, the generative AI engineer role and work, courses and a roadmap, the study guide, preparation, and how hard the exam is.

## What is the Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate?

It is a Databricks certification validating skills in building generative AI solutions on Databricks: decomposing problems into LLM application designs, preparing data and chunking documents, building RAG chains and agents, using Vector Search and model serving, applying governance, and evaluating and monitoring applications.

The exam is a proctored, multiple-choice test, taken online or at a test centre, with around 45 questions in 90 minutes according to recent exam guides, and the certification is valid for two years. Databricks recommends hands-on experience with its generative AI tools before attempting it. Check the official certification page for the current exam guide, format and policies, since details are updated.

## What is the generative AI engineer role?

A generative AI engineer builds applications and systems on top of generative models, especially large language models: chatbots, RAG assistants, document processing, agents and content tools, taking them from prototype to reliable production.

The role blends software engineering with AI-specific skills: retrieval, prompt and context design, evaluation, fine-tuning when needed, safety, cost control and deployment. It differs from research roles that create new models, and overlaps with ML engineering and backend development. Employers look for people who can show working systems, measure their quality and explain trade-offs. Titles vary: the same work may be called AI engineer, LLM engineer, applied AI engineer or machine learning engineer, so read job descriptions for the actual responsibilities.

## What work does a generative AI engineer do?

Day to day, a generative AI engineer designs LLM features, builds ingestion and retrieval pipelines, writes and tests prompts, integrates tools and APIs, evaluates outputs against test sets, deploys services, monitors quality and cost, and works with product teams on requirements and risks.

Typical tasks include chunking and indexing documents, tuning hybrid search and reranking, adding citations and refusal rules, building agent workflows, fine-tuning small models with LoRA, setting up guardrails against prompt injection, and investigating failures from production logs. In my work, this ranges from RAG.NextUpgrad's retrieval pipeline to schema validation in DocuLens AI and QLoRA training in FineTune Studio.

## What is a good generative AI engineer course?

Good options include DeepLearning.AI's short courses on LLM apps, RAG, agents and evaluation; Hugging Face courses on transformers and agents; cloud provider learning paths such as Databricks Academy, Google Cloud and Microsoft Learn; and university courses on NLP for foundations.

Choose courses with hands-on projects, current tools and evaluation content, not just prompting tips. Combine one structured course with your own project: build a RAG assistant over real documents, then add evaluation, then deploy it. Certificates show effort, but a working, documented project demonstrates the skills employers hire for. Revisit your course choices every few months, since generative AI tools change quickly and older courses may teach deprecated interfaces.

## What is the Databricks generative AI engineer course?

Databricks Academy offers a "Generative AI Engineering with Databricks" learning path covering generative AI solution design, data preparation for RAG, building applications with Vector Search and Mosaic AI tools, deployment with model serving, and evaluation and governance, aligned with the certification.

It is available as self-paced online training and instructor-led sessions, and Databricks partners and customers may have access to more content. Work through it inside a real Databricks workspace, practising each step rather than only watching. The course maps closely to the exam's sections, making it the most direct preparation resource.

## What is the roadmap to become a generative AI engineer?

Start with Python and software engineering, then learn LLM fundamentals, prompting and structured output, embeddings and RAG, evaluation, agents and tool use, fine-tuning basics, and deployment with monitoring. Build a project at each stage.

A concise roadmap:

- **Months 1 to 2**: Python, APIs, Git, SQL, a web framework.
- **Months 3 to 4**: LLM APIs, prompting, a first RAG app.
- **Months 5 to 6**: hybrid retrieval, reranking, evaluation sets.
- **Months 7 to 8**: agents, tools, MCP, guardrails.
- **Months 9 to 10**: fine-tuning with QLoRA, deployment, cost control.
- **Ongoing**: hackathons, open source, a polished portfolio.

Add a platform certification, such as Databricks, if your target employers use it.

## What is the study guide for the Databricks GenAI Engineer Associate?

The official exam guide on the Databricks certification page is the study guide: it lists exam sections, objectives, recommended training and sample questions. Use it as a checklist, mapping each objective to documentation and hands-on practice.

Sections typically cover designing applications, data preparation, application development, assembling and deploying applications, governance, and evaluation and monitoring. For each, know the relevant Databricks features: Vector Search index types, model serving endpoints, Unity Catalog governance, agent and evaluation tools, and MLflow tracking. Supplement with documentation pages for each feature and build a small end-to-end RAG app in a workspace.

## What is the Databricks GenAI Engineer certification course structure?

The official preparation path combines the Databricks Academy generative AI engineering courses with the exam guide and practice in a workspace. Courses are organised around the exam domains, from solution design through data preparation, development, deployment, governance and evaluation.

Many learners supplement official material with practice questions and community notes, but rely on official sources for accuracy, since unofficial dumps can be outdated or wrong and violate exam policies. Sharing or using leaked exam questions can also lead to certification being revoked. Plan your study as modules: one week per domain, ending each week by building that part of a project, then a final week of review and practice questions.

## How do I prepare for the Databricks GenAI Engineer Associate?

Read the exam guide, complete the Databricks Academy generative AI course, then build an end-to-end RAG application in a Databricks workspace: ingest documents, create a Vector Search index, build a chain or agent, deploy it with model serving, and evaluate it.

Preparation tips:

- Know chunking strategies and when to use each.
- Understand Vector Search index types and syncing.
- Learn model serving options and how to choose models.
- Study governance with Unity Catalog and guardrails.
- Practise evaluation concepts and MLflow tracking.
- Take official sample questions and review mistakes.

Hands-on practice matters most, because scenario questions test applied judgement.

## How hard is the Databricks GenAI Engineer Associate exam?

It is moderately difficult. Engineers who have built RAG systems and used Databricks usually find it manageable with a few weeks of focused preparation. Those with only theoretical knowledge or no Databricks experience find it harder, because questions are scenario-based and platform-specific.

The challenge is choosing the best option among plausible ones, which requires understanding trade-offs in chunking, retrieval, model choice, deployment and evaluation. General RAG experience helps a lot, but learn Databricks-specific features and terminology. Budget practice time in a real workspace; it turns abstract objectives into concrete knowledge.

# What is vector search in Databricks? Indexes, GCP, Redis, SQLite, cost, and is it dead
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/databricks-vector-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vector search in Databricks, called Mosaic AI Vector Search, is a managed service that indexes embeddings from your Delta tables and serves fast similarity search for RAG and recommendation applications, governed through Unity Catalog. It keeps indexes in sync with source data automatically. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, so this page covers Databricks Vector Search and its indexes, vector search on Google Cloud, Redis and SQLite, cost, whether vector search is dead, how Google uses it, and vector search engines.

## What is vector search in Databricks?

Mosaic AI Vector Search is Databricks' built-in vector database. It creates vector indexes from Delta tables, serves similarity queries through endpoints, and integrates with Unity Catalog for access control and lineage, so retrieval follows the same governance as your data.

It supports embeddings computed by Databricks-managed embedding models or your own, metadata filtering, and hybrid search combining keyword and vector similarity. Typical uses are RAG over enterprise documents stored in the lakehouse, product recommendations and semantic search. Its main advantage is integration: if your data and pipelines already live in Databricks, you avoid copying data to a separate vector database and managing sync yourself.

## How do I use vector search in Databricks?

Create a vector search endpoint, then create an index from a Delta table with a primary key and either a text column for managed embeddings or an embedding column. Query it with the Python SDK, REST API or SQL.

```python
from databricks.vector_search.client import VectorSearchClient
index = VectorSearchClient().get_index(endpoint_name="docs_ep", index_name="main.rag.docs_idx")
hits = index.similarity_search(query_text="refund policy", columns=["id", "text"], num_results=5)
```

Enable Change Data Feed on the source table for syncing. In RAG apps, pass retrieved text to a model serving endpoint and log retrievals. Check the documentation for current SDK names and options, which evolve.

## What is a vector search index in Databricks?

A vector search index is the searchable structure built from your data's embeddings. Databricks offers Delta Sync indexes, which automatically stay in sync with a source Delta table, and Direct Vector Access indexes, where you write and update vectors yourself through the API.

Delta Sync indexes can compute embeddings for you from a text column using a model endpoint, or use embeddings you computed in the table. Sync can be triggered or continuous. Direct Vector Access suits applications that produce vectors outside the lakehouse or need real-time writes. Both support filters on metadata columns. Choose Delta Sync when your source of truth is a Delta table, which is the common case.

## What is vector search in GCP?

On Google Cloud, Vertex AI Vector Search, formerly Matching Engine, is the managed vector search service built on Google's ScaNN technology for low-latency search at large scale. Google Cloud also offers vector search in AlloyDB and Cloud SQL with pgvector, BigQuery and Firestore.

Choose Vertex AI Vector Search for very large, high-throughput workloads; AlloyDB or Cloud SQL for applications that want vectors next to relational data; BigQuery for analytics-style similarity over warehouse data; and Firestore for app developers already using it. Vertex AI also offers RAG-focused services that manage chunking, embedding and retrieval for you.

## Can Redis do vector search?

Yes. Redis supports vector similarity search through its query engine, with vector fields indexed using exact FLAT or approximate HNSW indexes, plus filtering on other fields and hybrid queries. Newer Redis versions also add a dedicated vector data structure.

Redis keeps data in memory, so vector search is very fast, which suits real-time recommendations, semantic caching of LLM responses and session-level retrieval. The trade-off is memory cost for large collections. Many teams use Redis as a semantic cache in front of a model: if a new question's embedding is very close to a previous one, return the cached answer, saving cost and latency.

## Can SQLite do vector search?

Yes, through extensions. sqlite-vec adds vector storage and similarity search to SQLite with no external dependencies, and runs anywhere SQLite runs, including browsers via WebAssembly and mobile devices. Some SQLite-based databases, such as libSQL, add native vector support.

SQLite vector search suits local-first apps, desktop tools, mobile apps, prototypes and small to medium collections, where running a separate server would be overkill. Brute-force search over tens of thousands of vectors is fast enough for many uses. For millions of vectors with heavy concurrent traffic, a server database or dedicated vector store is more appropriate.

## Is vector search expensive?

It can be cheap or expensive depending on scale. Costs come from computing embeddings, storing vectors, keeping indexes in memory and serving queries. Small projects can run on an existing PostgreSQL database at almost no extra cost; billions of vectors need serious infrastructure.

Ways to control cost:

- Use an existing database with vector support before adding a new service.
- Choose smaller embedding dimensions where quality allows.
- Quantise vectors to cut memory, rescoring top results.
- Embed once and cache; re-embed only changed content.
- Filter by metadata to reduce search space.

Measure cost per thousand queries and storage per million vectors for your setup before committing.

## Is vector search dead?

No. Claims that it is dead usually come from long-context models that read whole documents and from coding agents that search with tools like grep instead of embeddings. Both are useful, but neither replaces retrieval over large knowledge bases.

What is changing is that vector search is no longer used alone. Strong systems combine keyword search, vector search, metadata filters and reranking, and agents can choose among these tools. Long context helps after retrieval, letting models read more of the retrieved material. For millions of documents, fast similarity search remains essential, so expect vector search to be a standard component rather than a hype topic.

## Does Google use vector search?

Yes. Google has described using neural matching and language models such as BERT in Search to understand the meaning of queries and pages beyond keywords, and it open-sourced ScaNN, its vector similarity search library, in 2020. Recommendations across its products rely on embeddings too.

Google's public explanations say AI systems help connect concepts in queries to relevant pages, alongside many other ranking signals. Its cloud products, such as Vertex AI Vector Search, are built on the same research. For website owners, this means writing clearly about topics in natural language matters more than exact keyword repetition, because semantic matching recognises related wording.

## What is a vector search engine?

A vector search engine is software that stores vectors and returns the most similar ones to a query vector, using approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. It powers semantic search, recommendations and RAG retrieval.

Options include libraries such as FAISS, ScaNN and hnswlib for in-process search; vector databases such as Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate and Pinecone; search engines with vector support such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Vespa; and database extensions such as pgvector. Choose by scale, filtering needs, hybrid search support, operations capacity and where your data already lives.
