# Face recognition guide: biometrics, Python, InsightFace, detectors, losses, training
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/face-recognition-python-insightface-arcface/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Face recognition systems detect a face, convert it into an embedding and compare it with stored templates, with quality depending on detectors, training losses, cameras and lighting. I built FaceVision, which runs face detection, recognition and liveness in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web and stores only embeddings in PostgreSQL, so this page covers how face biometrics work, recognition in the dark, a Python tutorial, InsightFace versus face_recognition, detectors, Hikvision, loss functions, training time and phone use. How does face recognition biometrics work? Enrolment captures your face and converts it into a template, usually an embedding vector, stored securely. At verification, a new image is converted the same way and compared with the template; if similarity exceeds a threshold, access is granted. The threshold balances false accepts, where the wrong person gets in, against false rejects, where you are refused. Liveness detection checks that a real person is present rather than a photo or mask. Secure systems store templates in protected hardware or encrypted databases and never keep raw images unnecessarily. FaceVision follows this principle, storing embeddings in PostgreSQL rather than photos. Even templates deserve strong protection, since biometrics cannot be changed like passwords. Periodic re-enrolment helps as appearance changes. How does face recognition work in the dark? Systems with infrared hardware, such as iPhone Face ID and Windows Hello cameras, work in darkness because they illuminate your face with invisible infrared light and capture infrared images or depth maps. Phones relying on the normal front camera struggle in low light, so some brighten the screen to light your face, with mixed results. Infrared imaging also resists some spoofing, since photos look different in infrared. For custom systems, add infrared cameras or illumination for night use, such as attendance at entrances. Plan for glare and backlighting during the day as well. Test in the lighting conditions where the system will actually run, since accuracy can drop sharply in poor light. What does a face recognition tutorial in Python cover? A typical tutorial captures images with OpenCV, detects faces, aligns them, computes embeddings with a pretrained model, stores embeddings for known people, and identifies new faces by comparing embeddings with cosine similarity and a threshold. Also asked as: face recognition tutorial python Beginners often start with the face_recognition library for a few lines of code, then move to InsightFace models for higher accuracy. A FastAPI service can expose enrolment and matching endpoints, storing embeddings in PostgreSQL, the same stack FaceVision uses. Keep code modular so you can swap models later. Add liveness checks, consent prompts and tests across lighting and demographics. Evaluate false accept and false reject rates on a validation set before using the system for anything important. InsightFace vs face_recognition: which should you use? face_recognition, built on dlib, is easy to start with and runs on CPUs, but its models are older. InsightFace provides state-of-the-art detection and ArcFace recognition models with better accuracy on hard cases, and GPU or ONNX acceleration. An important difference is licensing: InsightFace's pretrained model weights are released for non-commercial research use, so commercial products need licensed models or ones trained on permissively licensed data. face_recognition's dlib models are more permissive but less accurate on difficult images. For learning, either works; for production, weigh accuracy, licence, speed and maintenance. Test both on your own images, including varied angles and lighting. What are good pre-trained models for face or head detection? Strong face detectors include RetinaFace and SCRFD from the InsightFace project, OpenCV's lightweight YuNet, Google's MediaPipe face detector and YOLO models fine-tuned for faces. For head detection in crowds, models trained on datasets such as CrowdHuman work well. Also asked as: can anyone recommend me a very good pre-trained model for face or head detection Choose by speed, accuracy and hardware: YuNet and MediaPipe run fast on CPUs and phones, SCRFD offers excellent accuracy-speed trade-offs, and RetinaFace provides landmarks useful for alignment. Head detectors help when faces are turned away, such as counting people in queues. Check licences before commercial use, and evaluate on images resembling your deployment, since detectors trained on frontal photos may miss small or angled faces. What is the difference between Hikvision face detection and face recognition? In Hikvision and similar CCTV systems, face detection notices that a face is present and captures a snapshot or triggers an event. Face recognition goes further, comparing captured faces against a stored face library to identify specific people. Also asked as: hikvision face detection vs face recognition Detection works on many cameras, while recognition usually needs compatible cameras or recorders with face analytics and configured face libraries. Recognition raises much greater privacy and legal obligations, including consent, purpose limitation and data retention rules under laws such as India's data protection law. Use detection for counting or alerts where identity is unnecessary, and recognition only with clear justification, notices and secure handling of biometric data. Review vendor firmware updates regularly for security fixes. Why is plain softmax loss not preferred for face recognition? Plain softmax loss trains features that separate known identities but does not make same-person features tightly clustered or different people far apart. Face recognition must compare unseen people, so it needs highly discriminative embeddings. Also asked as: why is a general/original softmax loss not preferred in fr (face recognition Margin-based losses, such as SphereFace, CosFace and ArcFace, normalise features and class weights and add an angular or cosine margin, forcing embeddings of the same identity closer and different identities further apart. This greatly improves verification on new faces, which plain softmax handles poorly. ArcFace's additive angular margin became the standard for training modern face recognition models, including many used in production systems and open-source toolkits. Understanding this loss helps when choosing thresholds. How long does it take to train a face recognition neural network? Roughly, training a strong model such as ArcFace with a ResNet backbone on millions of face images takes about a day or more on several modern GPUs, while fine-tuning a pretrained model on a small dataset takes minutes to hours. Also asked as: how long it takes to train face recognition deep neural network? (rough estimation Time depends on dataset size, backbone depth, image resolution, number of GPUs and training epochs. Large public face datasets have licensing and privacy issues, so most teams use pretrained models rather than training from scratch. Fine-tuning helps adapt to specific conditions, such as infrared cameras or particular demographics. Track verification accuracy on a held-out set throughout training. Budget extra time for data cleaning, evaluation and threshold tuning, which often take longer than training itself. Should you use face recognition on your phone? Yes, if your phone uses secure face unlock, such as iPhone Face ID or Class 3 Android face unlock, it offers strong convenience with good security. Camera-only face unlock is fine for convenience but weaker than fingerprint or a strong PIN. Also asked as: should i use face recognition on my phone Consider your situation: if someone could hold the phone to your face while you are unaware, enable eyes-open or attention requirements, and know how to temporarily disable biometrics quickly. Use a strong passcode as the backup, since it protects your device when biometrics are bypassed. For sensitive apps, such as banking, check which biometric methods they accept. Face data on phones stays in secure hardware, not on company servers. How does face recognition work on Samsung phones? Samsung Galaxy face recognition uses the front camera to capture a 2D image of your face and compares it with your registered face data stored securely on the phone. It is designed for convenience rather than high security. Samsung notes that face recognition is less secure than a PIN, pattern, password or fingerprint, and it is not accepted for Samsung Pass or payments. Settings include an option requiring open eyes and a faster recognition option that slightly reduces security. Registering an alternative look helps with glasses or hairstyles. For stronger protection, use the fingerprint sensor for sensitive tasks and keep face recognition for quick unlocking.

# Does FAISS use cosine similarity? ANN, HNSW, BM25, semantic search and RAG thresholds
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/faiss-cosine-similarity-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


FAISS supports cosine similarity indirectly: normalise your vectors to unit length and use an inner product index, because the inner product of unit vectors equals cosine similarity. FAISS, Meta's library for fast similarity search, also offers approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as IVF, PQ and HNSW. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense retrieval with BM25, so this page covers FAISS metrics and indexes, how search works, cosine versus BM25 and semantic search, when cosine misleads in RAG, and similarity thresholds in LangChain.

## Does FAISS use cosine similarity?

Not directly by name. FAISS provides L2 distance and inner product indexes. To use cosine similarity, normalise all vectors with `faiss.normalize_L2` and use an inner product index such as `IndexFlatIP`; scores then equal cosine similarity.

Normalise both the stored vectors and every query vector, otherwise inner product favours longer vectors. Many embedding models already output unit-length vectors, in which case inner product and cosine give the same ranking, and even L2 distance ranks identically, since for unit vectors squared distance equals two minus twice the cosine. In LangChain's FAISS wrapper, setting the distance strategy to inner product or enabling L2 normalisation achieves cosine behaviour. Check your model's documentation for normalisation.

## What does FAISS use for search?

FAISS uses vector indexes and distance metrics: exact flat indexes that compare against every vector, and approximate indexes such as inverted files, product quantization and HNSW graphs, with L2 or inner product as the metric.

Indexes can be combined through the index factory; for example, a string such as IVF4096,PQ64 creates an inverted file with 4,096 clusters and product-quantized codes. FAISS is written in C++ with Python bindings, uses SIMD instructions on CPUs, and supports GPUs for very fast batch search. It is a library, not a database, so persistence, metadata filtering and updates are your responsibility, or are handled by frameworks that wrap it.

## Does FAISS use approximate nearest neighbour search?

Yes, optionally. FAISS offers both exact search with flat indexes and approximate nearest neighbour search with IVF, PQ, HNSW and LSH indexes, which trade a small loss in recall for much faster queries and lower memory.

Exact flat search is ideal up to hundreds of thousands of vectors, especially on GPU. Beyond that, ANN indexes become necessary: IVF searches only the closest clusters, controlled by nprobe; PQ compresses vectors so billions fit in memory; HNSW navigates a graph for low-latency queries. Tune parameters by measuring recall against exact search on a sample of queries, choosing the cheapest setting that meets your recall target.

## Does FAISS use HNSW?

Yes. FAISS includes HNSW indexes, such as `IndexHNSWFlat`, which build a hierarchical navigable small world graph over vectors for fast approximate search, with M controlling graph connectivity and efSearch controlling search breadth.

HNSW in FAISS offers excellent speed and recall without a training step, but uses more memory than compressed indexes and does not support removing vectors easily. Increase efSearch for better recall at the cost of latency, and choose M around 16 to 64 depending on accuracy needs. For very large collections, combining IVF with PQ is more memory-efficient, while HNSW suits datasets that fit comfortably in RAM and need low latency. It is also the default choice in many vector databases.

## How does FAISS similarity search work?

You add vectors to an index, then search with query vectors; FAISS returns the k nearest vectors and their distances. Flat indexes compute distances to every vector; approximate indexes narrow candidates first, using clusters, compressed codes or graphs.

In Python: create `index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(dim)`, call `index.add(vectors)` with a float32 NumPy array, then `distances, ids = index.search(queries, k)`. IDs map back to your documents through a list or dictionary you maintain. Approximate indexes such as IVF need `index.train(sample)` before adding vectors. Save indexes with `faiss.write_index` and load them with `faiss.read_index`. Batch queries together for speed, since FAISS is optimised for matrix operations.

## Does BM25 use cosine similarity?

No. BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function that scores documents by term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length normalisation. It sums per-term scores rather than computing an angle between vectors.

Classic TF-IDF retrieval in the vector space model does use cosine similarity between sparse term vectors, which is where the confusion comes from. BM25 improved on it with term frequency saturation, so repeating a word has a diminishing effect, and length normalisation controlled by the parameters k1 and b, with typical defaults around 1.2 and 0.75. Cosine similarity on dense embeddings captures meaning, while BM25 captures exact term overlap, which is why hybrid retrieval combines both, often with reciprocal rank fusion.

## Does semantic search use cosine similarity?

Usually, yes. Semantic search embeds the query and documents into vectors and ranks documents by similarity, most often cosine similarity or the equivalent dot product on normalised vectors. Some systems use Euclidean distance instead.

Semantic search and cosine similarity are not the same thing: semantic search is the overall task of finding results by meaning, while cosine similarity is one scoring function used inside it. The embedding model matters far more than the metric: a good model makes similar meanings point in similar directions. Use the metric your embedding model was trained with, which its documentation states, and keep it consistent between indexing and querying.

## Is cosine similarity of embeddings really about similarity?

Not always. A 2024 paper with this title, from Netflix researchers, showed that for some learned embeddings, cosine similarity can produce arbitrary results, because training can rescale dimensions in ways that change cosine scores without changing the model's predictions.

Their analysis focused on matrix factorisation models with certain regularisation, but the lesson generalises: cosine scores depend on how embeddings were trained, and a high score does not guarantee semantic relevance. Modern sentence embedding models are trained specifically so cosine similarity is meaningful, which makes them more reliable. Still, validate on your data: check whether top results are actually relevant, and treat raw similarity scores as relative rankings rather than calibrated probabilities.

## Why does cosine similarity fail in RAG, and what should you use instead?

Cosine similarity on embeddings can rank passages that sound similar above passages that actually answer the question, miss exact terms such as codes and names, and give scores that are hard to threshold reliably across queries.

Fixes: combine dense retrieval with BM25 in hybrid search; rerank the top candidates with a cross-encoder that reads the question and passage together; use embedding models trained for retrieval with separate query and document modes; and add metadata filters. Base decisions on reranker scores rather than raw cosine values. RAG.NextUpgrad applies hybrid retrieval, fusion and reranking, then a confidence gate, so answers rely on evidence that actually supports them.

## How do you set a similarity threshold in a LangChain FAISS retriever?

Create the retriever with `search_type="similarity_score_threshold"` and pass `search_kwargs={"score_threshold": 0.5, "k": 5}`. Only documents whose relevance score exceeds the threshold are returned, up to k.

Relevance scores in LangChain are normalised to a zero-to-one range, but how they are computed depends on the distance strategy: FAISS defaults to L2 distance, converted into a relevance score, so pick thresholds by testing. Normalise embeddings and use inner product or cosine settings for more interpretable scores. Calibrate by running known relevant and irrelevant queries, then choose a threshold that keeps relevant results while filtering noise. Too strict a threshold returns nothing for valid questions, so log empty results.

# What is faiss-cpu? How FAISS works, large data, rotation, production use, and imports
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/faiss-cpu-production-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


faiss-cpu is the CPU-only Python package of FAISS, Facebook AI Similarity Search, Meta's open-source library for fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors such as text and image embeddings. You install it with pip and use it to find the nearest vectors to a query, exactly or approximately. Retrieval is central to RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers faiss-cpu, how FAISS works, rotations, large data, production use, FAISS versus Pinecone, a combined workflow, imports, and whether FAISS is a database.

## What is faiss-cpu?

faiss-cpu is the pip package that installs FAISS without GPU support, running on any machine's CPU. Install it with `pip install faiss-cpu`, then `import faiss` in Python. A GPU-enabled build exists for systems with supported NVIDIA GPUs, usually installed through conda.

The CPU version is fast enough for most applications up to millions of vectors, especially with approximate indexes, and is the easiest option for laptops, servers and cloud functions. It uses optimised CPU instructions and multithreading. Use the GPU build when indexing or searching very large collections where speed matters greatly. For most student projects and small RAG applications, faiss-cpu with a flat or HNSW index answers queries in milliseconds, so start there.

## How does FAISS work?

FAISS stores vectors in an index and answers queries by computing distances, L2 or inner product, between the query and candidates. Flat indexes compare against all vectors exactly; approximate indexes narrow the search with clustering, graphs or compressed codes.

Key index families: IVF partitions vectors into clusters and searches the nearest ones; HNSW navigates a graph of neighbours; product quantisation compresses vectors into short codes to save memory. Combinations, written as factory strings like "IVF1024,PQ32", balance memory, speed and recall. You tune parameters such as `nprobe` to trade accuracy for speed. FAISS also includes k-means clustering, useful on its own for grouping embeddings, for example clustering support tickets or documents by topic.

## Can FAISS handle rotation?

FAISS supports rotation as a vector transform: random rotations and learned rotations such as OPQ, optimised product quantisation, can be applied before quantisation to distribute information evenly across dimensions and reduce quantisation error.

If you mean finding rotated images or objects, FAISS itself does not provide rotation invariance; that depends on your embedding model. Use embeddings that are robust to rotation, or augment your index with embeddings of rotated versions. FAISS faithfully searches whatever vectors you give it, so invariances must come from how the vectors are produced.

## Can FAISS handle large data?

Yes. FAISS was designed for billion-scale search: with IVF and product quantisation, billions of vectors fit in memory as compact codes, and GPU builds accelerate indexing and search. Meta's research demonstrated billion-scale similarity search on GPUs.

Strategies for large data: choose compressed indexes such as IVF-PQ, train them on a representative sample, shard indexes across machines, use memory-mapped indexes for on-disk storage, and tune `nprobe` for recall. Measure recall against exact search on a sample. Beyond a single machine, distributed vector databases may be simpler than managing sharded FAISS yourself.

## Is FAISS good for production?

FAISS is production-grade as a search library: fast, mature and widely used inside large systems. But it is not a complete production service: you must add persistence, an API, concurrency handling, updates and deletes, metadata filtering, monitoring and backups.

It works well in production when the index is mostly static or rebuilt periodically, such as nightly re-indexing of a document collection, and when you control the serving process. For frequently changing data, many concurrent writers, or complex filters, a vector database built on similar algorithms saves engineering effort.

## How can FAISS be used in production?

A common pattern is building the index offline, saving it with `write_index` or `serialize_index`, loading it in each API server at startup, and serving searches through your own endpoint, with metadata stored in a regular database mapped by IDs.

Production checklist:

- Use `IndexIDMap` so results map to database IDs.
- Rebuild or update indexes on a schedule, swapping atomically.
- Store index files in object storage with versioned names.
- Load indexes read-only in multiple server instances.
- Monitor latency and recall with test queries.
- Keep the embedding model version recorded with each index.

## FAISS vs Pinecone: which should I choose?

Choose FAISS for free, local, fully controlled vector search embedded in your application, ideal for research, offline processing, prototypes and static indexes. Choose Pinecone for a managed database with persistence, scaling, filtering and updates without operating infrastructure.

FAISS costs nothing but engineering time and server resources; Pinecone costs a subscription but removes operational work. Data control favours FAISS; convenience favours Pinecone. Many teams use both at different stages: experiment with FAISS locally, then move to a managed or self-hosted database when the application needs live updates and multiple users.

## How do I prototype with FAISS and move to Pinecone?

Prototype retrieval with FAISS locally: embed your documents, build an index, test queries and tune chunking. When ready for production, create a Pinecone index with the same dimension and metric, upsert the same embeddings with metadata, and switch your retrieval code to query Pinecone.

Keep retrieval behind a small interface, such as functions `add`, `search` and `delete`, so switching backends changes one module. Use the same embedding model in both, or re-embed everything if you change it. Compare recall on your test questions after migration to confirm results match, then add Pinecone-specific features such as namespaces and metadata filters.

## How do I import FAISS in Python?

Install the package first with `pip install faiss-cpu`, then use `import faiss`. The import name is `faiss` regardless of whether you installed the CPU or GPU build.

Common problems: installing a package named "faiss" instead of "faiss-cpu", which does not work; using a Python version without available wheels; or mixing conda and pip installations. Check with `python -c "import faiss; print(faiss.__version__)"`. If installation fails on a new Python version, use a slightly older Python in a virtual environment, or install through conda-forge.

## Is FAISS a database?

No. FAISS is a library for vector similarity search and clustering that runs inside your application's memory. It has no built-in server, persistence layer, transactions, user management or metadata filtering like a database.

You can save and load indexes as files, and build database-like features around it, but for a ready-made vector database, use options such as Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Chroma, Pinecone or PostgreSQL with pgvector. Several of these use FAISS-like algorithms internally. Think of FAISS as an engine and vector databases as complete vehicles. Choosing between them depends on whether you want to build the rest of the vehicle yourself or prefer to drive one that is ready.

# FAISS explained: full form, vectors, vs Chroma, Pinecone and pgvector, metadata, storage
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/faiss-explained-vs-chroma-pinecone/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


FAISS, Facebook AI Similarity Search, is an open-source library from Meta for fast similarity search over dense vectors, used to find nearest neighbours among millions or billions of embeddings. It is a library, not a database, which explains most comparisons. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense retrieval with BM25, so this page covers FAISS's full form, what a FAISS vector is, why people choose it, how it differs from vector databases, comparisons with Chroma, Pinecone and pgvector, metadata and where to store indexes.

## What is the full form of FAISS?

FAISS stands for Facebook AI Similarity Search. It was released as open source by Facebook AI Research, now Meta AI, in 2017, and is written in C++ with Python bindings, with GPU support through CUDA.

The library came from research on billion-scale similarity search, described in a paper by Jeff Johnson, Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou, and it remains maintained by Meta on GitHub under the MIT licence. It is used widely in research and production, inside vector databases and frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex, and directly in applications needing fast nearest neighbour search. The name is usually pronounced like the word face.

## What is a FAISS vector?

A FAISS vector is simply a dense float32 vector, such as a text or image embedding, added to a FAISS index. FAISS stores these vectors, possibly compressed, and finds those nearest to a query vector.

Vectors must all share the same dimension, set when creating the index, and are passed as NumPy arrays of shape number of vectors by dimension. Each vector receives a sequential integer ID, or a custom ID with an IndexIDMap wrapper. Depending on the index type, FAISS keeps vectors exactly, quantizes them into compact codes, or links them in a graph. FAISS does not create vectors; an embedding model does, and FAISS only indexes and searches them.

## Why is FAISS better?

FAISS is fast, flexible and free: it offers many index types, from exact search to compressed and graph indexes, supports GPUs, scales to billions of vectors, and runs in-process without a server, which makes it ideal for research and embedded use.

Its index factory lets you combine methods, such as inverted files with product quantization, to trade memory, speed and recall precisely. Research benchmarks often use FAISS as a reference implementation. It is better than a full database when you want maximum control and performance in a single process. It is worse when you need database features, such as metadata filtering, updates from many clients, replication and access control, which require additional engineering.

## How does FAISS differ from other vector databases?

FAISS is a library, not a database. It provides vector indexes and search inside your process, while vector databases such as Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus or Pinecone add persistence, metadata filtering, APIs, replication, access control and operational tooling.

With FAISS, you manage saving and loading indexes, mapping IDs to documents, handling updates and scaling across machines. Vector databases handle those concerns for you and expose network APIs for multiple applications. Some databases, such as Milvus, can use FAISS-style indexes internally. Choose FAISS for prototypes, offline batch jobs, research and single-process apps; choose a vector database for multi-user production systems that need filtering, durability and concurrent writes.

## Which is better, FAISS or Chroma?

Chroma is easier for building applications: it stores documents, metadata and embeddings together, supports filters, and persists data automatically. FAISS is faster and more configurable for pure vector search at large scale but leaves storage and metadata to you.

For a RAG prototype with a few thousand to a few hundred thousand chunks, Chroma's developer experience usually wins. For very large collections, GPU acceleration or research on index types, FAISS gives more control. LangChain and LlamaIndex support both, so switching is straightforward. Compare them on your data if performance matters, measuring recall, latency and memory. For multi-user production, consider whether either fits, or whether a server-based vector database is better.

## Which is better, FAISS or Pinecone?

Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database with metadata filtering, scaling and operations handled for you. FAISS is a free library you run and manage yourself. Choose Pinecone for managed production; choose FAISS for control, cost and offline use.

Pinecone removes infrastructure work: no servers, automatic scaling, backups and an API usable from any service, at a usage-based cost. FAISS has no service fees, runs anywhere, including offline, and can be extremely fast, but you must build persistence, filtering, updates and scaling. Data residency matters too: Pinecone stores your vectors in its cloud. Teams often prototype with FAISS and move to a managed or self-hosted database when production needs grow.

## FAISS vs pgvector: which should you use?

Use pgvector when your application already uses PostgreSQL and you want vectors alongside relational data with SQL filters and transactions. Use FAISS for in-memory, high-performance search in a single process, research or offline pipelines.

pgvector gives durability, replication, backups and access control automatically through PostgreSQL, and handles millions of vectors well with HNSW indexes. FAISS offers more index types, GPU acceleration and finer control, and can be faster for huge in-memory workloads, but lacks database features. A common pattern: FAISS for experiments and evaluation of retrieval approaches, then pgvector or a vector database in production. Benchmark both with your data and filters before committing.

## Can FAISS store metadata?

No. FAISS indexes store only vectors and their integer IDs. Metadata such as document text, source, page or user permissions must be stored elsewhere and linked to FAISS IDs by your application.

Frameworks such as LangChain wrap FAISS with a docstore that keeps text and metadata in a Python dictionary, saved alongside the index, which is why LangChain's save_local writes both an index file and a pickle file. Filtering by metadata usually happens after search, by retrieving extra candidates and discarding those that do not match, which can hurt recall for selective filters. If metadata filtering is central, a vector database with native filters is usually a better choice.

## How do you map FAISS IDs to metadata?

Wrap your index with IndexIDMap, or IndexIDMap2, and add vectors with your own integer IDs, such as database primary keys. After search, use the returned IDs to look up metadata in a dictionary, SQLite table or database.

A practical setup: store documents in SQLite or PostgreSQL with an integer primary key, add vectors to FAISS with add_with_ids using the same keys, and query metadata with WHERE id IN the returned IDs. This keeps the mapping stable even after deletions. For pre-filtering, some indexes accept an IDSelector to restrict search to allowed IDs. Keep the index and metadata store in sync when inserting or removing documents, ideally in one update routine.

## Where should you store a FAISS index?

Save the index to disk with faiss.write_index and load it with faiss.read_index. Store the file locally, on a mounted volume in containers, or in object storage such as S3 and download it at startup.

Large indexes can be memory-mapped with the IO_FLAG_MMAP flag for some index types, reducing startup time and RAM use. Version index files together with their metadata store and the embedding model name, since mismatches break results. For services with multiple replicas, either load a read-only index in each replica and rebuild periodically, or move to a vector database designed for shared, updatable storage. Back up indexes like any other critical data.

# What is a FAISS index? How it works, using it, saving it, and FAISS vs Chroma, Qdrant
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/faiss-index-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A FAISS index is the core data structure of FAISS, Meta's open-source library for efficient similarity search: you add vectors, such as text or image embeddings, and query for the nearest neighbours of a new vector, exactly or approximately, on CPUs or GPUs. FAISS is widely used inside RAG pipelines, research and other vector databases. I build retrieval systems like RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers FAISS indexes, how they work, using, growing and saving them, and comparisons with ChromaDB, Milvus, Qdrant and Pinecone.

## What is a FAISS index?

A FAISS index stores vectors in a structure optimised for nearest-neighbour search. FAISS offers many index types, from `IndexFlatL2`, which compares the query with every vector exactly, to approximate indexes such as IVF, HNSW and product quantisation that trade a little accuracy for big speed and memory gains.

You choose an index by collection size, memory budget, speed and recall requirements. Index factory strings, such as "IVF4096,PQ64", let you compose index types concisely. FAISS runs in memory within your application, which makes it very fast but means you manage persistence, updates and metadata yourself, unlike a database. Many vector databases and frameworks use FAISS-style algorithms internally, so understanding its index types helps you tune any vector search system.

## How does a FAISS index work?

Flat indexes compute distances to all vectors, guaranteeing exact results. IVF indexes cluster vectors around centroids and search only the closest clusters. HNSW indexes build a multi-layer graph of neighbours and navigate it. Product quantisation compresses vectors into short codes so billions fit in memory.

At query time, FAISS computes distances, L2 or inner product, between the query and candidate vectors, returning the top-k IDs and distances. Parameters such as `nprobe` for IVF or `efSearch` for HNSW control the speed-recall trade-off. GPU versions accelerate both building and searching for very large collections.

## How do I use a FAISS index?

Install FAISS, create an index with your vector dimension, add vectors as a float32 NumPy array, then search with query vectors to get distances and indices of nearest neighbours.

```python
import faiss, numpy as np
d = 384
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)                 # inner product on normalised vectors = cosine
vecs = np.random.rand(1000, d).astype("float32")
faiss.normalize_L2(vecs); index.add(vecs)
q = vecs[:1].copy()
D, I = index.search(q, 5)
print(I[0], D[0])
```

Map returned indices back to your documents with a separate list or dictionary. For cosine similarity, normalise vectors and use an inner-product index. Install the CPU build with `pip install faiss-cpu`, or a GPU build where available for your platform.

## How do I add vectors to a FAISS index incrementally?

Call `index.add()` again with new vectors; flat and HNSW indexes accept additions at any time. To control IDs, wrap the index in `IndexIDMap` and use `add_with_ids`, which lets you map results to database IDs and remove vectors later.

IVF and product quantisation indexes must be trained once on representative data with `index.train()` before adding; you can then add vectors incrementally, but if the data distribution shifts a lot, retrain for good recall. HNSW supports adding but not efficient removal. For frequent updates and deletes, a vector database is often more convenient than managing FAISS yourself.

## How do I write a FAISS index to memory?

Use `faiss.serialize_index(index)` to convert an index into a NumPy byte array in memory, and `faiss.deserialize_index(array)` to restore it. For files, use `faiss.write_index(index, "index.faiss")` and `faiss.read_index`.

In-memory serialisation is useful for storing indexes in databases, object storage, caches or sending them between processes. Remember to save your ID-to-document mapping alongside the index, since FAISS stores only vectors and integer IDs. For large indexes, memory-mapped reading options reduce loading time and RAM use. A common pattern in web services is building the index offline, uploading the serialised bytes to object storage, and loading them at startup, so every server instance has the same index without rebuilding. Version the file name with the embedding model and date, so you never mix indexes built with different models.

## Why choose FAISS over ChromaDB?

Choose FAISS for maximum speed and control, large-scale or GPU-accelerated search, research and benchmarking, and embedding vector search directly in your application without running a database. It offers many index types and tuning options.

Choose ChromaDB when you want a simple, developer-friendly database with persistence, metadata filtering, document storage and an API out of the box, especially for prototypes and small to medium RAG apps. FAISS requires you to build those features yourself. Many teams prototype with Chroma for convenience and use FAISS where performance or custom indexing matters.

## FAISS vs ChromaDB: what is the difference?

FAISS is a C++ library with Python bindings for similarity search; it has no built-in persistence layer, metadata filtering or server. ChromaDB is an open-source vector database that stores embeddings, documents and metadata, supports filtering, and runs embedded or as a server.

Chroma is easier for typical RAG use: add documents, query with filters, persist automatically. FAISS is faster to tune for large collections and offers GPU support and advanced compression. For a student RAG project, Chroma or pgvector reduces glue code; for research on retrieval efficiency, FAISS gives more control.

## What is the difference between FAISS and Milvus?

FAISS is a library for in-process vector search. Milvus is a distributed, open-source vector database built for production at large scale, with persistence, replication, filtering, multiple index types and management tools. Milvus can use FAISS-style indexes internally.

Use FAISS for embedded search, offline jobs and experiments. Use Milvus when many users and services need a shared vector database with updates, deletes, scaling across machines and operational features. Milvus adds infrastructure complexity, so choose it when scale and concurrency justify running a distributed system.

## What is the difference between FAISS and Qdrant?

FAISS is a search library; Qdrant is a vector database written in Rust with an API, persistence, payload filtering during search, hybrid search with sparse vectors, quantisation and distributed mode. Qdrant uses its own HNSW implementation rather than FAISS.

Qdrant suits applications needing filtered search, multiple clients and production operations. FAISS suits applications that keep vectors in memory inside one process, or research comparing index types. Qdrant also offers a local mode for development, giving a database-like experience without a separate server.

## What is the difference between FAISS and Pinecone?

FAISS is a free, open-source library you run yourself; Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed cloud vector database with APIs, scaling, metadata filtering and hybrid search, with no infrastructure to manage.

FAISS gives control, zero licence cost and offline use, but you handle persistence, scaling and updates. Pinecone trades control and cost for convenience and managed reliability. For prototypes and research, FAISS or local databases work well; for production teams without operations capacity, managed services like Pinecone reduce effort. Evaluate recall, latency and cost on your own data. Keeping retrieval behind a small interface in your code makes it easy to start with FAISS and switch to a managed service later.

# When to use async in FastAPI: how it works, asyncio, Starlette, Pydantic, Flask, React
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-async-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Use async in FastAPI when your endpoint spends time waiting on I/O that has async libraries, such as calling AI model APIs with an async HTTP client, querying databases through async drivers, or streaming responses; write `async def` and `await` those calls. For blocking libraries, use plain `def`, and FastAPI runs it in a thread pool. FastAPI powers the back ends of my AI products, including FaceVision's embedding service, so this page covers async decisions, how it works, Starlette and Pydantic, Flask, Django and React.

## When should I use async in FastAPI?

Use async when handling many concurrent requests that mostly wait on network or disk I/O: calling external APIs such as language models, querying databases with async drivers, reading from caches, and streaming data. Async lets one process serve many waiting requests efficiently.

Do not use async for CPU-heavy work, such as image processing or running local models, which blocks the event loop; offload that to worker processes, background task queues or thread pools. For simple CRUD apps with low traffic, sync code is fine. Async shines in AI services, where requests often wait seconds for model responses, and in real-time features like WebSockets. FineTune Studio, for example, streams live training loss to the browser over WebSockets, a natural fit for async endpoints.

## When should I use async def in FastAPI?

Use `async def` when everything inside the endpoint that waits is awaitable, for example `await client.get()` with httpx or `await session.execute()` with an async database driver. Use plain `def` when you call blocking libraries, such as the standard requests library or a sync database driver.

The key mistake is calling blocking code inside `async def`, which freezes the event loop and slows every request. If you must call blocking code in an async endpoint, use `run_in_threadpool` or `asyncio.to_thread`. When unsure, plain `def` is safe because FastAPI runs it in a thread pool automatically, while still performing well for many applications.

## Why is FastAPI async?

FastAPI is async because it is built on Starlette and the ASGI standard, designed for Python's async and await features. This lets a single server process handle thousands of concurrent connections, such as slow API calls, long-polling and WebSockets, without a thread per request.

Async matters most for I/O-bound services, which is most web APIs: they spend their time waiting for databases, networks and other services. By switching between requests while each waits, the event loop keeps CPUs busy and latency low. FastAPI still supports sync endpoints, so you can adopt async gradually where it helps.

## How does async work in FastAPI?

An ASGI server such as Uvicorn runs an event loop. When an `async def` endpoint awaits I/O, it yields control, letting the loop process other requests; when the I/O completes, the endpoint resumes. Sync `def` endpoints run in a thread pool so they do not block the loop.

Dependencies can also be async or sync, and FastAPI resolves them before calling your endpoint. Background tasks run after the response is sent. For streaming, `StreamingResponse` with an async generator sends data as it is produced, ideal for streaming language model tokens to users, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with cited answers.

## Does FastAPI use asyncio?

Yes. FastAPI runs on asyncio by default through Starlette and the AnyIO library, which also supports the Trio event loop. You write standard `async` and `await` code, and the ASGI server manages the asyncio event loop.

You can use asyncio features inside endpoints, such as `asyncio.gather` to run several API calls concurrently, timeouts with `asyncio.wait_for`, and async libraries like httpx, asyncpg and redis-py's asyncio client. Avoid creating your own event loops inside endpoints; work within the one the server provides. For example, a RAG endpoint can run keyword and vector searches concurrently with `asyncio.gather`, cutting retrieval latency roughly to that of the slower search rather than the sum of both.

## Does FastAPI use Starlette?

Yes. FastAPI is built on top of Starlette, a lightweight ASGI framework that provides routing, requests and responses, middleware, WebSockets, background tasks and static files. FastAPI adds data validation, dependency injection and automatic API documentation on top.

Because of this, Starlette features work directly in FastAPI: custom middleware, `StreamingResponse`, `FileResponse` and WebSocket endpoints. Knowing Starlette helps when you need lower-level control, such as custom middleware for logging or authentication. Performance largely comes from Starlette and the ASGI server underneath.

## How does FastAPI use Pydantic?

FastAPI uses Pydantic models to validate and parse request data, such as JSON bodies, query parameters and headers, converting types automatically and returning clear 422 errors for invalid input. It also uses Pydantic for response models, filtering and serialising output.

From the same models, FastAPI generates the OpenAPI schema, which powers the interactive documentation at `/docs`. Pydantic version 2, with its Rust-based core, made validation much faster. Use separate models for input, database records and output, so internal fields such as password hashes never leak into API responses.

## When should I use FastAPI vs Flask?

Choose FastAPI for APIs needing validation, automatic documentation, async I/O, high concurrency or streaming, including AI and machine learning services. Choose Flask for simple, synchronous web apps, quick prototypes, or projects relying on Flask's large extension ecosystem.

FastAPI's type-hint-driven design reduces boilerplate and catches errors early, and its generated docs help front-end teams. Flask is minimal and flexible, with many tutorials and extensions for templates, authentication and admin panels. For new API-first projects, especially those calling language models, FastAPI is usually the better default. Flask has added async support, but FastAPI was designed around it from the start.

## Can I use Django and FastAPI together?

Yes. Common patterns include running Django for the admin panel, ORM and traditional pages, and FastAPI for high-performance or async API endpoints, either as separate services sharing a database, or by mounting both under one ASGI application.

Using Django's ORM inside FastAPI requires care, since it is mostly synchronous; run ORM calls in a thread pool or use its async query methods where available. Many teams find it simpler to keep them as separate services. A gradual migration is also common: keep existing Django pages running and build new API features in FastAPI, sharing authentication through tokens. Alternatively, Django Ninja offers a FastAPI-like API style within Django itself.

## Can I use FastAPI with React?

Yes, it is a popular stack: FastAPI serves a JSON API, and a React front end, built with Vite or Next.js, calls it over HTTP. Enable CORS in FastAPI for your front-end origin during development and in production if domains differ.

Practical setup: define Pydantic models for API contracts, generate TypeScript types from FastAPI's OpenAPI schema, use authentication with tokens or cookies, and deploy the front end to a static or Next.js host and FastAPI to a server or container platform. For AI features, stream responses from FastAPI to React to show answers as they generate.


---

# FastAPI for AI applications: async endpoints for LLM calls, dependency injection, streaming responses, and the patterns that hold up in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why is FastAPI the default choice for serving AI applications?

**Because an AI application spends most of its request time waiting on slow network calls, a model API, an embedding call, a vector database query, and FastAPI's async support means the server can handle other requests during that wait instead of blocking a whole worker thread on it [1][6]. Combined with automatic request validation from type hints, a built-in docs UI, and dependency injection for clean wiring of providers and settings, it removes most of the boilerplate a Flask-based service would need to hand-build for the same job.**


Both production systems I run day to day, a RAG platform and a document extraction service, are FastAPI applications underneath, and the async layer is not a nice-to-have, it is the difference between a server that serves five concurrent users and one that serves fifty on the same hardware [11][12].

> A synchronous web server serving LLM calls is a waiter who stands at one table until the kitchen finishes a dish, ignoring everyone else in the restaurant. Async is the waiter who takes the next order while the first dish cooks.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does async actually help when the model call is still slow?

**The model call itself is not made faster by async; a five-second generation still takes five seconds. What async changes is what the server does during that five seconds: instead of one worker thread sitting idle waiting for the response, `await`ing an async HTTP call to the model API frees that worker to handle other incoming requests, and resumes this one when the model's response arrives [6]. One process can then hold many concurrent slow requests in flight, which is exactly the shape of load an LLM-backed API sees.**



## What is the single most common FastAPI mistake in AI apps?

**Calling a synchronous client inside an `async def` route. If your model provider's SDK, or your database driver, does not itself support async and you call it directly inside an async route without offloading it, that call blocks the event loop exactly the way a fully synchronous server would, silently cancelling the whole benefit of using FastAPI. The fix is to use the provider's async client if one exists, or run the blocking call in a thread pool with `run_in_threadpool` so it does not block the event loop while it waits.**



## How does dependency injection fit into an AI application?

**FastAPI's dependency injection system is where the clean project structure of settings, providers, and database sessions actually gets wired into each incoming request [2]. A `get_settings()` dependency provides typed configuration; a `get_llm_client()` dependency provides the model provider instance; a `get_db_session()` dependency provides a database session scoped to the request and closed automatically afterward. Routes declare what they need as parameters, and FastAPI resolves and injects them, which keeps route functions thin and makes swapping a provider or a database a change in one place, not a search-and-replace across the codebase.**




## How do I stream LLM responses token by token?

**Return a `StreamingResponse` whose body is an async generator that yields chunks as they arrive from the model provider's streaming API, rather than collecting the full response before returning anything [4]. Most model providers expose a streaming mode over server-sent events specifically for this [5]. The user sees the answer appear progressively, which cuts perceived latency dramatically even though total generation time is unchanged, because the wait for the first token is far shorter than the wait for the whole answer.**



## When do I need background tasks versus a real task queue?

**FastAPI's built-in `BackgroundTasks` is for quick, fire-and-forget work tied to a single request's lifecycle, sending a notification email after a response is returned, with no need to track its status or retry it [3]. A real task queue, Celery or an equivalent, is for anything that needs retries, scheduling, monitoring, or to survive the web server restarting, a long document-processing job, a nightly re-embedding run, a batch of API calls that must complete even if the request that triggered them is long gone [8]. Reaching for background tasks when you actually need a queue is how "fire and forget" jobs quietly disappear when the server restarts mid-job.**



## What does a clean FastAPI layer for an AI app look like?

**Routes stay thin: parse the request, resolve dependencies, call into the application's core logic, return a response, ideally streamed. All the actual work, retrieval, generation, validation, sits in the modules described in a proper project structure, not inline in the route function [10]. Settings come from dependency injection, never read directly from the environment inside a route. Errors from the model provider are caught and translated into clean HTTP error responses, not leaked as raw provider exceptions.**



## FastAPI interview questions for AI roles

**Explain why async matters specifically for LLM-backed APIs. Describe how dependency injection would wire a swappable model provider. Explain how you would stream a model's response to a frontend. Compare BackgroundTasks with a real task queue and say when each applies. Describe the most common way a FastAPI app silently loses its async benefits. The strongest answer includes a concurrency bug you found and fixed, not just the theory.**



## Where should I start?

**Take an existing script that calls a model API and wrap it in a FastAPI route with a streaming response and one dependency for the client. An evening turns a script into a real, concurrent-capable service.** For a hands-on session on serving AI applications with FastAPI, from a script to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Why is FastAPI so popular? Install, docs, ORM choices and production use
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-guide-orm-production/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs, popular because it is fast to write and fast to run: you declare inputs with Python type hints, and FastAPI validates requests, converts data and generates interactive documentation automatically. It is the backend I used across my NextUpgrad applications, including RAG.NextUpgrad and FaceVision's embeddings service. This page covers its popularity and history, installation, the docs, how it achieves performance, ORM choices, production use, how it compares with Node.js, and FastAPI Cloud.

## Why is FastAPI so popular?

FastAPI is popular because it combines very quick development with strong correctness: type hints drive request validation, editor autocompletion and documentation, while async support gives good performance. Developers write less code and catch errors earlier.

Other reasons: automatic OpenAPI documentation with interactive Swagger UI, clear error messages for invalid requests, dependency injection for things like database sessions and authentication, and excellent documentation. It also fits the AI era well: most machine learning and LLM work happens in Python, so FastAPI is the natural way to wrap models, RAG pipelines and agents in a web API. For students, its tutorial is one of the best introductions to building APIs properly.

## When was FastAPI invented?

FastAPI was created by Sebastián Ramírez and first released in December 2018. It builds on Starlette for web handling and Pydantic for data validation.

It grew quickly over the following years as teams adopted it for machine learning services and microservices, and it became one of the most used Python web frameworks alongside Django and Flask. Its design reflected newer Python features, such as type hints and async, that older frameworks predated. The project is open source under the MIT licence and maintained on GitHub with a large community.

## How do I install FastAPI?

Create a virtual environment, install FastAPI with its standard extras, write a small app and run it with the FastAPI CLI.

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
```

```python
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

```bash
fastapi dev main.py        # development server with auto-reload
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` to see the interactive documentation. For production, use `fastapi run` or a server setup such as Uvicorn with multiple workers behind a reverse proxy. Pin versions in a `requirements.txt` file, keep the virtual environment out of Git, and read settings such as database URLs from environment variables, so the same code runs on your laptop and in deployment.

## What are FastAPI's docs?

FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI schema for your API and serves interactive documentation at `/docs`, using Swagger UI, and alternative documentation at `/redoc`. They update as you change your code.

The docs list every endpoint, its parameters, request bodies and response models, derived from your type hints and Pydantic models, and let you send test requests from the browser. Add descriptions, examples and tags in your code to make them clearer. For public APIs you can disable them or protect them in production. The underlying OpenAPI schema, at `/openapi.json`, can generate client libraries for front ends and other services.

## How does FastAPI achieve high performance?

FastAPI runs on ASGI, an asynchronous server interface, using Starlette and servers such as Uvicorn, so it can handle many concurrent requests efficiently when endpoints use `async` and non-blocking I/O. Pydantic's fast validation core adds to this.

Performance in practice depends on your code: blocking calls, such as a synchronous database driver or heavy CPU work inside an `async` endpoint, slow everything down. Use async database drivers or define those endpoints with plain `def`, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool. For CPU-heavy tasks, such as running a large model, use background workers or separate model servers. Most real bottlenecks are databases and external API calls, not the framework.

## Does FastAPI have an ORM?

No. FastAPI does not include an ORM; it leaves data access to you. Most projects use SQLModel or SQLAlchemy for SQL databases, or an ODM such as Beanie for MongoDB.

This keeps FastAPI focused and flexible: you choose the database layer that suits your project and can use raw SQL when needed. A common pattern is a dependency that provides a database session to each request and closes it afterwards, plus Alembic for schema migrations. Keep database models separate from API schemas when they differ, so you never accidentally expose fields like password hashes in responses.

## What is the best ORM for FastAPI?

SQLModel is the most natural choice for many projects because it is made by FastAPI's author and combines SQLAlchemy and Pydantic, so one class can serve as both the database table and the API schema. SQLAlchemy 2.0 is the most powerful and flexible option for complex applications.

Choose by need:

- **SQLModel**: simple CRUD apps and learning; less boilerplate.
- **SQLAlchemy 2.0**: complex queries, large codebases, full control; async support available.
- **Tortoise ORM**: an async-first, Django-like ORM.
- **Beanie**: MongoDB with Pydantic models.

Whatever you pick, use migrations with Alembic for SQL databases, connection pooling, and tests against a real database, not only mocks.

## Can FastAPI be used in production?

Yes. FastAPI is used in production by many companies and startups for APIs and machine learning services. Production readiness depends on how you deploy and operate it, not on the framework.

A production checklist:

- Run with `fastapi run` or Uvicorn workers behind a reverse proxy, or in containers.
- Use environment variables for configuration and secrets.
- Add structured logging, metrics and health checks.
- Validate inputs strictly and set request size and timeout limits.
- Handle authentication and rate limiting.
- Run database migrations and keep backups.
- Write tests with FastAPI's TestClient and run them in CI.

RAG.NextUpgrad and my other NextUpgrad apps shipped this way, with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics.

## FastAPI vs Node.js: which should I use?

Use FastAPI when your backend is close to Python's ecosystem, such as machine learning, data processing, RAG and AI agents. Use Node.js when your team works in JavaScript or TypeScript across front end and back end, or you rely on its large web ecosystem.

Both handle high concurrency well with async I/O. Node.js frameworks such as Express, Fastify and NestJS are mature and widely used; TypeScript gives strong typing comparable to FastAPI's type hints. FastAPI's automatic validation and docs are excellent out of the box. Many teams use both: a Next.js front end with its own server routes, and a FastAPI service for AI features, communicating over a clean API.

## Is FastAPI Cloud free?

FastAPI Cloud is a deployment platform from the team behind FastAPI, introduced to make deploying FastAPI apps simple. Its availability, plans and any free tier depend on its current offering, so check its official website.

FastAPI itself is free and open source, and you can deploy it on many platforms with free tiers for small projects, such as container hosts and serverless platforms that support Python. For student projects, a free tier on a platform such as Render, Railway or a cloud provider's free allowance is usually enough. Watch for cold starts on free tiers, keep secrets in environment variables, and add a health endpoint so the platform can check your app.

# What is FastAPI in Python? Uses, examples, running it, Docker and templates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-python-examples/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


FastAPI is a Python framework for building web APIs: you write functions with type hints, and FastAPI turns them into HTTP endpoints with automatic request validation, JSON responses and interactive documentation. It is widely used to serve machine learning models and LLM features, and it is the backend I used for RAG.NextUpgrad and my other NextUpgrad applications. This page explains what it is used for, shows examples, covers running it with and without Uvicorn and in notebooks, and gives a Dockerfile and production template guidance.

## What is FastAPI in Python?

FastAPI is an open-source Python web framework for building APIs quickly and correctly. It uses standard Python type hints with Pydantic models to validate inputs and shape outputs, and runs on ASGI servers for asynchronous performance.

You define endpoints as functions decorated with the HTTP method and path, such as `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")`. FastAPI reads the type hints to parse path, query and body parameters, rejects invalid requests with clear errors, and documents everything automatically at `/docs`. It also provides dependency injection, which handles shared resources such as database sessions and authentication cleanly. The result is less boilerplate and fewer bugs than hand-written validation.

## What is FastAPI used for in Python?

FastAPI is used to build REST and JSON APIs, serve machine learning and LLM models, power retrieval-augmented generation backends, create microservices, handle webhooks, and build internal tools and admin backends.

Common examples:

- An inference endpoint that runs a model and returns predictions.
- A RAG API that retrieves passages and streams a cited answer.
- A backend for a React or Next.js front end.
- Webhook receivers for payment or messaging services.
- Data and automation APIs that other teams call.

Its async support suits I/O-heavy work, such as calling databases and external APIs; for heavy CPU work, pair it with background workers. Because it is plain Python, the code that loads a model or a vector index in a notebook moves into an endpoint with little change, which is why data scientists and ML engineers adopt it quickly.

## How do I use FastAPI in Python?

Install it, create an app, define endpoints with type hints and Pydantic models, and run it with the FastAPI CLI. The interactive docs at `/docs` let you test endpoints immediately.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str
    top_k: int = 5

@app.post("/ask")
def ask(q: Question):
    return {"question": q.text, "top_k": q.top_k, "answer": "stub"}
```

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
fastapi dev main.py
```

Send an invalid body, such as a string for `top_k`, and FastAPI returns a clear 422 error explaining what is wrong.

## What are some FastAPI examples in Python?

Typical examples are a CRUD API with a database, a file upload endpoint, an authenticated endpoint with dependencies, a streaming response for LLM output, and a background task. Here is a streaming example.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import time

app = FastAPI()

def tokens():
    for word in "Retrieval augmented generation grounds answers in documents".split():
        yield word + " "
        time.sleep(0.1)

@app.get("/stream")
def stream():
    return StreamingResponse(tokens(), media_type="text/plain")
```

Streaming like this is how chat interfaces show answers as they are generated. The FastAPI documentation has tutorials for each pattern, from path parameters to security.

## How do I run a FastAPI server?

During development, run `fastapi dev main.py`, which starts a server with auto-reload on port 8000. In production, run `fastapi run main.py` or Uvicorn with several worker processes, usually behind a reverse proxy.

Production basics: set the host to `0.0.0.0` inside containers so the server is reachable, choose the number of workers based on CPU cores, configure timeouts, and run behind a proxy or load balancer that handles HTTPS. Keep settings in environment variables. Add a health endpoint for monitoring and container orchestration.

## How do I run FastAPI with Uvicorn?

Install Uvicorn, then point it at your app object with `module:variable` syntax, for example `uvicorn main:app --reload` for development or with workers for production.

```bash
uvicorn main:app --reload                               # development
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4  # production-style
```

The FastAPI CLI uses Uvicorn under the hood, so `fastapi run` and `uvicorn` give similar results; the CLI just picks sensible defaults. Use `--reload` only in development, since it watches files and restarts. In containers, a single Uvicorn process per container with scaling handled by the platform is a common pattern.

## Can I run FastAPI without Uvicorn?

Yes. FastAPI is an ASGI application, so any ASGI server can run it, such as Hypercorn or Granian. Uvicorn is simply the most common and the default used by the FastAPI CLI.

Alternative servers may offer features such as HTTP/2 or different performance characteristics; benchmark with your workload before switching. For testing, you do not need a server at all: FastAPI's `TestClient` calls your app directly in Python, which is how unit tests usually work. Serverless platforms that support ASGI can also host FastAPI through adapters. Whichever server you choose, keep application code independent of it, so switching servers later is a one-line change in your start command or container configuration rather than a rewrite.

## Can I run FastAPI in a Jupyter notebook or Colab?

Yes, with care. For testing logic, use `TestClient` in the notebook to call endpoints without a server. To run a real server, start Uvicorn in a background thread so it does not block the notebook's event loop.

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
client = TestClient(app)
print(client.post("/ask", json={"text": "What is RAG?"}).json())
```

For a live server in Colab, you would also need a tunnel to reach it from outside, which exposes your app publicly, so protect it and stop it afterwards. For anything beyond quick experiments, move the code into a `.py` file and run it with the FastAPI CLI locally or in a container.

## What is a good Dockerfile example for Python FastAPI?

A simple, production-friendly Dockerfile uses a slim Python base image, installs dependencies first for caching, copies the app, and runs it with the FastAPI CLI on all interfaces.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["fastapi", "run", "main.py", "--port", "8000"]
```

Add a `.dockerignore` to keep virtual environments and secrets out of the image, pass configuration through environment variables, and run as a non-root user for better security. Build with `docker build -t myapi .` and run with `docker run -p 8000:8000 myapi`.

## What is a production-ready FastAPI template?

The FastAPI team maintains a full-stack template with FastAPI, SQLModel, PostgreSQL, a React front end, Docker Compose, authentication, migrations and tests, which is a good reference for production structure.

What a production setup should include, whether from a template or your own:

- **Structure**: routers by feature, separate schemas and models, a settings module.
- **Database**: SQLModel or SQLAlchemy with Alembic migrations.
- **Security**: authentication, CORS configuration, input limits, secrets in environment variables.
- **Observability**: structured logging, metrics, health checks.
- **Quality**: tests with TestClient, linting and CI.
- **Deployment**: Dockerfile, Compose for local services, and a platform for production.

Start from a template, but understand every piece; delete what you do not need.

# What is FastAPI in simple words? Starting a server, GET example, WebSockets and auth
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-simple-words-websockets/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


In simple words, FastAPI is a Python framework that lets you build web APIs, the back-end services apps talk to, quickly and safely: you write normal Python functions with type hints, and FastAPI turns them into web endpoints, checks incoming data, and creates interactive documentation automatically. It is popular for AI services because Python is the language of AI. FastAPI powers back ends in my products, including FaceVision, so this page explains FastAPI and APIs simply, starting a server, a GET example, WebSockets and their authentication, choosing between FastAPI and Flask, and AI agents simply.

## What is FastAPI in simple words?

FastAPI is a tool for building the part of an app that runs on a server and answers requests. You write Python functions, mark them with a route like `/users`, and FastAPI makes them available over the internet, checking that incoming data is correct.

Imagine a restaurant: the front end is the menu customers see, and the API is the kitchen taking orders and sending dishes back. FastAPI helps you build the kitchen with clear rules about what orders look like. It is fast to write, fast to run, and generates a web page at `/docs` where you can test every endpoint without extra tools.

## What is an API, and what is FastAPI?

An API, application programming interface, is a set of rules that lets one program request data or actions from another, for example a mobile app asking a server for your order history. Web APIs usually exchange JSON over HTTP.

FastAPI is a framework for building web APIs in Python. You define endpoints, the URLs and methods such as GET and POST, and the data they accept and return; FastAPI handles routing, validation, conversion to JSON and documentation. Other frameworks include Flask and Django in Python, and Express in JavaScript. FastAPI stands out for type-hint-based validation and automatic docs.

## How do I start with FastAPI?

Install Python, create a virtual environment, install FastAPI, write a small app in `main.py`, and run it with the FastAPI command. Then open the automatic documentation in your browser to test it.

Steps:

- `python -m venv .venv` and activate it.
- `pip install "fastapi[standard]"`.
- Create `main.py` with `app = FastAPI()` and one route.
- Run `fastapi dev main.py`.
- Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

Next, follow the official tutorial: path and query parameters, request bodies with Pydantic, dependencies, databases and testing. Build a small project, such as a notes API, as you learn. Writing tests with FastAPI's TestClient from the start makes later changes much safer.

## How do I start a FastAPI server?

For development, run `fastapi dev main.py`, which starts a server with automatic reload on code changes. For production, run `fastapi run main.py` or Uvicorn directly, such as `uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4`.

On hosting platforms, set the start command to bind to the platform's port, often from a `PORT` environment variable. Use multiple workers or a process manager for production traffic, and put a reverse proxy in front for HTTPS. If the server does not start, check for import errors, a port already in use, or a wrong module path in the command.

## What is a FastAPI GET example?

A GET endpoint returns data. This example returns a greeting and accepts an optional query parameter:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/greet/{name}")
def greet(name: str, lang: str = "en"):
    message = "Namaste" if lang == "hi" else "Hello"
    return {"message": f"{message}, {name}"}
```

Visiting `/greet/Asha?lang=hi` returns `{"message": "Namaste, Asha"}`. FastAPI validates that `name` and `lang` are strings and documents both in `/docs`. Add response models to control output, and use path parameters for identifiers and query parameters for options and filters.

## Can I use WebSockets in FastAPI?

Yes. FastAPI supports WebSockets for real-time, two-way communication, such as chat, live dashboards, notifications and streaming progress. Define an endpoint with `@app.websocket`, accept the connection, then send and receive messages in a loop.

```python
from fastapi import WebSocket
@app.websocket("/ws")
async def ws(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    while True:
        text = await websocket.receive_text()
        await websocket.send_text(f"echo: {text}")
```

Handle disconnects with `WebSocketDisconnect`, and use a connection manager for broadcasting. FineTune Studio streams live training loss to the browser this way. For multiple server instances, share messages through Redis pub/sub or a similar broker, since each process only knows its own connections. For one-way streaming, such as AI responses, server-sent events or streaming HTTP responses are often simpler than WebSockets.

## How do I authenticate WebSockets in FastAPI?

Browsers cannot set custom headers such as Authorization when opening a WebSocket, so header-based dependencies like HTTPBearer often fail. Instead, pass a token in a query parameter, a cookie, or the first message, validate it before accepting, and close the connection with a policy-violation code if invalid.

Dependencies with `Depends()` do work on WebSocket endpoints, but they must read from sources the WebSocket provides, such as `Query` or `Cookie`, and raise `WebSocketException` rather than `HTTPException`. Prefer short-lived tokens, since query strings may appear in logs, or issue a one-time ticket from an authenticated HTTP endpoint. Always use secure WebSockets, `wss://`, in production.

## When should I choose FastAPI?

Choose FastAPI for API-first back ends, especially when you want automatic validation and documentation, async I/O for calling external services, streaming responses, or Python-based AI and machine learning features.

It fits mobile app back ends, microservices, AI inference and RAG services, internal tools' APIs and webhook receivers. Its type hints make large codebases easier to maintain, and the generated OpenAPI schema helps front-end teams. For full websites with server-rendered pages and an admin panel, Django may be more complete; for tiny scripts, Flask or FastAPI both work.

## Why choose Flask over FastAPI?

Choose Flask when you want maximum simplicity for small synchronous apps, rely on Flask's mature extension ecosystem, maintain existing Flask code, or build server-rendered pages with Jinja templates where API validation and async matter less.

Flask has a huge body of tutorials, extensions for authentication, admin and forms, and a gentle learning curve. FastAPI has advantages for modern APIs, but Flask remains perfectly capable for many projects. Team familiarity matters: a team experienced in Flask may deliver faster with it. For new AI-heavy APIs, FastAPI is usually the stronger default.

## What is an AI agent in simple words?

An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to work towards a goal by deciding steps and taking actions with tools, such as searching the web, reading files or updating a system, rather than only answering a question.

For example, asking an agent to "find three laptops under my budget and make a comparison table" leads it to search, read product pages, compare specifications and build the table. Agents need limits and supervision because they can make mistakes. Many AI agents run on back ends built with frameworks like FastAPI, which expose their tools as API endpoints.
