# How to get Gemini Pro for free, and what Gemini Pro offers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-pro-free-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


You can use Gemini Pro for free in three ways: the free Gemini app gives limited access to Google's Pro model, Google AI Studio lets developers try Pro models with free quotas, and Google has run time-limited offers that include the paid Google AI Pro plan at no cost for eligible students and for some telecom customers in India, such as Jio users. This page explains those routes, what the Pro plan adds, how Gemini, Flash, Pro and thinking modes differ, daily limits, family sharing, and how Gemini relates to Antigravity.

## How can I get Gemini Pro for free?

Use the free Gemini app, which includes limited access to the Pro model, use Google AI Studio for free developer access, or claim an official offer that includes Google AI Pro at no cost if you are eligible.

The options in order of effort:

- **Free Gemini app**: sign in at gemini.google.com or the mobile app; free accounts get some Pro model use with lower limits.
- **Google AI Studio**: a developer playground where you can try current models, including Pro, with free usage quotas.
- **Official offers**: Google has run student offers and telecom partnerships that include the paid plan for a limited period.

Offers change often, so confirm eligibility on Google's own pages. Avoid "free Gemini Pro" links shared in groups; they are a common route for phishing and account theft.

## Is Gemini Pro free for students?

Google has offered its paid AI plan free for a limited period to students in several countries, including India, through verification with a college email or student ID. Whether an offer is open today depends on the country and date.

When an offer is live, you sign in with a personal Google account, verify student status through Google's verification partner, and the plan is applied for the stated period. It usually renews at the normal rate afterwards unless you cancel, so note the end date. Even without an offer, students can do a lot on the free tier: explaining concepts, debugging code, summarising lecture notes and planning projects. NotebookLM, also from Google, is free and very good for studying from your own notes and papers.

## How do I get Gemini Pro with Jio?

Reliance Jio and Google announced a partnership in 2025 that gives eligible Jio users access to Google AI Pro at no cost for a limited period. Eligible users claim it from the MyJio app with the Google account they want to use.

Open the MyJio app, look for the Google Gemini or Google AI Pro offer banner, check the eligibility conditions, which have depended on age group and plan, and follow the steps to link your Google account. The benefit then appears in the Gemini app and Google One. Rules, eligible plans and duration are set by Jio and Google and have changed since launch, so rely on the MyJio app and Google's announcement, not on screenshots shared online. Never enter OTPs or passwords on links that claim to unlock the offer.

## What does Gemini Pro offer?

The Google AI Pro plan gives higher access to Google's most capable Gemini models, longer context for big files, Deep Research, video and image generation with higher limits, Gemini inside Gmail and Docs, NotebookLM with higher limits, and extra cloud storage.

For students and developers the useful parts are:

- More use of the Pro model and thinking modes for hard maths and code.
- Deep Research, which browses many sources and writes a cited report.
- Uploading long PDFs and codebases thanks to a large context window.
- Gemini in Gmail, Docs and Sheets for drafting and analysis.
- Higher limits in Google's coding tools.

The exact feature list and limits change as Google updates the plan, so check the plan page on Google One. If you mostly ask quick questions, the free tier is enough.

## What is the difference between Gemini and Gemini Pro?

Gemini is Google's family of AI models and the name of its assistant app. Gemini Pro refers either to the Pro model, the most capable tier in a Gemini generation, or to the Google AI Pro subscription that gives more access to it.

The model family has tiers: Flash-Lite for the cheapest, fastest tasks, Flash for most everyday work, and Pro for complex reasoning and coding. Some generations also add a deeper thinking mode on top. The Gemini app picks a model for you unless you choose one. The subscription changes your limits and features, not the model itself: a free user and a paid user asking the Pro model the same question get the same quality of answer, but the free user runs out sooner.

## What is the difference between Gemini Flash and Pro?

Flash is the faster, cheaper model tuned for everyday tasks and high volume. Pro is the more capable model for complex reasoning, difficult code and long multi-step work, and it is slower and more expensive per request.

In practice:

- Use **Flash** for summaries, emails, quick explanations, extraction from documents and chat features in your app.
- Use **Pro** for debugging a tricky bug, designing a system, solving hard maths, or long analysis where a wrong step costs more than waiting.

For developers building with the Gemini API, Flash is usually the right default because latency and cost matter at scale. Start with Flash, measure where it fails, and route only those cases to Pro. That routing pattern is how most production AI apps keep costs under control.

## When should I use Gemini Pro vs thinking mode?

Pro is a model tier; thinking is a way of running a model, where it reasons step by step before answering. Use a thinking mode when the task needs several steps of logic, and a standard fast mode when it does not.

Thinking helps with maths and physics problems, competitive programming, debugging, planning a project and comparing options with many constraints. It adds waiting time and uses more of your limits, so it is wasted on simple questions, rewriting text or quick facts. If an answer from the fast mode seems shallow or contradicts itself, rerun the same prompt with thinking on. For developers, the Gemini API exposes thinking controls on models that support it, so you can set how much reasoning to spend per request.

## How many Gemini Pro queries do I get per day?

It depends on your plan: free accounts get a small daily allowance of Pro model prompts, and paid plans get much more. Google lists the current limits in the Gemini Apps help centre, and they change from time to time.

Limits are also counted per feature: Pro model prompts, Deep Research reports, image generation and video generation each have their own allowance. When you reach a limit, the app usually falls back to a faster model or asks you to wait. To stretch a free allowance, use Flash for routine tasks, write one clear, complete prompt instead of many short follow-ups, and save Pro and thinking for the problems that need them. Developers using the API have separate rate limits shown in Google AI Studio.

## Can I share Gemini Pro with family?

Partly. Google AI Pro is a Google One plan, and its cloud storage can be shared with up to five family members in a Google One family group. Whether the Gemini features are shared too depends on the plan and country.

Set up a family group from your Google account, invite members, then enable sharing in Google One settings. Each member keeps their own private files and chats; sharing never exposes your Gemini conversations or Drive files to others. Google has been extending AI benefits to family members in some regions, so check the Google One help pages for your country before assuming everyone in the group gets Pro features. Offer-based plans, such as student or telecom offers, may have their own sharing rules.

## Does Gemini Pro include Antigravity?

Antigravity is Google's agent-first coding environment and is offered separately from the Gemini app. Individuals have been able to use it without a paid plan within rate limits, and Google AI subscriptions have come with higher limits.

Antigravity runs coding agents that plan and carry out tasks across an editor, a terminal and a browser, using Gemini models and some models from other providers. Because it is new, its pricing, limits and the benefits attached to Google AI plans have changed several times, so check Google's Antigravity site and the plan page before deciding. For learning to code with AI, the free options, such as Antigravity's free limits, Gemini in the browser, or Gemini Code Assist's free tier for individuals, are usually enough.

# Can Gemini make videos? Length, sound, photo to video, editing, analysis and watermarks
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-video-generation-veo/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, Gemini can create short videos from text prompts or photos using Google's Veo models, typically eight-second clips with generated sound, with daily limits that depend on your plan. It can also analyse videos you upload. I build AI products on several model providers and follow their multimodal features closely, so this page covers video creation, length, sound, photo to video, failed generations, editing, video analysis, the watermark you may notice, and why Gemini makes mistakes.

## Can Gemini create videos?

Yes. In the Gemini app, you can describe a scene and Gemini generates a short video with Google's Veo model, including motion, camera movement and, with recent versions, audio. Availability and daily limits depend on your subscription and country.

Write prompts like a director: subject, action, setting, style, camera angle, lighting and sound, for example a slow dolly shot of a tea stall at dawn with steam rising and soft street ambience. Shorter, concrete prompts usually work better than long stories. Developers can access Veo through the Gemini API and Vertex AI, and Google's Flow tool offers more control for filmmakers. Generated videos follow Google's usage policies, which restrict harmful or deceptive content.

## How long are Gemini videos?

Videos generated in the Gemini app are typically eight seconds long, at 720p or 1080p depending on the model and tool. Each generation produces one short clip rather than a full-length video.

Generation usually takes a minute or two, depending on load. Clip length is limited because video generation is computationally expensive and quality degrades over longer durations. For longer content, creators generate several clips and combine them in an editor, keeping characters and style consistent through careful prompts or reference images. Specifications change with model updates, so check Google's current help pages for exact durations, resolutions and daily generation limits for your plan.

## Can Gemini make videos longer than 8 seconds?

Not in a single generation in the Gemini app, where clips are about eight seconds. Google's Flow tool can extend scenes by generating continuations, and you can stitch multiple clips together in any video editor.

To make a longer piece, plan a storyboard of shots, generate each shot as a separate clip, keep descriptions of characters, clothing, lighting and style identical across prompts, and use the last frame of one clip as a reference for the next where supported. Then edit the clips together with music and transitions in tools such as CapCut, DaVinci Resolve or Google Vids. Consistency between clips is the hardest part, so review each one before generating the next.

## Does Gemini make videos with sound?

Yes, with Veo 3 and later models. Gemini can generate native audio together with the video, including sound effects, ambient noise, music and spoken dialogue with matching lip movements, based on your prompt.

Describe the audio explicitly for best results: background sounds, music mood, and dialogue in quotes with who speaks it. Results vary: speech may be slightly off, and complex conversations can drift out of sync. If you need precise narration, generate the video and record or synthesise the voiceover separately, then combine them in an editor. Generating realistic voices of real people without consent is restricted and can be harmful, so use original characters.

## Can Gemini make videos from photos?

Yes. Gemini's photo-to-video feature lets you upload an image and describe the motion and sound you want, then Veo animates it into a short clip. It suits bringing illustrations, product shots or landscapes to life.

Use photos you own or have rights to, and avoid animating images of real people without consent, since policies restrict misleading or harmful content involving identifiable people. Describe movement precisely, such as gentle wind moving the leaves while the camera slowly zooms in, and specify audio. Results work best with clear subjects and simple backgrounds. Like other Gemini videos, outputs carry watermarks, and features may vary by plan and region.

## Why is Gemini not generating videos?

Common causes: your plan or country does not include video generation yet, you reached the daily limit, the prompt triggered safety filters, the service is busy, or you are using a work or school account where the feature is disabled.

Fixes: check that the video option appears in the Gemini app for your account; wait for the daily limit to reset; rephrase prompts that mention real people, brands, violence or other restricted content; try again later if generation stalls; update the app or switch to the web version; and sign in with a personal account if admin settings block the feature. Google's Gemini Apps Help pages list current availability by plan and region.

## Can Gemini edit videos?

Not in the sense of a timeline editor. Gemini can analyse your video, suggest cuts, write captions and scripts, and generate new clips, but it does not directly trim, splice or colour-grade your existing video files.

For AI-assisted editing, combine Gemini with editing tools: ask Gemini to summarise footage and list timestamps of key moments, then cut those in an editor; generate B-roll clips with Veo to fill gaps; and draft titles and descriptions. Google Vids offers AI help for creating work videos, and YouTube's creation tools include AI features. As tools evolve, more direct editing may arrive, so check current features in Google's apps.

## How does Gemini analyse videos?

Gemini models are natively multimodal: they process sampled video frames, typically about one frame per second, along with the audio track, so they can describe scenes, transcribe speech, answer questions and point to timestamps.

You can upload a video file or share a YouTube link in the Gemini app, or send video through the Gemini API, and ask questions such as summarise this lecture, list the steps shown, or when does the speaker mention the deadline. Long videos consume many tokens, so very long recordings may need splitting. Fast motion between sampled frames can be missed, so ask for timestamps and verify important details by watching the relevant segments.

## Why is there a flickering Gemini logo on videos?

The logo is usually Gemini's visible watermark, added to AI-generated videos to show they were made with Google's tools. Compression or playback in some apps can make the overlay appear to flicker.

Gemini videos also carry SynthID, an invisible digital watermark that can identify Google AI-generated content even after edits. The visible mark helps viewers recognise AI content, which matters as realistic video becomes easy to create. Do not try to remove watermarks to pass videos off as real footage; that can mislead people and may violate terms. If the flicker appears in your own exports, re-encode with a higher bitrate or try a different player to check whether it is a playback artefact.

## Why does Gemini make so many mistakes?

Like all language models, Gemini predicts plausible text rather than looking up guaranteed facts, so it can hallucinate, misread ambiguous prompts, rely on outdated knowledge, or make arithmetic and reasoning slips, especially on niche or recent topics.

Reduce mistakes by giving context and constraints, asking it to search the web or use uploaded documents, requesting sources, breaking complex tasks into steps, and choosing a stronger model for hard reasoning. Typos and odd lettering can appear in generated images and videos because image models render text imperfectly. For important uses, verify key facts. In my own products, grounding answers in retrieved evidence with citations, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, is the most reliable way to cut errors.

# Why does Gemini add a watermark? SynthID, images, text, and who owns Gemini
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gemini-watermark-synthid/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini adds watermarks so that images, video and audio it generates can be recognised as AI-made. Many images carry a small visible Gemini mark, and Google embeds an invisible digital watermark called SynthID in generated media, designed to survive cropping, compression and filters. This page explains why, how it applies to edited photos and to text, how to check for watermarks, why removing them is a bad idea, who made and owns Gemini, and the real risks of using it.

## Why does Gemini add a watermark?

To make AI-generated content identifiable. As generated images and videos become realistic, watermarks help people, platforms and fact-checkers tell synthetic media from real photos and footage, reducing misinformation and misuse.

Google uses two layers. A visible mark tells viewers at a glance that an image came from Gemini. SynthID, developed by Google DeepMind, embeds an imperceptible signal in the content that detection tools can read even after common edits. Google has also joined industry efforts on content provenance, such as the C2PA standard, which attaches information about how content was made. Watermarking is part of responsible deployment and increasingly expected by platforms and regulators.

## Why does Gemini add a watermark to images?

Generated and AI-edited images can be mistaken for real photos, so Gemini marks them. A visible watermark appears on many images created in the Gemini app, and SynthID is embedded invisibly in the pixels.

The invisible watermark matters more than the visible one: a logo can be cropped out, but SynthID is designed to remain detectable after resizing, compression, colour changes and screenshots, though no watermark is impossible to defeat. Whether a visible mark appears can depend on the product, plan and feature, and Google has changed this over time. For professional use, check the current terms for your plan, and in any case disclose that an image is AI-generated when it could mislead.

## Does Gemini put a watermark on photos you edit?

Yes. When Gemini edits a photo with AI, the result is treated as AI-generated or AI-modified media and receives SynthID, and often a visible mark, even though it started as your own photo.

That is intentional: an edited photo with a changed background, added objects or altered faces is exactly the kind of image that could mislead if presented as unedited. For harmless uses, such as a cleaner background for a project poster, the watermark simply records the edit. For official documents, such as ID or passport photos, do not use AI edits at all; use a real photo and approved tools. Never edit images of other people in ways they have not agreed to.

## Does Gemini add a watermark to text?

Google has developed SynthID for text, which subtly adjusts how the model chooses words to embed a statistical signal, and it has applied this in its Gemini products. Unlike images, text watermarks are fragile and do not prove authorship.

Text watermarking works by nudging token choices in a way that is invisible to readers but detectable statistically over enough text. Heavy editing, paraphrasing, translation or very short passages weaken the signal. Google published the method and open-sourced a version for developers. For students, the key point is that neither watermarks nor "AI detectors" are reliable judges of whether an essay was AI-written; follow your college's rules on AI use and be transparent about how you used it.

## Can you tell if text was written by Gemini?

Not reliably by reading it, and not reliably with public AI detectors, which produce many false positives, including on genuine human writing. SynthID text detection exists, but it needs access to the watermark scheme and enough unedited text.

Signs often cited, such as generic phrasing, certain words or very even structure, appear in human writing too, so they are weak evidence. If you are a teacher or reviewer, ask the writer to explain their work, show drafts or discuss the topic; understanding is the real test. If you are a student using AI, keep your notes and drafts, write in your own voice, and declare AI assistance where required. Accusations based only on detector scores are unfair and often wrong.

## How do I check for a Gemini watermark?

Look for the visible Gemini mark on the image, and use Google's SynthID verification tools, which Google has made available for checking whether content contains its watermark, including through the Gemini app for images.

Upload or share the image to the verification feature and it reports whether SynthID was detected. A negative result does not prove an image is real: it may come from another AI tool that uses no watermark, or the watermark may have been damaged. Provenance metadata under the C2PA standard can also show an image's history where supported. For news and claims that matter, combine tools with traditional checks: reverse image search, the original source and context.

## What is the best Gemini watermark remover?

Removing watermarks to hide that an image is AI-generated is deceptive, can break Google's terms of use, and may break platform rules or laws in some places, so this page does not recommend tools for it. The invisible SynthID watermark is also designed to survive most edits.

If the visible mark gets in the way of a legitimate use, better options are: check whether your plan or a different Google tool offers outputs suited to professional use; generate the image with enough margin and compose it in a design tool without hiding its origin; or use stock photos or your own photography where a real image is needed. Labelling content as AI-generated is increasingly expected and builds trust with your audience.

## Who made Gemini?

Gemini was made by Google DeepMind, Google's AI research lab, formed in 2023 by merging Google Brain and DeepMind. Google announced the first Gemini models in December 2023.

The models were developed by large teams across Google DeepMind and Google Research, building on Google's earlier work, including the Transformer architecture published by Google researchers in 2017. The Gemini app, previously called Bard, is built by Google's product teams on these models. Gemini models are also available to developers through Google AI Studio, the Gemini API and Vertex AI on Google Cloud.

## Who owns Gemini?

Google owns Gemini. Google is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., so Alphabet is the ultimate parent company. Gemini products follow Google's terms of service and privacy policy.

That ownership matters for data: conversations in the Gemini app are stored in your Google account according to your activity settings and may be reviewed to improve services, as Google discloses; work and school accounts follow their organisation's Google Workspace settings. Developers using the Gemini API agree to Google's API terms, which differ between free and paid tiers. Read those terms before sending sensitive information.

## Is Gemini dangerous?

Gemini is not dangerous in itself, but like any powerful AI tool it has real risks: confident wrong answers, privacy exposure if you share sensitive data, realistic fake images in the wrong hands, and over-reliance that weakens your own skills.

Use it safely:

- Verify facts, especially health, legal and financial information, with official sources.
- Keep passwords, OTPs, identity numbers and other people's private information out of chats.
- Review activity settings and delete conversations you do not need kept.
- Label AI-generated images and never create misleading images of real people.
- Use it to learn faster, not to skip learning.

Google applies safety filters and watermarking, but responsible use is still up to you.

# GenAI and LLM interview questions with answers: RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, agents, evaluation and system design, from both sides of the table
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What do GenAI engineer interviews actually ask?

**Six things, in some order: LLM fundamentals, tokens, context, attention, hallucination; RAG, how you build and evaluate retrieval; fine-tuning, when and how with LoRA; prompting and agents, including safety; evaluation and cost, how you know it works and what it costs; and one system design where you assemble the pieces. Plus a walkthrough of a project you built, which is where most decisions get made. Definitions get you past the first minute. Trade-offs and stories get you the offer.**


I have sat on both sides: interviewing candidates for SCULT INDIA and being interviewed for GenAI roles. The pattern is consistent enough that this page is the preparation I now give mentees, with the answers I would want to hear. Longer notes are on the portfolio [11][12].

> The question is never really "what is RAG". The question is "have you built one, and do you know what broke". Answer the second question every time.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## LLM fundamentals: what will they ask?

**Expect: what is a token and why does it matter for cost; what is the context window and one failure mode of long contexts; explain attention in one minute; what is hallucination and how do you manage it; open-weight versus API models for a given product; what is the difference between a base model and an instruct model. Answer each with the concept in one sentence, then a consequence for a product you built.**



## RAG interview questions

**Expect: explain RAG end to end; why is chunking important and how do you choose a size; why add keyword search to embeddings; what does a reranker do; how do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation; how do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer; how would you handle multi-tenant documents. Every question maps to a stage of the pipeline; know the pipeline and you know the questions.**



The paper to cite is Lewis et al. [1]; the metric framework most interviewers know is RAGAS [7]. The answer that separates candidates is to the evaluation question: "I measure retrieval recall on twenty labelled questions before I look at a single generated answer, because a system can be faithful to the wrong passage."

## Fine-tuning interview questions

**Expect: when would you fine-tune instead of using RAG; explain LoRA and QLoRA; how do you prepare a dataset; how do you read a loss curve; what is catastrophic forgetting; how do you evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly; can you fine-tune GPT. The trap question is "how would you teach the model our product facts", and the right answer is "I would not, I would retrieve them, and fine-tune only for the voice and format".**



## Prompt engineering and agent interview questions

**Expect: system prompt versus user prompt and why the split matters for security; what is prompt injection and how do you limit its damage; when does chain-of-thought help and when does it waste tokens; how do you test a prompt; what is an agent and where does the model's judgement actually belong; how would you stop an agent taking a harmful action; when is a workflow better than an agent. Safety questions are where candidates who have only prototyped get exposed.**


The references interviewers respect: chain-of-thought [5], ReAct for agents [6], OWASP for security [9], and Anthropic's guide for the workflow-versus-agent distinction [10]. The answer to "how do you stop a harmful action" is not a clever prompt; it is least-privilege tools and a human confirmation for anything irreversible.


## Evaluation and cost questions

**Expect: how do you know your system works; what metrics do you track; how do you test a prompt change before deploying; how much does this feature cost per month; how would you cut that cost in half; what do you log. The interviewer is testing whether you treat an LLM system like software. Answer with a fixed evaluation set, metrics per stage, a CI check, tokens logged per request, and a cost model: input plus output tokens times price times requests.**



## System design questions for GenAI roles

**Expect one design in 30 to 45 minutes: a support chatbot over company documents, a document extraction service, a coding assistant, a voice assistant for a regional language. Structure it: clarify users and constraints, draw the request path, name each component and its failure mode, say what you would measure, estimate cost, and state what you would cut for version one. Interviewers grade the trade-offs you name unprompted, not the boxes you draw.**



## Behavioural and project questions

**Expect: tell me about a project; what broke and what did you do; a time you disagreed with a technical decision; how you handle a requirement you think is wrong; why this role. For the project question, use one project and go deep: the problem, the decision you made, the failure you hit, the fix, the measured result. My RAG platform's confidence gate exists because of a failure; that story has done more for me in interviews than any definition.**


My separate note on the "tell me about a project" question, with the structure and a worked example, is on the portfolio [13].

## Coding rounds for GenAI roles

**Expect Python: parse and validate a JSON output against a schema; implement reciprocal rank fusion over two ranked lists; write a retry with backoff around an API call; chunk a text by paragraphs with a size cap; compute cosine similarity; write a small evaluation loop. Rarely leetcode-style puzzles. Write clear, typed, tested code, talk while you write, and handle the edge case out loud. The interviewer is watching how you work, not whether you finish.**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    """Fuse ranked lists of ids; 1/(k+rank) per list, summed. A common coding-round question."""
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```

## How should freshers prepare for a GenAI interview?

**Build one RAG project and one fine-tune before the interview, so every answer has a story. Read four papers: transformer, RAG, LoRA, QLoRA. Write the evaluation set for your project, because the evaluation question is where freshers lose. Rehearse the project walkthrough with a timer, failure by failure. Prepare three questions to ask about how the team evaluates and ships. Then be honest about what you have not done; the sentence "I have not done that, here is how I would start" gets hired.**



## Questions to ask the interviewer

**How do you evaluate model changes before they ship? What does your logging show for a bad answer? How often do requirements change and how do you handle it? Who owns prompt versions? What was the last production incident and what changed after? These tell you whether the team treats LLM systems as engineering, and they tell the interviewer you do.**



## Want a mock interview or a session for your batch?

**I run GenAI interview preparation sessions for final-year batches and tech clubs, with a live system design and a project walkthrough clinic.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Top GenAI and LLM interview questions, plus how to answer coding rounds
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-llm-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The top GenAI interview questions test three things: whether you understand how large language models work (tokens, embeddings, attention), whether you can design a real system with them (retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, evaluation, cost), and whether you can explain a project you built in depth. Coding rounds still test data structures and algorithms in Python or Java. This page lists the questions that come up most and how to answer them, the types of interview rounds, the coding problems to practise, and how to perform in a live coding round.

## What are the top GenAI interview questions?

Expect questions on how LLMs work, how RAG and fine-tuning differ, how to evaluate outputs, how to reduce hallucinations, and how to control cost and latency. Then expect a deep dive into your own project.

Questions that come up again and again:

- What is a transformer, and what does attention do?
- What are embeddings, and how is semantic search built on them?
- RAG or fine-tuning: when would you use each?
- How do you chunk documents, and how do you choose chunk size?
- How do you evaluate a RAG system? Separate retrieval recall from answer faithfulness.
- How do you reduce hallucinations? Grounding, citations, refusal on weak evidence.
- What is LoRA, and why does it make fine-tuning cheaper?
- How do you handle prompt injection in an app with tools?

Answer each with a concept, a trade-off and an example from something you built.

## What do GenAI interviews actually test?

They test whether you can ship, not just define terms. Interviewers check fundamentals, judgement about trade-offs, and evidence that you have built and debugged a real GenAI feature.

A typical GenAI role interview has a screening call, a coding round, a machine learning or GenAI concepts round, a system design round such as "design a document question-answering system for a company", and a project deep dive. The deep dive decides many offers. Prepare a two-minute walkthrough: the problem, the architecture, one hard bug, and how you measured quality. When I describe RAG.NextUpgrad, the parts that make the conversation are the specific choices: hybrid dense plus BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, and a confidence gate that refuses to answer on weak evidence. Specifics show you built it.

## What are the most asked LLM interview questions?

The most asked LLM questions cover architecture, training, inference and safety. A focused list beats memorising fifty answers you cannot explain.

Prepare short, clear answers to these:

- What is tokenisation, and why do token counts matter for cost?
- Self-attention and multi-head attention, in plain words.
- Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder models: examples of each.
- Pretraining versus instruction tuning versus RLHF.
- What does temperature do? What is top-p sampling?
- What is a context window, and what happens when you exceed it?
- KV cache: why it speeds up generation.
- Quantisation: what 4-bit loading trades away.
- LoRA and QLoRA: what is trained and what is frozen.
- Why do models hallucinate, and how do you measure it?

For each, have one sentence of definition and one practical consequence.

## What do LLM interview questions test?

They test whether you understand why models behave as they do, so you can make engineering decisions: which model to use, how to prompt it, when to retrieve, when to fine-tune, and how to keep cost and latency under control.

Interviewers rarely want maths for its own sake. A question about temperature is really asking whether you know to use low temperature for extraction and higher for brainstorming. A question about context windows is asking whether you know that stuffing more text can make answers worse, and that retrieval of the right passages beats long prompts. A question about fine-tuning is asking whether you know it changes behaviour and format, while RAG supplies facts. Link every answer to a decision you would make in a product.

## What types of questions are asked in an interview?

Most tech interviews mix four types: technical concept questions, coding problems, design questions, and behavioural questions about how you work with people and handle problems.

What each type looks for:

- **Concept questions** check fundamentals in your area, such as Python, databases, networks or LLMs.
- **Coding problems** check problem solving and clean code under time pressure.
- **Design questions** check how you structure a system and reason about trade-offs.
- **Behavioural questions**, such as "tell me about a conflict in your team", check ownership and communication.

For behavioural answers use the STAR structure: situation, task, action, result. Prepare five stories from projects, hackathons or college work that you can adapt to most questions.

## What are the top Python coding interview questions?

Common Python coding questions are classic problems on arrays, strings and hash maps, plus Python-specific checks on lists, dictionaries, generators and complexity.

Practise these until you can solve them cleanly:

- Two Sum with a dictionary in one pass.
- Valid parentheses with a stack.
- Longest substring without repeating characters with a sliding window.
- Group anagrams with a dictionary of sorted keys.
- Merge intervals after sorting.
- Top K frequent elements with `collections.Counter` or a heap.
- Binary search on a sorted array, and its variants.
- Level-order traversal of a binary tree with `collections.deque`.

Also expect Python questions: list versus tuple, how dictionaries work, mutable default arguments, generators and `yield`, and the time complexity of common operations.

## What are the top coding interview questions in Java?

Java coding rounds use the same core problems as any language, with extra questions on collections, object-oriented design and Java specifics such as `HashMap` internals and immutability.

The problem list overlaps with Python: Two Sum, reverse a linked list, detect a cycle, merge two sorted lists, valid parentheses, binary tree traversals, lowest common ancestor, number of islands with BFS or DFS, and simple dynamic programming such as climbing stairs and coin change. Java-specific topics to revise:

- `HashMap` versus `TreeMap` versus `LinkedHashMap`, and how hashing and collisions work.
- `String` immutability, `StringBuilder`, and `equals` versus `==`.
- Interfaces versus abstract classes.
- Checked versus unchecked exceptions.
- Basic concurrency: threads, `synchronized` and `ExecutorService`.

Write clean method signatures and name variables well; it shows.

## How do I answer coding interview questions?

Talk through a clear process: clarify the problem, give a simple solution, improve it, write clean code, then test it with edge cases. Interviewers grade your reasoning as much as the final answer.

A structure that works in every round:

- Restate the problem and ask about input size, edge cases and constraints.
- Describe a brute-force solution and its complexity in one sentence.
- Find the bottleneck and improve it, usually with a hash map, two pointers, sorting or a heap.
- Write the code while explaining each part.
- Walk through a small example and edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates.
- State the final time and space complexity.

If you get stuck, say what you are trying. Silence is the worst signal in a coding round.

## How should I code during an interview?

Write readable code first and clever code never. Use clear names, small helper functions and simple control flow, and test as you go rather than at the end.

Practical habits:

- Choose the language you are fastest in, usually Python, unless the role requires another.
- Write the function signature and a few test calls before the body.
- Prefer standard library tools such as `collections` and `heapq` in Python.
- Avoid premature optimisation; get a correct solution, then improve it.
- Handle edge cases explicitly instead of hoping they work.

In online assessments, read all the problems first and start with the one you can finish. Partial but correct solutions often score better than ambitious unfinished ones.

## Where can I practise coding interview questions?

LeetCode is the standard practice platform, and NeetCode organises the most useful LeetCode problems by pattern with video explanations. HackerRank and Codeforces are also widely used for assessments and contests.

Practise by pattern, not at random: arrays and hashing, two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search, linked lists, trees, graphs, heaps, backtracking and dynamic programming. Solve a few problems per pattern until you can recognise it in a new problem. Track problems you could not solve and redo them a week later. Add timed mock interviews with a friend, a mentor or an AI interviewer that asks you to explain aloud. For GenAI roles, also build and deploy one small RAG project, because a working project answers many interview questions at once.

# Generating synthetic data with ChatGPT, Copilot, LLMs and Python, plus healthcare uses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/generate-synthetic-data-chatgpt-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Synthetic data can be generated with chat assistants such as ChatGPT and Copilot, with LLM pipelines, or with Python libraries that model real distributions. Each suits different needs, from quick test fixtures to privacy-safe research datasets. I built FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning, where training data quality decides results, so this page covers ChatGPT, Copilot and generative AI, LLM and Python methods, where synthetic data comes from, whether it can replace real data, and uses in healthcare and market research. Can ChatGPT generate synthetic data? Yes. ChatGPT can generate synthetic text, such as questions, reviews and dialogues, and tabular data, either directly as CSV or JSON or by writing and running Python code that creates larger files with libraries such as Faker and NumPy. For small datasets, describe the schema, number of rows, value ranges and relationships, and ask for edge cases. For larger or statistically realistic data, ask it to write a script, which you can run and modify. Watch for repetitive examples and unrealistic distributions, so request variety explicitly and check summary statistics. Never paste real personal data to model from, and review OpenAI's terms if you plan to use outputs to train other models. Can Copilot generate synthetic data? Yes. GitHub Copilot can write scripts and test fixtures that generate synthetic data, such as Faker-based factories for users and orders, while Microsoft 365 Copilot can create sample tables in Excel or draft example records in documents. For developers, Copilot is most useful for producing data generators inside your codebase: seeded factories for tests, SQL insert scripts for development databases and mock API responses. Ask it to include boundary values, missing fields and unusual characters, which catch bugs. Review generated code for correctness and keep a fixed random seed so tests are reproducible. For business users, Copilot in Excel can produce realistic-looking sample data for demos and training spreadsheets. Can generative AI create synthetic data? Yes. Generative AI is one of the main ways to create synthetic data: language models produce text, diffusion models produce images, and specialised models such as CTGAN or variational autoencoders produce tabular data mirroring real distributions. Each type learns patterns from real data, then samples new examples. Image generators create training images for rare defects or unusual conditions, while text models create instruction datasets, conversations and labelled examples. Simulation complements generative AI, especially for robotics and autonomous driving, where rendered environments produce perfectly labelled data. Quality depends on how well the generator captures real variation, so always validate synthetic data against real samples before relying on it. How do you generate synthetic data using an LLM? Define the schema and target distribution, write a prompt template, vary seeds such as topics, personas and difficulty, request structured JSON output, generate in batches, then deduplicate, filter low-quality examples and validate against real data. Also asked as: how to generate synthetic data using llm Diversity is the main challenge, so build a seed list covering the space you need, such as fifty topics times five personas, rather than asking for many examples in one prompt. Use moderate temperature, and ask for edge cases explicitly. Filter with rules and an LLM judge, then review random samples by hand. Libraries such as distilabel organise these pipelines. For fine-tuning data, test the result with base-versus-tuned evaluation, as in FineTune Studio. How do you generate synthetic data in Python? Use Faker or Mimesis for realistic fake records, NumPy and SciPy for values from chosen distributions, scikit-learn's make_classification and make_regression for machine learning test sets, and SDV for synthetic tables learned from real data. Also asked as: how to generate synthetic data in python For test data, Faker creates names, addresses, emails and dates in many locales, including Indian formats. For statistical realism, fit an SDV model, such as GaussianCopula or CTGAN, on real data and sample new rows, then evaluate quality with SDMetrics. For classification experiments, make_classification controls the number of features, informative features and class balance. Set random seeds for reproducibility, save datasets with their generation scripts, and document the assumptions behind each distribution. Where does synthetic data come from? Synthetic data comes from rules and templates, statistical models fitted to real data, simulations such as game engines and digital twins, and generative AI models, including language models, GANs and diffusion models. Most methods start from real data or expert knowledge. Statistical and generative models learn patterns from real samples, so their quality and biases reflect that source. Simulations encode physics and scenarios designed by engineers, producing labelled images or sensor data. Rule-based generators follow formats specified by developers, suiting software testing. Knowing the origin matters, because it determines what the data can represent faithfully and where it may mislead, such as rare cases the source never contained. Can synthetic data replace real data? Not fully. Synthetic data can supplement real data, protect privacy, fill gaps and enable early testing, but final models and decisions should be validated on real data, since synthetic data can miss rare patterns or carry generator biases. Some tasks rely heavily on synthetic data successfully, such as software testing, simulation-trained robotics with real-world fine-tuning, and instruction tuning with LLM-generated examples. But a 2024 Nature paper on model collapse found that models trained repeatedly on generated data can degrade, losing diversity. The safest approach mixes synthetic with real data, measures performance on a real held-out test set, and tracks where synthetic examples help or hurt. Treat synthetic data as a tool, not a substitute for reality. What is the difference between real and synthetic data? Real data is collected from actual events, people or measurements. Synthetic data is generated artificially to resemble real data's structure and statistics, without corresponding to real individuals or events. Real data captures true complexity, including rare cases and messy errors, but may be scarce, costly, biased or restricted by privacy laws. Synthetic data is cheap to scale, privacy-friendlier and easy to label, but only as faithful as its generator, and it may smooth over important outliers. Real data is the ground truth for evaluation; synthetic data is best for augmentation, testing and sharing. Many projects use both, with clear labels showing which records are synthetic. What is synthetic data in healthcare? In healthcare, synthetic data means artificial patient records, medical images or clinical trial data generated to resemble real populations without exposing real patients. It supports research, software testing, education and AI development under strict privacy rules. Synthea, an open-source tool from MITRE, generates realistic synthetic patient histories, widely used for testing health software and interoperability standards such as FHIR. Generative models create synthetic medical images to augment rare conditions in training data. Benefits include faster data access and safer sharing, but risks remain: re-identification from poorly generated data and clinical patterns that do not match reality. Validate with clinicians, measure privacy risk, and confirm models on real, approved datasets before clinical use. How does synthetic data work in market research? In market research, synthetic data often means simulated survey responses or synthetic personas generated by language models conditioned on demographic profiles, used to pretest questionnaires, explore hypotheses and estimate likely reactions quickly. Also asked as: how synthetic data in market research works A 2023 study by Argyle and colleagues found that language models can reproduce some aggregate opinion patterns from real surveys, but such simulations also flatten diversity, reflect training biases and miss emerging trends. Synthetic panels are therefore best for early exploration, such as refining question wording or generating hypotheses, not for final decisions. Validate key findings with real respondents. Synthetic data also helps share research datasets safely, by generating records that preserve statistical relationships without exposing participants' identities.

# How long has generative AI existed? Agentic AI, OpenAI, vibe coding, art, music, apps
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/generative-ai-history-timeline/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Generative AI feels new, but it builds on decades of research; it became mainstream only in late 2022, when ChatGPT and image generators reached millions of people. Related ideas, from agents to AI music, have their own longer histories. I build AI products and teach students how the field evolved, so this page covers how long generative AI has existed, when it went mainstream, its development history, agentic AI, OpenAI, vibe coding, AI art and music, AI in production and AI apps. How long has generative AI existed? Simple generative models existed for decades, from statistical text generators to neural networks producing text and images. Modern generative AI took shape from 2014, when generative adversarial networks appeared, and accelerated after the transformer architecture arrived in 2017. Earlier milestones include Markov chain text generation described by Claude Shannon in 1948 and recurrent neural networks generating text in the 2010s. Variational autoencoders in 2013 and GANs in 2014 made realistic image generation possible. OpenAI's GPT models from 2018 showed that large transformers trained on text could write fluently. By 2022, diffusion models and chat interfaces brought these capabilities to everyday users. Each era expanded what machines could create. How long has generative AI been mainstream? Generative AI became mainstream in late 2022. Image generators such as Midjourney and Stable Diffusion spread during 2022, and ChatGPT's launch on 30 November 2022 brought conversational AI to millions within weeks. In 2023, generative features entered search engines, office software and phones, and businesses began adopting them widely. By 2024 and 2025, generative AI was built into products used daily by hundreds of millions of people, from writing assistants to coding tools and image editors. Adoption speed surprised even many researchers. Its mainstream era is therefore only a few years old, which explains why norms, regulations and best practices are still developing quickly. How long has generative AI been in development? Research behind generative AI spans more than seventy years, from early statistical language models to neural networks. The current wave builds on breakthroughs from 2014 to 2020: GANs, transformers, large-scale pretraining and diffusion models. Key steps include word embeddings in 2013, sequence-to-sequence models in 2014, attention mechanisms in 2015, the transformer in 2017, GPT and BERT in 2018, GPT-3 in 2020 showing few-shot abilities, and diffusion models reaching high image quality by 2021. Reinforcement learning from human feedback, refined between 2017 and 2022, made models helpful conversational assistants. Hardware advances, especially GPUs, made scaling possible. Each advance built on earlier work, compounding progress. How long has agentic AI been around? Agents have been studied in AI since its early decades, but agentic AI built on language models emerged in 2022 and 2023, with research such as ReAct and projects such as AutoGPT. Mainstream agent products arrived from 2024. Also asked as: how long has open ai been around · how long has ai apps been around Classic agents included planning systems, game-playing programs and reinforcement learning agents, such as those that mastered Go in 2016. Language models made general-purpose agents practical by understanding instructions and calling tools. Coding agents, browser agents and enterprise agents appeared in 2024 and 2025, including computer use, Claude Code and OpenAI's Operator. Agentic AI as a mainstream term is therefore only a few years old, though its foundations are decades older. How long has OpenAI been around? OpenAI was founded in December 2015 as a non-profit research organisation. It created a capped-profit company in 2019 and restructured its for-profit arm as a public benefit corporation in 2025, while the non-profit retained control. Its early work covered reinforcement learning and robotics, before shifting focus to large language models with GPT in 2018. GPT-3 in 2020, DALL-E in 2021 and ChatGPT in 2022 made it one of the most influential AI companies. Partnerships, especially with Microsoft, funded large-scale training. Its governance changes drew wide public attention. OpenAI's history reflects the broader shift of AI from academic research to products used by hundreds of millions of people. How long has vibe coding been around? The term vibe coding was coined by Andrej Karpathy in February 2025 to describe building software by prompting AI and accepting its code without close review. The practice grew from AI coding assistants available since 2021. GitHub Copilot launched as a preview in 2021, and chat-based coding with ChatGPT followed in late 2022. As models improved and agentic coding tools such as Cursor, Claude Code and app builders appeared, non-programmers began creating working apps through conversation. The term spread rapidly in 2025 and was widely discussed in media and dictionaries. Vibe coding is new as a term, but its foundations are only a few years older. How long has generative AI art been around? Computer-generated art dates to the 1960s and 1970s, with programs such as Harold Cohen's AARON. Neural network art emerged with Google's DeepDream in 2015 and GAN-generated images from 2018, and text-to-image tools went mainstream in 2022. OpenAI's DALL-E in 2021 showed images generated from text descriptions, followed in 2022 by DALL-E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion, which made high-quality image generation widely accessible. Since then, image models have improved in realism, text rendering and editing. Artists also use these tools as creative instruments. Generative art has raised debates about copyright, artist consent and labelling, leading to lawsuits, licensing deals and provenance standards for AI-generated images. How long has generative AI music been around? Algorithmic music dates to the 1950s, with the Illiac Suite composed by computer in 1957, and David Cope's experiments in the 1980s. Neural music generation advanced with OpenAI's Jukebox in 2020, and text-to-song tools such as Suno and Udio spread in 2023 and 2024. Google's MusicLM in 2023 generated music from text descriptions, and later tools created full songs with vocals from prompts. Record labels sued AI music companies in 2024 over training data, and licensing agreements followed as the industry adapted. Generative music is now used for backing tracks, prototyping and content creation. Questions about artist rights, attribution and authenticity remain central as the technology improves. How long has AI been used in production systems? AI has run in production for decades: expert systems in the 1980s configured computer orders at companies such as DEC, spam filters and recommendation engines spread in the late 1990s and 2000s, and deep learning entered products around 2012. Also asked as: how long has ai been in production Speech recognition, image search, translation and fraud detection adopted deep learning in the 2010s, often invisibly; many users never noticed these systems were AI. Generative AI added a new wave of production uses from 2023, such as chat assistants, coding tools and document processing. Production AI requires monitoring, evaluation and governance, lessons learned through decades of earlier deployments. Today's AI engineers build on that history, as I do with products such as RAG.NextUpgrad. How long have AI apps been around? Consumer AI apps date back over a decade: Siri launched on iPhone in 2011, Google Now in 2012 and Amazon's Alexa in 2014. Generative AI apps, such as ChatGPT's mobile apps in 2023, started a new wave of AI-first applications. Before assistants, AI powered apps behind the scenes, through recommendations, photo search and keyboard predictions. Since 2023, app stores have filled with chat assistants, image generators, AI tutors and productivity tools, and major apps added AI features. Building AI apps has become accessible to students, with APIs, open models and frameworks lowering barriers. The five NextUpgrad apps I shipped in 2026 reflect how quickly a small team can now build useful AI products.

# Generative AI vs AI, ML, LLMs, predictive AI, agents and OpenAI: the differences explained
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/generative-ai-vs-ai-differences/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Artificial intelligence is the broad field of making machines perform tasks that normally need human intelligence; generative AI is the part of AI that creates new content, such as text, images, code, audio and video, rather than only classifying or predicting. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are generative AI; spam filters and fraud scores are traditional AI. I build generative AI products such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, so this page clears up how generative AI differs from AI, ML, LLMs, predictive, discriminative and explainable AI, agents and OpenAI.

## What is the difference between generative AI and AI?

AI is the umbrella term covering all techniques that let machines perceive, reason, learn and act, from rule-based systems and search algorithms to machine learning. Generative AI is a subset that generates new content similar to its training data.

Most AI before 2022 was not generative: recommendation engines, image classifiers, speech recognition, route planners and fraud detection. Generative AI became mainstream with large language models and image generators. Both can work together: a document system might use classic AI to classify documents and generative AI to summarise them. Every generative AI system is AI, but most AI systems are not generative.

## What is the difference between generative AI and traditional AI?

Traditional AI typically analyses existing data to classify, detect, rank or predict, such as approving loans, recognising faces or forecasting demand, often with task-specific models. Generative AI produces new content and handles open-ended tasks through prompts.

Traditional models are usually smaller, cheaper, more predictable and easier to evaluate with clear metrics like accuracy. Generative models are flexible general-purpose tools but cost more to run, can hallucinate, and are harder to evaluate. Many real systems combine them: traditional models for structured decisions and scoring, generative models for language, summaries and interaction.

## What is the difference between generative AI and machine learning?

Machine learning is the approach of learning patterns from data instead of writing explicit rules; it includes classification, regression, clustering and more. Generative AI is built with machine learning, specifically deep learning, but focuses on generating new data.

So generative AI is a subset of machine learning: all modern generative models are trained with ML techniques, but most ML models, such as decision trees predicting churn, are not generative. Learning ML fundamentals, such as data splits, evaluation and overfitting, remains valuable for anyone working with generative AI, because the same principles apply when fine-tuning or evaluating models.

## What is the difference between generative AI and an LLM?

An LLM, large language model, is a specific kind of generative AI model trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate language. Generative AI is broader, including image, video, audio, music and 3D generators as well as LLMs.

ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are built on LLMs, many now multimodal, accepting images and audio. Stable Diffusion and Midjourney are generative image models, not LLMs. LLMs are also used in non-generative ways, such as embeddings for search or classification. In everyday conversation, people often use "generative AI" to mean LLM-based chatbots, but the field is wider.

## What is the difference between generative AI and predictive AI?

Predictive AI forecasts outcomes or values from historical data, such as next month's sales, a customer's likelihood to churn or a machine's failure risk. Generative AI creates new content, such as a report, email, image or code.

They answer different questions: predictive AI asks "what will happen?" or "which category?", while generative AI asks "what should this content be?". They combine well: a predictive model flags customers likely to churn, and a generative model drafts personalised retention messages for staff to review. Predictive models are easier to measure with accuracy metrics; generative outputs need human or model-based evaluation.

## What is the difference between generative AI and discriminative AI?

In machine learning theory, discriminative models learn the boundary between classes, modelling the probability of a label given the input, such as "is this email spam?". Generative models learn how the data itself is distributed, so they can produce new examples.

Logistic regression, support vector machines and most classifiers are discriminative. Naive Bayes, hidden Markov models, GANs, diffusion models and language models are generative. Discriminative models are often more accurate for pure classification; generative models can create data, handle missing information and model uncertainty. Modern systems frequently combine both approaches.

## What is the difference between generative AI and explainable AI?

They address different questions. Generative AI is a type of AI that creates content. Explainable AI is a set of methods and goals for making AI decisions understandable to humans, such as showing which features influenced a prediction.

Explainability matters for all AI, especially in high-stakes areas like lending, healthcare and hiring, where people need to understand and contest decisions. For generative AI, explainability is hard because outputs come from billions of parameters; practical approaches include citations to sources in RAG, showing reasoning steps, and interpretability research into model internals. Grounded answers with citations, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, are a practical form of transparency.

## What is the difference between generative AI and AI agents?

Generative AI produces content when prompted. AI agents use generative models, usually LLMs, as their reasoning engine, but add tools, memory and a loop that lets them plan and take actions towards a goal, such as searching, editing files or updating systems.

A chatbot answering a question is generative AI; an assistant that books a meeting by checking calendars, drafting an invite and sending it after your approval is an agent. Agents are built on generative AI but involve more engineering: tool design, permissions, error handling and monitoring. Not every agent is generative, but most modern ones are.

## What is the difference between agentic AI and generative AI, with an example?

Generative AI creates outputs in response to prompts; agentic AI pursues goals by deciding and executing multiple steps with tools. Example: asking generative AI "write a leave application" gives you text; asking an agentic system to "apply for leave next Friday" might check your calendar, fill the HR form, submit it after approval and notify your team.

Agentic systems add autonomy, tool use and planning on top of generative models, which brings more value and more risk. They need guardrails, such as limited permissions, human approval for consequential steps, logs and evaluation of success rates. Many practical systems sit in between: workflows with a few AI-driven decisions.

## What is the difference between generative AI and OpenAI?

Generative AI is a field of technology; OpenAI is a company that builds generative AI products, including ChatGPT, GPT models, image and video models, and developer APIs. Many other companies and open-source communities also build generative AI.

Other major developers include Anthropic with Claude, Google with Gemini, Meta with Llama, Mistral, Alibaba with Qwen, and DeepSeek, plus open-source projects worldwide. Saying "OpenAI" when meaning generative AI is like saying a brand name for a whole category. For building products, you can choose among many providers or open models, and multi-provider designs reduce dependence on any one company.

# How to use GGUF in ComfyUI: install ComfyUI-GGUF, where files go, LTX-2 and Qwen
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/gguf-comfyui-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To use GGUF models in ComfyUI, install the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node, put the GGUF model file in ComfyUI's unet or diffusion_models folder, restart, and replace the normal model loader in your workflow with the "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node. GGUF files are quantised, so large image and video models fit on GPUs with less memory. Quantisation is central to my FineTune Studio work with QLoRA, so this page covers what GGUF is, installing and placing files, a tutorial, examples, and LTX-2 and Qwen setups.

## How do I use GGUF in ComfyUI?

Install ComfyUI-GGUF, place your `.gguf` diffusion model in `ComfyUI/models/unet`, restart ComfyUI, then load it with the "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node instead of the standard checkpoint or diffusion model loader.

Everything else in the workflow stays the same: text encoders, VAE, sampler and output nodes. If the model needs a text encoder that is also in GGUF format, load it with the GGUF CLIP loader nodes. Start from a known working workflow for the model, such as the examples in the model's repository, and swap only the loader, so you change one thing at a time when debugging.

## Can I use GGUF in ComfyUI?

Yes, through the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, which adds loaders for GGUF-quantised diffusion models and text encoders. Native ComfyUI support has expanded over time, but the custom node remains the standard route for most GGUF models.

GGUF lets you run large models, such as modern image and video transformers, on consumer GPUs that cannot hold full-precision weights. The trade-off is some quality loss at lower bit widths and sometimes slower speed than optimised formats. Check that the GGUF file matches a model architecture the node supports; the repository lists supported models and updates as new ones appear.

## What are GGUF models in ComfyUI?

GGUF models are model weights saved in the GGUF file format, which came from the llama.cpp project and stores tensors, often quantised to 8, 6, 5, 4 or fewer bits, together with metadata. In ComfyUI, they are usually quantised versions of diffusion and video models or text encoders.

File names show quantisation levels, such as Q8_0, Q5_K_M or Q4_K_S. Higher numbers keep more quality and use more memory; lower numbers save memory with more quality loss. Q8 is close to full precision, Q5 and Q4 are popular balances, and lower levels suit very limited GPUs. Compare outputs on your own prompts to choose.

## Where do I install the GGUF node in ComfyUI?

Install ComfyUI-GGUF into the `ComfyUI/custom_nodes` folder, either through ComfyUI-Manager by searching for "GGUF", or with Git, then install its Python requirement and restart ComfyUI.

With Git:

```bash
cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes
git clone https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF
pip install --upgrade gguf
```

For the Windows portable build, use the embedded Python, for example `python_embeded\python.exe -s -m pip install -r ComfyUI\custom_nodes\ComfyUI-GGUF\requirements.txt` from the portable folder. After restarting, search the node menu for "GGUF" to confirm the loaders appear. If they do not, check the ComfyUI console for import errors, which usually point to a missing `gguf` package installed into a different Python environment from the one ComfyUI uses. Keep the node updated, since support for new model architectures arrives in updates.

## Where do I put GGUF files in ComfyUI?

Put GGUF diffusion or video model files in `ComfyUI/models/unet` or, in newer ComfyUI versions, `ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models`. The "Unet Loader (GGUF)" node lists files from these folders.

If a file does not appear in the loader's dropdown, check that it is in the right folder, has the `.gguf` extension, and that you restarted ComfyUI or refreshed the node list. Do not put GGUF diffusion models in the `checkpoints` folder, which is for full checkpoint files containing model, text encoder and VAE together. Keep a consistent naming scheme with the quantisation level in the filename.

## Where do I put GGUF text encoder models in ComfyUI?

Put GGUF text encoder files, such as quantised T5 or other language encoders used by image and video models, in `ComfyUI/models/clip` or `ComfyUI/models/text_encoders`, and load them with the GGUF CLIP loader nodes.

Models such as Flux use two text encoders, so use the dual CLIP loader variant with one GGUF and one standard encoder if needed. VAE files stay in `models/vae` and load with the normal VAE loader. Quantising text encoders saves significant memory, because some encoders are larger than you might expect, with modest effect on prompt understanding at Q8 or Q5.

## Is there a ComfyUI-GGUF tutorial?

Yes. The ComfyUI-GGUF repository's README explains installation, supported models and loader nodes, and many community video tutorials walk through specific models. A simple tutorial flow follows.

Steps:

- Install ComfyUI and confirm a standard workflow runs.
- Install ComfyUI-GGUF and its Python dependency.
- Download a GGUF quantisation of your model from its Hugging Face page.
- Place the model, text encoder and VAE in their folders.
- Open an example workflow for the model and swap in GGUF loaders.
- Generate, then compare Q8 and Q4 outputs and speed.

Monitor GPU memory to choose the highest quality that fits.

## What are some ComfyUI-GGUF examples?

Common examples include running Flux image models in Q4 or Q5 on GPUs with limited memory, video models such as Wan or LTX variants with GGUF transformers, and combining GGUF models with LoRAs for styles or characters.

Model repositories on Hugging Face that publish GGUF files often include example workflows as images or JSON that you can drag into ComfyUI. Check that example workflows match your installed node versions; outdated workflows may reference renamed nodes. When sharing your own workflows, note the quantisation level and node versions so others can reproduce results.

## How do I install and configure LTX-2 GGUF models in ComfyUI?

Update ComfyUI and ComfyUI-GGUF to recent versions, download an LTX-2 GGUF quantisation along with the required VAE and text encoder listed on the model card, place each in its folder, and load an official or model-card workflow, replacing the model loader with the GGUF loader.

Video models are memory-hungry, so start with short clips, low resolution and fewer frames, then scale up. Use the sampler settings recommended on the model card, since video models are sensitive to steps and schedulers. If you run out of memory, try a lower quantisation, enable ComfyUI's memory-saving options, or offload the text encoder to the CPU. New model releases often need the latest ComfyUI version, so update before troubleshooting.

## How do I use Qwen-Image-Layered GGUF in ComfyUI?

Update ComfyUI and ComfyUI-GGUF, download the GGUF quantisation and the matching text encoder and VAE from the model's page, place them in the correct folders, and start from the workflow provided by the model authors or quantisation publisher, swapping in GGUF loaders.

Layered image models output separate layers, such as foreground and background, so check the workflow's output nodes to save each layer, often as PNGs with transparency. Read the model card for supported resolutions and prompts. As with any new architecture, if loading fails, confirm your ComfyUI and node versions support the model, since support usually arrives in updates shortly after release.
