# Are hackathons important? Downsides, coding, beginners, placements and resume tips
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathons-important-beginners-resume/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Hackathons are worth it for most students because they compress learning, teamwork and shipping into a weekend, but they have real downsides when they replace deeper work. I won first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee with KrishGyan and at BYTEBATTLE with Annapurna, and I mentor students preparing for events, so this page covers why hackathons matter, why they can be bad, coding needs, beginners, non-CS and school students, placements and resumes. Are hackathons really important? Hackathons are important as accelerated practice: you scope a problem, build a working prototype, present it and get feedback, all within a day or two. They are not mandatory, but they build skills classes rarely teach. The real value is in shipping under constraints, working in a team with different skills, and explaining your project to judges. They also connect you with mentors, sponsors and peers who later become collaborators. Several of my products began this way: KrishGyan, which delivers farming advice in a farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp, and Annapurna, a surplus-food coordination app, both started as hackathon builds. Their importance depends on what you do after the event. Why can hackathons be bad? Hackathons can be bad when they reward flashy demos over working software, encourage sleepless crunch, or replace sustained learning. Some events favour polished pitches, and many projects are abandoned the moment the event ends. Also asked as: why hackathons are bad Other downsides: teams split work so narrowly that members learn little outside their part; judging can be rushed or inconsistent; and constant participation crowds out fundamentals, internships and deep projects. Code written in a rush often has poor structure and security. Reduce these problems by choosing events with real problem statements, sleeping properly, rotating roles within the team and continuing the best projects afterwards. Treat hackathons as one part of growth, not a replacement for steady practice. Do hackathons require coding? Most hackathons expect working prototypes, so at least one team member usually codes. But teams also need design, research, product thinking, presentation and domain knowledge, so non-coders can contribute meaningfully. Some events are explicitly open to no-code tools, design or business tracks, ideathons and policy challenges. Designers create interfaces and flows, domain experts shape the problem and the judges' understanding, and presenters often decide how the project is received. If you cannot code yet, learn the basics of a no-code builder or help with front-end design. Many beginners pick up coding at hackathons by pairing with experienced teammates, which is one of the fastest ways to learn practical development. Are hackathons for beginners? Yes. Many hackathons welcome beginners, with workshops, mentors and beginner prizes. Major League Hacking events and campus hackathons often run introductory sessions on Git, APIs and deployment before building starts. To get started, join with friends or form a team at the event, pick a simple idea you can finish, and use templates or starter kits. Focus on learning and finishing rather than winning. Ask mentors for help early instead of staying stuck for hours. After the event, write a short post about what you built and learned. A first hackathon often builds more confidence than any tutorial, even without a prize, because you see an idea become a working demo. Are hackathons only for students? No. Hackathons run for professionals, companies, governments and communities, not just students. Corporate internal hackathons, open-source sprints, civic tech events and online global hackathons on Devpost welcome people of many ages and backgrounds. Professionals join to explore new technologies, build side projects, network or win prizes. Companies run internal hackathons to test ideas and break silos between teams. Governments use them to crowdsource solutions to public problems, such as the Smart India Hackathon, which mainly involves students but partners with ministries and organisations. Some events are restricted, for example student-only or women-only tracks, so check eligibility rules. Many online hackathons let you join from anywhere, individually or in teams. Are hackathons only for CS students? No. Hackathons welcome students from every branch and field. Teams benefit from mechanical, electronics, biology, business, design and humanities students, who bring domain knowledge and perspectives that pure computer science teams lack. Many winning ideas come from domain problems in agriculture, healthcare, logistics or education, where non-CS teammates understand real users. Hardware hackathons need electronics and mechanical skills, while social impact challenges value research and communication. Non-CS students can also learn enough Python or no-code tools to prototype. KrishGyan, built for farmers, shows how much a deep understanding of users shapes a strong hackathon project. Check each event's tracks, since many offer categories designed for non-programmers. What are the best hackathons for high school students? Good options include Hack Club events and community hackathons, high school friendly events listed by Major League Hacking, Technovation Girls, the Congressional App Challenge in the United States, and in India, the ATL Marathon for school innovators. Many university hackathons also accept high school students, so check eligibility on Devpost and MLH listings. Online hackathons remove travel barriers. For beginners, choose events with workshops and mentors, and aim to finish a simple, working project. School students can also start a club and host a small hackathon, which builds leadership. Participation at this stage builds portfolios for college applications and teaches teamwork early, as long as academics stay balanced. Are hackathons important for placements? Hackathons help placements by giving you projects, stories and skills that interviewers value, and some companies hire directly from their own hackathons. They are not a replacement for fundamentals, coding interviews or internships. In interviews, a hackathon project gives you a concrete example to discuss: the problem, your role, technical choices, trade-offs under time pressure and what you would improve. Wins and finalist positions signal initiative, especially for startups. Company-run hackathons and coding challenges sometimes lead to interview shortcuts or internship offers. Still, recruiters weigh problem solving, core subjects and real experience heavily, so balance hackathons with data structures practice and longer projects that show depth. Do hackathons look good on a resume? Yes, when presented with outcomes. Hackathons show initiative, teamwork, speed and the ability to ship. Wins, finalist positions and projects with live demos or code strengthen a resume, especially for early-career roles. Also asked as: do hackathons look good on resume A list of event names alone adds little. Recruiters care about what you built, your role and results, such as a first prize, a deployed prototype or users after the event. Projects continued after the hackathon carry more weight than abandoned prototypes. Link to GitHub repositories and demos so reviewers can verify your work. As experience grows, keep only the most significant hackathons on the resume and move the rest to a portfolio page or LinkedIn. What is the best way to list hackathons and programming competitions on a resume? Create an Awards and Competitions section, or list major hackathon projects under Projects. For each, include the event, result, year, a one-line project description, your role and the technologies used. Use a consistent format, for example: First Prize, Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee, for KrishGyan, which gives farming advice over WhatsApp in the farmer's own voice and language. For programming competitions, give ranks or percentiles with the platform and contest, such as Codeforces rounds or ICPC regionals. Order entries by significance, keep each to one or two lines, and link to code or demos. Mention notable outcomes, such as a pilot or continued development after the event.

# How to convert handwriting to text, and turn text into handwriting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/handwriting-to-text-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, you can convert handwriting to text. Handwritten text recognition, a form of OCR built for handwriting, is now built into phones, notes apps and AI assistants: point Google Lens or Apple's Live Text at a page, write with a stylus in a notes app, or upload a photo of your notes to an AI model. It also works in reverse: you can make typed text look like your handwriting with a custom font. This page explains how recognition works and walks through scanning, copying, converting, translating and creating handwriting.

## What is handwritten text recognition?

Handwritten text recognition (HTR) is technology that reads handwriting from images or pen strokes and turns it into editable text. It is a specialised form of optical character recognition (OCR), which originally targeted printed text.

Handwriting is harder than print because letters vary between people, join together and slant. Modern HTR uses deep learning models that read whole lines or pages, using context to guess unclear words, much as people do. Two modes exist: offline recognition from photos or scans, and online recognition from stylus strokes, which also uses the order and direction of each stroke and is more accurate. Results are good on neat writing and weaker on messy notes, unusual scripts and mixed languages, so proofreading is always needed.

## Can you convert handwriting to text?

Yes. Phone tools such as Google Lens and Apple's Live Text, notes apps with stylus support, cloud OCR services, and AI models such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude can all turn handwriting into editable text.

Which to use:

- **A few lines**: Google Lens or Live Text on your phone.
- **Stylus notes**: convert inside Samsung Notes, Apple Notes or OneNote.
- **Pages of notes**: photograph them and ask an AI assistant to transcribe, keeping headings and lists.
- **Forms and documents at scale**: cloud services such as Google Cloud Vision or Azure AI Document Intelligence.

In my OCR & Speech Workspace, OCR runs page by page so each piece of text keeps its page number; that is worth copying for long notes, so you can always find the original.

## Can you scan handwriting to text?

Yes. Photograph or scan the page in good light, then use a tool that recognises handwriting. On phones, the camera with Google Lens or Live Text does it directly; on computers, upload the scan to an OCR tool or AI assistant.

For the best results:

- Use even light without shadows and hold the phone parallel to the page.
- Scan at a decent resolution; most phone cameras are enough.
- Crop to the text and avoid busy backgrounds.
- Write in dark ink on plain paper when you know you will scan.
- For multiple pages, use a scanner app to create a single PDF first.

Then proofread, focusing on names, numbers and technical terms, where errors cluster.

## How do I copy handwritten text from an image?

On Android, open the image in Google Photos or Lens, tap Lens, select the text and copy it. On iPhone, open the photo, press and hold the text with Live Text, and copy. On a computer, upload the image to Google Lens in the browser or to an AI assistant.

If selection fails, the writing may be too unclear or the image too small; try a sharper photo or zoom in on the section. AI assistants are often better than Lens for long passages because they use context: upload the image and ask "transcribe this handwriting exactly, keep line breaks, mark unclear words with [?]". Marking uncertain words is important, because AI may otherwise guess confidently. For sensitive documents, prefer on-device tools.

## Can notes apps convert handwriting to text?

Yes. Apple Notes on iPad with Apple Pencil can convert handwriting to text and lets you write directly into text fields with Scribble; Samsung Notes converts handwriting with S Pen; Microsoft OneNote has ink-to-text conversion.

Notes apps work best with stylus input because they record strokes, which makes recognition more accurate than reading a photo. They also keep handwritten notes searchable even without converting them. Typical workflow: take notes by hand during class, then select a section and convert it when you need typed text for an assignment or to share. Check the app's language settings; recognition supports many languages, but mixed scripts and abbreviations may need manual fixes.

## Can you translate handwriting to text?

Yes. Google Translate's camera mode and Google Lens can read handwriting and translate it into another language, and AI assistants can transcribe and translate a photo in one step.

Point Google Translate's camera at the note or import a photo, choose the source and target languages, and it overlays or lists the translation. For longer handwritten letters or notes, upload the photo to an AI assistant and ask: "Transcribe this handwritten text in its original language, then translate it into English, and mark any words you are unsure of." Translation errors compound recognition errors, so for anything important, such as official documents, have a fluent person check the result.

## How do I turn handwriting into editable text on a computer?

Photograph or scan your pages, then use OneNote's text extraction, Google Drive's OCR when opening an image or PDF with Google Docs, or an AI assistant for higher accuracy on messy notes. Paste the result into your document and proofread.

A practical study workflow: scan a week's notes into one PDF, upload it to an AI assistant, and ask for a clean transcription with the original headings and bullet points, followed by a one-page summary. Keep the original scans, because transcription mistakes happen. If you write notes digitally with a stylus, convert inside the notes app instead, which is more accurate than photographs. For printed text, standard OCR is near perfect; it is handwriting that needs checking.

## How do I turn text into my handwriting?

Create a font from a sample of your handwriting with a handwriting-font service: you fill in a template with each character, scan or photograph it, and the service generates a font file you install and type with.

Steps that work:

- Download the service's template and write each character neatly with a dark pen.
- Scan at good resolution and upload.
- Install the generated font file on your computer.
- Adjust spacing and size in your word processor.

Uses include personalised cards, design projects and notes. Typed "handwriting" always looks more regular than real writing, which people can notice. Do not use it to fake work that must be handwritten, such as assignments or exam sheets where handwriting is required; that is academic misconduct.

## Is there an app that converts text to handwriting?

Yes. Handwriting-font creators, text-to-handwriting websites that render typed text on a ruled-page image, and design tools with handwriting fonts all do this. Some robots and plotters even write with a real pen from typed text.

Choose by purpose: for design and greeting cards, a handwriting font in Canva or your word processor is enough; for a personal touch, a font made from your own writing; for a realistic page image, a text-to-handwriting generator. Check privacy terms before uploading samples of your handwriting, which is personal data. And again, do not use these tools to submit handwritten work you did not write by hand.

## What text looks like handwriting?

Handwriting-style fonts make typed text look handwritten. Free options on Google Fonts include Caveat, Indie Flower, Patrick Hand, Kalam and Shadows Into Light, and the Handwriting category lists many more.

Pick by mood: Patrick Hand and Kalam are neat and readable, Caveat looks like quick notes, Indie Flower is playful. Kalam also supports Devanagari, useful for Hindi text. For readability, use handwriting fonts for headings, quotes or short notes, not long paragraphs, and keep body text in a clean font. On websites, load fonts efficiently and check that they render well on phones.

# How agentic AI works: goals, vs gen AI and LLMs, departments, guides and courses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-agentic-ai-works-vs-gen-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Agentic AI describes systems that pursue goals with some autonomy: they plan, take actions with tools, observe results and adjust, usually with a language model as the reasoning engine. It builds on generative AI but goes further than producing content. I build AI products with retrieval, fallbacks and confidence gates, such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page explains how agentic AI works simply and technically, what it works toward, how it differs from gen AI, AI agents and LLMs, departments, and guides and courses. How does agentic AI actually work? Agentic AI works in a loop: it receives a goal, plans steps, takes an action such as searching, calling an API or editing a file, observes the result, and decides the next step, repeating until the goal is met or it needs help. For example, asked to prepare a competitor summary, an agent might search the web, open several pages, extract key facts, notice a missing detail, search again, then write a cited report. A language model makes each decision, while tools let it act beyond text. Memory keeps track of progress, and guardrails limit what it may do. The loop is simple; reliability comes from good tools, clear instructions, limits and evaluation. How does agentic AI work technically? Technically, an agent system sends the model a system prompt, the goal, conversation history and tool definitions as JSON schemas. The model returns either text or a structured tool call, which the application executes before appending the result and calling the model again. Around this core sit several components: an orchestrator that runs the loop and enforces step limits; state storage, often a database or checkpointer; retrieval for knowledge; permission checks for tools; tracing that logs every call; and error handling with retries. Protocols such as the Model Context Protocol standardise how agents connect to tools and data. Multi-agent systems add coordinator agents that delegate subtasks to specialist agents and merge their results. What does agentic AI work toward? Agentic AI works toward goals defined by people: completing a task, such as resolving a support ticket, fixing a bug or compiling a report, within the constraints, permissions and success criteria its designers set. Goals should be specific and measurable, such as tests passing or a form fully completed, since vague goals lead to wandering or premature stopping. Designers also define what the agent must not do, such as spending money or deleting data without approval. Agents do not have their own desires; they optimise for the objective in their instructions, which is why poorly specified goals can produce technically correct but unwanted results. Clear stopping conditions matter as much as goals. Is agentic AI the same as generative AI? No. Generative AI creates content such as text, images or code in response to a prompt. Agentic AI uses generative models to take actions toward goals across multiple steps, with tools, memory and some autonomy. A generative AI chatbot writes an email when asked; an agentic system can read your inbox, draft replies, check your calendar and schedule meetings, asking approval before sending. Agentic AI is built on generative AI, so it inherits its strengths and weaknesses, including hallucination. The shift adds new risks, since actions affect the real world, and new requirements, such as permissions, monitoring and evaluation of multi-step behaviour rather than single responses. Are AI agents and agentic AI the same? They are closely related. An AI agent is a specific system that acts toward a goal with tools. Agentic AI is the broader approach or property of systems that act with autonomy, often involving one or many agents. Also asked as: is agentic ai and gen ai same In practice, people use the terms interchangeably. Some writers reserve agentic AI for systems with significant autonomy, planning and multi-agent coordination, while calling simpler tool-using assistants AI agents. Anthropic distinguishes workflows, where code defines the steps, from agents, where the model directs its own process; both count as agentic systems. What matters more than labels is how much autonomy the system has, which actions it can take, and what oversight exists. What is the difference between agentic AI and an LLM? An LLM is a model that predicts text. Agentic AI is a system that uses an LLM as its reasoning engine, adding tools, memory, goals and a control loop so it can act and complete multi-step tasks. Also asked as: difference between agentic ai and llm An LLM alone answers within one response and cannot check facts, run code or change anything outside the conversation. Wrapped in an agent, the same model can search, calculate, query databases and verify its own work through tool results. That makes agents more capable but also more complex to build and test. Many agent failures come from system design, such as unclear tools or missing context, rather than from the LLM itself, so engineering around the model matters greatly. Can agentic AI work without an LLM? Yes. Agents existed long before LLMs: reinforcement learning agents playing games, robots using planning algorithms, trading bots and rule-based software agents. Modern general-purpose agentic AI, however, mostly relies on LLMs for flexible reasoning and language understanding. Also asked as: can agentic ai work without llm Without an LLM, agents need hand-built rules, search algorithms or models trained for one specific environment. These remain valuable where reliability and speed matter, such as industrial control or logistics optimisation. Hybrid systems are common: an LLM interprets requests and plans, while classical planners, optimisation solvers or rule engines execute critical decisions predictably. In RAG.NextUpgrad, a confidence gate checks whether retrieved evidence is strong enough before the model answers, a simple decision layer around the LLM. Can agentic AI models run departments? Not on their own today. Agents can run many processes within departments, such as triaging support tickets, reconciling invoices or screening applications for completeness, but humans still set goals, handle exceptions, make judgement calls and remain accountable. Some companies describe departments where agents handle most routine volume while small human teams supervise, review edge cases and improve the system. Fully autonomous departments face obstacles: agents make errors that compound over long tasks, struggle with ambiguous situations, and cannot carry legal or ethical responsibility. A realistic goal is agent-assisted departments, where measurable workflows are automated with approval steps, audit logs and clear escalation paths to people. What does a complete guide to agentic AI cover? A complete guide covers what agents are, when to use them versus simpler workflows, core patterns such as tool use, planning, reflection and multi-agent coordination, memory and retrieval, frameworks, evaluation, safety, deployment and costs. Also asked as: agentic ai complete guide Strong free guides include Anthropic's Building effective agents, OpenAI's A practical guide to building agents and Google's Agents whitepaper. They agree on key advice: start with the simplest solution, add autonomy only when it clearly helps, design tools carefully, and keep humans in control of risky actions. Supplement guides with hands-on building, since agent behaviour surprises even experienced engineers. Revisit guides periodically, as patterns evolve with new models and protocols. What is a complete agentic AI course? Complete courses include the free Hugging Face Agents Course, Microsoft's AI Agents for Beginners, LangChain Academy's LangGraph courses and DeepLearning.AI's short courses on agents, which together cover fundamentals, frameworks, multi-agent systems and evaluation. Also asked as: agentic ai complete course A complete course should progress from LLM basics and tool calling to building agents by hand, then frameworks, memory, RAG, multi-agent design, the Model Context Protocol, evaluation, guardrails and deployment, with projects at each stage. Paid courses on Udemy or Coursera add structure but should be checked for recency. Finish with a capstone agent that completes a real workflow end to end, with logs and measured success rates, which proves skill better than any certificate.

# How AI agents are created: what they are, types, Claude agents, coding agents, and costs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-ai-agents-are-created/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


AI agents are created by giving a language model a goal, a set of tools it can call, instructions and memory, and wrapping it in a loop where it decides the next step, acts, observes the result and continues until the task is done or a limit is reached. They differ from chatbots because they take actions. I build AI systems with tool use and multi-provider fallback, so this page explains agents in detail, how they are built, LLMs and tools, types, whether they work, Claude agents, coding agents and costs.

## What are AI agents, explained in detail?

An AI agent is software that perceives its situation, decides what to do and takes actions to achieve a goal, with some autonomy. Modern AI agents use a language model to plan and choose actions such as searching, running code, calling APIs or editing files.

The core loop: receive a goal, think about the next step, call a tool, read the result, update the plan, and repeat. Memory holds conversation history, notes or retrieved knowledge. Guardrails limit which tools it can use, how many steps it takes and which actions need human approval. Examples include research agents that search and summarise, coding agents that fix bugs and run tests, and support agents that look up orders and draft replies.

## How are AI agents created?

Choose a capable model, define tools as functions with clear names, descriptions and input schemas, write instructions describing the goal and rules, add memory or retrieval if needed, and run a loop that executes tool calls and feeds results back to the model.

Practical steps:

- Start with one narrow task and a clear definition of done.
- Give the agent only the tools it needs, with permissions scoped tightly.
- Log every step for debugging.
- Set limits on steps, time and cost.
- Require human approval for irreversible actions.
- Build an evaluation set of real tasks and measure success rate.

Anthropic's guidance recommends starting with simple workflows and adding autonomy only where it measurably helps.

## Are AI agents LLMs?

No. Agents use large language models as their reasoning engine, but an agent is the whole system: the model plus tools, instructions, memory, a control loop and guardrails. The same LLM can power a simple chatbot or a complex agent.

Think of the LLM as the brain and the agent as the brain plus hands and a job description. The LLM decides what to do; the surrounding code executes actions, enforces limits and checks results. That is why two agents using the same model can perform very differently: tool design, prompts, error handling and evaluation make most of the difference.

## Are AI agents tools?

Agents use tools and can themselves be offered as tools to other agents or applications. Tools are specific capabilities, such as a search API, a calculator or a database query, that the agent decides when and how to call.

Standards such as the Model Context Protocol let agents connect to many tools and data sources through a common interface, so one agent can use files, calendars, code repositories and business systems. In multi-agent systems, an orchestrating agent may call specialised sub-agents as if they were tools. From a user's perspective, an agent is a tool that can carry out multi-step work, but it needs supervision unlike a deterministic tool.

## How many types of agents are there in AI?

Classic AI textbooks, notably Russell and Norvig's, describe five types: simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents, utility-based agents and learning agents, in increasing sophistication.

Simple reflex agents react to current input with rules; model-based agents track the state of the world; goal-based agents plan towards goals; utility-based agents choose actions that maximise a measure of success; learning agents improve from experience. Modern LLM agents are often described differently: single-agent tool users, multi-agent systems with roles, and workflow agents following predefined paths with model decisions at certain steps.

## Do AI agents actually work?

Yes, for well-scoped tasks with clear success criteria, good tools and human oversight, such as coding tasks with tests, research summaries with sources, and routine data processing. They still struggle with long, ambiguous tasks, unreliable tools and situations needing judgement.

Coding agents show real progress on benchmarks built from real software issues, and teams use them daily. Failures include getting stuck in loops, misreading tool output, overconfident wrong actions and errors compounding across many steps. The practical approach is to deploy agents where mistakes are cheap and checkable, measure success rates, and keep humans in the loop for consequential decisions.

## How do Claude AI agents work?

Claude agents use Claude's tool-use ability: developers describe tools with names and schemas, Claude decides when to call them and with what inputs, the application runs the tool and returns results, and Claude continues until it finishes the task.

Anthropic provides building blocks: tool use in the API, the Claude Agent SDK, which packages the agent loop used by Claude Code, support for the Model Context Protocol to connect external tools, and computer use for operating interfaces. Claude Code is itself an agent that reads codebases, edits files and runs commands with permission checks. Good agent design still matters more than the model alone.

## Can I build AI agents with Claude?

Yes. You can build agents with the Claude API's tool use, write your own loop in Python or TypeScript, use the Claude Agent SDK for a ready-made loop with tools and permissions, or use frameworks such as LangGraph with Claude models.

A first project: an agent with two tools, `search_docs` over your documents and `create_ticket` in a task tracker, that answers questions and files tickets when it cannot resolve them, with approval before creating each ticket. Log every tool call, cap the number of steps, and test on twenty real requests. Keep API keys in environment variables and scope tool permissions narrowly.

## Which AI agents are best for coding?

Popular coding agents include Claude Code, GitHub Copilot's agent features, Cursor's agent mode, OpenAI's Codex, Aider and others. The best one depends on your editor, models, codebase size and how much autonomy you want.

Choose by testing on your own repository: give each agent the same three tasks, such as fixing a bug, adding a feature with tests and refactoring a module, and compare correctness, the quality of diffs and how much supervision they needed. Agents perform best with good tests, clear project instructions and small, well-defined tasks. Review every change before merging, especially security-sensitive code.

## How do AI agents spend your money?

Agents spend money in two ways: model usage, where every step consumes tokens billed by providers, and actions, such as calling paid APIs, launching cloud resources or making purchases if given payment access. Long loops and large contexts multiply costs.

Controls to put in place:

- Set hard budgets on tokens, steps and time per task.
- Use cheaper models for simple steps and stronger ones only where needed.
- Never give agents unrestricted payment credentials.
- Require human approval for purchases, transfers and resource creation.
- Monitor spending with alerts and logs.

Emerging agent payment systems add spending limits and authorisation, but treat any agent with financial access as a security risk.

# How do businesses use GenAI? How it works, studios, workshops, courses, and failures
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-businesses-use-genai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Generative AI, or GenAI, uses models trained on huge amounts of data to create new content, text, images, code, audio and video, in response to prompts. Businesses use it to answer customers, draft content, write code, process documents and search internal knowledge. I build GenAI products, from RAG.NextUpgrad to DocuLens AI, and give workshops and talks on building with AI, so this page explains how GenAI works, whether it is a tool, business uses, studios, workshops, courses, the 5-day intensive, learning paths, and why projects fail.

## How does GenAI work?

GenAI models learn patterns from vast datasets, then generate new content that follows those patterns. Language models predict the next token given previous text; image models, often diffusion models, learn to turn random noise into images step by step, guided by text descriptions.

Training happens in stages: pretraining on broad data teaches general knowledge and language; fine-tuning and human feedback teach the model to follow instructions helpfully and safely. At use time, your prompt and any retrieved documents form the context, and the model generates output based on probabilities. It does not look facts up unless connected to search or documents, which is why grounding with retrieval matters for accuracy.

## What is GenAI technology?

GenAI technology is the set of models, tools and infrastructure for generating content: large language models, image and video generators, speech synthesis, code assistants, plus the platforms, APIs, vector databases and orchestration tools used to build applications with them.

Core components in business applications include a model accessed through an API or hosted privately, prompts and system instructions, retrieval for grounding in company data, tools for taking actions, evaluation for quality, and guardrails for safety and privacy. The technology changes quickly, but these building blocks stay stable, which is why learning them is more valuable than chasing each new model release.

## Is GenAI a tool?

GenAI is better described as a technology or capability than a single tool. It powers many tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Midjourney and countless features inside existing software like email, documents and design apps.

For individuals, GenAI tools act as assistants for writing, research, coding and creativity. For organisations, GenAI is a capability to integrate into products and processes, which needs data, engineering, evaluation and governance. Treating it as "just a tool" leads to shallow adoption; treating it as a capability to design around leads to real productivity gains.

## How do businesses use GenAI?

Common business uses include customer support assistants grounded in help articles, drafting marketing and sales content, coding assistants for developers, document processing such as extracting invoice data, internal knowledge search over policies and reports, meeting summaries, and data analysis with natural language.

Examples by function: support teams deflect routine questions with RAG chatbots; legal teams review contracts faster with clause extraction; HR answers policy questions; engineers ship code faster; operations teams automate document workflows. Successful companies start with high-volume, low-risk tasks, measure time saved and quality, and keep humans reviewing outputs that affect customers or decisions.

## What is a GenAI studio?

A GenAI studio is usually a cloud workspace for experimenting with generative models: writing and testing prompts, comparing models, tuning parameters, grounding with data, and moving prototypes into applications. Google's Vertex AI Studio, formerly called Generative AI Studio, is a well-known example.

Other platforms offer similar playgrounds, such as Google AI Studio for the Gemini API, Azure AI Foundry and Amazon Bedrock's playgrounds, and some universities and companies run internal "GenAI studios" giving staff safe access to models. Studios are good for prototyping; production systems still need code, evaluation, security and monitoring.

## What is a GenAI workshop?

A GenAI workshop is a hands-on session teaching participants to use or build with generative AI: prompting techniques, using AI tools for work, building chatbots or RAG apps, evaluating outputs and understanding risks. Formats range from a two-hour introduction to multi-day bootcamps.

Effective workshops are practical: participants build something, such as a document question-answering app or an AI workflow, on real examples. In my campus sessions, a live build of a small AI app followed by a roadmap for further learning engages students far more than slides about AI's potential. Graph database providers, cloud companies and communities also run workshops with sample projects on GitHub.

## Is there a GenAI course with certification?

Yes. Options include Google Cloud and Microsoft Learn generative AI learning paths with badges and certifications, DeepLearning.AI and Coursera courses with certificates, AWS's generative AI training, and platform certifications such as the Databricks Generative AI Engineer Associate.

Choose based on goals: business-oriented courses explain uses and strategy; technical courses teach APIs, RAG, agents and deployment. Certificates show initiative, but employers value a working project more: build a RAG app or AI workflow with evaluation results alongside any course. Check whether certificates are free or paid, and whether the provider is respected in your target industry.

## What is the 5-day GenAI intensive course?

Google and Kaggle have run free, live "5-Day Gen AI Intensive" courses, combining daily whitepapers, podcasts, codelabs on Kaggle and livestreamed sessions with Google experts, covering foundation models, prompting, embeddings, agents and MLOps for generative AI. Later editions focused on AI agents.

The course materials, including whitepapers and notebooks, remain available on Kaggle after the live run, so you can work through them at your own pace. Watch Kaggle and Google's announcements for future live editions, which include community discussion and capstone projects. It is a strong, free, structured introduction for developers with Python basics.

## How do I learn GenAI?

Start with how generative models work and how to prompt them well, then learn to build with APIs, retrieval, evaluation and agents, completing a project at each step. Python and basic web development help a lot.

A learning path:

- Use AI tools daily and learn prompting fundamentals.
- Take a foundations course such as Generative AI for Everyone.
- Learn Python and call an LLM API.
- Build a RAG app over real documents with citations.
- Add evaluation and simple agents with tools.
- Deploy with FastAPI and share your project.

Join hackathons to practise building fast under real constraints.

## Why isn't GenAI working in my organisation?

Most GenAI projects stall because of unclear business goals, poor or inaccessible data, no evaluation of quality, weak integration into real workflows, and lack of user trust, rather than because the models are not capable enough.

Fixes: pick specific, measurable use cases; clean and organise the knowledge the system needs; build evaluation sets before launch; integrate into tools people already use; design for human review; and train staff. Security and privacy concerns need clear policies, not blanket bans. Start small, prove value with numbers, then scale what works rather than launching broad, vague initiatives.

# How ChatGPT is made and responds, why it lags, images, tutorials, and LLM-ready sites
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-chatgpt-works-tutorial/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


ChatGPT is made by training large language models on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, then fine-tuning them with example conversations and human feedback so they follow instructions helpfully and safely. When you send a message, the model generates a response token by token, using the conversation and any tool results such as web searches. I build AI products on several model providers, so this page covers how ChatGPT is made and responds, Claude's reliability, lag, images, tutorials for work and agents, LLM-ready websites, and its history.

## How is ChatGPT made?

ChatGPT is built in stages. First, a large transformer model is pretrained on vast text and code to learn language patterns and knowledge. Then supervised fine-tuning teaches it to respond like an assistant using example conversations, and reinforcement learning from human feedback refines it towards responses people prefer.

Further training adds reasoning, tool use, safety behaviours and multimodal abilities such as understanding images and speech. Around the model, OpenAI builds the product: chat interface, memory, search, file analysis, image generation, voice and agent features, plus safety systems. The models run on large GPU clusters in data centres. Each new model generation goes through safety testing and evaluation before release, documented in system cards that describe capabilities and known limitations.

## How does ChatGPT generate responses?

ChatGPT converts your message and the conversation into tokens, processes them through the neural network, and predicts the most likely next token, repeating until the response is complete. Sampling settings add controlled variety, so answers differ slightly each time.

For many requests, the model decides to use tools first: searching the web, running code, reading files or generating images, then includes those results in its context before writing. Reasoning models think through steps internally before answering. The model does not look up a fact database by default, which is why grounding with search or documents improves accuracy.

## How does Claude generate reliable responses?

Claude, like other assistants, generates text by predicting tokens, and Anthropic trains it with methods including Constitutional AI, using written principles, plus human feedback, to be helpful, honest and harmless, including acknowledging uncertainty rather than inventing answers.

Reliability in practice comes from grounding and good prompts: giving Claude source documents and asking it to quote or cite them, enabling web search for current facts, allowing "I don't know", and asking for step-by-step reasoning on complex tasks. In applications, retrieval with citations and evaluation of outputs, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, matter more than the model alone.

## Why is ChatGPT lagging?

ChatGPT lags because of high demand, long conversations it must reread, large uploads, reasoning or research modes that take extra time, image generation, slow internet connections, or browser extensions and outdated apps.

Fixes:

- Start a new chat when one becomes very long.
- Choose a faster model for simple questions.
- Upload fewer or smaller files.
- Disable heavy extensions or try a private window.
- Update the app or clear the browser cache.
- Check OpenAI's status page for incidents.

If lag appears only on one network, test another connection to rule out network problems.

## Can ChatGPT generate images?

Yes. ChatGPT can generate images from text descriptions and edit uploaded images, such as changing styles or backgrounds, using OpenAI's image models, with limits depending on your plan.

For better images, describe the subject, style, composition, lighting and text you want included, then refine through follow-up messages. ChatGPT can also create charts with code, and diagrams and documents as files. Images include provenance information marking them as AI-generated. Follow OpenAI's usage policies, and avoid misleading images of real people. Students use image generation for presentation visuals, posters and project mock-ups; for professional design work, combine it with proper design tools for precise layouts and brand consistency.

## What is a simple ChatGPT tutorial for beginners?

Open chatgpt.com or the app, sign in, type a clear request, and refine with follow-ups. Start with tasks like explaining a concept, summarising text, drafting an email or brainstorming ideas, and learn to give context and format instructions.

Beginner tips:

- Say who you are and what you need: "I am a first-year student; explain recursion simply."
- Ask for a format: bullets, table, steps or word limit.
- Paste text or upload files for summaries and questions.
- Ask follow-ups instead of starting over.
- Verify important facts and sources.

Explore features gradually: projects, custom instructions, voice and image tools.

## How do I use ChatGPT at work?

Use ChatGPT for drafting and editing documents and emails, summarising meetings and reports, analysing spreadsheets, brainstorming, preparing presentations and learning new topics, while following your organisation's policies on data and AI use.

Practical workplace uses: turn meeting notes into action items, draft first versions of proposals, analyse CSV data for trends, prepare interview questions, and explain technical concepts to non-technical colleagues. Use business plans with data protections for company information, avoid pasting confidential data into personal accounts, and review all outputs before sharing, since you remain responsible for accuracy.

## How do I use ChatGPT agent mode?

On supported plans, select agent mode, describe a multi-step task, such as researching products and building a comparison spreadsheet, and ChatGPT works through it with a virtual browser and tools, showing its steps and asking permission before important actions.

Tips: give a clear goal, constraints and output format; stay available for confirmations; watch progress and interrupt if it goes off track; and verify results. Avoid giving the agent access to sensitive accounts unless necessary, and be cautious with tasks involving payments or personal data. Agents work best on well-defined tasks with checkable results.

## How do I make a website LLM-ready for ChatGPT and other assistants?

Make your site easy for AI systems to read and cite: clear, factual content in server-rendered HTML, structured data such as JSON-LD with schema.org types, a clean sitemap, crawlable pages without heavy JavaScript gating, and documented APIs, for example with OpenAPI, if you want assistants to take actions.

For an e-commerce site, product pages should include structured product data, availability and clear descriptions. Some sites add an llms.txt file summarising key pages for language models. If you offer an API, an OpenAPI specification lets developers connect ChatGPT actions or agents to it. Measure results by checking whether AI assistants cite and describe your pages accurately.

## How long has ChatGPT been out?

ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022, so it has been publicly available since late 2022, nearly four years as of late 2026. It grew from a free research preview into one of the most widely used software products in the world.

Major milestones since launch include paid plans, GPT-4, plugins and then custom GPTs, voice conversations, image generation, web search, desktop apps, projects, agent features and the Atlas browser. Model generations have continued to improve reasoning, multimodality and tool use. Its launch triggered the broader generative AI wave across the industry.

# How chunking works: memory, examples, and chunking vs parsing, embedding and chinking
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-chunking-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Chunking works by combining separate pieces of information into larger, meaningful units, so the mind, or a computer system, handles fewer, richer pieces. In memory, chunks connect to knowledge you already have; in AI, chunks are document passages prepared for retrieval; in language processing, chunks are phrases. I design document chunking for RAG.NextUpgrad and teach study techniques to students, so this page explains how chunking works, memory capacity, examples, and how chunking differs from mnemonics, grouping, scaffolding, parsing, embedding and chinking.

## How does chunking work?

Chunking works by recognising patterns and relationships that let several items be treated as one unit. The letters F, B, I become one chunk, "FBI", because they match a familiar acronym stored in long-term memory, freeing working memory for other information.

The process depends on prior knowledge: experts chunk more because they recognise more patterns. A chess master sees a familiar opening as one chunk; a beginner sees many separate pieces. Chunking can be automatic, from experience, or deliberate, such as grouping study material by topic. In software and AI, chunking organises code into functions and documents into passages, applying the same principle of meaningful units. Understanding chunking helps you study better and design better systems, because both depend on presenting information in pieces the processor, human or machine, can handle well.

## What is chunking in memory?

In memory research, chunking is the process of organising information into meaningful units, chunks, that working memory can hold as single items. It explains how people remember more than the small capacity of working memory would otherwise allow.

George Miller popularised the idea in 1956, and later research refined working memory capacity to roughly four chunks for many tasks. Chunks are stored and retrieved as wholes, linked to long-term memory structures called schemas. This is why meaningful material is far easier to remember than random lists: meaning creates chunks.

## Does chunking increase memory capacity?

Not literally. Chunking does not add slots to working memory, which stays limited to a few items. It increases how much information each slot holds, so the effective amount you can remember and process grows substantially.

For example, remembering 12 random letters is hard, but remembering four familiar three-letter words containing the same letters is easy, because there are only four chunks. With expertise, chunks become larger and richer, which is why experts appear to have better memory in their field but not in general. Long-term learning, not memory hacks, is what builds powerful chunks.

## What are examples of chunking in memory?

Common examples include phone numbers grouped into blocks, card numbers in sets of four, acronyms such as NASA or ISRO, remembering a recipe as a few stages instead of many steps, and learning song lyrics by lines and verses rather than individual words.

Study examples: remembering the steps of mitosis as four stages, grouping historical events by era, chunking a programming concept into "input, process, output", and learning a speech as an opening, three points and a close. Musicians chunk notes into phrases, and drivers chunk routes into familiar segments. Each example turns many details into a few meaningful units.

## What is the difference between chunking and mnemonics?

Chunking organises information into meaningful groups based on structure or existing knowledge. Mnemonics are memory aids that attach information to easy-to-remember cues, such as acronyms, rhymes, images or the method of loci, even when the cue is unrelated to meaning.

They often work together: an acronym is both a mnemonic and a chunking device, compressing several items into one memorable word. Chunking tends to build understanding, because it relies on real relationships; mnemonics help with arbitrary lists, such as the order of planets. For deep learning, prefer meaningful chunking; for memorising lists, mnemonics are efficient. Combining them, by first understanding a topic's structure and then adding a mnemonic for its key terms, gives both comprehension and quick recall in exams.

## What is the difference between chunking and grouping?

Grouping simply arranges items together, for example by colour, position or category. Chunking forms meaningful units that function as single items in memory, usually because the group matches a pattern or concept you already know.

Grouping can support chunking, as with phone numbers split into blocks, but grouping alone does not guarantee chunks if the groups lack meaning. In design, visual grouping, such as spacing and boxes, helps users perceive structure; in learning, chunking builds lasting knowledge structures. A list of shopping items grouped by aisle becomes a set of chunks when each aisle triggers a familiar set of items.

## What is the difference between chunking and scaffolding?

Chunking breaks content into manageable pieces. Scaffolding is temporary support a teacher provides to help learners accomplish tasks they cannot yet do alone, such as hints, examples, templates or guided steps, gradually removed as competence grows.

Teachers often use both: they chunk a lesson into short segments and scaffold each with worked examples and guided practice, then reduce support. Chunking is about how content is structured; scaffolding is about how much help the learner gets. In mentoring students, I scaffold first projects with templates and checkpoints, then expect them to plan the next project themselves.

## What is the difference between chunking and parsing?

In document processing, parsing extracts text and structure from files, such as headings, paragraphs, tables and page numbers from a PDF, while chunking splits that extracted content into passages for indexing and retrieval. Parsing comes first; chunking depends on its output.

Poor parsing ruins chunking: if tables are scrambled or columns merged, chunks contain nonsense. In linguistics and NLP, parsing means analysing full grammatical structure, while chunking, or shallow parsing, identifies only phrases such as noun phrases. For RAG systems, investing in good parsing, including OCR for scans, is often the biggest quality improvement.

## What is the difference between chunking and embedding?

Chunking splits documents into smaller passages; embedding converts each passage into a vector of numbers representing its meaning. In RAG pipelines, chunking happens first, then each chunk is embedded and stored in a vector index for similarity search.

Chunk size affects embedding quality: very long chunks blend multiple topics into a vague vector, while very short chunks lose context. Embedding models also have input limits, which cap chunk length. Choosing chunk boundaries along document structure, then embedding with a model suited to your language, gives the best retrieval. Changing either step requires re-indexing.

## What is the difference between chunking and chinking?

In natural language processing, chunking groups words into phrases, such as noun phrases like "the large vector database", often using patterns over part-of-speech tags. Chinking removes words from a chunk, defining what should be excluded, such as verbs or prepositions.

Libraries such as NLTK let you write chunk grammars with rules to include patterns and chink rules to exclude tokens, useful for information extraction tasks like finding entity names. These classic techniques are less common now that neural models handle phrase extraction, but they remain useful for lightweight, interpretable pipelines and for learning NLP fundamentals.

# How do hackathons work? AI rules, timing, how many per year, prizes, themes, age limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-do-hackathons-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Hackathons work as time-boxed build events: teams register, receive themes or problem statements, build a prototype in 24 to 48 hours, and demo it to judges for prizes. Thousands run every year, online and in person, with rules on themes, AI tools and age. I have competed in 10+ hackathons, winning first prizes including Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, so this page explains how they work, community views, ChatGPT rules, AI hackathons, timing, frequency, prizes, themes, age limits and where to find them.

## How do hackathons usually work?

Registration opens weeks before; teams of two to five form; the event starts with an opening session announcing themes or problem statements; teams build for a fixed period with mentor support; then they submit code and a demo for judging.

Judging usually happens in rounds: a quick screening of all submissions, then finalist presentations to a panel. Criteria commonly include innovation, technical complexity, design, impact and presentation quality. In-person events provide food, Wi-Fi and spaces to work overnight; online events run on Discord or Slack with video demos. Some hackathons are multi-stage, such as idea submissions first and then a build round for shortlisted teams. Read each event's schedule and rules before registering.

## What are hackathons, according to the community?

Community discussions describe hackathons as intense, fun weekends of building with friends, learning new tools fast and meeting people, with prizes as a bonus. Veterans stress that the experience and connections matter more than winning.

Common views: beginners learn more in one hackathon than in weeks of tutorials; sponsor-heavy events can feel like marketing, so choose ones with good mentors and fair judging; and polished demos sometimes beat deeper technical work, which frustrates some participants. Many recommend treating hackathons as practice in scoping and shipping. Others warn about burnout from repeated all-nighters, suggesting sleep and realistic goals. Overall, the community sees them as valuable for students building portfolios and networks.

## Do hackathons allow ChatGPT?

Most modern hackathons allow ChatGPT and other AI assistants, treating them like any developer tool, but rules vary. Some require disclosure, some ban pre-written code, and a few exam-style or beginner contests restrict AI to keep competition fair.

Organisers increasingly publish explicit AI policies, often allowing assistants for coding help while requiring that the core idea and integration be built during the event, and asking teams to list the tools they used. Judges then focus on originality, product thinking and whether the team understands its code. If the rules are silent, ask organisers before relying heavily on AI. Being open about tools builds trust and avoids disqualification disputes after the results are announced.

## How do AI hackathons work?

AI hackathons follow the usual format but centre on building with models: teams use APIs or open models for features like chat assistants, RAG, agents, vision or speech, often with free API credits from sponsors.

Organisers usually provide model access, sample datasets, starter templates and mentors who know the sponsor's tools. Judging emphasises useful applications, responsible design and technical depth, such as evaluation, grounding or clever tool use, rather than a simple wrapper around a chatbot. Strong teams prepare a reusable stack beforehand, such as a FastAPI backend with retrieval and streaming, then spend the event on the problem and demo. Explain how you handle errors and hallucinations, since judges ask.

## When do hackathons happen?

Hackathons run all year, but college hackathons cluster around academic calendars, often during the autumn and spring semesters, tech fests and weekends. Large online hackathons and corporate challenges are announced throughout the year.

Many events run over a weekend, from Friday evening or Saturday morning to Sunday afternoon, so students and professionals can join without missing classes or work. Online hackathons may run for days or weeks with flexible schedules. National events, such as Smart India Hackathon, follow multi-month timelines with idea submissions months before the finale. Follow platforms and communities to see upcoming events, since registration often closes weeks before the hackathon starts.

## How many hackathons happen in a year?

Thousands. Platforms such as Devpost, Devfolio, MLH and Unstop together list many thousands of hackathons yearly, from small college events to large global online competitions, plus countless internal company hackathons that are never publicly listed.

MLH alone supports hundreds of student hackathons each season, and Devpost hosts many online challenges at any time. In India, college tech fests, corporate challenges and government events add many more. The exact total is unknown because counting depends on what qualifies, such as ideathons or coding contests. For participants, the takeaway is abundance: you can likely find an event every month that fits your interests and skill level, online or nearby.

## Do hackathons have prizes?

Most do. Prizes include cash, gadgets, cloud credits, internships or interview opportunities, incubation support, sponsor products and certificates, with categories such as best overall, best beginner team and best use of a sponsor's API.

Sponsor tracks often offer separate prizes, so a team can win for using a particular tool well even without placing overall. Some events focus on learning and offer only certificates, swag and recognition. Read the prize rules carefully: some require submitting by strict deadlines, joining follow-up programmes, or meeting tax and identity requirements to receive payment. Winning helps, but the project, skills and connections are the lasting rewards, so choose events that match your goals.

## Do hackathons have themes?

Many do. Themes or tracks, such as healthcare, education, fintech, sustainability, AI and open innovation, guide what teams build. Some hackathons give specific problem statements, while others are open, letting teams build anything.

Themes help judges compare projects fairly and help sponsors get solutions relevant to their interests. Open innovation tracks reward creativity across domains. Government hackathons such as Smart India Hackathon publish detailed problem statements from ministries and organisations. Choose a theme where you understand the users, have relevant skills or can access data, rather than the most fashionable one. Read theme descriptions carefully, since projects outside the stated tracks may be ineligible for prizes.

## Do hackathons have an age limit?

It depends on the event. Many require participants to be at least 18, or allow younger participants with guardian consent; student hackathons require enrolment; and some events have upper limits, such as youth competitions or early-career programmes.

Student hackathon organisers usually require minors to submit a guardian consent form, and venues or sponsors may add restrictions. School-level hackathons exist specifically for younger students. Corporate and open innovation challenges may require adult participants to sign legal agreements. Always check the official rules and code of conduct, and email organisers if eligibility is unclear, because breaking eligibility rules can lead to disqualification even after winning.

## Where can you find hackathons?

Community recommendations include Devpost, MLH's events calendar, Devfolio and Unstop for India, lu.ma and Eventbrite listings, Kaggle competitions, and university tech fest pages. Discord servers and developer communities share upcoming events quickly.

Follow organisers and sponsors on LinkedIn and X, join student tech clubs and communities, and subscribe to developer newsletters that list events. Companies such as cloud and AI providers announce hackathons on their blogs. Set alerts on platforms for themes you like. For Indian students, college fest websites and government portals, including Smart India Hackathon, are key sources. Student communities, such as TechVerse Enclave, which I founded, are good places to share opportunities and find teammates.

# How does BM25 work? Meaning, who developed it, uses in AI, Python, Qdrant and pgvector
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-bm25-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


BM25 works by scoring each document for a query: for every query word, it rewards documents where the word appears often, gives more weight to rare words, and adjusts for document length so long documents do not win just by being long. It is the default ranking in many search engines and the keyword half of hybrid retrieval in RAG. RAG.NextUpgrad fuses BM25 with dense vector search, then reranks, so this page explains how BM25 works, its name and origins, its role in AI, implementing it, and support in Qdrant and pgvector.

## How does BM25 work?

For each query term, BM25 multiplies an inverse document frequency weight, higher for rare terms, by a term frequency component that grows with repetitions but saturates, normalised by document length relative to the average. The document's score is the sum over query terms.

Two parameters shape it: `k1`, typically 1.2 to 2.0, controls saturation, so the tenth occurrence adds much less than the first; and `b`, typically 0.75, controls length normalisation. An inverted index lists which documents contain each term, so only matching documents are scored, making BM25 fast at scale. Preprocessing such as lowercasing, stemming and tokenisation strongly affects results, especially for Indian languages and mixed-language text.

## What does BM25 stand for?

BM25 stands for "Best Matching 25". "Best Matching" refers to a family of ranking functions developed for the Okapi information retrieval system, and 25 identifies the particular variant that became standard.

It is often called Okapi BM25 after that system. Variants exist, such as BM25F, which weights fields like titles and bodies differently, and BM25+, which adjusts for very long documents. In everyday engineering conversations, "BM25" simply means keyword relevance ranking as implemented in tools such as Lucene, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and many libraries.

## Who developed BM25?

BM25 was developed by Stephen Robertson, Steve Walker and colleagues working on the Okapi system at City University London, building on probabilistic retrieval theory by Robertson and Karen Spärck Jones. It was presented through the TREC evaluations in the mid-1990s.

Spärck Jones had earlier introduced inverse document frequency, the idea that rare terms matter more, in 1972, a foundation of BM25. Robertson and Hugo Zaragoza later wrote the standard theoretical review of BM25 in 2009. Their work remains one of the most influential contributions to search, still used in production systems decades later. Its longevity shows how well-designed simple methods can outlast many more complex ideas.

## What is BM25 in AI?

In AI applications, BM25 is used as a lexical retriever: it finds documents containing the query's exact words, complementing embedding-based semantic search. In RAG systems, BM25 catches names, codes, acronyms and rare terms that vector search can miss.

It also serves as a baseline in information retrieval research, since neural retrievers must beat BM25 to be considered useful, and it often remains competitive on new domains. Learned sparse models, such as SPLADE, extend BM25's idea by learning which terms matter. In practice, combining BM25 with dense retrieval through reciprocal rank fusion gives more robust retrieval than either alone.

## Where is BM25 used?

BM25 powers keyword search in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Apache Solr and Lucene-based systems, MongoDB Atlas Search, many website and documentation search tools, and libraries for Python and other languages. It is used in RAG pipelines as the keyword retriever in hybrid search.

You meet BM25 whenever you search documentation, e-commerce catalogues, support articles, logs or code with keyword-based search engines. Researchers use it as a standard baseline. In RAG.NextUpgrad, BM25 retrieves candidates alongside vector search, and reciprocal rank fusion merges both lists before reranking.

## Is BM25 a reranker?

Usually no. BM25 is typically a first-stage retriever: it scores the whole indexed collection and returns top candidates quickly. Rerankers, such as cross-encoder models, then reorder a small set of candidates with more expensive, more accurate scoring.

BM25 can technically rerank a candidate set produced by another method, for instance rescoring vector search results by keyword overlap, but neural rerankers generally do this better. The common pipeline is: BM25 and vector retrieval in parallel, fusion, then a cross-encoder reranker on the top 20 to 50 results, then the language model. Each stage trades speed for accuracy. Measuring recall after each stage shows where your pipeline loses good candidates.

## How do I implement BM25?

Tokenise documents, build an inverted index of term frequencies, compute each term's inverse document frequency and the average document length, then score each query by summing BM25 contributions for its terms over matching documents.

Steps:

- Tokenise and normalise text: lowercase, remove punctuation, optionally stem.
- For each term, count how many documents contain it.
- Compute IDF, commonly log of N minus df plus 0.5, over df plus 0.5, plus 1.
- Store term frequencies per document and document lengths.
- For a query, sum IDF times saturated, length-normalised term frequency.
- Sort documents by score.

For production, use a search engine or library rather than writing your own. Writing it once yourself, though, is an excellent way to understand ranking and to debug search results later.

## How do I implement BM25 in Python?

The quickest way is the `rank_bm25` library: tokenise your documents, build a `BM25Okapi` index, then score queries. For larger collections, use a search engine such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or a Postgres extension.

```python
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
docs = ["refunds are processed within 7 days", "hostel fees are due in july", "refund policy for courses"]
bm25 = BM25Okapi([d.split() for d in docs])
print(bm25.get_top_n("refund policy".split(), docs, n=2))
```

Improve tokenisation with lowercasing, stemming and stop-word handling. LangChain's BM25 retriever wraps this library for quick hybrid RAG experiments.

## Does Qdrant support BM25?

Yes, through sparse vectors. Qdrant supports sparse vectors with an IDF modifier, so you can store BM25-style term weights and have Qdrant apply inverse document frequency at query time. Libraries such as FastEmbed generate BM25 sparse vectors for Qdrant.

This lets you run keyword and semantic search in one database: store a dense vector and a sparse BM25 vector per chunk, then use Qdrant's hybrid query to fuse results with reciprocal rank fusion. Check the documentation for the current recommended setup, since Qdrant's hybrid search features have evolved across versions.

## Does pgvector support BM25?

No. pgvector handles dense vector similarity only. PostgreSQL's built-in full-text search provides keyword ranking with functions such as `ts_rank`, which is not BM25, though it works well for many applications.

For true BM25 in Postgres, use extensions such as ParadeDB's pg_search, which adds BM25 indexes, or other community BM25 extensions. A common hybrid setup combines pgvector for semantic search with full-text or BM25 search in the same database, fusing results in SQL with reciprocal rank fusion. That keeps the whole hybrid pipeline inside PostgreSQL. Check an extension's maintenance status and managed-hosting support before relying on it in production.
