# How does chunking help? Memory, cognitive load, education, tasks, AI and semantic chunking
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-chunking-help/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Chunking helps by grouping separate pieces of information into larger, meaningful units, so your limited working memory handles a few rich chunks instead of many isolated items. It makes learning, remembering and doing complex work easier, and the same idea is used in AI, where documents are split into chunks for retrieval. I design document chunking in RAG.NextUpgrad and teach students study strategies, so this page covers why chunking works, memory and cognitive load, education, tasks, AI and semantic chunking, and the golf meaning.

## Why is chunking used?

Chunking is used to overcome the limits of working memory, which can hold only a few items at once. By grouping items into meaningful units, people can process, remember and use much more information at the same time.

It is used in studying, teaching, instructional design, user interface design, presentations, programming and memory techniques. Phone numbers, card numbers and postcodes are chunked into groups for this reason. In software and AI, chunking organises code into functions and documents into retrievable passages. In every case, the goal is the same: make complex information manageable. It is one of the most transferable thinking tools, useful from exam preparation to designing software architecture.

## Why does chunking work?

Chunking works because working memory capacity is limited to roughly four meaningful units, but each unit can contain a lot of information if it connects to knowledge already stored in long-term memory. A familiar pattern counts as one chunk, however many parts it has.

For a beginner, "for i in range(10):" is many separate symbols; for an experienced programmer, it is one familiar chunk, a loop. Expertise largely consists of building bigger, richer chunks through practice, which is why experts process situations faster. Chunking also creates structure, making information easier to retrieve later because related items are stored together.

## How does chunking help with memorising?

Chunking helps memorising by reducing the number of items to remember and linking them into meaningful groups: remembering "IIT", "NIT", "IIIT" as one category of institutes, or a speech as three main sections, is easier than many separate facts.

Techniques: group related facts into categories; create acronyms and mnemonics; find patterns, such as rhythms in numbers; connect new information to things you already know; and summarise each section into a few key points. Practise recalling chunks without notes, then expand each chunk into details. Combined with spaced repetition, chunking makes long-term memory far more reliable.

## How does chunking help manage cognitive load?

Cognitive load theory, developed by John Sweller, describes the limited mental effort available for processing new information. Chunking reduces this load by presenting information in smaller, structured pieces and building schemas, organised knowledge that lets learners treat complex ideas as single units.

When too much new information arrives at once, learners become overloaded and learn little. Breaking lessons into short segments, mastering each before moving on, and using worked examples reduce extraneous load, leaving capacity for real understanding. As schemas form, tasks that once overwhelmed learners become manageable, freeing attention for higher-level thinking.

## What is chunking in education?

In education, chunking means breaking learning content into small, manageable segments, each with a clear focus, often followed by practice or reflection, so students can process and retain information without overload.

Teachers chunk lessons into short explanations followed by activities, split long readings into sections with questions, and break projects into milestones. Instructional designers create short video lessons and modules for the same reason. Chunking also applies to assessments: smaller, frequent quizzes help retention more than single large exams. The approach supports learners of all ages, especially those new to a subject.

## What are examples of chunking in education?

Examples include teaching a programming concept in ten-minute segments with exercises after each, splitting a chapter into sections with summary questions, grouping vocabulary by theme, and breaking a semester project into weekly milestones with feedback.

More examples:

- Mathematics: solving one step type at a time before combining steps.
- Languages: learning phrases as units rather than single words.
- History: organising events by period and cause.
- Science: diagrams grouping processes into stages.
- Coding bootcamps: one concept per day with a mini project.

At my campus sessions, a three-year roadmap split into one focus per year works the same way.

## How does task chunking work?

Task chunking breaks a large, intimidating task into small, concrete steps that each feel achievable. Instead of "build my final-year project", the first chunk is "write a one-paragraph problem statement", then "sketch three screens", and so on.

It works because small tasks are easier to start, reduce procrastination, give frequent feelings of progress, and make planning and estimation more accurate. Combine it with time-boxing, such as focusing for 25 to 50 minutes per chunk, and a visible checklist. In software teams, breaking features into small tickets and pull requests is task chunking applied to engineering.

## Where are chunking strategies used in AI?

In AI, chunking strategies are used most in retrieval-augmented generation: documents are split into chunks that are embedded, indexed and retrieved to answer questions. Chunking also appears in processing long texts that exceed model context limits, streaming audio for speech recognition, and splitting code for analysis.

Strategies include fixed-size chunks with overlap, recursive splitting by paragraphs and sentences, structure-aware chunking by headings and tables, semantic chunking, and parent-child chunking. In RAG.NextUpgrad and the OCR and Speech Workspace, chunk boundaries follow document structure and keep page numbers, so answers cite the right page. Chunking quality strongly affects retrieval accuracy.

## How does semantic chunking work?

Semantic chunking splits text where the meaning changes rather than at fixed lengths. It embeds sentences, measures similarity between neighbouring sentences, and starts a new chunk where similarity drops sharply, indicating a topic shift.

This keeps related sentences together, which can improve retrieval for documents without clear headings, such as transcripts or long emails. It costs more to compute and does not always beat simpler structure-aware chunking, so evaluate it on your own questions. Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex provide semantic splitters with adjustable thresholds for how big a meaning change must be. Set minimum and maximum chunk sizes too, so a long unbroken topic does not become one huge chunk.

## Why am I chunking my golf wedges?

In golf, "chunking" or hitting it fat means the club strikes the ground before the ball, losing distance. With wedges, it usually comes from weight hanging on the back foot, the ball too far forward, an early release of the wrists, or trying to scoop the ball into the air.

Common fixes: keep more weight on the lead foot through impact, position the ball centrally or slightly back for pitches, keep hands ahead of the ball, and focus on striking down and through. Drills, such as placing a towel behind the ball, help train a clean strike. A coach or video of your swing identifies the specific cause quickly.

# How does face recognition work? Detection, embeddings, thresholds and liveness, from building FaceVision
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-face-recognition-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How does face recognition work?

**Face recognition works in four steps. A detector finds each face in the image and its landmarks. The face is aligned and cropped to a standard size. A recognition network turns the crop into an embedding, a vector of a few hundred numbers in which faces of the same person land close together. Finally the system compares that embedding with stored ones and declares a match when the distance falls under a threshold. Everything else, liveness, enrolment, privacy, is engineering around those four steps.**


The embedding idea comes from FaceNet, which trained a network so that the Euclidean distance between two face vectors directly measured how likely they were the same person [1]. ArcFace sharpened it with an angular margin loss that spreads identities further apart, and it is the recipe behind most open models today [2].

I built FaceVision in 2026 as a browser-only detection, recognition and liveness system: the camera frames never leave the device, only embeddings are sent to a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, and no image is ever stored [13]. This page is what that build taught me, with the papers underneath each step.

> The moment you decide never to store a face image, half your privacy problems disappear and the other half become simple. Store the vector, throw away the pixels.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FaceVision</cite>

## What is the difference between face detection and face recognition?

**Face detection finds faces: it returns bounding boxes and usually landmarks for eyes, nose and mouth, for every face in a frame, and it does not know or care who they are. Face recognition takes one detected face and identifies or verifies the person. Detection is the first stage of recognition, but a security camera that counts people, or a phone that focuses on a face, needs only detection.**



MTCNN was the standard detector for years [3]; RetinaFace improved accuracy on small and turned faces and remains a strong default [4]. Google's MediaPipe ships a fast detector that runs on phones and in browsers [11].

## What is a face embedding, and how are faces compared?

**A face embedding is a fixed-length vector, often 128 or 512 numbers, produced by a network trained so that the same person's faces cluster together and different people's faces sit apart. Comparison is a distance: cosine similarity or Euclidean distance between two vectors. If the distance is below a threshold, the system calls it a match. The threshold is not part of the model; it is a decision you make from your own error data.**



The embedding is why you never need to store the face image. A vector cannot be turned back into a photograph in any useful way, it is far smaller, and it can be compared in a database index like any other vector. FaceVision stores exactly this: the vector, the user id, the timestamp, nothing visual [13].

## How do I choose the match threshold?

**Collect pairs of embeddings from your real users and cameras, labelled same-person or different-person, then plot the two error rates as the threshold moves: false accepts, a stranger let in, and false rejects, the right person turned away. Choose the threshold that meets your risk. A door lock wants false accepts near zero and tolerates retries; a class attendance system tolerates a few false accepts and hates queues. Never ship a vendor's default threshold blind.**



NIST's ongoing Face Recognition Technology Evaluation publishes false match and false non-match rates for hundreds of algorithms under controlled conditions, and it is the reference for what state-of-the-art accuracy looks like [5]. It also shows how far the same algorithm's numbers move between a mugshot-quality image and a webcam frame, which is why your own data matters more than the leaderboard.

## Why does face recognition fail?

**For a short list of reasons that repeat everywhere: low light and backlight, motion blur, extreme pose, masks and sunglasses, low-resolution or heavily compressed cameras, faces too small in the frame, enrolment photos that look nothing like daily conditions, and a threshold tuned on a different population. Twins and close relatives are a real limit for some models. Most "the AI is broken" tickets are a camera or lighting problem.**



On twins: FaceVision, like every embedding system I have tested, sometimes cannot separate identical twins at a threshold that still rejects strangers. For high-stakes use, that is a reason to add a second factor, not a reason to loosen the threshold.

## Is face recognition biased, and how accurate is it across groups?

**Accuracy differs across demographic groups for most algorithms. NIST's 2019 demographic study measured higher false positive rates for some groups than others, with the size of the gap depending strongly on the algorithm [6]. The gap has narrowed in recent evaluations but has not vanished. The practical response is to test on your own user population, report the error rates per group, and choose a threshold and a fallback that protect the worst-served group, not the average.**


For a college attendance system in India, the relevant test set is your own students under your own classroom lights, not a benchmark shot in a studio elsewhere.

## What is liveness detection, and why do I need it?

**Liveness detection, also called presentation attack detection, checks that the face in front of the camera is a live person and not a printed photo, a phone screen showing a photo or video, or a mask. Without it, any recognition system that unlocks or pays can be defeated by a picture from social media. Active liveness asks the user to do something, blink, turn, follow a dot. Passive liveness analyses a single frame or short clip for texture, depth cues and screen artefacts.**



ISO/IEC 30107 defines the framework and terminology for presentation attack detection and the metrics vendors quote [7]. Texture analysis, the observation that a re-photographed face carries colour and frequency artefacts a live face does not, is one of the classic passive approaches [8]. FaceVision uses a passive check on the device before any embedding is computed, so a photo held to the camera is rejected before it can even be compared [13].


## Can I run face recognition in the browser, without a server seeing the face?

**Yes. ONNX Runtime Web runs detection, recognition and liveness models in the browser using WebAssembly or WebGPU [10]. The camera frame stays on the device, the models produce an embedding locally, and only the embedding travels to your API for comparison and storage. It is slower than a GPU server for large galleries, but for verification and small identification sets it is fast enough, and it removes the biggest privacy and compliance burden: you never possess a face image.**


The architecture of FaceVision, which is the concrete version of this answer:


Models are exported to ONNX from PyTorch or taken from open toolkits such as InsightFace, which publishes ArcFace-family recognition models and RetinaFace detectors [9]. Quantising them shrinks download size and speeds inference on phones, at a small accuracy cost you should measure.

## How do I build a face recognition attendance system?

**Enrol each person with three to five embeddings taken under the real classroom conditions, on the same kind of camera. At check-in, detect, run liveness, embed and compare against the enrolled set for that class only, which keeps the gallery small and the false-match rate low. Log the score, not the image. Add a fallback for rejections, such as a one-time code, so a bad lighting day does not stop a class. Publish the privacy notice before the first day.**


Attendance is the most common student project in this space and the one most often built wrong: images saved to a folder, a global gallery of thousands, no liveness, a threshold copied from a tutorial. Built right, with per-class galleries, on-device liveness and embeddings-only storage, it is also a strong portfolio piece, because you can explain each decision.

## Is face recognition legal in India, and how do I handle privacy?

**Facial data is biometric personal data, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sets the framework for processing personal data with notice, consent, purpose limitation and security obligations [12]. Rules and enforcement continue to develop, so treat this as the direction, not legal advice. The engineering answer is independent of jurisdiction: collect consent, tell people what is stored and for how long, store embeddings rather than images, delete on request, and restrict who can run a search.**



I wrote a longer note on what changed in my own practice after FaceVision, and most of it is the list above [14].

## Which library or model should I use for face recognition?

**For a Python prototype: InsightFace for detection and ArcFace-family recognition, or the face_recognition library for simplicity at lower accuracy [9]. For phones and browsers: MediaPipe for detection [11] and an ONNX-exported ArcFace model in ONNX Runtime Web for recognition [10]. For anything that unlocks or pays: add a liveness model and test it against printed photos and phone screens yourself before you believe its numbers.**



## What are common face recognition interview questions?

**Explain detection versus recognition versus verification versus identification. Explain what an embedding is and why distance measures similarity. Explain how you would set a threshold and what false accept and false reject mean. Explain what liveness detection defends against. Explain how you would design the system so no face image is stored. If you can answer these from a project you built, you are ahead of most candidates.**



## Where should I start with a face recognition project?

**Build verification first, not identification: enrol yourself and two friends, run detection and embedding in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, store only embeddings, and plot your own false accept and false reject curve from a hundred attempts. Then add passive liveness and try to fool it with a photo of yourself. That project teaches every concept on this page and is exactly the shape of FaceVision.**


If your college wants a hands-on session on computer vision that respects privacy from the first line of code, that is one of the talks I offer. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does Gemini AI work? Gems, videos, graphs, limits, credits, speed and water use
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-gemini-ai-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini AI works as a family of large multimodal models from Google: transformer networks trained on huge amounts of text, code, images, audio and video, which predict the next part of a response from everything in the conversation. The Gemini app, formerly Bard, wraps these models with Google Search, tools and integrations. I build AI products that switch between model providers, Gemini among the options, so this page covers how it works and what it offers, Gems, video and graphs, limits and credits, speed, water use and photo editing.

## How does Gemini AI work?

Gemini models are transformer neural networks trained to predict the next token on vast multimodal data, then tuned with human feedback to follow instructions. They are natively multimodal, so text, images, audio and video are processed in one model rather than bolted together.

Newer versions use mixture-of-experts designs, activating only parts of the network per request for efficiency, and support very long context windows, so they can read long documents or hours of video. "Thinking" variants reason step by step before answering. In the Gemini app, the model can call tools such as Google Search for current information, code execution and Google apps, then combine results into an answer.

## What does Gemini AI offer?

Gemini offers a chat assistant for writing, research, coding and learning, with image understanding, image generation and editing, video generation on eligible plans, Deep Research reports, Canvas for documents and code, Gems, and integrations with Gmail, Docs, Drive and other Google apps.

Developers use Gemini models through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, or Vertex AI on Google Cloud, with features such as long context, structured output, function calling and grounding with Search. Gemini is also built into Android, Chrome and Workspace. Paid plans add stronger models, higher limits and more storage; check Google's plan pages for current features in India.

## What are Gemini AI Gems?

Gems are custom versions of Gemini that you set up with instructions, and optionally files, for tasks you repeat, such as a study coach, an email editor or a coding helper. Instead of re-explaining context each time, you open the Gem and start.

Create one from the Gems section: give it a name, describe its role and rules, add reference files, test it, then save. Google also provides premade Gems, such as a learning coach. Good Gem instructions are specific: who it helps, what to do, what format to use and what to avoid. Gems can be shared, which helps teams use consistent prompts.

## Can Gemini AI generate videos?

Yes, on eligible plans. The Gemini app generates short videos from text prompts using Google's Veo models, and newer Veo versions can produce synchronised audio. Google's Flow tool offers more control for filmmaking with Veo.

Availability, length and daily limits depend on your plan and region. Generated videos carry SynthID watermarks identifying them as AI-made. For best results, describe the subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting and style in your prompt. Gemini can also help write scripts and storyboards even when video generation is unavailable on your plan.

## Can Gemini AI generate graphs?

Yes. Gemini can create charts by writing and running code from data you provide or upload, and can build interactive charts in Canvas. In Google Sheets, Gemini helps create charts and formulas from your spreadsheet data.

Ask specifically: "Create a bar chart of monthly sign-ups from this CSV, with months on the x-axis." Check the underlying numbers, because charts are only as accurate as the data interpretation. For repeatable charts, ask Gemini for the Python or spreadsheet formula it used, so you can rerun it yourself. For diagrams such as flowcharts, it can produce Mermaid code or images.

## Does Gemini AI have a limit?

Yes. Gemini apps have usage limits that depend on your plan and the model or feature, such as daily prompts for the most capable models, image and video generations, Deep Research reports and file uploads. Free users have lower limits than paid subscribers.

When you reach a limit, Gemini may switch you to a lighter model or ask you to wait until it resets. Developers face separate API rate limits by tier in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. Google's Gemini Apps Help pages list current limits, which change as models and plans change. For heavy use, a paid plan or the API with your own quota is more predictable.

## How do Gemini AI credits work?

Some Google AI plans include monthly AI credits that are spent on generation-heavy features, such as video creation in Flow and Whisk. Each generation consumes credits based on the model and settings, and unused monthly credits typically do not carry over.

Higher plans include more credits, and Google has offered ways to top up. Credits are separate from ordinary chat usage limits. Check your plan's page or the Flow interface to see your balance and the credit cost of each option before generating, since higher-quality video models cost more credits per clip.

## Why is Gemini AI so slow?

Gemini can feel slow when using a "thinking" model that reasons before answering, processing long documents or videos, running Deep Research, generating images or video, during high demand, or because of your network or browser.

Fixes:

- Switch to a faster model for simple tasks.
- Start a new chat when conversations get very long.
- Upload smaller files or only relevant pages.
- Check your connection and disable heavy browser extensions.
- Try the mobile app or another browser.

For applications calling the API, stream responses so users see text immediately, and add fallback providers for outages, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with multi-provider fallback.

## Does Gemini AI use water?

Yes, indirectly. Data centres that run Gemini use water for cooling. In 2025, Google reported that a median Gemini Apps text prompt used about 0.26 millilitres of water, roughly five drops, along with a small amount of energy.

That figure covers typical text prompts; image and video generation and long-context or reasoning tasks use more. At global scale, totals add up, which is why companies report on efficiency, renewable energy and water replenishment. Measurement methods differ across companies, so compare figures carefully. You can reduce your own footprint by choosing lighter models for simple tasks.

## How do I use Gemini as a photo editor?

Upload a photo in the Gemini app and describe the edit in plain language, such as "remove the background clutter" or "change the shirt to blue", and Gemini's image model edits it while keeping the rest consistent. You can refine with follow-up instructions.

Tips:

- Make one change at a time for precise control.
- Describe what to keep: "keep the face and pose unchanged".
- Use reference images for style or objects.
- Download the result in full resolution.

Edited images include SynthID watermarks marking AI involvement. Only edit photos you have rights to, and never create misleading images of real people.

# How does OCR work? From Tesseract to document AI: turning scanned PDFs and invoices into searchable, structured text
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-ocr-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is OCR and how does it work?

**OCR, optical character recognition, converts images of text, a scanned page, a photo of a receipt, a PDF that is really a picture, into machine-readable text. It works in three stages: detection finds where text is on the page, recognition reads the characters in each region, and layout analysis puts the pieces back in reading order with their structure, paragraphs, columns, tables. Modern systems do all three with neural networks; older ones like classic Tesseract use hand-built image processing for the first and third.**


The distinction that saves the most time: a "PDF" may already contain text, in which case you do not need OCR at all, only extraction. Check with a PDF library first; PyMuPDF will tell you in one call whether a page has a text layer [11]. OCR is for pages that are only pixels.

I built two document systems in 2026 that sit on top of OCR: DocuLens AI, which extracts and compliance-checks invoices and contracts with schema validation [13], and the OCR & Speech Workspace, which OCRs large PDFs concurrently in page batches and turns each document into a searchable knowledge base with page-level citations [12]. This page is the pipeline underneath both.

> Nobody wants OCR. They want the total from the invoice, the clause from the contract, the answer from the manual, with the page number. OCR is the first ten percent of that.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building DocuLens AI</cite>

## What are the stages of an OCR pipeline?

**Preprocess the image: deskew, denoise, binarise, fix resolution. Detect text regions and their orientation. Recognise the characters in each region into strings with confidence scores. Reconstruct layout: reading order, columns, paragraphs, tables, headers and footers. Post-process: spell-check against a lexicon, normalise numbers and dates, attach page and position to every span. Then either store the text for search or pass it to an extraction step.**



Detection is where CRAFT-style networks replaced connected-component heuristics, finding text at odd angles and sizes [3]. Recognition moved from character classifiers to sequence models, and TrOCR showed a pure transformer encoder-decoder could read lines end to end with pre-trained vision and language models [4]. Layout is where the hardest problems remain, and where document-understanding models entered.

## What is Tesseract, and is it still good?

**Tesseract is the open-source OCR engine originally developed at HP and later at Google, now maintained as a community project [1]. Version 4 added an LSTM-based recogniser, which made it good on clean, printed, well-scanned text in dozens of languages, and it remains free, offline and scriptable, with OCRmyPDF wrapping it to add text layers to scanned PDFs [10]. It is still the right tool for clean printed pages at zero cost. It is the wrong tool for photos, handwriting, complex tables and forms.**



Smith's 2007 overview of the engine's architecture is still the best short explanation of how a classic OCR engine thinks about a page [2].

## How do vision-language models change OCR?

**Vision-language models read the page image directly and output text, structure or answers, without a separate detection and recognition stage. They handle mixed layouts, tables, handwriting and low-quality scans far better than classic engines, they can output Markdown with headings and tables preserved, and they can be asked for specific fields in one step. The cost is that they run as API calls or on a GPU, they can hallucinate plausible text where the image is unreadable, and they need validation downstream.**


LayoutLM pre-trained on text plus its position on the page and set the pattern for document understanding [5]; Donut showed that a model could go straight from pixels to structured output with no OCR engine at all [6]. Mistral's document API is one of several commercial options that return page text as Markdown with tables and images preserved [7], and it is what the OCR & Speech Workspace uses for its page batches [12].


The hallucination row is the one to remember. A classic engine produces garbage on a bad scan and you can see it is garbage. A language model produces a fluent, wrong invoice total. Validation is not optional.

## How do I OCR a PDF for free?

**If the PDF already has text, extract it with PyMuPDF or a similar library and skip OCR [11]. If it is a scan, run OCRmyPDF, which uses Tesseract to add an invisible text layer so the PDF becomes searchable and copyable [10]. For photos or messy pages, PaddleOCR or EasyOCR in a short Python script. For the best quality on hard documents at some cost, a vision-language document API. All of the open tools run offline on a laptop.**


The check-then-OCR pattern in Python:

```python
import fitz  # PyMuPDF

doc = fitz.open("scan.pdf")
for page in doc:
    text = page.get_text()
    if text.strip():
        use(text, page.number + 1)          # already has a text layer
    else:
        pix = page.get_pixmap(dpi=300)       # render, then OCR this page only
        text = ocr_engine(pix.tobytes("png"))
        use(text, page.number + 1)
```

Keep the page number with every span from the first line. Every citation, search result and audit trail later depends on it.

## How do I OCR large PDFs quickly?

**Split by page, process pages concurrently in batches sized to your engine's or API's rate limit, and merge in page order. A 500-page manual is 500 independent jobs; a concurrency of eight turns an hour into minutes. Cache results by document hash and page, so a re-upload does not re-OCR. Store text per page, not per document, so retrieval and citations stay page-precise.**


Page-batched concurrency is the design of the OCR & Speech Workspace: pages fan out to the document API in batches, results land in a per-page store with the page number, and the document becomes a scoped knowledge base whose answers cite exact pages [12].


## How accurate is OCR, and how do I improve it?

**On clean 300 DPI scans of printed English, modern engines exceed 99 percent character accuracy. Accuracy falls with low resolution, skew, shadows, coloured backgrounds, unusual fonts, handwriting and dense tables, and it falls hardest on the characters that matter most in business documents: digits. Improve it by fixing the input first, resolution, deskew, contrast, then choosing the right engine for the page type, then validating with rules, and only then by trying a bigger model.**



## What is document AI, and how is it different from OCR?

**Document AI is OCR followed by understanding: classifying the document type, locating the fields that matter, extracting them into a schema you defined, validating them, and returning confidence per field. OCR gives you a wall of text. Document AI gives you an invoice number, a vendor, line items and a total, typed and checked. The extraction may use a language model with a strict output schema, a layout model trained on forms, or both.**



DocuLens AI is the field-and-validation layer: extraction through a language model constrained to a JSON schema, then deterministic checks and a compliance score computed the same way every time, so finance and legal users can rely on it [13].

## How do I extract invoice data I can trust?

**Define the schema first: the fields, their types, and the rules between them. Extract with a model constrained to that schema, or with a layout model trained on invoices. Then validate deterministically: line items must sum to the subtotal, tax must match the rate, dates must parse, the invoice number must match the vendor's pattern, currency must be stated. Flag anything that fails for a human. Score each document the same way every time. Never let the model be the last word on a number.**



Determinism matters because the same invoice must produce the same result on Tuesday as on Monday. That is why DocuLens computes scores from rules, not from a model's opinion [13].

## Can OCR read handwriting?

**Partly. Handwriting recognition on clean, separated block letters works reasonably with modern models; cursive, mixed scripts and forms with lines through the text remain hard. Vision-language models do better than classic engines, and confidence scores plus human review are essential. For Indian forms, mixed Hindi and English handwriting on printed templates, the practical approach is to recognise the printed template's fields, then OCR each handwritten field region separately with the expected type as a constraint, and route low-confidence results to a person.**


## Which OCR should I use: Tesseract, PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, or an API?

**Tesseract via OCRmyPDF for clean scanned documents at zero cost [1][10]. PaddleOCR when you need tables, multilingual pages and production quality on your own hardware [8]. EasyOCR for a quick script [9]. A vision-language document API when documents are messy, layouts matter and you can pay per page and validate the output [7]. Most real pipelines use two: a cheap engine first, an expensive model only on pages the cheap one fails.**




## What are common OCR and document AI interview questions?

**Explain the three stages and where errors come from. Compare classic OCR with vision-language models, including the hallucination risk. Describe how you would OCR a 1,000-page PDF quickly. Explain how you would validate an extracted invoice. Describe how page-level citations work in a document chatbot. If you have built one extraction pipeline with validation, you can answer all of them.**



## Where should I start with an OCR project?

**Take twenty real documents you have, invoices, marksheets, notes, and build the check-then-OCR script above with Tesseract. Measure character accuracy on five pages by hand. Then swap in a vision-language model for the pages that fail and add three validation rules. You will have learned every concept on this page, and the pipeline will be the shape of a real product.** My longer design note on the pipeline is on the portfolio [14]. For a hands-on document AI session at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does speech to text work? Whisper, real-time transcription architecture, Indian languages, and building a live transcription feature
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-speech-to-text-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is speech to text and how does it work?

**Speech to text, also called automatic speech recognition or ASR, converts spoken audio into written text. Audio is captured as a waveform, converted into a spectrogram of frequencies over time, split into short segments at speech boundaries, and fed to a model that maps acoustic patterns to words, using a language model to pick likely sequences. Post-processing adds punctuation, casing, numbers and speaker labels. Modern systems such as Whisper do the acoustic and language modelling in one transformer trained end to end.**


Two ideas made end-to-end recognition practical: connectionist temporal classification, which lets a network output text without aligning every frame to a character [6], and self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled audio, which wav2vec 2.0 showed could cut labelled data needs dramatically [5]. Whisper then trained a transformer on 680,000 hours of weakly labelled multilingual audio and made robust, open transcription available to anyone with a GPU or a patient CPU [1][2].

I built live speech-to-text into the OCR & Speech Workspace in 2026, alongside page-batched OCR and document chat, so that a spoken question could be transcribed, matched against a document and answered with page citations [13]. This page is the pipeline and the decisions underneath that feature.

> Transcription accuracy on a benchmark is a fact about the benchmark. The only number I ship on is word error rate measured on my users' audio, on their phones, in their rooms.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is Whisper, and why did it matter?

**Whisper is OpenAI's open-weight speech recognition model family, released in 2022, trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask audio [1]. It transcribes in dozens of languages, translates to English, detects language, and is robust to accents, background noise and technical vocabulary in ways earlier open models were not. It comes in sizes from tiny to large, so it runs on a laptop CPU at the small end and on a modest GPU at the large end. It made high-quality transcription free to self-host, which changed what students and small teams can build.**



For most projects, faster-whisper on a server or whisper.cpp on a device is the practical choice; the official implementation is the reference [2][3][4].

## How do I build real-time speech to text?

**Capture audio in small frames, run voice activity detection to find where speech starts and stops, buffer frames into chunks of a few seconds, transcribe each chunk as it closes, and stream partial text to the user while a final pass reconciles boundaries and punctuation. Latency is decided by chunk length and model size, not by the network. Over WebSockets or WebRTC from the browser, with the model on a server or on the device, this is a solved architecture; the work is in the boundaries.**



Silero VAD is the small, fast detector most pipelines use to find speech boundaries [7]. Speaker diarisation, who spoke when, is a separate model; pyannote.audio is the common open choice [8]. My architecture write-up covers the WebSocket flow and the trade-off between chunk length and latency in detail [14].

## How accurate is speech to text, and how do I measure it?

**Accuracy is measured as word error rate, WER: substitutions plus deletions plus insertions divided by the words in the reference transcript, so lower is better. Modern models reach single-digit WER on clean English benchmarks and much worse on noisy rooms, accents, domain vocabulary and phone audio. Measure on fifty clips of your own users' audio with hand-corrected transcripts; jiwer computes WER in a few lines [11]. Then fix the biggest error class, which is usually names and numbers.**



## How do I handle Hindi, Indian languages and code-mixing?

**Use a multilingual model and test it on real speakers, because English benchmark numbers say nothing about Hindi, Tamil or Hinglish. Whisper supports many Indian languages with widely varying quality across them [1]. AI4Bharat publishes models and datasets tuned for Indic languages that often outperform general models on Indian speech [9], and Common Voice has crowd-sourced Indian-language audio you can evaluate on [10]. Code-mixed speech, Hindi and English in one sentence, remains the hardest case; measure it separately.**


KrishGyan, the assistant that won Changethon at IIT Roorkee, took voice notes from farmers in their own language and answered by voice; the recognition step was where the demo lived or died, and the fix was always testing on real recordings from real phones rather than trusting a model card.


## Should I use an API or self-host a model?

**Self-host with faster-whisper or whisper.cpp when audio is sensitive, volume is high, or you need to run offline or on device. Use a transcription API when you want the best quality on hard audio without owning GPUs, when volume is low, or when you need features such as diarisation and word timestamps out of the box. Many products do both: on-device for live captions, an API for the final high-accuracy transcript. Price per minute of audio and privacy terms decide it.**



The OCR & Speech Workspace uses a provider's audio capability for transcription alongside its document models, because the product's users upload documents to the same provider anyway and the privacy boundary was already drawn there [12][13].

## What is speaker diarisation, and do I need it?

**Diarisation labels which speaker said each segment, turning a transcript into a dialogue. It is a separate model that clusters voice embeddings over time, and it adds latency and errors of its own, especially when speakers overlap or the count is unknown. You need it for meeting minutes, interviews and call analysis. You do not need it for dictation, voice commands, captions of a single speaker, or search over a recording. Add it only when the product shows speakers.**


## What are the common uses of speech to text?

**Voice assistants and voice-first apps for users who do not type; meeting and lecture transcription with summaries; live captions for accessibility; call centre analytics; medical and legal dictation; searchable archives of recordings; voice input for forms in the field. In India, voice-first interfaces in regional languages are the highest-leverage use, because they reach the people every text interface excludes.**



## Speech to text versus text to speech, and other terms

**Speech to text, STT or ASR, turns audio into words. Text to speech, TTS, turns words into audio. Voice cloning is TTS in a specific voice. Natural language understanding interprets the transcribed text. A voice assistant chains all of them: recognise, understand, respond, speak. People search for these interchangeably; they are different models with different failure modes.**



## What are common speech recognition interview questions?

**Explain the pipeline from waveform to text. Define word error rate and its three components. Explain what voice activity detection does and why chunking matters for latency. Compare self-hosting Whisper with an API. Describe how you would evaluate a model for Hindi. Explain what diarisation is and when it is unnecessary. Each answer is a section above, and the best proof is a live transcription demo you built.**



## Where should I start with a speech project?

**Record ten voice notes on your phone, transcribe them with faster-whisper on your laptop, correct the transcripts by hand, and compute the word error rate. Then try a smaller and a larger model and a second language. That afternoon teaches the whole page.** For a hands-on session on voice-first apps, speech recognition and document AI at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does Tesseract work? OCR tutorial, Google's role, apps, Infinity Stones and Minecraft
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-tesseract-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tesseract, the open-source OCR engine, works by analysing an image's layout to find blocks and lines of text, then reading each line with an LSTM neural network that outputs characters, words and their positions. It runs locally on CPUs and supports over 100 languages. I use OCR in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page explains how Tesseract works, Google's role and ownership, a Python tutorial and apps, then the other Tesseracts: Marvel's Infinity Stone questions and the Minecraft mod block.

## How does Tesseract work?

Tesseract processes an image in stages: it binarises the image into black and white, analyses page layout to find text blocks, lines and words, then recognises each text line with an LSTM neural network trained on many fonts and languages, and finally assembles the text.

Since version 4, the LSTM engine reads whole lines as sequences, which handles connected and variable fonts better than the older character-by-character approach, still available as a legacy mode. Page segmentation modes control how Tesseract interprets layout, for example a single line, a block or a full page. Output formats include plain text, hOCR, ALTO XML, TSV with word positions and confidence, and searchable PDF. Accuracy depends heavily on input quality: clean scans at around 300 DPI give excellent results, while photos with shadows, skew or busy backgrounds need preprocessing first.

## How does Google relate to Tesseract?

Tesseract was created at Hewlett-Packard, open-sourced in 2005, and Google sponsored and led much of its development for years, with original developer Ray Smith continuing the work at Google, adding languages and the LSTM recogniser.

Google described the engine in a 2007 paper, "An Overview of the Tesseract OCR Engine". Google's own cloud OCR services, such as Cloud Vision, are separate, more powerful systems; Tesseract is the open-source engine anyone can run. "Google Tesseract" usually just means Tesseract OCR, reflecting Google's past sponsorship. Google's involvement helped Tesseract gain support for many languages, including Indian scripts such as Devanagari, Tamil and Bengali.

## Who owns Tesseract OCR?

No company owns Tesseract OCR in the commercial sense. It is open-source software under the Apache 2.0 licence, maintained by a community of contributors on GitHub, with copyright held by its contributors and originally HP and Google.

Anyone can use, modify and distribute it, including in commercial products, under the licence terms. Because it is community-maintained, check the repository's activity, releases and issues for support, rather than expecting a vendor. Many companies build products on top of Tesseract, and some offer commercial support for it.

## What is a simple Tesseract tutorial in Python?

Install Tesseract on your system, install pytesseract and Pillow with pip, then load an image and call `image_to_string`. Preprocess with OpenCV for better results on photos.

```python
from PIL import Image
import pytesseract
text = pytesseract.image_to_string(Image.open("notice.png"), lang="eng", config="--psm 6")
print(text)
data = pytesseract.image_to_data(Image.open("notice.png"), output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
```

`image_to_data` returns word boxes and confidence scores, useful for highlighting or filtering low-confidence words. On Windows, set `pytesseract.pytesseract.tesseract_cmd` to the executable path if it is not on PATH. Experiment with page segmentation modes for different layouts.

## What is a Tesseract app?

There is no single official Tesseract app; Tesseract is an engine that many apps use. Scanner and OCR apps on phones and desktops, including some open-source ones, embed Tesseract to extract text from photos and documents, and graphical front ends make it easier to use without the command line.

On Android, apps built on Tesseract libraries offer offline OCR; on desktops, tools such as gImageReader provide a GUI for Tesseract, and OCRmyPDF uses it to make searchable PDFs. Other apps named "Tesseract" may be unrelated products. When choosing an OCR app, check whether it works offline, which languages it supports and how it handles your privacy.

## Is the Tesseract the Space Stone?

In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the Tesseract is not itself the Space Stone; it is the cube that contains it. The Space Stone, one of the six Infinity Stones, gives the Tesseract its power to open portals and teleport across space.

In Avengers: Infinity War, Thanos crushes the Tesseract to reveal the blue Space Stone inside and adds it to his gauntlet. So the films treat the Tesseract as a container, much like Loki's scepter contains the Mind Stone and the Orb contains the Power Stone. In casual conversation, fans often use the names interchangeably.

## Is the Tesseract the Mind Stone?

No. The Tesseract contains the Space Stone. The Mind Stone is the yellow stone in Loki's scepter in The Avengers, which later became part of Vision in Avengers: Age of Ultron.

Both objects appear in The Avengers: Loki uses the Tesseract to open a portal for the Chitauri invasion and the scepter to control minds. Their colours help distinguish them: blue for space, yellow for mind. Thanos takes the Mind Stone from Vision in Infinity War, completing his set of stones.

## What is the difference between the Tesseract and the Space Stone?

The Tesseract is the cube-shaped container; the Space Stone is the Infinity Stone inside it, the actual source of the power to manipulate space. Without the stone, the cube is an empty vessel.

The Tesseract's history spans Asgard, Norway, the Second World War, S.H.I.E.L.D., Captain Marvel's story and the Avengers, while the Space Stone, as one of the six stones created at the universe's beginning in Marvel lore, predates it. Thanos needed the stone, not the cube, which is why he destroyed the Tesseract. In the comics, the equivalent object is the Cosmic Cube, with a different origin.

## How does the Tesseract work in Minecraft?

In Minecraft mods, notably Thermal Expansion in older versions and standalone Tesseract mods in newer ones, a Tesseract is a block that wirelessly transfers items, fluids and energy between Tesseracts set to the same frequency, even across long distances and dimensions.

You place Tesseracts at each location, set a shared frequency, and configure whether each sends or receives items, fluids or power. Pipes or machines connected to one Tesseract can then deliver resources to another far away. It is popular for linking bases, mining outposts and power systems. Exact behaviour depends on the mod and version, so check the mod's documentation.

## Is there a Minecraft Tesseract tutorial?

Yes. Mod wikis and video tutorials explain crafting and configuring Tesseracts for the specific mod and Minecraft version you use, including recipes, frequency settings and input-output modes.

General steps:

- Install the mod pack or mod that adds Tesseracts.
- Check the recipe with a recipe viewer such as JEI.
- Craft at least two Tesseracts.
- Place them where you need to send and receive resources.
- Set the same frequency on both and configure modes.
- Connect pipes, conduits or machines.

Test with a small item flow first, then scale up your network.

# How face recognition works: embeddings, thresholds, verification vs identification, tools
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-face-recognition-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Face recognition detects a face, aligns it, converts it into an embedding, a vector of numbers describing facial features, and compares that embedding with stored ones using a similarity threshold. Good systems never need to store face images at all. I built FaceVision, which runs detection, recognition and liveness checks in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web and stores only embeddings in PostgreSQL, never images, so this page explains how it works, key terms, alternatives, libraries and real-world uses.

## How does face recognition work with embeddings and thresholds?

A detector finds the face, landmarks align it, and a neural network converts it into an embedding, often 128 or 512 numbers. Recognition compares embeddings by cosine similarity or distance: if similarity exceeds a threshold, the faces are considered a match.

The threshold trades false matches against false rejections, so tune it on labelled pairs from your users and conditions. Since matching needs only embeddings, systems can avoid storing face images, reducing harm if data leaks and simplifying privacy compliance. FaceVision follows this design: images are processed in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, only embeddings reach the FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, and liveness checks help block photos or screens held up to the camera.

## What is the difference between face identification, verification and recognition?

Face verification is one-to-one: is this person who they claim to be, as in phone unlock. Face identification is one-to-many: who is this person among a gallery of known people. Face recognition is the umbrella term covering both.

Verification compares a probe embedding with one enrolled template and applies a threshold. Identification compares against many templates, returning the best match above a threshold or no match, and its error rates grow with gallery size, so thresholds must be stricter. Face detection, finding faces in an image, is a separate earlier step and does not identify anyone. Identification raises bigger privacy and legal concerns, so it needs clear consent, purpose limits and oversight.

## How can you do face recognition without neural networks?

Classic methods include Eigenfaces, which uses principal component analysis on face images; Fisherfaces, which uses linear discriminant analysis; and Local Binary Patterns Histograms, which describes local texture. OpenCV's face module implements all three.

These methods need aligned, well-lit, frontal faces and work best on small, controlled datasets, such as a few dozen people in consistent lighting. Detection can also be done without neural networks using Haar cascades, or HOG features with a linear classifier, as in dlib. Accuracy is far below modern deep embeddings on real-world images with varied poses and lighting, so use classic methods for learning, constrained hardware or teaching demonstrations rather than security-critical systems.

## Can a face recognition system be trained only on synthetic faces?

Yes, partly. Research datasets such as Microsoft's DigiFace-1M and other generated-face datasets have trained recognition models without real identities, reducing privacy concerns, but models trained only on synthetic faces usually perform worse than those trained on real faces.

The gap comes from differences in texture, lighting, expressions and demographic variety between synthetic and real images. Combining synthetic data with a smaller real dataset, or fine-tuning on real data, narrows it. Synthetic data also helps balance demographics and add pose or accessory variations that real datasets lack. If you go synthetic-first, evaluate thoroughly on real benchmarks and across demographic groups, since performance differences between groups matter greatly for fairness.

## How do you add new people to face recognition without retraining?

With embedding-based recognition, you do not retrain to add people: compute embeddings for a new person's enrolment photos and add them to the gallery. The pretrained embedding model already generalises to unseen faces.

Store several embeddings per person, or their average, captured under different angles and lighting, and update them over time as appearance changes, for example after verified successful matches. Retraining or fine-tuning the embedding network is only needed when performance on your population or conditions is poor, and then techniques such as replaying samples from earlier data help avoid catastrophic forgetting. This enrolment approach is how FaceVision and most modern systems scale to new users.

## OpenCV vs face_recognition: which should you use?

OpenCV is a broad computer vision library; its face modules provide detection and classic recognisers, plus a DNN module for modern models. face_recognition is a simple Python library built on dlib that detects faces and computes 128-dimensional embeddings in a few lines.

face_recognition is great for quick prototypes and learning, with functions to locate faces, compute encodings and compare them with a tolerance. Its dlib model is older and less accurate on difficult images than modern models. OpenCV offers more control, video handling and deployment options, and can run newer detectors such as YuNet and recognisers such as SFace. For production, consider modern embedding models through InsightFace or ONNX Runtime, with liveness detection added.

## DeepFace vs face_recognition: which is better?

DeepFace is a Python framework that wraps many face recognition models, such as ArcFace, FaceNet and VGG-Face, and detectors, plus analysis of age, emotion and other attributes. face_recognition provides one dlib-based model with a very simple API.

DeepFace lets you compare models and pick a stronger one, such as ArcFace, often giving better accuracy than face_recognition's default model, at the cost of heavier dependencies. face_recognition remains easier for beginners. For either, set thresholds on your own data and measure false accept and false reject rates. Be careful with attribute analysis such as emotion or gender prediction, which is unreliable and raises ethical concerns; focus on consented, clearly scoped use cases.

## Iris vs face recognition: which is more accurate?

Iris recognition is generally more accurate and stable than face recognition, because iris patterns are highly distinctive and change little over life. Face recognition is more convenient, works at a distance and with ordinary cameras, but is affected by pose, lighting, ageing and expression.

Iris systems need near-infrared cameras and close, cooperative capture, which suits border control, national ID enrolment and high-security access. India's Aadhaar programme captures iris scans and fingerprints alongside face photos. Face recognition suits phones, attendance and access where convenience matters. Multimodal biometrics combine methods for higher assurance. Both require liveness or presentation attack detection to resist photos, masks or printed irises, and careful privacy safeguards.

## What makes the best face recognition door lock?

Look for locks with 3D or infrared face recognition, which resists photos and works in darkness, local processing on the device, a backup unlock method such as a PIN or key, and strong encryption for stored templates.

Check reviews for recognition speed and false rejections in real conditions, battery life, and how the lock behaves when power or Wi-Fi fails. Prefer brands that publish security practices and provide firmware updates. Avoid locks that rely only on 2D cameras without liveness, which photos can sometimes fool. Consider privacy: understand whether face data leaves the device and whether cloud features can be disabled. For rentals or shared homes, get consent from everyone enrolled.

## What is a good face recognition tutorial?

A practical tutorial path: detect faces with OpenCV or a modern detector, compute embeddings with face_recognition or InsightFace, enrol a few known people, then match new images by cosine similarity with a tuned threshold.

Then extend it: process webcam video, add a simple liveness check such as blink or head-movement prompts, store embeddings in PostgreSQL or a vector store instead of images, and measure accuracy on your own test photos. Courses in computer vision cover the theory, while hands-on projects teach thresholds and failure cases. Always use consenting participants, explain how data is handled, and follow local laws, since face data is sensitive personal information in many jurisdictions.

# How does Gemini work? Gemini vs Google Assistant, Home, Messages, Workspace, AI Mode
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-gemini-works-google/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Gemini is Google's family of multimodal AI models and the assistant app built on them, which understands text, images, audio, video and code and is now built into Android, Google Home, Messages, Workspace, Photos and Search. I build AI products on several model providers, so this page explains how Gemini works, how it compares with Google Assistant, whether to use it on Google Home, in Messages and with Workspace, which model powers AI Mode, Gemini in Photos, and how to get started.

## How does Gemini work?

Gemini models are large transformer-based neural networks trained on vast amounts of text, code, images, audio and video, so they can understand and generate across these formats. The Gemini app sends your prompt to these models, which predict a response token by token.

Around the core model, Google adds instruction tuning and safety training, tools such as Google Search for grounding, connected apps such as Gmail, Maps or YouTube, and memory of your preferences if enabled. Different model sizes serve different needs: Flash models for speed, Pro models for harder reasoning, and on-device Nano models in some phones. Like all language models, Gemini can make mistakes, so verify important facts, especially numbers, dates and claims without sources.

## Gemini vs Google Assistant: what is the difference?

Google Assistant was built for quick commands: timers, smart home control, calls and simple answers. Gemini is a generative AI assistant that holds conversations, writes, analyses images and documents, and reasons through complex requests, while increasingly handling Assistant's tasks too.

Google has been replacing Google Assistant with Gemini on Android phones, and on smart speakers and displays through Gemini for Home. Gemini is more capable for open-ended help, such as planning a trip or summarising an email thread, and supports natural follow-up questions. Some routine actions were initially slower or missing in Gemini, but coverage has grown. Gemini also relies more on cloud processing, so review privacy settings when you switch.

## Should you use Gemini or Google Assistant?

For most people, Gemini is now the better choice, because it handles both everyday commands and complex questions, and Google is moving its devices to Gemini. If you rely on a specific Assistant routine that Gemini does not yet support, keep Assistant for now.

Try Gemini for a week with your common tasks: alarms, reminders, smart home control, messages, navigation and questions. Check that routines, voice match and device controls work as before. On Android, you can usually choose the default assistant in settings while both remain available. Consider privacy: Gemini conversations may be stored and reviewed according to your activity settings, so adjust Gemini Apps Activity if you prefer shorter retention. The choice will narrow as Assistant is phased out.

## When does Gemini come to Google Home?

Google announced Gemini for Home in October 2025, replacing Google Assistant on Nest speakers and displays, with early access starting in the United States and a wider rollout over the following months. Availability depends on your country, language and device.

Gemini for Home brings natural conversation to smart speakers, more flexible smart home commands, such as turning off all the lights except the kitchen, and camera features like summaries of events on supported Nest cameras, some of which require a subscription. Check the Google Home app for an upgrade prompt and current eligibility. Older devices may get a reduced feature set. If you rely on routines, review them after the switch to confirm they still run correctly.

## Should you use Gemini in Google Messages?

Use it if you want quick help drafting replies, brainstorming or asking questions without leaving the Messages app. Gemini in Messages works as a separate chat with Gemini; it does not read your other conversations unless you share content with it.

It is convenient for rewriting a message more politely, translating text, or organising outings with friends. Treat it like any AI chat: avoid sharing sensitive personal information, passwords or private details about others. Conversations with Gemini in Messages are handled under your Gemini Apps Activity settings, so review them in your Google account. If you prefer a clean messaging app, you can ignore the Gemini chat, and it will not affect your normal messaging.

## Should you connect Gemini to Google Workspace?

Connect it if you want Gemini to search and summarise your Gmail, Drive and Docs, such as finding a document or summarising an email thread. It saves time, but it gives the assistant access to personal and work data, so weigh convenience against privacy.

For work or school accounts, your administrator controls whether Gemini can access Workspace data, and enterprise terms typically restrict how data is used. For personal accounts, review the Gemini Apps Privacy Hub to understand how connected content and activity are handled, and turn off connections for apps you do not want included. Start with one app, such as Drive, test usefulness, and verify answers against the original documents, since summaries can miss details or misread context.

## Which Gemini model does Google AI Mode use?

Google's AI Mode in Search runs on a custom version of Google's latest Gemini models, adapted for search with query fan-out, which breaks a question into many sub-searches and combines the results into one answer with links.

When AI Mode launched widely in 2025, Google said it used a custom version of Gemini 2.5, and it has since upgraded AI Mode as newer Gemini models arrived. Because the model is customised for Search, its behaviour differs from the Gemini app even when the underlying generation is similar. For developers, the closest public equivalent is grounding Gemini API calls with Google Search, which returns answers with source citations.

## Why does Google AI Mode not appear in Gemini?

AI Mode is a feature of Google Search, not of the Gemini app, so you will not find it inside Gemini. Open it from the AI Mode tab or button in Google Search on the web or in the Google app.

If AI Mode does not appear in Search either, it may not be available in your country, language or account type yet, or it may be disabled for work or school accounts by administrators. Update the Google app, sign in with a personal account, and check Search Labs if you are in an early-access region. The Gemini app offers its own web-grounded answers and Deep Research, which serve similar needs from inside Gemini.

## How does Gemini in Google Photos work?

Google Photos uses Gemini for Ask Photos, which lets you search your library with natural questions, such as what did we eat on our beach trip, and for editing features that understand requests like remove the person in the background.

Ask Photos combines Gemini's language understanding with Photos' existing image analysis: faces you have labelled, locations, dates and recognised objects. It can answer questions that need reasoning across photos, like when your child learned to swim, and it shows the matching photos as evidence. Google has said it does not train generative AI products outside Photos on your personal Photos data, and some features are limited to certain countries and languages, so check availability in your settings.

## How do you get started with Gemini?

Open gemini.google.com or the Gemini app, sign in with your Google account, and start with a concrete task: summarise a document, plan a study schedule, explain code or analyse a photo. Use follow-up questions to refine answers rather than writing one long prompt.

Next, explore features: upload files and images; use Deep Research for reports with sources; create Gems, custom assistants with saved instructions; connect apps such as Gmail or Drive if you want personal context; and try Canvas for editing documents and code. For developers, Google AI Studio offers free experimentation with Gemini models and an API key for building apps. Google's own learning resources and Grow with Google courses cover practical everyday use.

# How GGUF works: when to use it, quants, file locations, GGML, safetensors and FP8
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-gguf-works-vs-safetensors/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


GGUF is the single-file model format used by llama.cpp and tools built on it, such as Ollama and LM Studio. It packs a model's weights, usually quantized, together with metadata such as architecture, tokenizer and chat template, so models load quickly and run on ordinary hardware. I fine-tune models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio and run them locally, so this page explains how GGUF works, when to use it, how to choose models and quants, where files go, and how GGUF compares with GGML, safetensors and FP8.

## What does GGUF mean for LLMs?

For LLMs, GGUF means a model packaged for local inference with llama.cpp-based tools. A GGUF file contains everything needed to run the model: weights, tokenizer, hyperparameters and prompt template, typically in a quantized form.

The name is commonly expanded as GPT-Generated Unified Format, with GG linked to Georgi Gerganov, who created llama.cpp. In practice, seeing GGUF in a Hugging Face repository name tells you the model is ready for Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp or GPT4All, usually offered in several quantization levels. It is the dominant format for running open models on laptops, desktops and CPUs, while safetensors remains standard for training and GPU servers.

## How does a GGUF file work?

A GGUF file has a header, a key-value metadata section, tensor descriptions and aligned tensor data. Metadata stores the architecture, context length, tokenizer vocabulary, special tokens and chat template; tensor entries record names, shapes, data types and offsets.

Because tensor data is aligned, loaders can memory-map the file: the operating system pages weights into memory as needed instead of reading the whole file upfront, which makes loading fast. Each tensor can use a different quantization type, so sensitive layers may keep higher precision. New metadata keys can be added without breaking older readers, which is why GGUF replaced its predecessors. Tools such as gguf-py in llama.cpp let you inspect metadata and tensor types.

## How do GGUF models run?

A llama.cpp-based runtime reads the GGUF metadata to build the model architecture, maps the quantized weights into memory, and runs inference on CPU or GPU backends such as CUDA, Metal or Vulkan, dequantizing blocks on the fly.

You choose how many layers to offload to the GPU; the rest run on the CPU, which lets models larger than VRAM still run, slowly. The runtime keeps a KV cache for the conversation, whose size grows with context length. Chat templates from metadata format prompts correctly. Ollama and LM Studio wrap this process with model management, a chat interface and an OpenAI-compatible API, so applications can use local GGUF models like hosted ones.

## When should you use GGUF?

Use GGUF when you want to run models locally on laptops, desktops or CPU servers, especially with limited VRAM, through llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio. It suits private, offline and low-cost inference.

GGUF is less suitable for training or fine-tuning, which use safetensors with PyTorch, and for high-throughput GPU serving, where engines such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM with formats like FP8, AWQ or GPTQ usually deliver more requests per second. A common workflow: fine-tune in safetensors with QLoRA, merge the adapter, convert to GGUF with llama.cpp's conversion script, quantize, then run locally. That is how small custom models end up on ordinary machines.

## Which GGUF model should you use?

Pick the model by task and hardware, then the GGUF version. For chat on a laptop, a 7 to 8 billion parameter instruct model is a good start; for coding, choose a coding model; for weaker machines, try 1 to 4 billion parameter models.

Download from reputable uploaders on Hugging Face, ideally the model creator or well-known quantizers, and read the model card for licence, context length and recommended settings. Prefer instruct or chat versions for assistants and base versions only for completion tasks. Check that your runtime supports the architecture, since brand-new models need recent llama.cpp versions. Test two or three candidates on your real prompts, comparing quality and speed, before settling on one.

## Which GGUF quant should you use?

Q4_K_M is the usual default, balancing size and quality. Use Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have spare memory and want better quality, Q8_0 for near-original quality, and Q3 or IQ quants only when memory is very tight.

Quality loss grows sharply below about 4 bits, especially for smaller models, so a larger model at Q4 often beats a smaller model at Q8. Importance-matrix quants, marked imatrix or IQ, preserve quality better at low bits. Coding, maths and structured output tasks are more sensitive to quantization than casual chat, so test those carefully. Leave memory for the KV cache, which grows with context length, when deciding how large a quant fits.

## Where should you put GGUF files?

It depends on the tool. LM Studio keeps models in its models folder, in publisher and model subfolders, or imports them with `lms import`. Ollama imports a GGUF through a Modelfile with a FROM line pointing to the file. llama.cpp loads any path you pass.

For text-generation-webui, place GGUF files in its models directory. In ComfyUI, GGUF image model weights, used through the ComfyUI-GGUF extension, typically go in the models unet folder. Keep large models on a fast SSD with plenty of space, and avoid duplicating files across tools; some users point several apps at one shared folder. After moving files, refresh or restart the app so it detects them, and keep the model card alongside for reference.

## What is the difference between GGUF and GGML?

GGML is the tensor library behind llama.cpp, and also the name of the older model file format. GGUF replaced the GGML file format in August 2023, adding extensible metadata, a single self-contained file and better compatibility across versions.

Old GGML files broke when new model types or settings appeared, because the format lacked flexible metadata; GGUF stores architecture details, tokenizer and templates as key-value pairs, so new information can be added without breaking readers. Modern llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio no longer load old GGML model files, so convert or re-download them. The ggml library itself continues as the computation engine under llama.cpp and related projects.

## What is the difference between GGUF and safetensors?

Safetensors is a safe, fast format from Hugging Face for storing tensors, used by PyTorch and Transformers for training and GPU inference, usually in 16-bit precision. GGUF is a llama.cpp format for local inference, usually quantized and bundled with metadata.

Safetensors checkpoints are often split into shards with separate config and tokenizer files, while GGUF puts everything in one file. Both avoid the code-execution risks of pickle files. Use safetensors for fine-tuning, research and serving with vLLM or Transformers; convert to GGUF for Ollama, LM Studio and CPU or mixed CPU-GPU inference. llama.cpp includes scripts that convert Hugging Face safetensors checkpoints into GGUF, followed by quantization to your chosen level.

## What is the difference between GGUF and FP8?

GGUF is a file format; FP8 is a numeric precision, 8-bit floating point. FP8 weights are used for fast inference and training on recent GPUs with hardware FP8 support, usually stored as safetensors and served by engines like vLLM.

GGUF files typically use integer block quantization, such as 4 or 8 bits, designed for CPUs and consumer GPUs, while FP8 targets data-centre GPUs such as NVIDIA Hopper and newer, where it nearly doubles throughput compared with 16-bit with little quality loss. Choose FP8 for high-volume GPU serving and GGUF for local, memory-constrained or CPU inference. In image models such as Flux, both appear as options: FP8 for capable GPUs, GGUF quants for limited VRAM.
