# How long does it take to become an AI engineer? Degrees, PCB, self-taught, GenAI, Google
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-long-to-become-ai-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Becoming an AI engineer usually takes one to two years of focused learning if you start with basic programming, or three to six months if you are already a software developer. AI engineers build products with models: retrieval, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation and deployment. I started BCA in 2023, have led engineering at SCULT INDIA since 2024, and built five AI apps for NextUpgrad in 2026, so this page covers timelines, how to start, self-taught and GenAI paths, degrees, PCB, difficulty, Google and career fit.

## How long does it take to become an AI engineer?

From zero programming, expect about 12 to 24 months of consistent study and projects to become job-ready for junior AI engineering roles. A working software developer can transition in roughly 3 to 6 months, because backend, API and deployment skills transfer directly.

The timeline depends on hours per week, prior maths and coding, and whether you build real projects. A degree takes three or four years but covers broader foundations; self-study can be faster but needs discipline. Milestones help: Python and Git in the first months, then APIs and a first RAG app, then agents, fine-tuning basics and evaluation, then deployment and a portfolio. Being job-ready means you can ship and explain a working AI product, not finish a course list.

## How do you start to become an AI engineer?

Start with Python and basic software skills: functions, data structures, Git, APIs and JSON. Then call a model API, build a small chatbot, and expand it into a document question answering app with retrieval and citations.

A good first month: learn Python basics, build a command-line app, and make your first API call to a language model. Month two: learn embeddings and vector search and build a RAG app over your notes. Month three: add a web interface with FastAPI or Next.js and deploy it. Along the way, read official documentation, join a community such as a college tech club, and share progress publicly on GitHub so others can review your work.

## How do you become a self-taught AI engineer?

Follow a structured roadmap, build projects continuously, and get feedback from real users or developers. Free resources are enough: provider documentation, Hugging Face courses, fast.ai, roadmap.sh's AI engineer roadmap and open-source code.

Self-taught engineers succeed by proving skills publicly: a portfolio of two or three deployed AI apps with clear READMEs, evaluation results and write-ups of design decisions. Contribute to open-source AI projects, join hackathons to work in teams under deadlines, and find mentors who review your code. The main risk is gaps in fundamentals, so schedule time for data structures, databases, networking and basic statistics. Employers hiring for AI engineering often weigh shipped work as much as degrees.

## How do you become a GenAI engineer?

A generative AI engineer builds applications with large language models and other generative models. Learn prompting, RAG, agents and tool calling, fine-tuning with methods like LoRA, evaluation, and deployment, on top of solid Python and backend skills.

Build a portfolio that shows each layer: a RAG app with hybrid retrieval and citations, an agent with tools and guardrails, a fine-tuned small model with a before-and-after evaluation, and a deployed app with monitoring. My NextUpgrad apps follow this pattern: RAG.NextUpgrad for retrieval with reranking and a confidence gate, and FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning with live loss charts and base-versus-tuned evaluation. Understanding cost, latency and failure modes separates engineers from demo builders.

## What degree do you need to become an AI engineer?

Common degrees are B.Tech or B.E. in computer science, AI or data science, BCA followed by MCA, and B.Sc in computer science, mathematics or statistics. A master's helps for research-heavy roles but is not required for most AI engineering jobs.

Many applied AI teams care more about whether you can build and ship than about the degree title, though some large companies and government roles filter by degree. Choose a programme that gives you strong programming, data structures, databases, linear algebra, probability and some machine learning. I am a BCA student who leads engineering at SCULT INDIA; the degree gave structure, while projects, hackathons and real products built my AI engineering skills.

## Can I become an AI engineer with PCB?

Yes. Students with physics, chemistry and biology in 12th can become AI engineers, though some routes need mathematics. Many BCA and B.Sc programmes accept students from any stream or let them study mathematics later, while most B.Tech programmes require mathematics.

Options include BCA or B.Sc in computer science or data science at universities that admit PCB students, adding mathematics through a board such as NIOS where eligibility needs it, or a biology-related degree combined with programming, leading to AI in healthcare, bioinformatics or drug discovery. Check each college's eligibility rules before applying. Whatever route you choose, learn Python early and build up mathematics, especially linear algebra and probability, which AI work relies on.

## Is it hard to become an AI engineer?

It is challenging but achievable. The difficulty is less about genius and more about consistency: learning programming, some mathematics and many tools, then building projects that work reliably rather than only in demos.

The hard parts are debugging, understanding why models fail, evaluating quality, and keeping up with fast-changing tools. The field also rewards communication: explaining trade-offs to teammates and users. What makes it easier is that resources are free and plentiful, communities are welcoming, and you can see progress quickly by building. Studying a little every day and finishing projects beats occasional intense bursts. Mentors and peers shorten the path significantly, so join a community early.

## How do you become an AI engineer at Google?

Google hires AI and machine learning engineers through its careers site, usually requiring strong computer science fundamentals, coding interviews on data structures and algorithms, machine learning knowledge, and evidence of building real systems.

Prepare on three fronts: practise algorithm problems until you can solve medium-level questions clearly in about 40 minutes, study ML system design and fundamentals, and build substantial projects or open-source contributions. Students can target internships, which often convert into full-time offers. Referrals help your application get seen, so network at conferences, hackathons and developer events such as Google Developer Groups. Many Google AI roles also value research experience or publications, especially in research-focused teams.

## Should I become an AI engineer?

Community discussions, such as on Reddit, mostly say yes if you enjoy building software and learning constantly, and no if you only want a trending title. AI engineering is software engineering with models, not a shortcut around it.

Common advice from practitioners: learn solid software engineering first, avoid course collecting, build real products, and expect the tools to change every few months. Many warn that entry-level roles are competitive and that strong fundamentals matter more than knowing the latest framework. Choose it if you like debugging, experimenting and explaining your work, and if you are comfortable with uncertainty. If you prefer stable, slowly changing work, data engineering or backend roles may suit you better.

## Can anyone become an engineer?

Most people who commit to steady learning can become software or AI engineers; you do not need to be a genius or a topper. What you need is curiosity, persistence, problem-solving practice and enough mathematics for your chosen area.

Backgrounds vary widely: engineers come from commerce, arts and science streams, career changes and self-teaching. Formal engineering titles in some fields, such as civil or electrical, require specific degrees and licences, while software and AI roles are more open to skill-based paths. Start small, build consistently, and seek feedback. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023, and I tell each of them the same thing: build and ship regularly, because where you start matters less than how consistently you practise.

# How many jobs has AI replaced or created? Global and India numbers to 2030
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-many-jobs-has-ai-replaced/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


No one has a precise count of jobs replaced by AI, because companies rarely attribute layoffs to a single cause and most AI changes tasks rather than eliminating whole roles. What exists are tracked layoff announcements, surveys and projections, such as the World Economic Forum's estimate of 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced by 2030. I lead engineering at SCULT INDIA and build AI products, so this page separates measured numbers from forecasts, globally and in India.

## How many jobs has AI replaced?

There is no reliable global total. Layoff trackers capture only announcements where companies name AI as the reason, which undercounts quiet changes such as roles not refilled, and overcounts cases where AI is a convenient explanation for cost cutting.

In the United States, Challenger, Gray & Christmas, which tracks announced job cuts, began listing AI as a reason in 2023; AI-attributed cuts have risen but remain a small share of all announced cuts. Larger effects show up indirectly: slower hiring for entry-level writing, support and junior coding roles, and teams doing more work with the same headcount. Treat viral claims of millions already replaced with suspicion unless they cite a clear method and source.

## Where has AI replaced jobs?

The clearest effects are in customer support, content writing and translation, data entry and back-office processing, basic graphic design, and some junior programming and testing tasks, where AI tools already handle much of the routine work.

Freelance marketplaces saw early shifts, with fewer simple writing and translation gigs as generative AI spread. Call centres and help desks use chatbots and agents to resolve common queries, reducing demand for first-line staff. Media and marketing teams produce more content with fewer people. In software, AI coding assistants raise productivity, so some companies hire fewer juniors. Physical work, healthcare and skilled trades have seen far less replacement so far, because software alone cannot do those jobs.

## How has AI affected jobs?

Mostly by changing tasks within jobs. Workers use AI to draft, summarise, code, analyse and search faster, while expectations rise: employers want people who can use these tools and still check their output.

Effects differ by group. Experienced workers often gain the most because they can judge AI output; some entry-level roles shrink because the routine tasks juniors used to learn on are automated. New skills appear in job descriptions, such as prompt design, AI tool fluency and evaluation. Some industries report productivity gains, others report disappointing pilots. In engineering teams, AI tools speed up routine drafting, while design, review and debugging still need engineers who understand the system.

## What jobs has AI created?

AI has created roles such as AI engineer, machine learning engineer, MLOps engineer, data annotator and AI trainer, AI product manager, prompt and conversation designer, AI safety and policy specialist, and AI evaluation and red-teaming roles.

It also expands demand in supporting fields: data engineering, cloud infrastructure, chip design, data centre construction and operations, cybersecurity, and AI governance and compliance. Many existing jobs gained AI components, such as marketers running AI-assisted campaigns and analysts building AI workflows. Some of these roles, like data labelling, are unstable gig work, while engineering and governance roles are in high demand. The pattern matches earlier technologies: new work appears around building, running and regulating the technology.

## How many jobs has AI created?

As with losses, there is no precise global count, because AI skills spread across many job titles. Job postings and professional network data show rapid growth in roles requiring AI skills, especially since 2023, though from a small base.

LinkedIn's Economic Graph and similar sources track rising demand for AI engineering and AI literacy across countries, and AI talent hiring has grown faster than overall hiring in many markets. Indirect jobs, in data centres, chips and energy, add more. Counting is hard because a marketer who now uses AI is not a new job, while an AI engineer at a startup is. Watch trends in postings for your target role rather than headline totals.

## How many AI jobs were expected to be created by 2025?

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2020 projected that by 2025, about 85 million jobs could be displaced and about 97 million new roles could emerge, across the economies it surveyed, covering automation broadly rather than AI alone.

Now that 2025 has passed, the picture is mixed: generative AI arrived faster than that report expected, but large-scale net job losses did not appear in employment statistics, and many new roles involved data, AI and digital skills. The lesson is that projections describe direction better than exact numbers. The WEF's later reports, in 2023 and 2025, updated the estimates with generative AI included and extended the horizon to 2027 and 2030.

## How many AI jobs will be created by 2030?

The WEF's Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects about 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced between 2025 and 2030 across all trends, a net gain of 78 million, with AI and big data specialists among the fastest-growing roles.

Not all 170 million are AI jobs: the largest absolute growth includes farmworkers, delivery drivers, care workers and sales staff, driven by demographics, the green transition and economic trends. AI-specific roles are smaller in number but grow fastest in percentage terms. The report also expects about 39 percent of workers' core skills to change by 2030, which is why employers emphasise reskilling. Use these projections to choose growing skills, not to predict your personal job security.

## How many jobs will AI displace?

Projections vary by method. The WEF expects 92 million jobs displaced by 2030 across all drivers, Goldman Sachs estimated generative AI could expose the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs to automation, and the IMF found 40 percent of global employment exposed to AI.

Exposure is not displacement: an exposed job may be augmented, with AI taking some tasks and people doing more valuable ones. Displacement depends on adoption speed, regulation, costs and how firms choose to use productivity gains, either to cut staff or to grow output. History suggests technology displaces specific tasks and roles while creating others, but transitions can be painful for individuals. Plan for change in your field rather than betting on any single headline number.

## How many AI and ML jobs are there in India?

India has one of the world's largest pools of AI talent and a large number of AI and ML openings, spread across IT services, global capability centres, startups and product companies. Exact counts vary by job portal and date.

NASSCOM and industry reports have repeatedly highlighted strong demand for AI and data skills and a gap between demand and qualified supply, especially for experienced engineers. Job portals typically list thousands of openings for titles such as machine learning engineer, data scientist and AI engineer, with more roles asking for generative AI skills. For an accurate current number, search major portals with consistent filters and track it monthly, since postings change quickly and duplicates inflate counts.

## How many jobs have been lost due to AI in India?

There is no official count of jobs lost to AI in India. Companies rarely attribute layoffs to AI alone, and government employment data does not separate AI as a cause, so any precise figure you see is an estimate.

What is visible is slower hiring for some entry-level roles in IT services, BPO and customer support, as companies automate routine work and focus on productivity. At the same time, global capability centres and AI-focused startups in India are hiring for new skills. For students and early-career workers, the practical response is to build skills AI cannot easily replace: system design, domain knowledge, communication and the ability to build and supervise AI tools.

# How does mentorship work? Career mentorship, UPSC mentoring, and mentorship vs leadership
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-mentorship-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Mentorship works as an ongoing relationship in which a more experienced person guides someone's growth through regular conversations, feedback, advice and introductions, focused on the mentee's goals. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023, led 20+ campus sessions, and lead a 14-member engineering team at SCULT INDIA, so this page covers how mentorship works, career mentorship and growth, finding a mentor, guidance versus mentorship, UPSC mentoring, and how mentorship relates to leadership.

## How does mentorship work?

A mentor and mentee agree on goals, meet regularly, often every two to four weeks, and discuss progress, challenges and decisions. The mentor shares experience, asks questions, gives honest feedback and opens doors; the mentee does the work and drives the agenda.

Good mentorships have structure: clear goals at the start, an agreed meeting rhythm, preparation before each session, and follow-up actions. They can be formal, through company or college programmes, or informal, growing from a professional relationship. Formats include one-to-one, group mentoring, peer mentoring and reverse mentoring, where a junior teaches a senior, often about new technology. Relationships usually last months to years and end or evolve when goals are met.

## What is career mentorship?

Career mentorship is guidance from someone further along a career path who helps you choose directions, build skills, navigate workplaces and make decisions about jobs, education and growth. It focuses on your long-term development, not one task.

A career mentor might help a student pick between higher studies and a job, review a resume and portfolio, prepare for interviews, plan skill-building, or think through an offer. In technology, mentors often review code and projects and suggest communities and hackathons. The best career mentors share both successes and mistakes, and help you think rather than telling you what to do. In my mentoring, I start from a student's goal and work backwards to projects they can build.

## How can mentorship help in career growth?

Mentorship speeds up growth by giving you feedback you would not get alone, helping you avoid common mistakes, expanding your network, and building confidence to take on bigger challenges such as new roles, projects or competitions.

Specific benefits include clearer goals, faster skill development through targeted advice, introductions to opportunities, and honest perspective during setbacks. Mentors also model professional habits: how to communicate, prioritise and handle conflict. Mentorship helps the mentor too, who sharpens leadership and communication skills. For maximum benefit, be proactive: bring specific questions, act on advice and report back, so your mentor can see progress and invest more in you over time.

## Where can I find personalized career mentorship?

Start close: seniors and alumni from your college, teachers, managers and colleagues, and members of professional communities. Formal options include college mentorship programmes, company programmes, and platforms such as ADPList that connect mentees with volunteer mentors.

Communities are excellent sources: tech clubs, open-source projects, hackathons, meetups, and online groups where experienced people help newcomers. LinkedIn works when you send a short, specific message showing you have done your homework, such as asking about one decision rather than requesting general guidance. Start with a single conversation, not a request for long-term mentorship; relationships grow when you follow up with results. Paid mentoring services exist, but check reviews and credentials carefully before committing.

## What is the difference between mentorship and career guidance?

Career guidance is usually short-term and informational: a counsellor or session helps you understand options, courses and careers. Mentorship is a longer relationship focused on your personal growth, with ongoing feedback and support from someone with relevant experience.

Guidance answers questions such as which degree leads to which careers, or how admissions work, often through aptitude tests and information sessions. Mentorship goes further: it adapts to your progress, challenges your thinking and helps you act on decisions over time. Both are useful. Students often need guidance first, to choose a path, and mentorship after, to grow along it. Campus sessions I lead, such as the VSICS induction for 100+ first-years with a three-year roadmap, act as guidance that can lead to mentorship.

## Is mentorship necessary for UPSC?

Mentorship is not necessary to clear the UPSC Civil Services Examination; many candidates succeed through self-study using standard books, the syllabus, previous papers and test series. A good mentor can, however, save time and improve answer writing and strategy.

Mentorship helps most with planning a realistic study schedule, choosing an optional subject, getting feedback on written answers, and managing stress during a long preparation. Mentors who have appeared in the examination or have strong teaching experience can spot weaknesses quickly. The risk is dependence: preparation still requires disciplined daily study. Before paying for any programme, check what the mentor actually provides, such as answer evaluation and one-to-one time, and speak to past students.

## Which mentorship is best for UPSC?

The best UPSC mentorship is the one that matches your stage, medium of instruction and weaknesses, rather than the most advertised brand. Look for personalised feedback, especially on answer writing, and regular one-to-one reviews of your progress.

Evaluate options using clear criteria: mentor experience with the examination, batch size, frequency of individual sessions, quality of answer evaluation, availability in Hindi or English medium as needed, and genuine reviews from past candidates rather than toppers' photos in advertisements. Free resources, such as official UPSC notifications, previous papers and discussion groups, cover much of what you need. Try a short trial or demo session before committing, and make sure the plan fits your own schedule.

## Is mentorship a leadership role?

Yes, mentorship is a form of leadership, though not a formal position. Mentors influence others' growth through guidance, example and support, which are core leadership skills, even when they have no authority over the mentee.

Many organisations treat mentoring as a leadership development step, because it builds listening, coaching, feedback and empathy. Engineers often begin leading by mentoring interns or juniors before managing teams. Leading engineering at SCULT INDIA, I find that mentoring juniors and leading a team draw on the same habits: setting clear expectations, giving honest feedback, and helping people solve problems themselves instead of solving the problems for them.

## What is the difference between mentorship and leadership?

Leadership is guiding a group toward shared goals, often with formal authority and responsibility for results. Mentorship is a one-to-one or small-group relationship focused on an individual's development, usually without authority over their work.

A leader is accountable for the team's outcomes and makes decisions that affect everyone; a mentor is accountable only for honest, useful support. Leaders can mentor, and good ones do, but they also handle strategy, priorities and performance. Mentors can come from outside your organisation, which lets them give perspective without politics. They are not the same, but strong leadership includes mentorship, and strong mentors use leadership skills such as listening and clear communication.

## Why is mentorship important in leadership?

Mentorship lets leaders develop people, not just direct tasks. It builds trust, grows future leaders, spreads knowledge across the team, and improves retention, because people stay where they feel invested in.

Leaders who mentor create teams that solve problems independently, which frees the leader to focus on direction and strategy. Mentoring also keeps leaders humble and informed, since mentees share frontline problems and fresh ideas. Leadership pipelines depend on it: organisations that mentor juniors have successors ready when leaders move on. The same applies to communities: student groups such as TechVerse Enclave, which I founded and which has 500+ members, grow when experienced members guide newcomers.

# How much does an LLM API cost? Token pricing explained, a cost model you can run, and 12 ways to cut the bill without cutting quality
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-much-does-an-llm-api-cost/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How much does an LLM API cost?

**LLM APIs charge per token, priced per million tokens, with input, what you send, and output, what the model writes, priced separately, and output typically costing three to five times more per token. Your cost for one request is input tokens times the input rate plus output tokens times the output rate. Your monthly cost is that times the number of requests. Rates differ by model tier by more than a hundredfold, and they change often, so the providers' pricing pages are the only source of current numbers [1][2][3].**


I will not print price figures on this page, because they would be wrong within months and this site only states what can be checked. What does not change is the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what lets you estimate a feature's cost before you build it. My five production AI apps in 2026 all ran on small budgets; one, a full RAG platform, fits in about 220 MB on a free tier [13]. The habits that made that possible are below, and the longer notes are on the portfolio [10][11].

> The API bill is a design decision you made in the prompt template. Every passage you send, every token you let the model write, is a line item.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a token, and how many are in my request?

**A token is the unit the model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word, more for code and for Indic scripts. A request's input tokens include the system prompt, the conversation history, any retrieved documents and the user's message; output tokens are the answer. Count them with the provider's tokeniser before you estimate anything [9]. A "short question" over a RAG system can be three thousand input tokens once five passages are attached.**



## How do I estimate the monthly cost of an AI feature?

**Build one real request, count its input and output tokens, and multiply. Then multiply by requests per day and by thirty. Then multiply by two, because production prompts grow and users retry. Do this before building, and again after the first week of real traffic, because estimates are usually wrong in the same direction: more tokens per request than planned, and more requests from a few heavy users than from the average.**



```python
def monthly_cost(in_tok: int, out_tok: int, in_rate: float, out_rate: float, per_day: int) -> float:
    """in_rate/out_rate are the provider's prices per million tokens for the chosen model."""
    per_request = (in_tok * in_rate + out_tok * out_rate) / 1_000_000
    return per_request * per_day * 30 * 2     # x2: growth, retries, prompt creep
```

## Why are RAG systems expensive, and how do I make them cheaper?

**Because every question resends the retrieved passages, and passages are the largest part of the prompt. A system that stuffs ten chunks pays for ten chunks on every turn. Fixes, in order of impact: rerank to five or fewer passages; keep chunks tight and structure-aware so each passage carries only what is needed; cache the system prompt and any fixed prefixes where the provider supports it [4]; trim conversation history to the last few turns plus a summary; and refuse early, with a confidence gate, so unanswerable questions never reach the model.**


Sending fewer, better passages also improves answers, not just cost: models attend poorly to the middle of long contexts [8]. In RAG.NextUpgrad, reranking to five passages and gating weak queries cut prompt size and stopped the most expensive category of request, the confident wrong answer that a user then retries three times [13].

## What is prompt caching, and how much does it save?

**Prompt caching lets a provider store a prefix of your prompt, typically the system prompt, tool definitions and large fixed documents, and charge a much lower rate when the same prefix is reused within a time window [4]. For applications with long system prompts or shared documents across many requests, the saving on input tokens is large. It requires structuring prompts so the fixed part comes first and the variable part last, which is good prompt hygiene anyway.**


## How do I cut LLM costs without hurting quality?

**Twelve levers, roughly in order of payoff. Most teams pull three and stop; the first six are structural and the rest are operational.**




## Is self-hosting an open model cheaper than an API?

**At high, steady volume or under strict privacy requirements, yes: a GPU serving an open model through vLLM has a fixed monthly cost regardless of tokens [7]. At low or spiky volume, no: the GPU sits idle, and you pay for the engineer who keeps it running. The break-even depends on your token volume, the model size you need, and whether you already have operations capacity. Many teams do both: a small self-hosted model for cheap high-volume tasks and an API for the hard ones.**




## Which provider is cheapest?

**It changes monthly, and cheapest per token is the wrong question. Compare cost per solved task: a cheaper model that needs two retries or a longer prompt costs more. Use a routing layer such as OpenRouter to compare prices and models across providers without many keys [6], test the top two or three on your evaluation set, and pick by quality per rupee. My decision framework for choosing a provider, with the questions beyond price, is on the portfolio [12].**


## How do I stop a surprise bill?

**Set a hard monthly spending cap at every provider. Add per-user daily request and token limits in your code. Set max output tokens on every call. Alert at fifty percent of budget and again at eighty. Log tokens and cost per request with the user id. Fall back to a smaller model or a polite refusal when the daily budget is exhausted. Never ship an API key in client code. One viral post or one abusive script is enough to find the control you skipped.**



## What does an LLM feature cost at student or startup scale?

**Small, if designed with the levers above. A RAG assistant for a college club with a few hundred questions a day, five reranked passages, a capped answer and a mid-tier model costs less per month than a couple of coffees; the same assistant with ten unranked passages, unlimited output and a top-tier model for every request costs many times more for slightly worse answers. Free tiers from providers cover prototypes entirely. The difference is design, not budget.**



## LLM cost interview questions

**Estimate the monthly cost of a described feature out loud. Explain why output tokens matter more. Name three structural ways to cut a RAG system's cost. Explain prompt caching. Say when you would self-host and how you would decide. Describe the controls that prevent a runaway bill. Interviewers use these to find out whether you have run something real; a number from a system you operated is the best answer.**



## Where should I start?

**Take one request from your current or planned app, count its tokens with the provider's tokeniser, run the cost model above with today's prices, and set a spending cap before you do anything else.** For a session on shipping AI features that survive real users and real budgets, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does object detection work? Models, CNNs, LLMs, Gemini, OpenCV, and coding one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-object-detection-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Object detection works by running an image through a neural network that predicts, for each object it finds, a class label such as "person" or "car", a confidence score and a bounding box around it. It answers both "what" and "where", unlike classification, which only labels the whole image. Face detection is the first step in FaceVision's browser pipeline, before recognition and liveness checks. This page covers how detection works, what it achieves, models, CNNs, LLMs and Gemini, OpenCV, and how to code and train a detector.

## How does object detection work?

A detection network extracts features from the image with a backbone, then a detection head predicts boxes and class scores at many positions and scales. Overlapping predictions for the same object are merged with non-maximum suppression, leaving one box per object.

One-stage detectors such as YOLO predict boxes and classes in a single pass, which makes them fast for real-time video. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN first propose candidate regions, then classify and refine them, often with higher accuracy on small objects. Transformer detectors such as DETR predict a set of objects directly using attention. Training uses images with labelled boxes and losses for both location and class.

## What is object detection in AI?

In AI, object detection is the computer vision task of locating and identifying multiple objects in images or video. Its output is a list of objects, each with a category, a bounding box and a confidence score.

It sits between classification, which labels a whole image, and segmentation, which labels every pixel. Variants include face detection, pedestrian detection, text detection for OCR, and 3D detection for autonomous vehicles using depth or lidar. Detection is often the first stage of larger systems: detect faces, then recognise them; detect products, then read their labels; detect vehicles, then track them.

## What does object detection accomplish?

Object detection lets machines find and count things in visual data automatically, enabling decisions such as alerting, measuring or acting. It turns raw images into structured information: what objects exist, where they are, and how many.

Applications include safety monitoring for helmets and protective gear, retail shelf analysis, traffic counting, wildlife monitoring with camera traps, defect detection in manufacturing, medical findings in scans, document layout analysis, and robotics grasping. Combined with tracking, it follows objects across video frames, supporting analytics such as footfall counting. Its value depends on accuracy in your specific conditions, which is why custom training is common.

## What are the main object detection models?

Popular families include the YOLO series for fast real-time detection, Faster R-CNN and Mask R-CNN for accuracy and instance masks, SSD and RetinaNet as earlier one-stage designs, and transformer-based models such as DETR, RT-DETR and open-vocabulary detectors such as Grounding DINO and OWL-ViT.

Choosing a model: YOLO variants for speed on edge devices and video; two-stage models where small-object accuracy matters most; open-vocabulary detectors when you need to detect objects described in text without training on them. Benchmarks on the COCO dataset compare accuracy and speed, but test on your own images. Check licences carefully: some popular implementations use copyleft licences with obligations for commercial products.

## Is object detection based on CNNs?

Often, but not always. Many detectors, including most YOLO versions and Faster R-CNN, use convolutional neural network backbones to extract features. Newer detectors use vision transformers or hybrid designs, and some use transformers in the detection head even with CNN backbones.

CNNs remain popular because they are efficient and run well on phones and edge hardware. Transformer detectors such as DETR simplify the pipeline by removing hand-designed steps like anchor boxes, and perform strongly with large-scale pretraining. In practice, the choice depends on available models, hardware and accuracy needs, not on CNN versus transformer ideology.

## Can LLMs do object detection?

Text-only LLMs cannot see images, so they cannot detect objects. Multimodal models that accept images can describe objects and, in some cases, return bounding box coordinates when prompted, making zero-shot detection possible without training.

This is useful for prototyping, rare categories and flexible queries such as "find every red helmet". Trade-offs: slower and more expensive per image than dedicated detectors, less precise boxes, and less consistent results. A practical pattern is using a multimodal model to pre-label images, reviewing labels by hand, then training a fast dedicated detector for production use.

## Can Gemini do object detection?

Yes. Gemini models can return bounding boxes for objects when asked, in coordinates normalised to the image size, and some versions can also return segmentation masks. Google's documentation shows how to request boxes with a prompt and parse the output.

Ask for structured JSON output listing labels and box coordinates, then convert them to pixel positions for drawing. Gemini works well for flexible, descriptive queries, such as "detect all items that are not in their packaging". For real-time video, high frame rates or offline use, a dedicated detector on the device is faster and cheaper. Validate Gemini's detections on a sample of your images before relying on them.

## Can OpenCV do object detection?

Yes. OpenCV's DNN module runs pretrained detection models, such as YOLO or SSD in ONNX format, and older classical detectors such as Haar cascades for faces and HOG for pedestrians. OpenCV also handles the surrounding work: reading video, resizing frames and drawing boxes.

Haar cascades are fast but less accurate than deep learning detectors; use them only for simple, controlled cases. For modern accuracy, export a trained detector to ONNX and run it with OpenCV DNN or ONNX Runtime. OpenCV's face detection now includes a neural network detector that is far more robust than older cascades.

## How do I code object detection?

The quickest start is a pretrained YOLO model with the Ultralytics Python library: load the model, run it on an image or webcam, and read the boxes.

```python
from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO("yolo11n.pt")             # small pretrained model
results = model("street.jpg")
for box in results[0].boxes:
    print(model.names[int(box.cls)], float(box.conf), box.xyxy.tolist())
```

Install with `pip install ultralytics`. Use `results[0].show()` to view boxes, or pass `source=0` for a webcam. Check the licence before commercial use. For browsers, export to ONNX and run with ONNX Runtime Web, as FaceVision does for its models.

## How do I make my own object detector?

Collect images of your objects in realistic conditions, label bounding boxes with a tool such as Label Studio or CVAT, split into training, validation and test sets, and fine-tune a pretrained detector. A few hundred labelled images per class often gives useful results.

Steps:

- Define classes clearly and label consistently.
- Include varied lighting, angles, backgrounds and object sizes.
- Fine-tune a small pretrained model first; scale up if needed.
- Evaluate with mean average precision and by looking at mistakes.
- Add hard examples where the model fails, and retrain.
- Export and test speed on your target device.

Data quality matters more than model choice for most custom detectors.

# How does OCR work step by step? OCR models, offline use, libraries, training, PDFs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-ocr-works-step-by-step/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


OCR, optical character recognition, works in steps: the image is cleaned up, text regions are detected, each line or word is read by a recognition model, and the output is corrected and assembled into text with its layout. The result is searchable, editable text from scans, photos and PDFs. I use OCR in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page covers OCR scanning, each step, how models work, offline use, the best libraries, improving results, training a model and making OCR PDFs.

## What is OCR scanning?

OCR scanning means scanning a document or photographing it and running optical character recognition so the text becomes machine-readable, rather than just a picture of text. You can then search, copy, edit and index it.

Many scanners and phone apps run OCR automatically and produce searchable PDFs. Uses include digitising records, extracting data from invoices and forms, making books searchable, reading receipts in expense apps and making documents accessible to screen readers. Without OCR, a scanned PDF is just images: you cannot search it or select its text, and AI tools cannot read it reliably.

## How does OCR work step by step?

OCR follows a pipeline: capture the image, preprocess it, detect text regions, recognise characters and words, then post-process and reconstruct layout.

Steps in detail:

- **Capture**: scan or photograph the document.
- **Preprocess**: convert to greyscale, remove noise, fix skew and adjust contrast.
- **Layout analysis**: find blocks, columns, lines, tables and reading order.
- **Detection**: locate words or lines of text.
- **Recognition**: convert each text image into characters with a neural model.
- **Post-processing**: apply dictionaries or language models to fix errors.
- **Output**: plain text, structured data, or a PDF with a hidden text layer.

Each step's quality affects the next, so preprocessing often matters most.

## How do OCR models work?

Modern OCR models use deep learning: a detection network finds where text is, and a recognition network reads the cropped text as a sequence. Classic recognisers combine convolutional networks for visual features with recurrent layers and CTC loss to output character sequences.

Newer recognisers use transformers, such as TrOCR, treating OCR like translation from image to text. Vision language models go further, reading whole pages, understanding layout and tables, and returning structured output like Markdown. They handle complex documents better but cost more and can occasionally hallucinate text, so validate outputs. For scanned PDFs, the OCR and Speech Workspace uses Mistral's OCR model in page batches for layout-aware text.

## Does OCR work offline?

Yes. Many OCR tools run entirely on your device: Tesseract on desktops and servers, PaddleOCR and EasyOCR in Python, Google's ML Kit on Android and iOS, Apple's Live Text on Apple devices, and Tesseract.js in browsers.

Offline OCR protects privacy, since documents never leave your machine, works without internet, and has no per-page cost. Cloud OCR services and vision language models often give better accuracy on complex layouts, handwriting and poor scans, but require sending data to a provider. Choose based on document sensitivity, accuracy needs and volume.

## Which OCR library is best?

It depends on the documents. Tesseract is a solid free choice for clean printed text; PaddleOCR is strong for photos, complex layouts and Asian scripts; EasyOCR is simple for scene text; and vision language model OCR leads on complex documents.

How to choose:

- **Clean scans, many languages, CPU only**: Tesseract.
- **Photos, receipts, signboards**: PaddleOCR or EasyOCR.
- **Tables, forms, mixed layouts**: layout-aware OCR or vision language models.
- **Mobile apps**: Google ML Kit or Apple's Vision framework.

Always benchmark on 50 to 100 of your own documents, measuring character or field accuracy, before committing.

## What is the best OCR library for Python?

Popular Python options are pytesseract, a wrapper for Tesseract; EasyOCR, simple and deep-learning based; PaddleOCR, accurate with layout tools; docTR, with good detection and recognition models; and newer document OCR toolkits for layout and tables.

Start with pytesseract for clean documents because it is lightweight and fast on CPUs. Move to PaddleOCR or EasyOCR for photos and difficult images, ideally with a GPU. For PDFs with tables and structure, try layout-aware tools or a vision language model API. Combine OCR with OpenCV preprocessing for better results on noisy images.

## Is there a free OCR library for Android?

Yes. Google's ML Kit Text Recognition is free and runs on the device, supporting Latin, Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese and Korean scripts. Tesseract is also available on Android through community libraries such as Tesseract4Android.

ML Kit is usually the easiest and fastest choice: add the dependency, pass a camera frame or image, and receive text blocks, lines and elements with bounding boxes. Tesseract offers more language coverage and control but needs language data files and more setup. For Java or Kotlin apps, both integrate well; test accuracy and speed on low-end devices your users actually have.

## How do I improve OCR scanning results?

Improve the input first: scan at around 300 DPI, use even lighting without shadows, keep pages flat and straight, and choose greyscale or colour with good contrast. Then preprocess: deskew, denoise, binarise and crop margins.

More tips:

- Set the correct language or languages in your OCR tool.
- Choose the right page segmentation mode for single lines or blocks.
- Remove backgrounds and watermarks where possible.
- Split multi-column pages before recognition.
- Use a dictionary or validation rules for fields like dates and IDs.
- Try a stronger model for handwriting or complex layouts.

Measure accuracy on a sample before and after each change.

## How do I train an OCR model?

For Tesseract, fine-tune an existing language model with its tesstrain tools using line images and matching text. For deep learning OCR, fine-tune a pretrained recogniser such as TrOCR or a PaddleOCR model on labelled crops of your text.

Steps:

- Collect real samples and transcribe them accurately.
- Add synthetic data by rendering text in fonts and backgrounds like your documents.
- Split data into training, validation and test sets.
- Fine-tune from a pretrained model rather than training from scratch.
- Measure character error rate on the test set.

Fine-tuning works well for specific fonts, forms or handwriting styles; general OCR is better left to existing models.

## How do I make an OCR PDF?

Use OCRmyPDF, a free command-line tool built on Tesseract, to add a searchable text layer to scanned PDFs: `ocrmypdf input.pdf output.pdf`. Adobe Acrobat and many scanner apps also create searchable PDFs.

OCRmyPDF keeps the original page images and places invisible text underneath, so the PDF looks the same but becomes searchable and selectable. Add `-l eng+hin` for multiple languages, `--deskew` to straighten pages and `--skip-text` to skip pages that already have text. Searchable PDFs are also much better inputs for RAG systems, which need real text to retrieve from.

# How Ollama works: vs vLLM, Llama, ChatGPT, Unsloth, Hugging Face, LM Studio, coding
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-ollama-works-vs-vllm-lm-studio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Ollama is a free tool that downloads and runs open language models on your own computer with one command, exposing a local API that apps can call. It is the easiest way to start with local LLMs, while servers with many users need engines such as vLLM. I fine-tune open models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio, so this page covers how Ollama works, vLLM and speed, Llama, ChatGPT, Unsloth, Hugging Face, coding, LM Studio and AnythingLLM, and SDKs. How does Ollama work? Ollama runs a local server that downloads quantized open models, loads them into GPU or CPU memory, and serves them through a command line and a REST API on port 11434. It builds on llama.cpp-style inference for efficient local performance. When you run a command such as ollama run with a model name, Ollama pulls the model from its library if needed, chooses how many layers fit on your GPU, offloads the rest to system memory, and starts a chat. Applications call the same server through its native API or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Modelfiles customise system prompts, parameters and adapters. Ollama unloads idle models after a timeout to free memory for other work. What is the difference between Ollama and vLLM? Ollama is built for easy local use by one person or a small team, running quantized models on laptops, desktops and Macs. vLLM is a high-throughput serving engine for GPUs, designed to handle many concurrent users efficiently in production. Also asked as: difference between ollama and huggingface vLLM uses PagedAttention to manage the key-value cache efficiently and continuous batching to serve many requests at once, plus tensor parallelism across GPUs. It mainly runs full-precision or GPU-quantized models on NVIDIA and AMD hardware. Ollama prioritises simplicity: one install, one command, automatic CPU and GPU offloading. A common path is prototyping with Ollama, then deploying with vLLM when real traffic arrives. Both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs, easing the switch. Ollama vs vLLM: which is faster? For a single user, Ollama and vLLM can feel similar, depending on model and quantization. Under many concurrent requests, vLLM is far faster in total throughput, because continuous batching serves many users together on the same GPU. Also asked as: ollama vs vllm speed Ollama processes a limited number of parallel requests per model, so latency grows as users increase. vLLM keeps GPU utilisation high, giving much better tokens per second across all users. On machines without a supported GPU, such as many laptops and Macs, Ollama is the practical choice since vLLM targets data-centre GPUs. Benchmark your own model, hardware and expected concurrency, measuring time to first token and total throughput, before deciding. What is the difference between Ollama and Llama? Llama is a family of open-weight language models created by Meta. Ollama is an independent tool for running language models locally, including Llama and many others, such as Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, DeepSeek and gpt-oss. The similar names cause confusion, but they are separate projects: Meta trains and releases Llama models under its community licence, while Ollama packages models into an easy-to-run format and provides the local server. You can run Llama through Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM or Hugging Face Transformers. When choosing a model in Ollama, compare families on your tasks, since Llama is no longer the only strong option. What is the difference between Ollama and ChatGPT? ChatGPT is OpenAI's cloud assistant running proprietary models on OpenAI's servers, with features such as search, image generation and memory. Ollama runs open models on your own computer, keeping data local and working offline, without per-message limits. ChatGPT generally offers stronger reasoning and broader features, needing no hardware. Ollama trades some capability for privacy, control and no recurring cost beyond your hardware and electricity. Local models are excellent for drafting, summarising, coding help and private documents, especially mid-size models on a capable GPU. Many people use both: ChatGPT for demanding tasks and Ollama for sensitive data or offline work. Interfaces such as Open WebUI give Ollama a ChatGPT-like experience. What is the difference between Ollama and Unsloth? Unsloth is a library for fine-tuning open models quickly with less memory, using LoRA and QLoRA. Ollama is a tool for running models locally. They complement each other: fine-tune with Unsloth, then run the result in Ollama. Unsloth can export fine-tuned models to GGUF format, which Ollama imports through a Modelfile, so you can chat with your custom model locally. Unsloth also publishes quantized versions of popular models on Hugging Face, which Ollama can pull directly. The workflow suits domain assistants: prepare a dataset, fine-tune with QLoRA, evaluate against the base model, as FineTune Studio does with base-versus-tuned comparisons, then serve the tuned model locally. What is the difference between Ollama and Hugging Face? Hugging Face is a platform hosting hundreds of thousands of models and datasets, plus libraries such as Transformers for training and running models in Python. Ollama is a local runtime that makes running quantized models simple through one command. They work together: Ollama can pull GGUF models directly from Hugging Face repositories, giving access to far more models than Ollama's own library. Hugging Face Transformers offers full flexibility for research, fine-tuning and custom pipelines, but requires Python and more setup. Ollama suits developers and users who just want a model running behind an API. Use Hugging Face to discover and fine-tune models, and Ollama to serve them locally. Can Ollama write code? Yes. With coding models such as Qwen2.5-Coder, Qwen3-Coder, Devstral or CodeLlama, Ollama can write, explain and refactor code, and it integrates with editors through extensions such as Continue and Cline for chat and autocomplete. Quality depends on model size and your hardware: 7B models handle autocomplete and small functions, while 14B to 32B models produce better multi-step code. Agentic coding with local models works for focused tasks but trails frontier cloud models on large refactors. Increase the context length in Ollama settings for coding, since defaults can be short and truncate files. Always review generated code and run tests, as with any AI assistant. LM Studio vs Ollama vs AnythingLLM: which should you use? LM Studio is a desktop app with a graphical interface for discovering, downloading and chatting with local models, plus a local server. Ollama is command-line and server-first, ideal for developers. AnythingLLM is an all-in-one app for chatting with documents and agents, using backends like Ollama. Choose LM Studio if you prefer clicking to typing, want to browse Hugging Face models visually or use Apple's MLX on Macs. Choose Ollama for scripting, integrating with apps and running as a background service. Choose AnythingLLM when you want document RAG, workspaces and agents without coding, connecting it to Ollama or LM Studio for the model. Many people combine them, since they solve different layers of the local AI stack. What Ollama SDKs exist, including for Go? Ollama offers official Python and JavaScript libraries, and because Ollama itself is written in Go, its repository includes a Go API client package. Its OpenAI-compatible endpoint also lets you use OpenAI SDKs in many languages. Also asked as: ollama sdks in go: overview and code examples In Go, the api package provides a client for chat, generation, embeddings and model management, with streaming responses through callbacks. Community libraries cover languages such as Rust, Java and C#. Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex include Ollama integrations. For portability, many developers use the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which lets the same code switch between Ollama locally and cloud providers in production. Check each library's documentation for supported features, such as tool calling and images.

# How pgvector works: uses, history, vs Elasticsearch, scaling, IVFFlat, and unused indexes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-pgvector-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


pgvector is an open-source extension that makes PostgreSQL a vector database: it adds a vector column type, distance operators for cosine, Euclidean and inner product, and approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, HNSW and IVFFlat, so you can run similarity search with ordinary SQL next to your relational data. PostgreSQL is central to my stack, so this page explains what pgvector means and how it works, uses and history, comparison with Elasticsearch, scaling and production readiness, IVFFlat indexes, why indexes go unused, and enabling it in pgAdmin.

## What does pgvector mean?

pgvector is short for "PostgreSQL vector": "pg" is the common abbreviation for PostgreSQL, and "vector" refers to the numerical vectors, usually AI embeddings, the extension stores and searches.

Practically, it means you can add a column like `embedding vector(768)` to a table and query for the rows most similar to a given vector. It turns Postgres into a combined relational and vector database, so applications such as RAG systems can keep documents, metadata, users, permissions and embeddings in one place, with transactions and backups covering everything.

## How does pgvector work?

pgvector stores vectors in table columns and adds operators that compute distances: `<->` for Euclidean, `<=>` for cosine and `<#>` for negative inner product. Queries order rows by distance to a query vector and take the top results; indexes speed this up by searching approximately.

Without an index, Postgres compares the query with every row, which is exact but slow for large tables. HNSW indexes build a graph of nearest neighbours and walk it towards the query; IVFFlat indexes cluster vectors and search only nearby clusters. Postgres's planner decides when to use the index, and normal features, such as WHERE filters, joins and row-level security, combine with vector search.

## What is pgvector used for?

pgvector is used for semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, duplicate and near-duplicate detection, image and face similarity search, and clustering, all within PostgreSQL rather than a separate vector database.

Teams choose it when they already run Postgres and want simpler architecture: one database to back up, secure and operate. A RAG app might store chunks with their embeddings, document metadata and access rules in the same tables, then combine vector search with Postgres full-text search for hybrid retrieval. FaceVision-style systems can store face embeddings with user records, protected by the same database controls.

## When was pgvector created?

pgvector was created by Andrew Kane and first released in 2021. It grew rapidly in popularity from 2023, when RAG applications made vector search a mainstream need, and gained HNSW indexes in version 0.5.0 that year.

Since then, releases have added half-precision and binary vectors, sparse vectors, parallel index builds, iterative index scans for filtered queries and many performance improvements. Major cloud providers now offer pgvector on managed Postgres services. Because features differ between versions, check which version your database runs, especially on managed platforms.

## pgvector vs Elasticsearch: which should I use?

Use pgvector when your data already lives in PostgreSQL and you want vector search alongside relational queries, transactions and simple operations. Use Elasticsearch when you need advanced full-text search, analytics and aggregations at large scale, with vector search as an addition.

Elasticsearch has richer text analysis, language analysers and distributed search features, but adds another system to operate and keep in sync with your database. pgvector keeps everything in one place, and Postgres full-text search covers basic keyword needs; extensions add BM25 if required. For many RAG applications with up to a few million chunks, pgvector is simpler and sufficient.

## Is pgvector scalable?

Yes, for many workloads. With HNSW indexes, enough memory and tuning, pgvector handles millions to tens of millions of vectors with low latency. Beyond that, partitioning, read replicas, quantisation with half-precision vectors, and careful hardware sizing extend its range.

Limits appear with very large collections, very high query rates, or heavy filtering combined with vector search, where specialised vector databases may perform better. Plan capacity by estimating memory for vectors and indexes, testing query latency at your target scale, and monitoring. Many teams start with pgvector and only move vector workloads elsewhere if measurements demand it.

## Is pgvector production ready?

Yes. pgvector is widely used in production by companies of all sizes and is supported on major managed Postgres services. It benefits from PostgreSQL's mature reliability features: write-ahead logging, replication, backups, point-in-time recovery and access control.

Production practices: use HNSW indexes for most workloads, build indexes after bulk loads with enough maintenance memory, monitor query plans and latency, keep pgvector updated, and test recall against exact search on a sample. Combine with connection pooling for many concurrent clients. As with any database, load testing at expected scale before launch avoids surprises.

## What are IVFFlat indexes in pgvector, and how do they work?

An IVFFlat index divides vectors into clusters, called lists, using k-means. At query time, it compares the query with each cluster's centroid, searches only the closest clusters, called probes, and returns the nearest vectors found there.

Settings: `lists` sets the number of clusters at build time, often around rows divided by 1,000 for up to a million rows; `ivfflat.probes` sets how many clusters to search at query time, trading speed for recall. Build IVFFlat after loading representative data, since clusters come from existing vectors. HNSW usually offers better speed and recall without a training step, so IVFFlat is mainly useful when build time or memory matters more.

## Why is my pgvector index not being used?

Common reasons: the query does not use `ORDER BY embedding <operator> query LIMIT n`, the operator does not match the index's operator class, such as cosine queries on an L2 index, the table is small enough that a sequential scan is cheaper, or filters and joins lead the planner to another plan.

Fixes: write queries in the order-by-distance-with-limit form, create the index with the operator class matching your distance, run `ANALYZE` after loading data, check plans with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and for filtered queries consider partial indexes, partitioning or iterative scans in newer versions. Casting issues, such as comparing different dimensions, also prevent index use.

## How do I enable pgvector in pgAdmin?

First install pgvector on the database server, or use a managed service that includes it. Then, in pgAdmin, open the Query Tool for your database and run `CREATE EXTENSION vector;`, or right-click Extensions under the database and create the "vector" extension through the dialog.

You need privileges to create extensions. Confirm installation by expanding Extensions in pgAdmin or running `SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'vector';`. If the extension is not listed as available, it is not installed on the server; pgAdmin is only a client and cannot install server software. Enable it separately in each database where you need vectors.

# How RAG works: chatbots, rerankers, LangChain, image indexing and multimodal pipelines
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-rag-works-chatbots-images/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, makes a language model answer from your documents: it retrieves relevant passages for each question and adds them to the prompt, so the answer is grounded and can cite sources. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, reranking, cited streaming answers and a confidence gate, so this page explains how RAG works, why it is used, RAG chatbots, their limits, LangChain, rerankers, and indexing images and structured data.

## How does RAG work?

RAG has two phases. Indexing splits documents into chunks, embeds them and stores them in a search index. At query time, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks for a question and gives them to the language model, which answers using that context.

A full pipeline: parse documents, including OCR for scans; chunk by structure with overlap; embed chunks and build both vector and keyword indexes; for each question, rewrite it if needed, run hybrid retrieval, fuse and rerank results; build a prompt with the top passages and instructions to cite and refuse when unsure; and stream the answer with citations. Evaluation then checks whether retrieval found the right passages and whether answers stayed faithful to them.

## Why is RAG used?

RAG is used to give language models access to knowledge they were not trained on, such as private company documents or recent information, while reducing hallucination and enabling citations. Updating documents is far cheaper than retraining a model.

Specific benefits: answers grounded in approved sources; citations users can verify; access control, since retrieval can respect each user's permissions; fresh information without fine-tuning; and smaller models that perform well when given the right context. That is why RAG powers support assistants, internal knowledge search, legal and policy question answering, and study tools. It does not make answers perfect; retrieval quality and prompt design still decide whether the model gets the right evidence.

## How does a RAG chatbot work?

A RAG chatbot runs the retrieval pipeline on every message: it turns the user's question, plus relevant conversation history, into a search query, retrieves passages from its knowledge base, and generates a reply grounded in those passages.

Follow-up questions need care. If a user asks "what about the second option?", the chatbot must rewrite it into a standalone query using the conversation, otherwise retrieval fails. Good RAG chatbots also track the sources shown, stream answers with citations, refuse or ask for clarification when evidence is weak, and log questions without good answers so the knowledge base can be improved. The chat interface is simple; the retrieval and grounding behind it do the real work.

## What are RAG chatbots?

RAG chatbots are conversational assistants that answer from a specific knowledge base, such as product documentation, company policies or course material, by retrieving relevant passages before generating each answer, rather than relying only on the model's training.

They are common in customer support, HR and IT help desks, education, legal research and healthcare information services. Their strengths are accuracy on domain questions, citations and easy updates. Typical stacks combine a document parser, an embedding model, a vector or hybrid search engine, a reranker and a language model, with a web or messaging interface. The OCR & Speech Workspace I built adds document-scoped RAG with page citations, so answers point to the exact page they came from.

## Are all chatbots RAG?

No. Many chatbots answer only from the model's training data, follow scripted flows, or call APIs and tools without retrieving documents. RAG is one design choice, used when answers must come from specific, changing or private knowledge.

Rule-based chatbots, common in older customer service bots, follow decision trees and predefined responses. General assistants like ChatGPT use the model's knowledge and may add web search, which is a form of retrieval. Agentic chatbots call tools such as order lookups or calendars. Many production assistants combine approaches: scripted flows for common tasks, tools for actions, and RAG for knowledge questions. Choose based on what the user needs answered and how often the knowledge changes.

## Why do RAG-only chatbots disappoint?

RAG-only chatbots disappoint when retrieval fails, documents are messy, questions need reasoning across many sources, or users want actions rather than answers. A chatbot that can only search and summarise will struggle with tasks like checking an order or comparing data.

Common failures: poor chunking splits answers across fragments; vector-only search misses exact terms; no reranking puts weak passages first; missing query rewriting breaks follow-ups; and no refusal behaviour produces confident wrong answers. Fixes include hybrid retrieval, rerankers, structured data access through tools or SQL, agentic multi-step retrieval for complex questions, evaluation sets and confidence gates. RAG works best as one component in a system, not as the whole product.

## Can LangChain be used for RAG?

Yes. LangChain provides document loaders, text splitters, embedding integrations, vector store connectors, retrievers including ensemble retrievers for hybrid search, and chains or LangGraph workflows that assemble prompts with retrieved context.

A basic LangChain RAG app loads documents, splits them with a recursive text splitter, embeds them into a vector store such as Chroma or Qdrant, creates a retriever, and composes a chain that formats retrieved passages into a prompt for a chat model. LangGraph adds control for agentic RAG, such as deciding when to retrieve again. LlamaIndex and Haystack are strong alternatives, and plain Python is viable when you want full control over every retrieval step.

## Why is a reranker used in a RAG pipeline?

A reranker improves precision. First-stage retrieval is fast but approximate, so relevant passages may sit at rank 15 instead of rank 1. A reranker, usually a cross-encoder, reads the question and each candidate together and reorders them by true relevance.

Since the language model only sees the top few passages, putting the best evidence first directly improves answers and reduces hallucination. Rerankers are slower than embeddings, so they run on a short list, typically the top 20 to 100 fused results. Options include open-source cross-encoders and hosted rerank APIs. In RAG.NextUpgrad, reranking sits between fusion and the confidence gate, so weak evidence is detected before the model writes an answer.

## How do you index images for RAG?

Three common approaches: convert images to text with OCR and captions, then index the text; embed images directly with a multimodal model such as CLIP so text queries find similar images; or embed page screenshots with document-retrieval models like ColPali.

For scanned documents, OCR with layout extraction is usually the most reliable, since text search and citations stay simple. For charts and diagrams, generate descriptive captions with a vision-language model and store them alongside the image reference. For photo collections, multimodal embeddings work well. Store metadata such as page number, document ID and image path, so answers can cite and display the original image. At answer time, pass the image itself to a vision model when details matter.

## How do you build a generalised RAG pipeline for text, images and structured data?

Route each data type to the retrieval method that suits it: text through hybrid search, images through captions or multimodal embeddings, and structured data through SQL or API tools rather than embeddings. A router or agent decides which sources each question needs.

Use a shared ingestion layer that normalises documents into chunks with consistent metadata: source, type, page, permissions and timestamps. Tables can be stored both as text summaries for retrieval and as rows for precise queries. At query time, an agent can run text retrieval, query a database with generated SQL, and fetch image descriptions, then combine the evidence into one cited answer. Evaluate each path separately, since failures in one modality hide easily in combined results.
