# How Tesseract OCR works: AI, GPU, Windows use, stdout output, and better alternatives
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-tesseract-ocr-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tesseract OCR works in stages: it converts the image to black and white, finds blocks, lines and words in the page layout, reads each text line with an LSTM neural network trained on many fonts and languages, and outputs text with word positions and confidence scores. It runs offline on ordinary CPUs and is free under Apache 2.0. I use OCR in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page explains how Tesseract and OCR in general work, AI and GPU questions, its status and history, Windows use, printing to stdout, and better alternatives.

## How does Tesseract OCR work?

Tesseract first preprocesses the image, using adaptive thresholding to separate text from background. Layout analysis then finds text blocks, lines and words. The LSTM recogniser reads each line as a sequence, predicting characters, and a final step assembles words, lines and paragraphs into output.

Settings shape this process: the language model, selected with `-l`, determines character sets and dictionaries; the page segmentation mode, `--psm`, tells Tesseract whether to expect a full page, a single block, a single line or a single word; and the OCR engine mode chooses the LSTM or legacy engine. Clean, high-resolution input matters more than any setting. Scanning at around 300 DPI, straightening pages and increasing contrast often improves accuracy more than switching engines, so preprocess before blaming the OCR.

## How does OCR technology work in general?

OCR systems capture an image, clean it up, detect where text is, recognise characters or whole lines with trained models, and post-process results with language knowledge to fix errors, producing machine-readable text, often with positions and confidence.

Early OCR matched characters against templates, which only worked for specific fonts. Later systems extracted features and used statistical classifiers. Modern OCR uses deep learning: detection networks find text regions, and recognition networks such as CNN-LSTM models or transformers read them. The newest systems, vision language models, read entire pages including layout and tables, outputting structured formats like Markdown.

## Does Tesseract OCR use AI?

Yes, in the machine learning sense. Since version 4, released in 2018, Tesseract uses an LSTM recurrent neural network trained on large amounts of text images to recognise lines. Older versions relied on traditional pattern matching, still available as the legacy engine.

It is not a large language model and does not understand meaning, so it cannot infer missing words from context the way modern vision language models can. That makes it predictable and fast, but less capable on messy or complex documents. For many applications, its machine learning recogniser plus good preprocessing is enough. You can even fine-tune its LSTM models on your own fonts or scripts with the project's training tools when standard models struggle.

## Does Tesseract OCR use a GPU?

No, not in practice. Tesseract runs on the CPU. Older versions had experimental OpenCL support, but it was never reliable and is not recommended. Tesseract can use multiple CPU threads for some operations.

For faster batch processing, run several Tesseract processes in parallel on different pages, setting `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1` per process, which often uses CPU cores more efficiently than one multi-threaded process. If you need GPU-accelerated OCR, use deep learning toolkits such as PaddleOCR, EasyOCR or docTR, or cloud OCR services.

## Does Tesseract OCR still work and is it maintained?

Yes. Tesseract is actively maintained by an open-source community on GitHub, with releases fixing bugs and improving performance, and it remains one of the most widely used OCR engines, embedded in countless tools such as OCRmyPDF.

Its core recognition approach has not changed dramatically since version 4, so newer deep learning and vision language model OCR often outperform it on difficult inputs. For clean scans of printed text, it still works very well, offline and free. Check the releases page for the latest version, and use packaged builds from trusted sources.

## Why was Tesseract OCR developed?

Hewlett-Packard developed Tesseract in the 1980s and 1990s as a research project to improve OCR for its scanners, aiming for better accuracy than commercial OCR engines of the time. It performed strongly in a 1995 independent accuracy test.

After years without development, HP open-sourced it in 2005, so others could build on it. Google then sponsored its development, using OCR at scale, for example in digitisation projects, and added many languages and the LSTM recogniser. Its open-source release turned it into the default free OCR engine for developers and researchers. That openness is why so many Indian-language digitisation and accessibility projects could build on it without licence costs.

## Who made Tesseract OCR?

Tesseract was created at Hewlett-Packard Laboratories, with Ray Smith as its lead developer. After HP open-sourced it, Ray Smith continued leading its development at Google for many years, and a community of contributors maintains it today.

Ray Smith described the engine's design in the 2007 paper "An Overview of the Tesseract OCR Engine", which remains a good introduction to its architecture. Today, maintainers and contributors from around the world manage releases, language data and documentation through the tesseract-ocr GitHub organisation.

## Which OCR is better than Tesseract?

For harder documents, several options outperform Tesseract: PaddleOCR and EasyOCR for photos and scene text, cloud services such as Google Document AI, Azure AI Document Intelligence and Amazon Textract for forms and tables, and vision language model OCR, such as Mistral OCR, for complex layouts.

Tesseract remains competitive for clean printed text, offline use and zero cost. Choose based on your documents: benchmark candidates on twenty representative pages, measuring accuracy on fields you care about, speed and cost. In the OCR and Speech Workspace, Mistral OCR handles scanned PDFs because layout and table fidelity matter for retrieval with page citations.

## How do I use Tesseract OCR on Windows?

Install Tesseract with the UB Mannheim Windows installer, add its folder to your PATH, open Command Prompt, and run `tesseract image.png output` to create output.txt. Use `-l` for languages and `--psm` for layout modes.

Examples:

- `tesseract scan.png out -l eng` writes out.txt.
- `tesseract scan.png out -l eng+hin` reads English and Hindi.
- `tesseract scan.png out pdf` creates a searchable PDF.

For Python on Windows, install pytesseract and set `pytesseract.pytesseract.tesseract_cmd` to the executable path if needed. Graphical front ends exist if you prefer not to use the command line.

## Can tesseract-ocr print the result to stdout?

Yes. Use `stdout` as the output name: `tesseract image.png stdout` prints recognised text to standard output instead of writing a file. You can also pass `-` as the input to read the image from standard input.

This makes Tesseract easy to use in shell pipelines, for example `tesseract scan.png stdout -l eng | grep "Invoice"`, or from other programs that capture output. Combine with config options, such as `--psm 6`, as usual. For structured output with positions, use `tsv` or `hocr` output formats, which can also be printed to stdout.

# How to ask someone to be your mentor, questions to ask, mentor vs teacher and origins
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-ask-for-a-mentor/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To ask someone to be your mentor, start with a specific, small request, such as one conversation about a decision, show you have done your homework, and let the relationship grow from follow-ups rather than a formal ask. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023, so this page covers how to ask, what to ask a career mentor, how mentors differ from teachers, the Greek origin of the word, where mentorship came from, mentor duties, mentoring founders and academics, and what makes a great mentor.

## How do you ask someone to be your mentor?

Do not open with "will you be my mentor". Ask for something specific and small: fifteen minutes of advice on a decision, feedback on a project, or how they handled a situation you face. Show what you have already tried.

Example message: I am a second-year BCA student building a RAG project and saw your talk on retrieval; could I ask you two questions about evaluating it, over a short call or by message? Afterwards, act on their advice and report back with results. If conversations continue naturally, you can propose a regular rhythm, such as monthly check-ins. Respect their time, accept a no gracefully, and remember that mentorship grows from demonstrated effort.

## What questions should you ask your career mentor?

Ask questions that draw on their experience and your specific situation: what skills mattered most early in their career, what they would do in your position, which mistakes to avoid, and how they evaluate opportunities.

Useful questions: What would you focus on in my first two years? How do you decide between two offers? What separates good engineers from great ones in your team? How did you get your first leadership responsibility? What should I stop doing? Which people or communities should I connect with? Bring context each time, such as a project, a decision or a draft resume, so answers are concrete rather than generic.

## Is a mentor a teacher?

A mentor teaches, but is not a teacher in the formal sense. Teachers deliver structured lessons to groups and assess learning; mentors guide an individual's broader growth through experience, advice and example, usually outside a curriculum.

A teacher can become a mentor when the relationship extends beyond the classroom, such as advising a student on career choices or projects. Likewise, a senior engineer mentoring a junior teaches skills, but without exams or a syllabus. The word mentor emphasises a personal, ongoing relationship and the mentee's goals, while teacher emphasises instruction and knowledge transfer. Both roles matter, and the best teachers often act as mentors for some students.

## What is the difference between a mentor and a teacher?

Teachers follow a curriculum, teach groups, set assignments and assess performance within a course. Mentors focus on one person's goals, offer guidance from experience, and support decisions about careers, skills and personal growth over time.

Other differences: teaching is usually formal and time-bound, while mentoring is often voluntary and open-ended; teachers have authority over grades, while mentors usually have no authority over the mentee; and teaching transfers defined knowledge, while mentoring develops judgement and confidence. Mentors can be peers, seniors or professionals outside your field. Students benefit from both: teachers build foundations, and mentors help apply them to real choices and opportunities beyond the syllabus.

## Is mentor a Greek word?

Yes. Mentor comes from Greek mythology: in Homer's Odyssey, Mentor is an old friend of Odysseus who is entrusted with the care of his son, Telemachus. The goddess Athena takes Mentor's form to guide Telemachus.

The modern sense of mentor as a wise adviser became popular through the 1699 French novel The Adventures of Telemachus by François Fénelon, in which Mentor plays a central guiding role. From there, the word entered English and other languages as a common noun. The verb to mentor appeared much later, in the twentieth century. The story's lesson still fits today: a mentor guides growth through presence, wisdom and encouragement.

## Where did mentorship first come into practice?

Mentorship is ancient: experienced people have guided younger ones in families, crafts and philosophy for millennia, such as Socrates teaching Plato. The idea took its name from Homer's Odyssey, and craft apprenticeships formalised it for centuries.

Medieval guilds paired apprentices with masters for years of practical training, combining skill transfer with guidance on conduct and career. Formal workplace mentoring programmes spread in the 1970s and 1980s, and Kathy Kram's 1985 book Mentoring at Work shaped how organisations understand career and psychosocial mentoring. Today mentoring appears in schools, universities, companies, startups and online communities, often supported by structured programmes and platforms that match mentors and mentees.

## What is a mentor's job description?

A mentor's role is to guide a mentee's development: meet regularly, help set goals, share experience, give honest feedback, suggest resources and connections, encourage reflection, and maintain confidentiality and professional boundaries.

In formal programmes, a mentor description often lists the time commitment, such as one hour every two weeks for six months; required experience; responsibilities, such as preparing for sessions and tracking goals; and expectations around safeguarding, especially with students or minors. Paid mentor roles on education platforms add teaching sessions, reviewing work and reporting progress. Good mentors listen more than they talk, ask questions before advising, and help mentees make their own decisions rather than deciding for them.

## Why is mentorship essential for entrepreneurs?

Entrepreneurs face many first-time decisions, about customers, hiring, fundraising and product, with little margin for error. Mentors who have built companies help them avoid costly mistakes, see blind spots, make introductions and stay resilient through setbacks.

Accelerators and incubators build programmes around mentorship for this reason. Useful mentors challenge assumptions, share specific experiences rather than generic advice, and connect founders to customers, investors and talent. Founders should seek several mentors with different strengths, such as product, sales and finance, and test advice against their own data, since every startup's context differs. Experienced outside perspectives often reveal problems that a team is too close to see.

## How do you mentor someone in academia?

Academic mentoring helps students and early researchers with research skills, writing, publishing, conferences, funding and career choices. Set expectations early, meet regularly, give specific feedback on work, and support independence rather than doing work for them.

Good academic mentors explain unwritten rules, such as how peer review works or how to approach potential collaborators, introduce mentees to networks, and discuss careers both inside and outside academia. They model research integrity and help mentees handle rejection, which is common. Agree on authorship and responsibilities early to avoid conflict. For students from first-generation or underrepresented backgrounds, mentors can make a large difference by making hidden expectations visible.

## What makes someone a top mentor, according to developers?

When developers describe their best mentors in community discussions, common themes appear: the mentor gave real responsibility early, explained the reasoning behind decisions, reviewed code patiently and honestly, and believed in them before they believed in themselves.

Many recall a senior engineer who let them make manageable mistakes, then helped them learn from them, or a manager who shielded them from noise while pushing them to grow. Others mention authors and open-source maintainers whose writing or reviews acted as mentorship at a distance. The pattern is clear: great mentors combine high standards with genuine care. If you mentor others, aim for both, and your mentees may name you one day.

# How to be a mentor at work and in college: technical mentors, culture, word origin
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-be-a-mentor-at-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To be a good mentor at work, listen before advising, share specific lessons from your own experience, give honest and kind feedback, and help your mentee grow towards their goals, not yours. In college, mentors are faculty or seniors who guide students through studies and careers. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023 and lead a 14-member engineering team at SCULT INDIA, so this page covers college mentoring, workplace mentoring and culture, technical mentors, mentoring on resumes, and where the word comes from.

## What is a mentor in college?

A college mentor is a faculty member, senior student or alumnus who guides students on academics, skills, careers and personal challenges. Many colleges assign faculty mentors to groups of students, and peer mentoring programmes pair first-years with seniors.

Good college mentors help students choose electives and projects, prepare for internships, balance studies with clubs and hackathons, and find support when struggling. Seniors are especially useful for practical questions, like which skills to learn first or how placements work. At the VSICS induction seminar in July 2025, I gave over 100 first-year students a three-year roadmap, because early direction saves students from drifting through their first year.

## What is the mentor and mentee relationship in college?

The mentor is the experienced guide; the mentee is the student being guided. In a healthy relationship, the mentee drives it with goals and questions, and the mentor offers perspective, feedback and connections.

What makes it work: regular check-ins, even brief ones; clear goals, such as landing an internship by third year; honesty in both directions; and the mentee acting on advice and reporting back. Mentors should respect boundaries and avoid making decisions for students. Mentees should come prepared rather than expecting the mentor to set the agenda. Many of my strongest mentoring relationships started with a student showing a half-built project and asking what to fix next.

## How do I be a mentor at work?

Start by understanding your mentee's goals, then meet regularly, listen more than you talk, share specific experiences including mistakes, give actionable feedback, and look for opportunities to stretch and showcase them.

Practices that work:

- Ask what they want to achieve in six months and a year.
- Use their real work, a pull request or design, as material.
- Share how you think, not just what to do.
- Give feedback soon, specifically and privately.
- Introduce them to people and projects that help their growth.
- Celebrate progress and credit them publicly.

Leading a team, I find mentoring through code reviews and architecture discussions teaches more than formal sessions.

## How do I build a mentorship culture?

Build it through visible leadership, simple structures and recognition: leaders mentor openly, mentoring time is expected rather than extra, pairing is easy, and people who mentor well are recognised in reviews and promotions.

Steps for a team or organisation:

- Make mentoring part of senior roles' expectations.
- Pair new joiners with a buddy for their first months.
- Use code reviews, pair programming and demos as everyday mentoring.
- Run short internal talks where people share lessons.
- Create spaces for questions without judgement.
- Measure outcomes such as onboarding time and internal promotions.

Communities work the same way: TechVerse Enclave grew to over 500 members because seniors kept answering juniors' questions and juniors later did the same.

## What is a technical mentor?

A technical mentor is an experienced engineer or technologist who guides others in technical skills and decisions: writing better code, designing systems, debugging, choosing tools and growing as an engineer. They focus on craft, not only career advice.

Technical mentors appear in companies, open-source projects, bootcamps and hackathons. At hackathons, technical mentors help teams unblock problems, scope features and fix integration issues within hours. I have mentored at more than ten hackathons, and the most useful help is usually scoping: helping a team cut features so they finish one working flow rather than five broken ones.

## What does a technical mentor role involve?

A technical mentor role involves reviewing code and designs, pairing on problems, explaining concepts, suggesting learning resources, setting stretch tasks, and giving feedback on technical growth. In formal roles, it may include onboarding new engineers and running workshops.

Typical responsibilities:

- Conduct code reviews with explanations, not just corrections.
- Guide architecture and design decisions.
- Help debug and teach debugging methods.
- Recommend learning paths for skills gaps.
- Assess progress and give structured feedback.
- Model good engineering practices: testing, documentation, communication.

The best technical mentors make themselves less necessary over time by building the mentee's independent judgement.

## What is the difference between a technical mentor and an associate trainer?

A technical mentor gives personalised, ongoing guidance to individuals or small teams, adapting to their projects and goals. An associate trainer delivers structured training programmes, such as courses or bootcamp modules, to groups, following a curriculum.

Trainers focus on teaching content consistently and assessing learners against set outcomes; mentors focus on applying skills in real work and solving each person's specific problems. Training builds foundations efficiently; mentoring turns knowledge into judgement. Many organisations combine them: new hires attend training sessions, then work with mentors on real tasks. Job titles vary by company, so read the role description for specifics.

## Should I put mentoring on my resume?

Yes, if it is substantial and relevant. Mentoring shows leadership, communication and expertise. List it under experience, leadership or volunteering with specifics: who you mentored, how many, and outcomes.

Examples of strong entries: "Mentored 12 junior developers through onboarding, cutting average ramp-up time" or "Mentored student hackathon teams; three teams reached finals." Avoid vague lines like "mentored others" without context. For student resumes, peer mentoring, teaching assistant work and community leadership are worth including. Be ready to discuss it in interviews with a concrete story of helping someone improve.

## Does the word "mentor" come from the Odyssey?

Yes. The word comes from Mentor, a character in Homer's Odyssey, an old friend of Odysseus who is entrusted with the household when Odysseus leaves for the Trojan War. The goddess Athena takes Mentor's form to guide Odysseus's son Telemachus.

The modern meaning, a wise and trusted adviser, became common after the French writer François Fénelon's 1699 novel "Les Aventures de Télémaque" made Mentor a central guiding figure. So the word reached English through the Greek epic and its later retellings. It is a good reminder that mentorship is an ancient idea: guidance passed from the experienced to the next generation.

## Does Mentor die in the Odyssey?

No. Mentor does not die in the Odyssey. He survives the story, which ends with Athena, again in Mentor's form, bringing peace between Odysseus and the families of the suitors he killed.

Much of what "Mentor" does in the poem is actually Athena in disguise: encouraging Telemachus to seek news of his father, travelling with him, and later standing beside Odysseus during the fight with the suitors. The real Mentor appears only briefly. Readers sometimes confuse him with other characters who do die, such as many of the suitors, so check the specific book and passage if you are studying the text.

# What course should I do to become an AI engineer? Paths after BCA, MCA or no degree
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-become-ai-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To become an AI engineer, a computing degree such as B.Tech, BCA, B.Sc or MCA helps, but the course that matters most is the one you build yourself: Python and software engineering, then language model APIs, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation, agents and deployment, proven through real projects. I am a BCA student who leads engineering at SCULT INDIA and shipped five production AI apps in 2026, so this page covers courses, paths with BCA, MCA or no degree, ML versus AI engineers, LLM engineering, projects, demand and AI's effect on the role.

## What course should I do to become an AI engineer?

Choose a computing degree you can access, such as B.Tech in computer science or AI, BCA, B.Sc computer science or MCA, then add focused learning through free and paid courses aligned with AI engineering. The degree opens doors; skills and projects get you hired.

Useful courses: Harvard's free CS50 and CS50 AI for fundamentals; DeepLearning.AI short courses on LLM apps, RAG and agents; Hugging Face courses on transformers; and cloud provider courses on deployment. Follow a roadmap such as roadmap.sh's AI Engineer map. Do not collect certificates without building: after each course, ship a project that uses what you learned. Pair formal study with one long-running project you keep improving, because depth in one real system teaches retrieval, evaluation, deployment and debugging together, which no single course covers.

## How do I become an AI engineer?

Build strong programming and software engineering skills, learn to use language models through APIs, master retrieval and evaluation, then agents and deployment, while shipping projects and joining hackathons. Internships and open-source contributions convert skills into job offers.

A practical sequence:

- Python, Git, APIs, SQL and one web framework.
- LLM fundamentals: prompting, structured output, costs.
- RAG: embeddings, chunking, hybrid search, reranking, citations.
- Evaluation: test sets and metrics.
- Agents and tools, including MCP.
- Deployment: FastAPI, Docker, cloud, monitoring.

Document every project with a write-up and demo, and share it publicly. Hackathons accelerate this: building under time pressure with feedback from judges and mentors teaches prioritisation that self-study rarely does.

## How do I become a machine learning engineer without a degree?

It is possible but harder, because some employers filter by degree. Compensate with a strong public portfolio, open-source contributions, competition results, certifications from recognised providers, and networking that leads to referrals.

Learn mathematics fundamentals, linear algebra, probability and statistics, alongside Python, machine learning with scikit-learn, deep learning with PyTorch and deployment. Build projects that show the full lifecycle: data collection, training, evaluation, serving and monitoring. Startups and smaller companies are often more open to candidates without degrees. Consider distance or online degrees from recognised universities if formal credentials become a barrier.

## Can I become an AI engineer after BCA?

Yes. BCA teaches programming, databases and web development, a solid base for AI engineering, which is mostly about building software around models. Many AI engineering roles care about what you can build, not whether your degree says B.Tech.

My path is an example: during BCA, I built and shipped production AI apps, including a RAG platform, a fine-tuning studio and browser-based face recognition, and won national hackathons. BCA students should start early: learn AI tools in the second year, join hackathons, seek internships, and build a portfolio. Some employers prefer B.Tech or postgraduates for certain roles, which MCA can address later if needed.

## Can I become an AI engineer after MCA?

Yes. MCA adds depth in software engineering and computing, and its two-year programme gives time for AI specialisation, a major project and an internship. MCA graduates regularly move into AI and ML roles.

Use MCA strategically: choose AI-related electives, make your final project an AI system with real users and evaluation, do an AI-focused internship, and build a portfolio alongside coursework. Learn practical tools the syllabus may not cover, such as LLM APIs, vector search and deployment. Employers will judge your projects and problem-solving more than the degree title.

## What is the difference between an ML engineer and an AI engineer?

ML engineers typically train, optimise and deploy machine learning models, working with data pipelines, feature engineering, training infrastructure and model serving. AI engineers typically build applications using existing models, especially language models, through APIs, retrieval, agents and product integration.

The roles overlap and titles vary by company. ML engineering demands more mathematics and modelling depth; AI engineering demands more software and product skills, plus evaluation of model behaviour. Both need strong coding and deployment skills. Many engineers move between them; fine-tuning work, like QLoRA in FineTune Studio, sits right at the boundary.

## How do I become a great LLM engineer?

Go beyond calling APIs: master retrieval quality, evaluation, prompt and context design, fine-tuning when appropriate, inference optimisation, cost control and safety. Great LLM engineers measure everything and know why their systems fail.

Habits of strong LLM engineers:

- Build evaluation sets before optimising.
- Read failures by hand, not just metrics.
- Understand tokenisation, context limits and sampling.
- Know when to use RAG, fine-tuning or both.
- Design for failure with fallbacks and refusals.
- Keep up with research but test claims on your own data.

Ship systems people use, and write about what you learned. Explaining a failure you fixed, such as retrieval missing exact product codes until you added keyword search, shows more skill than listing frameworks.

## What is the best AI engineer project for a portfolio?

The best project solves a real problem for real users, is deployed with a public demo, includes evaluation results, and has a clear write-up explaining architecture and trade-offs. Depth beats variety: one excellent project outweighs ten tutorials.

Strong examples: a RAG assistant over real documents with hybrid search, citations and a refusal threshold; a document extraction tool with schema validation; a fine-tuned small model with base-versus-tuned comparisons; a browser-based vision app that protects privacy; or an agent that automates a real workflow with logs and approvals. My own portfolio grew from projects like these, each with a live demo.

## Are AI engineers in demand?

Yes. Organisations across industries are building AI features, assistants and automations, and need engineers who can integrate models reliably, securely and cost-effectively. Reports such as the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs place AI and big data skills among the fastest-growing.

Demand is strongest for engineers who can ship production systems, not just prototypes: retrieval, evaluation, deployment, monitoring and security. Entry-level competition is high, so portfolios, internships and hackathon results matter. Demand also extends beyond pure AI companies: banks, healthcare, retail, education and government teams all need people who understand both software and AI.

## Will AI replace AI engineers?

AI is automating parts of the job, such as writing boilerplate code, generating tests and drafting prompts, but it increases demand for engineers who can design systems, judge quality, ensure safety and take responsibility for outcomes.

The role is shifting from writing every line to specifying, supervising and verifying AI-generated work, and from building single features to orchestrating agents and pipelines. Engineers who adapt, using AI tools heavily while deepening judgement in architecture, evaluation and security, become more productive and more valuable. Those who only do routine coding face more pressure, so focus on skills that require understanding, not repetition.

# How to become an AI engineer in India: the GenAI engineer roadmap, skills, projects and salary reality, from a BCA to shipping five production apps
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-become-an-ai-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What does an AI engineer actually do?

**In 2026 an AI engineer, often titled GenAI engineer, applied AI engineer or LLM engineer, builds products on top of existing models: retrieval systems over company documents, fine-tuned models for narrow tasks, agents that call tools, evaluation harnesses that prove the system works, and the deployment, monitoring and cost control around all of it. Training foundation models from scratch is a research role at a handful of labs and is not what most job posts mean.**


My own week is the evidence. In the first half of 2026 I shipped five production AI applications at NextUpgrad: a RAG platform, a fine-tuning platform, a document intelligence service, a browser-only face recognition system and an OCR and speech workspace [10]. None involved training a model from scratch. All involved Python, an API framework, a database, Docker, tests, and a lot of evaluation. That is the job.


> Nobody hired me for what I knew. They hired me for what I had shipped and could explain failure by failure.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I become an AI engineer with no experience?

**Build in public, in this order: learn Python well enough to write a small service; learn one web framework and deploy something live; build a RAG system over documents you care about; fine-tune a small model on a dataset you made; build an agent with one real tool; write an evaluation for each. Publish every project with a README, a live URL and a demo video. Apply with those links, not with a course certificate.**



That timeline is what I told 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction in July 2025, and it is the shape of my own path from a BCA in India to leading engineering at an agency and shipping production AI systems [11]. It is not fast. It is faster than any alternative I have seen work.

### Can I become an AI engineer from BCA, or a tier-3 college?

**Yes. I did a BCA at VSICS, not an IIT B.Tech, and the interviews that mattered never asked about the college; they asked about RAG.NextUpgrad and what broke in it. Companies filter on degree when they have nothing else to look at. Give them something else: live projects, hackathon results, public writing, a GitHub that shows steady work. The degree becomes a footnote.**


What a BCA lacks compared with a B.Tech is usually maths depth and campus placement access. Fix the first with one solid linear algebra course and by reading papers with a notebook open; fix the second by going where the companies are, hackathons, communities, cold outreach, instead of waiting for a placement cell.

## What skills does an AI engineer need in 2026?

**Python fluently, including async and packaging. One API framework, FastAPI or similar. SQL and one database, plus a vector index. The LLM stack: prompting, RAG, fine-tuning with LoRA, tool calling and agents, evaluation. Deployment: Docker, a CI pipeline, logging and metrics, one cloud or platform. Enough maths to read a paper and reason about embeddings and loss curves. And the soft skill that decides senior roles: writing a clear spec and a clear README.**



The foundational papers are short and readable; the RAG paper [2] and the LoRA paper [3] are the two I ask every mentee to read in their first month, with Anthropic's agents guide as the practical companion [1].

## Which programming language and courses should I start with?

**Python, without debate, plus enough JavaScript or TypeScript to build an interface when a project needs one. For courses: the official Python tutorial [4], the FastAPI documentation [5], Hugging Face's free LLM and agents courses [6], fast.ai's practical deep learning course for intuition [7], and Andrew Ng's machine learning specialisation if you want the classical foundation [8]. All free or nearly. Spend more time building than watching.**


On certificates: I have never seen one change a hiring decision at SCULT INDIA or anywhere I have interviewed. I have seen a deployed project with a clear README change many.

## What projects should I build for an AI engineer portfolio?

**Five projects that together cover the stack: a RAG assistant over a real document set with measured recall; a fine-tuned small model with a base-versus-tuned comparison; an agent with one real tool and a safety boundary; a computer vision or speech application with a privacy decision explained; and one boring, useful web app for a real person or club. Each live at a URL, each with a README that states the problem, the decision you made, and the result.**



The RAG project is the one recruiters ask about most, because it is the one they are hiring for most. My longer write-up on which projects lead to interviews is on the portfolio [13].

### How do I build a GitHub profile recruiters read?

**Pin five repositories, each with a README that has the problem in one sentence, a screenshot or demo link, how to run it, and what you would do next. Commit steadily rather than in bursts. Delete or archive tutorial clones. Add a profile README with your role, city, and three links: portfolio, LinkedIn, email. Recruiters spend under two minutes; make those minutes land on finished things.**


## How do I get an AI internship or a first job?

**Apply where the work is visible: startups, agencies and small product companies that ship AI features, and remote roles that hire on portfolios. Cold email founders with one line about their product and a link to a project that resembles it. Enter hackathons, because judges and sponsors hire. Post one build a week on LinkedIn. Treat the first role as the one that produces the stories you need for the second.**


My first serious work came through a community I built, TechVerse Enclave, and through hackathons, not through a placement cell. That is not an argument against placement cells; it is an argument for not waiting for one.


## What is the salary of an AI engineer in India?

**I will not give you a number, because the numbers that circulate online are unmeasured and this page only reports what can be checked. What I can tell you from hiring and being hired: pay tracks the company tier and city far more than the title; a GenAI engineer at a funded startup in Bengaluru and one at an agency in a smaller city are different bands for the same skills; remote roles for foreign companies pay more and hire on portfolios; and the fastest way to raise your number is a second offer, not a longer wait.**



## Can I get a remote AI job from India?

**Yes, and remote roles are where portfolios matter most, because the company cannot see your college and does not care. Target companies that already hire remotely, contribute to open-source projects they use, apply with a project that mirrors their product, and be ready for asynchronous, written communication, which is a skill you can practise by writing READMEs and posts. Time-zone overlap with Europe is India's structural advantage.**


## How long does it take to become an AI engineer?

**Twelve to eighteen months of steady building, alongside a degree, gets most people to a hireable portfolio: Python, one deployed app, RAG, a fine-tune, an agent, all live. Faster is possible with full-time focus; slower is normal with exams. The variable that matters is shipped projects per quarter, not hours of video watched.**



## What are common AI engineer interview questions?

**Explain a RAG system you built and what failed. Compare RAG with fine-tuning and say when you would choose each. Explain LoRA in one minute. Describe how you evaluated a system and what metric you chose. Design an agent for a task and name its guardrails. Estimate the cost of an LLM feature. Write a function under time pressure. The pattern: they want to know you have shipped and can reason about trade-offs, not that you memorised definitions.**


## Is AI engineering a good career, and will AI replace AI engineers?

**It is a good career for people who like building and are comfortable with tools changing every year. The models will keep getting better at writing code, which changes the job from typing to specifying, evaluating and integrating. Engineers who can define a problem, judge an output and ship a system will be more valuable, not less. Engineers whose only skill is producing code from a clear spec are the ones at risk, in AI and everywhere else.**




## Where can I get help on this path?

**Ask. I mentor students through TechVerse Enclave, run sessions at colleges, and answer real questions by email.** The full roadmap article with resources is on the portfolio [12]. If your college wants a career session on GenAI engineering, or a workshop that ends with every student having a deployed project, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to build a developer portfolio website: what to include, what to cut, free hosting, and the three-second test recruiters actually apply
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-a-developer-portfolio-website/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What should a developer portfolio website include?

**A home page that states what you build in one sentence and links everywhere else. Three to five project write-ups, each with the problem, the decision you made, a demo or screenshot, and what you would do differently. An about section that is two paragraphs, not a biography. A contact method that is one click away. Talks or writing if you have them. Nothing else. The whole site should answer what do you build, is it real, and how do I reach you, inside ten seconds of landing.**


My own site exists for exactly this, and it is the page every organiser and recruiter opens before a call [9]. My longer notes on the README format that feeds project pages, and on which projects to include, are on the portfolio [7][8].

> A portfolio site is not a museum of everything you have touched. It is three doors, each opening onto something real.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I write a project page that gets read?

**Problem in one sentence: who had it and what it cost them. The decision you are proud of, in three sentences, including the trade-off. A demo video or three screenshots, never a wall of code. What you would do differently now, which shows growth more than any feature list. A link to the repository and, if it exists, a live demo. Skip the tech stack badge wall at the top; put it at the bottom if at all. A reader should understand the project without opening the code.**



## Which projects should I put on my portfolio?

**Three to five, chosen for range and depth, not for count. One that solved a real problem for a real person. One that shows a technical decision you can defend for twenty minutes. One that is live and usable right now. Cut anything that is a tutorial clone, a copy of a template, or unfinished. A portfolio with three strong projects reads as more capable than one with twelve thin ones, because reviewers judge by the best page they see, not the total.**


## What should I leave off my portfolio?

**Certificates, unless a project sits behind them. A skills matrix with progress bars, which nobody trusts. Every course you have completed. Tutorial clones with no changes of your own. A blog if you are not going to keep writing, better a single pinned post than an abandoned feed. Stock photography. A dense biography above the fold. The test is simple: does this page help someone decide to talk to you in the next thirty seconds; if not, cut it.**




## Where should I host a portfolio for free?

**GitHub Pages for a fully static site, free forever on a public repository, with a custom domain supported [2]. Netlify and Vercel's free tiers for a site with a build step, also generous and free for personal use [3]. Cloudflare Pages as another free, fast option [4]. A `.dev`, `.me` or `.in` domain costs a small yearly fee if you want one; the hosting itself should never cost anything for a personal portfolio. Avoid managed website builders with monthly fees; a static site is simpler, faster and free.**



## How fast and accessible should it be?

**Fast enough that it loads before the recruiter's attention moves on: a static site with optimised images and no heavy frameworks for a simple portfolio easily hits good Core Web Vitals scores [1]. Accessible enough that a screen reader can navigate it: real headings, alt text on images, sufficient colour contrast, keyboard-navigable links [5]. Neither takes more than an afternoon to get right, and both are things a recruiter or organiser will notice without naming, as a site that either feels solid or feels broken.**


## How do I keep it updated without it becoming a chore?

**Update it the moment something changes: a project ships, a talk happens, a link breaks. Do not schedule quarterly overhauls, which is how portfolios go a year stale. Keep the write-up template from this page in a notes file so a new project page takes twenty minutes, not a weekend. Delete a project the moment you would not want it asked about; an outdated portfolio actively works against you, so removing is as valid an edit as adding.**



## What mistakes do developer portfolios make?

**A home page with no clear statement of what you build. A skills wall that reads like a résumé keyword dump. Ten projects, all thin. Broken links to deleted repositories or dead demos. No way to contact you without hunting. A design so custom it is confusing to navigate. Copy-pasted README text with no framing for a human reader. Every one of these is fixed by the ten-second test: would a stranger know what to do next.**



## Developer portfolio interview questions

**"Walk me through a project on your site" is the most common opener once a recruiter has read it, so every project page should survive twenty minutes of follow-up questions. Prepare the decision, the trade-off, the failure and the fix for each of your three to five projects before the interview, not during it. The portfolio's job is to earn this question; your job is to answer it well.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick your best three projects, write the problem-decision-demo-lesson page for the first one tonight, and deploy on GitHub Pages or Netlify this week.** For a session on building a technical portfolio that gets you interviews, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to build an AI app and deploy it for free: architecture, stack, hosting, costs and the checklist that survives real users
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-an-ai-app/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I build an AI app?

**Build a normal web application and put the model call behind one function. The front end collects input and shows output, the API validates the input, calls the model with a prompt and any retrieved context, validates the output, stores what happened, and returns it. Add authentication, a database, logging and a deploy pipeline, and you have an AI app. The model is one dependency, and everything around it is what makes the product work when a stranger uses it.**


I shipped five production AI applications between February and July 2026, a RAG platform, a fine-tuning platform, a document extraction service, a browser face recognition system and an OCR and speech workspace, each with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics [12]. The stack below is the one they share, and the checklist at the end is what each of them taught me the hard way.

> The model call is thirty lines. The other three thousand lines are why the app is still up next month.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the architecture of an LLM app?

**Five layers. A client: a web page, a mobile app, a WhatsApp bot. An API layer that authenticates, validates and rate-limits. A model layer: the prompt, the provider client, retries and fallbacks, and optionally retrieval, tools or a fine-tuned model. A data layer: a relational database for users and logs, a vector index for documents, object storage for files. And an operations layer: deploy pipeline, logs, metrics, alerts. Most AI apps are small enough that the API and model layers live in one service.**



The longer write-up of the FastAPI and Next.js version of this, with the folder layout, is on the portfolio [13].

## Which tech stack should I use for an AI app?

**Python for the back end, because every model library, SDK and example is in Python, with FastAPI for the API [1]. Postgres for data, with pgvector when you need embeddings [3]; Supabase gives you Postgres, auth and storage on a free tier [4]. Any front end you already know, plain HTML, React or Next.js. Docker to package it [2]. GitHub Actions to test and deploy [8]. One platform host. Add nothing else until a real need appears.**



On frameworks such as LangChain: excellent for a first prototype and for loaders; for production, I write the model wrapper myself, because a bug under three abstraction layers costs a day and a bug in my own fifty lines costs ten minutes.

## How do I deploy an AI app for free?

**Package the app in Docker and deploy to a platform with a free or trial tier: Railway, Render or Fly.io for a container, Hugging Face Spaces for a demo with a GPU option, Supabase for the database, and a static host such as GitHub Pages, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages for the front end. Free tiers sleep or cap hours, so design the app to start fast and hold no state in memory. The model API itself is not free beyond trial credits, so budget tokens from day one.**



Free tiers change; the platform documentation is the source of truth and this table is a map, not a guarantee [4][5][6][7]. RAG.NextUpgrad, with hybrid retrieval, reranking and streaming, runs in about 220 MB of memory on a free tier, which is the proof that a real AI app does not need a large server [12]. My deployment write-up walks through it step by step [14].


## How much does it cost to run an AI app?

**Hosting can be zero at first. The model API is the real bill: input tokens plus output tokens, times the price per million, times requests. Estimate it before launch: measure the tokens of a typical request, multiply by expected daily requests, multiply by the provider's rate. Then set a hard monthly cap at the provider, a per-user daily limit in your code, and an alert at half the cap. An app with no cap is one viral post away from a bill you did not plan.**



## How do I make an AI app reliable?

**Wrap every model call with a timeout, a bounded retry with backoff, and a fallback to a second provider or a smaller model with the same prompt. Validate outputs against a schema and fail closed when they do not parse. Stream responses so users see progress. Make the app stateless so it can restart. Test the prompt against a fixed set of inputs in CI. Log every request with its tokens, latency and outcome. My apps fall back across providers automatically, and that single feature has kept them up through several API outages.**


```python
async def generate(prompt: str, schema: type[BaseModel]) -> BaseModel:
    for provider in PROVIDERS:                      # identical prompt, ordered by preference
        for attempt in range(2):
            try:
                raw = await asyncio.wait_for(provider.complete(prompt, max_tokens=800), timeout=30)
                return schema.model_validate_json(raw)   # fail closed if it does not parse
            except (TimeoutError, ProviderError, ValidationError) as e:
                log.warning("provider=%s attempt=%d err=%s", provider.name, attempt, e)
                await asyncio.sleep(0.5 * (attempt + 1))
    raise ServiceUnavailable("all providers failed")
```

## How do I secure an AI app?

**Treat every input, and every document or tool result the model reads, as untrusted. Keep instructions in the system prompt and data in delimited user content. Give tools the least permission they need and require a human confirmation for irreversible actions. Never put secrets in prompts. Rate-limit per user. Validate outputs before acting on them. Log prompts and outputs with user consent and a retention policy. OWASP's list of LLM application risks is the checklist to review before launch [9].**


The most common student mistake is the API key in the front-end code, where anyone can read it and run up your bill. The key lives on the server, always, and the server enforces the limits.

## Should I build an AI agent or a simple app?

**A simple app, until a decision appears that you cannot write as code. Most "AI agents" that succeed in production are workflows: code decides the steps, a model does the language work at each step. Reach for a real agent loop only when the task is open-ended and the model must choose actions at run time, and then add limits, permissions and confirmations before anything else [11].**



## How do I get users for an AI app?

**Build it for a group you belong to, your class, your club, a family business, and put it in front of them the day it works. Ask what they tried to do that failed, and fix that. Post a demo video where those people are. Ten real users teach more than a thousand sign-ups from a launch post, and they are how a student project becomes a line on a resume that a recruiter believes.**



## What mistakes kill AI apps after demo day?

**No cap on API spend. The key in the front end. No logs, so the first complaint is undebuggable. State held in memory on a host that sleeps. Prompts edited in production with no test set. One provider and no fallback. No per-user limits, so one script drains the budget. A model output acted on without validation. Each is on the checklist above; each I have either done or watched a mentee do.**



## What are common AI app interview questions?

**Design an LLM feature end to end and name where it can fail. Estimate its monthly cost. Explain how you would handle a provider outage. Explain where prompt injection can enter and what limits its damage. Describe how you would test a prompt change. Say what you would log. Each answer is a section above, and the best evidence is a live app you can open during the interview.**



## Where should I start?

**Take a problem someone near you has, build the smallest version with FastAPI, one model call with a timeout and a fallback, Postgres on Supabase, Docker, and deploy it on a free tier this weekend. Log everything. Show it to three people. Then read the checklist again.** All five of my production apps are open source and follow this shape [12]. If your college wants a workshop that ends with every student having a deployed AI app, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to build a Copilot agent, how it works, and what it can do
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-build-copilot-agent/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To build a Copilot agent, open Microsoft 365 Copilot and use Agent Builder for a simple agent made of instructions and knowledge, or use Copilot Studio when the agent needs actions, API calls, triggers or multi-step workflows. An agent combines instructions, knowledge sources and actions, and a language model decides how to use them for each request. This page shows how to create one and how it works, then answers what agents can do: read PDFs and SharePoint lists, call APIs, send email, run on a schedule, call other agents and be shared, plus which agent to use for coding.

## How do I create a Copilot agent?

In Microsoft 365 Copilot, choose to create an agent, describe what it should do in plain language, add knowledge such as SharePoint sites or files, test it in the preview pane, and share it. For actions and workflows, build it in Copilot Studio instead.

A first agent in under an hour:

- **Purpose**: one narrow job, such as answering questions about your department's policies.
- **Instructions**: who it serves, what it should and should not answer, tone, and when to hand over to a person.
- **Knowledge**: the SharePoint site or documents that hold the answers.
- **Starter prompts**: three example questions users can click.
- **Test**: ask twenty real questions, including tricky ones, and fix instructions where answers go wrong.

Start narrow; a focused agent that answers well beats a broad one that guesses.

## How does a Copilot agent work?

When a user sends a message, the agent's orchestrator reads its instructions, decides whether to search its knowledge sources, call an action or reply directly, runs those steps, and has the language model compose an answer, citing sources where it used them.

Knowledge searches retrieve relevant passages, respecting each user's permissions, which is retrieval-augmented generation. Actions are tools with descriptions, such as "create a ticket" or "look up an order", and the model picks them based on those descriptions, so clear names and descriptions matter. In Copilot Studio you can also define topics, fixed conversation paths for cases that must follow exact steps. Every conversation can be reviewed in analytics and transcripts, which is how you improve the agent after launch.

## Which Copilot agent is best for coding?

For coding, use GitHub Copilot: agent mode in VS Code and other editors for interactive multi-file changes, and the Copilot coding agent on GitHub for issues you hand off and review as pull requests. Microsoft 365 agents are built for work content, not codebases.

GitHub Copilot's agents can read the repository, run commands and tests, and iterate on failures. Give them well-scoped tasks with acceptance criteria, keep a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file with build and style rules, and review every change through normal code review. For comparison, other strong coding agents include Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex and Google's Gemini CLI; try one real task in each if your team is choosing.

## Can a Copilot agent read a PDF?

Yes. Agents can use PDFs as knowledge, either uploaded directly in Agent Builder or Copilot Studio, or stored in a SharePoint site or OneDrive folder the agent searches. They answer from the text and cite the document.

Results are best with text-based PDFs; scanned PDFs need text recognition first, so run OCR on them before adding them. Large manuals answer better when split into sensible sections with clear headings. Keep one current version of each document, because outdated copies lead to conflicting answers. In my OCR & Speech Workspace, page-batched OCR and page citations made answers on scanned documents checkable, which is the same principle: clean text in, citations out.

## Can a Copilot agent read a SharePoint list?

Yes. Copilot Studio agents can use SharePoint lists as knowledge for questions, and can read and update list items through the SharePoint connector as actions. Results respect the user's permissions on the list.

Use the list as knowledge when users ask questions such as "which laptops are available in the IT pool?". Use connector actions when the agent must do something precise, such as filter items, create a new request or update a status, because actions return exact records rather than a summarised search. Clear column names and consistent values help the model a lot. For large lists, filter in the action rather than asking the model to scan everything.

## Can a Copilot agent call an API?

Yes. In Copilot Studio, agents call APIs through prebuilt connectors, custom connectors, Power Automate flows, or REST API actions defined with an OpenAPI description. In Microsoft 365 Copilot, developers add API plugins to declarative agents.

Steps for a custom API: describe the endpoints in an OpenAPI file with clear operation names and descriptions, set up authentication such as OAuth or an API key stored securely, add it as an action, and write instructions on when to use it. Test with realistic requests and check the inputs the model sends, since vague parameter descriptions lead to wrong calls. Validate responses and handle errors, so the agent says "I could not reach the system" instead of inventing an answer.

## Can a Copilot agent send an email?

Yes, through an action such as the Office 365 Outlook connector or a Power Automate flow in Copilot Studio. Agents can also draft emails for the user to review and send, which is safer for most cases.

For anything external or important, have the agent draft and ask for confirmation before sending, and log what was sent. Decide whose mailbox sends the email: the signed-in user's or a shared service account, which changes permissions and how replies are handled. Limit who can trigger email actions and what recipients are allowed, to avoid misuse or accidental mass emails. Test with your own address before connecting real users.

## Can a Copilot agent be scheduled?

Yes. Copilot Studio supports autonomous agents with triggers, including recurring schedules and events such as a new file, email or record, so an agent can run without a user starting a chat.

Examples: every Monday at 9 a.m., summarise last week's support tickets and post the summary to a Teams channel; when a new invoice lands in a folder, extract the fields and create an approval request. Scheduled agents run under a configured identity, so check what data and actions that identity can reach. Add monitoring: review run history, set alerts for failures, and keep a human approval step before irreversible actions. Power Automate scheduled flows are an alternative when the logic is fixed and needs no AI judgement.

## Can a Copilot agent call another agent?

Yes. Copilot Studio supports multi-agent setups, where a main agent hands specific tasks to other agents, such as an IT agent passing a request to a separate HR or procurement agent, each with its own knowledge and actions.

Multi-agent designs work well when domains are clearly separate and owned by different teams. They add complexity: more places for errors, harder debugging and more permissions to manage. Start with one agent and split only when instructions become too long or knowledge sources conflict. Give each agent a clear description of what it handles, because the orchestrator chooses agents by those descriptions, just as it chooses actions. Test hand-offs with tricky requests that sit between two domains.

## Can a Copilot agent be shared?

Yes. You can share agents with specific people, security groups or the whole organisation, depending on your role and your organisation's policies. Copilot Studio agents can also be published to channels such as Teams, websites and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Before sharing, check that everyone who will use the agent may see its knowledge sources; agents respect user permissions for SharePoint content, but uploaded files and some connectors may expose data more widely. Admins can control who may create and share agents and review agents across the organisation. Give the agent an owner who reviews conversations and updates its knowledge, because an unmaintained agent quietly goes out of date.

# How to do side projects: meaning, design, ideas, finishing, marketing and grades
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-do-side-projects/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A side project is something you build outside your main studies or job, for learning, fun, a portfolio or a possible business. For developers and students, side projects are often the clearest proof of skill. My own products, from KrishGyan and Annapurna to the five NextUpgrad AI apps, were built alongside my BCA studies, so this page covers what side projects mean, how to start and design one, ideas, grades versus projects, community views, why projects stall, when to commit, and marketing them.

## What does side project mean?

A side project is work you do in addition to your primary job or studies, usually self-directed: an app, tool, website, open-source library, blog or experiment. It is driven by interest or learning rather than obligation.

In music, a side project is a band or album that members create apart from their main group, which explains some unrelated search results. In tech, side projects range from weekend experiments to products that become companies; several well-known products started as side projects inside or outside companies. For students, side projects show initiative and practical skill beyond coursework, and they give you real stories for interviews about decisions, bugs and trade-offs you handled yourself.

## How do you do a side project?

Pick a small problem you care about, define the smallest version that is useful, build it in short regular sessions, ship it publicly, and improve it based on feedback. Finishing a small project beats abandoning an ambitious one.

Practical habits: schedule fixed time, such as two evenings a week; keep a short task list; use familiar tools so you spend time building, not configuring; deploy early with free tiers; and write a README as you go. Share progress in public to stay accountable. Set a deadline for version one, about two to four weeks, and cut features ruthlessly to hit it. Afterwards, decide whether to continue, polish or move on.

## How do you design a side project?

Start with the user and one core job: who is it for, what problem does it solve, and what single flow proves value. Sketch that flow on paper, list the minimum features, and choose a simple architecture you can build and run cheaply.

A design checklist: a one-sentence purpose; user stories for the core flow; rough wireframes; a data model; API and storage choices; a deployment plan; and what you will deliberately leave out. Prefer boring, proven technology, such as FastAPI, Next.js and PostgreSQL, unless learning a new tool is the goal. Design for change: keep components simple and decoupled, add tests around critical logic, and log errors so you can debug once real users arrive.

## What are good side project ideas?

Good ideas solve a problem you or people near you actually have: a study planner for your course, a RAG assistant over college notes, an expense splitter for hostel friends, a local language voice bot, or a tool that automates a boring task.

Developer-focused ideas include a CLI tool, a browser extension, a GitHub Action, an API wrapper or an open-source library improvement. AI ideas include a document question answering app with citations, a fine-tuned small model for a narrow task, or an agent that triages your email. Pick ideas where you can get real users, even ten, since feedback teaches more than features. Avoid cloning popular apps unless you add a clear twist.

## What are the best side projects for senior software developers?

Senior developers benefit most from projects that stretch them in new directions: learning a new domain such as AI, contributing to important open-source projects, building tools that solve team problems, writing or teaching, and small products with real users.

Options include building infrastructure tools others adopt, maintaining an open-source library, publishing deep technical writing, mentoring through community projects, or launching a niche software product to learn sales and marketing. Exploring AI engineering through a real application, such as a RAG system with evaluation, keeps skills current. Seniors should choose projects that compound reputation and learning, and keep scope realistic given limited time, family and work commitments.

## Low marks or side projects: which matters more?

Community discussions usually say strong side projects can outweigh average marks for many software jobs, especially at startups, but very low marks can block campus placements and some employers that filter by grades. Aim for both where possible.

Practical balance: keep marks above common cutoffs used by recruiters in your context, often around 60 to 70 percent in Indian campus drives, while investing most extra time in projects that demonstrate skill. Explain trade-offs honestly in interviews, showing what you built and learned. Postgraduate admissions and some government roles weigh marks more heavily, so consider your goals. Projects open doors marks cannot, but marks can close doors before anyone sees your projects.

## Why do side projects remain unfinished?

Common reasons are scope creep, perfectionism, choosing new technology that slows progress, losing motivation after the exciting start, and burnout from adding projects on top of full workloads. Most unfinished projects never had a clear, small definition of done.

Fixes: define version one as a single core flow and ship it within weeks; keep a done list to see progress; use tools you know; work in short, regular sessions instead of occasional marathons; and share progress publicly for accountability. If motivation fades, ask whether the project still serves your goals, and archive it guilt-free if not; abandoning deliberately is better than dragging it on. Rest matters too, since tired people do not ship.

## When is a side project worth committing to?

Commit when there are signals beyond your own excitement: real users returning, people asking for features, measurable learning you value, or a clear path to income or career benefit, and when you can sustain the time without hurting your main responsibilities.

Test before committing: ship a minimal version, share it with a small audience, and watch behaviour rather than compliments. Weekly active users, retention and unsolicited feedback are strong signals. Consider opportunity cost: what else could the same hours achieve? If signals are strong, set goals for the next three months and review them. If the project is mainly for learning, commitment can be lighter: finish, document and move on when the lessons are captured.

## What is on a side project marketing checklist?

A simple checklist: a clear one-line description, a landing page with screenshots or a demo video, a README for developer tools, a launch post in relevant communities, and a way to collect emails or feedback.

More items: post on platforms where your users gather, such as Reddit communities, Product Hunt, Hacker News or LinkedIn; write a short article explaining why you built it and what you learned; share progress updates; add basic analytics; set up SEO basics such as titles, descriptions and a sitemap; and respond quickly to early users. Marketing is ongoing, not one launch day, so plan a few posts over the following weeks.

## What does the community say about side projects?

Community discussions highlight side projects that solved the creator's own problem, taught a valuable skill, or found a small loyal audience. Popular advice is to build things you would use yourself and to finish small projects before starting new ones.

Frequently praised examples include personal finance trackers, browser extensions, automation scripts, niche directories, open-source developer tools and small AI utilities. Many developers say their side projects led to jobs, freelance clients or startups, while others valued the learning most. Common warnings include spending months on features nobody asked for and neglecting health. The shared lesson: start small, ship publicly, listen to users, and treat every project as a learning investment.
