# How do I job search? A practical guide with LinkedIn, Google and AI tools
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-job-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To job search well, decide on two or three target roles, set saved searches with alerts on LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri and Google's job results, tailor your resume for each application, ask for referrals, and track every application in one sheet. Treat it as a weekly system, not a daily scroll. This page shows how to search on each platform, what a job search engine is, how to use AI tools without hurting your chances, which strategies work for students and freshers, and how to handle job search fatigue.

## How do I job search?

Pick a specific target, such as "junior Python backend developer" or "GenAI intern", then run a weekly routine: find roles, tailor and send a set number of applications, follow up, and practise interviews.

A routine that works for students and early-career engineers:

- **Target list**: 20 to 30 companies you would genuinely join, plus two or three role titles.
- **Alerts**: saved searches on LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri, Internshala and Google so new roles reach you within a day.
- **Applications**: five to ten tailored ones a week beat fifty generic ones.
- **Referrals**: message engineers at target companies with a short note and your best project.
- **Tracker**: company, role, date, contact, status and next step in one spreadsheet.

Review the tracker every Sunday and adjust what is not getting replies.

## How do I job search on LinkedIn?

Open the Jobs tab, search a precise title, then filter by date posted, experience level, location and remote options. Save the search with alerts on, and apply to fresh roles within a day or two.

Make your profile searchable first: a headline with your target role and core skills, a featured section with your best project, and skills that match the job descriptions you want. Use Boolean search in the keyword box, for example `"machine learning" AND (intern OR fresher) NOT senior`. Easy Apply is quick but crowded, so for roles you care about, also find someone on the team and send a short message. Recruiters notice candidates who post about what they build, so share project updates regularly.

## How do I job search on Google?

Search a role plus "jobs", for example "data analyst jobs India" or "remote Python developer jobs". Google shows a jobs panel that gathers listings from many sites, with filters for date, type and location.

Open the panel to filter by date posted, job type and employer, and turn on alerts for the search so new listings arrive by email. Each listing links to where you can apply, often the company's own careers page, which is usually the best place to apply. Google can show these listings because employers mark up job posts with structured data. Search operators help too: `site:greenhouse.io "machine learning intern"` or `site:lever.co "backend engineer"` surfaces roles posted on the applicant tracking systems many startups use.

## How do I job search on Indeed?

Enter a job title or skill and a location, or "remote", then filter by date posted, job type, experience and salary details where shown. Upload a resume, create a profile and set job alerts for your main searches.

Indeed aggregates listings from company sites as well as roles posted directly on it, so it is wide but noisy. Sort by date and focus on listings from the last few days. Read the full description before applying and match your resume's wording to the skills it asks for, because many employers screen applications with keyword filters. Be careful with listings that ask for payment, personal documents early, or chats on messaging apps before any interview; genuine employers do not charge candidates.

## What is a job search engine?

A job search engine collects job listings from many sources, such as company career pages, job boards and recruiters, and lets you search them all in one place. Indeed and Google's job results are examples.

A job board, by contrast, mainly hosts listings that employers post directly on it. In practice the line blurs: LinkedIn, Naukri and Indeed both host and aggregate. For freshers in India, combine one or two general engines with specialist sources: Internshala for internships, Wellfound for startups, the careers pages of companies you admire, and community job channels in developer groups. The engine finds roles; your application still has to stand out.

## Which AI job search tool is best?

There is no single best one. The most useful AI help is a general assistant such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini used to tailor your resume, prepare for interviews and research companies, plus the AI features already built into LinkedIn and job platforms.

Use AI for:

- Comparing your resume with a job description and listing the gaps.
- Rewriting bullet points to show impact, then checking every claim is true.
- Drafting short referral and follow-up messages in your own voice.
- Mock interviews: ask for technical and behavioural questions for the exact role.

Be wary of auto-apply tools that send hundreds of applications for you. They often produce poor matches, can break platform rules and can leave a bad impression with recruiters who see the same generic message twice.

## Does AI job search work?

AI makes the preparation faster and better; it does not get you hired on its own. Tailored applications, strong projects and referrals still decide outcomes, and AI helps you produce those faster.

Where it clearly helps is speed: tailoring a resume to a job description takes minutes instead of an hour, and mock interviews are available at any time. Where it hurts is when output is generic. Recruiters read many AI-written cover letters that sound the same, and a resume stuffed with keywords but no evidence fails the first human read. The test is simple: could you defend every line in an interview? If not, rewrite it. Your projects, your GitHub and the way you talk about what you built carry more weight than any tool.

## How do I use AI for job search?

Give the assistant the job description and your resume, ask for the three biggest gaps and a tailored version, then edit it yourself. Use it the same way for messages, company research and interview practice.

A prompt that works: "Here is a job description and my resume. List the skills the role needs that my resume does not show. Then rewrite my project bullets to match the role, using only facts from my resume." Paste the result into your own document and fix the voice. For interviews: "Ask me five interview questions for this role, one at a time, and grade my answers." Never paste personal documents such as ID numbers into an assistant, and never let it invent experience or numbers.

## What job search strategies actually work?

The strategies that work are targeting, referrals, proof of skill and consistency: a focused list of roles, warm introductions, public projects that match those roles, and a steady weekly pace.

For students and freshers in tech, ranked roughly by return on effort:

- **Referrals**: a short message to an engineer at the company, with a link to a relevant project.
- **Projects**: one or two deployed projects that match the role, with a clear README.
- **Hackathons and communities**: they create contacts and stories for interviews.
- **Tailored applications** through company career pages.
- **Cold applications** on large portals, kept as a background routine.

When I speak to first-years, the roadmap I give is foundations first, then hackathons and internships, then placements or a startup. The job search is easier when the earlier steps are done.

## What is job search fatigue?

Job search fatigue is the exhaustion and loss of motivation that builds up after weeks of applications, rejections and silence. It is common, and it usually shows as procrastination, low-effort applications or giving up on good roles.

Ways to manage it:

- Set process goals you control, such as five tailored applications a week, instead of outcome goals.
- Time-box the search to fixed hours and keep other parts of life, such as learning, exercise and friends, running.
- Keep building one project during the search so you make visible progress.
- Track replies to see what works, and change your approach rather than only increasing volume.
- Talk to peers or a mentor; feedback on your resume often fixes the real problem fast.

If low mood persists for weeks, talk to someone you trust or a professional.

# How to learn in public: start, community advice, blog platforms, personal brand, speaking
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-learn-in-public/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Learning in public means sharing what you learn as you learn it, through posts, notes, projects, talks and open code, so others benefit and you get feedback, accountability and visibility. It is one of the fastest ways for students to build skills and a reputation together. I share technical work through my site and campus sessions, having led 20+ of them, so this page covers what it means, how to start, community advice, build-in-public updates, blog platforms, personal branding and public speaking.

## What is learning in public?

Learning in public is the habit of sharing your learning process openly: writing notes, publishing projects, explaining concepts, asking questions and documenting mistakes, rather than learning privately and only showing finished results.

The idea, popularised among developers by the writer Shawn Wang, known as swyx, is that teaching what you just learned deepens understanding, attracts feedback from experts, and builds a public record of growth that employers and collaborators can see. It does not require being an expert; beginners often help other beginners best because they remember what was confusing. The core mindset is generosity and honesty: share useful things, admit gaps, and improve publicly.

## How do you learn in public?

Pick a topic you are learning, and share small outputs regularly: a short post explaining a concept, a GitHub repository with notes, a demo video of a project, or a thread summarising what you built this week.

Make it useful to others: write the explanation you wished you had found, include code and screenshots, and link resources. Share where your audience is, such as LinkedIn, X, a blog or developer communities. Ask questions openly and credit people who help. Consistency beats perfection: a short weekly post for six months builds more than one perfect article. This site, with its answer pages on RAG, fine-tuning and careers, is part of my own learning in public.

## How do you start learning in public?

Start this week with one small post: what you learned, a problem you solved, or a resource you found useful. Keep it short, specific and honest. Your first posts do not need an audience; they build the habit.

A simple starter plan: set up a GitHub profile with a README and one project; choose one platform for writing; commit to one post per week for eight weeks; and keep a running notes file of things worth sharing. Use templates such as today I learned, how I fixed this error, or what I built this week. Expect little response at first. Engagement grows as you help people consistently over months.

## What does the community say about learning in public?

Community discussions are mostly positive: people report faster learning, job leads and new friends from sharing their journeys. Common cautions are avoiding performative posting, burnout from chasing engagement, and sharing confidential work details.

Practical advice from these discussions: focus on helpfulness rather than self-promotion; share real code and specific lessons instead of vague motivation; engage with others' posts, not only your own; and keep a sustainable pace. Introverts suggest written formats like blogs and GitHub notes instead of videos. Many recommend starting in communities where you already participate, such as Discord servers or subreddits, before broadcasting widely. Quality and consistency matter more than follower counts.

## What are good build-in-public blogs and update formats?

Good build-in-public updates share real numbers and decisions: what shipped, what users said, what failed and what comes next. Formats include weekly or monthly changelogs, devlogs, open metrics dashboards from indie founders, and project retrospectives.

Effective updates are regular, concise and honest, including mistakes and reasoning, which makes them valuable to readers building similar things. Many indie developers publish monthly updates on personal blogs or newsletters, and open-source maintainers write release notes and roadmaps. Start with a simple template: goals for the period, what was done, metrics, lessons and next steps. Avoid sharing sensitive customer data or security details, and keep updates focused on what others can learn.

## What is the best platform for a technical blog?

Popular choices are a personal site with a static site generator, such as Hugo, Astro, Jekyll or Next.js, hosted on GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel; or hosted platforms such as Hashnode, Dev.to, Medium and Substack.

A personal domain gives you ownership, control over design and long-term search value, which community discussions usually recommend. Hosted platforms offer built-in audiences and easier setup. Many writers do both: publish on their own site and cross-post to Dev.to or Medium with canonical links pointing home. Choose Markdown-based tools if you write code-heavy posts, and make sure code blocks, images and RSS feeds work well. The platform matters less than writing consistently.

## How do you build your personal brand?

Decide what you want to be known for, such as building RAG systems or mentoring students, then consistently share work, insights and help in that area across a website, GitHub, LinkedIn and talks. Reputation follows useful, visible work.

Practical steps: create a simple website with your bio, projects and contact details; keep profiles consistent in name, photo and description; publish case studies of real work; speak at college events or meetups; and help others in communities. Be authentic and accurate: never inflate achievements, since trust is the whole point of a brand. My own brand rests on verifiable work: five NextUpgrad AI apps, hackathon wins and 20+ campus sessions.

## How can beginners learn public speaking skills?

Start small and practise often: speak in class, present a project to friends, record yourself explaining a topic for two minutes, and join a club such as Toastmasters or a college speaking society. Confidence comes from repetition.

Prepare well: know your opening and closing lines, structure the talk around three points, and rehearse aloud with a timer. Focus on the audience's needs rather than your nerves. Watch recordings to fix filler words, pace and body language. Ask for specific feedback after each attempt. Technical speakers benefit from demos, which shift attention from the speaker to the work. Most confident speakers started out nervous; repetition is what changed them.

## How do you learn English public speaking?

Build English fluency and speaking confidence together: speak English daily in low-stakes settings, read aloud, shadow talks by repeating after speakers, and practise short structured talks on familiar topics before tackling formal presentations.

Prepare scripts at first, then move to bullet points to sound natural. Learn key phrases for openings, transitions and conclusions. Record yourself and compare with fluent speakers for pronunciation and pacing, focusing on clarity rather than accent. Join English-speaking clubs, online conversation groups or Toastmasters. Remember that audiences value clear ideas over perfect grammar; many successful speakers present confidently in their second language by keeping sentences simple.

## How do you build a career in public speaking?

Build expertise first, then a speaking reputation: develop a topic you know deeply, speak at free events such as colleges, meetups and webinars, record talks, gather testimonials, and gradually approach conferences and organisations that pay speakers.

Create a speaker page with your topics, bio, photos, past talks and contact details, and make booking easy. Network with event organisers and say yes to diverse audiences early. Combine speaking with related work, such as workshops, training, consulting or courses. Speaking careers usually grow alongside a professional career rather than replacing it at first. For students, campus sessions are a great start: they build skill, references and a body of talks.

# How to learn Python for AI in 2026: the roadmap from zero to shipping an LLM app, what to skip, and the projects that prove it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-learn-python-for-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I learn Python for AI?

**Learn the Python that ships software, then point it at models. In practice: variables, functions and data structures; reading and writing files and JSON; calling HTTP APIs; virtual environments and packages; classes when you need them; async when you have many calls; tests. Then, with that base, call a model API, build a small FastAPI service around it, and deploy it. Twelve weeks of building gets a beginner to a live LLM application. Twelve weeks of tutorials gets a beginner to week thirteen of tutorials.**


All five production AI systems I shipped in 2026 are Python services: a RAG platform, a fine-tuning platform, a document extraction service, a face recognition backend and an OCR and speech workspace [14]. The Python inside them is not exotic. It is the Python in this roadmap, used carefully, with tests.

> Nobody has ever asked me to reverse a linked list in Python at work. Everybody has asked me why the API call timed out. Learn for the second question.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How much Python do I need for AI?

**Less than the tutorials suggest, and different. You need: core syntax and data structures; functions with type hints; modules and packages; file and JSON handling; error handling; HTTP requests; virtual environments; the standard library's pathlib, json, datetime, logging and asyncio; classes and dataclasses; and writing tests. You do not need, at first: metaclasses, decorators beyond using them, deep NumPy, or competitive-programming tricks. Those come when a project demands them.**



## What is the roadmap from zero to an AI app?

**Twelve weeks, four projects, each deployed. Weeks one to three: fundamentals through a command-line tool that reads a file and produces a report. Weeks four to six: HTTP and APIs through a script that calls a model API and saves structured output. Weeks seven to nine: a FastAPI service with a database, deployed on a free tier. Weeks ten to twelve: a RAG application over documents you know, with an evaluation set. Every week, one commit a day, and a README that explains what you built.**



The longer version, with resources per week, is on the portfolio [13].

## Which Python libraries matter for AI in 2026?

**For calling models: the provider SDKs, or plain httpx and requests [5][6]. For services: FastAPI with Pydantic for validation [4][7]. For data handling: json and pathlib from the standard library, pandas when tables appear. For retrieval: an embeddings client and pgvector or FAISS. For training and fine-tuning: PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT and TRL, learned when you fine-tune, not before. For tests: pytest [8]. For environments: uv or venv with pip [9]. Learn each when a project needs it.**



Frameworks such as LangChain are fine for a first prototype; I recommend calling the SDKs directly for your first real project so you understand every line you ship.

## Should I learn NumPy, pandas and maths first?

**No, not first. For an applications career in GenAI, you can build and deploy your first LLM app without NumPy. Learn pandas when you have a table to analyse, NumPy when you touch vectors directly, and the maths, linear algebra and probability, alongside your first embedding and fine-tuning projects, where it has a purpose. Learning them first is how students spend six months on prerequisites and never ship. For a research or classical ML path, reverse the order.**



## What are the best free resources to learn Python for AI?

**The official Python tutorial for the language itself [1]. Automate the Boring Stuff for practical scripting [2]. Python for Everybody for a gentle structured course [3]. FastAPI's documentation, which is a course in itself [4]. Hugging Face's free LLM course once you are calling models [10]. fast.ai for deep learning intuition when you get there [11]. Google Colab for a free notebook and GPU [12]. All free. Pick one per stage, finish it by building, and do not collect courses.**



## What should my first Python AI project be?

**A script that reads a folder of your own notes or PDFs, calls a model API to summarise each one into structured JSON, validates the JSON with Pydantic, and writes a report. It touches files, HTTP, error handling, structured data and tests, and it is useful to you. Then wrap it in FastAPI and deploy it. Then add retrieval so you can ask questions across the notes. Three steps, three months, one growing project, live at a URL.**


```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Summary(BaseModel):
    title: str
    key_points: list[str]
    open_questions: list[str]

def summarise(path: Path) -> Summary:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    raw = call_model(f"Summarise into JSON with title, key_points, open_questions:\n\n{text}")
    return Summary.model_validate_json(raw)          # fails loudly if the model drifts

report = [summarise(p).model_dump() for p in Path("notes").glob("*.md")]
Path("report.json").write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
```

That is a week-four project, and a version of it is the seed of every document system I have shipped.

## What mistakes keep students stuck in Python tutorials?

**Watching instead of typing. Starting a fourth course before deploying a first project. Learning NumPy for months before calling a single API. Skipping virtual environments and losing a week to dependency conflicts. Never writing a test, so every change is scary. Copying assistant output without reading it. Treating tracebacks as failures instead of instructions. The fix for all of them is the same: ship something small every week and read the errors.**


## Python for AI interview questions

**Expect practical Python: parse and validate JSON, write a retry with backoff around an API call, chunk text by paragraphs with a size cap, compute cosine similarity, use a dict to count or group, write a small async fan-out over many API calls, and write a test for one of those. Rarely puzzles. Interviewers want typed, readable code and a candidate who talks through edge cases; the coding round for GenAI roles is a work sample, not an exam.**





## Where should I start today?

**Install Python, create a virtual environment, and write a script that reads one file and prints a summary of it. Tomorrow make the summary come from a model API. By the weekend, put it in a repository with a README.** For a workshop at your college that takes a room from zero Python to a deployed AI app, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to mentor junior developers, find a tech mentor, and why mentoring matters with AI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-mentor-junior-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To mentor junior developers, set clear goals together, give them real work with support, review their code with explanations rather than rewrites, and meet regularly to discuss growth, not only tasks. I lead a 14-member engineering team at SCULT INDIA and have mentored more than 200 students since 2023, so this page covers mentoring juniors, why mentoring matters more with AI, tech and career mentors, finding one, qualifications, reverse mentoring, starting a corporate scheme and Frontend Mentor.

## How do you mentor junior developers?

Pair real responsibility with support: give juniors meaningful tasks slightly above their level, explain context and expectations, review their code with reasons, and hold regular one-to-ones about growth. Let them struggle productively before stepping in, but never leave them stuck for days.

Practical habits: write onboarding docs and a first-week plan; pair-program on unfamiliar areas; ask questions instead of giving answers, such as "what would happen if this request fails?"; praise specific good decisions publicly and correct privately; and share how you debug, not just the fix. Track progress with small goals, like owning a feature end to end. Make it safe to ask questions, because juniors who hide confusion learn slowly and ship bugs.

## Why does mentoring matter more in the AI era?

AI tools let juniors produce code quickly without understanding it. Mentors supply what AI cannot: judgement about trade-offs, knowledge of the system's history, review of whether generated code is correct and secure, and career guidance.

Many routine tasks juniors once learned on are now automated, so deliberate mentoring replaces learning by repetition. Mentors should teach juniors to read and question AI output, write tests, debug without assistance when needed, and explain their code in reviews. A useful rule for teams: every AI-assisted change needs an engineer who can explain why it works. The goal is engineers who use AI to go faster while understanding the system deeply enough to own it.

## Why do we need a mentor?

A mentor shortens the learning curve: they help you avoid common mistakes, give honest feedback you would not get alone, open doors to opportunities, and help you make better decisions about skills, projects and careers.

Self-learning gives knowledge, but mentors give perspective: which skills matter now, how teams really work, and how to handle setbacks. They also hold you accountable, which turns plans into action. You do not need one mentor for everything; different people can help with code, careers, public speaking or entrepreneurship. Mentors are most useful when you bring specific questions and act on advice, then report back on what happened.

## What is a tech mentor?

A tech mentor is an experienced engineer, designer, data scientist or technical leader who guides someone's growth in technology: reviewing code and projects, suggesting learning paths, explaining industry practices and advising on technical career decisions.

Tech mentors can be senior colleagues, open-source maintainers, community leaders or volunteers on mentoring platforms. Sessions might include code reviews, system design discussions, mock interviews, project feedback or help choosing between job offers. Good tech mentors teach thinking, not just answers: how to break down problems, read documentation, debug methodically and communicate decisions. For students, a tech mentor can turn scattered learning into a focused plan of projects and skills.

## Why do you need both a technical and a career mentor?

Technical mentors make you better at the work: code quality, architecture and tools. Career mentors make you better at navigating work: choosing roles, negotiating, building visibility, handling conflict and planning long-term growth. One person rarely excels at both.

Technical skill alone can leave you underappreciated if you cannot communicate impact or choose the right opportunities; career savvy without depth does not last. A senior engineer on your team may be ideal for code reviews, while someone outside your company can give unbiased career advice. Many professionals build a small personal board of advisers: a technical mentor, a career mentor, peers at the same level, and someone more junior who keeps them current.

## How do you find a mentor in tech?

Look where experienced people already help others: open-source projects, developer communities, meetups, hackathons, college alumni networks, and mentoring platforms such as ADPList. Start by contributing or asking a specific question, not by asking someone to be your mentor.

Make it easy to help you: share your goal, what you have tried and a precise question. Follow up with results, which shows you act on advice and makes people want to continue. At work, ask your manager to connect you with a senior engineer, or join internal mentoring programmes. In student communities such as TechVerse Enclave, which I founded, newcomers meet mentors by joining projects and events where experienced members are already active.

## What qualifications do you need to be a mentor?

Usually no formal qualification is required. You need relevant experience a step or more ahead of your mentee, genuine interest in their growth, listening skills, honesty and reliability. Formal programmes may require training or background checks, especially when working with minors.

Being a few years ahead is enough to help someone starting out; many great mentors are peers just one stage further along. Useful skills include asking good questions, giving constructive feedback, sharing failures openly and respecting the mentee's choices. Mentoring certifications exist and can help in coaching careers, but they matter less than experience. Start by mentoring one person in an area you know well, then reflect on what worked before taking on more.

## What could you learn from a mentor half your age?

Plenty. Reverse mentoring pairs a younger person with a more senior one, usually to share knowledge of new technology, AI tools, social media, current culture and how younger customers and colleagues think.

Senior professionals use reverse mentoring to stay current with tools such as AI assistants, modern development practices and digital platforms, while the younger mentor gains exposure to leadership thinking and organisational context. It works when both treat it as a real exchange, set goals, and stay curious rather than defensive. Many companies run formal reverse mentoring programmes. Age matters less than expertise: anyone who knows something you do not can teach you.

## How do you begin a corporate mentorship scheme?

Define the goal, such as faster onboarding, retention or leadership development; secure leadership support; recruit and train mentors; match pairs thoughtfully; set expectations for meeting frequency and duration; and measure outcomes. Start with a small pilot before scaling.

Practical steps: survey employees about needs; create a simple application form capturing goals and skills; match based on goals, not just seniority; give mentors a short guide and a first-meeting agenda; run cohorts of three to six months; and collect feedback midway and at the end. Recognise mentors' time in performance reviews, since unrewarded mentoring fades. Software platforms can help with matching and tracking, but the relationships themselves need human attention.

## What is Frontend Mentor and how does it work?

Frontend Mentor is a platform offering real-world front-end coding challenges with professional designs. You download the design files and assets, build the project in HTML, CSS and JavaScript or a framework, then submit your solution for community feedback.

It suits beginners and intermediate developers who want portfolio projects that look professional. A good workflow: start with newbie challenges, focus on semantic HTML and responsive CSS, deploy with GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel, then compare your solution with others and request feedback. Later challenges add JavaScript, APIs and frameworks. Combine it with a human mentor who reviews your code, since community comments vary in depth. Treat each challenge as a chance to practise accessibility too.

# How to negotiate a salary offer, even as a fresher: timing, percentage, scripts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-negotiate-salary-offer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To negotiate a salary offer, wait until you have it in writing, research what the role pays, then thank the employer and ask for a specific, justified figure, framed around the value you bring and your enthusiasm for the job. Most employers expect some negotiation. I mentor students through placements and lead an engineering team at SCULT INDIA, so this page covers negotiating offers, freshers' options, whether negotiating is bad or common, what percentage to ask, going above the range, timing, and asking for a raise after a year.

## How do I negotiate a salary offer?

Get the offer in writing, research market pay for the role, decide your target and walk-away numbers, then respond warmly with one specific request and a short reason. Negotiate the whole package, not just base pay.

A simple script: "Thank you, I'm excited about this role. Based on market data for similar roles and my experience with X, I was hoping for a base closer to [figure]. Is there flexibility?" Then stop talking and listen. Consider joining bonus, variable pay, notice buyout, remote days, learning budget, title and start date. Knowing your alternative, such as another offer, gives you confidence. Get any agreed changes in a revised written offer.

## Can freshers negotiate salary?

Yes, freshers can negotiate, but room varies. Campus placements with fixed packages for a batch usually leave little flexibility, while off-campus offers from startups and mid-size companies often have more.

Even when base pay is fixed, freshers can sometimes negotiate start date, location, joining bonus, relocation support, team or role, and training. Your leverage as a fresher comes from proof: internships, shipped projects, hackathon wins and competing offers. Students I mentor who had a live project and a clear demo had noticeably better conversations than those relying only on grades. If the answer is no, accept gracefully; how you negotiate is remembered more than whether you did.

## How should a fresher negotiate salary?

Negotiate politely, with evidence, and only once you have an offer. Research the typical range for the role and city type, highlight specific skills or projects that justify more, and ask a question rather than making a demand.

Steps for freshers:

- Find ranges on Glassdoor, AmbitionBox and from seniors at the company.
- List your proof: internships, projects with users, certifications, competing offers.
- Ask: "Is there any flexibility on the base or a joining bonus?"
- If base pay is fixed, ask about the review cycle and when a raise is possible.
- Respond within the deadline and confirm everything in writing.

Never invent a competing offer; recruiters talk, and it can cost you the job.

## How do freshers negotiate salary in an interview?

Avoid naming a number early in interviews if you can; ask about the budgeted range instead. If pressed, give a researched range whose bottom you would accept, and say you are flexible for the right role.

A good response to "What are your salary expectations?": "I'm focused on finding the right role and learning. Could you share the budgeted range for this position?" If they insist: "Based on my research for similar roles, a range of [figures] seems fair, but I'm open depending on the full package." Save real negotiation for after the offer, when the company has decided it wants you and you have the most leverage.

## Is it bad to negotiate salary?

No. Polite, reasoned negotiation is professional and expected in most companies. It rarely leads to an offer being withdrawn; what damages relationships is aggressive ultimatums, dishonesty, or repeatedly reopening agreed terms.

Some situations call for care: government jobs and campus batches with fixed pay, very small organisations with tight budgets, or offers already at the top of a published band. In those cases, negotiate non-salary terms instead. Also negotiate once, comprehensively, rather than item by item. Employers often respect candidates who advocate for themselves calmly, because the same skill matters when working with clients and stakeholders.

## Is it common to negotiate salary?

Yes, especially for experienced hires and in the private sector, where recruiters often build in some room expecting negotiation. Many candidates still accept the first offer, often from anxiety rather than because the offer was final.

Norms vary by company type: large firms have structured bands and approval processes, startups may trade salary for equity or flexibility, and campus programmes are mostly standardised. Women and first-generation professionals are often less likely to negotiate, which compounds pay gaps over time, since future raises build on the starting figure. Asking once, respectfully, is normal.

## What percentage should I negotiate on a salary offer?

A common range is asking for roughly 10 to 20 percent above the initial offer, if market data and your experience support it. Smaller asks suit offers already near market rate; larger ones need strong justification, such as a competing offer.

Base your number on research, not a fixed rule: if the offer is well below market, asking for more than 20 percent can be reasonable; if it is already generous, a smaller increase or better benefits may be smarter. Ask for a specific figure rather than a range, because people usually settle near the bottom of any range you give. Expect the company to meet you partway.

## Can I negotiate above the salary range?

Sometimes. Ranges are often set by budgets and bands, but exceptional candidates, scarce skills, competing offers or a more senior title can justify going above. Companies can also move you to a higher band or add a joining bonus.

If an offer is at the top of the range, ask whether the role could be levelled up given your experience, or whether a one-time bonus, extra leave or an early salary review is possible. Be realistic: some organisations, especially with published pay scales, cannot exceed their bands. If the gap between the range and your needs is large, it may not be the right role.

## When should I negotiate salary for a new job?

Negotiate after you receive a written offer and before you accept it. That is when your leverage is highest: the company has chosen you, and you have not committed. Respond within the stated deadline.

Before the offer, discuss expectations in general terms; after accepting, reopening pay damages trust. If you need time, ask: "Could I have until Friday to review the full offer?" If you are waiting for another company's result, tell them you have an offer with a deadline; they may speed up. Have the conversation on a call where possible, then confirm in writing.

## How do I negotiate a salary raise after a year?

Document your impact over the year with specific results, research current market pay for your role, and ask your manager for a dedicated conversation, ideally before the annual budget or review cycle is finalised.

Prepare a one-page summary: projects delivered, problems solved, responsibilities added, and measurable outcomes such as time saved or revenue influenced. Then say: "I'd like to discuss my compensation given my contributions this year." If the answer is "not now", ask what specific results would justify a raise and when you can revisit it, and write that down. Sometimes a title change or new responsibilities come first, with pay following at the next cycle.

# How to negotiate your first tech job offer in India: what freshers can actually negotiate, the script, and the mistakes that cost the most
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-negotiate-your-first-tech-job-offer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Can a fresher actually negotiate a tech job offer?

**Yes, more often than freshers assume, and the ask itself carries almost no risk when done politely and after the offer is already extended. Companies build a negotiation buffer into most offers precisely because they expect some candidates to ask; a fresher who never asks simply leaves that buffer on the table. The risk people fear, the offer being pulled for asking, is genuinely rare for a reasonable, polite ask after an offer letter exists; it happens far more often as a scare story than as a real outcome.**


Most students I mentor accept the first number out of fear the offer will vanish if they ask for anything; watching that fear turn out to be misplaced, again and again, is why this page exists.

> The worst realistic outcome of a polite, reasonable ask is "no, this is final." The worst outcome of never asking is guaranteed: you get exactly the first number, every time.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is actually negotiable in an entry-level offer?

**The base salary is the most visible lever, but rarely the only one. Joining bonus, sometimes easier to move than base since it is a one-time cost to the company. Start date, useful if you need time to finish exams, travel, or simply breathe between college and work. Remote or hybrid flexibility, where the role allows it. Sign-on equipment or relocation support. Even the level or designation, in some structures, if your background genuinely supports it. Ask about the whole package, not only the headline number, since some of these move more easily than base pay does.**



## How do I know what to ask for?

**Research real compensation data for the specific company, role and level before naming a number, using sources like Levels.fyi and Glassdoor rather than guessing [1][2]. Anchor your ask to that data, not to a vague sense that "more would be nice." A specific, researched ask, "I've seen this role bands around X for this level, is there room to move closer to that," is far more persuasive than an unspecific "can you do better."**



## What is the actual script for negotiating without a competing offer?

**Thank them for the offer, confirm genuine enthusiasm for the role, then ask specifically and briefly: "I'm excited about this role. Based on what I've seen for similar positions at this level, is there flexibility on the base salary?" No bluff, no ultimatum, no apology. If the answer is no on base, ask about the joining bonus or start date next, since a single "no" on one lever does not mean no on all of them.**



## Do I need a competing offer to negotiate?

**It helps, because it gives the company a concrete number to react to, but it is not required. A well-researched, specific, polite ask moves numbers on its own more often than people expect, especially for a first offer where companies have built in some room precisely because they expect this conversation. Never bluff about a competing offer you do not have; it is easily discoverable through informal networks, and being caught bluffing costs far more trust than simply not having leverage in the first place.**



## What mistakes cost the most in salary negotiation?

**Bluffing about an offer that does not exist, which is discoverable and destroys trust immediately if caught. Negotiating over email in a way that reads as an ultimatum instead of a conversation. Accepting a verbal promise of a later raise instead of getting the actual number in the offer letter. Negotiating only the base and never asking about the rest of the package. Being so afraid of losing the offer that the ask never happens at all, guaranteeing the outcome you were afraid of by default.**



## Salary negotiation interview and follow-up questions

**Recruiters sometimes ask directly what compensation you are expecting; answer with a researched range, not a vague deflection or an unresearched high number. If pressed for your current or previous salary where legally relevant, answer honestly but redirect to the value you bring for this specific role rather than anchoring entirely to a past number.**



## Where should I start?

**Before you accept your next offer, look up real compensation data for that company and role, and ask one specific, polite question about the number. That single habit, repeated at every offer for the rest of your career, compounds.** For a career session on negotiating your first tech offer, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to participate in your first hackathon: where to find hackathons in India, how to form a team, what to prepare, and what to expect in 24 to 48 hours
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-participate-in-your-first-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I participate in a hackathon for the first time?

**Find one on Devfolio, Unstop, MLH, Devpost or Hack2skill that welcomes beginners, register two to four weeks ahead, form a team of two to four through the event's team-finding channel or your college, set up your laptop and accounts the week before, and arrive with one small idea you could finish in half the time available. Then build the smallest working version, demo it honestly, and write down what you learned. The first hackathon teaches you how hackathons work; the second one is where you start winning.**


My first hackathon was a mess: a team that met at registration, an idea that needed three days, a demo that did not run. Three later wins came from doing the opposite of everything on that day [8]. This page is what I wish someone had handed me before the first one.

> Nobody wins their first hackathon by being brilliant. They win their fourth by having learned what the first three taught.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a hackathon, and what actually happens?

**A hackathon is a timed building competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, where small teams build a working prototype around a theme or a problem statement and demo it to judges. It opens with a briefing and problem statements, then the build, with mentors circulating and checkpoints or mid-way reviews, then submissions with a repository and a video, then three-minute pitches, then results. Online hackathons run the same way over Discord and a submission portal. Food, sleep and the demo working are the three things beginners underestimate.**



## Where do I find hackathons in India?

**Devfolio lists most large student hackathons in India, including college fests, and has team-finding built in [1]. Unstop lists corporate and college hackathons plus case competitions [2]. Major League Hacking runs a global season of student hackathons with many in India [3]. Devpost is where company-sponsored online hackathons live [4]. Hack2skill hosts corporate and government-partnered events [5]. Smart India Hackathon is the national one, run through your college [6]. Beyond the platforms, follow your college's coding club, nearby college fests, and community Discord and WhatsApp groups, where smaller, beginner-friendly events appear first.**



## How do I get shortlisted?

**Most hackathons with more applicants than seats shortlist on the application. Fill in every field. Link a GitHub with at least two repositories that have READMEs, even small ones. Write the "why do you want to attend" answer specifically: what you want to build or learn, not "to gain experience". If the hackathon asks for an idea, give a small concrete one. Apply early; late applications compete for fewer seats. Apply to several; acceptance is partly luck.**


## How do I find a hackathon team?

**Post in the event's team-finding channel, on Devfolio or Discord, with three lines: what you can do, what you want to learn, and when you are free to talk. Ask in your college coding club and your class group. Say yes to a team that has a skill you lack, even if you do not know them. A team of three with one person who can build a frontend, one who can build a backend or model, and one who can design and pitch is enough. Two committed people beat four who vanish at midnight.**



The longer version of finding a team, including how to handle a teammate who disappears mid-event, is on the portfolio [9].


## What should I prepare the week before?

**The boring things that eat hours on the day. Laptop updated, editor and Python or Node set up, Git configured, GitHub account with SSH working. Accounts created and API keys tested for the tools you might use, kept in a `.env` file. A starter template you have run once: a frontend, an API, a database, deployed somewhere free. A charger, an extension cord, a power bank, headphones, a water bottle, snacks, a change of clothes for offline events. And a plan for the demo video, because recording at 6 a.m. with no plan is how good projects submit bad videos.**



## What should a beginner build at a hackathon?

**One feature that works end to end, for one specific person, with a demo you can show in ninety seconds. A receipt reader for a hostel mess. A notice-board summariser for your college WhatsApp. A form that fills itself from a photo. Use APIs for the hard parts and spend your hours on the flow and the demo. Do not build a platform, a marketplace, a social network or anything with "ecosystem" in the description. The judging rewards a thing that runs, and beginners lose by attempting things that cannot run in 36 hours.**



My list of what to build at a first hackathon, with the scope test I still use, is written up separately [10].

## How do I manage the 24 to 48 hours?

**Decide the idea and the demo path in the first hour and do not revisit it. Split work by interface: one person owns the frontend, one the backend, one the model or data, with the API contract written down first. Have something that runs end to end, however ugly, by the halfway mark. Eat on a schedule. Sleep in shifts if it is overnight; a team with two hours of sleep each builds better than a team with none. Freeze the build with two hours left. Record the video and rehearse the pitch on the frozen build.**



## What if I do not know how to code well yet?

**Come anyway, with a role. Teams need someone to design screens, write the pitch, make the video, test the flow, talk to mentors and keep the plan. Learn one thing during the event by pairing with the builder on one small piece. Use no-code and low-code tools for parts of the demo where they fit. Judges care whether the thing works and whether the team understood the problem, not whether every member wrote code. By your second hackathon you will have shipped something, which is the fastest way to learn to code well.**


## How do I make the first hackathon count even if I lose?

**Ship something that runs, however small. Talk to at least three mentors and two other teams. Write down what broke and why. Post about it the same week with a screenshot, the lesson and a thank-you to the organisers. Keep the repository clean with a README and a video link. Add the event to your LinkedIn as experience. Register for the next one before the memory fades. Every win I have had traces back to a loss I wrote about.**



## Hackathon FAQ for beginners

**Do I need a team? Most events allow solo, but a team of two or three is easier and more fun. Do I need an idea before? Usually not; problem statements come at the start, and platforms often let you form teams first. Is it free? Student hackathons almost always are, and offline ones usually feed you. Can first-years join? Yes, and many events have first-timer tracks. Online or offline? Offline for the first one if you can; the energy and the mentors help.**



## Where should I start?

**Open Devfolio or Unstop tonight, pick one hackathon four weeks out, register, and post a three-line team-finding message. The rest of this page applies from there.** For a hackathon workshop at your college that covers picking, building and pitching in a weekend, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM: formats, chat templates, how much data, synthetic data, validation and the checklist before you train
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prepare-a-dataset-for-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM?

**Start with a written spec of the behaviour you want, then collect or write examples that follow it exactly: for each, the input a user would give and the ideal output, in the chat format the base model expects. Deduplicate, validate every row against the spec, hold out a validation split, measure token lengths, and read a random sample by eye. The dataset is the fine-tune; the training run only copies what is in it, including its inconsistencies.**


FineTune Studio, the platform I built in 2026, validates the uploaded dataset before it lets a run start, because the most common reason a run produced a bad model had nothing to do with hyper-parameters: the data was inconsistent, mis-templated or leaked into the validation split [12]. This page is that validation, explained.

> Write twenty examples by hand before anything else. If twenty consistent examples are hard to write, the spec is not ready, and the fine-tune will faithfully learn the confusion.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FineTune Studio</cite>

## What should the spec contain?

**One paragraph: who the user is, what they send, what the model must produce, in what format, with what tone, and what it must do when the input is unclear or out of scope. Then three example pairs that follow it. Every later example is checked against this paragraph. A spec you cannot write in a paragraph is a task you are not ready to train.**


## Which dataset format should I use: Alpaca, ShareGPT or chat messages?

**Use the messages format, a list of role and content turns, system, user, assistant, because it maps directly onto the chat template every modern model uses and onto what TRL's trainer expects [7]. Alpaca's instruction, input and output fields [1] and ShareGPT's multi-turn conversations are older JSON shapes that convert to messages trivially. The format is a container; what the model actually sees is the template rendered from it.**



A row in the messages format, which is also the shape most APIs accept [9]:

```json
{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a support agent for Acme. Answer only from the provided policy. If the policy does not cover the question, say so and offer to escalate."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Policy: Refunds within 14 days with receipt.\n\nQuestion: I bought it 20 days ago, can I return it?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "The policy allows refunds within 14 days of purchase with a receipt, so a return at 20 days is outside the window. I can escalate this to a supervisor if you would like."}
]}
```

## What is a chat template and why does it matter?

**A chat template is the exact string layout a model was trained on for conversations: the special tokens that mark the start and end of each turn and which role speaks. Every model family uses a different one. If you train with the wrong template, or hand-write the tokens with a small mistake, the model learns garbage or produces it at inference. Always render examples with the tokenizer's own template function [6], and use the same template when you serve the model.**


```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
text = tok.apply_chat_template(row["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False)
# never build this string by hand; the template lives with the model
```

Template mismatch is the single most common cause of a fine-tuned chat model that "does not work", in my experience and in the support questions FineTune Studio users asked. My longer note on formats and templates is on the portfolio [11].

## How much data do I need to fine-tune an LLM?

**For tone, style and output format: a few hundred high-quality examples produce a visible, stable change. For a classification or extraction skill: a few thousand covering the classes and the edge cases. For adapting to a domain's language: tens of thousands. Below about a hundred, put the examples in the prompt instead. LIMA showed that a thousand carefully curated examples were enough to teach strong instruction-following, and that quality mattered more than quantity [2].**



These are orders of magnitude from experience, not laws; the only reliable number comes from training on half your data and checking whether the other half still improves the model.

## Can I use synthetic data for fine-tuning?

**Yes, and most fine-tuning datasets today are partly synthetic: a stronger model generates examples from your spec, from seed examples, or from documents. Self-Instruct and Alpaca showed the approach at scale [3][1]. It works when you filter hard: validate every generated row against the spec, remove duplicates and near-duplicates, spot-check by hand, and mix in real examples so the model does not learn the generator's tics and refusals. Unfiltered synthetic data teaches a copy of the generator, not your task.**



## How do I clean and deduplicate the dataset?

**Normalise whitespace and encoding. Remove exact duplicates, then near-duplicates by comparing normalised text or embeddings, because duplicated training data both wastes compute and makes models memorise [5]. Remove rows that violate the spec: wrong format, wrong language, refusals you did not intend, outputs that reference the prompt. Strip personal data you do not have consent to train on. Measure token lengths and trim or split outliers so no row exceeds your training sequence length.**



The Hugging Face Datasets library handles the mechanics, loading, mapping, filtering and splitting, for datasets of any size [8]. My own pre-training validation checklist, which FineTune Studio runs automatically, is written up separately [10].


## How do I split training and validation data?

**Hold out ten to twenty percent, chosen so that near-duplicates of a training row never land in validation, or the validation loss lies to you. For grouped data, all rows from one document, one user or one conversation go to the same split. Keep a third, small test set of examples you wrote by hand and never look at during tuning, for the final honest comparison of base versus fine-tuned.**


## What is label masking, and should I train on the user turns?

**Label masking means computing the loss only on the assistant's tokens, so the model learns to produce answers rather than to predict the user's questions. Most trainers do this for you when you use the messages format with a chat template and an assistant-only loss option [7]. Training on user turns wastes capacity and can teach the model to continue user text. Mask them unless you have a specific reason not to.**


## What are common dataset mistakes?

**Mixing two specs in one dataset, so the model learns to flip between them. Hand-writing chat tokens. Duplicated rows inflating confidence. A validation split that shares documents with training. Outputs that mention the instruction. Ten variations of the same easy example and none of the hard cases. Personal data nobody consented to. Not reading any rows. A model can only be as consistent as its data, and it will be exactly as inconsistent.**



## Dataset interview questions

**How much data do you need for a style fine-tune versus a skill? What is a chat template and what happens if you get it wrong? How do you generate synthetic data without teaching the generator's habits? How do you prevent leakage between splits? What is label masking? Each answer above is a paragraph; the best evidence is a dataset you built and a model whose behaviour you can trace to specific rows.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick one narrow behaviour, write the paragraph spec and twenty examples tonight, render them with the tokenizer's template, and read them back. Then generate two hundred more synthetically, filter them against the spec, and hold out twenty. That dataset will fine-tune a small model on a free GPU tomorrow.** For a hands-on fine-tuning workshop at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to prompt ChatGPT: system prompts, courses and prompts for resumes and images
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prompt-chatgpt/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To prompt ChatGPT well, tell it the goal, give the context it needs, set constraints such as length and audience, and say exactly what format you want, adding an example when format matters. Then refine with specific follow-ups. Behind every chat sits a system prompt that sets the assistant's role; you can add your own layer through custom instructions, Projects or a custom GPT. This page covers prompting basics, system prompts, courses, and ready-to-use prompts for roadmaps, resumes, images, photo edits and interior design.

## How do I write a good ChatGPT prompt?

Include four things: the goal, the context, the constraints and the output format. "Explain recursion" becomes "I am a first-year BCA student. Explain recursion with one everyday analogy and one Python example, in under 200 words, then give me two practice problems."

Habits that improve answers:

- Give background: your level, purpose and audience.
- Paste the material: the text, code or data you are asking about.
- Specify format: bullet points, table, JSON, word count.
- Show an example of the output you want.
- Ask for steps or reasoning on complex problems.
- Ask what it needs to know before answering, for open-ended tasks.

When the answer misses, say precisely what to change instead of repeating the same prompt.

## What is the system prompt in ChatGPT?

The system prompt is a hidden set of instructions that defines the assistant's role, rules and behaviour before your messages. In ChatGPT, OpenAI writes a system prompt, and your custom instructions, Project instructions or a GPT's instructions add to it.

System-level instructions shape every reply in a conversation: tone, what to refuse, what tools to use, how to format answers. That is why the same model can act as a tutor in one GPT and a code reviewer in another. In the OpenAI API, developers write these instructions themselves as system or developer messages. Good system prompts are specific about role and boundaries, short enough to follow, and tested on real examples.

## How do I add a system prompt in ChatGPT?

Use custom instructions in ChatGPT's settings for rules that apply to all chats, Project instructions for one subject or project, or create a custom GPT with its own instructions for a reusable assistant.

Where each fits:

- **Custom instructions**: who you are and how you like answers, for every chat.
- **Projects**: instructions plus files for a course, a client or a long piece of work.
- **Custom GPT**: a shareable assistant with instructions, knowledge files and optional actions.

Example instruction for a study Project: "You are my tutor for Operating Systems. Use the attached syllabus. Explain with examples, then ask me one question to check understanding. Do not write my assignments." Test with a few questions and refine.

## Can you change ChatGPT's system prompt?

You cannot replace or remove OpenAI's own system prompt in the ChatGPT app, but you can add your own instructions on top through custom instructions, Projects and custom GPTs. Developers using the API control the whole system prompt themselves.

Your added instructions shape tone, format and focus, but cannot override OpenAI's safety policies. Prompts found online claiming to "unlock" or "jailbreak" ChatGPT usually break the terms of use and produce unreliable output. If you need full control, for example for a product, use the API, where you write the system or developer message, choose the model and set parameters. In the app, clear custom instructions plus good prompts achieve almost everything most users need.

## Is there a ChatGPT prompt engineering course for developers?

Yes. DeepLearning.AI's free short course "ChatGPT Prompt Engineering for Developers", taught with OpenAI, covers prompting principles and building with the API. OpenAI's and Anthropic's official prompt engineering guides are also free and kept up to date.

For developers, prompting is one part of a larger skill set: structured outputs with JSON schemas, tool calling, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation with test sets, and managing cost and latency. After a short course, build a small app, such as an extractor that turns emails into structured data, and measure accuracy on fifty examples while you change prompts. That teaches more than any certificate, and gives you a project to show.

## What is a good ChatGPT prompt for a learning roadmap?

Give your starting point, goal, time available and preferred style, and ask for a week-by-week plan with projects and checkpoints. For example:

```
I am a second-year BCA student who knows basic Python. My goal is to get an
internship as a GenAI engineer in six months. I can study 2 hours a day.
Create a week-by-week roadmap with: topics, one free resource per topic,
a small project every two weeks, and a checkpoint question to test myself.
Prioritise building over watching videos.
```

Then ask follow-ups: "make weeks 5 to 8 more practical" or "replace paid resources with free ones". Revisit the roadmap monthly and adjust to your progress. A roadmap you follow beats a perfect one you abandon.

## How do I prompt ChatGPT for a resume?

Give it the job description and your real experience, and ask it to tailor and tighten, using only facts you provided. Never let it invent experience, numbers or skills.

A prompt that works:

```
Here is a job description and my current resume. 1) List the skills the role
needs that my resume does not show. 2) Rewrite my project bullets to match the
role, using strong verbs and only facts from my resume. 3) Suggest a 2-line
summary. Keep it to one page. Flag anything you are unsure about.
```

Then edit the output in your own voice. Check every claim, because you must defend each line in an interview. Remove personal details such as ID numbers before pasting your resume into any chatbot.

## How do I prompt ChatGPT for images?

Describe the subject, setting, style, lighting, composition and any text, and say what the image is for. For example: "A flat illustration for a college hackathon poster: four students around laptops, sticky notes on a wall, bright orange and white palette, top-down view, space at the top for a title."

Tips:

- Name the style: photo, watercolour, flat vector, 3D render, pencil sketch.
- Specify aspect ratio for posters, slides or social posts.
- Put exact text in quotes and check spelling in the result.
- Refine with one change at a time: "same image, but evening light".
- Avoid real people's likeness, trademarks and copyrighted characters.

Label AI-generated images where they could be mistaken for real photos.

## How do I write ChatGPT photo editing prompts?

Upload the photo and say exactly what to change and what must stay the same. For example: "Replace the background with a plain light grey studio wall. Keep the person, clothing, face and lighting on the face unchanged. Do not add or remove objects."

Prompts for common edits:

- "Remove the person in the background on the right; fill naturally."
- "Make it look like evening golden-hour light, keep everything else the same."
- "Extend the image to a 16:9 frame, continuing the scenery naturally."
- "Convert to a clean black-and-white portrait with soft contrast."

AI edits regenerate the image, so faces and small details can shift; check carefully. Do not use AI-edited photos for official documents, and never edit images of others without consent.

## How do I prompt ChatGPT for interior design?

Upload a photo of the room or give its dimensions, describe how you use it, your style and budget level, and ask for a layout, colour palette, furniture list and a visual concept. Specific constraints produce useful ideas.

Example prompt:

```
Here is a photo of my 10 x 12 ft hostel-style study room with one window on the
left wall. I need a desk for two monitors, storage for books and space for a
bed. Style: minimal, warm wood, plants. Suggest a layout, a colour palette with
paint names to look for, and a shopping list by priority. Then generate an
image of the redesigned room from the same angle.
```

Treat the image as inspiration; measure everything before buying.

# How to run Ollama: locally, offline, on CPU, Mac, Raspberry Pi and phones
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-run-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To run a model with Ollama, install it and type `ollama run` followed by a model name, such as `ollama run llama3.2`; Ollama downloads the model the first time, loads it, and opens a chat in your terminal, while also serving it on a local API for your apps. Everything runs on your own machine, offline once the model is downloaded. This page explains the command, how local inference works, offline and CPU-only use, laptops and Macs, Raspberry Pi, Android and iPhone, and running GGUF models from Hugging Face.

## How do I use ollama run?

Run `ollama run <model>` in a terminal. If the model is not installed, Ollama pulls it first; then it loads the model into memory and opens an interactive chat. Type your message, and `/bye` to exit.

Useful variations:

```bash
ollama run llama3.2                         # chat
ollama run qwen2.5:7b "Explain BM25 in one line"   # one-off prompt
ollama run llama3.2 --verbose               # shows tokens per second
```

Inside the chat, `/set parameter num_ctx 8192` raises the context window and `/show info` displays model details. After the first run, the same model is available to apps through `http://localhost:11434`. Use `ollama ps` to see whether it is running on GPU or CPU.

## How does Ollama run models locally?

Ollama loads a model file, usually a quantised GGUF model, into your RAM or GPU memory and runs inference with the GGML engine, the same family of code behind llama.cpp, using your CPU, GPU or both.

When you send a prompt, Ollama applies the model's chat template, tokenises the text, runs the model to generate tokens one by one, and streams them back. It keeps the model loaded for a few minutes between requests so follow-ups are fast, then unloads it to free memory. Quantisation, storing weights in 4 or 8 bits instead of 16, is what lets billion-parameter models fit on ordinary laptops. Nothing is sent to external servers unless you use Ollama's optional cloud models.

## Can Ollama run without internet?

Yes. Once a model has been downloaded, Ollama runs completely offline; prompts and responses never leave your machine. You need internet only to install Ollama and pull or update models.

This makes it useful for travel, poor connectivity, privacy-sensitive documents and air-gapped environments. To prepare, pull the models you need while online, and if you use tools on top of Ollama, such as a web UI or LangChain, make sure their dependencies are installed too. Models can be copied between machines by copying the models folder, which helps when internet is slow. Cloud models in Ollama, by contrast, always need a connection.

## Can Ollama run on CPU only?

Yes. Ollama runs on CPU when no supported GPU is available, though more slowly. Small models, of 1B to 4B parameters, are comfortable on modern CPUs; 7B to 8B models work but respond more slowly.

Tips for CPU-only use: pick small, quantised models; keep the context window modest; close memory-heavy apps; and prefer machines with more RAM and newer CPUs, which have faster vector instructions. Apple Silicon Macs are a special case: their unified memory and GPU make local models fast even without a separate graphics card. For tasks such as embeddings, classification and short answers, small CPU models are often good enough.

## Can I run Ollama on my laptop?

Yes. Most modern laptops can run Ollama. With 8 GB of RAM, use 1B to 4B models; with 16 GB, 7B to 8B models at 4-bit run well; with 32 GB or a GPU with 8 GB or more of video memory, larger models become practical.

Check your setup with `ollama run llama3.2 --verbose` and look at tokens per second: above roughly 10 tokens per second feels responsive for chat. Plug in the charger for long sessions, since power-saving modes slow inference. If your laptop has an NVIDIA GPU, keep drivers updated so Ollama uses it. For heavier models, consider Ollama's cloud models or a remote GPU server.

## How do I run Ollama on a Mac?

Download the Mac app from ollama.com, move it to Applications and open it; the `ollama` command is then available in Terminal. Run `ollama run llama3.2` to start.

Apple Silicon Macs, with M-series chips, run local models efficiently because the GPU shares fast unified memory with the CPU; a Mac with 16 GB can run 7B to 8B models smoothly, and more memory allows larger models. Intel Macs work on CPU, more slowly. Keep the app running in the menu bar so the local API stays available for other tools. Models are stored in `~/.ollama/models`; set `OLLAMA_MODELS` to move them to an external drive if space is tight.

## Can you run Ollama on a Raspberry Pi?

Yes, on recent 64-bit Raspberry Pi models with a 64-bit operating system, using the Linux install script. Expect it to be slow: use very small models, around 1B to 3B parameters, and short contexts.

A Raspberry Pi 5 with 8 GB of RAM is the practical minimum for a usable experience with tiny models. It is a great learning project and can power simple offline assistants, home automation commands or classification tasks, but not fast chat with larger models. Cooling matters, as sustained inference heats the board. For anything heavier, run Ollama on a laptop or server and let the Pi call it over the network.

## Can Ollama run on Android?

Not officially. Ollama provides installers for Windows, macOS and Linux, not Android. Some enthusiasts run it on Android through Linux environments such as Termux, but performance and support vary.

For on-device AI on Android phones, apps built for mobile, which run small models with frameworks optimised for phones, are a better choice, and Google's on-device Gemini Nano powers some built-in features. A practical alternative is to run Ollama on your laptop or a home server and connect to it from your phone over your local network through a web UI, keeping the API protected and off the public internet.

## Can you run Ollama on an iPhone?

No. Ollama does not run on iOS. To use local models on an iPhone, use apps designed to run small models on-device, or connect from your iPhone to Ollama running on a Mac or server on your network.

Apple's own on-device models power Apple Intelligence features on supported iPhones. Third-party apps can run small open models on recent iPhones, with limits on model size because of memory. The remote approach often gives the best experience: run Ollama with a capable model on your Mac, put a chat UI in front of it, and open that UI in Safari on your iPhone over Wi-Fi.

## Can Ollama run GGUF models?

Yes. GGUF is Ollama's native format. You can run GGUF models from Hugging Face directly by reference, or import a local GGUF file with a Modelfile and `ollama create`.

```bash
ollama run hf.co/<user>/<repo>                 # GGUF repo on Hugging Face
```

```
# Modelfile
FROM ./my-model.Q4_K_M.gguf
PARAMETER temperature 0.3
```

```bash
ollama create my-model -f Modelfile && ollama run my-model
```

Choose a quantisation that fits your memory, such as Q4_K_M for a balance of size and quality. Make sure the chat template matches the model, or answers will be odd; models from Ollama's library and many Hugging Face repos include it.
