# How to set up a hackathon: length, what it includes, origins, demos, prizes, judging
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-set-up-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Setting up a hackathon means defining a purpose and audience, securing a venue or platform, sponsors, mentors and judges, publishing themes and rules, and running a well-paced schedule from kickoff to demos. I have competed in 10+ hackathons and founded the TechVerse Enclave community, so this page covers setting one up, ideal length, what hackathons include, where the name came from, whether hackathons count as experience, giving demos and SIH presentations, prize money, and how judges should give feedback and report.

## How do you set up a hackathon?

Define the goal and audience, pick dates and format, secure a venue or online platform, recruit sponsors, mentors and judges, publish themes, rules and judging criteria, open registrations, and plan logistics such as food, Wi-Fi, power and schedules.

Work backwards from the event: two to three months before, confirm sponsors and the venue; six weeks before, open registration and announce tracks; two weeks before, brief mentors and judges and run team formation sessions; on the day, keep strict timings for kickoff, mentor rounds, submission and demos. Use Devfolio, Devpost or Unstop for applications and submissions, and a Discord server for communication. Afterwards, publish results quickly and send feedback forms.

## How long should a hackathon last?

Most hackathons last 24 to 48 hours, often across a weekend. Shorter formats of 8 to 12 hours suit beginners and corporate events, while online hackathons may run for one to several weeks with flexible schedules.

Twenty-four hours is enough for a focused prototype; 36 to 48 hours allows more polish and rest. Longer online events let participants balance work or classes, but momentum can fade, so add checkpoints such as midpoint demos. Consider your audience: first-year students may prefer a single long day without overnight stays, while experienced developers enjoy weekend sprints. Whatever the length, protect time for judging, so demos are not rushed at the end.

## What does a hackathon include?

A typical hackathon includes an opening ceremony, a theme or problem statement announcement, team formation, building time with mentor support, workshops or talks, meals and breaks, a submission deadline, demo presentations, judging and a closing ceremony with prizes.

Many also include sponsor challenges with separate prizes, networking sessions with recruiters, fun activities such as quizzes or games during long nights, and swag. Online hackathons replace physical elements with live streams, Discord channels, scheduled office hours and recorded demo videos. Participants usually need to submit a code repository, a short description and a demo video or presentation. Good events also include a code of conduct and clear support channels for help.

## Where did the name hackathon come from?

Hackathon combines hack, in the sense of creative programming, and marathon. The term appeared in 1999, used independently by OpenBSD developers for a cryptography coding event and by Sun Microsystems for a programming challenge at its JavaOne conference.

Hack originally meant a clever solution or playful technical exploration, especially in early computing cultures at universities, before it took on its security meaning. Hackathons spread through the 2000s via tech companies and startup culture, with internal company hackathons producing well-known features. By the 2010s, student hackathons, government innovation challenges and corporate events had made the format global, including large national programmes in India such as Smart India Hackathon.

## Does a hackathon count as experience?

Usually not as formal work experience, since it is not employment. List hackathons under Projects, Achievements or Extracurricular activities, unless the hackathon led to an internship or contract, which then counts as experience.

Hackathons still demonstrate experience in a broader sense: building under deadlines, teamwork, product thinking and presenting to judges. In interviews, treat them as project experience and describe your role, technical decisions and results. For freshers without internships, strong hackathon projects can fill much of the experience gap. Be accurate in applications: do not label a hackathon as a job, since background checks and interviewers may question it. Wins and finalist places deserve a clear line of their own.

## How do you give a hackathon demo?

Show the product working on its core flow within the first minute, narrate what the user sees and why it matters, and keep the demo short and rehearsed. Prepare a backup video in case the live demo fails.

Before the demo, reset the app to a clean state, pre-fill test data, close unrelated tabs and notifications, increase font sizes, and test the projector and internet. Use realistic data, such as an actual user scenario, rather than placeholder text. Explain only the essential technology, then return to impact. End by stating what you built during the event and what is next. Have a teammate ready to answer technical questions while the presenter continues.

## How do you give a Smart India Hackathon presentation?

Use the official SIH presentation template when provided, and cover the problem statement, your proposed solution, technical approach, feasibility, impact and benefits, research and references, and a demo or prototype screenshots, in a clear, concise flow.

Evaluators look for a precise understanding of the problem owner's needs, a workable technical plan and realistic deployment. Use diagrams for architecture and workflows, avoid dense text, and cite data sources. Highlight what makes your approach better than existing solutions. Prepare for questions on scalability, cost, security and integration with government systems. Rehearse as a team so every member can explain their part, and keep the presentation within the allotted time.

## Does a hackathon give money?

Many hackathons award cash prizes to winners, and some offer sponsor prizes, travel support or stipends. Others give non-cash rewards such as gadgets, cloud credits, internships, incubation support or certificates.

Prize structures vary widely: student events may offer modest rewards, while large sponsored, government or Web3 hackathons can offer substantial prize pools across tracks. Read the prize rules for eligibility, payment timelines and tax requirements, since organisers may deduct tax at source and request identity documents. Participation itself is usually free. Treat money as a bonus: most of a hackathon's value comes from skills, projects, mentorship and connections that continue after the event.

## How should hackathon judges give feedback that students use?

Make feedback specific, actionable and balanced: name one thing that worked, one or two improvements with a concrete next step, and a resource or example. Students act on precise advice far more than on general praise or criticism.

Good judges ask questions before critiquing, connect feedback to the judging criteria, and separate product, technical and presentation notes. Written feedback, even three bullet points per team, is more useful than a quick verbal comment students forget. Encourage teams that did not win by pointing to what would make the project competitive next time. Organisers can help by providing a feedback form for judges and sharing compiled notes with every team after results.

## What should a hackathon judge include in a post-event report?

Include scores and rationale for top projects, observations on overall project quality, notes on whether judging criteria and time slots worked, any fairness or eligibility concerns, and suggestions for problem statements, mentoring and logistics next time.

Organisers use these reports to improve future events and to give teams useful feedback, so be specific: which tracks produced strong work, where teams struggled, whether problem statements were clear, and whether demo time was sufficient. Flag issues such as pre-built projects or rule violations with evidence. Recommend promising teams for follow-up support, such as incubation or mentorship. Keep the report concise, ideally a page or two, and submit it soon after the event.

# How to start a tech community on campus: from five friends to 500 members, the sessions, the structure and the mistakes, from building TechVerse Enclave
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-start-a-tech-community-on-campus/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I start a tech community on campus?

**Pick one topic you can teach for an hour, book a room, tell five people, and run the session this week. Then run one next week. A community is a weekly session that happens whether five or fifty people attend; everything else, the name, the logo, the group chat, the sponsors, comes after the habit exists. TechVerse Enclave started in 2023 as a hackathon team and a handful of friends learning web development together. It has since grown past 500 members, and I have mentored more than 200 students through it. The first six months were the hardest and the most important.**


The full playbook, with the timeline and the numbers, is on the portfolio [1][3]. This page is the version for someone starting Monday.

> Nobody joins a community. They come to a session, and they come back to the next one because it happened. The community is the coming back.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, founder of TechVerse Enclave</cite>

## What should the first session be?

**Something you built last month, shown live, then a hands-on hour where everyone leaves with a version running. A first session about "introduction to AI" attracts fifty curious people who never return. A first session where ten people deploy their first web page attracts ten people who return with friends. Teach what you know; the second session can be taught by whoever learned fastest.**



The session format I still use, with timings, is written up separately [4]: ten minutes of story, twenty of demonstration, forty of hands-on, and a public artefact from every attendee.

## How do I get people to show up and keep coming?

**Same time, same place, every week, announced the day before, with photos and a recap the same day. Make the first-timer's experience good: someone greets them, the setup instructions were sent in advance, they leave with something working. Ask every attendee to bring one person. Celebrate small ships publicly. Growth came for TechVerse Enclave when members started teaching, because each new teacher brought their own circle.**



## How should a student community be organised?

**Small roles with names: a lead, a sessions lead who owns the calendar, a content lead who posts, an outreach lead who invites speakers and talks to faculty, and a treasurer if money exists. A shared calendar planned a month ahead. A written handover document from day one, because the founders graduate. A faculty coordinator who signs forms and books rooms, kept informed monthly. Nothing more until the weekly session has run for a semester.**



The mistake that kills most college clubs is not low attendance; it is a founding batch that graduates without a handover. The lessons post covers what I got wrong here first [2].

## How do I get speakers, mentors and judges?

**Invite practitioners with a concrete ask: a topic from their own work, two dates, the audience, the format, what you offer. Start with alumni and engineers in your city, then people who already post about speaking at colleges. Many, including me, speak for free for student communities. Build a record first: a speaker says yes faster to a community with photos of ten past sessions than to one with a plan. Then ask each speaker for the next thing, judging your hackathon, monthly office hours.**


My detailed guide to writing the invitation is a separate page on this site; the short version is six things in one email and a follow-up after five days.


## How do I run a hackathon as a student community?

**Start with a 12-hour internal build day for your own members, then a one-day campus hackathon, then a bigger one with outside teams. Fix the rubric and the timeline before you fix the theme. Recruit judges who have built things and brief them for fifteen minutes. Protect the demo slot: three minutes each, a hard stop, a working projector. Sponsors come after the first successful event, not before. TechVerse Enclave's first hackathon was an afternoon in a classroom; the ones after had partners because the first one had photos.**


The organiser guide with the timeline, rubric and budget lines is on the portfolio [5].

## How do I get sponsors, funding and partner programmes?

**Programmes first, money second. Google Developer Groups on Campus, Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors, the GitHub Campus Program and Major League Hacking give student communities structure, resources, swag, speakers and credibility, for free [6][7][8][9]. Apply once you have a semester of sessions to show. Local companies sponsor food and prizes for hackathons when you show them last year's photos and this year's plan. College funding follows visible activity, so make the activity visible first.**


## How does a community help your career?

**In every way that a certificate does not. My teammates for three winning hackathons came from it. My first clients came from it. The sessions I ran inside it became the sessions colleges invited me to give. The people I mentored became referrals. Recruiters read "founded a 500-member developer community and mentored 200 students" as leadership evidence no course provides. And teaching every week is the fastest way to actually understand what you are learning.**



## What mistakes do new communities make?

**Spending the first month on a name and a logo. Announcing a big event before running a small session. Founders doing everything and burning out. No handover, so the club dies with a batch. Chasing sponsors before there is anything to sponsor. Measuring the group chat's size instead of the room's. Every one of these I made or watched; the fix for all of them is the weekly session.**



## Can you help our community get started?

**Yes. I run sessions on building and running student communities, speak at inaugurations of new clubs, and connect organisers with the playbook and the templates.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite. Free for student communities.

# How to structure an LLM project in Python: folder layout, config, prompts as files, evals, and the patterns that survive past the notebook
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-structure-an-llm-project-in-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should I structure an LLM project in Python?

**As a proper package under `src/`, with separate modules for the model provider, prompts, retrieval, domain logic, API or CLI, and evaluation; typed settings loaded from environment variables; prompts stored as versioned files rather than string literals; Pydantic schemas at every model boundary; a `tests/` folder with a golden set and an `eval` command; and a task runner so `make eval` or `uv run eval` works on any machine. The structure exists so the model can change, the prompts can change and the retrieval can change without touching each other.**


Both production systems I maintain, the RAG platform and the document extraction service, share this shape, and the shape is why a provider swap in one took an afternoon rather than a week [11][12]. My shorter note on the layout is on the portfolio [13]. This page is the full version with the reasons.

> The first time you change models, the structure pays for itself. The second time you change prompts without a test set, you learn why the eval folder exists.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What does the folder layout look like?

**A `src/yourapp/` package with `providers/`, `prompts/`, `retrieval/`, `core/`, `api/` and `eval/` inside it; `tests/` beside `src/` with fixtures and a golden set; `data/` for local indexes and samples, gitignored where large; `scripts/` for one-off jobs; `pyproject.toml`, `Makefile` or task file, `.env.example`, `README.md`. The src layout prevents the common bug of importing the local folder instead of the installed package [1] and forces you to install the project properly.**



## How should I handle configuration and secrets?

**A single typed settings object loaded from environment variables, using Pydantic Settings or equivalent [2]: model names, endpoints, temperature, chunk sizes, feature flags, all with types and defaults. Secrets come from the environment and never from the repository; commit a `.env.example` with the keys and no values [10]. Every module receives the settings object or the specific values it needs; nothing reads `os.environ` directly. This is what lets the same code run on your laptop, in CI and in production.**



## Where should prompts live?

**In files, one per prompt, under `src/app/prompts/`, loaded by a small function that fills placeholders and records which version was used. A prompt is a piece of program logic that happens to be in English; treating it as a string literal buried in a function makes it impossible to diff, review or test. Name files by purpose and version, keep a changelog line at the top, and run the golden set whenever one changes. Templates with explicit placeholders beat f-strings, because the template can be reviewed without the surrounding code.**



## How do I handle model outputs safely?

**Define a Pydantic model for every structured output and parse at the boundary [3]. Use the provider's structured output or tool-calling mode to constrain generation where available [7][8], then still validate, because constraints reduce but do not eliminate malformed output. On failure, retry once with the validation error in the prompt, then fall back to a safe default or a human queue. The rest of the codebase receives typed objects and never raw model text.**


DocuLens is built on this rule: a strict schema per document type, validation at the boundary, deterministic rules afterwards, and a review queue for anything that fails [12]. It is the difference between a demo and a system a finance team trusts.


## How do I set up evaluation in the project?

**A `golden/` folder with labelled cases as JSON or JSONL: input, expected output or expected properties, tags. An `eval` module that runs every case through the real pipeline, computes metrics, retrieval recall, format validity, faithfulness judged by a model or rules, latency, cost, and writes a report. A command, `make eval` or `uv run eval`, that prints the score and exits non-zero if it drops below a threshold. Run it in CI on every prompt or retrieval change. Twenty cases is enough to start; grow it from production failures.**



## How should I log and trace?

**Structured logs, JSON in production, with a request ID that follows the call through retrieval, generation and validation [9]. Log the prompt version, model name, token counts, latency, retrieved document IDs and validation outcome for every call. Store prompts and outputs for a bounded time, with sensitive data redacted, so a failure report can be reproduced. When a user says the answer was wrong, you should be able to find exactly what the model saw.**


## Which tools should I use for the project itself?

**uv for environments and dependencies, because it is fast and produces a lockfile [4]. Ruff for linting and formatting in one tool [5]. pytest for tests [6]. Pydantic for schemas and settings [2][3]. FastAPI if the app serves HTTP. A Makefile or a task runner with `setup`, `test`, `eval`, `run` and `lint` targets so nobody memorises commands. Pre-commit hooks that run Ruff. Nothing exotic; boring tools mean a new contributor is productive in an hour.**



## How do I package and deploy it?

**A Dockerfile that installs from the lockfile, copies `src/`, and runs the API with a production server. Settings from environment variables, so the same image runs everywhere. Health and readiness endpoints. Indexes and data mounted or fetched at startup, not baked into the image if they change. A CI pipeline that runs lint, tests and evals before building the image. Deployment specifics depend on the host; the structure makes them small.**



## What mistakes make LLM projects unmaintainable?

**Prompts as f-strings scattered through functions. Provider calls made directly from business logic, so a model swap touches everything. Raw model text parsed with regex in five places. No golden set, so every change is a guess. API keys in the repository. A notebook as the only entry point. No request IDs, so failures cannot be traced. Everything in one file called `main.py` at two thousand lines. Each is fixed by one folder on this page.**



## Interview questions on LLM project structure

**Explain how you would structure a RAG application so the model can be swapped. Where do prompts live and how are they versioned? How do you validate outputs? What is in your eval set and when does it run? How do you handle secrets? How would you debug a wrong answer reported by a user? A repository that answers these by its layout is the strongest evidence you can bring.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your current notebook and create the six folders. Move the model call into providers, the prompt into a file, the output into a schema, and five examples into a golden set with an eval command. Two hours, and the project can now change safely.** For a workshop on shipping LLM applications from notebook to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to take part in a hackathon: skills, AI rules, worth it, SIH, and running one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-take-part-in-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To take part in a hackathon, find an event on platforms such as Devfolio, Unstop, Devpost or MLH, form or join a team, register before the deadline, prepare your tools, and build a focused demo during the event. I have competed in 10+ hackathons, winning first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats and placing top 3 at an IIT Kanpur hackathon, so this page covers taking part, skills, AI rules, whether hackathons and certificates are worth it, SIH, and running one.

## How do you take part in a hackathon?

Find events on Devfolio, Unstop, Devpost, MLH or your college's notices; read the rules, themes and eligibility; form a team of two to four with complementary skills; register before the deadline; and complete any screening round, such as an idea submission.

Before the event, set up your laptop with the tools you will use, prepare a project template with authentication or a basic frontend, and research the problem statements. During the event, agree on one core feature, divide work clearly, commit code often, and stop adding features a few hours before the deadline to polish the demo. Practise your pitch twice. After the event, publish the project on GitHub and thank organisers and mentors.

## What is the use of a hackathon?

Hackathons turn learning into building under real constraints. Participants gain practical skills, teamwork experience, portfolio projects, feedback from experts, networking with sponsors and peers, and sometimes prizes, internships or startup ideas.

For organisers and sponsors, hackathons generate fresh solutions, test developer tools, find talent and build communities. Governments use them to source ideas for public problems. For students, a single weekend can teach more about scoping, prioritising and shipping than a semester of isolated assignments, because everything must work by a deadline in front of judges. Projects from my own teams, such as KrishGyan and Annapurna, won first prizes at hackathons, which gave them early validation.

## What skills do you need for a hackathon?

A strong team covers building, design and pitching: one or two developers comfortable with a stack such as Python, FastAPI, Next.js or Flutter, someone who can design simple interfaces, and someone who can explain the idea clearly to judges.

Useful technical skills: Git and GitHub for collaboration, calling APIs, a database such as PostgreSQL or Firebase, quick deployment with platforms like Vercel or Render, and increasingly AI APIs for language and vision features. Equally important are soft skills: scoping a problem to fit the time, dividing tasks, communicating under pressure and presenting confidently. Beginners can still join; many events welcome first-timers and value learning, so bring curiosity and willingness to help.

## How do you learn hackathon skills?

Build small projects end to end before the event: a web app with a database, an API integration and a deployment. Each one teaches the full cycle you will repeat under time pressure at a hackathon.

Practise in timed sprints: give yourself a weekend to build and deploy something useful. Learn one stack deeply rather than many superficially, so you are not learning tools during the event. Watch demo videos of past winners on Devpost to see what judges value. Join beginner-friendly hackathons and college events, contribute to a teammate's project, and review what went wrong afterwards. Communities like TechVerse Enclave run sessions where students learn these skills together.

## Can you use AI during a hackathon?

Usually yes, unless the rules forbid it. Most modern hackathons allow AI coding assistants and AI APIs, and many have AI tracks. Always read the rules, because some events require all code to be written during the event or restrict generated content.

Use AI to speed up boilerplate, debugging, documentation and design ideas, but make sure your team understands every part of the code, because judges ask technical questions. Be transparent: mention the AI tools and APIs you used in your submission. Judges reward original problem framing and working integration more than code volume, so AI is most valuable when it frees time for user research, testing and a polished demo rather than when it generates features you cannot explain.

## Can you use ChatGPT in a hackathon?

In most hackathons, yes: ChatGPT and similar assistants are treated like other developer tools. Check the rules for restrictions on pre-written code or generated assets, and disclose significant use if the organisers ask.

Good uses include brainstorming features, generating test data, explaining errors, drafting README files and preparing pitch scripts. Risky uses include copying large code blocks you do not understand, using unverified facts in your pitch, and pasting private sponsor data into a public chatbot without permission. If your product itself calls an AI model, design it carefully: validate outputs, handle failures, and show judges how you prevent wrong answers, since reliability impresses more than flashy demos.

## Is a hackathon worth it?

Yes, for most students and developers. Even without winning, you get a finished project, practical experience, teammates and feedback. The cost is a weekend of time and energy, which pays back quickly in skills and portfolio material.

Hackathons are less worth it if you only collect participation certificates without building anything meaningful, or if you join so many that coursework and health suffer. Choose events whose themes interest you and whose judges or sponsors you want to meet. Measure value by what you learned and shipped, not by the number of events attended. My own hackathon projects, including KrishGyan, became some of the strongest items in my portfolio.

## Is a hackathon certificate worth it?

A participation certificate alone carries little weight with recruiters. Winner, finalist or special mention certificates from reputed events carry more, especially when linked to a project people can see and try.

Put the project first on your resume: what you built, the tech stack, your role and the result, such as first prize or top 3 out of a stated number of teams. Link the GitHub repository and a demo video. Certificates help as supporting evidence, for example in college applications or internal records, but interviewers will ask about the work, not the paper. A strong project from an unknown event beats a certificate from a famous one with nothing to show.

## Is Smart India Hackathon worth it?

Yes, for students who want to solve real problems from ministries, public organisations and industry. Smart India Hackathon offers national visibility, mentoring, government and industry exposure, and for winners, recognition and prizes that look strong on a resume.

It is demanding: internal college selection, proposal screening and a long grand finale require serious preparation. Choose a problem statement your team understands and can prototype credibly, and research the organisation that posed it. Even if you are not selected for the finale, preparing a proposal teaches problem analysis and documentation skills. Treat it as one of several events, alongside community and college hackathons that offer more frequent practice.

## How do you run a successful hackathon?

Start with a clear purpose and audience, secure a venue or online platform, sponsors and judges, publish themes and rules early, and plan the schedule, food, internet, mentors and judging criteria in detail. Success comes from preparation and communication.

Key practices: recruit volunteers with defined roles; run a pre-event session on themes and team formation; keep Wi-Fi, power and food reliable for in-person events; schedule mentor rounds; publish transparent judging rubrics; and keep demos to strict time slots. Make beginners welcome with workshops and starter kits. Afterwards, share results, photos and feedback forms quickly, and publish winning projects. Participants return to events where they feel supported and judged fairly, which matters more than prize size.

# How to test VRAM: errors, OCCT, overclock stability, temps, and how much you need
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-test-vram/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To test VRAM, run a dedicated video memory test such as OCCT's VRAM test or memtest_vulkan to check for errors, while monitoring memory usage and temperature with GPU-Z, HWiNFO or nvidia-smi. For overclocks, add game or benchmark runs and watch for artefacts or falling scores. VRAM matters greatly in AI: it decides which models you can run and fine-tune, which is why FineTune Studio uses 4-bit QLoRA. This page covers what VRAM does, performance, testing for errors, overclocks, temperatures, usage, and how much you need.

## What is the purpose of VRAM?

VRAM, video random access memory, is the dedicated high-speed memory on a graphics card. It holds the data the GPU works on: textures, geometry, frame buffers and shaders in games, and model weights, activations and batches in AI workloads.

Because VRAM sits right next to the GPU with very high bandwidth, the GPU can process huge amounts of data quickly. If a task needs more memory than the VRAM available, data spills to slower system RAM, or the program fails with an out-of-memory error. In machine learning, VRAM capacity is often the main limit: a model must fit, along with its working memory, for training or fast inference.

## Does VRAM help performance?

More VRAM helps when you would otherwise run out. Then it prevents stuttering, texture pop-in, lower settings or crashes. If your workload already fits comfortably, extra VRAM adds little; GPU core speed and memory bandwidth matter more.

In games, high resolutions and texture settings use more VRAM, and running short causes stutter. In AI, VRAM decides whether a model fits at all: a 7-billion-parameter model needs roughly 14 GB in 16-bit precision but about 4 to 5 GB in 4-bit form. Larger VRAM also allows bigger batch sizes and longer contexts. So for AI work, VRAM capacity is often the single most important GPU specification.

## How do I test VRAM?

Run a dedicated VRAM test that writes and reads patterns across most of the memory and reports errors. OCCT's VRAM test and memtest_vulkan are popular choices; older tools such as MemTestCL also exist. Run tests for at least 30 to 60 minutes.

A basic routine:

- Close other GPU applications and update drivers.
- Open a monitoring tool to watch memory usage, clocks and temperatures.
- Run the VRAM test on as much memory as possible.
- Note any reported errors; zero errors is the only pass.
- Follow with a demanding game or benchmark to check real-world stability.

Errors at stock settings suggest faulty memory or overheating, and may justify a warranty claim.

## How do I test VRAM on a GPU in practice?

Choose a tool that supports your GPU and operating system: OCCT on Windows for NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, memtest_vulkan on Windows and Linux through Vulkan, and vendor tools such as nvidia-smi for monitoring NVIDIA cards.

For AI machines, a practical test is also running a real workload: load a model that uses most of the VRAM and run inference or training for an hour, watching for crashes, NaN losses or errors. Check that the reported VRAM size matches your card's specification in GPU-Z or nvidia-smi; a mismatch can indicate a counterfeit or misconfigured card, which is worth checking with second-hand purchases.

## How do I test VRAM with OCCT?

Open OCCT, choose the VRAM test, set it to use most of the available memory, and start the test while OCCT's monitoring shows clocks, usage and temperatures. Let it run for at least 30 minutes, and longer for overclocks.

OCCT reports errors as they occur and stops or flags the test. Any error means the memory is not stable at current settings. If errors appear on a stock card, check cooling and drivers, then retest; persistent errors suggest hardware problems. Save the test report as evidence if you contact the seller or manufacturer. OCCT also offers GPU core and power tests, useful for checking whole-system stability.

## How do I test VRAM for errors?

Run memtest_vulkan or OCCT's VRAM test, which write known patterns to memory and verify them, counting mismatches. Any reported error indicates a problem with memory chips, the memory controller, cooling or overclock settings.

Visual symptoms can also indicate VRAM errors: coloured artefacts, flickering textures, checkerboard patterns, driver crashes and system freezes under load. Errors only during long runs often point to overheating; errors immediately suggest faulty memory or unstable clocks. Reset any overclock to default, retest, and if errors persist at stock settings with good temperatures, the card likely needs repair or replacement.

## How do I test VRAM overclock stability?

Raise the memory clock in small steps with a tool such as MSI Afterburner, run a VRAM error test after each step, then confirm with benchmarks and games. Watch for errors, artefacts, crashes and, importantly, falling benchmark scores.

Modern GDDR memory uses error detection and retries, so an unstable overclock may not crash but silently lose performance as errors are corrected. If scores drop as you raise clocks, you have passed the stable point; step back down. Test with long runs, since instability can appear after heat builds up. For AI training, avoid aggressive memory overclocks entirely, because silent errors can corrupt results over long jobs.

## How do I check VRAM temperatures?

Use HWiNFO or GPU-Z to read memory temperature sensors, often labelled "memory junction temperature" on cards with GDDR6X, while running a VRAM test or heavy workload. Check your card's specification for its memory throttle point.

Memory can run hotter than the GPU core, especially on cards with memory chips on the back of the board. High memory temperatures cause throttling, errors and reduced lifespan. Improve them with better case airflow, cleaning dust, adjusting fan curves, or replacing thermal pads on older cards if you are comfortable doing so. For long AI training runs, monitor temperatures periodically and keep the room and case well ventilated.

## How do I see what's using my VRAM?

On Windows, open Task Manager, go to the Details tab, and add the "Dedicated GPU memory" column to see each process's VRAM use; the Performance tab shows total usage. On NVIDIA systems, run `nvidia-smi` to list processes and their memory.

Browsers, game launchers, video players and background AI tools can hold VRAM. In Python, frameworks cache memory: PyTorch's `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` and `memory_reserved()` show usage, and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` releases cached blocks. If VRAM stays full after closing an app, a process may still be running; end it or restart. For machine learning, close other GPU apps before loading large models.

## What is a good amount of VRAM?

It depends on use. For 1080p gaming, 8 GB is a practical minimum today, with 12 GB or more preferable for higher resolutions and settings. For AI, 8 GB runs small models, 12 to 16 GB runs and fine-tunes 7B models with QLoRA, and 24 GB or more handles larger models.

VRAM on graphics cards cannot be upgraded; you must replace the card, so buy with headroom. For AI students on a budget, free or low-cost cloud GPUs and 4-bit quantisation stretch limited VRAM a long way. Tools such as Hugging Face's model memory estimator help predict how much a given model needs before you download it.

# How to use Gemini, and what AI apps, agents, Cursor and vibe coding actually look like
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-use-gemini-ai-looks/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To use Gemini, open the Gemini app or gemini.google.com, sign in with your Google account, type or speak what you need, and refine the answer with follow-up messages; you can also upload files and images, choose models, and use tools like Deep Research. Many people also wonder what AI tools look like before trying them. I build AI products and use these tools daily, so this page covers using Gemini, its interface, when to use Deep Research or NotebookLM, Gemini versus Bixby, and what AI agents, agentic AI, Cursor and vibe coding look like.

## How do I use Gemini?

Open the Gemini app on Android or iPhone, or visit gemini.google.com, sign in, and type a request in the prompt box. Ask follow-up questions to refine, upload files or photos with the plus button, and choose a model or tool such as Deep Research when needed.

Tips for better results:

- Give context: who you are, the goal and the format you want.
- Ask for step-by-step explanations when learning.
- Upload documents to summarise or question them.
- Use Gems for tasks you repeat.
- Check important facts using the sources it cites.

On Android, Gemini can also act as your phone assistant, activated by holding the power button or saying the wake phrase.

## Is Gemini easy to use?

Yes. Gemini works like a chat app: you type or speak naturally and get answers, with no technical setup. Features such as file uploads, image generation and voice conversations are available from simple buttons.

Getting great results takes a little practice: specific prompts with context work far better than vague ones, and complex tasks benefit from breaking them into steps. Students often start by asking it to explain concepts, quiz them, or summarise notes. Its integration with Google apps, such as Gmail, Docs and Drive, makes it especially convenient for people already using Google services.

## What does Gemini look like?

Gemini looks like a chat interface: a large prompt box at the bottom with buttons for uploads, tools and voice, a model selector, the conversation in the centre, and a sidebar listing past chats, Gems and settings. On phones, it appears as an app or an overlay above other apps.

Responses can include text, images, code blocks, tables and links to sources, with buttons to copy, share, regenerate or export to Google Docs. Canvas opens a side panel for editing documents or code, and Deep Research displays a plan and progress before delivering a report. The design changes as Google updates the product, but the chat-centred layout stays.

## When should I use Gemini Deep Research?

Use Deep Research for questions that need many sources and a structured report: market overviews, comparisons of tools, literature summaries, background research before a project, or planning trips and purchases with detailed criteria.

Do not use it for quick facts or simple questions, where normal chat is faster. Give a clear scope: the question, audience, time period, sources to prioritise and desired structure. Review and edit the research plan before it runs. Deep Research takes several minutes and has daily limits, so save it for questions that genuinely need depth, and verify key claims in the cited sources.

## When should I use Gemini vs NotebookLM?

Use Gemini for general questions, writing, brainstorming, coding and web-connected research. Use NotebookLM when you want answers grounded only in your own sources, such as lecture notes, papers or reports, with citations pointing to exact passages.

NotebookLM is ideal for studying a course, analysing a set of research papers, or onboarding with company documents; it also creates study guides and audio overviews. Gemini is better for open-ended tasks and current information from the web. Many students combine them: NotebookLM to understand course material, Gemini to explore beyond it.

## Should I use Gemini or Bixby?

On Samsung Galaxy phones, use Gemini for open-ended AI tasks such as questions, writing, summarising and image understanding, and Bixby for Samsung-specific device controls, such as changing settings or controlling Samsung apps and devices.

Samsung integrates Gemini into many Galaxy AI features, and you can set Gemini as your default assistant, replacing the side button shortcut if you prefer. Bixby remains useful for quick phone commands and Samsung ecosystem control. Try both for a week with your typical tasks; many users keep Gemini as the main assistant and use Bixby for routines and device settings.

## What does an AI agent look like?

To users, an AI agent often looks like a chat or task panel that shows a plan, the steps it is taking, tool calls such as "searching" or "editing file", progress updates, and requests for approval before important actions. Behind the scenes, it is code connecting a model to tools.

Examples: a coding agent showing file diffs and terminal commands; a research agent displaying sources it is reading; a browser agent highlighting where it clicks; and business agents in dashboards listing tickets processed and actions awaiting approval. Good agent interfaces make every action visible and reversible, so people can trust and correct them.

## What does agentic AI look like in practice?

In practice, agentic AI looks like systems completing multi-step tasks: an assistant that reads incoming invoices, extracts fields, checks them against purchase orders and queues exceptions for a person; or a coding agent that implements a feature, runs tests and opens a pull request for review.

The common pattern is goal, plan, tool use, observation and adjustment, with guardrails such as step limits, permissions and human approvals. Dashboards show what agents did and why, and logs allow audits. Most successful agentic systems today handle narrow, well-defined processes rather than open-ended goals.

## What does Cursor AI look like?

Cursor looks much like Visual Studio Code, because it is built on VS Code: a file explorer, code editor tabs and a terminal, plus an AI side panel for chat and agent mode, inline AI suggestions as you type, and diff views showing proposed AI changes.

You can select code and ask the AI to edit it, chat about the codebase, or let the agent make multi-file changes that you accept or reject. Settings let you choose models and add project rules. VS Code users usually feel at home immediately, and most VS Code extensions and themes work in Cursor.

## What does vibe coding look like?

Vibe coding looks like a conversation with an AI coding tool: you describe a feature, the AI writes code across files, you run the app, describe what is wrong or what to add next, and repeat, often accepting changes without reading every line.

A typical session: "Build a study planner with a calendar view", run it, "add reminders", run it, paste an error, "fix this", and so on, with the app evolving quickly. It feels fast and creative for prototypes. Done responsibly, it also includes git commits after each working step, tests, and reading the parts of the code that handle data and security.

# How to use Hugging Face: Transformers explained, install, cache, tokens and history
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-use-hugging-face/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To use Hugging Face, browse the Hub for a model or dataset, then load it in Python with the Transformers library: a pipeline runs a task in a few lines, and the same library handles fine-tuning. Hugging Face also hosts demos called Spaces and offers paid compute. FineTune Studio is built on Transformers, PEFT and TRL, so I use this stack daily. This page covers what Hugging Face is, how it earns money, how Transformers works, its licence and history, installation, where models are cached, and fixing token errors.

## How do I use Hugging Face?

Create a free account, search the Hub for a model suited to your task, read its model card for usage and licence, then run it with the Transformers library or the model's recommended code. For a quick start, use a pipeline.

```python
from transformers import pipeline
classify = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
print(classify("The new hostel rules are clear and fair."))
```

From there, explore datasets with the `datasets` library, try models in Spaces demos, fine-tune with `Trainer` or TRL, and share your own models and datasets. Use access tokens for gated or private models, and check each model's licence before commercial use. Many models also run through other tools, such as Ollama after conversion. Start with small models so downloads and experiments stay fast on a laptop.

## What is Hugging Face?

Hugging Face is a company and platform at the centre of open AI: the Hub hosts hundreds of thousands of models, datasets and Spaces demos, and its open-source libraries, such as Transformers, Datasets, Tokenizers, PEFT, TRL and Diffusers, make those models usable.

Think of it as GitHub for machine learning: people publish models with model cards, version them with git, and others download, use and fine-tune them. Companies such as Meta, Google, Mistral and Alibaba release open models there. For learners, Hugging Face also provides free courses on NLP, LLMs, agents and diffusion. It started in 2016 as a chatbot app before pivoting to open-source tools. Its community features, such as discussions on model pages, are often the fastest way to learn a model's quirks.

## How does Hugging Face make money?

Hugging Face earns revenue from paid services on top of its free platform: subscriptions such as Pro and Enterprise Hub plans, Inference Endpoints for deploying models on managed infrastructure, paid compute for Spaces, and enterprise contracts with security, support and private hosting.

It has also raised significant venture funding from major technology companies. The model mirrors other open-source businesses: free tools and hosting build a huge community, and organisations pay for convenience, scale, security and support. For individuals and students, nearly everything needed to learn and build is free.

## What is a transformer in Hugging Face?

In Hugging Face, "transformer" refers both to the neural network architecture behind modern language and vision models and to the Transformers library that implements these models. The library provides thousands of pretrained transformer models with a common interface.

The architecture, introduced in 2017, uses self-attention to process sequences, and variants include encoders like BERT for understanding, decoders like Llama and GPT-style models for generation, and encoder-decoders like T5 for translation and summarisation. In the library, each model has a configuration, tokenizer and model class, loaded with `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModel` classes from a Hub name.

## How does Hugging Face Transformers work?

Transformers downloads a model's configuration, weights and tokenizer from the Hub, builds the model in PyTorch, or other supported frameworks, and runs it. The tokenizer converts text to token IDs, the model processes them, and outputs are decoded back to text or labels.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
ids = tok("What is RAG?", return_tensors="pt")
print(tok.decode(model.generate(**ids, max_new_tokens=40)[0]))
```

Pipelines wrap these steps for common tasks. The library also supports quantised loading, multi-GPU inference and training with `Trainer`.

## Is Hugging Face Transformers open source?

Yes. The Transformers library is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, developed on GitHub with thousands of contributors. You can use it freely, including commercially, under the licence terms.

Note that models on the Hub have their own licences, separate from the library: some are fully open, such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, while others have custom licences with restrictions, such as acceptable use policies or limits on commercial use. Always check the model card's licence before deploying a model in a product, especially for client work. Some datasets also carry licences that affect how models trained on them may be used.

## When did Hugging Face Transformers come out?

The library began in late 2018 as "pytorch-pretrained-bert", a PyTorch port of Google's BERT. It was renamed "pytorch-transformers" in 2019 as more models were added, then "transformers" later that year, with TensorFlow support.

Its paper, "Transformers: State-of-the-Art Natural Language Processing", was presented in 2020. Since then, it has grown to support text, vision, audio and multimodal models, quantisation, and integration with training libraries. Its rapid adoption made Hugging Face the default place to share and use open models. Early versions focused on text models like BERT and GPT-2; the library's unified Auto classes, which load any supported architecture by name, were a major reason it spread so quickly through research and industry.

## How do I install the Hugging Face Transformers library?

Install it with pip in a virtual environment, along with PyTorch: `pip install transformers torch`. Add extras as needed, such as `accelerate` for multi-GPU and large models, `datasets` for data, and `peft` and `trl` for fine-tuning.

Steps:

- Create and activate a virtual environment.
- Install PyTorch matching your CUDA version from the PyTorch site if you have a GPU.
- Run `pip install transformers accelerate`.
- Test with a small pipeline example.
- Log in with `huggingface-cli login` or the newer `hf auth login` for gated models.

Pin versions in your requirements file, since new releases sometimes change behaviour.

## Where does Hugging Face Transformers save models?

By default, downloaded models are cached in `~/.cache/huggingface/hub` on Linux and macOS, and in `C:\Users\<you>\.cache\huggingface\hub` on Windows. Each model is stored once and reused across projects.

Change the location by setting the `HF_HOME` environment variable, or `HF_HUB_CACHE` for the hub cache specifically, useful when your system drive is small. You can also pass `cache_dir` when loading a model. Use `huggingface-cli scan-cache` or the newer `hf cache` commands to see sizes and delete unused models. To save a fine-tuned model elsewhere, use `save_pretrained` with your chosen folder.

## How do I fix a "no token found" error when downloading from Hugging Face?

This error usually appears when downloading gated or private models without authentication. Accept the model's licence on its Hub page, create an access token in your account settings, then log in with the CLI or set the `HF_TOKEN` environment variable.

Steps:

- Visit the model page and accept its terms if it is gated.
- Create a read access token in Hugging Face settings.
- Run `huggingface-cli login` or `hf auth login` and paste the token.
- Or set `HF_TOKEN` in your environment or `.env` file.
- Retry the download.

Never commit tokens to git. If you use notebooks on shared platforms, store the token in the platform's secrets feature.

# How to win a hackathon: what judges score, how to pick an idea, and the demo that works live, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is a hackathon?

**A hackathon is a timed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, sometimes a few weeks online, where small teams build a working prototype that solves a stated problem and then pitch it to judges. The output is a demo, not a plan. The prize is usually cash, credits or an incubation offer, but the lasting value is the project, the repository and the people you built it with.**


The word blends "hack", in the sense of building something quickly, with "marathon". In India the format ranges from a two-day event in a college seminar hall to Smart India Hackathon, the government-run national competition with a months-long process [1]. AI hackathons are the same format with problem statements that expect a model, an agent or a data pipeline in the solution.

I have been on both sides of the table: three first prizes as a builder, at IIT Roorkee, CSJMU and MeetKats, a loss I learned more from than any win, and time as a judge and mentor at college events. This page is the version of the talk I give students, with the parts that made the difference between winning and not.

> Every hackathon I won, we solved a smaller problem than the teams we beat. Every hackathon I lost, we tried to solve a bigger one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does a hackathon work?

**Registration opens weeks ahead. Teams form, usually two to five people. On the day, organisers reveal or confirm the problem statements, the timer starts, and teams build. Mentors circulate. At the end, each team submits code and a short deck and gets a few minutes to demo and answer questions. Judges score against a rubric, and prizes follow.**



The single most important line in that timeline is "skeleton with the demo path stubbed end to end" in the first six hours. A team that can click through a fake version of the final demo at hour 6 will have a real one at hour 30. A team that builds features in isolation integrates at hour 33 and demos a crash.

## How do I find and join a hackathon in India?

**Devfolio and Unstop list most Indian college and company hackathons, Major League Hacking lists student events worldwide, Devpost covers global online ones, and Smart India Hackathon runs through colleges via its official portal. Follow the tech clubs of IITs, NITs and nearby colleges on Instagram and LinkedIn, because campus hackathons are announced there first. Register early; good events fill.**



Sources for these listings are the platforms themselves [2][3][4][5]. My recommendation for a first-year: one campus hackathon within a two-hour train ride, in person, before any online one. You learn more from watching thirty teams demo in one room than from a month of tutorials.

### Can a beginner participate in a hackathon?

**Yes, and you should, before you feel ready. Most college hackathons have a beginner track or no prerequisites at all. Join a team where one person can already build a basic web or Python app, take the role that matches what you can do, design, research, presentation, testing, and build the skill of finishing under a deadline. Nobody is judged on their first hackathon; they are judged on their demo.**


## How do I pick a hackathon idea that can win?

**Pick a problem a specific person has, that you can demonstrate end to end in three minutes, where the hardest part is something your team can actually build in the time you have. Start from the problem statement's audience, list five problems that person has, choose the one with the clearest before-and-after, and cut everything that is not on the path from the user's pain to your demo.**


Ideas that won for us, and why:

- **KrishGyan, Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee.** Farming advice in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp: pest control, crop health and weather, spoken back, no reading or typing needed. It won because the demo was a voice note in and a voice note out, which any judge could follow, and because the audience was real and underserved [6].
- **BrandHive, Product Genesis at CSJMU.** A platform for small businesses and emerging influencers to grow organically without a marketing budget. It won because we showed the whole loop, not a slide of features [7].
- **Annapurna, BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats.** Coordinating surplus food between donors, NGOs and volunteers, with four roles and a verified-impact layer. It won on clarity of roles and a demo that walked one meal from a hotel kitchen to a shelter [8].

And the one that did not: STROT, where we built more and explained less, and a simpler team took the prize [9]. That loss is why every timeline I give now starts with cutting scope.


### What are good AI hackathon project ideas?

**The winning AI ideas apply a model to one narrow workflow with real inputs: voice-first advice for people who do not type, document extraction for a specific paper form, a RAG assistant over one institution's documents, a vision check for one quality problem, an agent that completes one repetitive task end to end. "ChatGPT for X" loses to "this one task, done, with this evidence".**


A frame that produces ideas fast: pick an audience, farmers, first-year students, small shops, clinics, college offices; pick a friction, a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document; ask what the AI removes. KrishGyan came out of exactly that frame: farmers, the reading barrier, voice.

## What do hackathon judges actually look for?

**Judges score four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not just a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually use it; and problem solving, did you understand the problem before you built. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. A working demo of a modest idea beats a slide deck of a grand one every time.**



These four criteria, feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a room as a judge, and the ones I wrote about after sitting on panels [10]. The weights change; the questions do not.


### What questions do judges ask in Q&A?

**Who is this for and have you spoken to them? What happens when this fails? How is this different from the existing solution? What would you build next with a month? Which part did you write yourselves versus take from a library? Judges use Q&A to find out whether you understand your own project, so short honest answers beat confident vague ones.**


## How do I pitch a hackathon project?

**In three minutes: thirty seconds on who has the problem and what it costs them, ninety seconds of live demo on the happy path, thirty seconds on how it works with one architecture slide, and thirty seconds on what you would do next and what you are asking for. Say the user's name, not the technology's, in the first sentence. Rehearse it three times with a timer.**



For Smart India Hackathon the format is more formal and the template is prescribed, but the same order inside it wins: problem, demo, how, next. Teams that open with a slide of technologies lose the room in the first fifteen seconds.

### How do I give a demo that works live?

**Freeze your code at least two hours before demos. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine you will present from, on the venue Wi-Fi if you can. Seed the data so the demo never depends on a live network call you do not control. Record a backup video of the full path and have it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk.**


The demo that failed for us at STROT failed on a live API call over venue Wi-Fi. Every demo since has run on seeded data with a recorded fallback, and none has failed.

## How should a hackathon team be formed?

**Three people with three roles: one who builds the core, one who owns the interface and the data, one who owns the problem, the deck and the pitch and also tests everything. Decide roles before the event, not at hour one. A friend who cannot code but can research users and present is worth more than a fourth developer.**


Every first prize we won was a team of three with those roles. Teams of five spend their first three hours negotiating and their last three merging conflicts.


## What is Smart India Hackathon and how do I crack it?

**Smart India Hackathon is a national competition run by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell in which student teams solve problem statements posted by government ministries and industry. Teams register through their college, are shortlisted internally, then compete at the national level. To do well: pick a problem statement whose owner you can reach, build a working prototype early, and make the presentation about the ministry's outcome, not your stack.**


The official portal carries the current year's problem statements, timeline and eligibility, and it changes each cycle, so read it rather than any summary, including this one [1]. What stays constant: the internal college round eliminates most teams, so treat the internal presentation as the real competition, and the national judges are domain experts from the problem's ministry, so the domain matters more than the demo polish.

## Do hackathons help your career or resume?

**Yes, when you turn them into evidence: a public repository with a readable README, a two-minute demo video, and a short write-up of the problem, the decision you made and the result. A line saying "participated in 6 hackathons" does nothing. A line saying "1st prize, Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee, built a voice-first farming assistant over WhatsApp" with a link does the work of a semester of grades.**


On LinkedIn, add the hackathon under Honours & awards with the issuer and date, and post the demo video the same week; hackathon posts travel further than any other student content, in my experience running a 500-member community. On the resume, one line per win, with the problem and the result, and the repository link.

## What mistakes make teams lose?

**Building for 34 hours and presenting for 2. Choosing a problem to impress rather than to solve. No roles, so everyone builds the same screen. A live demo that depends on Wi-Fi. A deck that opens with the tech stack. Not talking to a single real user. Sleeping zero hours and demoing incoherently. Every one of these is cheaper to avoid than to recover from.**



## What should I do after the hackathon?

**Within a week: clean the repository, write the README, publish the demo video, and post the story. Within a month: decide whether the project deserves users, and if so, ship the smallest real version. Annapurna went from a hackathon prize to a tool people used because we kept the roles that worked and threw away the parts built for the judges.**



## Can I invite a judge or mentor to my college hackathon?

**Yes. Organisers can reach me for judging, mentoring or a session on hackathon strategy before your event, on-site across India or remote. What I need from you is the date, the format, the problem statements if fixed, and the rubric you plan to use, or I will bring the four-criteria one above.**


The details and the invite form are at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite, and my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com. Free for student communities.

# How to win hackathons: what winners do, what to learn, using AI, and are they worth it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-hackathons/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To win hackathons, choose a specific real problem, build one complete working flow rather than many half-features, make the demo reliable, and pitch it clearly: user, problem, live demo, how it works, impact. Teams that finish and explain well beat teams with bigger ideas and broken demos. I have won first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, finished top three at an IIT Kanpur hackathon, and mentored at more than ten, so this page shares what actually works.

## How do I win hackathons?

Win by solving a narrow, real problem for a specific user, delivering a working end-to-end demo, and pitching it with clarity and evidence. Judges remember one flow that works far more than ambitious plans.

A winning approach:

- Spend the first hour defining the user, problem and one core flow.
- Deploy a skeleton early so integration problems surface quickly.
- Cut features ruthlessly; finish the core.
- Polish the demo path and record a backup video.
- Prepare a pitch: problem, demo, how it works, impact, next steps.
- Rehearse answers about technical choices and limitations.

Pick themes where you have domain insight; it shows. Talk to mentors early in the event: they often know what judges care about and can save you hours of wrong turns.

## How do people actually win hackathons?

Most winners combine a sharp problem statement, a demo that works live, and a confident, honest pitch. Behind that, they usually come prepared: a team with clear roles, a familiar tech stack, starter templates and experience from previous events.

KrishGyan won Changethon 2025 because the demo showed exactly the promised flow: a farmer asking a question in their own voice and language over WhatsApp and getting useful advice. Annapurna won BYTEBATTLE by coordinating surplus food with a simple, working system. Neither was the most technically complex project in the room; both solved a clear problem and worked flawlessly on stage.

## What should I learn to win hackathons?

Learn to build a complete app fast: one front-end framework, one back-end framework, a database, deployment, and calling AI model APIs. Add Git teamwork, basic UI design and pitching. Depth in a fast stack beats shallow knowledge of many.

A practical skill set:

- Next.js or React for the front end.
- FastAPI or Node.js for the back end.
- PostgreSQL or Supabase for data and auth.
- LLM APIs, embeddings and simple RAG for AI features.
- Deploying to Vercel, Railway or similar in minutes.
- Figma basics and a clean component library.
- A three-minute pitch structure.

Practise by building small projects in one day before events. Keep a personal starter template with authentication, a database connection and deployment already configured, so the event's hours go into the problem itself.

## How do I win hackathons with AI?

Use AI in two ways: as a building assistant, speeding up coding, debugging and design, and as a product feature, such as retrieval-augmented answers, document understanding, voice interfaces or agents that solve the user's problem.

Judges are now used to AI projects, so a chatbot wrapper rarely impresses. Stand out by grounding AI in real data with citations, handling local languages, adding evaluation or confidence checks, and showing why AI is necessary for the problem. Be ready to explain your model choices, prompts, failure cases and costs. Read each event's rules on AI-assisted coding and disclose use where required.

## Are hackathons worth it?

Yes, for most students. Even without winning, you gain fast, practical learning, portfolio projects, teamwork experience, mentors' feedback, and connections with peers, sponsors and recruiters. Wins add credibility and sometimes internships or funding.

They are less worth it if you attend many events without finishing projects or reflecting on lessons, or if they hurt your studies and health. Choose events that match your interests, prepare beforehand, and continue your best projects afterwards. Several opportunities in my own journey came from people I met at hackathons, which no certificate captures.

## What does the community say about whether hackathons are worth it?

Community discussions, such as on Reddit, generally say hackathons are worth it for learning, networking and portfolio building, especially early in your career, while warning against treating them as guaranteed paths to jobs or chasing participation certificates.

Common advice: go with a goal, such as learning a new framework or meeting companies; prioritise events with good mentors and sponsors; build something you would show in an interview; and avoid burnout from back-to-back events. Some experienced developers say returns diminish after many events, at which point open source or internships may teach more.

## What are hackathons in college?

College hackathons are coding events organised by colleges, student clubs, tech fests or companies, where student teams build projects in a fixed time, often 24 to 36 hours, judged on innovation, execution and presentation.

They range from internal department events to national competitions such as Smart India Hackathon, where colleges first run internal rounds. College hackathons are usually beginner-friendly, with mentors, workshops and themes relevant to students. They are an excellent first step: you learn to build quickly, work in a team, and present your work, skills that matter in placements and beyond.

## Which hackathons should I join in college?

Start with your college's internal hackathons and beginner-friendly online events, then join inter-college and national events as your skills grow. Smart India Hackathon, tech fest hackathons at IITs and NITs, and company-sponsored events are strong options.

A progression:

- **First year**: internal events and online beginner hackathons.
- **Second year**: inter-college and tech fest hackathons, one themed event in your interest area.
- **Third year onwards**: national events, company challenges and Smart India Hackathon.

Follow Devfolio, Unstop and Major League Hacking for listings, and choose events with mentors and clear judging.

## What are the best hackathons for college students?

Strong choices include Smart India Hackathon, Major League Hacking member events, hackathons at IIT and NIT tech fests, company challenges such as those run by large technology firms, Web3 and AI-themed events on Devfolio, and Google's student programmes such as the Solution Challenge when running.

"Best" depends on your goals: national recognition, learning a new technology, meeting specific companies or building social impact projects. Look at past winners and sponsor lists to judge quality. Well-organised events publish clear rules and judging criteria, provide mentors and treat participants well.

## Do hackathons look good on college applications?

Yes. For college or postgraduate applications, hackathons show initiative, practical skills, teamwork and the ability to build under pressure. Wins or strong projects with real users stand out more than participation alone.

Describe them concretely: what problem you solved, your role, the technology, and results such as awards or users. Link to code or a demo if the application allows. For job applications, hackathon projects work the same way on resumes. One meaningful project you continued developing after the event is more impressive than a long list of participations.

# How to write a tech resume as a fresher in India: the one-page format, what to put instead of a skills wall, and a free resume website that beats a PDF
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-a-tech-resume-for-freshers-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should a fresher write a tech resume?

**One page. A header with your name, one line describing what you build, and links to email, GitHub and a portfolio, no photo, no objective paragraph. A projects section with three entries, each with the problem, the decision, and a measurable outcome, ahead of education. A short skills line, not a wall. Education below projects, since for a fresher the projects are the evidence and the degree is context. Nothing that needs a second page has earned its place yet.**


I have reviewed enough fresher resumes at hackathons and campus sessions to see the same mistakes repeat: a skills wall with forty items, an objective paragraph nobody reads, and projects buried under a "certifications" section three times its length. This page is the fix, plus the free resume-website option that often works better than the PDF itself [6].

> A resume is not a list of everything you know. It is three pieces of evidence that you can do the job, arranged so a tired recruiter finds them in ten seconds.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should be at the top of the resume?

**Your name, a phone number, an email you actually check, and three links: GitHub, a portfolio or LinkedIn, and one more if relevant. Under that, one line: what you build and one proof, the same sentence your LinkedIn headline should carry [3]. Not "Computer Science student seeking opportunities". Not a paragraph. One sentence a recruiter can read while scrolling past forty other resumes.**



## What goes in the projects section, and how should it read?

**Three projects, each three lines: the problem in one sentence, the decision or hard part in one sentence, and the outcome in one sentence, ideally with a number. "Built a RAG system over 40 pages of college documents; added a confidence gate after early demos returned wrong answers confidently; recall at 5 improved from 61 percent to 89 percent, measured on a 30-question set." That is one project entry. It proves you can scope, iterate, and measure, in three lines.**



My guide to which projects to choose for this section, and the ones that actually get interviews, is written up separately [7].

## Should I have a skills section, and what should it look like?

**A short line or two, grouped by category, not a wall with progress bars: "Languages: Python, JavaScript. Tools: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Git, Docker." No percentages, no five-star ratings for how well you know a language, which nobody trusts and which ATS systems ignore anyway. List what you can actually discuss for ten minutes in an interview, and nothing you would freeze on if asked a follow-up question.**




## How do I get past an ATS without gaming it?

**Use plain, standard section headings, Experience, Projects, Education, Skills, so parsing software reads them correctly. Avoid tables, columns, text boxes and graphics that confuse a parser, however good they look to a human eye. Mirror the language of the job posting honestly where it matches what you actually did, a posting that says "REST APIs" should be met with "REST APIs" in your resume if that is what you built, not a synonym. None of this is gaming a system; it is writing clearly enough that both a machine and a human parse the same document correctly.**


## What should education look like for a fresher?

**Degree, institution, graduation year, and a CGPA only if it genuinely helps, one line, below the projects section. Coursework only if a specific course is directly relevant and not implied by the degree itself. No list of every subject studied. A recruiter reading a fresher's resume already expects a degree; the projects section is what differentiates one BCA or B.Tech graduate from another.**


## Should I use a resume website instead of a PDF?

**Both, for different moments. Send a clean one-page PDF when a form or an email asks for a resume, since that is the expected format. Link a simple resume or portfolio website in the header for everyone who wants more, because it can hold live demo links, a longer project write-up, and updates without you re-sending a file [6]. A resume website is not a replacement for the PDF; it is the deeper layer the PDF's links point to.**



## What mistakes do freshers make on tech resumes?

**A two-page resume with a full page of certificates and half a project. An objective paragraph that says nothing a recruiter could not guess. A skills wall claiming expert-level everything. Projects described by technology stack instead of outcome, "Built using React, Node.js, MongoDB" with no sentence on what it did or what was hard. Broken links to private repositories. A resume never updated after the first draft, still listing a project from first year as the newest thing built.**



## Tech resume interview questions

**Not asked directly, but tested by every "walk me through a project" question: can you defend every line on the resume for ten minutes without notes. If a bullet point cannot survive a follow-up question, it should not be on the resume. The strongest resumes are the ones the candidate wrote entirely from memory of what they actually did.**



## Where should I start?

**Cut your current resume to one page tonight: header, three projects in three lines each, a short skills line, education last. Then link a portfolio site from the header.** For a resume and portfolio workshop that turns a semester of projects into an interview-ready one-pager, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
