# How to write a speaker bio: length, what to include, examples, and a template
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-speaker-bio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A speaker bio is a short, third-person summary of who you are, what you have done and what you speak about, used by organisers in brochures, websites, social posts and on-stage introductions. A good one makes people want to hear you in a few seconds. I have spoken at more than 20 campus sessions and keep bios in several lengths for organisers, so this page covers what a speaker bio is, length, what to include, examples, short bios, writing your own, conference and college fest bios, and a template.

## What is a speaker bio?

A speaker bio is a brief professional introduction, usually written in the third person, that event organisers use to present you to audiences. It explains your current role, credibility and topic, and is often read aloud by the host before you speak.

It appears on event websites, programmes, posters, social media announcements and speaker slides. Unlike a resume, it is selective and audience-focused: it highlights what makes you relevant to this audience and topic, not your whole career. Keep a headshot and links ready alongside it, since organisers usually ask for both together.

## How do I write a speaker bio?

Start with your name and what you do now, add two or three specific achievements that prove credibility, connect them to the topic you speak about, and end with a personal touch or a call to action, such as where to find you.

Steps:

- Write a one-line positioning statement: who you are and what you do.
- List achievements with numbers: projects shipped, people taught, awards won.
- Pick the two or three most relevant to the audience.
- State your speaking topics in plain language.
- Write in the third person, in active voice.
- Read it aloud; it should sound natural when a host introduces you.

## How long should a speaker bio be?

Keep three versions: a short bio of about 50 words for social posts and programmes, a medium bio of about 100 words for event pages, and a long bio of about 200 words for detailed listings. A host introduction should take under 30 seconds to read.

Organisers often give word limits; follow them exactly. Longer is not better: the audience only remembers a few facts, so choose the strongest ones. If you speak on different topics, keep topic-specific variants that emphasise relevant experience. Update all versions whenever you have a new achievement, so you never send outdated information.

## What should I include in a speaker bio?

Include your name, current role and organisation, your area of expertise, two or three specific achievements, your speaking topics, and optionally a human detail and where to connect with you. Leave out unrelated jobs, long lists and vague adjectives.

Specifics beat claims: "has mentored more than 200 students since 2023" is stronger than "passionate mentor". Mention credentials only if they matter to the audience. Use numbers, named products, awards and events. Avoid inflating anything; organisers and audiences notice, and credibility is the whole point of a bio. A short personal note, such as a hobby or mission, makes you relatable.

## What are some speaker bio examples?

Here is my own medium-length bio as an example: "Pranjul Rathour leads engineering at SCULT INDIA, an AI-first studio, where he heads a 14-member team. In 2026 he shipped five production AI applications, from a RAG platform to browser-based face recognition. He has mentored more than 200 students since 2023, won first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee and Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025, and speaks on building and shipping AI products."

Notice the structure: current role, proof with numbers, recognitions, then speaking topic. A designer's bio might highlight products designed and users reached; a researcher's might highlight publications and applications. Adapt the structure, not the wording.

## How do I write a short speaker bio?

For about 50 words, keep three elements: who you are now, one or two strongest proofs, and what you speak about. Cut everything else.

Example: "Pranjul Rathour leads engineering at SCULT INDIA and has shipped five production AI apps. He has mentored over 200 students and won first prizes at Changethon 2025 and Vividhotsava 2025. He speaks on building real AI projects and careers in AI."

Short bios are used on posters, social media and programmes where space is tight, so they should still be specific. Avoid starting with "I am passionate about"; start with your role and results. Read it in ten seconds; if it takes longer, trim.

## How do I write a speaker bio for myself?

Write in the third person, as if someone else were describing you, because hosts read bios aloud and programmes present them that way. Gather facts first, choose the most relevant, then write plainly without modesty or exaggeration.

Many people find self-promotion awkward; treat it as reporting facts. Ask a friend or mentor what they would say about you, which often reveals strengths you underplay. Get feedback on a draft from someone in your target audience. For first-person contexts, such as your own website's about page or LinkedIn, rewrite the same content in the first person, keeping the same specifics.

## How do I write a speaker bio for a conference?

Match the conference's audience and theme: emphasise expertise and results relevant to the track, mention your organisation and role clearly, and include the topic of your talk. Follow the organiser's word limit and format, and submit a professional headshot.

Conference audiences care about credibility in the specific domain, so highlight related work: systems built, research, open-source projects, or past talks. Include links if the platform allows, such as your website or LinkedIn. Avoid listing everything you have done; choose what makes attendees think "this person can teach me something useful about this topic".

## How do I write a speaker bio that gets me booked for college fests?

Show students why you are relevant to them: practical achievements they aspire to, such as shipped projects, hackathon wins, internships or startups, plus the specific value of your session, like a roadmap, live demo or career guidance. Make it easy to invite you.

College organisers look for speakers who connect with students, not just impressive titles. Mention past campus sessions and audience sizes, for example a seminar for over 100 first-year students, and offer clear session formats and topics. Include a link to an invite page with your topics, formats and contact details, which makes it easy for organisers to say yes quickly.

## Is there a speaker bio template?

Yes. Use this structure and fill in your details: "[Name] is [role] at [organisation], where [what you do]. [Key achievement with a number]. [Second achievement or recognition]. [He/She/They] [speak/speaks] on [topics], helping [audience] [outcome]. [Optional personal detail or where to connect]."

Example filled in: "Riya Sharma is a backend engineer at a fintech startup, where she builds payment APIs used by thousands of merchants. She won first prize at a national hackathon in 2025. She speaks on APIs, system design and internships, helping students land their first engineering roles." Adapt each sentence to your audience and keep versions in three lengths.

# What is a technical blog? How to start, write great posts, length, and examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-technical-blog/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A technical blog is a blog where developers, engineers or companies share explanations, tutorials, project write-ups and lessons about technology, written for practitioners who want to understand or build something. Writing one deepens your own understanding, builds a public record of your skills, and helps others solve problems. I document projects such as RAG.NextUpgrad and FineTune Studio in public write-ups, so this page covers what technical blogs and posts are, starting and creating one, writing great posts, length, examples, platforms, and blogs in technical communication.

## What is a technical blog?

A technical blog publishes articles about technical topics: how-to tutorials, explanations of concepts, project case studies, debugging stories, comparisons of tools, and opinion pieces grounded in experience. Its audience is usually developers, engineers, students or technical decision-makers.

Individuals use technical blogs to learn in public and build reputation; companies use engineering blogs to share how they build systems, attract talent and support users. The best technical blogs combine accuracy with clear writing and practical value: readers should leave able to do or understand something they could not before. Many developers say writing regularly made them better engineers, because explaining a system exposes gaps that coding alone can hide.

## What is a technical blog post?

A technical blog post is a single article that explains a specific technical topic or solves a specific problem, often with code, diagrams, commands and results. Common types are tutorials, explainers, case studies, troubleshooting guides and comparisons.

A strong post has a clear title stating the problem, a short introduction with context and what the reader will get, structured sections with steps or explanations, working code samples, visuals, a summary, and links to sources or repositories. It respects the reader's time by getting to the point and showing rather than only telling. It also states the versions of tools and libraries used, so readers know whether the instructions still apply.

## How do I start a technical blog?

Pick a platform, choose a focus area, and publish your first post about something you recently learned or built. Do not wait for the perfect design or a long list of ideas; consistency matters more than launch polish.

Starting steps:

- Choose topics you work on, such as RAG, web development or DevOps.
- Set up a blog on your own domain or a developer platform.
- Write your first post on a problem you solved this month.
- Publish on a regular schedule, such as twice a month.
- Share posts where your audience is, such as LinkedIn and communities.
- Keep a list of ideas from questions you get asked.

## How do I create a technical blog site?

Create one with a static site generator, such as Astro, Hugo, Jekyll or Next.js, hosted free on GitHub Pages, Vercel or Netlify, or use a developer blogging platform such as Hashnode or dev.to that handles hosting for you.

Owning your domain is valuable long term: your content and search ranking stay yours even if platforms change. A common approach is to publish on your own site and cross-post to dev.to or Hashnode with a canonical link pointing back. Make sure the site supports code highlighting, images, RSS, good mobile reading and fast loading. Keep posts in Markdown in a git repository for easy versioning. Add simple analytics to learn which posts readers find through search, and write more on those topics.

## How do I write a technical blog post?

Start with the reader's problem, show the solution step by step with working code and results, explain why each step matters, and end with a summary and next steps. Write a draft quickly, then edit for clarity and accuracy.

A writing process:

- Define the reader and the one thing they should learn.
- Outline sections before writing.
- Write the steps and code first, then the explanations.
- Test every code sample exactly as published.
- Add diagrams or screenshots where words are slow.
- Cut unnecessary words and jargon; define terms you keep.
- Ask someone to follow the post and note where they got stuck.

## What makes a great technical blog?

Great technical blogs are accurate, specific, practical and honest. Each post solves a real problem, includes tested code and evidence, explains trade-offs, and admits limitations. Readers trust them because the author clearly built and measured what they describe.

Other qualities: clear titles that match what people search for; consistent publishing; readable formatting with headings, short paragraphs and code highlighting; diagrams for architecture; and links to sources and repositories. Original experience is the strongest differentiator, such as "how we cut retrieval failures by adding keyword search", which generic AI-written content cannot copy.

## How long should a technical blog post be?

As long as needed to solve the problem completely, and no longer. Quick fixes can be a few hundred words; tutorials and deep dives often run 1,000 to 2,500 words or more. Readers value completeness more than brevity for technical topics.

Structure matters more than length: use headings so readers can skim to the part they need, put the answer or key steps early, and move long background to linked posts. If a post grows beyond 3,000 words, consider splitting it into a series. Measure engagement, such as time on page and comments, to learn what your readers find useful.

## What are some technical blog examples?

Strong examples include company engineering blogs from Netflix, Stripe, Cloudflare, Uber and Airbnb, which explain how they build large systems, and individual blogs by engineers who write deep, practical posts on programming, AI and infrastructure.

Study examples for structure and tone: how they state the problem, use diagrams, share numbers, and explain decisions. Cloudflare's posts are known for detailed incident analyses; Stripe's for clarity; many individual blogs for honest learning journeys. For AI topics, look for posts that include evaluation results rather than just demos, which is what separates practical engineering writing from hype.

## What are the best technical blog sites and platforms?

For hosting your own blog, GitHub Pages, Vercel and Netlify with a static site generator are popular and free. For built-in audiences, dev.to, Hashnode and Medium are common developer platforms. For reading, engineering blogs and aggregators such as Hacker News surface quality posts.

Choose based on goals: own your domain for long-term reputation and search ranking; use platforms for initial reach; combine both with canonical links. Avoid platforms that paywall or restrict your content if you want maximum reach. Whatever you use, keep source files backed up so you can move platforms later. Writing consistently in one place builds an audience faster than scattering posts across many platforms.

## What is a blog in technical communication?

In technical communication, a blog is an informal, regularly updated channel for sharing technical information, such as product updates, tutorials, release notes, best practices and stories, complementing formal documentation such as manuals and API references.

Blogs are more conversational and timely than documentation, helping explain why changes happened and how to use new features. Technical writers use them to reach users, gather feedback and support community learning. Frameworks such as Diátaxis distinguish tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation; blog posts often blend tutorial and explanation styles, linking to official documentation for reference details.

# How transformers work in AI: next tokens, positions, GPT, encoders and long inputs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-transformers-work-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Transformers are the neural network architecture behind modern language models such as GPT, Claude and Gemini. Introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, they use self-attention to relate every token to every other token in parallel. I fine-tune transformer models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio, so this page covers what transformers are, how LLMs work, next-token prediction, positional encoding, why GPT is a transformer, encoders and decoders, input limits, long sequences, gibberish output and workshop ideas. What are transformers in AI? Transformers are a neural network architecture that processes sequences, such as text, by using self-attention to weigh how much each token relates to every other token. They power large language models, translation, speech recognition and vision models. Before transformers, recurrent networks processed text one word at a time, which was slow and struggled with long-range connections. Transformers process all tokens in parallel, making training on huge datasets efficient on GPUs. A transformer stacks layers, each with multi-head attention and a feed-forward network, plus residual connections and normalisation. The same design now handles images in vision transformers, audio in Whisper and protein structures, making it the most influential architecture in modern AI. How do LLM transformers work? An LLM transformer converts text into tokens, maps each token to an embedding vector, passes the vectors through many layers of self-attention and feed-forward networks, and outputs a probability for every possible next token. In each attention layer, every token creates query, key and value vectors. Attention scores, computed from queries and keys, decide how much each token draws information from earlier tokens, so a pronoun can attend to the noun it refers to. Multiple heads capture different relationships in parallel. Stacking dozens of layers builds increasingly abstract representations. Training adjusts billions of weights so predictions match real text, and later fine-tuning teaches the model to follow instructions and hold conversations. How is the next token predicted in transformers? The final layer produces a score, or logit, for every token in the vocabulary. A softmax turns these into probabilities, and a decoding method picks one token, which is appended to the input before predicting the next. Greedy decoding always picks the most likely token, which is predictable but can repeat. Sampling adds variety: temperature reshapes the probabilities, while top-k and top-p limit choices to likely candidates. This loop repeats token by token until the model emits an end token or hits a length limit. A key-value cache stores earlier attention results, so each new token needs only incremental computation. That is why longer outputs take proportionally longer to generate. What is positional encoding in the transformer model? Positional encoding gives a transformer information about token order, since self-attention alone treats input as an unordered set. The original transformer added fixed sine and cosine patterns of different frequencies to each token's embedding. Also asked as: what is the positional encoding in the transformer model Without position information, the cat chased the dog and the dog chased the cat would look identical. Later models use alternatives: learned position embeddings in GPT-2 and BERT, and rotary position embeddings, called RoPE, in Llama, Qwen and many modern models, which encode relative positions by rotating query and key vectors. ALiBi adds distance-based penalties to attention scores. Methods such as RoPE scaling help extend context length beyond what a model saw during training. Why is GPT called a transformer? GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer: generative because it produces text, pre-trained because it first learns from huge text datasets, and transformer because its architecture is a decoder-only transformer. OpenAI introduced GPT in 2018, building on the 2017 transformer paper but keeping only the decoder stack with masked self-attention, which lets each token attend only to earlier tokens. This suits next-token prediction. Later versions scaled the same idea with more parameters, more data and training techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback. Reasoning models add training that encourages longer thinking before answering, but they remain transformer-based in their core architecture. When should you use an encoder, a decoder or both in a transformer? Use encoder-only models, such as BERT, for understanding tasks like classification, search embeddings and entity extraction. Use decoder-only models, such as GPT and Llama, for generating text. Use encoder-decoder models, such as T5, for transforming input into output, like translation or summarisation. Also asked as: which situation will helpful using encoder or decoder or both in transformer model Encoders see the whole input at once, which gives rich representations for embeddings and classifiers, and they are smaller and cheaper to run. Decoder-only models dominate today because one model can handle almost any task through prompting, including summarisation and translation. Encoder-decoder models remain strong for speech recognition, as in Whisper, and specialised translation. In RAG systems, an encoder often creates embeddings for retrieval while a decoder writes the answer. Why do transformers have a fixed input length? Transformers have a maximum context length because self-attention compares every token with every other, so memory and compute grow quadratically with length, and because models are trained on sequences up to a certain length. Position encodings are also learned or tuned for a specific range, so performance degrades beyond it. Context limits have grown from 512 tokens in BERT to hundreds of thousands or millions in modern models, thanks to efficient attention kernels such as FlashAttention, RoPE scaling and training on longer sequences. Still, long inputs cost more, and models may overlook information in the middle of long contexts. Exceeding the limit causes truncation or errors, so long documents need chunking. How do you handle long sequences with transformers? Split long inputs into chunks that fit the context window, use retrieval to pass only relevant parts, or choose a long-context model. For summarisation, process chunks separately and combine the summaries in a second pass. Also asked as: how to handle long sequences with transformers Retrieval-augmented generation is often the best approach: index the document, retrieve the most relevant passages for each question and send only those, which is how RAG.NextUpgrad and the document-scoped RAG in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace work. For classification of long texts, sliding windows with overlap and aggregated predictions help. Technically, efficient attention variants, such as sparse attention or sliding-window attention, extend practical lengths. Always test whether the model actually uses information from all parts of a long input. Why is my transformer language model generating meaningless text? Meaningless output usually comes from a mismatched tokenizer, a wrong chat template, broken or overly aggressive quantization, bad sampling settings such as very high temperature, an undertrained model, or a fine-tune that damaged the base model. Check that the tokenizer matches the model exactly, and apply the model's chat template for instruction-tuned models. Lower the temperature and set a sensible repetition penalty. If you trained the model, inspect the loss curve: a loss that never fell means undertraining, while gibberish after fine-tuning often signals a learning rate that was too high or data formatting errors. Test the base model first to isolate whether the problem lies in your changes. FineTune Studio's base-versus-tuned comparison catches this early. What are good transformers workshop ideas? Good workshop ideas include visualising attention in a small pretrained model, building a tiny character-level transformer from scratch, comparing tokenizers, and fine-tuning a small model on a classification task with Hugging Face Transformers. For beginners, start with a hands-on demo: tokenize sentences, predict next tokens and adjust temperature to see the effects. For intermediate groups, implement self-attention in NumPy or PyTorch and train a tiny model on a small text dataset, following Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT. Advanced sessions can cover LoRA fine-tuning, RAG pipelines or evaluation. Keep each session project-based, with notebooks that run on free Google Colab GPUs, so every participant leaves with working code.

# How does a vector database work? Examples, choosing one, and do you need it for RAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-vector-databases-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector database stores embeddings, numeric vectors that represent meaning, together with the original data and metadata, and answers queries by finding the vectors closest to a query vector. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes make this fast even over millions of items. That is the retrieval step behind semantic search and RAG. This page explains how it works and what vector search is, gives examples, helps you choose, answers whether RAG needs one and how to build one, covers Supabase, NoSQL and dimensions, and whether vector databases are dead.

## How does a vector database work?

You insert items with an embedding vector, an ID and metadata. The database adds each vector to an index. At query time, you send a query vector, and the database uses the index to return the nearest stored vectors, optionally filtered by metadata.

Exact search compares the query with every vector, which is slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate indexes. HNSW builds a layered graph where each vector links to near neighbours, and search walks the graph towards the query. Inverted-file indexes cluster vectors and search only the nearest clusters. Product quantisation compresses vectors to save memory. Databases add what libraries lack: persistence, updates and deletes, filtering, access control, replication and scaling.

## What is vector search in a database?

Vector search finds items whose embeddings are most similar to a query embedding, measured by cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. It retrieves by meaning rather than exact words.

For example, searching "laptop overheating" can find a help article titled "fan noise and high temperature on notebooks" even with no shared keywords. Many databases now support vector search alongside their normal queries: PostgreSQL with pgvector, OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, MongoDB Atlas and others. Combining vector search with keyword search, called hybrid search, usually gives the best results, because keywords catch exact terms such as product codes that embeddings blur.

## What are some examples of vector databases?

Examples include pgvector for PostgreSQL, Pinecone as a managed service, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus as open-source dedicated vector databases, Chroma for lightweight local use, and vector search features in OpenSearch, Elasticsearch and MongoDB Atlas.

Related tools that are not full databases: FAISS, a library for fast similarity search in memory, and hnswlib, an index library. Cloud providers also offer vector capabilities in their managed databases and storage services. The landscape changes quickly, but the core ideas, embeddings, approximate indexes, filtering and hybrid search, stay the same across products.

## Which vector database should I choose?

Choose the simplest option that meets your needs: pgvector if you already use PostgreSQL, Chroma or FAISS for prototypes, Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus for a dedicated open-source service, and Pinecone if you want fully managed scaling.

Questions to decide:

- How many vectors now and in a year: thousands, millions or billions?
- Do you need metadata filters, multi-tenancy or access control?
- Do you need keyword plus vector search?
- Who will operate it: your team or a vendor?
- Where must data live for privacy or compliance?

For most student and startup projects, pgvector on a hosted PostgreSQL is enough. Measure retrieval recall on your own questions before switching for performance reasons.

## Does RAG need a vector database?

RAG needs retrieval, not necessarily a dedicated vector database. For small document sets, an in-memory index such as FAISS, or pgvector in your existing database, is enough; some systems even use keyword search alone.

What RAG really needs is good retrieval: clean chunks, a suitable embedding model, hybrid keyword plus vector search, reranking and evaluation. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion and re-ranking in about 220 MB on a free tier, which shows that heavy infrastructure is not required. Move to a dedicated vector database when scale, filtering, concurrency or operations demand it.

## How do I create a vector database for RAG?

Chunk your documents, embed each chunk with one embedding model, store chunks with their vectors and metadata in a vector store, then retrieve with the same model at query time. With PostgreSQL and pgvector, it is a table with a vector column and an index.

```sql
create extension if not exists vector;
create table chunks (id bigserial primary key, doc text, page int, content text, embedding vector(768));
create index on chunks using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
-- query: nearest 5 chunks to a query embedding
select doc, page, content from chunks order by embedding <=> $1 limit 5;
```

Match the vector dimension to your model, add a full-text index for keyword search, and store page numbers for citations.

## Does Supabase have a vector database?

Yes. Supabase supports vector storage and search through pgvector, a PostgreSQL extension, so you can store embeddings next to your other data and query them with SQL or through Supabase's client libraries.

Enable the extension, create a table with a vector column, add an index, and write a database function for similarity search that your app calls. Supabase's AI documentation includes guides for semantic search and RAG. Because it is PostgreSQL, you also get row-level security for access control, joins with user data and transactions, which dedicated vector databases may not offer. For student projects, Supabase's free tier is a convenient way to build a full RAG backend.

## Is a vector database NoSQL?

Usually it is described as a NoSQL-style system, because dedicated vector databases do not use relational tables and SQL as their main model. But vector search also exists inside SQL databases, such as PostgreSQL with pgvector.

Dedicated vector databases expose APIs for collections of points or objects with vectors and metadata, closer to document stores. SQL databases with vector extensions let you mix vector similarity with joins, filters and transactions. The classification matters less than the features you need: query language, filtering, consistency, scale and operations. Many teams prefer keeping vectors in the same database as their application data to avoid syncing two systems.

## Is a vector database 3D?

No. Vectors in a vector database usually have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, such as 384, 768 or 1536, not three. Each dimension is a learned feature of meaning, not a spatial direction.

Three-dimensional pictures of embeddings in tutorials are simplifications made with dimension-reduction methods such as PCA, t-SNE or UMAP, which squash high-dimensional vectors into two or three dimensions for visualisation. They help intuition, showing that similar items cluster, but distances in the picture are distorted. Search always happens in the full high-dimensional space.

## Is the vector database dead?

No, but it is changing. Vector search is becoming a standard feature of general-purpose databases and storage services, long context windows reduce the need for retrieval in some cases, and agentic search with keywords works for some tasks. Dedicated vector databases still matter at large scale and for specialised needs.

The durable part is retrieval itself: most AI applications still need to find the right information quickly, cite it and control access. Whether that runs in a dedicated vector database, PostgreSQL with pgvector, a search engine or a library depends on scale and team. Focus on retrieval quality and evaluation, and keep your design portable, so the storage choice can change as the market does.

# How does vector search work? History, Postgres speed, and other meanings of vector
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-vector-search-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vector search finds items by similarity of meaning or content: an embedding model turns each document, image or query into a vector of numbers, and the search returns the stored vectors closest to the query vector. It powers semantic search, recommendations and the retrieval step in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains how it works and what it is used for, its history, checking vector size, making Postgres vector and trigram search fast, how Postgres became a strong vector database, and the other meanings of "vector" in graphics and physics.

## How does vector search work?

Each item is converted into an embedding vector by a model and stored in an index. A query is embedded with the same model, and the index returns the vectors with the highest similarity, usually cosine similarity or dot product, along with their items.

Comparing a query with every stored vector is exact but slow at scale, so systems use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. HNSW builds a graph linking each vector to near neighbours and walks it towards the query; inverted-file indexes cluster vectors and search only nearby clusters; quantisation compresses vectors to save memory. These trade a little accuracy for large speed gains. In production, vector search is usually combined with keyword search, filters and reranking.

## What is vector searching used for?

Vector searching is used wherever you need to find things that are similar in meaning or content, not just matching words: semantic search, question answering over documents, recommendations, duplicate detection, image and audio search, and memory for AI agents.

Examples: a support portal that finds help articles for a question phrased differently from the article; an e-commerce site that recommends similar products; a photo app that finds pictures by description; and a RAG chatbot that retrieves passages from a college handbook before answering. Its weakness is exact identifiers, such as order numbers, which keyword search handles better, so hybrid search is common.

## How long have vector databases been around?

Similarity search over vectors has been studied for decades in information retrieval and computer science, but dedicated vector databases as a product category became prominent around 2019 to 2022, driven by deep learning embeddings and then by large language models.

Key milestones include research on approximate nearest-neighbour methods, libraries such as FAISS released in 2017, graph indexes such as HNSW published in 2016, and then databases and services built around them, along with vector extensions for existing databases such as pgvector for PostgreSQL. After ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, RAG made vector search a mainstream need, and many general databases added vector features.

## When were vector databases introduced?

Purpose-built vector databases emerged in the late 2010s, with open-source and managed products appearing around 2019 to 2021 and growing rapidly after 2022. Before that, teams used libraries and search engines with custom code for vector similarity.

The timeline matters less than the trend: vector search is becoming a standard feature rather than a separate category. Today you can choose dedicated vector databases, vector extensions in relational databases, search engines with vector support, or libraries for in-memory use. Pick based on scale, filtering needs and the database your team already runs.

## How do I check a vector's size?

For embeddings, the size is the vector's dimension: the number of values it contains, such as 384, 768 or 1536. In Python, check `len(vector)` or `array.shape`; the model card lists its embedding dimension, which must match your index configuration.

```python
emb = model.encode("hello")      # sentence-transformers example
print(len(emb))                  # e.g. 384
```

Mismatched dimensions are a common error when switching embedding models: the index was created for one size and new vectors have another. In pgvector, the column type `vector(768)` fixes the dimension. In programming languages, "vector size" can also mean the number of elements in a dynamic array, such as `std::vector::size()` in C++.

## How do I get sub-second trigram or vector search in Postgres on long strings?

Use the right index for each kind of search, search on shorter fields where possible, and limit candidates before expensive ranking: a GIN trigram index with `pg_trgm` for fuzzy text, an HNSW index with pgvector for semantic search, and filters applied with indexed columns.

Tips that help:

- Index trigrams on the field users actually search, not entire long documents.
- For long text, split into chunks with their own rows and embeddings.
- Use `LIMIT` and rely on index-ordered queries for vectors.
- Tune HNSW search parameters for the recall and speed you need.
- Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm indexes are used.

Combining trigram or full-text results with vector results through rank fusion gives hybrid search inside one database.

## How did PostgreSQL become a better vector database?

PostgreSQL became a strong vector database through the pgvector extension, which added a vector data type, distance operators and approximate indexes, notably HNSW, plus later improvements such as more efficient storage options and better query performance.

Advantages of using Postgres for vectors: vectors live alongside your relational data, so you get joins, transactions, backups and row-level security in one system; full-text search enables hybrid retrieval; and the operational tooling is mature. Limits appear at very large scale or extreme query loads, where specialised vector databases may perform better. For most applications, starting with Postgres and pgvector is a sensible default.

## Is vector better than raster?

In graphics, vector images, made of shapes and paths, scale to any size without losing sharpness and are ideal for logos, icons and illustrations. Raster images, made of pixels, are better for photographs and detailed textures. Neither is better overall.

Use vector formats such as SVG for logos, diagrams and UI icons, especially on websites, where they stay crisp on every screen and are often small files. Use raster formats such as JPEG, PNG or WebP for photos. Many projects use both: an SVG logo and WebP photos. This "vector" is unrelated to vector search, although both use the mathematical idea of vectors.

## What is a free vector in physics?

In physics, a free vector is a vector defined only by its magnitude and direction, not by a specific point of application, so it can be moved parallel to itself without changing its meaning. Displacement and velocity of a rigid body's translation are common examples.

It contrasts with a bound or fixed vector, tied to a specific point, such as a force acting at a particular point on a body, where the point of application affects rotation, and a sliding vector, which can move along its line of action. The same vector concept, a list of components with magnitude and direction, underlies embeddings in AI, where each dimension is a learned feature.

## What is the vector method?

The vector method usually refers to solving problems in mathematics and physics using vectors: representing quantities with magnitude and direction, and using operations such as addition, dot products and cross products to find results like angles, areas and forces.

In geometry, vector methods prove properties of shapes and find distances and angles without coordinates for every point. In physics, they resolve forces and motions into components. In machine learning, vector methods represent data as vectors and use similarity measures, which is the basis of vector search: cosine similarity is simply the dot product of two normalised vectors, measuring how closely they point in the same direction.

# How YOLO works: training, PyTorch, segmentation, classification, labelling and licences
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-yolo-works-training/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


YOLO, You Only Look Once, is a family of real-time object detection models that predict bounding boxes and classes for a whole image in a single pass of a neural network. Modern versions also handle segmentation, classification, pose and oriented boxes. I run vision models in FaceVision with ONNX Runtime Web, so this page explains how YOLO and its training work, its PyTorch roots, when to use it, segmentation and classification, commercial use, labelling data, and how it compares with Detectron2 and MMDetection.

## How does the YOLO algorithm work?

YOLO passes the whole image through a convolutional backbone, combines features at several scales in a neck, and uses detection heads to predict box coordinates and class scores at many positions at once. Overlapping duplicate boxes are then removed.

The original YOLO divided the image into a grid, with each cell predicting boxes; later versions added anchor boxes, multi-scale feature pyramids and, more recently, anchor-free heads that predict box centres and distances directly. Post-processing applies a confidence threshold and non-maximum suppression, which keeps the highest-scoring box among heavily overlapping ones; some recent versions train to avoid needing NMS. One forward pass for the whole image is what makes YOLO fast enough for real-time video.

## How does YOLO training work?

Training feeds labelled images through the network, compares predicted boxes and classes with ground truth using box regression and classification losses, and updates weights with gradient descent over many epochs.

Ultralytics training is a single command: `yolo detect train data=data.yaml model=yolo11n.pt epochs=100 imgsz=640`, where data.yaml lists image paths and class names. Starting from pretrained weights, called transfer learning, needs far fewer images; typical custom datasets start with a few hundred images per class. Built-in augmentations such as mosaic, scaling and colour shifts improve robustness. Watch validation mean average precision, not just loss, and keep the best checkpoint. Then export with `yolo export` to ONNX or TensorRT for deployment.

## Does YOLO use PyTorch?

Most modern YOLO versions do. Ultralytics YOLOv5, YOLOv8 and YOLO11 are built on PyTorch, as are YOLOv7, YOLOv9 and YOLOv10. The original YOLOv1 to v3 used Darknet, a framework written in C and CUDA.

PyTorch makes training and customisation accessible in Python, while export to ONNX, TensorRT, OpenVINO, CoreML and TFLite allows deployment without PyTorch. Other implementations exist in TensorFlow, in PaddlePaddle with PP-YOLO, and in JAX, but the PyTorch versions have the largest communities. For browsers, models are exported to ONNX and run with ONNX Runtime Web or converted for TensorFlow.js, which is how I run vision models client-side in FaceVision.

## When should you use YOLO?

Use YOLO when you need fast object detection on images or video with a known set of classes, especially in real time or on edge devices: counting, tracking, safety monitoring, inspection, robotics and retail analytics.

Consider alternatives when you need maximum accuracy on small or crowded objects, where larger transformer detectors may win; when classes are open-ended, where open-vocabulary detectors such as Grounding DINO help; or when you need detailed scene understanding, where vision-language models fit better. YOLO's strengths are speed, mature tooling, easy training and broad export options, which make it the default starting point for most practical detection projects.

## Which YOLO model should you use for segmentation?

Use the segmentation variants of recent Ultralytics models, named with a -seg suffix, such as yolo11n-seg for speed or yolo11m-seg and larger for accuracy. They output instance masks alongside boxes and classes.

Choose the size by hardware: nano and small for edge devices and real-time video, medium for balanced servers, large and extra-large for offline accuracy. For very precise masks, such as medical or measurement tasks, compare against dedicated segmentation models or SAM-based pipelines, which produce finer boundaries. Train on polygon-labelled data in YOLO segmentation format, and evaluate with mask mean average precision rather than box metrics alone. Higher input resolution improves thin structures and small objects.

## How does YOLO segmentation work?

YOLO segmentation models add a mask branch to the detector. A small network produces a set of prototype masks for the whole image, and each detected object predicts coefficients that combine those prototypes into its own mask.

This approach, inspired by YOLACT, keeps segmentation fast because masks are built from shared prototypes rather than computed separately per object. The combined mask is cropped to the object's bounding box and thresholded to produce the final instance mask. Training uses polygon labels converted to masks, with a mask loss added to box and class losses. The result is real-time instance segmentation, useful for robotics, agriculture and video effects.

## Can you use YOLO for classification?

Yes. Ultralytics provides classification variants, with a -cls suffix, trained on ImageNet, which classify a whole image into one class. Train them on folders of images organised by class name with a single command.

Use classification when each image contains one main subject, such as identifying plant diseases from leaf photos or sorting product images. Use detection when images contain multiple objects or you need locations. Classification datasets are cheaper to label, since you only sort images into folders. Compare YOLO classification models with alternatives like EfficientNet or ViT if accuracy is critical, and export the best model to ONNX or TFLite for deployment on phones.

## Can you use YOLO commercially?

Yes, but check the licence. Ultralytics YOLO models are AGPL-3.0, which requires releasing your source code if you distribute the software or offer it over a network, unless you buy an Ultralytics Enterprise licence.

Some YOLO versions use GPL-3.0, which also has copyleft obligations. Permissively licensed alternatives include YOLOX and RF-DETR, both under Apache 2.0. Pretrained weights and datasets can carry their own terms, such as COCO image licences, so review all three: code, weights and data. For internal tools that are never distributed, obligations may differ, but get legal advice for commercial products rather than relying on assumptions.

## How do you label training data for YOLO?

Use an annotation tool such as Label Studio, CVAT or Roboflow to draw boxes, then export in YOLO format: one text file per image, each line holding a class index and the normalised centre x, centre y, width and height.

Organise images and labels into train and validation folders, and list paths and class names in a data.yaml file. Label consistently: decide rules for partial objects, occlusion and tiny objects, and write them down. Include varied backgrounds, lighting and negative images without objects. Use model-assisted labelling to speed up later batches, correcting predictions instead of drawing every box. Review a random sample for errors, since label quality strongly affects accuracy.

## YOLO vs Detectron2 vs MMDetection: which trains faster?

For typical custom datasets, Ultralytics YOLO usually trains fastest and is easiest to set up. Detectron2 and MMDetection are research toolboxes offering many architectures, such as Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN and DETR variants, with more configuration and often slower training.

Speed depends on model size, image resolution, batch size and hardware, so benchmark on your own data. YOLO's training pipeline is optimised for single commands and strong defaults; Detectron2, from Meta, suits teams extending Mask R-CNN-style models; MMDetection, from OpenMMLab, offers the widest model zoo for research comparisons. Choose YOLO for fast iteration and deployment, and the toolboxes when you need specific architectures or research reproducibility.

# How does YOLO work? The AI model explained, YOLOv8, people detection, and TensorFlow
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-yolo-works/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


YOLO, short for "You Only Look Once", is a family of AI models for real-time object detection: in a single pass through a neural network, it finds every object in an image, draws a bounding box around each, and labels it, such as person, car or helmet. Its speed made it the standard for video and edge applications. I build browser-based vision in FaceVision, where detection comes before recognition, so this page explains YOLO, how it and YOLOv8 work, people detection, and using TensorFlow to build, train and load models.

## Is YOLO an AI model?

Yes. YOLO is an AI model, specifically a family of deep learning models for object detection in computer vision. Given an image or video frame, it outputs bounding boxes, class labels and confidence scores for the objects it recognises.

Versions have evolved since the original 2015 paper by Joseph Redmon and colleagues, with many later releases from different teams, including Ultralytics' popular versions. Pretrained YOLO models detect 80 everyday object classes from the COCO dataset, and you can fine-tune them for custom objects such as defects, products or safety equipment. They run on GPUs, CPUs, phones and edge devices. That flexibility made YOLO a favourite for hackathon demos, traffic counting, retail analytics and safety monitoring.

## What does YOLO mean in AI?

In AI, YOLO stands for "You Only Look Once", meaning the model looks at the whole image once and predicts all objects in a single forward pass, instead of running a classifier over many proposed regions. That single pass is why it is fast.

The name plays on the slang phrase "you only live once", but in computer vision it describes the detection approach. Earlier detectors, such as R-CNN, proposed regions first and classified each separately, which was slow. YOLO reframed detection as one regression problem from image pixels to boxes and class probabilities, enabling real-time video detection.

## Is YOLO a deep learning model?

Yes. YOLO models are deep convolutional neural networks, with recent versions incorporating attention components, trained end to end on labelled images using backpropagation. They have a backbone that extracts features, a neck that combines features at multiple scales, and a head that predicts boxes and classes.

Training requires images with bounding box labels, typically thousands, though fine-tuning a pretrained model needs far fewer for new classes. Like other deep learning models, YOLO benefits from GPUs for training and data augmentation such as mosaic, flips and colour changes. For deployment, models are exported to formats like ONNX, TensorRT, TFLite or CoreML.

## How does YOLO work?

YOLO divides the image into a grid of locations and, at each, predicts bounding boxes, a confidence that an object is present, and class probabilities. Predictions at multiple scales catch small and large objects, and non-maximum suppression removes duplicate boxes for the same object.

The backbone network processes the whole image once, producing feature maps rich in visual patterns. The detection head converts these features into box coordinates and class scores. During training, losses penalise wrong positions, wrong classes and missed objects. At inference, you set a confidence threshold to keep reliable detections, trading recall against false positives.

## How does YOLO work step by step?

Step by step: resize and normalise the image, pass it through the backbone to extract features, combine features at different scales in the neck, predict boxes and class scores in the head, filter by confidence, then apply non-maximum suppression to keep the best box per object.

In detail:

- **Preprocess**: letterbox-resize to the model's input size, such as 640 by 640.
- **Backbone**: convolutional layers detect edges, textures, then object parts.
- **Neck**: feature pyramid layers merge fine and coarse features.
- **Head**: predicts box coordinates, objectness and classes per location.
- **Post-process**: confidence threshold, then non-maximum suppression.
- **Output**: boxes, labels and scores mapped back to the original image.

## How does YOLO v8 work?

YOLOv8, released by Ultralytics in 2023, uses a CSP-style convolutional backbone, a feature pyramid neck, and an anchor-free, decoupled head that predicts box centres and classes separately, improving accuracy and simplifying training.

Anchor-free detection removes the need for predefined anchor box shapes, adapting better to varied objects. Training uses modern techniques such as mosaic augmentation, task-aligned label assignment and distribution focal loss. YOLOv8 also supports segmentation, pose estimation and classification with the same framework. Newer Ultralytics versions follow similar principles with further efficiency improvements.

## What is the best YOLO model for human detection?

For people detection, start with a small pretrained YOLO model, such as a nano or small variant from a recent Ultralytics release, since "person" is one of the COCO classes. Choose larger variants if accuracy matters more than speed.

Then evaluate on footage from your actual cameras, because angle, lighting, crowd density and resolution strongly affect results. Fine-tune with a few hundred labelled frames from your environment to improve accuracy significantly. For tracking people across frames, add a tracker such as ByteTrack. Handle privacy carefully: detecting people raises consent and data protection obligations, so minimise storage and blur faces where possible.

## How do I implement a YOLO model using TensorFlow?

Use KerasCV or its successor KerasHub, which provide YOLOv8-style detectors in Keras with TensorFlow, or export an Ultralytics YOLO model to TensorFlow SavedModel or TFLite for inference in TensorFlow environments.

With Keras, load a pretrained backbone, build the detector, prepare your dataset with bounding boxes in the expected format, compile with the appropriate losses, and train with `model.fit`. For mobile deployment, convert to TFLite. Exporting from Ultralytics is often simpler: train in PyTorch, then run `model.export(format="tflite")` or `format="saved_model"`, and verify outputs match before deploying.

## How do I train a TensorFlow model?

Prepare data with `tf.data`, define a model with Keras layers or a pretrained backbone, compile it with an optimiser, loss and metrics, then call `model.fit` with training and validation data, monitoring results with callbacks such as early stopping.

```python
import tensorflow as tf
model = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=(28, 28)),
                             tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
                             tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, validation_split=0.1)
```

For vision tasks, start from a pretrained model and fine-tune; it needs far less data. Use callbacks such as `EarlyStopping` and `ModelCheckpoint` to stop when validation loss stops improving and keep the best weights, and use a GPU, locally or on Colab, for anything beyond small datasets.

## How do I load a model in TensorFlow?

Save a Keras model with `model.save("model.keras")` and load it with `tf.keras.models.load_model("model.keras")`. For deployment, export a SavedModel and load it with `tf.saved_model.load`, or convert to TFLite for mobile.

Common issues: custom layers or losses need to be registered or passed through `custom_objects` when loading; version mismatches between TensorFlow releases can break loading, so record versions; and saving only weights requires rebuilding the same architecture before calling `load_weights`. Test the loaded model on a few inputs to confirm predictions match the original.

# Hugging Face Transformers: sentiment, translation, search, GPT-2, Unsloth, spaCy, Ollama
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hugging-face-transformers-sentiment-unsloth-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Hugging Face Transformers is a widely used open-source library for loading, running and fine-tuning pre-trained models for text, vision and audio, backed by the Hugging Face Hub of shared models and datasets. I built FineTune Studio on Transformers, PEFT and TRL for QLoRA fine-tuning with live loss and base-versus-tuned evaluation, so this page covers a sentiment analyzer, examples, translation training, semantic search preprocessing, GPT-2 segmentation faults, small models, Unsloth, spaCy, Ollama and the LLM course. How do you build a simple sentiment analyzer with Hugging Face Transformers? The quickest way is the pipeline function with the sentiment-analysis task, which downloads a default English model fine-tuned on movie reviews and returns a label and score for any text you pass, in a few lines of Python. Also asked as: how to build a simple sentiment analyzer using hugging face transformer For better results on your own domain, pick a model from the Hub that matches your language and text type, such as a multilingual model trained on tweets, or fine-tune one. To fine-tune, load a labelled dataset with the datasets library, tokenize it with AutoTokenizer, load AutoModelForSequenceClassification with the right number of labels, and train with the Trainer class. Evaluate accuracy and F1 on a held-out split, then save the model and reuse it through the same pipeline call. Wrap it in a FastAPI endpoint to serve predictions in an app. What are some Hugging Face Transformers examples? The Transformers repository includes ready-to-run example scripts for text classification, token classification, question answering, summarization, translation, language modelling, image classification and speech recognition, each training or evaluating models from the command line. Look in the examples folder of the GitHub repository, where PyTorch scripts such as run_glue.py and run_translation.py accept a model name, dataset and training arguments. The documentation's task guides walk through each task step by step with code, and the Hub hosts community notebooks. Everyday examples include pipelines for summarisation, zero-shot classification, named entity recognition, image captioning and speech recognition, plus text generation with chat models. Start by running an example unchanged, then swap in your own data, which teaches the library's patterns faster than writing from scratch. How do you train an encoder-decoder translation model with Hugging Face Transformers? Load a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model, such as a MarianMT, T5 or mBART checkpoint, with AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, tokenize source sentences and targets together, then fine-tune with Seq2SeqTrainer and evaluate translations with BLEU or chrF. Also asked as: how do i train a encoder-decoder model for a translation task using hugging face transformers Prepare a parallel dataset of sentence pairs and pass targets through the tokenizer's text_target argument so labels are created correctly. Use DataCollatorForSeq2Seq to pad inputs and labels, and enable predict_with_generate so evaluation produces real translations. For T5, add a task prefix such as translate English to German. Starting from a model already trained on your language pair, such as an OPUS-MT model, needs far less data than training from scratch. For Indian languages, look at models such as AI4Bharat's IndicTrans2. Read sample outputs too, since BLEU alone can hide fluency problems. What preprocessing does semantic search with Hugging Face Transformers need? Clean and normalise text, split long documents into chunks within the model's maximum sequence length, encode chunks and queries with the same embedding model, apply its pooling method, and normalise vectors so cosine similarity works correctly. Also asked as: what preprocessing is needed for semantic search using pre-trained hugging face transformers The Sentence Transformers library handles tokenization, pooling and normalisation for embedding models from the Hub. Remove boilerplate, such as navigation text or repeated headers, but keep meaningful structure, such as headings, which can be prepended to each chunk for context. Use overlapping chunks so ideas are not cut in half. Some models, such as the E5 family, expect query and passage prefixes, so follow each model card. Store metadata, such as source and page, with each vector for citations. For better recall, combine dense search with BM25, the hybrid approach RAG.NextUpgrad uses. How do you fix a segmentation fault when training GPT-2 with Hugging Face Transformers? Segmentation faults usually come from native library conflicts rather than your Python code: mismatched PyTorch, CUDA, tokenizers or sentencepiece builds, packages mixed from conda and pip, or multiprocessing problems in data loading. Also asked as: how to fix segmentation fault when training gpt-2 model using hugging face transformers Create a fresh virtual environment, install PyTorch for your exact CUDA version, then current transformers, tokenizers and accelerate. Run with python -X faulthandler to see which call crashed. Set the data loader's num_workers to zero and TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM to false to rule out multiprocessing issues. Reduce batch size in case memory pressure triggers native crashes. Also fix common GPT-2 setup errors: it has no padding token, so set the pad token to the end-of-sequence token, and resize token embeddings after adding new tokens. If problems persist, run the same script on Colab to isolate your machine. Why are small language models on Hugging Face outperforming larger ones? Small models now beat older, larger ones on many benchmarks because of better training data, far more training tokens per parameter, distillation from stronger models and improved post-training, such as instruction tuning and preference optimisation. Microsoft's Phi work showed that carefully curated, textbook-quality data lets small models punch above their size, and Hugging Face's SmolLM models follow a similar data-first approach. Modern small models are often trained on trillions of tokens, well beyond compute-optimal estimates, which raises quality at a fixed size. Caveats matter: benchmark scores can be inflated by test contamination, and small models still trail large ones on broad knowledge, long-context reasoning and rarer languages. For focused tasks, a fine-tuned small model is often cheaper, faster and good enough, which is why QLoRA fine-tuning is so popular. How does Unsloth compare with Hugging Face? Unsloth is not a replacement for Hugging Face; it is an open-source library that speeds up and slims down fine-tuning of supported models, working with Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT and TRL and saving models in standard formats. Also asked as: unsloth vs hugging face Unsloth rewrites key parts of training with custom GPU kernels, and its maintainers report substantially faster LoRA and QLoRA training with lower memory use, letting larger models fit on a single consumer or free notebook GPU. The standard Hugging Face stack supports far more architectures, distributed training options and research flexibility. Choose Unsloth for fast, memory-efficient fine-tuning of popular open models on limited hardware; choose plain Transformers, PEFT and TRL, as FineTune Studio uses, when you need broad model support or custom training loops. Both can push models to the Hub. How does spaCy compare with Hugging Face Transformers? spaCy is a production NLP library for fast pipelines, such as tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition and dependency parsing, often on CPU. Hugging Face Transformers provides state-of-the-art transformer models for many tasks, including text generation. Also asked as: spacy vs hugging face transformers spaCy excels at efficient, structured processing of large text volumes, rule-based matching and integrating NLP into applications through a consistent API. Transformers excels at accuracy, fine-tuning and modern tasks such as summarisation, question answering and chat. They combine well: spacy-transformers lets spaCy pipelines use transformer models from the Hub as their backbone. Use spaCy when you need speed, linguistic annotations and simple deployment; use Transformers when you need top accuracy, generative models or custom fine-tuning. Many projects use spaCy for preprocessing and Transformers for the heavy modelling. How does Ollama compare with Hugging Face Transformers? Ollama is an easy tool for running quantised models locally, built on llama.cpp, with a simple command line and an OpenAI-compatible API. Transformers is a Python library for loading, fine-tuning and running models with full control. Also asked as: ollama vs hugging face transformers Ollama focuses on inference: pull a model, run it and call it from apps, including GGUF models pulled directly from the Hugging Face Hub. It does not train models. Transformers supports training, fine-tuning, research and inference in full or reduced precision, but needs more setup and usually a GPU for speed. A common workflow combines both: fine-tune with Transformers and PEFT, merge the adapters, convert to GGUF, then serve locally with Ollama. Choose Ollama for quick local chat and prototyping, and Transformers when you need to change or train the model itself. What is the Hugging Face Transformers LLM course? The Hugging Face LLM Course, formerly the NLP Course, is a free online course teaching transformers, tokenizers, datasets, fine-tuning and sharing models on the Hub, with newer chapters on fine-tuning large language models and reasoning. It runs in the browser with notebooks you can execute on Colab, and its source lives in the huggingface/course repository on GitHub, where the community contributes translations and fixes. Hugging Face also offers free courses on agents, computer vision, audio, diffusion models and deep reinforcement learning. Work through the chapters in order, run every notebook, then fine-tune a small model on your own dataset to consolidate what you learned. Pair the course with the Transformers documentation's task guides, which go deeper into specific tasks and training options.

# Hybrid search and reranking in RAG: BM25 plus embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoders, and why this pair fixes most bad answers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-and-reranking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every query, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, and merges their ranked results into one list. Keyword search catches exact terms, product codes, names, error numbers and rare words that embeddings blur together. Embedding search catches paraphrases and meaning that share no words with the document. Fusing them gives higher recall than either alone, and the fusion itself can be a dozen lines of code with no tuning.**


Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and a cross-encoder reranker is the core of RAG.NextUpgrad's query path, and it is the part of the platform that moved retrieval recall most on the labelled question set [13]. My shorter notes on each half are on the portfolio [11][12]. This page is the pair together, with the papers and the code.

> Users ask for "error E-4021" as often as they ask "why did my upload fail". Only one of those is a semantic query. Ship both retrievers or you will fail half your users.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does vector search alone miss results?

**Because embeddings compress meaning and lose exact strings. A product code, a person's name, an error number, an acronym or a version string carries little meaning to the model, so its vector lands near other codes and names rather than near the exact match. Numbers and negation blur too. Dense retrieval was shown to beat keywords for open-domain questions on average [3], and the average hides exactly the queries that matter most in support, legal and technical corpora.**


## What is BM25, and why is it still used?

**BM25 is a ranking function from classical information retrieval that scores a document for a query by how often the query's terms appear in it, weighted by how rare each term is across the collection and normalised for document length [1]. It needs no training, runs in microseconds over an inverted index, and finds exact terms perfectly. It cannot see that "reset my password" and "credential recovery" are the same request, which is exactly what embeddings are for. Together they cover each other's blind spots.**



Learned sparse models such as SPLADE bring some semantic expansion to the keyword side [6], and late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover exact-term precision on the dense side [5]. Both are worth knowing; BM25 plus a dense model plus fusion remains the practical default.

## What is reciprocal rank fusion?

**Reciprocal rank fusion merges several ranked lists into one by giving each document a score equal to the sum, over every list it appears in, of one divided by a constant plus its rank in that list. Documents ranked high in either list rise; documents ranked high in both rise most. The constant, usually 60, dampens the influence of top ranks. It needs no score normalisation, because it uses ranks not scores, and Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher showed it beating more complex fusion methods [2].**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)

fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense_top_40, bm25_top_40)[:30]   # then rerank these
```

That function is in RAG.NextUpgrad almost exactly as written, because the paper's simplicity is the point: no learned weights, no score scales to reconcile, nothing to retune when you swap an embedding model [13].

## What is reranking, and why not just retrieve more?

**A reranker is a model that reads the question and a candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare a query vector with passage vectors that were computed separately, for speed; a cross-encoder looks at the pair jointly, which is far more accurate but too slow to run over the whole corpus. So you retrieve wide with the fast methods, thirty to fifty candidates, and rerank narrow, to the best three to eight. Retrieving more without reranking sends noise to the model, and models use long contexts unevenly [8].**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho and remains the recipe [4]; Sentence Transformers publishes pretrained rerankers you can run on a CPU for small candidate sets [10].


## How do I choose k at each stage?

**Measure recall at each boundary on a labelled question set. Retrieve enough from each retriever that recall at the fusion output is above ninety percent; forty each is a common starting point. Fuse and keep enough that the reranker sees every plausible passage, twenty to fifty. Rerank down to what the model needs, three to eight, and check recall at that k is still above eighty-five. If recall drops sharply at the rerank step, the reranker is wrong for your domain; if it drops at fusion, one retriever is starving the other.**




## How much does hybrid search and reranking improve results?

**On the labelled sets I have worked with, fusion raised recall at thirty over either retriever alone, and the reranker raised recall at five without touching recall at thirty, which is exactly what each is supposed to do. Public benchmarks such as BEIR show dense models varying widely across domains and BM25 remaining a hard baseline on several [7], which is the research version of the same lesson. Your gain depends on your queries: corpora heavy in codes, names and numbers gain most from BM25; corpora of prose gain most from the reranker.**



## How do I implement hybrid search?

**Keep a keyword index alongside the vector index: Postgres full-text search or a BM25 library over the same chunks [9]; Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate and others also offer sparse or hybrid support. At query time, run both, fuse with the function above, rerank with a cross-encoder from Sentence Transformers or a hosted reranking API [10], and send the top few to the model. The whole path is a few hundred lines; the design decisions are the k values and the reranker choice.**



## When is hybrid search not worth it?

**Rarely, but there are cases. A tiny corpus where everything fits in the prompt does not need retrieval at all. A corpus of pure prose with no codes or names, where the reranker alone recovers what dense misses. A latency budget so tight that even microseconds matter, which is unusual. In every other case I have seen, the cost of a second retriever is small and the recall gain on exact-term queries is large. Default to hybrid and let your measurements argue you out of it.**



## Hybrid search and reranking interview questions

**Explain why embeddings miss exact terms and BM25 misses paraphrase. Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it needs no normalisation. Explain the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder and why you cannot rerank the whole corpus. Describe how you would choose k at each stage and measure it. Say when you would use learned sparse or late interaction models. A retrieval system you built and ablated is the best evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Add BM25 next to your vector search over the same chunks, fuse with the twelve-line function, and measure recall at thirty on twenty real questions before and after. Then add a cross-encoder and measure recall at five. Both changes take an afternoon and usually deliver the largest quality jump the system will ever see.** For a hands-on retrieval session at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
