# Hybrid search explained: what it combines, vector vs BM25, RRF, engines and production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Hybrid search combines keyword search, usually BM25, with vector search over embeddings, then merges the results, so you catch both exact terms like product codes and meaning-based matches like paraphrases. It is the default retrieval pattern for serious RAG systems. RAG.NextUpgrad uses hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and reranking, so this page explains what hybrid search combines, how it compares with vector and full-text search, RRF versus reranking, engines that support it, and production practice.

## What does hybrid search combine?

Hybrid search combines lexical retrieval, which matches exact words using methods like BM25, with semantic retrieval, which matches meaning using dense embedding vectors. Both run on the same query, and their ranked results are merged into one list.

Merging usually uses reciprocal rank fusion, which combines positions rather than raw scores, or a weighted sum of normalised scores. Some systems use learned sparse vectors, such as SPLADE, as the lexical side. The combination works because the two methods fail differently: keyword search misses synonyms and paraphrases, while vector search can miss exact identifiers, rare names and numbers. Together they raise recall, and a reranker can then sort the merged candidates precisely.

## Hybrid vs vector search: which is better?

Hybrid search is usually better for real-world retrieval, especially in RAG over technical, legal or product documents. Pure vector search works well for conversational, paraphrased queries but struggles with exact terms like error codes, SKUs, names and acronyms.

Benchmarks on varied datasets often show hybrid retrieval matching or beating either method alone, though results depend on your data. Vector-only systems are simpler to run and fine for small, homogeneous corpora. The cost of hybrid is extra indexing and a fusion step, both cheap with modern engines. Test on your own queries: build a small labelled set, compare recall at 10 for keyword, vector and hybrid, and choose based on measured results.

## Full-text search vs semantic search: what is the difference?

Full-text search finds documents containing the query's words, using inverted indexes, stemming and ranking functions like BM25. Semantic search finds documents with similar meaning, using embeddings, even when they share no words with the query.

Full-text search is fast, explainable and precise for exact terms, filters and phrases; it is built into PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and SQLite. Semantic search handles natural language questions, synonyms and cross-lingual matching, but needs an embedding model and a vector index, and its results are harder to explain. For user-facing search and RAG, combining them gives the best of both, with full-text catching exact matches and semantic search catching intent.

## BM25 vs dense retrieval: how do they compare?

BM25 scores documents by term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalisation; it needs no training and generalises well to new domains. Dense retrieval embeds queries and documents with a neural model and ranks by vector similarity, capturing meaning.

On benchmarks such as BEIR, BM25 remained a surprisingly strong baseline across domains, while dense retrievers excelled on data similar to their training but sometimes underperformed on unfamiliar domains. Modern embedding models have narrowed that gap. BM25 is cheap and transparent; dense retrieval costs embedding compute and memory. Because their errors differ, combining them through fusion is common practice, and fine-tuning the embedding model on your domain can further improve dense results.

## RRF vs reranking: what is the difference?

Reciprocal rank fusion merges several ranked lists by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each document, with k often set to 60. Reranking rescores a candidate list with a more powerful model, usually a cross-encoder that reads the query and document together.

They solve different problems and work well together. RRF is a cheap, training-free way to combine BM25 and vector results without calibrating their incompatible scores. A reranker is slower and costs compute per pair, but judges relevance far more precisely, so it runs only on the top 20 to 100 fused candidates. The typical pipeline is hybrid retrieval, then RRF fusion, then reranking, then the top few passages go to the language model; RAG.NextUpgrad follows this order.

## What are hybrid search engines?

Hybrid search engines are search systems that support both keyword and vector retrieval in one query, with built-in fusion. Most major search engines and vector databases now offer it natively.

They store an inverted index for text and a vector index, such as HNSW, for embeddings, and expose a hybrid query that runs both and merges results with RRF or weighted scores. Some also support sparse vectors, metadata filters and reranking stages. The term can also describe consumer search engines that blend traditional ranking with AI-generated answers. For developers, choosing an engine with native hybrid search avoids running and syncing two separate systems.

## What are some examples of hybrid search engines?

Examples include Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, Vespa, Pinecone with sparse-dense vectors, Azure AI Search, MongoDB Atlas, and PostgreSQL combining full-text search with pgvector.

Each implements fusion differently: Weaviate has a hybrid query with an alpha weighting between keyword and vector, Qdrant fuses dense and sparse vectors with RRF in its query API, and Elasticsearch supports RRF retrievers. Application frameworks add it too: LangChain's ensemble retriever combines BM25 and vector retrievers, and Open WebUI offers a hybrid search option for its document RAG, combining BM25 with embeddings and an optional reranker. Pick based on scale, hosting and existing infrastructure.

## What is hybrid search in OpenSearch?

OpenSearch supports hybrid search through a hybrid query that combines a lexical match query with a neural or k-NN vector query, then normalises and combines their scores using a search pipeline with a normalization processor.

You define a search pipeline specifying a normalisation technique, such as min-max or L2, and a combination technique, such as an arithmetic mean with weights for each sub-query. Newer versions also support score-ranker processors with reciprocal rank fusion. Embeddings can be generated at ingest and query time through OpenSearch's ML Commons models or supplied by your application. Tune weights on a labelled query set, because the best balance between keyword and vector varies by dataset.

## What is hybrid search in Azure AI Search?

In Azure AI Search, a hybrid query runs full-text search and vector search in parallel within one request, then merges results using reciprocal rank fusion. You send the search text and a vector query together.

You can add semantic ranking on top, which uses Microsoft's language models to rerank the top results and produce captions, a combination Microsoft recommends for RAG. Integrated vectorisation can generate embeddings during indexing and querying. Filters, scoring profiles and field weights still apply. Typical settings retrieve a few dozen candidates from each method, fuse them, rerank semantically, and pass the top passages to the language model with citations.

## How do teams do hybrid search in production?

A common production setup: BM25 and dense retrieval in the same engine, RRF fusion, a cross-encoder or hosted reranker on the top 50 or so candidates, metadata filters for permissions and freshness, and an evaluation set to tune everything.

Practical lessons: chunk documents sensibly with titles and section headers included; keep embeddings and the text index in sync on updates; cache frequent queries; log queries with zero or low-confidence results to find gaps; and measure recall and answer faithfulness, not just latency. Add query rewriting for conversational follow-ups. In RAG.NextUpgrad, a confidence gate after reranking refuses to answer when evidence is weak, which prevents confident wrong answers when retrieval fails.

# Image classification: vs segmentation and localization, small data, datasets, tutorial
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/image-classification-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Image classification assigns a label to a whole image, such as cat, defect or healthy leaf, and is the foundational computer vision task. Modern classifiers use convolutional networks or vision transformers, usually fine-tuned from pretrained models. I build vision systems, including FaceVision, so this page explains image classification, how it differs from segmentation and localization, its relation to machine vision, non-neural methods, small datasets, how many images you need, regression versus classification, datasets and tutorials.

## What is image classification in machine learning?

Image classification is the task of predicting which category an image belongs to, from a fixed set of classes. A model takes pixels as input and outputs probabilities for each class, choosing the most likely label.

Models learn from labelled examples: thousands of images tagged with their correct class. Convolutional neural networks such as ResNet and EfficientNet, and vision transformers, dominate today, usually starting from weights pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on the target data. Variants include multi-label classification, where an image can have several labels, and fine-grained classification, such as identifying bird species. Accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrices measure performance.

## Image segmentation vs image classification: what is the difference?

Classification gives one label, or a few, for the whole image. Segmentation labels every pixel, outlining exactly where each class or object appears. Classification answers what is in the image; segmentation answers where, precisely.

Segmentation comes in semantic form, labelling pixels by class, and instance form, separating individual objects. It needs pixel-level annotations, which cost far more to create than image labels, and models are heavier. Use classification when location does not matter, such as sorting product photos or flagging whether a scan is abnormal; use segmentation when shapes or areas matter, such as measuring tumour size, crop coverage or road lanes. Detection, with bounding boxes, sits between them.

## What do image classification and localization refer to?

Classification identifies what the main object in an image is; localization finds where it is, usually with a bounding box. Classification with localization outputs both a label and a box for a single main object.

Object detection generalises this to multiple objects, giving a class and box for each. Localization models add a regression head that predicts box coordinates alongside the classification head. Early ImageNet challenges included a classification and localization track. Today, most applications needing location use detection models such as YOLO directly. Localization techniques like class activation maps can also show which image regions influenced a classifier's decision, useful for explaining predictions.

## Is image classification a subset of machine vision?

Image classification is one task within computer vision, and it is widely used in machine vision, the industrial application of vision for inspection and automation. So it is a building block of both rather than a strict subset.

In machine vision, classification sorts products as pass or fail, identifies part types or grades produce quality, often running on cameras at production line speed. Machine vision also relies on measurement, barcode reading, alignment and detection. Computer vision, the broader research field, includes classification along with detection, segmentation, tracking, 3D reconstruction and generation. Knowing classification well prepares you for most other vision tasks, since many models extend classification backbones.

## Are there image classification algorithms that are not neural networks?

Yes. Classic approaches extract hand-crafted features, such as HOG, SIFT, colour histograms or local binary patterns, then classify them with algorithms like support vector machines, random forests, k-nearest neighbours or logistic regression.

Bag-of-visual-words models, which cluster local features into a vocabulary and classify histograms of visual words, were state of the art before deep learning. These methods train fast, need less data and run on weak hardware, which suits simple, controlled tasks like sorting objects by colour or shape. On complex natural images, neural networks are far more accurate. A hybrid option uses a pretrained neural network as a feature extractor with a classical classifier on top.

## How do you train an image classifier with a small dataset?

Use transfer learning: start from a model pretrained on ImageNet, freeze most layers, and train a new classification head on your images, then optionally fine-tune the last layers with a low learning rate.

Add data augmentation, such as flips, rotations, crops and colour changes, to create variety. Use early stopping and a validation set to prevent overfitting. With very small data, extract features with a pretrained model and train a simple classifier like logistic regression, or use zero-shot approaches with CLIP-style models, which can classify from text descriptions with no training at all. Clean, consistent labels matter more than quantity when data is scarce.

## How many photos do you need to train ResNet-50 for image classification?

With transfer learning, a few hundred images per class often give good results for distinct classes, while subtle, fine-grained classes may need thousands. Training ResNet-50 from scratch needs vastly more, typically hundreds of thousands of images.

Estimate empirically with a learning curve: train on 10, 25, 50 and 100 percent of your data and plot validation accuracy. If accuracy is still rising steeply at full data, more images will help; if it has plateaued, focus on label quality or model changes. Class balance, image variety and how different your images are from ImageNet also matter. Start with a small labelled set, measure, then collect more for the classes with the most errors.

## What are the best image classification datasets?

Classic benchmarks include MNIST and Fashion-MNIST for beginners, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 for small colour images, ImageNet for large-scale classification, and fine-grained sets like Stanford Dogs, CUB-200 birds and Oxford Flowers.

Domain datasets are useful for portfolio projects: PlantVillage for leaf diseases, chest X-ray collections for medical imaging research, EuroSAT for satellite land use, and food or retail product datasets. Hugging Face Datasets, Kaggle and TensorFlow Datasets host many with ready loaders. Check licences, especially for commercial use and medical data. For a standout project, collect and label a small dataset of your own for a real problem rather than reusing only benchmark data.

## Regression vs classification for images: what is the difference?

Image classification predicts a category, such as ripe or unripe. Image regression predicts a continuous number, such as a person's estimated age, a fruit's weight, or crop yield from field photos.

Architecturally they differ mainly in the output layer and loss: classification uses a softmax output with cross-entropy loss, while regression uses a single linear output with mean squared or absolute error. Some problems can be framed either way, such as age prediction as exact years or as age bands. Regression suits measurements where small errors are acceptable; classification suits decisions with distinct categories. Evaluate regression with error metrics such as mean absolute error.

## What is a good image classification tutorial?

PyTorch's transfer learning tutorial, TensorFlow's image classification guide, fast.ai's first lessons and Hugging Face's image classification fine-tuning guide each walk you from loading data to training and evaluating a classifier.

A practical path: train a simple CNN on CIFAR-10 to learn the basics, then fine-tune a pretrained ResNet or vision transformer on a small dataset of your own photos, add augmentation and a confusion matrix, and export the model to ONNX for deployment. Build a small web demo where users upload an image and see predictions with confidence scores. That end-to-end project teaches more than any single course chapter.

# Image classification: best models, small data, tutorials, detection, segmentation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/image-classification-models-tutorials/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Image classification assigns a label to a whole image, such as cat, defective part or ripe fruit. Modern systems use convolutional networks or vision transformers, usually fine-tuned from pretrained models rather than trained from scratch. I build vision products such as FaceVision, which runs detection and recognition in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, so this page covers the best algorithms and CNNs, Hugging Face models, small datasets, Python, PyTorch and TensorFlow tutorials, and how classification differs from detection, recognition and segmentation. What are the best image classification algorithms? The best modern algorithms are deep learning models: convolutional neural networks such as ResNet, EfficientNet and ConvNeXt, and vision transformers such as ViT, DeiT and Swin. Classic methods, such as SVMs on handcrafted features, now suit only very constrained problems. Accuracy depends more on pretraining and data than on the exact architecture. Models pretrained on large datasets, then fine-tuned on your images, consistently beat those trained from scratch. Self-supervised backbones such as DINOv2 and image-text models such as CLIP produce strong features that need little labelled data, and CLIP even classifies images zero-shot from text labels. Choose by accuracy, speed and deployment target: lightweight CNNs for phones and browsers, larger transformers for servers with GPUs. What is the best CNN model for image classification? ResNet-50 remains the standard baseline, EfficientNet and EfficientNetV2 offer excellent accuracy for their size, ConvNeXt matches vision transformers with a pure CNN design, and MobileNetV3 suits phones and edge devices. For most projects, start with a pretrained ResNet or EfficientNet, fine-tune on your data, and compare with ConvNeXt if you need more accuracy. CNNs still have advantages: built-in assumptions about local patterns help with smaller datasets, and they run efficiently on many devices. The timm library offers hundreds of pretrained CNNs with consistent interfaces, making comparisons easy. Measure accuracy and inference time on your target hardware, since a slightly less accurate model that runs fast may be better. What are the best image classification models on Hugging Face? Popular Hugging Face models include Google's ViT, Microsoft's ResNet-50, Meta's ConvNeXt and DINOv2, Swin Transformer, EfficientNet variants and OpenAI's CLIP for zero-shot classification. The timm collection adds hundreds more. Also asked as: best image classification models huggingface Filter the Hugging Face model hub by the image classification task and sort by downloads or recent activity. For quick experiments, the pipeline API runs any model in a few lines, and AutoModelForImageClassification lets you fine-tune with the Trainer. DINOv2 features with a simple linear classifier perform strongly with limited labels. Check each model card for training data, licence and expected input size. Export chosen models to ONNX for deployment, including in browsers, as FaceVision does with ONNX Runtime Web. What are the best image classification models for small datasets? For small datasets, fine-tune a pretrained model such as ResNet, EfficientNet or ConvNeXt, or extract features from DINOv2 or CLIP and train a simple classifier on top. Transfer learning lets a few hundred labelled images per class work well. Use strong data augmentation, such as random crops, flips, colour jitter and mixup, to reduce overfitting. Freeze most layers at first and train only the head, then unfreeze gradually with a low learning rate. With very few examples, try CLIP zero-shot classification or few-shot methods before labelling more. Use stratified cross-validation, since a small test set gives unstable metrics. Check class balance, and collect more data for confusing classes rather than adding images evenly. How do you do image classification in Python? Organise images into one folder per class, load them with a library such as torchvision, timm or Keras, apply resizing and normalisation, fine-tune a pretrained model, then evaluate accuracy and the confusion matrix on a held-out test set. Also asked as: image classification tutorial python A minimal workflow: split data into training, validation and test sets; choose a pretrained backbone; replace the final layer with one matching your number of classes; train for a few epochs with augmentation; and track validation accuracy. Save the best model, then test on unseen images. Libraries such as fastai or the Hugging Face Trainer reduce boilerplate. Use Google Colab for free GPU access when experimenting, and export the final model to ONNX or TorchScript for deployment. What does a PyTorch image classification tutorial cover? PyTorch tutorials typically load images with torchvision's ImageFolder and DataLoader, apply transforms, load a pretrained ResNet, replace its final layer, train with cross-entropy loss and an optimiser such as Adam or SGD, then evaluate on test data. Also asked as: pytorch tutorial image classification The official PyTorch tutorials include Training a Classifier, using the CIFAR-10 dataset, and Transfer Learning for Computer Vision, which fine-tunes ResNet on a small ants and bees dataset. Key concepts include moving tensors to the GPU, switching between train and evaluation modes, and disabling gradients during evaluation. Once the basic loop works, add learning rate schedulers, mixed precision training and early stopping. The timm library and PyTorch Lightning help scale experiments cleanly. What does a TensorFlow image classification tutorial cover? TensorFlow tutorials load images with tf.keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory, build or load a model from Keras Applications such as EfficientNet, compile it with a loss and optimiser, train with model.fit and evaluate with model.evaluate. Also asked as: tensorflow tutorial image classification The official TensorFlow image classification tutorial trains a small CNN on a flowers dataset, then adds data augmentation and dropout to reduce overfitting. A companion transfer learning tutorial fine-tunes a pretrained MobileNetV2. Keras makes the high-level workflow concise, while TensorFlow Lite, now called LiteRT, converts models for mobile and edge devices. Keras 3 can also run on PyTorch or JAX backends, so the same code works across frameworks. Use callbacks for checkpoints and early stopping. What is the difference between image detection and image classification? Image classification assigns one or more labels to the whole image, such as contains a dog. Object detection finds each object's location with a bounding box and labels it, such as two dogs at specific positions. Also asked as: image detection vs image classification Classification answers what is in the image; detection answers what and where. Detection models, such as YOLO, RT-DETR and Faster R-CNN, usually build on classification backbones and add components that predict boxes. Use classification for sorting images, quality checks on single items or medical image triage, and detection for counting, tracking or locating multiple objects. Detection needs more expensive labels, since each object requires a box, so choose the simplest task that solves your problem. What is the difference between image recognition and image classification? Image recognition is a broad term for identifying what is in an image, covering classification, detection and identifying specific instances. Image classification is a specific task: assigning predefined category labels to an image. Also asked as: image recognition vs image classification People often use the terms interchangeably. In practice, recognition sometimes means identifying a particular individual or item, such as face recognition, which compares embeddings to match a specific person rather than a general category. FaceVision uses this approach, detecting faces in the browser, then comparing embeddings stored in PostgreSQL, never storing the images themselves. Classification answers which category, while recognition can also answer which specific one. Clarify the exact task before choosing models, since the techniques differ. What is the difference between semantic segmentation and image classification? Image classification labels the whole image. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class, such as road, car or sky, producing a detailed map of where each category appears. Also asked as: semantic segmentation vs image classification Segmentation gives precise shapes rather than boxes or single labels, which matters for medical imaging, autonomous driving, satellite analysis and agriculture. Instance segmentation goes further, separating individual objects of the same class. Models include U-Net, DeepLab and SegFormer, while Meta's Segment Anything generates masks for any object without predefined classes. Segmentation labels take the most effort to create, so use classification or detection unless your application truly needs pixel-level detail.

# How to impress hackathon judges: what they look for, and how to do well
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/impress-hackathon-judges/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Hackathon judges look for a real problem, a working solution, sound technical choices, credible impact and a clear pitch, roughly in that order of weight at most events. I have sat on both sides of the table: winning first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, and judging and mentoring at others. This page shares what judges actually score, how to impress them and do well, what you do at a hackathon, whether it is hard, hackathon tests, Unstop and other sites, and where the word and idea came from.

## What do hackathon judges actually look for?

Most rubrics score five things: problem relevance, the working solution, technical execution, impact or feasibility, and presentation. Judges reward teams that solve a specific problem well over teams that attempt everything.

A typical rubric, seen from both sides:

- **Problem**: is it real, specific and important to an identifiable user?
- **Solution**: does the demo work live, end to end?
- **Technical depth**: are choices sensible, and can the team explain them?
- **Impact and feasibility**: could this be used, scaled or deployed?
- **Presentation**: is the story clear within the time limit?

As a judge, I trust teams that show what does not work yet and how they would fix it; honesty reads as understanding.

## How do I impress hackathon judges?

Lead with the user and the problem, show a live demo of one complete flow, explain why you chose your approach, quantify impact where possible, and answer questions directly and honestly.

Specific moves that work:

- Open with one person's problem, not your tech stack.
- Demo the core feature within the first minute or two.
- Mention one hard technical decision and why you made it.
- Show evidence: a user quote, a test result, a small dataset you validated on.
- Admit limitations and give a next-step plan.
- Keep slides minimal; the demo is the star.

KrishGyan stood out at Changethon 2025 because the demo showed a farmer asking in their own voice and language and getting a useful answer.

## How do I do well in a hackathon?

Pick a narrow problem, plan scope in the first hour, divide roles, integrate early, freeze features well before the end, and rehearse the demo and pitch several times.

A time plan for a 24-hour event:

- **Hour 0 to 1**: choose the problem, define one user and one core flow.
- **Hours 1 to 4**: skeleton app deployed, front end and back end connected.
- **Hours 4 to 16**: build the core feature; cut anything non-essential.
- **Hours 16 to 20**: polish, fix bugs, prepare slides.
- **Final hours**: rehearse, record a backup demo, rest a little.

Talk to mentors early; one good suggestion can save hours.

## What do we have to do in a hackathon?

In a hackathon, you form or join a team, choose or receive a problem, build a working prototype within the time limit, and present it to judges, usually with a short demo and slides. Organisers provide themes, rules, mentors and judging criteria.

The typical flow: registration and team formation, an opening session explaining rules and themes, building time with mentor check-ins, a submission deadline for code and slides, and final presentations. Some events add idea rounds before shortlisting. You are expected to write most of your project during the event, though rules on starter templates and AI tools vary, so read them.

## Is a hackathon hard?

Hackathons are demanding because of tight time limits, teamwork pressure and things breaking at the last minute, but they are designed to be accessible. Beginners regularly take part and learn a lot, especially at events with beginner tracks and mentors.

What makes them manageable: choosing a small problem, using tools you know, splitting work clearly, asking mentors for help, and aiming to finish something rather than to win your first time. Skills improve quickly with each event. The hardest part for many people is the first one; after that, you know what to expect.

## What is a hackathon test?

A hackathon test usually refers to an online assessment used to shortlist participants, such as a coding test, quiz or idea submission round, before the main build event. Hiring hackathons by companies often use coding tests to screen candidates.

Formats include timed coding problems, multiple-choice questions on fundamentals, and written idea proposals with a presentation. Prepare with practice problems on data structures and algorithms, review basics of the event's technology theme, and for idea rounds, write a clear problem statement, proposed solution and implementation plan. Read instructions carefully; many submissions fail on format rather than ideas.

## What is an Unstop hackathon?

Unstop is an Indian platform, formerly known as Dare2Compete, where companies and colleges host hackathons, coding contests, case competitions, quizzes and hiring challenges. An "Unstop hackathon" is a hackathon listed and run through it.

Students use it to discover competitions, register teams, submit entries and follow results. Many college tech fest events and company hiring hackathons appear there. As with any platform, read each event's rules, timeline, eligibility and prize terms, and prefer events from organisers you can verify. It is one of the easiest ways for Indian students to find many competitions in one place.

## What is the best hackathon website?

There is no single best one; use a few. Devfolio and Unstop list many Indian hackathons; Major League Hacking and Devpost list student and global events; Kaggle hosts data competitions; and college tech fest sites list campus events.

Tips for choosing events:

- Prefer events with clear judging criteria and mentors.
- Mix online events for volume with offline ones for networking.
- Check past winners' projects to understand the bar.
- Follow organisers on social media to catch registrations early.

Over time, you will learn which events suit your interests, whether AI, social impact, fintech or hardware.

## Why is it called a hackathon?

"Hackathon" combines "hack", in the programmer's sense of building something clever and quick, and "marathon", an intense, sustained effort. It describes an event where people build intensively for a fixed period.

The word has nothing to do with breaking into systems; "hacker" originally meant an enthusiastic, skilful programmer. Over time, hackathons spread beyond software to hardware, design, policy, health and social impact, but the core idea remains: small teams, short time, real prototypes. Variants include ideathons, focused on ideas, and datathons, focused on data analysis.

## Who invented the hackathon?

No single person invented it. The term appeared in 1999, used independently around events by the OpenBSD project and by Sun Microsystems around its JavaOne conference, where developers built software intensively over a short period.

Collaborative coding sprints existed before, but the name and format spread through the 2000s via tech companies, open-source communities and universities. Today hackathons run worldwide, from corporate innovation events to national programmes such as Smart India Hackathon. The format endures because it compresses learning, teamwork and creation into a memorable experience.

# Induction program guide: university, orientation, freshers, faculty, teachers, staff
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/induction-program-university-faculty-teachers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

An induction program introduces newcomers, whether first-year students, new teachers or employees, to an institution's people, values, rules and support so they settle in faster and perform better. Formats range from a single day to several weeks or years. I spoke at the VSICS induction on 6 July 2025 to more than 100 first-year students, sharing a three-year roadmap, so this page covers university and student induction, orientation, freshers parties, introductions, feedback, faculty and teacher induction, and effective employee induction. What is an induction program in a university? A university induction program is a structured welcome for new students at the start of the first year, introducing the campus, academic expectations, rules, support services, culture and the people students will learn alongside. Also asked as: what is induction program in university In India, AICTE made a three-week Student Induction Program mandatory for first-year students in technical programs, and the UGC's Deeksharambh guide encourages similar programs across universities. Activities include campus tours, talks by faculty and alumni, sessions on universal human values, creative arts, physical activity, local visits and introductions to departments, clubs and mentors. The goal is to ease the move from school, build relationships between students and teachers, and reduce early anxiety and dropout. Good programs also explain academic integrity, grading, attendance and where to get help. What does a student induction program mean? A student induction program is the set of activities that help newly admitted students adjust to college life before or during their first weeks of classes. Induction simply means bringing someone into a new role or community. Also asked as: what does student induction program meaning It covers practical matters, such as timetables, portals, library access and hostel rules, alongside personal ones, such as making friends, managing time and finding mentors. Many colleges assign senior student volunteers or faculty mentors to small groups. Some programs last a day; others extend over weeks with follow-up sessions. For students, induction is the best time to ask questions, join clubs and learn what opportunities exist, such as hackathons, research projects and coding communities. My talk at the VSICS induction focused on a three-year roadmap, because a clear plan early helps first-years use every semester well. Is an induction program the same as orientation? They overlap but are not identical. Orientation is usually short, often a day or two, and focused on information: rules, facilities, schedules and procedures. Induction is broader and longer, aiming to integrate newcomers socially, academically and culturally. Also asked as: is induction program and orientation same Many institutions use the words interchangeably, and orientation is often one part of a larger induction program. AICTE's three-week format is clearly induction, mixing values, activities and relationships, while a single welcome session is orientation. Workplaces follow the same pattern: orientation covers paperwork, policies and tools on the first day, while induction or onboarding continues for weeks or months until the person is productive. If your institution calls its program orientation, expect mostly information; if it calls it induction, expect activities and mentoring as well. Is an induction program the same as a freshers party? No. An induction program is an official, structured introduction to the institution organised by the college, while a freshers party is a social celebration, usually organised by senior students, to welcome first-years informally. Also asked as: is induction program and freshers party same Induction happens at the start of the academic year and covers academics, rules, values and support, often with attendance required. Freshers parties come later, after students have settled in, and include performances, games and titles such as Mr and Ms Fresher. Both help newcomers feel welcome, but in different ways. Freshers events must stay free of ragging, which is banned under UGC regulations, and induction programs usually explain anti-ragging rules and helplines. Treat induction seriously and enjoy the freshers party as a chance to make friends. How do you give an introduction in an induction program? Keep it short, around thirty to sixty seconds: your name, your background or previous school, your course, one or two interests, and what you hope to achieve. End with something memorable or an invitation to connect. Also asked as: how to give introduction in induction program For example, share your name, the course you joined, a hobby such as coding, music or sport, and a goal such as building a project in your first year. Speak slowly, make eye contact and smile, since warmth matters more than polish. Avoid reciting marks or long life stories. If you are nervous, rehearse once aloud and keep notes minimal. Listen to others' introductions and remember names; following up with someone who shares your interests is how friendships and project teams begin. Faculty introductions follow the same pattern, adding teaching areas and research interests. How do you give feedback for an induction program? Be specific, balanced and constructive: say which sessions helped and why, which felt unclear or too long, and what you would add or change. Concrete suggestions are more useful than general praise or complaints. Also asked as: how to give feedback for induction program Organisers usually collect feedback through forms with ratings and open comments. Mention particular speakers, activities or information that made a difference, such as a mentoring session or campus tour. Point out gaps, such as missing information about scholarships, portals or clubs. Suggest improvements, such as shorter talks, more interaction or a follow-up session after a month. Keep the tone respectful, since organisers and speakers give their time. If the form allows, separate feedback on content from feedback on logistics, such as timing, seating or audio. Honest feedback improves the program for next year's students. How do you apply for a faculty induction program? In India, newly appointed assistant professors usually attend a faculty induction program at a UGC Human Resource Development Centre, such as the month-long Guru-Dakshta program. Apply through the centre's website or notice, typically with a forwarding letter from your institution. Also asked as: how to apply faculty induction program Check the HRDC schedule for upcoming programs, fill in the application form, and attach your appointment letter and the head of institution's nomination or no-objection letter. Seats are limited, so apply early and confirm accommodation and fee details with the centre. Induction and orientation programs often count towards career advancement under UGC regulations, so keep the certificate safely. Online options for continuing development exist through SWAYAM, including the ARPIT refresher courses. Engineering faculty can also look at AICTE training programs, which follow similar nomination processes. What is the induction program for teachers? A teacher induction program supports newly qualified or newly hired teachers during their first years through mentoring, training, classroom observation and sometimes reduced workloads, helping them build skills and stay in the profession. Programs vary by country. In England, early career teachers complete a two-year induction with a mentor and a structured training framework. In India, college faculty attend induction programs at HRDCs, while school systems and private schools run their own training for new teachers. Common elements include a dedicated mentor, observation of experienced colleagues, feedback on lessons, workshops on classroom management, assessment and inclusion, and time for reflection. Strong induction helps new teachers survive a demanding first year, which is why many education systems invest in it. How long is a teacher induction program? It varies: faculty induction programs for new college teachers in India typically run about a month, while induction for beginning school teachers in many countries lasts one to two years, such as England's two-year early career teacher induction. Short workplace inductions for teachers joining a new school may last only a few days, covering policies, systems and timetables. Longer programs spread mentoring, observations and training across the first years of teaching, since skills develop through practice and feedback rather than a single course. Completion requirements, such as assessments or portfolios, differ by system. Check with your employer or education authority for the exact duration and conditions, especially when completion affects confirmation of appointment, certification or career progression. Plan your workload so induction supports rather than overwhelms you. What employee induction program is effective? An effective employee induction program gives clear role expectations, the tools and access needed on day one, a buddy or mentor, a structured plan for the first weeks, introductions to key people, and regular check-ins with feedback. Start before day one by sending schedules and setting up accounts. Mix information about the company, policies and culture with real work early, since small early wins build confidence. A thirty, sixty and ninety day plan sets clear milestones. Assign a buddy for informal questions, separate from the manager. Avoid overwhelming new hires with slides on the first day; spread content over weeks. For engineering teams, a small first task shipped in week one, clear documentation and pairing sessions speed things up. Gather feedback from new joiners and track time to productivity and early retention.

# Should I install Ollama? Install on Windows, Mac, Linux, WSL and Docker
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-ollama-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Install Ollama if you want to run open-weight language models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral or DeepSeek on your own machine, for privacy, offline use, learning or building prototypes without per-token costs. It installs in a few minutes on Windows, macOS and Linux, and runs in Docker. This page helps you decide, then covers installing on Windows including a D drive, where models are stored, macOS, Ubuntu, WSL, Docker and pulling models inside a container, and running DeepSeek models.

## Should I install Ollama?

Yes, if you want to learn how language models work hands-on, keep data private, work offline, or prototype apps without paying per token. No, if you only want the best answers for hard tasks, where hosted models such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are much stronger.

Your hardware decides the experience. With 8 GB of RAM you can run small models of a few billion parameters at usable speed. With 16 to 32 GB of RAM or a GPU with 8 GB or more of video memory, mid-size models become practical. Larger models need serious GPUs. Ollama itself is free and open source, and uninstalling it is simple, so trying it costs nothing but disk space: models range from a couple of gigabytes to tens of gigabytes each.

## How do I install Ollama on Windows?

Download the Windows installer from ollama.com, run it, and Ollama starts in the background with an icon in the system tray. Then open a terminal and run a model.

```powershell
ollama --version
ollama run llama3.2
```

The first `run` downloads the model, then opens an interactive chat; type `/bye` to exit. Ollama also serves an API on `http://localhost:11434`, which tools such as LangChain and Open WebUI use. If you have an NVIDIA or AMD GPU, keep its drivers updated so Ollama can use it; check with `ollama ps` while a model runs to see whether it is on the GPU or CPU.

## Can I install Ollama on the D drive?

Yes. The models are what take space, and you can store them on any drive by setting the `OLLAMA_MODELS` environment variable, for example to `D:\ollama\models`, then restarting Ollama. The installer also accepts a custom install directory.

Steps for the models folder:

- Quit Ollama from the system tray.
- Open "Edit environment variables for your account" in Windows settings.
- Add a variable `OLLAMA_MODELS` with the value `D:\ollama\models`.
- Start Ollama again and pull a model; it downloads to the new folder.

To install the program itself elsewhere, the Windows installer supports a directory option documented in Ollama's Windows guide. Moving existing models is as simple as moving the folder to the new path before restarting.

## Where does Ollama install models?

By default, models are stored in a `.ollama/models` folder in your home directory: `C:\Users\<you>\.ollama\models` on Windows and `~/.ollama/models` on macOS. On Linux, when installed as a service, they are under the `ollama` user's home, typically `/usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models`.

Set `OLLAMA_MODELS` to change the location on any system. Models are stored as layered blobs with manifests, so the folder will not show friendly filenames; use `ollama list` to see installed models and `ollama rm <name>` to delete one and free space. Several models can share layers, so deleting one may free less space than its listed size. If disk space is tight, keep only the models you actually use.

## How do I install Ollama on a Mac?

Download the macOS app from ollama.com, move it to Applications and open it. It adds the `ollama` command to your terminal, and you can run a model straight away with `ollama run llama3.2`.

Apple Silicon Macs, with M-series chips, run local models well because the GPU shares fast unified memory with the CPU, so a Mac with 16 GB or more can run mid-size models comfortably. Intel Macs work but are slower. You can also install through Homebrew if you prefer managing tools that way. Keep the app running in the menu bar so the local API at port 11434 stays available for other apps.

## How do I install Ollama on Ubuntu?

Run the official install script, which installs Ollama and sets it up as a systemd service that starts automatically.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama run llama3.2
```

Check the service with `systemctl status ollama` and view logs with `journalctl -u ollama`. For NVIDIA GPUs, install the proprietary drivers first; the script detects them. To change settings such as the models folder or listening address, edit the service with `sudo systemctl edit ollama` and add environment variables like `OLLAMA_MODELS` or `OLLAMA_HOST`, then restart the service. As with any script piped to a shell, you can download and read it first.

## Can I install Ollama on WSL?

Yes. Inside WSL 2 on Windows, install Ollama with the Linux install script, and with up-to-date NVIDIA drivers on Windows, Ollama in WSL can use the GPU. Alternatively, install the Windows version and call it from WSL over the local network.

Choose based on your workflow. If your projects live in WSL, running Ollama there keeps everything in one environment. If you also use Windows tools, the Windows app is simpler and you can reach it from WSL at the Windows host's address. Avoid running both at once on the same port. WSL needs enough memory allocated; if models fail to load, raise the memory limit in your WSL configuration.

## Should I install Ollama in Docker?

Docker is a good choice for servers, reproducible setups and running Ollama alongside other services such as a web UI or a database. On a personal laptop, the native installer is simpler and usually uses the GPU with less setup.

Run the official image with a volume so models persist:

```bash
docker run -d --name ollama -p 11434:11434 -v ollama:/root/.ollama ollama/ollama
```

For NVIDIA GPUs, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and add `--gpus=all`. With Docker Compose, you can define Ollama, Open WebUI and your app together. Do not expose port 11434 to the internet without authentication in front of it; the Ollama API has no built-in login.

## How do I pull Ollama models in a Docker container?

Run the `ollama pull` command inside the running container with `docker exec`, and the model is saved in the mounted volume, so it survives restarts.

```bash
docker exec -it ollama ollama pull llama3.2
docker exec -it ollama ollama list
docker exec -it ollama ollama run llama3.2 "Explain BM25 in one line"
```

For automated setups, pull models in a start-up script or call the API's pull endpoint from your app on first run. Keep the volume, named `ollama` above, when updating the image, so you do not re-download models. If another container needs Ollama, connect them on the same Docker network and use `http://ollama:11434` as the address.

## Can I install DeepSeek on Ollama?

Yes. DeepSeek's open-weight models, including distilled versions of its reasoning model, are available in Ollama's library. Run one with `ollama run deepseek-r1`, adding a size tag to choose a smaller or larger variant.

Pick a size that fits your memory: small distilled versions run on ordinary laptops, while the largest DeepSeek models need multiple high-end GPUs and are not practical locally. Reasoning models print their thinking before the final answer, so expect longer responses. Running locally means your prompts stay on your machine, which addresses privacy concerns some people have about using hosted services. Test on your own tasks; smaller distilled models are much weaker than the full model.

# How to install OpenCV with pip, conda, VS Code, PyCharm and Jupyter
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-opencv-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To install OpenCV for Python, run `pip install opencv-python` in the environment you use, then `import cv2` in your code. Use `opencv-contrib-python` if you need extra modules, and a `-headless` variant on servers without a display. Most installation problems come from installing into a different Python environment from the one your editor or notebook runs. This page covers pip and conda, VS Code, PyCharm and Jupyter, macOS and Linux, and two functions everyone uses early: resize and findContours.

## How do I install OpenCV?

For Python, create a virtual environment, activate it, and run `pip install opencv-python`. Check it with `python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"`.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install opencv-python
python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__version__)"
```

For C++ projects, install OpenCV through your system's package manager or build it from source with CMake, following the official installation guides. For most students, the Python package is enough for image processing, video and classic computer vision, and pairs well with NumPy, and with PyTorch or ONNX Runtime for deep learning models.

## Can you pip install OpenCV?

Yes. The official Python packages on PyPI are `opencv-python` for the main modules, `opencv-contrib-python` for main plus extra modules, and `opencv-python-headless` and `opencv-contrib-python-headless` for servers without GUI functions.

Rules that avoid strange errors:

- Install only one of these packages in an environment; they conflict.
- Use headless versions in Docker and on servers, where `cv2.imshow` is not needed.
- Upgrade pip first if installation tries to build from source: `python -m pip install --upgrade pip`.
- Use `python -m pip` so pip matches the Python you run.

If `import cv2` fails after installing, the package is almost certainly in another environment.

## How do I install OpenCV in VS Code?

Open your project folder, create a virtual environment, select it as the interpreter with "Python: Select Interpreter" in the command palette, then run `pip install opencv-python` in VS Code's terminal, which uses that environment.

If VS Code shows "Import cv2 could not be resolved", the editor is using a different interpreter from the one where you installed OpenCV. Check the interpreter shown in the status bar, select the `.venv` one, and reload the window. Also confirm the integrated terminal has the environment activated before installing. Install the Python extension from Microsoft for IntelliSense and debugging support.

## How do I install OpenCV in PyCharm?

Open Settings, then Project, then Python Interpreter, make sure your project's virtual environment is selected, click the plus button, search for `opencv-python` and install it. Or run `pip install opencv-python` in PyCharm's terminal, which uses the project interpreter.

If the import still fails, check that the run configuration uses the same interpreter as the project. PyCharm can create a separate environment per project, so a package installed in one project will not appear in another. For autocompletion of `cv2`, recent OpenCV packages include type hints; if completion is poor, restart PyCharm so it re-indexes the environment.

## How do I install OpenCV in a Jupyter Notebook?

Install OpenCV into the same environment as the notebook's kernel. The safest way is to run `%pip install opencv-python` in a notebook cell, which installs into the active kernel, then restart the kernel.

If you use several environments, register each as a Jupyter kernel with `python -m ipykernel install --user --name myenv` and select the right kernel in the notebook. Note that `cv2.imshow` opens a separate window and does not display inline; in notebooks, convert the image from BGR to RGB with `cv2.cvtColor` and show it with Matplotlib's `plt.imshow`. In Google Colab, OpenCV is usually preinstalled, and Colab provides a patched display helper for images.

## How do I install OpenCV through conda?

Use the conda-forge channel: `conda install -c conda-forge opencv`, inside a conda environment you created for the project. Then `import cv2` as usual.

```bash
conda create -n cv python=3.11
conda activate cv
conda install -c conda-forge opencv
```

Avoid mixing conda's OpenCV with a pip-installed OpenCV in the same environment, because they can conflict. If you mostly use pip packages, a plain virtual environment with `opencv-python` is simpler. Conda is useful when you also need other compiled libraries that conda manages well, such as specific scientific packages.

## Does OpenCV work on Mac?

Yes. OpenCV works on macOS, including Apple Silicon Macs, through pip with `pip install opencv-python` or through conda-forge or Homebrew. Prebuilt wheels support both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

Tips for Mac users: use a Python from python.org, Homebrew or a virtual environment rather than the system Python; grant camera permission to your terminal or editor in System Settings when using `cv2.VideoCapture(0)`; and remember that `cv2.imshow` windows need `cv2.waitKey` to refresh. For deep learning inference on Apple Silicon, combine OpenCV for image processing with frameworks that use the Mac's GPU.

## Does OpenCV work on Linux?

Yes. OpenCV works very well on Linux, which is the most common platform for computer vision servers and research. Install it with pip in a virtual environment, or through your distribution's package manager.

On servers and in Docker, use `opencv-python-headless` to avoid GUI dependencies; otherwise you may see errors about missing libGL libraries, which you can fix by installing the system library or switching to the headless package. For GPU-accelerated OpenCV functions with CUDA, you need to build from source with CUDA enabled; the pip packages do not include CUDA support. Many projects instead run deep learning on the GPU with PyTorch or ONNX Runtime and use OpenCV for pre- and post-processing.

## How does OpenCV resize work?

`cv2.resize` scales an image to a new width and height, computing new pixel values with an interpolation method. Note that the size argument is `(width, height)`, while NumPy image shapes are `(height, width, channels)`.

```python
import cv2
img = cv2.imread("photo.jpg")
small = cv2.resize(img, (640, 360), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)       # shrinking
big = cv2.resize(img, None, fx=2, fy=2, interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)  # enlarging by factor
```

Use `INTER_AREA` for shrinking, which avoids moire patterns, and `INTER_LINEAR` or `INTER_CUBIC` for enlarging. To keep the aspect ratio, compute one dimension from the other. For OCR, upscaling small text images often improves recognition.

## How does OpenCV findContours work?

`cv2.findContours` traces the boundaries of white shapes in a binary image and returns them as lists of points, plus a hierarchy describing which contours are inside others. You then measure, filter or draw them.

```python
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
_, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(binary, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
big = [c for c in contours if cv2.contourArea(c) > 500]
cv2.drawContours(img, big, -1, (0, 255, 0), 2)
```

Use `RETR_EXTERNAL` for outer shapes only, `RETR_TREE` for nested ones. Objects should be white on black; invert the threshold if needed. Contours are useful for counting objects, measuring sizes and cropping documents.

# How to install Tesseract OCR and languages, its history, and the Marvel Tesseract's story
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-tesseract-ocr-history/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To install Tesseract OCR, use the UB Mannheim installer on Windows, `sudo apt install tesseract-ocr` on Debian and Ubuntu, or `brew install tesseract` on macOS, then add language packs for the scripts you need, such as Hindi. Tesseract began at Hewlett-Packard in the 1980s and became open source in 2005. I use OCR in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page covers installing Tesseract and languages, its origins and release history, and, because the name is shared, the Marvel Tesseract's story.

## How do I install Tesseract on Windows?

Download the Windows installer from the UB Mannheim Tesseract page, run it, and during setup select additional languages if needed. Then add the install folder, usually C:\Program Files\Tesseract-OCR, to your PATH environment variable.

Verify by opening a new Command Prompt and running `tesseract --version`. If Windows cannot find it, check the PATH entry and restart the terminal. For Python, install pytesseract with pip and, if needed, point it to the executable path in code. Avoid unofficial download sites; the UB Mannheim builds are the widely recommended Windows packages linked from Tesseract's documentation. If you only need OCR occasionally, Windows Subsystem for Linux is an alternative: install the Linux package inside it and run Tesseract from there.

## How do I install Tesseract OCR on Linux and macOS?

On Debian or Ubuntu, run `sudo apt install tesseract-ocr`; on Fedora, `sudo dnf install tesseract`; on macOS with Homebrew, `brew install tesseract`. Then check with `tesseract --version` and list installed languages with `tesseract --list-langs`.

For Python projects, add `pip install pytesseract` and, optionally, OpenCV for preprocessing. In Docker images, install the system package in your Dockerfile so the engine is available inside the container. Distribution packages may lag the newest release; build from source or use project repositories if you need the latest features, though most users are fine with packaged versions.

## How do I install a language in Tesseract OCR?

Install the language's traineddata file into Tesseract's tessdata folder. On Linux, use packages such as `tesseract-ocr-hin` for Hindi; on Windows, select languages in the installer or copy traineddata files into the tessdata folder; on macOS, Homebrew's `tesseract-lang` adds many languages.

Then use the language code with `-l`, such as `tesseract scan.png out -l hin+eng` for Hindi and English. Official files come from the tessdata repositories, in three variants: tessdata_fast for speed, tessdata_best for accuracy, and the standard set. Check with `tesseract --list-langs` that the language appears. Set the `TESSDATA_PREFIX` environment variable if Tesseract looks in the wrong folder.

## Who created Tesseract OCR?

Tesseract was created at Hewlett-Packard Laboratories, with development led by Ray Smith, starting in 1985. HP released it as open source in 2005, and Google sponsored its development for many years, with Ray Smith continuing to lead the work there.

Today, Tesseract is maintained by an open-source community on GitHub. Its major architectural change came with version 4, which added an LSTM neural network recogniser, greatly improving accuracy. The project's longevity, nearly four decades, makes it one of the oldest continuously developed OCR engines still in wide use. Its design has been documented in research papers, which helped it become a reference point for later OCR systems.

## Where did Tesseract OCR come from?

Tesseract came from HP Labs research in the late 1980s and early 1990s, aimed at improving OCR for HP's scanners. It performed strongly in the 1995 OCR accuracy evaluation by the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, then development paused until HP open-sourced it in 2005.

After open-sourcing, Google took on much of the development, adding languages and improvements, and used OCR heavily in projects such as book scanning. The name comes from the four-dimensional shape, the tesseract, suggesting something beyond the ordinary. The engine's open availability made it the default OCR choice for developers and researchers worldwide.

## When did Tesseract come out?

Tesseract development began in 1985 at HP, its open-source release came in 2005, version 3 arrived in 2010, and version 4, with the LSTM neural network engine, was released in 2018. Version 5 followed in 2021 with further improvements.

Each major version improved accuracy, language support and performance. Check the GitHub releases page for the current version, and prefer versions 4 and above for their neural recogniser. The Marvel Tesseract first appeared on screen in 2011's Captain America: The First Avenger and in Thor's post-credits scene the same year, while the geometric term dates back to 1888.

## Where did the Tesseract come from in the Avengers films?

In the films, the Tesseract was kept on Asgard and hidden on Earth in Norway by Odin centuries ago. The Red Skull found it during the Second World War, Howard Stark later recovered it from the ocean, and S.H.I.E.L.D. studied it until Loki stole it in The Avengers.

Captain Marvel adds that it was used in Mar-Vell's secret laboratory in the 1990s, where the cat-like Flerken, Goose, swallowed it before returning it to S.H.I.E.L.D. In Marvel comics, the equivalent object is the Cosmic Cube, created by scientists, with a different origin story from the films.

## Why does Loki want the Tesseract?

Loki wants the Tesseract because it contains the Space Stone, which can open portals across space. In The Avengers, Thanos offers Loki an army, the Chitauri, to conquer Earth in exchange for the Tesseract, and Loki uses it to open a portal for the invasion.

Loki's motives include ruling Earth, proving himself after his rejection on Asgard, and the influence of Thanos, who gave him the scepter containing the Mind Stone. The Tesseract was both the invasion's key and Thanos's real prize. After the Avengers defeat him, Thor takes Loki and the Tesseract back to Asgard.

## Why did Loki take the Tesseract in Avengers: Endgame?

In Endgame, the Avengers travel back to 2012 to collect Infinity Stones, but the plan goes wrong: in the chaos at Stark Tower, the Tesseract slides across the floor to the captured Loki, who seizes the chance and teleports away with it to escape.

This creates a branched timeline, the premise of the Disney+ series Loki, where the Time Variance Authority captures this variant Loki and confiscates the Tesseract. Meanwhile, Tony Stark and Steve Rogers travel to 1970 to take another version of the Tesseract from a S.H.I.E.L.D. base to complete the mission.

## Where is the Tesseract now in the Marvel films?

In the main timeline, the Tesseract no longer exists: Thanos crushed it in Avengers: Infinity War to take the Space Stone. The 1970 Tesseract borrowed in Endgame was returned to its own time by Captain America after the final battle.

The variant Tesseract taken by Loki in 2012 was confiscated by the Time Variance Authority in the Loki series, where Infinity Stones are treated as ordinary objects. So the answer depends on the timeline. For the real-world Tesseract OCR engine, the answer is simpler: it is actively maintained on GitHub and installable on every major operating system.

# Is AI a good career in India? Roles, what hiring actually looks like, what fresher paths exist, and how to get in without an IIT tag
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/is-ai-a-good-career-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Is AI a good career in India?

**Yes, if you build things, and the qualifier matters more than the yes. Companies across India are adding AI features to products and hiring engineers who can ship them; the roles pay at or above general software roles at the same level, and the work is genuinely interesting. But entry-level AI hiring demands proof of shipped work earlier than most fields, and a stack of certificates without a deployed project does not get interviews. I got into GenAI work from a BCA programme without a placement cell by building and posting weekly, and that path is open to anyone willing to do the same [9].**


This page is my honest answer to the question students ask me most at campus sessions, with the industry references that back it [1][2][3] and the paths I have watched work and fail. My roadmap for GenAI engineering in India is written up separately [4].

> The question is never whether AI is a good career. It is whether you will be one of the people with something to show when the interview comes.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What AI roles actually exist in India?

**GenAI or AI engineer: builds features on top of models, RAG systems, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment; the most-hired role for freshers with projects. Machine learning engineer: trains and serves models, more infrastructure and data pipelines. Data scientist: analysis, experimentation, classical models, business communication. AI product engineer: full-stack developer who integrates AI well. Applied researcher or research engineer: papers and new methods, mostly requires a master's or PhD. Then MLOps, data engineering and annotation or evaluation roles around them. Most openings for freshers are in the first and fourth.**



## How does AI hiring actually work for freshers?

**Campus placements at top colleges bring companies to you; everywhere else, hiring happens through referrals, cold outreach, hackathons, communities and remote applications, and it evaluates what you have built. The interview usually has a coding round, a project deep-dive where you defend your decisions, and a system-design or take-home task such as building a small RAG or extraction pipeline. The project deep-dive is where most candidates fail and where a real shipped project makes you pass [6][7].**



## Do I need an IIT, NIT or IIIT degree?

**For campus placements at those colleges, the tag is the door. For everything else, it is a mild signal that a portfolio overrides. Remote companies, startups and most mid-size product firms evaluate the GitHub, the deployed demo and the interview, and referrals from communities and hackathons open the same doors a tag does [5][10]. I have watched BCA and tier-three B.Tech students get GenAI roles with strong projects and IIT students get rejected with none. The tag saves time; it does not substitute for work.**


## Do I need a master's or PhD for an AI career?

**Not for engineering roles, which are most of the roles. GenAI engineers, ML engineers, AI product engineers and MLOps engineers are hired on demonstrated ability to build. A master's helps for research roles and for some ML engineer roles at large labs, and a PhD is effectively required for research scientist positions. If you want to build products, build products; if you want to publish papers, the degree path is the right one. Choose by what you want to do daily, not by what sounds impressive.**



## What skills do AI jobs in India test for?

**Python, thoroughly. Working with model APIs and structured outputs. Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, evaluation. Fine-tuning basics with LoRA and when not to fine-tune. Evaluation: how you know it works. Deployment: an API, a container, a free-tier host, logging. Data handling and SQL. Git and a readable repository. Communication: explaining a technical decision to a non-technical person. Not tested for freshers in most roles: deriving backpropagation by hand, training models from scratch, or reciting paper titles.**



## What are the real risks of an AI career?

**Entry-level roles are competitive and demand shipped proof early, so students who only study fall behind students who build. Tools change fast, so the specific framework you learn will be replaced; the skills that persist are evaluation, data handling and systems thinking. Hype produces bad job descriptions and some companies that do not know what they need. Some roles labelled AI are data entry or annotation. And AI tools make junior generalist coding cheaper, which raises the bar for what a junior must bring. None of these is a reason to avoid the field; each is a reason to build rather than collect certificates.**



## What does a first AI job pay in India?

**Enough to be worth it, with wide variance by city, company type and role, and I will not invent numbers here. Startups and remote roles often pay above local service companies for the same skills; product companies pay above both for strong candidates. Compensation rises quickly in the first three years for engineers who ship. The practical advice: research current ranges on public sites for the specific role and city, and negotiate your first offer, because most freshers do not and leave money on the table [8].**


## Which path should I take: placement, remote, startup or freelance?

**Campus placement if your college has good AI hiring; it is the easiest door. Remote roles at foreign startups if you can show shipped work and communicate well; they pay well and evaluate portfolios [5]. Indian startups if you want to learn fast and take ownership early. Freelance and building for local businesses if you want cash flow and real users while you look, which is what I did. Many people combine them: a freelance project becomes a portfolio piece becomes a remote offer.**




## What should my first eighteen months look like?

**Months one to three: Python, one model API, one small deployed app. Months four to six: a RAG system over real documents, measured and deployed; start posting weekly. Months seven to nine: a vision or fine-tuning project with an evaluation; first hackathon. Months ten to twelve: an internship, freelance project or open-source contribution; second hackathon; polish the portfolio. Months thirteen to eighteen: apply widely, interview, iterate on feedback, and keep shipping. My full roadmap with the specific resources is on the portfolio [4].**



## Is AI a good career for non-CS students?

**Yes for engineering roles if you learn to program properly, which takes months of daily practice, not weeks. Domain knowledge is an advantage: a pharmacy student building a prescription reader, a commerce student building an invoice extractor, a biology student building a lab-report assistant each has a project no CS student can match. The route is the same: Python, one API, one deployed project, weekly posts, communities. My sessions for non-CS audiences exist because this route works [7].**



## Where should I start?

**Tonight: install Python, make one API call to a model, and put the script on GitHub with a README. This week: post what you built. Next month: a RAG system over documents you actually have. The career follows from the habit.** For a career session at your college on getting into AI from anywhere in India, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
