# Is GGUF a quantization method? Choosing GGUF quants, GPTQ vs AWQ, and GGUF in Ollama
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/is-gguf-a-quantization-method/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


GGUF is not itself a quantization method; it is a file format, created by the llama.cpp project, that stores a model's weights and metadata in one file. It supports many quantization types, such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0 and the I-quants, which is why "GGUF" is often used loosely to mean a quantized local model. Quantization is central to FineTune Studio's QLoRA training, so this page covers how GGUF quants work, choosing one, GGUF versus GPTQ and AWQ, the best methods, GPU loading, and using GGUF with Ollama.

## Is GGUF a quantization method?

No. GGUF, the GPT-Generated Unified Format, is a container format for model tensors plus metadata such as architecture, tokenizer and chat template. Within a GGUF file, tensors can be stored in full precision or in many quantized formats.

GGUF replaced the older GGML format in 2023 and is used by llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio and other local AI tools. The quantization happens when converting a model to GGUF with llama.cpp's tools, choosing a type such as Q4_K_M. So the accurate phrasing is "a Q4_K_M quantization stored in GGUF format". Single-file packaging is one reason GGUF became the standard for local models.

## How does GGUF quantization work?

llama.cpp quantization splits weights into small blocks and stores each block as low-bit integers plus scale factors, so values can be approximately reconstructed during inference. K-quants use a two-level structure of super-blocks and sub-blocks with their own scales for better accuracy.

The suffixes describe variants: Q4 means roughly 4 bits per weight; "_K" means K-quant; "_S", "_M" and "_L" mean small, medium and large mixes, where more important tensors get higher precision. I-quants, such as IQ4_XS, use more sophisticated encodings and often an importance matrix computed from calibration text to protect influential weights. Lower bits save memory and speed up inference with some quality loss.

## Which GGUF quantization should I use?

Q4_K_M is the usual default: a good balance of size, speed and quality for most models. Choose Q5_K_M or Q6_K for better quality if memory allows, Q8_0 for near-original quality, and Q3 or IQ3 variants only when memory is very tight.

Rules of thumb:

- Pick the highest quality that fits fully in your GPU memory with room for context.
- Larger models at lower bits often beat smaller models at higher bits.
- Very small models suffer more from aggressive quantization.
- Coding and maths are more sensitive than chat; test those tasks specifically.

Always compare two or three quants on your own prompts before settling.

## How do Q4_K_M, IQ4_XS and IQ4_NL compare?

All three are roughly 4-bit. Q4_K_M is a K-quant with a medium mix, slightly larger and very widely used. IQ4_XS is an I-quant that is smaller for similar quality, especially with an importance matrix. IQ4_NL uses a non-linear quantization grid and suits some hardware paths.

In practice, IQ4_XS often gives quality close to Q4_K_M at a smaller size, helpful when you are just short of fitting a model in VRAM. I-quants can be slower on some CPUs and older backends, while K-quants are well optimised everywhere. Differences in output quality are usually small; measure perplexity or task accuracy on your workload if it matters, and choose for speed and fit.

## GPTQ vs GGUF vs AWQ: which quantization method is right for me?

Use GGUF for local inference with llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio, especially on CPUs, Macs or mixed CPU and GPU setups. Use GPTQ or AWQ for GPU serving with engines such as vLLM or Transformers, where they integrate with fast GPU kernels.

GPTQ quantizes weights using second-order information to minimise error; AWQ protects weights tied to large activations; both target GPU inference at around 4 bits. GGUF offers many quantization levels and runs almost anywhere. For a production API on GPUs serving many users, AWQ or GPTQ with vLLM is common; for laptops, desktops and edge devices, GGUF is usually simplest.

## What is the best quantization method for LLMs?

There is no single best method; it depends on hardware and use. For GPU serving, AWQ and GPTQ at 4 bits, or FP8 on GPUs that support it, are strong. For local use, GGUF K-quants and I-quants work well. For fine-tuning on limited memory, QLoRA's 4-bit NF4 is standard.

Evaluate on your tasks: measure quality on a test set, latency, throughput and memory. Quality loss grows below 4 bits, and multilingual or reasoning tasks can degrade more than benchmarks suggest. In FineTune Studio, the base model loads in 4-bit NF4 for training, while deployment formats are chosen separately for the serving environment.

## Can I fully load a GGUF model on the GPU?

Yes. In llama.cpp, offload all layers with the GPU layers option, such as `-ngl 99`; in Ollama, models load as many layers as fit on the GPU automatically, with settings to adjust. The model must fit in VRAM along with the context cache.

If it does not fit, layers stay on the CPU and generation slows. Options: choose a smaller quant, reduce context length, quantize the KV cache where supported, or use a smaller model. Check memory use with nvidia-smi or Ollama's process status. Full GPU offload gives the biggest speed improvement for local inference, often several times faster than CPU.

## Does Ollama use GGUF?

Yes. Ollama runs models in GGUF format under the hood, built on llama.cpp technology. Models you pull from the Ollama library are GGUF files packaged with templates and parameters, and you can import your own GGUF files.

You can also run GGUF models directly from Hugging Face with Ollama by referencing the repository, for supported models. Ollama adds model management, an API, automatic GPU offloading and a simple interface on top of the format. Because it uses GGUF, the same quantization choices apply: tags such as q4_K_M or q8_0 indicate which quant you are pulling.

## How do I import a GGUF file into Ollama?

Create a text file named Modelfile with a `FROM` line pointing to your GGUF file, add the chat template and parameters if needed, then run `ollama create` to register the model and `ollama run` to use it.

```bash
# Modelfile contents: FROM ./my-model-Q4_K_M.gguf
ollama create my-model -f Modelfile
ollama run my-model
```

If the model's chat template is not detected, copy it from the original model card into the Modelfile's TEMPLATE section, since a wrong template causes poor answers. This is how fine-tuned models, such as QLoRA results exported to GGUF, become local Ollama models.

## How can I run local GGUF models without the command line?

Use a graphical app: Ollama's desktop app lets you chat with installed models, LM Studio lets you search, download and run GGUF models from Hugging Face entirely through its interface, and web interfaces such as Open WebUI connect to Ollama in a browser.

LM Studio is especially beginner-friendly: it shows which quantizations fit your hardware, downloads them, and provides a chat window and a local API server. Importing custom GGUF files into Ollama still typically uses a Modelfile, though GUI front ends can help. For students without coding experience, these apps make local, private AI accessible on ordinary laptops.

# Is voice to text AI? Speech recognition types, best models and apps
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/is-voice-to-text-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, voice to text is AI. Modern speech recognition uses deep neural networks trained on large amounts of transcribed audio to turn speech into text, whether it is your phone's keyboard dictation, Google's speech services or OpenAI's Whisper. Older systems used statistical models, which also count as machine learning. This page explains what kind of AI speech recognition is, whether it is generative AI, the best models and apps, how to dictate on a MacBook, and how AI voices, text to speech and voice-overs differ.

## Is voice to text AI?

Yes. Voice to text, also called speech recognition or speech to text, uses AI models that learn from data how sounds map to words. Every mainstream dictation and transcription tool today is built on deep learning.

The model listens to audio, converts it into a representation of sound frequencies over time, and predicts the most likely words, using context to choose between similar-sounding options. That is why accuracy improved so much in the last decade: models trained on far more audio handle accents, noise and natural speech better. Still, errors cluster on names, numbers, technical terms and mixed languages, such as Hindi and English in the same sentence, so proofread anything important.

## Is all speech to text AI?

Practically all modern speech to text is AI, using machine learning models. Very early systems used rule-based pattern matching on a few words, and simple voice commands on old devices used small templates, but those are rare today.

Speech recognition moved from template matching in early research, to statistical models such as hidden Markov models combined with language models, which are a form of machine learning, to end-to-end deep learning in the 2010s and transformers today. So whether a tool is "AI" is not really in question; what differs is how capable the model is, whether it runs on your device or in the cloud, and what data it was trained on.

## Is speech to text generative AI?

Usually it is classed as perception or recognition AI rather than generative AI, because it transcribes what was said instead of creating new content. But many modern systems, such as Whisper, use a generative transformer decoder that produces the transcript token by token.

The distinction matters in practice because generative-style decoders can occasionally invent text, for example during long silences or background music, which a pure recognition approach is less prone to do. When multimodal language models transcribe audio, they can also summarise, translate or answer questions about it, which is clearly generative. For transcripts that must be exact, such as legal or medical records, use systems built for verbatim transcription and review the output.

## What type of AI is voice to text?

Voice to text is an application of deep learning in the field of automatic speech recognition (ASR), part of speech and language processing. Models are usually trained with supervised learning on paired audio and transcripts.

Common architectures include encoder-decoder transformers, as in Whisper, and models trained with connectionist temporal classification or transducer methods, which suit streaming. Many systems add a language model to improve word choices. On-device recognition, as on modern phones, uses compact models for speed and privacy, while cloud services use larger models for accuracy. In my OCR & Speech Workspace, live speech-to-text sits alongside document chat, because once speech is text, retrieval and summarisation work on it too.

## Is Google speech to text AI?

Yes. Google's speech recognition, in Android voice typing, Google Assistant, YouTube captions and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, is built on deep learning models trained on large speech datasets in many languages.

Google Cloud Speech-to-Text offers models for different needs, such as long recordings, phone calls and live streaming, with features such as automatic punctuation, word timestamps and speaker diarisation, and support for Indian languages. Gemini models can also transcribe audio and then summarise or translate it. For developers, the choice between Cloud Speech-to-Text and Gemini depends on whether you need verbatim transcripts with timing at scale, or understanding of the content.

## What is the best speech to text AI model?

There is no single best model for every language and audio type. Strong options include OpenAI's Whisper, which is open source, plus commercial models from Google, Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI and specialist providers. Public benchmarks such as Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard compare open models.

Choose by your needs:

- **Free, private, offline**: Whisper or optimised versions such as faster-whisper and whisper.cpp.
- **Live captions**: a streaming cloud API.
- **Indian languages and mixed speech**: test providers with Indian-language models on your own samples.
- **Meetings**: services with speaker diarisation.

Benchmark on ten of your own recordings; word error rates on public datasets do not always match your accents and noise.

## What is the best speech to text AI app?

For everyday dictation, your device's built-in voice typing is best: Gboard on Android, Dictation on iPhone and Mac, and voice typing on Windows. For meetings, use the transcription in Teams, Google Meet or Zoom. For recordings, Word's Transcribe or a Whisper-based app works well.

Choose by use:

- **Notes and messages**: built-in keyboard dictation.
- **Lectures**: a recorder app with transcription, or Whisper on your laptop afterwards.
- **Interviews and podcasts**: tools with speaker labels and editing.
- **Privacy-sensitive audio**: apps that run on the device.

Check how the app handles your data, since recordings can contain personal information, and get consent before recording other people.

## How do I use speech to text on a MacBook Air?

Turn on Dictation in System Settings, under Keyboard, then press the dictation key, the microphone key on newer keyboards, or the Fn or Globe key twice, and start speaking in any text field. Press it again or click Done to stop.

Tips:

- Say punctuation, such as "comma", "full stop" and "new line", or let automatic punctuation handle it where supported.
- Choose your language and add more in Dictation settings; English (India) is available.
- Dictation on Apple Silicon Macs can run on the device for many languages, which is faster and more private.
- For longer recordings, transcribe audio files with an app or Whisper rather than live dictation.

Proofread names and technical terms after dictating.

## What is the difference between an AI voice and text to speech?

Text to speech is the technology that converts written text into spoken audio. "AI voice" usually refers to modern neural text to speech, which sounds natural, or to voice cloning, which imitates a specific person's voice from samples.

Older text to speech sounded robotic because it stitched together recorded sounds or used simple synthesis. Neural TTS generates speech with natural rhythm, emotion and emphasis, and some systems take style instructions such as "excited" or "calm". Voice cloning raises serious consent and fraud risks, so reputable services require permission from the voice owner. When you use AI voices in videos or apps, disclose that the voice is synthetic where listeners might assume it is human.

## What is the difference between a voice-over and text to speech?

A voice-over is a human recording narration, usually a professional voice artist or the creator. Text to speech generates narration from text with a synthetic voice, without anyone recording.

Choose voice-over for emotion, brand voice, nuance and trust, such as ads, documentaries and personal content. Choose text to speech for speed, cost, easy updates and many languages, such as tutorials, accessibility features, prototypes and internal training. Modern TTS is good enough for many explainer videos, but listeners still notice in long or emotional content. A common workflow is to draft narration with TTS to check timing, then record the final version yourself.

# Jobs after BCA: scope, best roles, Google, BCA vs B.Tech, and getting a well-paid job
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/jobs-after-bca/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


BCA jobs are the roles Bachelor of Computer Applications graduates take in software and IT: developer, web developer, tester, data analyst, technical support, system administrator, and increasingly cloud, cybersecurity and AI roles. BCA graduates do get good jobs when they combine coursework with real projects, internships and in-demand skills. I am a BCA student at VSICS who leads engineering at SCULT INDIA and shipped five production AI apps in 2026, so this page covers BCA job scope, where to apply, the best roles, Google, BCA versus B.Tech, and landing a well-paid job.

## What is a BCA job?

A BCA job is any role suited to Bachelor of Computer Applications graduates, typically in software development, IT services, testing, data, networking and technical support, where BCA skills in programming, databases and web development apply directly.

Common titles include software developer, web developer, Android developer, QA tester, data analyst, IT support engineer, database administrator and technical content writer. Employers include IT services firms, product companies, startups, banks, e-commerce companies and government organisations. As skills grow, BCA graduates move into senior development, architecture, product and leadership roles, just like other computing graduates.

## What are the BCA course and job opportunities?

BCA is a three or four-year undergraduate programme covering programming, data structures, databases, operating systems, networking, web development and software engineering. Job opportunities span development, testing, data, cloud, cybersecurity, IT support and AI-related roles.

Graduates can also pursue MCA, MBA in IT or data science programmes, or specialised certifications. Government roles, banking IT positions and teaching are further options. The course gives foundations; specialisation decides opportunities. Choose a direction by your third semester, such as web development or AI, and build projects in it. The three-year roadmap I shared at the VSICS induction follows this idea: fundamentals in year one, a specialisation and hackathons in year two, internships and a capstone in year three.

## What is the job scope after BCA?

The scope is broad and growing, because every industry needs software. Strong areas include full-stack web development, mobile apps, data analytics, cloud and DevOps, cybersecurity, quality engineering, and AI application development such as RAG systems and automation.

AI has expanded opportunities for BCA graduates: companies need people who can build AI features into products, automate workflows and evaluate AI systems, skills learned through projects rather than specific degrees. Freelancing, startups and remote roles add options. The scope is limited mainly by skills: graduates who only complete coursework face tougher competition than those with portfolios.

## Do BCA students get jobs?

Yes. Many BCA students get jobs through campus placements, off-campus applications, internships that convert to offers, startups and freelancing. Results depend heavily on skills, projects, communication and the effort put into job searching.

Some campus recruiters restrict eligibility to B.Tech graduates, so BCA students often rely more on off-campus hiring, internships and referrals. Build a GitHub portfolio, join hackathons, contribute to open source and practise interviews. In my experience as a BCA student, hackathon wins and shipped projects opened more doors than any certificate.

## Where can I get a job after BCA?

Look at IT services companies, which hire many freshers; product companies and startups, which hire on skills; banks and financial firms' IT teams; e-commerce and fintech companies; government IT departments; and remote roles with international startups.

Channels: college placement cell, LinkedIn, company career pages, Internshala for internships, the AICTE internship portal, the National Career Service, hackathons where sponsors recruit, and referrals from alumni and seniors. Apply consistently, tailor your resume to each role, and follow up professionally. Internships during BCA are the most reliable path to full-time offers. Track every application in a simple spreadsheet with dates, contacts and outcomes, and review it weekly to see which channels actually produce interviews.

## Which job is best for BCA students?

The best job matches your interests and growth goals. Software development, especially full-stack web development, offers the widest opportunities; data analysis suits those who enjoy numbers; cloud and DevOps suit infrastructure enthusiasts; and AI application development is growing fast.

For freshers, prioritise learning and mentorship over a slightly better first offer: a role at a strong engineering team or fast-growing startup builds skills that compound. Avoid roles with little technical growth unless they are stepping stones. Revisit your direction after one to two years, once you know what work energises you. Early roles are also where habits form, so choose teams that review code, write tests and ship regularly.

## Which BCA jobs pay the most?

Higher pay generally comes from software engineering at product companies and well-funded startups, especially in specialised areas such as backend systems, cloud architecture, cybersecurity, data engineering and AI or machine learning engineering.

Pay grows with demonstrated skill and impact rather than degree: experienced BCA graduates in these areas can match peers from any background. To move towards higher-paying roles, build depth in one in-demand area, ship real projects, contribute to open source, gain internship experience at product companies, and develop communication skills. Check current salary data on job sites for your city type and role.

## Can I get a job at Google after BCA?

It is possible but highly competitive. Google hires based on skills, problem solving and experience, and many roles do not strictly require a B.Tech. BCA graduates often reach companies like Google after gaining experience, completing an MCA or building an exceptional track record.

Prepare with strong data structures and algorithms, system design basics for experienced roles, real projects and open-source contributions. Google's student programmes and internships, when available, have specific eligibility, so check Google Careers. Referrals help get interviews; performance decides offers. Treat Google as one goal among many great engineering employers. Many engineers join after building strong records at startups or other product companies, where they gain the scale and ownership experience large companies look for.

## BCA vs B.Tech: which has better job opportunities in India?

B.Tech often has an advantage in campus placements, since many large recruiters target engineering colleges and some set B.Tech eligibility criteria. BCA graduates compete well in skill-based hiring at startups, product companies and through off-campus routes.

B.Tech provides deeper engineering and mathematics; BCA is more application-focused and shorter. Many BCA graduates pursue MCA to access postgraduate hiring and NIT programmes through NIMCET. In practice, after a few years of experience, skills and achievements matter far more than the undergraduate degree. Choose based on interests, budget and the path you can commit to.

## How do I get a well-paid job after completing BCA?

Specialise in an in-demand area, build two or three strong projects with real users, complete internships, practise data structures and interviews, and apply widely, especially to product companies and startups that hire on skills.

A plan:

- Pick a track: full-stack, data, cloud or AI engineering.
- Build and deploy projects with documented results.
- Do at least one internship before graduating.
- Join hackathons and open-source projects.
- Practise coding problems and mock interviews weekly.
- Use referrals from alumni and your network.

Consider MCA if your target employers prefer postgraduates, but do not wait for a degree to start building.

# What jobs is AI taking over? Most affected roles, timing, risks and safer careers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/jobs-ai-taking-over-safe-careers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

AI is taking over tasks more than whole jobs, with the biggest effects so far on customer support, translation, writing, data entry, basic coding and other routine knowledge work. Some roles shrink while new ones appear. I lead engineering at SCULT INDIA and mentor students on careers, so this page covers which jobs AI is taking over now and next, examples, timing, why it happens and why it hurts, whether to worry, safer careers, and what was automated around 2021. What jobs is AI taking over? AI is mainly taking over tasks within jobs: drafting text, answering routine customer queries, translating, transcribing, summarising documents, entering data and writing simple code. Roles built mostly on these tasks face the most pressure. Also asked as: what jobs are ai taking over The International Labour Organization's 2025 analysis found clerical support work the most exposed occupational group to generative AI, while most other jobs face partial exposure where AI changes tasks rather than replacing workers. Customer service, content writing, translation, bookkeeping and junior software roles are adapting fastest. Many workers now use AI to do more in the same time. Whether exposure leads to job losses depends on demand, regulation and how employers choose to deploy AI. Which jobs is AI taking over the most? The most affected jobs include customer service representatives, data entry clerks, administrative assistants, translators, transcriptionists, copywriters, proofreaders, telemarketers and some entry-level programming and analyst roles. Also asked as: what jobs are ai taking over the most The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 lists clerical roles, such as cashiers, data entry clerks and administrative secretaries, among the fastest-declining jobs through 2030. Research from Stanford's Digital Economy Lab in 2025 found declining employment for early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations such as software development and customer service, while experienced workers held steady. The pattern suggests AI hits tasks typically given to beginners hardest, which raises the importance of building judgement early. What jobs is AI going to take over? Over the next decade, AI agents are likely to automate more multi-step knowledge work: claims processing, routine legal document review, bookkeeping, scheduling, first-line technical support, basic research and parts of software testing. Also asked as: what jobs are ai gonna take over Physical automation will advance more slowly, but robotics and self-driving technology may affect warehouse work, delivery and some driving jobs. The World Economic Forum projects that technology will create more jobs than it displaces by 2030, with about 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced, though the new jobs need different skills. Growth areas include AI and data roles, cybersecurity, care work and green energy. Predictions vary widely, so watch actual hiring trends in your field. What are examples of AI taking jobs? Examples include companies replacing parts of customer support teams with AI chatbots, publishers cutting freelance writing and translation work, firms reducing transcription and data entry staff, and businesses slowing hiring of junior developers as coding assistants improve. Several companies have publicly said AI assistants now handle work equivalent to many support agents, while freelance platforms saw falling demand for simple writing and translation tasks after ChatGPT's release. In many cases, companies freeze hiring rather than lay people off, so the effect shows up as fewer openings. There are also counterexamples: some firms that cut staff for AI later rehired people when quality dropped. These examples show AI reshaping work unevenly rather than uniformly. When will AI start taking jobs? AI has already started affecting jobs. Automation has replaced routine tasks for decades, and since generative AI arrived in late 2022, measurable effects have appeared in writing, translation, customer support and entry-level technology hiring. The pace varies by industry and country. Adoption depends on cost, reliability, regulation and how easily tasks can be checked. Large-scale changes usually unfold over years, as companies redesign workflows, rather than overnight. In India, IT services, business process outsourcing and customer support are especially exposed, since they involve many standardised knowledge tasks. The practical question is not when, but which of your tasks AI can already do, and how you add value beyond them. Why is AI taking jobs away? AI takes jobs because it can now perform many language and pattern-based tasks quickly, around the clock and at lower cost than human labour, and businesses adopt tools that improve productivity and margins. Generative models made it possible to automate tasks that previously required human judgement about language, such as replying to customers, summarising documents or writing code. Companies under pressure to cut costs or grow without hiring adopt these tools first where output is easy to verify. Investor expectations and competition accelerate adoption. Yet AI still makes mistakes, so many deployments keep humans reviewing outputs, which changes jobs rather than removing them entirely. The economic incentive, not the technology alone, drives replacement decisions. Why is AI taking jobs bad? AI-driven job losses are harmful when workers lose income faster than they can retrain, when gains concentrate among a few companies, and when entry-level roles disappear, breaking the ladder people use to gain experience. Displacement hits some groups harder, such as clerical workers, who are disproportionately women in many countries according to the ILO, and young graduates seeking first jobs. Communities built around outsourced services may face regional impacts. There are also quality risks when AI replaces human judgement in sensitive areas such as healthcare or legal advice. Policies that help include retraining programmes, social safety nets and transparency about automation. Handled well, AI can also remove tedious work and create new roles. Should you be worried about AI taking jobs? Be alert rather than worried. If most of your work is routine and easy to verify, start adapting now. Most people will see their jobs change rather than disappear, and those who use AI well gain an advantage. Also asked as: should i be worried about ai taking jobs Practical steps: list your weekly tasks and mark which AI can already do; learn to use AI tools for those tasks so you become faster; invest in skills AI handles poorly, such as judgement, relationships, domain expertise and responsibility for outcomes; and build visible proof of your work. I advise the students I mentor to combine strong fundamentals with real projects that use AI. Anxiety is understandable, but action reduces risk far more than avoidance. What jobs are safe from AI taking over? Jobs that combine physical dexterity, human relationships, complex judgement and accountability are safest, such as nurses, electricians, plumbers, therapists, teachers, social workers, skilled trades, emergency responders and senior managers. No job is entirely untouched, but these roles depend on presence, trust and unpredictable environments that AI and robots handle poorly. Healthcare and care work also face growing demand from ageing populations. In technology, roles that own systems end to end, such as senior engineers, security specialists and AI engineers who build and evaluate AI systems, remain in demand. Safety comes less from job titles than from doing the hardest, most human parts of any role well. What jobs was AI taking over in 2021? In 2021, before generative AI became mainstream, automation mainly affected routine tasks: chatbots handling simple customer queries, robotic process automation for data entry and invoices, warehouse robots, self-checkout, and machine translation for basic content. Also asked as: what jobs are ai taking over in 2021 Predictive AI also automated parts of credit scoring, fraud detection, recommendation and document classification. Most of these systems handled narrow, rule-like tasks, so they affected repetitive clerical and manual roles rather than creative or professional work. The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 changed this, extending automation to writing, coding, analysis and conversation. Comparing 2021 with today shows how quickly the frontier moved from routine processing to knowledge work.

# Keyword vs vector search: FTS, grep, Elasticsearch, algorithms, models, DBs, SPLADE
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/keyword-vs-vector-search-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Keyword search matches the exact words in a query, while vector search matches meaning using embeddings, so each finds results the other misses. Production systems often combine both. In RAG.NextUpgrad I use hybrid retrieval, dense vectors plus BM25 merged with reciprocal rank fusion and then reranked, so this page compares keyword, full-text, grep and Elasticsearch with vector search, then covers examples, algorithms, models, databases, SPLADE and a short tutorial. Keyword vs vector search: what is the difference? Keyword search ranks documents by matching query terms, usually with BM25 over an inverted index. Vector search converts text into embeddings and finds documents whose vectors are closest in meaning, even without shared words. Keyword search excels at exact names, codes, error messages and rare terms, and it is fast, cheap and explainable. Vector search handles synonyms, paraphrases and natural language questions, such as matching car repair to automobile maintenance, but it can miss exact identifiers and is harder to debug. Hybrid search runs both and merges results, often with reciprocal rank fusion, then a reranker orders the final list. That combination is the pattern I use in RAG.NextUpgrad, because real users mix exact terms with vague questions. FTS vs vector search: which should you use? Full-text search, such as PostgreSQL's tsvector or SQLite FTS5, is keyword search built into a database, with stemming, stop words and ranking. Use it for exact terms, and use vector search for meaning-based queries. Many teams run both in the same database: PostgreSQL with full-text search and pgvector lets you combine scores in one SQL query, avoiding a separate search service. Full-text search needs no embedding model, updates instantly and costs little, while vector search requires embedding every document and query. For product search, documentation and RAG, a hybrid of the two usually gives the best relevance. Start with full-text search if queries are mostly keywords, and add vectors when users ask natural language questions. Grep vs vector search: when does each work? Grep finds exact text patterns, including regular expressions, by scanning files line by line. It has no ranking or understanding of meaning. Vector search ranks results by semantic similarity but cannot guarantee exact matches. Grep suits code, logs and configuration, where you know the identifier or error string, and it needs no index. Coding agents rely heavily on grep-style search because code has precise names that agents can guess and refine. Vector search suits natural language documents where wording varies. For large codebases, combine both: grep or symbol search for identifiers, and embeddings for questions such as where authentication is handled. Grep slows on huge corpora, while indexed search scales better. Elasticsearch vs vector search: are they different? Elasticsearch began as a keyword search engine built on Lucene and BM25, but it now supports vector search too, with dense vector fields, approximate kNN using HNSW and hybrid queries combining both. So the real comparison is Elasticsearch, or OpenSearch, versus dedicated vector databases such as Qdrant, Milvus or Pinecone. Elasticsearch is strong when you need mature keyword search, filtering, aggregations and analytics alongside vectors in one system. Dedicated vector databases can be simpler to operate for pure vector workloads and may offer more vector-specific features. Teams already running Elasticsearch often add vectors there rather than introducing a new database. Benchmark on your data and query patterns before choosing. What are examples of vector search? Common examples include semantic document search, retrieval for RAG chatbots, product recommendations, image search with models such as CLIP, near-duplicate detection, code search, and matching support tickets to known solutions. In RAG, vector search retrieves passages relevant to a question so the model answers from evidence. E-commerce sites find similar products from text or images. Music and video platforms recommend content from embedding similarity. Fraud and anomaly detection compare behaviour vectors. Face recognition compares face embeddings, as FaceVision does in the browser, storing embeddings rather than images. Each example follows the same pattern: convert items to vectors with a suitable model, index them, then search by similarity. What is the best vector search algorithm? HNSW, a graph-based approximate nearest neighbour algorithm, is the most widely used default, offering high recall and fast queries. Other strong options include IVF with product quantization for memory efficiency and DiskANN for huge datasets on SSDs. For small collections, up to perhaps tens of thousands of vectors, exact brute-force search is simple and accurate. HNSW trades memory for speed and suits most production workloads. IVF partitions vectors into clusters and searches only the nearest ones, and quantization compresses vectors to cut memory at some recall cost. Libraries such as FAISS implement many of these. Tune parameters such as ef_search in HNSW, measuring recall against exact search and latency on your data. What is the best model for vector search? There is no single best model. Strong embedding options include OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models, Cohere Embed, Voyage AI, and open models such as BGE-M3, E5, Nomic Embed and Qwen3 Embedding. The MTEB leaderboard compares them across tasks. Choose by language coverage, domain, context length, dimension size, licence and whether you need self-hosting. Multilingual models matter for Indian languages and mixed-language text. Smaller dimensions reduce storage and speed up search, and some models support shortening embeddings with little loss. Benchmarks rarely match your data, so build a small evaluation set of real queries with known relevant documents and measure recall for a few candidates. Use the same model for documents and queries. What are the top vector search databases? Popular choices include pgvector for PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone, Chroma and LanceDB, plus vector features in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Redis and MongoDB Atlas. Also asked as: top vector search dbs Pick based on scale and operations. pgvector suits teams already on PostgreSQL who want vectors beside relational data. Qdrant and Weaviate offer strong filtering and hybrid search, Milvus targets very large deployments, and Pinecone is fully managed. Chroma and LanceDB work well for local development and smaller apps. Check filtering performance, hybrid search support, backups, multi-tenancy and hosting options. For most projects, the database matters less than chunking, embedding choice and retrieval design, so do not over-optimise this decision early. What is SPLADE for sparse vector search? SPLADE is a learned sparse retrieval model. It uses a BERT-style model to assign weights to vocabulary terms for each document and query, including related terms not present in the text, producing sparse vectors searchable with an inverted index. Also asked as: splade for sparse vector search explained This combines the precision and efficiency of keyword search with some semantic understanding: a document about automobiles can receive weight for car even if it never uses that word. Because the vectors are sparse, they work with inverted indexes, and results are more interpretable than dense embeddings. SPLADE often performs strongly on retrieval benchmarks and pairs well with dense vectors in hybrid systems. Several vector databases support sparse vectors natively, making SPLADE practical in production. What does a basic vector search tutorial look like? Split documents into chunks, embed each chunk with an embedding model, store the vectors with their text in an index, embed the user's query with the same model, and return the nearest chunks by cosine similarity. A minimal Python version uses sentence-transformers for embeddings and FAISS or Chroma as the index, in under fifty lines of code. Next steps improve quality: add metadata filters, hybrid search with BM25, reciprocal rank fusion and a reranker. Evaluate with real questions, measuring whether the right chunk appears in the top results. Then add an LLM that answers from retrieved chunks with citations, and you have the core of a RAG system like RAG.NextUpgrad.

# How LangChain agents work: Deep Agents, MCP, Bedrock and agentic memory
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/langchain-agents-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A LangChain agent is a language model running in a loop with tools: the model decides which tool to call, LangChain executes it, the result goes back to the model, and the loop continues until the model gives a final answer. Modern LangChain builds agents on LangGraph, which manages state and control flow. This page explains how agents work and how to build one, what Deep Agents are, LangChain versus MCP and how they combine, using AWS Bedrock models, upgrading old retrieval chains to tools, and what agentic approaches and agentic memory mean.

## How do LangChain agents work?

A LangChain agent gives a model a system prompt and a set of tools with names, descriptions and input schemas. On each step, the model either requests a tool call or answers; LangChain runs requested tools, appends the results to the conversation, and calls the model again.

This is the ReAct pattern: reason, act, observe, repeat. LangGraph underneath tracks the state, the message history and any custom fields, and lets you add limits, human approval steps, persistence so conversations resume later, and streaming of intermediate steps. The quality of an agent depends mostly on tool descriptions, instructions and the model's tool-calling ability, not on the framework. Keep tools few and well described.

## How do I build a LangChain agent?

Define tools as Python functions with docstrings, choose a chat model that supports tool calling, and create an agent with LangChain's agent constructor, then invoke it with a user message.

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def room_for(course: str) -> str:
    """Return the classroom for a course code such as BCA301."""
    return {"BCA301": "Room 4"}.get(course.upper(), "Unknown course")

agent = create_agent(model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5", tools=[room_for],
                     system_prompt="Answer timetable questions using tools. Say so if unsure.")
out = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is BCA301?"}]})
print(out["messages"][-1].content)
```

APIs evolve between versions, so check the current LangChain docs for the exact constructor and model identifiers.

## What are LangChain Deep Agents?

Deep Agents is LangChain's approach for agents that handle long, complex tasks. It adds a planning tool for keeping a to-do list, sub-agents for delegating focused work, a virtual file system for notes and intermediate results, and a detailed system prompt.

The idea comes from how capable coding and research agents work: they plan, break work into parts, write things down instead of keeping everything in context, and delegate. Deep Agents packages these patterns on top of LangGraph so you can build, for example, a research agent that searches, saves findings to files and writes a report. They cost more tokens than simple agents, so use them when tasks genuinely need many steps.

## What is the difference between LangChain and MCP?

LangChain is a framework for building LLM applications and agents in code. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open protocol for exposing tools, data and prompts to any AI application. They solve different problems and work together.

With LangChain you write your application: prompts, chains, agents, retrieval and state. With MCP you package tools as servers that any MCP-compatible client can use, such as Claude, IDE agents or your own LangChain agent. If you build a tool once as an MCP server, it works across many apps; if you build it only as a LangChain tool, it works in LangChain. Many teams use LangChain for app logic and MCP for shareable tools.

## Does LangChain support MCP?

Yes. The LangChain MCP adapters package lets LangChain and LangGraph agents load tools from MCP servers and use them like native tools.

The typical flow: start a client for one or more MCP servers, such as a database or GitHub server, load their tools through the adapter, and pass them to your agent. The agent then sees tool names and descriptions from the servers and can call them. Because MCP tools may perform real actions, apply the same care as with any tool: least privilege, trusted servers, and human approval for destructive operations. Check the adapter's README for current usage.

## Can I use LangChain agents with AWS Bedrock models?

Yes. LangChain's AWS integration provides chat model classes for Amazon Bedrock, so you can use Bedrock-hosted models, including Anthropic's Claude models and others, in LangChain agents, as long as the model supports tool calling.

Set up AWS credentials with permission to invoke the models, enable model access in the Bedrock console for your region, install the LangChain AWS package, and create the chat model with the Bedrock model ID. Then pass it to your agent constructor as usual. Bedrock suits organisations already on AWS for billing, data residency and security controls. Test tool calling with your chosen model, since capabilities differ between models.

## How do I combine retrieval chains, agents and tools in LangChain?

Wrap your retriever as a tool and give it to the agent, instead of using older built-in retrieval chain classes. The agent then decides when to search your documents, alongside other tools such as calculators or APIs.

For example, create a tool `search_handbook(query)` that queries your vector store and returns the top passages with IDs and page numbers. The agent calls it when a question needs documents and cites the passages in its answer. Conversation memory comes from the agent's message state and persistence, not a special chain. This design is clearer and more flexible than legacy chains, and it lets you add a confidence rule, such as declining when no passage scores well, which RAG.NextUpgrad applies before answering.

## What is the agentic approach?

The agentic approach means designing AI systems that pursue goals through multiple steps, using tools and checking results, instead of producing a single response to a single prompt.

It suits tasks with uncertain paths, such as research, debugging, or resolving a support issue across systems. It is not always better: for predictable tasks, a fixed workflow is cheaper, faster and more reliable. A practical middle ground is a mostly deterministic workflow with a few agentic steps where judgement is needed. Whatever the design, add limits, logs and evaluation, because agentic systems fail in more varied ways than single calls.

## What are agentic agents?

"Agentic agents" is a redundant phrase usually meaning AI agents with real autonomy: systems that plan, take actions with tools and adapt based on results, as opposed to simple chatbots that only reply.

The term is used loosely in marketing. When evaluating a product described as agentic, ask concrete questions: which tools can it use, what can it change, when does it ask for approval, how are its actions logged, and how is it evaluated. Those answers matter more than the label. For learning, build a small agent yourself with two tools and a step limit; it teaches more than any definition.

## What is A-MEM, agentic memory for LLM agents?

A-MEM is a research approach to memory for LLM agents in which the agent organises its own memories: it writes structured notes about experiences, links related notes, and updates older memories as new information arrives, inspired by note-taking systems.

The motivation is that simple memory, such as storing chat history or embedding past messages, retrieves poorly over long periods. Agentic memory lets the model decide what to store, how to tag and connect it, and when to revise it. For builders, the practical lessons are to store memories as structured, retrievable notes with metadata, to link related items, and to let memories be corrected. Evaluate memory systems on whether they improve later task performance, not just on how much they store.

# LangChain best practices: RAG, security, production, StrOutputParser, ChatOpenAI, examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/langchain-best-practices/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


LangChain works best when you use it deliberately: pin versions, keep chains simple with the runnable interface, trace everything, evaluate retrieval and answers, and keep security controls outside the model. I build RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval and a confidence gate, so this page covers general, RAG and security best practices, production criticism, StrOutputParser, OpenAI versus ChatOpenAI and where to import it, code and project examples, and hallucination checks with guardrails.

## What are LangChain best practices?

Pin package versions, use the modern runnable interface and LangGraph for complex flows, keep prompts and chains small and testable, trace runs with LangSmith or another tool, and evaluate quality on a fixed test set before every release.

More practices: import from the split packages, such as langchain-core and provider packages, rather than old monolithic paths; prefer structured output with schemas over parsing free text; handle errors with retries and fallbacks; stream responses for user-facing apps; and keep business logic in your own functions, calling LangChain where it adds value. Read release notes before upgrading, and write small integration tests that run your chains against recorded or cheap model calls.

## What are LangChain RAG best practices?

Chunk documents by structure with metadata, use hybrid retrieval, for example an ensemble of BM25 and vector retrievers, add a reranker, require citations in prompts, and evaluate retrieval separately from generation.

Store source, page and permissions in metadata and filter on them. Rewrite follow-up questions into standalone queries for chat. Limit context to the top few reranked passages instead of stuffing many. Return source documents with answers so users can verify. Measure recall at k for retrieval and faithfulness for answers with a test set, using LangSmith or evaluation libraries. RAG.NextUpgrad follows the same principles: hybrid retrieval, fusion, reranking and a confidence gate before answering.

## What are LangChain security best practices?

Treat model outputs and retrieved documents as untrusted. Limit tool permissions, never let models run arbitrary code or SQL without sandboxing and allow-lists, keep secrets in environment variables, and enforce access control in retrieval, not in prompts.

Defend against prompt injection: documents or web pages can contain instructions that hijack an agent, so separate data from instructions, validate tool arguments, and require human approval for consequential actions. Use read-only database credentials for query tools. Avoid deprecated components with known risks and keep packages updated for security fixes. Log tool calls for auditing, rate-limit endpoints, and filter personal data before sending it to external providers. Review LangChain's security policy for current guidance.

## Why do some say LangChain is not good for production?

Critics point to heavy abstractions that hide what is sent to models, frequent breaking changes in earlier versions, difficult debugging, and performance overhead, which made some teams replace LangChain with direct SDK calls in production.

Many issues have eased: packages are split and versioned, stable 1.0 releases exist, LangGraph offers explicit control for agents, and LangSmith provides tracing. Plenty of companies run LangChain in production successfully. The practical stance is selective use: keep core logic and prompts visible in your code, use LangChain where integrations save time, and avoid deep chains you cannot debug. If a component becomes a bottleneck or obscures behaviour, replace it with plain code.

## What does StrOutputParser do in LangChain?

StrOutputParser converts a chat model's message output into a plain string, extracting the text content. Placed at the end of a chain, such as prompt | model | StrOutputParser(), it makes the chain return text instead of a message object.

It also works with streaming, yielding text chunks as they arrive, which is convenient for chat interfaces. Use it when you want raw text; for structured data, use with_structured_output on the model or a JSON or Pydantic parser instead, which validate the output against a schema. Import it from langchain_core.output_parsers. It is one of the simplest runnables and a common final step in tutorials and production chains alike.

## What is the difference between OpenAI and ChatOpenAI in LangChain?

ChatOpenAI wraps OpenAI's chat models, taking a list of messages and returning a message, with support for tools, structured output and streaming. OpenAI wraps the older text completion interface, taking a string prompt and returning text.

Modern OpenAI models are chat models, so use ChatOpenAI for almost everything. The OpenAI completion class exists for legacy completion models and is rarely needed. ChatOpenAI integrates with LangChain's message types, such as system, human and AI messages, and supports features like bind_tools and with_structured_output. If tutorials use OpenAI from older LangChain versions, update them to ChatOpenAI from the langchain_openai package, which also supports OpenAI-compatible endpoints through a base URL.

## Where is ChatOpenAI in LangChain?

ChatOpenAI lives in the langchain-openai package. Install it with pip install langchain-openai and import it with from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI. Older paths, such as langchain.chat_models, are deprecated.

Set your OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, then create a model with `ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)` and call invoke with a message or string. Similar provider packages exist for other models: langchain-anthropic for ChatAnthropic, langchain-google-genai for Gemini, and langchain-ollama for local models. If you see import errors, check that the provider package is installed and versions are compatible with langchain-core. Pin versions in requirements to avoid surprises when packages update. Most IDEs auto-complete these imports once packages are installed.

## What does example LangChain code look like?

A minimal chain combines a prompt template, a chat model and an output parser with the pipe operator, then calls invoke with input variables. This pattern, the LangChain Expression Language, underlies most modern LangChain code.

```python
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template("Explain {topic} in two sentences.")
chain = prompt | ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini") | StrOutputParser()
print(chain.invoke({"topic": "vector databases"}))
```

From here, add a retriever for RAG, tools with bind_tools for agents, or with_structured_output for JSON. Use chain.stream for streaming output and chain.batch for many inputs at once, and trace runs in LangSmith while developing.

## What is a good example LangChain project?

A strong starter project is a document question answering app: load PDFs, split them, embed them into Chroma or pgvector, retrieve relevant chunks, and answer with citations through a FastAPI or Streamlit interface.

Extend it step by step: add hybrid retrieval with an ensemble retriever, a reranker, chat history with standalone question rewriting, and an evaluation set measuring retrieval recall and answer faithfulness. Then build a LangGraph agent that can choose between document search and a web search tool. Document the architecture, metrics and limitations in the README. This single project demonstrates most skills employers look for in AI engineers, from retrieval to evaluation.

## How do you detect hallucinations with Guardrails AI and LangChain?

Guardrails AI wraps model calls with validators that check outputs, such as schema validity, toxicity, or whether answers are supported by provided context. Combine it with LangChain by validating chain outputs before returning them, re-asking or refusing when checks fail.

For hallucination detection in RAG, use validators or evaluation models that compare each claim in the answer against retrieved passages, flagging unsupported statements. Check the Guardrails Hub for current validators and the integration pattern for your installed version, since APIs evolve. Add cheap checks first, such as requiring citations and verifying cited passages exist, then heavier model-based checks for high-risk answers. Log failures and review them, since validators also produce false positives.

# What is LangChain in Python? Install, Python 3.13, Ollama prompts, and how to learn it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/langchain-python-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


LangChain is an open-source framework, available as a Python library, for building applications with large language models: it gives you standard interfaces for chat models, prompts, tools, retrievers and agents, plus integrations with hundreds of providers and data sources. Its companion LangGraph handles stateful agents. I build RAG and AI products in Python with FastAPI, so this page covers what LangChain is, installing it, Python 3.13, tutorials and examples, system prompts with Ollama, and how and in what order to learn LangChain and LangGraph.

## What is LangChain in Python?

LangChain in Python is a set of packages that make it easier to build LLM applications: chat model wrappers with a common interface, prompt templates, output parsers, document loaders, text splitters, retrievers, tool calling and agents.

Its value is standardisation: you can switch from one model provider to another by changing one class, and connect components with a consistent interface. Typical uses are RAG chatbots over documents, agents that call tools and APIs, structured data extraction, and summarisation pipelines. The ecosystem includes LangGraph for controllable agent workflows and LangSmith for tracing and evaluation. For simple apps, calling a model's SDK directly can be simpler, so use LangChain when its abstractions save you real work.

## Is LangChain a Python library?

Yes. LangChain is distributed as Python packages on PyPI, mainly `langchain` and `langchain-core`, with separate integration packages such as `langchain-openai`, `langchain-anthropic` and `langchain-ollama`. There is also a JavaScript and TypeScript version.

The split into packages keeps dependencies light: you install only the integrations you use. `langchain-core` defines base interfaces; `langchain` contains higher-level components such as agents; `langchain-community` holds many third-party integrations; and LangGraph is a separate library for graph-based agents. LangChain is open source under the MIT licence, maintained by LangChain Inc. and a large community.

## How do I install LangChain in Python?

Create a virtual environment, then install LangChain and the integration for your model provider with pip, for example `pip install langchain langchain-openai` or `pip install langchain langchain-ollama`. Set your provider's API key as an environment variable.

Steps:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -U langchain langchain-openai
```

Keep API keys in environment variables or a git-ignored `.env` file, never in code. Pin versions in `requirements.txt` once your app works, because LangChain has evolved quickly and newer releases sometimes change interfaces. Check the documentation's installation page for current package names.

## Can I use LangChain with Python 3.13?

Yes, recent LangChain releases support current Python versions, including 3.13. Older LangChain versions or specific integration packages may lag, so check each package's supported versions on PyPI if installation fails.

If you hit errors on Python 3.13, the cause is usually a dependency without compatible wheels yet, such as a native library used by a particular integration. Solutions: upgrade LangChain and the integration to the latest versions, use Python 3.12 for that project with a tool such as pyenv or uv, or swap the problematic integration. Newer LangChain versions have also dropped support for old Python versions, so very old Python installations may need upgrading.

## Is there a good LangChain tutorial in Python?

Yes. The official LangChain documentation has tutorials for chat models, RAG, structured extraction and agents, and LangChain Academy offers free courses, including on LangGraph. Start with the official material, because many older blog tutorials use deprecated interfaces.

A suggested order:

- Call a chat model and stream a response.
- Build a prompt template and parse structured output.
- Load documents, split them, embed them and build a retriever.
- Combine retrieval and generation into a RAG chain with citations.
- Add tool calling, then build an agent with LangGraph.
- Trace runs with LangSmith or logging to debug.

Build one small project end to end rather than following many partial tutorials.

## What are some LangChain examples in Python?

Common examples include a chatbot with memory, RAG over PDFs, extracting structured data from emails into a schema, summarising long documents, SQL question answering over a database, and agents that call web search or internal APIs.

A minimal chain:

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", "Answer briefly."), ("human", "{q}")])
chain = prompt | ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
print(chain.invoke({"q": "What is RAG?"}).content)
```

The `|` operator composes components into a runnable chain that supports `invoke`, `stream` and `batch`. The documentation and the repository's cookbook contain many more examples.

## What is the right way to do system prompting with Ollama in LangChain?

Use `ChatOllama` from the `langchain-ollama` package with a chat prompt template that has a separate system message. The system message goes into Ollama's system role, so the model treats it as instructions rather than user text.

```python
from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a concise assistant. Answer in two sentences."),
    ("human", "{question}"),
])
chain = prompt | ChatOllama(model="llama3.1")
print(chain.invoke({"question": "What is chunking?"}).content)
```

Avoid the older completion-style `Ollama` class for chat models, and check that the model you pulled supports system prompts well.

## How do I learn LangChain?

Learn LLM fundamentals first, prompts, tokens, embeddings and tool calling, then LangChain's core concepts: chat models, prompts, runnables, retrievers and tools. Build a RAG app and a simple agent, using official docs and LangChain Academy.

Tips:

- Read the conceptual guide before copying code.
- Prefer current documentation over old videos and blog posts.
- Use LangSmith or detailed logging to see exactly what is sent to the model.
- Learn to evaluate: a small test set of questions with expected answers.
- Compare with calling the model SDK directly, to understand what the framework adds.

Discussion forums are useful for real-world pitfalls, but verify advice against the current docs.

## How long does it take to learn LangChain?

With solid Python, you can build a basic RAG app or chain in a few days, and become comfortable with core components in two to four weeks of regular practice. Production-grade skills, evaluation, agents and deployment, take a few months of real projects.

The framework is the smaller part; the harder skills are retrieval quality, prompt design, evaluation, cost control and handling failures. A focused plan: week one for basics and a chatbot, week two for RAG, week three for tools and agents with LangGraph, week four for evaluation and deployment with FastAPI. Building one complete project you can demo is worth more than finishing many courses.

## Should I learn LangChain or LangGraph first?

Learn LangChain's core concepts first, chat models, prompts, tools and retrievers, because LangGraph builds on them. Then learn LangGraph for agents and multi-step workflows that need state, loops, branching and human approval.

LangChain's newer agent features are themselves built on LangGraph, so you will meet both. If your app is a straightforward RAG pipeline or extraction task, LangChain components may be all you need. If you are building agents that call tools repeatedly, wait for human input or recover from errors, LangGraph gives you explicit control over each step, which makes behaviour easier to debug and test.

# What is LangChain in simple words? Who made it, when, who uses it, runnables, alternatives
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/langchain-simple-words-alternatives/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


In simple words, LangChain is a toolkit for building apps with AI language models: it provides ready-made pieces to connect a model to your documents, tools and APIs, and to chain steps together, so you write less glue code. It is available for Python and JavaScript and has a large ecosystem. I build RAG and AI products in Python, so this page explains what LangChain does and why it matters, who made it and when, where the company is, who uses it, runnables, a common LangGraph import question, and the best alternatives.

## What is LangChain in simple words?

LangChain is a set of building blocks for AI applications. Instead of writing everything yourself, you use its components: model wrappers to talk to AI models, prompt templates, document loaders, text splitters, retrievers for searching your data, and tools that let models call functions.

Think of it like a box of connectors for AI apps: plug a model into your PDFs to make a document chatbot, or into a search API to make a research assistant. It works with many model providers and databases through a common interface, so you can switch components without rewriting your app. Its companion, LangGraph, handles more complex agents. For example, a document chatbot in LangChain is a loader, a splitter, an embedding model, a vector store retriever and a chat model wired together in a few dozen lines.

## What does LangChain do exactly?

LangChain standardises how you call models, build prompts, retrieve documents, call tools and compose these steps into chains and agents. It provides hundreds of integrations with model providers, vector stores, document sources and tools.

Concretely, LangChain can: load documents from files, websites and databases; split them into chunks; embed and store them in vector stores; retrieve relevant chunks for questions; format prompts; call chat models with streaming; parse structured outputs; and run tool-calling agents. LangSmith, from the same company, traces and evaluates these applications.

## Why is LangChain important?

LangChain was important in making LLM application patterns, such as RAG, tool calling and agents, accessible to many developers quickly, and it remains widely used because of its integrations, community and ecosystem, including LangGraph and LangSmith.

Its common interfaces reduce vendor lock-in: switching from one model provider to another can be a small change. Tutorials, templates and community answers make learning faster. It also attracts criticism for abstraction complexity and frequent changes, which is why many teams use it selectively. Understanding it is valuable for AI engineers, even if you choose lighter tools for some projects.

## Who made LangChain?

LangChain was created by Harrison Chase, who released it as an open-source project. He later co-founded the company LangChain, Inc., with Ankush Gola, to develop LangChain, LangGraph and the LangSmith platform.

The open-source project grew rapidly through community contributions, with thousands of contributors adding integrations and features. The company is venture-backed and offers commercial products for tracing, evaluation and deployment, while the core libraries remain open source under the MIT licence. Before LangChain, Chase worked on machine learning teams at startups including Robust Intelligence; the project began as a side effort to package common patterns for building with language models.

## When was LangChain introduced?

LangChain was first released in October 2022, shortly before ChatGPT's launch, and its popularity exploded as developers rushed to build applications with language models in early 2023.

The JavaScript version followed in early 2023. Major milestones include the split into modular packages such as langchain-core, the introduction of LangGraph for stateful agents, LangSmith for observability, and stable 1.0 releases focused on agent building. Because it evolved quickly, older tutorials often use outdated interfaces, so prefer current documentation. When reading a tutorial, check its date and imports: code using `langchain.llms` or `LLMChain` usually predates the modern packages, while `langchain_core` and provider packages such as `langchain_openai` signal current style.

## Where is LangChain located?

LangChain, Inc. is a technology company based in the United States, and its team works across locations. The open-source project itself is global, developed on GitHub by contributors worldwide.

For practical purposes, the "location" that matters to developers is online: documentation on the LangChain website, code on GitHub, the LangChain Academy courses, and community forums. Company details, such as offices and leadership, are on LangChain's official website. Location also matters little for usage: the libraries run wherever your code runs, on a laptop, a server or a cloud function, and LangSmith offers hosted and self-hosted options for teams with data residency requirements.

## Who uses LangChain?

LangChain is used by startups, enterprises, researchers and individual developers to build chatbots, RAG systems over company documents, coding and research assistants, data extraction pipelines, and agents that automate workflows. Its packages see very large download numbers.

Users range from students learning AI engineering to large companies running production systems, some using LangGraph and LangSmith for complex agent workflows and monitoring. Others use only specific components, such as document loaders or text splitters, within their own architectures. Its popularity means many job descriptions for AI engineers mention LangChain or LangGraph.

## What are LangChain runnables?

Runnables are LangChain's standard interface for components: prompts, models, retrievers, parsers and custom functions all implement methods such as `invoke`, `stream`, `batch` and their async versions, so they can be combined consistently.

You compose runnables with the pipe operator, as in `prompt | model | parser`, creating a chain that is itself a runnable. Helpers such as `RunnableParallel` run branches concurrently, `RunnablePassthrough` forwards inputs, and `RunnableLambda` wraps your own functions. This design, called the LangChain Expression Language, gives every chain streaming, batching and tracing support automatically.

## Can CompiledGraph be imported from LangChain?

No, `CompiledGraph` belongs to LangGraph, not LangChain. When you build a graph with LangGraph's `StateGraph` and call `.compile()`, you get a compiled graph object; import related classes from the `langgraph` package, whose module paths have changed across versions.

If an import fails, check your installed LangGraph version and its API reference, since classes such as `CompiledStateGraph` live under `langgraph.graph.state` in recent releases. In many cases you do not need to import the class at all: use the object returned by `.compile()` and call `invoke` or `stream` on it. Keep LangChain and LangGraph versions compatible.

## What are the best LangChain alternatives?

Popular alternatives include LlamaIndex for data and retrieval-focused applications, Haystack for production search and RAG pipelines, DSPy for programmatically optimising prompts, Microsoft's Semantic Kernel, CrewAI and Agno for agents, provider SDKs with agent features, and plain API calls with small helper code.

Choose by need: LlamaIndex for document-heavy RAG; Haystack for structured pipelines; DSPy for systematic prompt optimisation; provider SDKs for simple, direct control; and LangGraph if you like LangChain's ecosystem but need explicit agent control. Many production teams use minimal frameworks, so understanding the underlying patterns matters more than any library. Whatever you choose, keep retrieval steps such as hybrid search, fusion and reranking inspectable, since those decide answer quality more than the framework does.
