# Ollama vs LM Studio, Ollama tutorials, embeddings, and a free local coding assistant
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/ollama-vs-lm-studio-tutorial/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Ollama and LM Studio are both free tools for running open-weight language models on your own computer. Ollama is command-line and API first, ideal for developers and servers; LM Studio is a polished desktop app for browsing, downloading and chatting with models, with a local server too. This page compares them, explains sharing models and embeddings, how Ollama makes money, beginner and Python tutorials for Ollama, embeddings, and how to set up a free local coding assistant.

## What are Ollama and LM Studio?

Ollama is an open-source tool that runs language models locally through a simple CLI, a background server and an API, with a library of ready-to-run models. LM Studio is a desktop application with a graphical interface for discovering models on Hugging Face, downloading them, chatting, and serving them through a local API.

Both run quantised GGUF models on CPUs and GPUs, keep data on your machine, and work offline after downloading models. Ollama shines when you build apps, script workflows or run on servers and Docker. LM Studio shines when you want to explore and compare models visually, adjust settings with sliders, and get started without the terminal. Many developers keep both installed.

## What is the difference between Ollama and LM Studio?

The main differences are interface, openness and deployment. Ollama is open source, terminal and API driven, and runs well headless on servers and in Docker. LM Studio is a free but closed-source desktop app with a rich GUI and model browser.

Other differences:

- **Model sourcing**: Ollama pulls from its library or Hugging Face GGUF repos; LM Studio searches Hugging Face directly in the app.
- **Configuration**: Ollama uses Modelfiles and environment variables; LM Studio uses visual settings.
- **APIs**: both offer local APIs, including OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
- **Terms**: check LM Studio's terms for work use; Ollama uses the MIT licence.

Performance is similar for the same model and quantisation when settings match.

## Should I use Ollama or LM Studio?

Use Ollama if you are a developer building apps, want scripting and automation, or will run models on a server. Use LM Studio if you prefer a graphical app for exploring models, comparing them and chatting, especially when starting out.

A practical combination: explore and shortlist models in LM Studio, then run the chosen model in Ollama for your application. If you need a web UI for a team, Ollama with a web interface is the common route. For laptops with modest hardware, both perform similarly; the deciding factor is workflow, not speed.

## Can I use Ollama models in LM Studio?

Often, yes, because both use the GGUF format. You can import GGUF files into LM Studio, including files you downloaded for Ollama, though each tool keeps its own model library and Ollama stores models as content-addressed blobs rather than named files.

The simplest approach is to download the same model in each tool from its own source, which avoids path and naming issues. If disk space is tight, find the GGUF blob Ollama uses with `ollama show --modelfile <model>`, which shows the file path, and import that file into LM Studio. Make sure the chat template is correct after importing, or responses may be odd.

## What is text embedding in LM Studio?

Text embedding in LM Studio means running an embedding model locally to convert text into vectors, available through its local server's embeddings endpoint, so your apps can do semantic search and RAG without a cloud API.

Download an embedding model in LM Studio, load it, and call the OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint from your code with the model name. Use the same embedding model for indexing documents and embedding queries. Local embeddings are free per request and private, which suits personal knowledge bases and prototypes. Ollama offers the same capability with embedding models such as `nomic-embed-text`.

## How does Ollama make money?

Ollama the software is free and open source. The company behind it offers paid cloud features, such as running large models on its servers with higher usage limits, alongside the free local tool, and it has raised venture funding.

This model is common in open-source infrastructure: a free, widely adopted local tool builds a large user base, and paid hosted services serve users who need more power or convenience. For local users, nothing changes: running models on your own hardware remains free. Check Ollama's website for current cloud plans and terms.

## Is there an Ollama tutorial for beginners?

Yes. Install Ollama from ollama.com, run a small model, chat with it, then call it from code. The first session takes about fifteen minutes.

```bash
ollama run llama3.2               # downloads and opens a chat
ollama list                       # installed models
ollama ps                         # what is loaded, CPU or GPU
ollama rm llama3.2                # remove a model
```

Next steps: try a coding model and an embedding model, connect a web UI for a browser chat, and call the local API from Python. Start with small models if your laptop has 8 GB of RAM; 7B to 8B models need around 16 GB for comfortable use.

## How do I use Ollama with Python?

Install the official `ollama` Python library and call `chat` or `generate` with a model name. Streaming is available for responsive apps.

```python
# pip install ollama
import ollama

resp = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2", messages=[
    {"role": "system", "content": "Answer in two sentences."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is retrieval-augmented generation?"}])
print(resp["message"]["content"])

for chunk in ollama.chat(model="llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Count to five"}], stream=True):
    print(chunk["message"]["content"], end="", flush=True)
```

You can also use the OpenAI SDK against Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which makes switching between local and hosted models easy. The library talks to the server at `localhost:11434` by default; create a client with a different host if Ollama runs on another machine or in Docker, and wrap calls in error handling so your app reports clearly when the server or model is not available.

## Is there an Ollama embeddings tutorial?

Pull an embedding model, call the embed function, and store the vectors for semantic search. With a few documents you can search in memory; for more, use a vector store.

```python
import ollama, numpy as np

docs = ["Paging divides memory into pages.", "BM25 ranks documents by keywords.", "Deadlocks block processes."]
vecs = np.array(ollama.embed(model="nomic-embed-text", input=docs)["embeddings"])
q = np.array(ollama.embed(model="nomic-embed-text", input=["how does keyword ranking work"])["embeddings"][0])
scores = vecs @ q / (np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(q))
print(docs[int(scores.argmax())])
```

Run `ollama pull nomic-embed-text` first. Use the same model for documents and queries, and add keyword search for exact terms.

## How do I run a free AI coding assistant locally?

Run a coding model on a local server, such as LM Studio or Ollama, then connect an editor extension in VS Code or a terminal coding agent such as opencode to that local server's API. Your code stays on your machine and there is no per-request cost.

Steps:

- Download a coding-tuned model that fits your GPU memory.
- Start the local server in LM Studio or Ollama.
- Configure your VS Code extension or terminal agent with the local API URL and model name.
- Use a small, fast model for autocomplete and a larger one for chat or agent tasks.
- Test on a small repository first and review every change.

Expect local models to be weaker than frontier hosted models on complex tasks; they are excellent for explanations, boilerplate and private code.

# Best online hackathon platforms, the point of hackathons, mentoring, planning and seasons
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/online-hackathon-platforms-mentoring/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best online hackathon platforms are Devpost, Devfolio, MLH, Unstop and Hack2skill, which list events, handle registrations and collect submissions. Hackathons exist to turn ideas into working prototypes quickly, while building skills and connections. I have competed in 10+ hackathons and founded the TechVerse Enclave community, so this page covers platforms and websites, the point of hackathons, hackathon programs, mentoring and finding mentors, attending, planning, hackathon season and ISRO's hackathon.

## What is the best online hackathon platform?

Devpost is the largest global platform for online hackathons, Devfolio is popular in India and Web3, MLH lists student events worldwide, Unstop covers Indian college competitions, and Hack2skill runs many government and corporate hackathons.

For organisers, choose by audience and features: Devfolio offers applications, judging and project pages; Devpost provides large reach and gallery pages; Hack2skill supports large-scale government challenges. For participants, the best platform is the one listing events in your interests and region. Create profiles on two or three, enable notifications for themes you like, and keep your past projects visible there, since judges and recruiters browse them. Discord servers usually handle real-time communication.

## What are the best hackathon websites?

Good websites for finding hackathons include Devpost, MLH's events page, Devfolio, Unstop, Hack2skill, HackerEarth, Kaggle for data competitions, lu.ma for community events, and official pages for government challenges such as Smart India Hackathon.

Each serves a niche: MLH for student events with codes of conduct and beginner support, Kaggle for long-running machine learning competitions, HackerEarth for corporate hiring challenges, and Devfolio and Unstop for Indian college events. Aggregator newsletters and community Discord servers also share opportunities. Bookmark a few, check them weekly, and register early, since popular events fill quickly or close applications weeks before the start date. Follow organisers on LinkedIn as well.

## What is the point of a hackathon?

The point is to build something useful quickly: teams turn an idea into a working prototype within a fixed time, learning, collaborating and testing ideas faster than normal projects allow.

For participants, hackathons build practical skills, portfolios, confidence and networks. For organisers and sponsors, they generate ideas, test developer tools, discover talent and engage communities. Governments use them to source solutions to public problems, and companies use internal hackathons to spark innovation outside normal roadmaps. The time pressure forces focus: teams must decide what matters most and cut everything else, a skill that transfers directly to real product work. Many startups and lasting friendships began this way.

## What is a hackathon program?

A hackathon program is the structured plan of an event: registration, opening ceremony, problem statements or tracks, team formation, building periods, mentor sessions, workshops, submission deadline, judging rounds and a closing ceremony with prizes.

Some organisations also run longer hackathon programs, such as multi-stage national challenges with idea submission, shortlisting, prototype development and grand finales, or recurring corporate innovation programs where winning ideas receive funding and mentoring. Smart India Hackathon is an example of a multi-month national program. A good program publishes timelines, rules, judging criteria and support channels in advance, so participants can plan their time and expectations. Check the schedule before registering so you can commit fully.

## How do you mentor at a student hackathon?

Help teams scope, unblock and present, without building for them. Ask what problem they are solving and what a working demo looks like, suggest cutting features, help debug blockers, and give pitch feedback before judging.

Walk around regularly rather than waiting to be asked, since beginners hesitate to request help. Ask questions that guide thinking: who is the user, what is the core flow, what can you finish by tonight? Share quick technical tips, such as deployment shortcuts or API usage. Encourage teams who struggle, and remind everyone to rest. Before demos, run practice pitches and help teams explain clearly what they built and what remains mocked.

## How do you find a mentor or guide for a hackathon?

Ask event organisers, who usually provide mentors during the hackathon; reach out to seniors, alumni and faculty who have competed before; and join community servers where experienced hackers help newcomers.

Before the event, find one person who can review your idea and tech stack; during it, use official mentor office hours actively. When asking, be specific: share your problem statement, approach and the exact blocker. Student communities, such as TechVerse Enclave, which I founded, and college coding clubs are good places to meet experienced members. Mentors value teams that come prepared, act on advice and report back, which also builds lasting relationships.

## How do you attend a hackathon?

Find an event, check eligibility, register before the deadline, form or join a team, and prepare your laptop and tools. On the day, attend the opening session, build, use mentors, submit before the deadline and present your demo.

For in-person events, bring a laptop, charger, extension cord, ID, water bottle and something warm for night sessions. For online events, test your internet, camera and screen sharing, and join the Discord early. Read the rules about pre-built code and AI tools. Introduce yourself to others, attend workshops, and talk to sponsors. Afterwards, publish your project on GitHub and share what you learned, which turns attendance into lasting portfolio value.

## How do you plan a hackathon?

Decide the purpose, audience, format and size; set dates and a budget plan; secure a venue or platform, sponsors, mentors and judges; prepare themes, rules and judging criteria; then market the event and manage registrations.

Create a timeline: three months out for sponsors and venue, two months for mentors and judges, six weeks for registrations, and two weeks for final logistics. Plan food, Wi-Fi, power, accessibility, safety and a code of conduct. Recruit volunteers with clear roles. Prepare starter resources, API credits and workshops. After the event, publish results, collect feedback, and share highlights to build momentum for the next edition.

## When is hackathon season?

Hackathons happen all year, but student hackathon seasons follow academic calendars: in India, many college events cluster from August to March, and in North America, the MLH season runs roughly from late summer to spring.

Online hackathons and corporate challenges run continuously, and national programs such as Smart India Hackathon follow their own multi-month cycles, typically with finales around December in recent years. Summer often brings online and corporate events, since students are free. October brings Hacktoberfest, an open-source contribution event rather than a typical hackathon. Follow platforms and set alerts, and plan around exams, since the busiest hackathon months often overlap with academic deadlines.

## Is ISRO's hackathon online?

ISRO's Bharatiya Antariksh Hackathon, run with Hack2skill, has used online rounds for registration, idea submission and early evaluation, with shortlisted teams progressing to later stages. Check the current edition's official rules for exact formats.

Problem statements typically involve space technology, satellite data, remote sensing and related applications, so teams benefit from skills in data science, computer vision and geospatial analysis. Follow ISRO's official announcements and the Hack2skill event page for dates, eligibility and team rules, and avoid unofficial sources. Even if you are not selected, working with satellite datasets from public Earth observation portals builds valuable skills for space and climate technology careers.

# Open source contribution for beginners: guide, roadmap, career value, platforms, repos
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-contribution-beginners/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To start open source as a beginner, pick a project you use, read its contributing guide, look for issues labelled good first issue, make a small, well-tested change, and open a clear pull request. Documentation fixes and tests are perfect first contributions. I build with open-source tools across Python, FastAPI and Next.js and mentor students on building portfolios, so this page covers a guide, roadmap, career value, interview answers, sharing contributions, maintaining your own project, platforms and beginner-friendly repositories.

## How do beginners start open source contribution?

Learn basic Git and GitHub, choose a project you use or care about, read its README and CONTRIBUTING file, find a good first issue, ask to be assigned if required, make the change on a branch, and open a pull request.

Start small: fix a typo in documentation, improve an example, add a missing test, or reproduce a reported bug with clear steps. Run the project's tests and linters locally before submitting. Write a pull request description explaining what changed and why, linking the issue. Respond politely to review comments and update your branch. Your first merged pull request teaches the workflow; after a few, take on larger features and help review others' work.

## What is a good guide to open source contribution?

GitHub's Open Source Guides, at opensource.guide, explain how to contribute, communicate and understand project governance, and the firstcontributions repository walks beginners through forking, cloning, committing and opening a pull request step by step.

A practical guide in brief: understand the project's purpose and code of conduct; set up the development environment; read open issues and discussions; pick one that matches your skills; communicate before large changes; follow coding style and commit message conventions; write tests; and keep pull requests focused on one change. Be patient, since maintainers are often volunteers. Non-code contributions, such as documentation, translations, design and issue triage, are equally valued in many projects.

## Why do open source contributions matter for your career?

Open source contributions are public proof of skill: employers can read your code, see how you collaborate in reviews, and judge your communication. They also teach real-world practices, such as testing, code review and working in large codebases.

Contributors build networks with maintainers and engineers at companies that use or sponsor projects, which can lead to referrals and job offers. Programmes such as Google Summer of Code and LFX Mentorship provide structured experience and stipends. For students without internships, a few meaningful merged contributions to known projects can be more convincing than certificates. Choose quality over quantity: one substantial, well-reviewed contribution says more than dozens of trivial typo fixes.

## How should you describe your most meaningful open source contribution?

Choose one contribution with real impact, then explain the problem, why it mattered to users, what you changed, challenges during review, and the outcome, such as a fixed bug affecting many users or a feature adopted in a release.

Structure it like a project story: context about the project, the issue, your investigation, the solution and trade-offs, how you handled maintainer feedback, and what you learned. Link the merged pull request so interviewers can check it. Smaller contributions are fine if you explain them thoughtfully, such as improving documentation that reduced repeated questions. Interviewers assess technical understanding, collaboration and communication, so emphasise how you worked with others, not just the code.

## How should you manage and develop your own open-source project?

Start with a clear README, a licence, contribution guidelines, a code of conduct and issue templates. Use labels such as good first issue, keep a roadmap, automate tests with CI, and release versions with changelogs.

Respond to issues and pull requests promptly, even briefly, since contributors leave when ignored. Set boundaries to avoid burnout: define scope, say no to features that do not fit, and invite trusted contributors to become maintainers. Use GitHub Discussions for questions, and keep documentation current. Semantic versioning helps users trust upgrades. If the project grows, consider funding through GitHub Sponsors or Open Collective, and document governance so decisions remain transparent.

## How do you share links to your open source contributions?

When recruiters ask for links, share direct URLs to merged pull requests, not just your profile. GitHub search with is:pr author:your-username is:merged lists all your merged pull requests across repositories, which you can filter and link.

Create a short contributions section on your resume or portfolio listing the project, a one-line description of each contribution, and its pull request link. Highlight contributions to well-known repositories and substantial changes first. Keep your GitHub profile README updated with a few featured contributions. If some work is in private repositories, describe it without links and explain the impact. Make sure your GitHub email and name match your resume, so contributions are clearly attributed to you.

## What is an open source contribution roadmap?

Month one: learn Git, the GitHub flow and one language well. Month two: make documentation and test contributions to one project. Month three: fix small bugs. Months four to six: implement features, review others' pull requests, and apply to mentorship programmes.

Pick projects in your area of interest, such as AI tooling, web frameworks or developer tools, so contributions compound into expertise. Join project chats or forums to understand priorities. Track your contributions and lessons in a log. Apply to Google Summer of Code, Outreachy or LFX Mentorship when you have a few merged pull requests, since applications value prior contributions. Over a year, aim to become a regular contributor recognised by maintainers in one or two projects.

## What is the best open source contribution platform or programme?

GitHub hosts most open-source projects and is the main platform. Structured programmes include Google Summer of Code, Outreachy, LFX Mentorship, Hacktoberfest each October, and in India, GirlScript Summer of Code and similar community programmes.

Discovery sites such as goodfirstissue.dev and up-for-grabs.net list beginner-friendly issues across many projects. GitLab, Codeberg and other forges host important projects too. Programmes with mentors suit beginners, since guidance shortens the learning curve, and some, like GSoC and Outreachy, offer stipends. Hacktoberfest encourages quality pull requests over a month, though maintainers dislike spam, so contribute meaningfully. Read each programme's eligibility and timelines early, since applications open months before.

## What are the best open source projects for beginners?

Good beginner projects are active, welcoming and well documented, with labelled beginner issues and responsive maintainers. Examples include documentation-heavy projects, popular libraries in your language, developer tools you use, and organisations that take part in mentorship programmes.

Python developers might look at projects in the scientific or AI ecosystem, such as documentation and examples for libraries they use; web developers at framework ecosystems and component libraries; and AI learners at tooling such as LangChain integrations, Hugging Face libraries or evaluation tools, which welcome example and documentation improvements. Check recent activity, average time to merge, and how maintainers treat newcomers in closed pull requests before investing effort.

## What is the best repository for open source contribution practice?

The firstcontributions repository on GitHub is designed for practice: you fork it, add your name to a file, and open a pull request, learning the full workflow safely. It links to further beginner-friendly projects.

After that practice, move to real projects through goodfirstissue.dev or GitHub's good first issue search across repositories in your language. Also look at curated awesome lists for beginner contributions, which collect welcoming projects. Practice repositories teach mechanics, but real contributions teach collaboration, so do not stay in practice mode long. A good next step is improving documentation or tests in a library you already use, since you understand its users and can spot real problems.

# What does open source mean? Open LLMs, and is OpenAI, Claude or Ollama open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-llms-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Open source means software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In AI, many "open" language models are more precisely open-weight: you can download and run the trained model, but the training data and full training code are not published. This page explains the meaning, which LLMs are open and which are best, why and how to run them, and answers whether OpenAI, Claude, Ollama, Pinecone and LangChain are open source.

## What does open source mean?

Open source means the source code is freely available under a licence that grants everyone the rights to use it for any purpose, study how it works, change it and share copies or improvements. The Open Source Initiative maintains the formal definition.

Common open-source licences include permissive ones such as MIT and Apache 2.0, which allow almost any use including commercial, and copyleft ones such as GPL and AGPL, which require sharing changes under the same licence in certain cases. "Source-available" licences publish code but restrict some uses, such as offering the software as a competing service; those are not open source by the strict definition. Always read the licence before building a product on a project.

## What are open-source LLM models?

Open-source or open-weight LLMs are language models whose trained weights are published for download, so you can run, inspect and fine-tune them yourself. Well-known families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases.

Licences vary: some use permissive licences such as Apache 2.0, while others have custom terms that restrict certain uses or very large companies. Few release full training data, so most are open-weight rather than open source in the strict sense. They are available on Hugging Face and through tools like Ollama, and many come in several sizes and variants, such as instruct, coding and vision models.

## What are the best open-source models?

The best open models change every few months. Strong general families include the latest Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral and Gemma releases, plus OpenAI's open-weight models; specialised coding and embedding models lead in their niches. The best choice depends on your hardware and task.

How to choose:

- **Laptop with 8 to 16 GB RAM**: 3B to 8B models at 4-bit quantisation.
- **Single strong GPU**: 14B to 32B models, or mixture-of-experts models with small active size.
- **Coding**: coder-tuned variants.
- **RAG**: a good open embedding model plus a mid-size instruct model.
- **Languages**: test Indian-language performance yourself if you need it.

Check recent independent evaluations and test on your own prompts before settling.

## Why use an open-source LLM?

Use open models for privacy, since data never leaves your infrastructure; for cost control at high volume; for customisation through fine-tuning; for offline or on-device use; and for independence from a single vendor's pricing and policy changes.

Trade-offs to weigh: frontier hosted models are still stronger on the hardest reasoning and coding tasks; you are responsible for hosting, updates, security and evaluation; and GPUs cost money even when idle. A common pattern is to use an open model for routine, high-volume or sensitive tasks and a hosted model for hard ones. FineTune Studio exists because adapting open models with QLoRA is one of the main reasons teams choose them.

## How do I run an open-source LLM?

The easiest way is Ollama: install it, then run `ollama run llama3.2` or another model, and use the local API from your code. For more control, use llama.cpp or LM Studio; for serving many users on a GPU server, use vLLM.

```bash
ollama run qwen2.5:7b
```

```python
import requests
r = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/chat", json={
    "model": "qwen2.5:7b", "stream": False,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in two sentences."}]})
print(r.json()["message"]["content"])
```

Match model size to your memory, check `ollama ps` to confirm GPU use, and keep the local API private unless protected by authentication.

## Is OpenAI open source?

OpenAI's flagship models, such as the GPT models behind ChatGPT, are proprietary and available only through its apps and API. OpenAI has released some open models and tools, including open-weight language models and the Whisper speech recognition model, and open-source libraries such as the Codex CLI.

Despite the name, OpenAI moved away from releasing its main models openly years ago, citing safety and competition. Its open-weight releases are a separate line from its frontier models. So you can run some OpenAI models locally, but not the ones powering ChatGPT. For truly local alternatives to GPT-class assistants, use the strongest open models your hardware allows.

## Is Claude an open-source LLM?

No. Claude, made by Anthropic, is a proprietary model family available through claude.ai, Claude Code, the Claude API and cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI. Its weights are not published.

Anthropic does publish research, safety work and open standards, such as the Model Context Protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data, which is open source. If you need a model you can run entirely on your own hardware, choose an open-weight model; if you need Claude's capabilities, use it through its official channels and review the data terms for your use case.

## Is Ollama open source?

Yes. Ollama is open source under the MIT licence, with its code on GitHub. It is free to use for running open models locally, and it offers optional cloud features with their own plans.

Ollama builds on the open GGML ecosystem that also powers llama.cpp. The models you run through Ollama have their own licences, separate from Ollama's, so check each model's licence for commercial use. Because it is open source, you can inspect what it does, run it fully offline, and contribute fixes. It is one of the simplest ways to start with open LLMs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

## Is Pinecone open source?

No. Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed vector database service. You use it through its cloud API and client libraries; the database itself is not open source.

If you need an open-source vector database, popular choices include Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Chroma, and pgvector, an open-source extension for PostgreSQL. Open options let you self-host for data control and avoid vendor lock-in, at the cost of running the infrastructure yourself. For many projects, especially student and early-stage ones, pgvector or Chroma is simpler and free, and you can move to a managed service later if scale requires it.

## Is LangChain open source?

Yes. LangChain is open source under the MIT licence, with Python and JavaScript libraries on GitHub. LangGraph, its framework for stateful agents, is also open source. The company offers paid hosted products, such as observability and deployment tools, alongside the open libraries.

LlamaIndex, another popular framework for RAG and agents, is also open source under the MIT licence. Open frameworks let you inspect how retrieval and agent loops work, which helps debugging. They change quickly, so pin versions, read migration notes when upgrading, and keep your own code's core logic simple enough that you could replace the framework if needed.

# Open source software and open source AI: what counts, and which models are open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-software-and-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Open source software is software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, change and share it; Linux, Python, PostgreSQL, Git and VS Code's core are famous examples. In AI the term is contested: most models called open source are really open-weight, meaning you can download the trained weights, while the training data and full code stay private. This page lists essential open source software, explains open source AI, names the open models and agents, answers whether Google AI, n8n, Next.js and Supabase are open source, and shows how to contribute.

## What is the best open source software?

The most valuable open source software for students and developers includes Linux, Git, Python, VS Code's open-source core, PostgreSQL, Docker's engine, Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, GIMP and Blender, plus AI tools such as PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and Ollama.

By need:

- **Development**: Git, Python, Node.js, VS Code's core, PostgreSQL, Redis.
- **AI and data**: PyTorch, scikit-learn, Jupyter, Hugging Face libraries, Ollama, llama.cpp.
- **Web**: Next.js, React, Supabase, FastAPI.
- **Everyday use**: Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, Thunderbird, Bitwarden.
- **Creative**: GIMP, Inkscape, Blender, OBS Studio, Audacity.

Much of the modern internet and nearly every AI product runs on open source. Learning to read and contribute to these projects is one of the best ways to grow as an engineer.

## What is an open source AI model?

An open source AI model is one whose weights, and ideally code and training details, are published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In practice, most models called open source are open-weight models with varying licence terms.

With an open-weight model you can download it, run it on your own hardware, fine-tune it with methods like QLoRA, and inspect its behaviour, which is not possible with closed models served only through APIs. Licences differ: some are fully permissive, such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, while others restrict commercial use above certain scales or certain uses. Always read the licence on the model card before building a product on a model.

## What does open source mean in AI?

The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition says an AI system is open source when it grants the freedoms to use, study, modify and share it, which requires access to the model weights, the full code for training and running it, and enough information about the training data to reproduce a substantially equivalent system.

By that standard, few popular models qualify fully, because companies rarely release complete training data details. That is why careful writers say open-weight for models whose weights are downloadable but whose data and training pipelines are not. Fully open models from research groups do exist and publish data, code and checkpoints. For most engineering decisions, the practical questions are: can I download the weights, does the licence allow my use, and can I fine-tune and deploy it?

## Which AI models are open source?

Widely used open-weight model families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases. Licences range from permissive to custom terms with restrictions.

Popular choices by use:

- **General chat and reasoning**: Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek models.
- **Small and on-device**: Gemma, Phi, small Llama and Qwen variants.
- **Coding**: coder variants of Qwen and others.
- **Embeddings for RAG**: open embedding models on Hugging Face.
- **Speech**: OpenAI's Whisper for transcription.

You can run them with Ollama, llama.cpp or vLLM, or through hosted providers. GPT, Claude and Gemini models are proprietary and only available through their companies' apps and APIs.

## Is Google AI open source?

Partly. Google's Gemini models are proprietary, available through Google's apps and APIs. Google also releases Gemma, a family of open-weight models, and open-sources major tools such as TensorFlow and JAX.

Gemma models come in several sizes, including small ones that run on laptops and phones, and variants for specific uses. They are released under Google's Gemma terms, which allow broad use, including commercial use, with some conditions, so read the licence. Google researchers also published the original Transformer architecture, which underpins almost all modern language models. For students, Gemma is a good open model for experiments and fine-tuning practice, while Gemini is accessible through AI Studio's free tier.

## Which AI agents are open source?

Open-source AI agents include coding agents such as OpenHands, Aider, Cline and the command-line agents Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, general agents such as Goose, and frameworks for building agents such as LangGraph, CrewAI and AutoGen.

Open-source agents let you inspect exactly what the agent does, run it with local models, and adapt it to your workflow. Many work with several model providers, so you can switch between hosted models and local ones through Ollama. Quality depends heavily on the model behind them: an open agent with a weak local model performs far worse than the same agent with a frontier model. Read the permissions model of any agent before letting it run commands on your machine.

## Is n8n open source?

Not by the strict definition. n8n's source code is public and you can self-host it, but it uses the Sustainable Use License, a fair-code licence that restricts some commercial uses, such as offering n8n itself as a paid service. The Open Source Initiative does not recognise that as open source.

n8n chose this model to keep the code visible and free for internal use while protecting its business from competitors reselling it. For most users, including students, individuals and companies automating their own workflows, self-hosting n8n is allowed. If you plan to build a product that embeds or resells n8n, read the licence carefully or contact n8n about commercial terms. Fully open-source alternatives exist for some automation needs.

## Is Next.js open source?

Yes. Next.js, the React framework maintained by Vercel, is open source under the MIT licence, and its code is on GitHub. You can use it for any project, commercial or not, and deploy it anywhere, not only on Vercel.

Vercel funds most of its development and offers hosting optimised for it, but self-hosting with Node.js or Docker is fully supported. The MIT licence only requires keeping the copyright notice. Next.js is a good project to learn from: its issues, discussions and examples show how a large open-source framework is run, and documentation fixes are a realistic first contribution.

## Is Supabase open source?

Yes. Supabase, a backend platform built on PostgreSQL, is open source, with most of its code under the Apache 2.0 licence on GitHub. You can use the hosted service or self-host the stack with Docker.

Supabase combines open-source components: PostgreSQL for the database, PostgREST for an automatic REST API, a Realtime server, authentication, storage and edge functions, plus pgvector support for AI applications such as RAG. Self-hosting gives you control over data location and costs, but you take on maintenance, backups and security. For student projects, the hosted free tier is usually the quickest start; check its current limits.

## How do I contribute to open source AI projects?

Pick a project you already use, read its contributing guide, start with documentation fixes, tests or issues labelled "good first issue", and open small, well-explained pull requests. Consistency matters more than size.

A practical path:

- Use the project in a real task and note where you got stuck.
- Improve the docs or examples that confused you.
- Reproduce a reported bug and add a failing test.
- Fix small bugs, following the project's style and running its tests.
- Join the community channels and help answer questions.

Hugging Face libraries, LangChain, Ollama, vLLM and many model evaluation tools welcome contributions. Contributions on GitHub are public evidence of skill, and maintainers notice reliable contributors.

# Open source vs proprietary LLMs: differences, ChatGPT vs open models, Llama, best picks
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-vs-proprietary-llms/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Open-source or open-weight LLMs publish their model weights so anyone can download, run and fine-tune them, while proprietary LLMs such as ChatGPT's models are accessed only through the provider's apps and APIs. The choice affects cost, privacy, control and capability. I build with both, using Groq-hosted Llama in DocuLens AI and multi-provider fallback in RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers the differences, choosing, ChatGPT versus open models, Llama 3's openness, open source versus open access, and the best open models.

## What is the primary difference between open source and proprietary LLMs?

Access to the model itself. Open models release weights you can download, inspect, run on your own hardware and fine-tune. Proprietary models stay on the provider's servers, used only through APIs or apps under their terms.

This difference drives everything else: open models give control over data, deployment, customisation and long-term availability, while proprietary models offer frontier capability, managed infrastructure and less operational work. Licences vary widely among open models, from permissive Apache 2.0 and MIT to custom licences with restrictions. Proprietary models can change or be retired by the provider, while open weights you have downloaded keep working. Many teams use both for different tasks.

## Closed vs open source LLMs: which should you choose?

Choose closed models when you need the strongest reasoning, multimodal features or fastest time to market with minimal infrastructure. Choose open models when privacy, data residency, cost at scale, customisation or offline use matter most.

Hybrid setups are common: route complex queries to a frontier API and routine tasks, such as classification or extraction, to an open model you host or rent. Evaluate on your own tasks, measuring quality, latency and cost per request, since benchmark rankings rarely match specific workloads. Consider operational skills: self-hosting needs GPU management and monitoring. Keep your application provider-agnostic, so switching between closed and open models stays easy.

## ChatGPT vs open source LLMs: how do they compare?

ChatGPT is a polished product with frontier models, tools, memory and multimodal features, ready to use. Open-source LLMs are models you run or host yourself, through apps such as Ollama, LM Studio or Open WebUI, with full control but more setup.

For general assistance, ChatGPT typically leads in capability and convenience. Open models have closed much of the gap for many tasks and win on privacy, offline use, cost control and customisation through fine-tuning. Developers building products often combine them: open models for high-volume or sensitive tasks, frontier APIs for the hardest cases. Students can learn more about how models work by running open ones locally, inspecting tokens, prompts and outputs directly.

## Is Llama 3 fully open source?

Not fully. Meta releases Llama 3 weights, the tokenizer and inference code under the Llama community licence, which permits most uses with conditions. It does not release the full training data or complete training code, and the licence is not OSI-approved.

In practice you have what you need to run, fine-tune and deploy Llama 3: the model architecture is a standard transformer supported by Hugging Face Transformers, the tokenizer is included, and many tools support it. To build your own model from scratch, you would need training data and infrastructure that Meta does not provide. For fully open models with data and code, look at projects such as AI2's OLMo.

## Open source vs open access: what is the difference?

Open source means code, and for AI ideally weights, data and training code, released under licences that allow use, modification and redistribution. Open access means content is free to read, such as research papers, without necessarily granting rights to modify or reuse it.

In AI, an important middle term is open weights: models whose weights are downloadable, but whose licences may restrict use or whose training data is undisclosed. The Open Source Initiative published an Open Source AI Definition in 2024 requiring sufficient information about data, plus code and weights under open terms. Many models called open source are really open-weight. Check the actual licence before commercial use, rather than relying on labels.

## What is the best open source AI LLM?

Leading open-weight families in 2026 include Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama, Mistral, Gemma and OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the strongest large models approaching frontier proprietary performance on many benchmarks. Rankings change frequently.

Choose by licence, size and task: Qwen and gpt-oss use Apache 2.0, DeepSeek uses MIT for many releases, while Llama and Gemma use custom terms. Large mixture-of-experts models need serious GPUs, while mid-size dense models run on a single high-memory GPU. Check leaderboards such as LMArena and task-specific benchmarks, then test on your own prompts. For coding, reasoning or multilingual needs, specialised variants often outperform general models of similar size.

## What is the best small open-source LLM?

Strong small models include Qwen3 variants from under one to eight billion parameters, Gemma 3 at 1 and 4 billion, Llama 3.2 at 1 and 3 billion, Microsoft's Phi models, and SmolLM from Hugging Face.

Small models suit phones, laptops, edge devices and fine-tuning for narrow tasks such as classification, extraction or routing. They are weaker at broad knowledge and long reasoning, so pair them with RAG for facts. Fine-tuning a small model on your task often beats prompting a large general one, at a fraction of the cost and latency. FineTune Studio demonstrates this pattern with QLoRA and base-versus-tuned comparisons. Test several on your data, since strengths differ by task.

## What is the best open-source LLM to run locally?

For most laptops with 8 to 16 GB of memory, 7 to 14 billion parameter models such as Qwen3, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 and gpt-oss-20b, quantized to 4 bits through Ollama or LM Studio, offer the best balance of quality and speed.

With 24 GB or more of VRAM or a high-memory Mac, larger models around 30 billion parameters become practical. Pick instruct versions for chat, coding models for programming, and vision models for images. Quantization level matters: Q4_K_M is a good default. Measure tokens per second and answer quality on your own tasks. Local models keep data private and work offline, which suits sensitive documents and travel.

## What is the best open-source LLM for RAG?

Good RAG models follow instructions closely, use long context well and cite sources faithfully. Strong open choices include Qwen instruct models, Llama 3.1 and later instruct models, Mistral models and gpt-oss, chosen by size for your hardware.

For RAG, retrieval quality matters more than model size: a mid-size model with excellent hybrid retrieval and reranking often beats a larger model with weak retrieval. Test whether the model answers only from provided context, refuses when evidence is missing, and handles your languages. Some models are fine-tuned specifically for grounded answers with citations. DocuLens AI uses Groq-hosted Llama for fast document processing, an example of open weights served by a managed provider.

## How do development communities differ for open and closed LLMs?

Open model communities collaborate publicly: people fine-tune, quantize, benchmark and share derivatives on Hugging Face, build tools like llama.cpp and Ollama, and discuss results openly. Closed model development happens inside companies, with outside developers using APIs.

Open communities move fast on efficiency, quantization, local inference and domain fine-tunes, and they can inspect models for safety and bias. Closed providers concentrate large compute and research teams, releasing frontier capabilities and polished developer platforms, with communities forming around their APIs, SDKs and forums. Both ecosystems influence each other: open research ideas spread to closed labs, and closed model techniques inspire open releases. Developers benefit by participating in both.

# OpenAI API guide: models, examples, cut-off replies, fine-tunes, Azure, Groq, Anthropic
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/openai-api-guide-comparisons/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The OpenAI API gives developers programmatic access to OpenAI's models for text, structured output, tools, images, audio and embeddings. Choosing the right model, handling cut-off responses, using fine-tuned models and understanding data handling are the practical basics. I build AI products across providers with multi-provider fallback, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers model choice, a working example, incomplete responses, fine-tunes, data storage on Azure and Bedrock, comparisons with Azure, Groq and Anthropic, API keys and chat UIs.

## What is the best OpenAI API model?

It depends on the task. Use OpenAI's current flagship model for complex reasoning and coding, a reasoning model for hard multi-step problems, and smaller mini or nano variants for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification or extraction.

Model names change often, so check OpenAI's models page for current options, context lengths and capabilities. Evaluate candidates on your own test set, measuring quality, latency and cost per request. Many production systems route requests: a small, fast model for most traffic and a stronger one for difficult cases. For embeddings, use text-embedding-3-small or large. Pin specific model versions in production, so behaviour does not change unexpectedly when aliases update.

## What does an OpenAI API example look like?

With the official Python SDK, create a client, call the Responses API or Chat Completions with a model name and input, and read the text output. The API key comes from the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable.

```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    input="Explain RAG in two sentences.",
)
print(response.output_text)
```

Add streaming for chat interfaces, structured outputs with JSON schemas for extraction, and tools for actions. Handle rate limit and timeout errors with retries and exponential backoff, log request IDs for debugging, and keep keys out of source code. The JavaScript SDK mirrors this pattern with the same parameters.

## How do you continue an incomplete response from the OpenAI API?

Check why it stopped: if the finish or status reason indicates the length limit, increase the maximum output tokens. To continue, send the conversation again with the partial answer as an assistant message and ask the model to continue exactly where it stopped.

Better still, avoid truncation: request concise outputs, split large tasks into sections, and stream long responses so users see progress. For structured outputs, truncation produces invalid JSON, so generate smaller objects or paginate. Remember that output limits differ by model, and reasoning models spend tokens on internal reasoning, so set generous limits for them. When stitching continuations, check the seam for repeated or missing words, since models may restart a sentence.

## How do you use your fine-tuned model through OpenAI's API?

When fine-tuning finishes, OpenAI gives you a model ID starting with ft:, which includes the base model, your organisation and a suffix. Pass that ID as the model parameter in API calls, exactly like a base model name.

Find the ID in the fine-tuning dashboard or by retrieving the fine-tuning job through the API. Use the same message format and system prompt as your training data for consistent behaviour. Fine-tuned models are private to your organisation and billed at fine-tuned rates. Evaluate them against the base model on held-out examples before switching traffic, and keep the base model as a fallback. You can also fine-tune again, starting from your previous fine-tuned model.

## Do Azure OpenAI or Amazon Bedrock store data sent through the API?

Both state that customer prompts and completions are not used to train foundation models. Azure OpenAI may retain prompts and completions for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, unless approved for modified monitoring; Amazon Bedrock states it does not store or log prompts and completions.

Specific features change this: stored conversations, assistants, files, batch jobs or fine-tuning data are kept until you delete them, and logging you enable yourself, such as Bedrock invocation logging to your own storage, keeps records under your control. Data residency depends on the regions you choose. Read each provider's current data privacy documentation, sign appropriate agreements for regulated data, and avoid sending more personal information than a task requires.

## Azure OpenAI vs OpenAI API: what is the difference?

Both serve OpenAI models. Azure OpenAI runs them inside Microsoft Azure with enterprise features: private networking, Microsoft Entra ID authentication, regional deployment choices and compliance certifications. The OpenAI API is OpenAI's own platform, often getting new models and features first.

Azure suits organisations already on Azure that need governance, data residency and integration with Azure services; you create deployments of specific models in chosen regions. The OpenAI API is simpler to start with and usually offers the newest capabilities sooner. Code is similar, since official SDKs support both, with differences in endpoints, deployment names and authentication. Check model availability per region on Azure, since not every model is offered everywhere.

## Groq vs OpenAI API: how do they compare?

Groq runs open models, such as Llama, Qwen and other open-weight families, on its custom LPU hardware with very fast token generation, through an OpenAI-compatible API. OpenAI serves its own proprietary models, which lead on many capability benchmarks.

Choose Groq when speed and cost matter and open models are good enough, such as real-time chat, voice agents or high-volume extraction; DocuLens AI uses Groq-hosted Llama for fast document processing. Choose OpenAI when you need its strongest reasoning, multimodal features or specific tools. Because Groq is OpenAI-compatible, switching often means changing the base URL, key and model name. Many teams use both, routing by task and keeping one as a fallback.

## Anthropic vs OpenAI API: how do they compare?

Both offer frontier models through similar APIs with streaming, tool calling, structured outputs, vision and long context. Anthropic's Messages API serves Claude models; OpenAI's Responses and Chat Completions APIs serve GPT and reasoning models. Strengths shift with each release.

Differences include prompt caching behaviour, how tools and system prompts are specified, extended thinking options, file handling and pricing structures. Developers often prefer one for coding or long-document analysis based on their own tests. Build with an abstraction layer, or clean interfaces in your own code, so you can switch or fall back between providers. Evaluate both on your actual prompts and data, measuring quality, latency and cost, rather than relying on benchmarks alone.

## What does an OpenAI API key look like?

OpenAI API keys are long secret strings that start with a prefix such as sk-, and newer project keys start with sk-proj-, followed by many random characters. Never share a real key or paste it into public code, forums or screenshots.

Create keys in the OpenAI dashboard, scoped to a project, and store them in environment variables or a secrets manager, loading them at runtime. Add .env files to .gitignore. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately and create a new one, then check usage for unexpected activity. Set usage limits and monitoring alerts. In frontend apps, never expose keys to browsers; call the API from your server, which keeps keys hidden.

## What is the best UI for the OpenAI API?

Popular self-hosted chat interfaces include Open WebUI, LibreChat and LobeChat, which connect to the OpenAI API and other providers with your own key. The OpenAI Playground is good for testing prompts and parameters.

Open WebUI offers RAG over documents, multiple models and user management, and also works with local models through Ollama. LibreChat supports many providers, plugins and multi-user setups. For building your own interface, the Vercel AI SDK's chat hooks or simple React components with streaming work well. Consider security: self-hosted UIs store keys and conversations, so deploy them with authentication and HTTPS, and control who can access them.

# What are OpenAI API keys? Getting one, data storage, models and expiry
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/openai-api-keys-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An OpenAI API key is a secret token that lets your own code call OpenAI's models through its API, with every request billed to your OpenAI account. You create keys on the OpenAI platform, keep them in environment variables, and use them with OpenAI's SDKs or plain HTTP. This page covers what keys are and look like, where to get one, expiry, what happens to your data, how the API works, which models it offers, whether the API is itself an LLM, who owns it, and, for comparison, how Gemini API keys work.

## What are OpenAI API keys?

OpenAI API keys are secret credentials that identify your project when your code sends requests to OpenAI's API. Anyone with your key can make requests charged to your account, so keys must be kept private like passwords.

Keys belong to projects within an organisation, so you can separate keys for different apps, set spending limits and permissions per project, and revoke a key without affecting others. Never put a key in front-end JavaScript, a mobile app, a public GitHub repository or a screenshot. Call the API from your backend and keep the key in an environment variable or a secrets manager. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately in the dashboard and create a new one.

## What does an OpenAI API key look like?

An OpenAI API key is a long random string beginning with `sk-`; newer project keys begin with `sk-proj-`. The full key is shown only once, when you create it, so copy it straight into a password manager or your `.env` file.

The dashboard later shows only a masked version, so if you lose it, create a new key. In code, read it from the environment rather than pasting it in:

```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()   # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment
```

Tools such as GitHub's secret scanning detect committed keys, and providers may disable keys found in public places, which is another reason to keep them out of code.

## Where do I get an OpenAI API key?

Sign up on the OpenAI platform, add billing details or credits for your organisation, then open the API keys page and create a key for your project. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription does not include API usage; the API is billed separately.

Steps:

- Create or sign in to your account on the OpenAI platform.
- Set up billing and, ideally, a monthly spending limit.
- Create a project for your app.
- Generate an API key in that project and copy it once.
- Store it as `OPENAI_API_KEY` in your environment.

Buy credits only from OpenAI's own platform. Websites selling "cheap OpenAI keys" are reselling stolen or shared keys, which breaks OpenAI's terms and can expose your data.

## Do OpenAI API keys expire?

OpenAI API keys do not expire automatically; they work until you revoke them. However, a key can stop working if it is deleted, if the project or organisation is suspended, if billing fails, or if OpenAI disables a key detected as leaked.

Good practice is to rotate keys periodically and whenever someone with access leaves a project. Use separate keys for development and production, and for each service, so revoking one does not break everything. If your app suddenly gets authentication errors, check the key in the dashboard, your billing status and whether the key belongs to the right project. Monitor usage so unexpected spikes, a sign of a leaked key, are noticed quickly.

## Does the OpenAI API store data?

OpenAI states that data sent through the API is not used to train its models by default. API inputs and outputs are retained for a limited period, typically up to 30 days, for abuse and misuse monitoring, unless you qualify for zero data retention.

Some features store data by design: files you upload, assistants, conversation state and stored responses persist until you delete them or as configured. Enterprise customers can get stronger commitments, including zero data retention for eligible endpoints and data residency options. Before sending personal or sensitive data, read OpenAI's current enterprise privacy page and your organisation's policies, minimise what you send, and avoid including identity numbers or passwords in prompts.

## How does the OpenAI API work?

Your code sends an HTTPS request with your API key, a model name and input such as messages or a prompt; OpenAI runs the model and returns the output, along with token usage that determines cost.

The main pieces:

- **Text generation**: send input and instructions, get a response; stream it for responsive UIs.
- **Tools**: let the model call your functions, search the web or run code.
- **Structured outputs**: require JSON that matches a schema.
- **Embeddings**: turn text into vectors for search and RAG.
- **Images and audio**: generate images, transcribe speech, synthesise voice.

Requests are stateless unless you use features that store conversation state. Handle rate-limit and server errors with retries and backoff, which the official SDKs do automatically.

## What models does the OpenAI API offer?

The OpenAI API offers families of models for different jobs: GPT models for text, reasoning and coding, smaller fast models for high-volume tasks, embedding models for search, image generation models, speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, and realtime models for voice.

Model names and versions change frequently, so check the models page for current options, context lengths and pricing. A practical approach: start with a mid-sized general model, measure quality on your task, then try a smaller model for cost or a reasoning model for hard cases. Pin a specific model version in production so behaviour does not change unexpectedly, and test before upgrading.

## Is the OpenAI API an LLM?

No. The API is the interface, a web service, through which you access OpenAI's models, many of which are large language models. The LLM is the model running behind it; the API is how your software talks to it.

The distinction matters when designing systems. You can swap the model behind the same API call, use multiple providers through similar interfaces, or run an open-weight LLM locally behind an OpenAI-compatible API, as tools like Ollama and vLLM offer. Your application logic, such as retrieval, validation and tools, sits outside the model. In RAG.NextUpgrad, multi-provider fallback works precisely because the app talks to models through interchangeable interfaces.

## Who owns the OpenAI API?

OpenAI owns and operates the OpenAI API. OpenAI is the company that develops the GPT models and ChatGPT. Microsoft is a major partner and investor and offers OpenAI models through its own Azure OpenAI Service, which is a separate product with Microsoft's terms.

If your organisation uses Azure, the Azure version may be preferred for billing, compliance and regional hosting; the API shape is similar but authentication, endpoints and model availability differ. For individual developers and students, the OpenAI platform is the direct route. In both cases, the usage policies of the provider apply to your application.

## How many Gemini API keys can I have?

You can create multiple Gemini API keys, typically within Google Cloud projects through Google AI Studio. Rate limits and quotas generally apply per project, not per key, so extra keys in one project do not give you more free usage.

Use multiple keys to separate environments or apps and to rotate keys safely, not to get around limits; doing that through many accounts or projects can break the terms of service. Restrict keys where possible, such as limiting which APIs a key can call, store them in environment variables, and delete unused keys. If you need higher limits, enable billing on the project, which moves it to higher usage tiers.

How does the OpenAI API charge? The OpenAI API charges per token: input tokens you send and output tokens the model generates, at rates that differ by model. Is the OpenAI API censored? OpenAI's models follow usage policies and safety training, so they refuse some harmful requests, such as instructions for serious harm. Developers cannot disable this training, but within policy the API is flexible for a wide range of legitimate applications. Also asked as: is openai api censored OpenAI provides a free Moderation endpoint to screen inputs and outputs in your application. Refusals sometimes affect legitimate uses, such as medical or security education, so give clear context about the purpose and audience, and document refusal cases you encounter to improve prompts. Applications must also follow the usage policies, and violations can lead to account suspension. Open-weight models offer more control for specialised needs, but you then take full responsibility for safety and misuse prevention. Why is the OpenAI API slow? Slowness usually comes from larger or reasoning models that think before answering, long prompts, long outputs, not using streaming, high reasoning effort settings, rate limiting or network latency. Peak demand can also add delay. Also asked as: why openai api is slow Enable streaming so users see output immediately, and choose smaller models for simple tasks. For reasoning models, lower the reasoning effort when tasks are easy. Keep prompts concise and reuse stable prefixes to benefit from prompt caching. Limit maximum output tokens to what you need. For background work, the Batch API trades speed for cost savings. Monitor latency by model, and add fallbacks to other providers for reliability, as RAG.NextUpgrad does. What is OPENAI_API_BASE? Changing the base URL points the OpenAI SDK at another endpoint, such as Azure OpenAI, a corporate proxy, or OpenAI-compatible providers like Ollama, Groq, OpenRouter or vLLM servers. This lets the same code work with different backends. If older tutorials use OPENAI_API_BASE and your code ignores it, you are probably on a newer library version, so switch to base_url. Keep endpoints and keys in configuration, not hard-coded. Where can you buy OpenAI API access? Buy API credits on OpenAI's developer platform under billing settings, using a card, with automatic recharge available. Organisations can also access OpenAI models through Azure OpenAI, billed through Microsoft Azure. Also asked as: where to buy openai api API credits are separate from ChatGPT subscriptions, so a ChatGPT Plus plan does not include API usage. Start with a small credit purchase while prototyping, set spending limits, and monitor usage. Invoices help with reimbursement and accounting. For enterprises, Azure procurement or direct agreements with OpenAI may offer better governance and billing options. Can you train or fine-tune models through the OpenAI API? Yes. You can fine-tune supported OpenAI models through the fine-tuning API, uploading examples in JSONL format. Options include supervised fine-tuning, preference fine-tuning and reinforcement fine-tuning for some reasoning models. You cannot train new models from scratch. Fine-tuning suits consistent formats, styles, classification and specialised tasks. Prepare high-quality chat-formatted examples, upload training and validation files, start a job and monitor loss. The tuned model receives its own ID for API calls, with its own usage pricing. Keep a held-out set to compare tuned and base models. Before fine-tuning, test prompting and retrieval, which solve many needs faster. For full control over weights, open models fine-tuned with QLoRA, as in FineTune Studio, are an alternative. How do you create an OpenAI API key? Sign in to OpenAI's developer platform, open the API keys section, choose a project, and create a new secret key. Copy it immediately, since it is shown only once, and store it securely, such as in an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable. Also asked as: how create openai api key Project-scoped keys limit access to a specific project's resources, and you can restrict permissions for each key. If you lose a key, create a new one and delete the old. Never paste keys into front-end code, public repositories or shared notebooks; leaked keys can be abused quickly. Rotate keys periodically and monitor usage for unexpected activity. Name keys clearly, such as by application and environment, to manage them later. Can the OpenAI API read images? Yes. Vision-capable OpenAI models accept images as inputs, by URL or base64 data, and can describe, compare, extract text from and reason about them. Separate image generation models create and edit images from prompts. Also asked as: can openai api read images Common uses include reading receipts, analysing charts and screenshots, classifying products and answering questions about photos. You can include several images in one request. Images consume input tokens based on size and detail settings, so choose lower detail when fine resolution is unnecessary. Verify extracted numbers, since vision models can misread small text. For scanned documents with complex layouts, dedicated OCR, such as the Mistral OCR my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace uses, may be more reliable. How many tokens can the OpenAI API handle? Limits depend on the model: context windows range from tens of thousands of tokens for older models to hundreds of thousands or around a million for newer ones, and maximum output tokens vary separately. Check the models page for exact values. Also asked as: how many tokens openai api The context window covers your prompt, conversation history, documents and the response. Rate limits also cap tokens per minute for your organisation tier. Use the tiktoken library to count tokens before sending requests and to estimate costs. Long contexts cost more and can reduce answer quality for details buried in the middle, so retrieve only relevant passages. Split very large documents into chunks or use retrieval instead. What are OpenAI API tokens? Tokens are chunks of text that models read and generate; in English, a token averages about four characters, or roughly three quarters of a word. The API measures usage and bills in tokens, separately for input and output. Tokens are not credentials and do not expire; they are units of text. Different languages tokenise differently, so Hindi and other Indian languages often use more tokens per word than English, increasing costs. Images and audio also convert to tokens. Count tokens with tiktoken, set maximum output limits, and keep prompts concise to control usage. Usage dashboards show token totals by model. Understanding tokens helps estimate costs and design applications that stay within context limits.
