# Pinecone vs Chroma, Pinecone's history, free tier and examples, plus vector DB basics
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-vs-chroma-free-tier/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database, while Chroma is an open-source, developer-friendly vector store you can run locally or in the cloud. Both store embeddings for semantic search and RAG. RAG.NextUpgrad pairs dense retrieval with BM25, so this page compares Pinecone and Chroma, covers Pinecone's founding, team, free tier, examples and product direction, then explains Python vector libraries, LangChain integration, vector databases versus pandas, and their role in prompts.

## Pinecone vs Chroma: which should you use?

Choose Pinecone for a fully managed service that scales without operating servers, with metadata filtering, namespaces and hybrid search. Choose Chroma for open-source, local-first development, quick prototypes and self-hosting, with an optional managed cloud.

Chroma can run embedded in Python with a few lines, making it ideal for learning and small apps, and you control where data lives. Pinecone suits production teams that prefer paying for operations over running infrastructure, especially with large or unpredictable workloads. Both integrate with LangChain and LlamaIndex. Consider data residency, cost at your scale, latency from your region, and how much filtering you need. Prototype quickly with Chroma, and benchmark both before production.

## When was Pinecone founded?

Pinecone was founded in 2019 by Edo Liberty, a former research director at Amazon Web Services and Yahoo, and launched publicly in 2021 as one of the first managed vector databases.

The company grew rapidly with the rise of generative AI in 2023, when RAG made vector search essential, and it raised significant venture funding. In 2024 it introduced a serverless architecture that separates storage from compute to reduce costs for large, infrequently queried indexes. Pinecone has since added integrated embedding and reranking models and assistant features for RAG. Its history mirrors the broader vector database market's growth alongside LLM applications.

## How many employees does Pinecone have?

Pinecone is a mid-sized startup; public professional profiles have shown a team in the low hundreds. Exact headcount changes over time, so check its LinkedIn company page or recent news for current figures.

For buyers, team size matters less than signals of stability and support: product release cadence, documentation quality, uptime history, security certifications such as SOC 2, support plans and customer references. Managed services carry vendor risk, so keep your retrieval layer behind a clean interface in your code and maintain exportable copies of source data and embeddings. That way, switching providers stays feasible if pricing, features or company circumstances change.

## Does Pinecone have a free tier?

Yes. Pinecone offers a free Starter plan with limited storage, indexes and usage, suitable for learning, prototypes and small projects. Paid plans add higher limits, more regions, support and enterprise features.

Free-tier indexes may be paused or limited after inactivity, and limits change over time, so check Pinecone's pricing page for current details. Use the free tier to test retrieval quality and latency with your real data before committing. Monitor usage to avoid surprises when moving to paid plans, since costs depend on storage, reads and writes. For fully free alternatives, self-host Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma or pgvector, accepting the operations work yourself.

## What are some Pinecone examples?

Pinecone's examples repository on GitHub, pinecone-io/examples, contains notebooks for semantic search, RAG with OpenAI and other providers, hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors, recommendation, image search and chatbots with LangChain.

A minimal example: create a serverless index with a dimension matching your embedding model, upsert vectors with IDs and metadata, then query with a vector and a metadata filter, getting the top matches with scores. Extend it by adding namespaces per user or tenant, hybrid queries, and reranking with Pinecone's hosted rerank models or your own. Run notebooks in Colab with a free-tier API key to learn the full workflow quickly.

## What is on Pinecone's roadmap?

Pinecone's recent direction has focused on serverless indexes, integrated inference for embedding and reranking, assistant tools for building RAG quickly, and enterprise features such as bring-your-own-cloud deployments and stronger security controls.

Specific future plans are announced on Pinecone's blog, changelog and events, so follow those for accurate information rather than third-party speculation. The broader market trend is toward managed retrieval platforms that handle chunking, embedding, hybrid search and reranking together, reducing glue code for developers. When evaluating any vendor roadmap, prioritise features already shipped and documented over announced ones, and design your system so it does not depend on unreleased capabilities.

## What are the best Python vector database libraries?

Popular Python options are Chroma for simple local and embedded use, FAISS for fast in-process search, the Qdrant client with its local mode, LanceDB for embedded columnar vector storage, and pgvector through psycopg for PostgreSQL.

Clients for Pinecone, Weaviate and Milvus are also strong choices when you use those databases. Choose by deployment: embedded libraries such as Chroma, LanceDB and FAISS need no server, while client libraries connect to running databases. For learning, Chroma is easiest; for performance experiments, FAISS; for production with filtering, Qdrant or pgvector. All integrate with LangChain and LlamaIndex, so you can swap them while keeping the rest of your RAG code.

## How does LangChain integrate with vector databases?

LangChain provides a common VectorStore interface with methods such as add_documents, similarity_search and as_retriever, and integration packages for many databases, including Chroma, FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and PGVector.

You create a vector store with an embeddings object, for example with from_documents on your chunks, and LangChain handles embedding and inserting. Then as_retriever turns it into a runnable retriever you can use in chains and agents, with options for metadata filters, top k and maximal marginal relevance. Because the interface is shared, switching databases mostly means changing the import and connection settings. Check each integration's documentation for features like hybrid search, which vary.

## Why use a vector database instead of a pandas DataFrame?

A DataFrame can hold embeddings and compute similarities with NumPy, which works for small datasets. Vector databases add approximate nearest neighbour indexes, persistence, filtering, updates and concurrent access, which DataFrames lack as data and traffic grow.

With pandas, every query compares against all rows in memory, fine for thousands of vectors but slow for millions. You also must load the whole dataset into memory and manage saving and concurrency yourself. Vector databases index embeddings for millisecond searches, store data durably, support metadata filters and serve many users at once. For experiments and notebooks, DataFrames are perfectly reasonable; for applications, move to a vector store once performance or reliability matters.

## Why are vector databases used in LLM prompt engineering?

They supply relevant context for prompts. Instead of pasting whole documents, a system retrieves the most relevant passages or examples from a vector database and inserts them into the prompt, grounding the model's answer in specific information.

Uses include RAG, where retrieved passages support answers with citations; dynamic few-shot prompting, where the most similar past examples are retrieved as demonstrations; and memory, where relevant earlier conversations are recalled. This keeps prompts short, current and focused, which reduces cost and hallucination. Prompt quality then depends on retrieval quality, so evaluate what gets retrieved, not just how the prompt is worded. RAG.NextUpgrad's confidence gate declines to answer when retrieval is weak.

# Pinecone vs Supabase for vector search: how each works, RAG in Supabase, and keys
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-vs-supabase/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Pinecone and Supabase solve vector search differently. Pinecone is a managed, vector-only database built for similarity search at scale. Supabase is a backend platform on PostgreSQL, with auth, storage and APIs, that does vector search through the pgvector extension. If your app already needs a database, Supabase keeps everything together; if vector search is the main workload at large scale, Pinecone removes operations work. I build RAG on PostgreSQL, so this page compares them and covers Supabase RAG, Python, self-hosting and keys.

## Pinecone vs Supabase: which should I use?

Use Supabase when you want embeddings next to your application data, with SQL joins, auth-based access control and one bill. Use Pinecone when you have very large vector collections, need managed scaling without tuning Postgres, or want a dedicated vector service.

Comparison:

- **Model**: Pinecone is vector-first; Supabase is Postgres with pgvector.
- **Filtering**: Pinecone uses metadata filters; Supabase uses full SQL.
- **Hybrid search**: Pinecone supports sparse-dense vectors; Supabase combines pgvector with Postgres full-text search.
- **Access control**: Supabase applies Row Level Security to vectors; Pinecone uses namespaces and API keys.
- **Operations**: both are managed; Supabase can also be self-hosted.

For most student and startup RAG apps, Supabase is simpler.

## How does Pinecone work?

You create an index with a dimension and distance metric, upsert vectors with IDs and metadata, and query with a vector to get the nearest matches. Pinecone manages storage, indexing, replication and scaling behind an API.

Its serverless architecture separates storage from compute, so you pay for what you store and query rather than provisioning servers. Namespaces partition an index, which suits multi-tenant apps where each customer's data must stay separate. Queries can include metadata filters, and Pinecone offers hosted embedding and reranking models in some configurations. You cannot see or tune the internal index algorithms, which is the trade-off for not running anything yourself.

## What is a Pinecone index?

A Pinecone index is the top-level container for your vectors, defined by vector dimension, distance metric such as cosine or dot product, and deployment type. All vectors in an index share the same dimension, matching your embedding model.

Inside an index, namespaces divide data, for example one per user or document set, and every vector has an ID, values and optional metadata. You can create separate indexes for different embedding models or environments, such as development and production. Changing embedding models means creating a new index and re-embedding your data, so record which model produced each index.

## Pinecone vs Chroma: when should I use each?

Use Chroma for local development, prototypes, notebooks and small applications, because it is open source and runs in-process with no setup. Use Pinecone for production workloads that need managed scaling, high availability and multi-tenant isolation.

A common path is starting with Chroma while you design chunking and prompts, then moving to a managed or database-backed store when the app has users. To make that move painless, put retrieval behind a small interface in your code with functions such as add, query and delete. Chroma also offers a hosted cloud service, so the line between them has narrowed; evaluate on your own data, cost and operational needs.

## How does Supabase store data?

Supabase stores application data in a PostgreSQL database, files such as images and PDFs in S3-compatible object storage, and user accounts in Postgres tables managed by its auth service. Vectors are stored in Postgres columns using pgvector.

Because everything is Postgres, you can join user records with documents and embeddings in one query, apply Row Level Security policies to every table, and use standard tools for backups and migrations. Supabase auto-generates REST and GraphQL APIs from your schema, and Realtime streams database changes to clients. Your data is portable: you can dump the database and move to any Postgres host.

## Can I use Supabase with Python?

Yes. Install the official client with `pip install supabase`, create a client with your project URL and key, then query tables, call database functions, upload files and manage auth from Python. You can also connect directly to Postgres with drivers such as psycopg.

```python
from supabase import create_client
sb = create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_KEY)
rows = sb.rpc("match_chunks", {"query_embedding": emb, "match_count": 5}).execute()
```

For backend services, such as a FastAPI app, use a server-side key kept in environment variables, never in front-end code. Async support exists for high-concurrency apps; check the client documentation for current options.

## How do I build strong RAG retrieval in Supabase with three files?

Three pieces cover it: a SQL migration that creates a chunks table with an embedding column, a full-text search column and indexes; a hybrid search function that merges vector and keyword results with reciprocal rank fusion; and an ingestion script that chunks, embeds and inserts documents.

Details:

- **Migration**: enable pgvector, add `vector` and `tsvector` columns, an HNSW index and a GIN index.
- **Function**: run both searches, rank each, fuse by summing one over rank plus a constant, return top results.
- **Ingestion**: split by headings, embed in batches, store source and page metadata.

Supabase's documentation includes a hybrid search example. This mirrors the hybrid design in RAG.NextUpgrad, where keyword and vector retrieval are fused before reranking.

## Can I self-host Supabase?

Yes. Supabase is open source, and its repository includes a Docker Compose setup that runs Postgres, the API gateway, auth, storage, realtime and the dashboard on your own server. Self-hosting suits data residency needs or full control.

Plan for operations: secure secrets and keys, configure HTTPS and SMTP for auth emails, back up Postgres regularly, monitor resources, and apply updates. Some managed-platform features may differ or require extra setup when self-hosting. For most teams starting out, the managed service is easier; self-host when you have a specific reason and the capacity to run it reliably.

## Should the Supabase anon key be public?

Yes, the anon key, or newer publishable key, is designed to be used in browsers and mobile apps, so it is effectively public. It is safe only if Row Level Security is enabled on every table with correct policies. Never expose the service role or secret key.

The anon key lets clients call your API as an unauthenticated or logged-in user, and RLS policies decide what each request can read or write. Without RLS, anyone with the key can read or modify your tables. Check every table in the dashboard's security advisor, test policies with different users, and keep privileged keys only on servers.

## When is pine cone season?

Outside software, pine cones mature and fall mostly in autumn, roughly September to November in the northern hemisphere, depending on the pine species and climate. Many species take about two years to mature their cones.

Collectors gather fallen cones for crafts and decorations, and some species' cones release seeds only after fire or heat. The database company borrowed the name, and its logo nods to the pine cone's ordered spiral pattern, which follows Fibonacci numbers, a fitting image for a product built on mathematical structure. For search, check whether results refer to the trees, crafts or the vector database.

# Pitch deck guide: purpose, slides, length, Canva, startup decks, PPT and pitch bibles
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pitch-deck-guide-slides-canva/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A pitch deck is a short presentation that explains a startup or project to investors, judges or partners: the problem, solution, market, traction, team and ask. At hackathons, it often decides results as much as the code. I won first prizes at Changethon 2025 with KrishGyan, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 with BrandHive and BYTEBATTLE with Annapurna, so this page covers a deck's purpose, contents, length, Canva, startup decks, timing, PPTs and pitch bibles. What is the purpose of a pitch deck? A pitch deck's purpose is to win the next step: a meeting, an investment, a prize or a partnership. It tells a clear story of the problem, your solution, why now, and why your team can win, in a few minutes. It is not meant to explain everything. A good deck creates enough interest and confidence that the audience wants to learn more. Investors use it to judge market size, traction and team; hackathon judges use it to judge impact, feasibility and execution. Decks also clarify your own thinking, since reducing a venture to a handful of slides exposes weak assumptions. Tailor each deck to its audience and the specific decision you want them to make. What does pitch deck mean in business? In business, a pitch deck is a brief slide presentation used to pitch a company, product or idea, usually to investors when fundraising, but also to customers, partners, accelerators or competition judges. The word deck comes from a deck of slides. Startups typically maintain two versions: a presentation deck with minimal text and strong visuals for live pitches, and a send-ahead deck with more detail that readers can understand without a speaker. Established companies use similar decks for sales, partnerships and internal proposals. In India, startup schemes, incubators and accelerators often ask for pitch decks with applications, so having a polished one ready saves time. How do you make a pitch deck for a startup? Start with your story, not slides: write one sentence describing what you do and for whom, then outline the problem, solution, market, product, traction, business model, competition, team and ask. Then design simple slides for each point. Also asked as: how to make pitch deck for startup Use a proven structure such as Sequoia's or Y Combinator's guidance, keeping one idea per slide with large text and real visuals, such as product screenshots and charts. Lead with your strongest proof, whether traction, a pilot or a demo. Practise the spoken pitch alongside the slides, since they work together. Get feedback from mentors and founders, then iterate. For hackathons, show the working demo early, as judges value proof that the product actually works. What should be included in a pitch deck? Core slides include the title and one-line pitch, problem, solution, why now, market size, product or demo, traction, business model, competition, go-to-market plan, team, and the ask, such as the funding sought and how it will be used. Also asked as: what should be included in pitch deck Adjust emphasis by stage: early decks rely on problem insight, team and early validation, while later decks need metrics such as revenue growth and retention. Include contact details on the last slide. Keep financial projections brief, with detailed models in an appendix. For hackathons, replace funding slides with impact, technical architecture and next steps. Every slide should answer a question the audience will have; cut anything that does not move the story forward. How many slides does a pitch deck have? Most pitch decks have 10 to 15 slides. Guy Kawasaki's popular 10/20/30 rule suggests 10 slides, 20 minutes and no font smaller than 30 points, and many investors prefer concise decks they can scan quickly. Hackathon decks are often shorter, five to eight slides, because pitches last only a few minutes. Send-ahead decks for investors may run slightly longer, with an appendix covering financial details, technical depth or customer case studies. Fewer, stronger slides almost always beat more slides. If you need many slides to explain the idea, the story probably needs simplifying. Test by presenting to someone unfamiliar with your project and noting where they get confused. How long should an investor pitch deck presentation be? Plan for about 10 to 20 minutes of presenting, leaving time for questions, though many first meetings are shorter. Demo days and competitions often allow only two to five minutes, so prepare short and long versions. Also asked as: how long should investor pitch deck be Investors often decide within the first few minutes whether they are interested, so lead with the problem, solution and strongest proof. Time each section while rehearsing, and cut content rather than speaking faster. Prepare a one-minute version for networking and a three-minute version for demo days. At hackathons, judges often ask questions immediately after short pitches, so anticipate likely questions about feasibility, users and next steps, and keep backup slides ready. How long does it take to make a pitch deck? A first draft can take one to three days if you already understand your business, and refining it through feedback usually takes a few weeks. Hackathon decks are often built in one or two hours near the end of the event. Also asked as: how long does a pitch deck take to make Most time goes into thinking, not design: sharpening the problem statement, gathering traction data, sizing the market and choosing the strongest story. Templates speed up design, letting you focus on content. Expect multiple rounds of feedback from mentors, advisers and practice audiences. Each fundraising round needs updates, so keep a master deck you revise regularly. At hackathons, assign one teammate to the deck while others finish the demo, then rehearse together. Can you make a pitch deck on Canva? Yes. Canva offers many free and premium pitch deck templates, easy editing, team collaboration, presenter mode and exports to PDF and PowerPoint, making it a popular choice for students, hackathon teams and early startups. Choose a clean template, then replace placeholder content with your own story, data and product screenshots; avoid cluttered layouts with tiny text. Keep fonts and colours consistent with your brand. Canva's charts work for simple metrics, though complex financials may be easier in spreadsheets, then pasted as images. Export a PDF for sending, since it displays consistently, and test the presentation on the actual screen or projector you will use. Google Slides and PowerPoint remain good alternatives. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a PPT? PPT refers to a PowerPoint file or slide presentation in general, while a pitch deck is a specific presentation designed to persuade investors, judges or partners. A pitch deck can be a PPT file or built in Canva, Keynote or Google Slides. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and ppt The difference is purpose and structure. A general presentation might teach, report or train, often with dense text. A pitch deck follows a persuasive storyline, problem, solution, proof and ask, with minimal text and strong visuals. College presentations often read like reports, so students preparing for hackathons or incubators should rewrite them into pitch format: fewer words, clearer claims and evidence on every slide. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a pitch bible? A pitch deck pitches a business to investors or judges. A pitch bible, or series bible, pitches a creative project, such as a television or animated series, describing its world, characters, tone, story arcs and episode ideas. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and bible Pitch bibles are used in film, television, animation and games to sell a concept to studios or networks and to keep writers consistent once production starts. They are often longer and highly visual, with character art and sample storylines. Pitch decks focus on markets, traction and returns. Some creative startups need both: a bible for the creative product and a pitch deck for the business that will produce and distribute it.

# Best pitch deck template: slides, structure, Canva, and presenting a pitch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pitch-deck-template-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best pitch deck template is a simple structure that tells one clear story: the problem, your solution, a demo or proof, the market, how you make money or create impact, traction, the team and what you are asking for. Design matters less than clarity and evidence. I have pitched and won Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 with BrandHive, along with two other hackathon first prizes, and judged other teams, so this page covers what a deck includes, slide counts and length, creating one, investor versus hackathon decks, Canva, format and how to present.

## What is the best pitch deck template?

The best template follows a proven order and keeps one idea per slide: title, problem, solution, demo or product, market, business model or impact, traction, competition, team, and the ask. Many founders adapt the structures published by well-known investors and accelerators.

A template that works for students and early founders:

- **Title**: name, one-line description, logo.
- **Problem**: a specific user and their pain, with evidence.
- **Solution**: what you built, in one sentence.
- **Demo**: screenshots or a live demo.
- **Market**: who and how many.
- **Business model or impact**.
- **Traction**: users, pilots, results.
- **Competition**: why you are different.
- **Team**: why you can build it.
- **Ask**: funding, mentorship, partnership or next step.

Large, readable text and one strong visual per slide beat crowded designs.

## What does a pitch deck include?

A pitch deck includes the problem, solution, product or demo, target market, business model, traction, competition, team and the ask. For hackathons, replace business details with impact, technical approach and next steps as the judging criteria require.

Each slide should answer a question the audience has: why does this matter, why now, why you, how will it grow, and what do you want from us. Include real evidence where you have it: user quotes, pilot results, a working prototype. Avoid long paragraphs, tiny charts and jargon; if a slide needs a long explanation, it needs to be simpler.

## How many slides should a pitch deck have?

For investors, ten to twelve main slides, with extra details in an appendix. For a hackathon pitch of three to five minutes, five to eight slides, because each slide needs time to land.

A rule of thumb is roughly one slide per thirty to sixty seconds of speaking. Fewer, stronger slides are better than many rushed ones. Keep backup slides for likely questions, such as technical architecture, data privacy or detailed financials, and show them only if asked. Judges and investors remember the story and the demo, not the slide count.

## How long should a pitch be?

Hackathon pitches are usually three to five minutes plus questions; investor pitches commonly run ten to twenty minutes; a quick verbal pitch should be under a minute. Always confirm the time limit and rehearse to fit it with margin.

Plan time deliberately: about a fifth on the problem, the largest share on the solution and demo, and a short close on impact, traction and the ask. Rehearse with a timer at least three times; most first drafts run long. Cut slides rather than speaking faster. Leaving time for questions often helps, because questions show what the audience cares about.

## How do I create a pitch deck?

Write the story first, then build slides. Draft a one-paragraph narrative, outline one slide per point, gather evidence and visuals, design simply, and rehearse with feedback.

Steps:

- Write the problem and solution in one sentence each.
- List the questions your audience will ask and answer each on a slide.
- Add proof: demo screenshots, user feedback, data.
- Use a clean template with large fonts and consistent colours.
- Practise aloud, get feedback from someone outside your team, and simplify.

Use AI tools to tighten wording or suggest structure, but make sure every claim is true and you can explain every number.

## How do I make a pitch deck for investors?

Focus on the opportunity and your ability to capture it: a painful problem, a solution customers want, evidence of traction, a large enough market, a credible business model, a strong team, and a clear funding ask with how you will use it.

Investor-specific tips:

- Lead with traction if you have it; it is the strongest evidence.
- Show market size with a clear, bottom-up calculation.
- Explain how you will acquire customers and what it costs, in principle.
- Address competition honestly and state your advantage.
- State the round size and the milestones it will reach.

Send a PDF version that reads well without you presenting, and keep a separate, more visual version for live pitches.

## Can I create a pitch deck on Canva?

Yes. Canva has many pitch deck templates and makes it easy to design clean slides, add images and charts, collaborate with teammates, and present or export to PDF or PowerPoint.

Tips for Canva decks: pick a minimal template and remove decorative elements, use one or two fonts, keep text large, and use your own product screenshots rather than stock images where possible. Export a PDF for sharing, and test the presentation on the actual screen or projector if you can. PowerPoint, Google Slides and Keynote work equally well; choose the one your team collaborates in most easily.

## Is a pitch deck a PPT?

A pitch deck is a presentation, and it can be made in PowerPoint, which saves files as PPTX, or in Google Slides, Keynote or Canva. "PPT" is often used loosely to mean any slide presentation.

When sharing, a PDF is usually best, because it looks the same on every device and cannot be accidentally edited. Some competitions, such as Smart India Hackathon, specify a template and format for idea submissions, so follow official instructions exactly. For live pitches, keep the presentation file and a PDF backup on your laptop and a USB drive or cloud link.

## How do I give a pitch?

Open with a hook about the problem, keep eye contact, tell the story slide by slide in your own words, show the demo confidently, close with your impact and ask, then handle questions calmly and concisely.

Presenting tips from the judge's table:

- Start with the user and their problem, not your technology stack.
- Rehearse the demo many times; have a recorded backup.
- Assign speaking parts so transitions are smooth.
- Do not read slides; slides support you.
- Answer questions directly, admit unknowns, and say how you would find out.

Teams that clearly explain what they built and why it matters usually outscore teams with more features and a confusing story.

## Is pitch deck one word or two words?

"Pitch deck" is two words. It means a short slide presentation used to pitch a business, product or idea to investors, judges, customers or partners.

You will also see "pitch presentation" or simply "deck" used in startup conversations, such as "send us your deck". In writing, keep it as two words without a hyphen when used as a noun, as in "our pitch deck", and some writers hyphenate it when used before another noun, as in "pitch-deck template", though "pitch deck template" without a hyphen is common and acceptable.

# Pitch deck tutorial: best format, tips, roadmap slide, VC and game examples, AI tools
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pitch-deck-tutorial-format-tips/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A pitch deck is a short slide presentation, usually 10 to 15 slides, that explains your problem, solution, market, traction, team and ask to investors, judges or partners. A good deck tells a clear story in minutes. I have pitched at hackathons and product competitions, winning Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 with BrandHive and Changethon 2025 with KrishGyan, so this page covers a tutorial, the best format, tips, the roadmap slide, deck types, examples and tools.

## What is a good pitch deck tutorial?

Build your deck in this order: write the story in one paragraph, outline one message per slide, add evidence, design simply, then rehearse with a timer. Start from the content, not a template, because design cannot fix an unclear story.

Step by step: write a one-sentence description of what you do; describe the problem in the customer's words; show the solution with a product screenshot or demo; prove demand with traction or validation; size the market honestly; explain the business model; show the team; and finish with your ask and how you will use it. Then cut every slide that does not support the decision you want the audience to make, and test the deck on someone outside your field.

## What is the best pitch deck format?

A proven format, close to Sequoia's and Y Combinator's guidance: title, problem, solution, why now, market, product, traction, business model, competition, team, financials or roadmap, and the ask. Ten to fifteen slides is typical.

Use 16:9 slides, one idea per slide, large readable text and a headline that states the takeaway, such as "Farmers lose crops because advice arrives too late", rather than a generic label like "Problem". Keep a separate appendix for detailed metrics and answers to expected questions. Send a PDF when emailing investors, since it displays consistently, and keep a version with speaker notes for live pitches. For hackathons, compress to five to seven slides plus a live demo.

## What are the best pitch deck tips?

Lead with the problem and why it matters, show proof rather than adjectives, keep slides visual and simple, and know your numbers cold. Investors and judges decide quickly, so your first two slides must make them want to see the rest.

More tips: use real customer quotes and data; show the product early; explain why your team is the one to solve this; be honest about competition instead of claiming none exists; keep text minimal and speak the details; and end with a specific ask. Guy Kawasaki's 10/20/30 rule, ten slides, twenty minutes, thirty-point font, is a useful starting discipline. Rehearse out loud many times, and prepare answers for the hardest questions you expect.

## What goes on a roadmap slide in a pitch deck?

A roadmap slide shows what you will achieve over the next 12 to 24 months, usually as milestones on a timeline: product launches, customer or revenue targets, key hires and expansion, tied to the funding you are raising.

Make milestones specific and measurable, such as launching in three more languages or reaching a set number of active users, rather than vague goals like scaling up. Link each milestone to the use of funds, so investors see how their support creates progress toward the next round. Keep it to four to six milestones and show what is already done. In hackathon pitches, a roadmap slide shows judges what happens after the event, which signals commitment beyond the weekend.

## What is the difference between an investor deck and a pitch deck?

The terms often mean the same thing. When distinguished, a pitch deck is a short, visual deck for presenting live, while an investor deck is a more detailed, text-rich version sent ahead of or after meetings for investors to read on their own.

A presentation deck relies on the speaker: big visuals, few words and a demo. A send-ahead investor deck must stand alone, so it includes more explanation, metrics, market data and financial details. Many founders keep both versions of the same story. Investors often skim emailed decks quickly, so even the detailed version needs clear headlines and a logical flow. Data rooms and financial models come later, during due diligence, not in the first deck.

## What is the difference between a proposal and a pitch deck?

A pitch deck persuades someone to invest in or back an idea, usually at an early conversation. A proposal is a detailed document offering specific work or a solution to a client, with scope, deliverables, timeline, pricing and terms.

Pitch decks are short, visual and story-driven, aiming for a next meeting or a yes in principle. Proposals are longer, precise and often contractual, answering a client's request or tender with exactly what will be delivered. A sales deck sits between them, presenting a product to potential customers. Use a pitch deck for investors, competitions and partnerships; use a proposal when a client is ready to evaluate a concrete offer and needs detail to approve it.

## What are some VC pitch deck examples?

Well-known public examples include Airbnb's early seed deck, YouTube's 2005 deck, LinkedIn's Series B deck shared by Reid Hoffman, and early decks from companies such as Uber and Buffer. Collections of these are widely available online.

Study them for structure, not style: Airbnb's deck states the problem, solution, market and business model in a few simple slides, and LinkedIn's annotated deck explains the reasoning behind each slide. Remember that famous decks succeeded partly because of strong teams and timing, so do not copy their exact formats. Also read guidance from investors, such as Sequoia's business plan outline and Y Combinator's seed deck advice, which explain what investors look for.

## What are some game pitch deck examples?

A game pitch deck shows the game's hook, genre, core gameplay loop, target audience, platforms, art style, unique features, monetisation, team, timeline and the support you need. Publishers expect to see gameplay early, ideally a video or playable prototype.

Many studios and publishers share template decks and talks about what they want, and game jam projects are a good source of prototypes to build pitches around. Strong game decks open with a one-line hook and key art, then show a short gameplay clip, comparable successful titles, and a realistic production plan. Keep it to 10 to 15 slides. Publishers care about scope and the team's ability to finish, so show prior shipped projects, even small ones.

## What is the best AI tool for pitch decks?

Popular AI tools include Gamma and Beautiful.ai, which generate full decks from a prompt or outline, Canva's AI design features, Microsoft Copilot in PowerPoint, and general assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for writing and structure.

Use AI for drafts, structure and design speed, but write the story and numbers yourself. AI-generated decks often look polished but generic, with vague claims that investors and judges see through quickly. A good workflow: write your narrative and key facts, ask an assistant to propose a slide outline and critique your argument, generate a first design, then edit every slide for accuracy and specificity. Never let AI invent metrics, quotes or market sizes.

## What is the best pitch deck software?

PowerPoint, Google Slides and Keynote remain reliable standards. Canva offers easy templates and design tools, Pitch focuses on collaborative startup decks, and Figma Slides suits design-heavy teams. Choose what your team can edit quickly and share reliably.

Canva is a strong choice for students and hackathon teams because its pitch deck templates, brand kits and real-time collaboration make good-looking slides fast; export to PDF or PowerPoint for compatibility. Google Slides works well for live collaboration in teams. Whatever tool you use, check how the deck renders on another computer and as a PDF, embed fonts, compress large images, and keep a backup copy offline in case the venue's internet fails.

# Pitch deck vs business plan, proposal, portfolio, treatment, report, profile and IM
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pitch-deck-vs-business-plan-proposal/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A pitch deck is a short, persuasive slide presentation, and many other business documents are easily confused with it, from business plans and proposals to film treatments and information memoranda. Knowing the differences helps you prepare the right document for each audience. I won first prizes at Changethon 2025 with KrishGyan, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 with BrandHive and BYTEBATTLE with Annapurna, so this page compares pitch decks with seven related documents and covers orientation, Series A decks and design. Is a pitch deck the same as a business plan? No. A pitch deck is a short visual presentation, usually 10 to 15 slides, designed to spark interest and win a meeting or investment. A business plan is a detailed written document covering strategy, operations, market analysis and financial projections. Also asked as: is pitch deck the same as business plan Investors today usually ask for a deck first and request deeper materials, such as financial models, during due diligence. Business plans remain useful for bank loans, grant applications, some competitions and internal planning, forcing founders to think through details. Many teams write a concise business plan or memo to clarify thinking, then distil it into a deck. The deck tells the story; the plan provides the evidence behind it. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a proposal? A proposal is a document offering to do specific work for a client or funder, detailing scope, approach, deliverables, timeline and budget, often in response to a request. A pitch deck persuades investors or judges to back a venture. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and proposal Proposals are judged on fit with stated requirements and feasibility, and often follow a required format, such as grant applications or tenders. Pitch decks have more freedom and focus on opportunity, traction and team. Some situations blend them, such as pitching a pilot to a company, where slides open the conversation and a proposal formalises the agreement. Match the document to what the audience must decide. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a portfolio? A portfolio showcases past work, such as designs, projects or case studies, to demonstrate skill and credibility. A pitch deck argues for a future venture or project, asking the audience to invest, partner or award a prize. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and portfolio Portfolios support hiring or client decisions by showing what you have done; decks support investment decisions by showing what you will do and why it will succeed. A pitch deck may include a slide on past achievements, such as hackathon wins or shipped products, which works like a mini portfolio for the team. Keep portfolios visual and evidence-rich, and decks focused on a single persuasive story. Link to your portfolio from the deck for curious readers. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a treatment? A treatment is a prose summary of a film or television story, describing plot, characters and tone, used to pitch creative projects to producers. A pitch deck presents a business opportunity to investors with market, traction and financial information. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and treatment Film and TV pitches sometimes use decks too, called lookbooks or pitch decks, combining visuals, comparable titles and audience information with the treatment's story. Startups in media may need both: a treatment for the creative project and a business deck for the company producing it. Treatments emphasise storytelling quality, while business decks emphasise evidence of demand and a credible plan to make money. Know your audience's industry norms before preparing either. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a project report? A project report documents completed or ongoing work in detail, such as objectives, methods, results and conclusions, often for academic evaluation or stakeholders. A pitch deck persuades an audience to support what comes next. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and project report Students often turn final year project reports into pitch decks for hackathons or incubators, which requires cutting detail and reframing: problem, solution, proof, impact and ask. Reports should be thorough and accurate; decks should be concise and memorable. Keep the report as supporting evidence, sharing it when judges or investors ask for depth, and use appendices for technical details they may request. Mixing the two produces cluttered slides that lose the audience quickly. What is the difference between a pitch deck and a company profile? A company profile introduces an established business to customers, partners or suppliers, covering history, services, clients and credentials. A pitch deck targets investors or judges with a specific ask, such as funding, and argues for future growth. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and company profile Profiles are descriptive and credibility-focused, often used in sales and procurement, while decks are persuasive and opportunity-focused. A startup may maintain both: a profile for business development and a deck for fundraising. Avoid sending a company profile to investors, since it rarely answers their questions about market size, traction, unit economics and the use of funds. Tailor each document to the reader's decision. What is the difference between a pitch deck and an information memorandum? An information memorandum is a detailed, confidential document prepared for selling a company or raising significant capital, often by advisers, covering operations, financials, risks and market in depth. A pitch deck is a short introduction to spark interest. Also asked as: difference between pitch deck and information memorandum Investors typically see a teaser or deck first, sign a confidentiality agreement, then receive the information memorandum for due diligence. Memoranda can run to dozens of pages with audited financials and legal details. Early-stage startups rarely need one, while later-stage fundraising and acquisitions often do. Accuracy matters greatly, since memoranda inform major financial decisions and may carry legal responsibilities. Should a pitch deck be landscape or portrait? Landscape, almost always. Most decks use a 16:9 widescreen format because they are presented on screens and projectors and read on laptops. Portrait suits printed documents or mobile-first reading but looks awkward when presented. Send decks as PDFs so layouts stay consistent across devices. If many readers view your deck on phones, keep text large and slides simple so they remain readable when shrunk. Vertical formats can work for social media summaries of your pitch, but keep the main deck landscape. Test the deck on the actual projector or video call setup you will use, since aspect ratios sometimes differ. How do you build a great Series A pitch and deck? A Series A deck must prove the business works and can scale: strong traction such as revenue growth, retention and efficient customer acquisition, a large market, a repeatable go-to-market approach, a capable team, and a clear plan for using funds. Also asked as: how to build a great series a pitch and deck Lead with your strongest metrics and show trends over time, not just snapshots. Explain what you have learned since earlier funding and why now is the moment to scale. Present milestones the round will achieve, such as market expansion or product launches. Prepare a data room with financials, contracts and metrics definitions for due diligence. Warm introductions from trusted contacts improve response rates. Practise answering hard questions on churn, competition and margins confidently. How do you design a better pitch deck? Use one idea per slide, large readable fonts, consistent colours and typography, strong visuals such as product screenshots and simple charts, plenty of whitespace and a clear narrative from problem to ask. Also asked as: how to design a better pitch deck (2015 Label charts clearly and highlight the key takeaway in each slide's title, so readers grasp the point in seconds. Replace bullet-heavy slides with diagrams or a single bold statement. Use real product images and customer evidence instead of stock photos. Keep design consistent with your brand, and check contrast for readability. Templates help, but customise them to your story. Test with someone unfamiliar with your project; if they cannot explain your idea after viewing it, simplify.

# What is privacy and security? The difference, and what it means for AI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/privacy-and-security-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Privacy is about who is allowed to collect, see and use information about a person, and for what purpose. Security is the set of technical and organisational controls that keep information safe from people who are not allowed. They overlap but are not the same: a system can be very secure and still misuse your data. This page explains the difference, why both matter, what they mean for data, apps, social media and iPhones, how they apply to AI systems including inference attacks, and what the HIPAA privacy and security rules cover.

## What is privacy and security?

Privacy is a person's right to control how information about them is collected, used and shared. Security is the protection of information and systems against unauthorised access, change or loss.

Put simply, privacy answers "should this data be collected and used this way?", and security answers "is this data protected from those who should not have it?". A privacy decision is limiting a sign-up form to the fields you actually need. A security control is encrypting the database that stores those fields and requiring two-factor authentication for the admins. Good systems design both together: collect less, protect what you keep, and delete it when the purpose is over.

## Do privacy and security mean the same thing?

No. Security is about protection; privacy is about appropriate use. You can have security without privacy, but you cannot have privacy without security.

Two examples make the difference clear. A company that encrypts all its data perfectly but sells your browsing history to advertisers has strong security and poor privacy. A company with a strong privacy policy that leaves its database open on the internet has good intentions and no real privacy, because anyone can read the data. Security is necessary for privacy but not enough. Privacy adds questions security does not ask: do you have consent, is this the minimum data needed, how long will you keep it, and can the person see or delete it?

## Why is privacy and security important?

They protect people from harm such as fraud, identity theft, stalking, discrimination and embarrassment, and they protect organisations from breaches, fines and lost trust. Laws in most countries now require both.

For individuals, leaked phone numbers, ID details and passwords lead directly to scams and account takeovers. For organisations, a single breach can mean regulatory penalties, legal claims and customers who never return. For engineers, privacy and security are also design quality: systems that collect less data are simpler to secure and cheaper to run. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data, so these are now legal requirements, not just good practice.

## What is data privacy and security?

Data privacy is the set of rules and practices for handling personal data properly: consent, purpose, minimisation, retention and individual rights. Data security is the protection of that data through encryption, access control, monitoring and backups.

A practical checklist for any app that stores user data:

- Collect only the fields you need and record why you need each one.
- Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest in the database.
- Give each person and service the least access they need.
- Log access to sensitive data and review the logs.
- Set retention periods and actually delete old data.
- Let users see, correct and delete their data.

Most data breaches come from ordinary failures: weak passwords, exposed storage buckets and unpatched software.

## What is digital privacy and security?

Digital privacy and security is the same idea applied to your online life: controlling what your devices, apps and accounts reveal about you, and protecting them from being hacked or misused.

The basics give most of the protection. Use a password manager and unique passwords, turn on two-factor authentication for email and banking, keep your phone and laptop updated, and install apps only from official stores. Review app permissions for location, contacts, camera and microphone, and remove the ones an app does not need. Be careful with public Wi-Fi for sensitive accounts, and treat unexpected links in messages as suspicious, because phishing is still the most common way accounts are lost. Your email account is the master key to the rest, so protect it most.

## What is privacy and security in AI?

In AI, privacy means controlling what personal data goes into training, prompts, logs and outputs. Security means protecting models and AI apps from attacks such as prompt injection, data leakage and model theft.

AI adds new risks to old ones. Models can memorise and repeat training data. Users paste personal or confidential information into prompts that may be logged. Prompt injection can trick an AI app into revealing data or taking actions it should not. Good practice is to minimise personal data, mask it before it reaches a model, restrict what tools an AI agent can call, and review the OWASP list of risks for LLM applications. In FaceVision I designed for this: recognition runs in the browser and the server stores face embeddings only, never images.

## What is a privacy inference attack in AI security?

A privacy inference attack tries to learn private information from a trained model's outputs, for example whether a specific person's record was in the training data, or a sensitive attribute about them.

The main types:

- **Membership inference**: deciding whether a given record was used in training, often because models are more confident on data they have seen.
- **Attribute inference**: predicting a sensitive attribute, such as a health condition, from other known features.
- **Model inversion and data extraction**: reconstructing training examples, or getting a language model to repeat memorised text.

Defences include differential privacy during training, which adds calibrated noise so no single record changes the model much, limiting how much detail outputs reveal, removing duplicates and personal data from training sets, and testing models with these attacks before release.

## What is privacy and security in online social media?

On social media, privacy is about who can see your posts, profile and contacts, and what the platform does with your data. Security is about protecting your account from takeover and your information from scraping and scams.

Steps worth taking on every platform: review who can see your posts and contact you, turn off location tagging, hide your phone number and email from your profile, and enable two-factor authentication. Be careful what you share: your college, daily routine and photos of documents give attackers more than you think. Check which third-party apps are connected to your account and remove old ones. Remember that "private" posts can still be screenshotted, and that the platform itself sees everything you post.

## What is privacy and security on iPhone?

On iPhone, Privacy & Security is the section of Settings where you control which apps can access your location, contacts, photos, camera, microphone and other data, and where security features such as Safety Check and Lockdown Mode live.

Useful settings to review:

- **Location Services**: set apps to "While Using" or "Never", and turn off precise location where it is not needed.
- **Tracking**: refuse app tracking requests so apps cannot follow you across other apps.
- **Photos and contacts**: give limited access instead of full access.
- **Safety Check**: review and reset who has access to your information.
- **Lockdown Mode**: an extreme protection mode for people facing targeted attacks.

Keep iOS updated, because many updates fix actively exploited security flaws.

## What are the HIPAA privacy and security rules?

HIPAA is a United States law for health information. Its Privacy Rule sets when protected health information may be used or disclosed; its Security Rule sets the safeguards required to protect electronic health information.

The Privacy Rule covers patients' rights, such as access to their records, and limits on how hospitals, insurers and their partners share data. The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards: risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption where appropriate and staff training. A third piece, the Breach Notification Rule, requires notice when protected data is exposed. If you build a health app for US clients you will meet HIPAA. In India, health data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and sector rules, so check the requirements for each market you serve.

# How to make a professional GitHub profile: README templates, URL, privacy, avatar fixes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/professional-github-profile-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A professional GitHub profile shows who you are and what you build within seconds: a clear photo or avatar, a short bio, a profile README, and pinned repositories with good descriptions and demos. For students and developers, it often works as a second resume. I lead engineering at SCULT INDIA and mentor students who use GitHub as a portfolio, so this page covers building a professional profile, README templates and ideas, profile links, changing your URL, privacy, profile views and avatar questions.

## How do you make a professional GitHub profile?

Add a clear profile photo, your real name, a one-line bio with your focus, your location if comfortable, and links to your portfolio and LinkedIn. Then create a profile README and pin your six best repositories.

Each pinned repository should have a descriptive name, a one-line description, topics, a README with screenshots or a demo link, setup instructions and a licence. Remove or archive abandoned experiments from pins. Commit regularly to real projects rather than gaming the contribution graph. Recruiters spend seconds on a profile, so make the first screen tell a story: what you build, with which stack, and proof that it works, such as a live demo or meaningful stars and contributors.

## What is the best GitHub profile README template?

Good templates are simple: a one-line introduction, what you are working on, your main skills, two or three featured projects with links, and how to contact you. Collections such as awesome-github-profile-readme on GitHub offer many examples to adapt.

To create one, make a public repository named exactly as your username and add a README.md; GitHub shows it at the top of your profile. Popular add-ons include stats cards, language charts and activity widgets, but use them sparingly, since too many badges look cluttered and slow to load. Prefer real content: a short paragraph about your work, links to live demos, and recent writing. Update it whenever your focus changes.

## What are good GitHub profile ideas?

Ideas that stand out: a short story of what you build and why, a featured project section with demo GIFs, a now-learning section, recent blog posts pulled automatically, and a clear call to action, such as how to hire or collaborate with you.

Developers also use GitHub Actions to update their README automatically with latest posts, recent releases or stats. Designers create custom banners or SVG graphics that match their portfolio. Keep accessibility in mind: add alt text to images and avoid text embedded only in pictures. A clean, honest profile focused on shipped work beats a flashy one with animated widgets and dozens of skill icons for technologies you barely know.

## What does a GitHub profile and its link look like?

A GitHub profile page shows your avatar, name, username, bio and links on the left; your profile README at the top; pinned repositories; and a contribution graph showing activity over the past year. Its link is github.com followed by your username.

For example, a profile link has the form github.com/your-username, and a repository link adds the repository name after it. To copy your link on a laptop, open your profile in a browser and copy the address bar, or click your avatar, choose Your profile, and copy the URL. Below the pinned section, visitors also see achievements, organisations you belong to and followers, depending on your privacy settings.

## Can you change your GitHub profile URL?

Yes, by changing your username in Settings, under Account, Change username. Your profile URL changes to the new username immediately. GitHub redirects most repository links, but your old profile URL stops working.

Before changing: update links on your resume, LinkedIn, portfolio and package registries; check that the new username is available and professional; and remember that someone else can claim your old username later, which could break redirects if they create repositories with the same names. Update git remotes in local clones to the new URLs to avoid confusion. Changing usernames repeatedly hurts discoverability, so choose one you will keep for years.

## Can you make your GitHub profile private?

Yes. GitHub offers a private profile setting that hides most of your profile details and activity from other users, and you can separately hide private contribution counts from the contribution graph.

Public repositories you own still remain visible to everyone, so make repositories private individually if needed. Your username, avatar and public contributions to other projects can still appear in those projects. For job searching, a public, curated profile is usually more helpful than a hidden one. If privacy is the concern, use a separate account for personal experiments, keep your email private in settings, and use GitHub's noreply address for commits. Review these settings occasionally, since options evolve.

## Can you see who viewed your GitHub profile?

No. GitHub does not show who viewed your profile. Repository owners can see aggregate traffic for their repositories, including views, unique visitors, clones and referring sites, for the last 14 days, but not individual identities.

Find this under a repository's Insights tab, then Traffic. Third-party view counter badges in profile READMEs count visits but cannot identify viewers either, and they are easily inflated. Stars, forks, follows and issues are better signals of genuine interest. If you want to know whether recruiters engage, track clicks on links from your resume or portfolio with your own analytics instead. Focus on making the profile useful rather than tracking every visit.

## Does a GitHub profile picture matter?

It matters a little. A clear, friendly photo or consistent avatar makes your profile recognisable and trustworthy, especially to recruiters and collaborators. It will not replace good projects, but a missing or careless picture creates a weaker first impression.

For job seeking, use a clear headshot with good lighting, matching your LinkedIn photo so people connect your profiles. A tasteful illustrated avatar or logo works too, especially in open-source communities, as long as it is consistent across platforms. Avoid offensive images, low-resolution photos and default avatars on your main account. Your bio, pinned projects and README matter far more, so spend most of your effort there.

## How does GitHub generate default profile pictures?

GitHub generates default avatars called identicons: a symmetric, pixelated pattern in one colour, created from a hash of your user ID. Each account gets a unique, consistent pattern until you upload your own picture.

The pattern is drawn on a small grid, mirrored horizontally for symmetry, with its colour also derived from the hash, which is why identicons look like simple pixel art. GitHub introduced them in 2013 to replace a generic placeholder. Libraries in many languages generate similar identicons from strings, which is useful for your own apps. If you want a custom avatar that still feels techy, you can make pixel art or use your identicon as a starting point.

## Why is your GitHub profile picture not updating?

Usually caching. GitHub serves avatars through a content delivery network, and browsers cache images, so the old picture may appear for a while. Hard refresh, clear the cache or check in a private window.

If it still fails, check the upload: images must be under GitHub's file size limit, about 1 MB, in PNG, JPG or GIF format, and you must click Set new profile picture after cropping. Some places, such as old commits, emails, third-party sites and README badges, cache avatars longer. Commits show the avatar of the account linked to the commit email, so make sure your git email is verified on your account.

# Prompt caching explained: speed, Claude, Bedrock, KV cache, prefix caching, Claude Code
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-caching-claude-bedrock-kv-cache/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt caching stores the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix, such as a long system prompt, tool definitions or documents, so later requests reuse it instead of recomputing. It cuts latency and input costs substantially for repeated context. I build RAG applications such as RAG.NextUpgrad, where stable instructions precede changing questions, so this page covers speed, Claude and Bedrock setup, how caching works, KV caching, production use, Claude Code, prompt structure, paged attention and best practices. Does prompt caching speed up inference? Yes, for requests sharing a long identical prefix. Cached prefixes skip the expensive prefill computation, reducing time to first token noticeably, often dramatically for very long prompts, and lowering the cost of cached input tokens. The speedup applies to processing input, not generating output, so responses with long answers still take time to write. Gains are largest when the cached part is long, such as a large document or detailed system prompt, and the changing part is short, such as a user question. The first request writes the cache and may cost slightly more; later hits within the cache lifetime are faster and cheaper. Measure time to first token before and after enabling caching. How does prompt caching work in Claude? In the Claude API, you mark cache breakpoints with cache_control on content blocks, such as the end of your system prompt or a document. Claude caches everything up to each breakpoint, and later requests with the identical prefix read from the cache. You can set up to four breakpoints, and content must exceed a minimum length to be cached. The default cache lifetime is five minutes, refreshed each time it is used, with an optional longer lifetime at a higher write cost. Responses report cache creation and cache read tokens, so you can verify hits. Cache writes cost somewhat more than normal input, while cache reads cost much less, making repeated context far cheaper. How do you enable prompt caching in AWS Bedrock? Amazon Bedrock supports prompt caching for supported models, including Claude and Amazon Nova. In the Converse API, add cachePoint blocks after the content to cache; with Claude's native request format, use cache_control as in Anthropic's API. Also asked as: how to enable prompt caching in aws bedrock Check which models and regions support caching in Bedrock's documentation, since availability expands over time. Responses include cache read and write token counts for monitoring. The same principles apply: put stable content first, keep it identical across requests, and place cache points after large static sections such as system prompts, tool definitions and reference documents. Combine caching with Bedrock's cross-region inference and batch options for cost and throughput planning. How does prompt caching technically work? Transformers compute key and value tensors for every input token during the prefill phase. Prompt caching stores those tensors for a prompt prefix, keyed by its exact content, so a later request with the same prefix can reuse them and only compute the new tokens. Providers keep cached tensors in fast GPU or host memory for a limited time, evicting them when unused. Because attention for later tokens depends on everything before them, only identical prefixes can be reused; changing one early token invalidates everything after it. This is why caching works on prefixes, not arbitrary middle sections. Serving engines track cached blocks with hashes, matching new requests against stored prefixes efficiently. Is prompt caching the same as KV caching? They are related but different. KV caching reuses key and value tensors within a single request, so generating each new token does not recompute earlier tokens. Prompt caching persists those tensors across separate requests that share a prefix. Every modern inference engine uses KV caching during generation; without it, producing long outputs would be extremely slow. Prompt caching extends the idea across requests, conversations or users, storing the prefill results of common prefixes for reuse. In self-hosted engines, this is called prefix caching. Both trade memory for speed, and both depend on the fact that attention for a token only looks at earlier tokens. Understanding both helps you reason about latency. How usable is prompt caching in production? Very usable, and often one of the easiest cost and latency wins. It shines for long system prompts, tool definitions, large documents, few-shot examples and multi-turn conversations where earlier messages repeat in every request. Common pitfalls include dynamic content early in the prompt, such as timestamps or user names in the system prompt, which break cache hits; inconsistent tool ordering; and low traffic, where caches expire before reuse. Monitor cache hit rates through the usage fields in responses, and alert when they drop after code changes. For RAG, caching helps when the same documents are queried repeatedly, less so when every request retrieves different passages. Document caching assumptions so teammates do not break them accidentally. How do you enable prompt caching in Claude Code? Claude Code uses prompt caching automatically, caching its system prompt, tool definitions, project instructions and conversation history, which keeps long sessions faster and cheaper. You do not need to configure anything to benefit. Also asked as: how to enable prompt caching in claude code Caching is why keeping a stable CLAUDE.md file helps: unchanged instructions stay cached across turns, and smaller, focused instructions cache efficiently. Environment variables exist to disable caching for debugging, but leaving it on is recommended. Very long sessions eventually compact or clear history, which resets parts of the cache. If you build your own agents with the Claude Agent SDK, caching behaviour is handled similarly, but verify with usage data that cache reads appear as expected. How should you structure prompts to make the most of prompt caching? Put stable content first and changing content last: tool definitions, system instructions, reference documents and examples at the start, then conversation history, then the new user message. Keep the stable part byte-for-byte identical between requests. Also asked as: how to structure prompts to make the most of prompt caching Avoid timestamps, random IDs or per-user details in early sections; move them to the end. Keep tool lists in a fixed order. Place cache breakpoints after large stable sections, and in multi-turn chats, after the latest message so the growing history is reused. For RAG, put shared reference material before retrieved passages. Test by sending two identical requests and confirming the second reports cache reads rather than writes. How does prompt caching work with paged attention and prefix caching? PagedAttention, introduced by vLLM, stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like memory pages in an operating system. Automatic prefix caching hashes these blocks so requests sharing the same prefix reuse existing blocks instead of recomputing them. Also asked as: how prompt caching works: paged attention and prefix caching Block-based storage reduces memory waste and lets engines share common prefixes, such as a system prompt, across many concurrent requests. SGLang's RadixAttention organises cached prefixes in a radix tree for efficient matching. Self-hosted deployments gain the same benefits as provider prompt caching: faster time to first token and higher throughput. Memory limits determine how many prefixes stay cached at once. Enable prefix caching in your serving engine's settings, and structure prompts with shared stable prefixes to maximise reuse. What is prompt caching, and what are its best practices? Prompt caching is a technique where a model provider or serving engine reuses the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix across requests, cutting latency and input cost. Best practices centre on stable prefixes, monitoring and matching cache lifetimes to traffic. Also asked as: what is prompt caching? best practices explained Order prompts with stable content first, mark breakpoints where providers require them, and avoid dynamic values early in the prompt. Monitor cache read and write tokens to measure hit rates. Choose longer cache lifetimes for content reused less often, weighing their higher write cost. Combine caching with smaller models and focused retrieval for further savings. Providers differ: OpenAI caches automatically above a size threshold, while Claude uses explicit breakpoints.
