# Prompt caching explained: examples, KV vs prefix caching, OpenAI vs Claude, RAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-caching-kv-prefix-openai-claude/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt caching lets an LLM provider reuse work it already did on a repeated prompt prefix, such as a long system prompt, tool definitions or a document, so later requests are faster and cheaper. Every major provider now offers some form of it. I build RAG apps such as RAG.NextUpgrad that stream cited answers over long context, so this page covers how prompt caching works, an example, a tutorial, KV, prefix and context caching, implicit versus explicit caching, OpenAI versus Claude, RAG and best practices. What is prompt caching and how does it work? Prompt caching stores the model's processed state for the start of a prompt, its key and value tensors, so a later request beginning with exactly the same tokens skips recomputing them. You pay less for those tokens and get the first token sooner. Also asked as: prompt caching: a complete technical guide · prompt caching tutorial The match is a prefix match: the cache helps only up to the first token that differs, so anything that changes between requests should come last. Providers set a minimum cacheable length, often around a thousand tokens, and keep entries for a limited time, typically minutes, refreshed whenever they are used. Caches are scoped to your organisation, so other customers never read your prompts. The benefit grows with prompt length and repetition, which makes caching most valuable for chat assistants, agents with large tool lists and document question answering. What is an example of prompt caching? A support bot sends the same long system prompt and product manual with every user question. With caching, the first request processes and stores that shared prefix, and every later question within the cache lifetime reuses it, paying full rate only for the new question. Multi-turn chat is another example: each turn resends the whole conversation, so caching the history means each new turn processes only the latest messages. Coding agents such as Claude Code benefit heavily, since they resend large tool definitions, instructions and file contents on every step of a loop, so keeping that prefix stable across a session matters. In each case, the usage fields in the response report how many input tokens were read from cache, which confirms the cache is actually hitting. How do you set up prompt caching step by step? Order your prompt from most stable to most variable: tools, system instructions, reference documents, conversation history, then the new user message. Then enable caching for your provider and measure cache hits in the usage data. On OpenAI, caching is automatic for long prompts, so the work is mostly ordering and keeping prefixes identical. On Claude, add a cache_control breakpoint to the last block you want cached, such as the end of the system prompt or a document, and add further breakpoints for content that changes at different rates. On Gemini, rely on implicit caching or create an explicit cache with a time to live. Send two identical requests a few seconds apart and check the cached token count in the second response. If hits stay at zero, remove timestamps, random IDs and reordered tools from the prefix. What is the difference between KV caching and prompt caching? KV caching happens inside a single request: during generation, the model stores the key and value tensors of earlier tokens so each new token attends to them without recomputing. Prompt caching keeps those tensors for a prompt prefix across separate requests. Also asked as: kv caching vs prompt caching Every modern inference engine uses a KV cache; without it, generating each token would reprocess the entire sequence. Its size grows with context length and batch size, which is why long contexts consume so much GPU memory. Prompt caching builds on the same data: instead of discarding the KV cache when a request ends, the server keeps the prefix portion and reuses it when another request starts with the same tokens. So KV caching speeds up generation within one answer, while prompt caching speeds up the prefill stage across many answers. What is the difference between prefix caching and prompt caching? They are largely the same idea under different names. Prefix caching is the term inference engines such as vLLM and SGLang use, while prompt caching is the name API providers give the billed feature built on it. Also asked as: prefix caching vs prompt caching In vLLM, automatic prefix caching splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, as in PagedAttention, and hashes each block together with the tokens before it, so any new request sharing those blocks reuses them. SGLang's RadixAttention stores prefixes in a radix tree for similar sharing across many requests. Hosted APIs such as OpenAI and Anthropic expose the same mechanism with pricing, minimum lengths and expiry rules. If you self-host open models, enable prefix caching in your server; if you call an API, follow the provider's caching rules. What is the difference between context caching and prompt caching? Context caching is Google's name for prompt caching in the Gemini API and Vertex AI. It comes in two forms: implicit caching, applied automatically, and explicit caching, where you create a named cache of content and reference it in later requests. Also asked as: context caching vs prompt caching Explicit context caches have a time to live you choose and are billed for storage while they exist, in addition to discounted reads. That suits large, reused material, such as a long video, a codebase or a set of manuals that many queries will reference over an hour or a day. Implicit caching needs no setup but gives no guarantee of a hit. Functionally, both reuse processed tokens just like other providers' prompt caching; the differences lie in control, lifetime and how storage is charged. What is the difference between implicit and explicit prompt caching? Implicit caching is automatic: the provider detects repeated prefixes and discounts them without code changes. Explicit caching requires you to mark what to cache, such as Claude's cache_control breakpoints or Gemini's cache objects, giving more control over hits and lifetime. Also asked as: implicit vs explicit prompt caching OpenAI's caching is implicit, applying to prompts above a minimum length, and Gemini offers implicit caching on recent models. Anthropic's caching is explicit, with a five-minute default lifetime and a longer one-hour option. Implicit caching is easier but less predictable, since request routing and eviction decide whether you hit. Explicit caching lets you keep a large document cached through a busy period, at the cost of managing breakpoints and, for Gemini, paying storage. Choose based on how predictable your traffic is. How does OpenAI's prompt caching compare with Claude caching? OpenAI caches automatically for prompts above a minimum length, discounting cached input with no code changes. Claude requires explicit cache_control breakpoints, charges a little extra to write the cache, and gives a deeper discount on cache reads. Also asked as: openai&#x27;s prompt caching vs claude caching In practice, OpenAI is simpler: order prompts well and caching happens, though hits depend on routing, and a prompt_cache_key parameter can improve them for shared prefixes. Claude gives more control: you choose exactly where caches end, can set up to four breakpoints, and can pick a longer lifetime for infrequent traffic. Both report cached tokens in usage fields, and both require exact prefix matches. For apps that call several providers, such as RAG.NextUpgrad with its multi-provider fallback, one stable prompt layout lets caching work whichever provider answers. How does RAG compare with prompt caching? They solve different problems and work well together. RAG retrieves a few relevant passages per question from a large corpus, while prompt caching makes it cheaper to resend the same large context repeatedly. Also asked as: rag vs prompt caching If your knowledge fits in the context window and many questions hit the same material, such as one handbook, caching the whole document can replace retrieval and avoid missed chunks. For large or changing corpora, RAG is still required, since you cannot cache millions of documents in one prompt. Combining them is common: cache the system prompt, tool definitions and stable reference material, then append retrieved passages and the question at the end. Retrieved chunks vary by query, so placing them early breaks the prefix. In a pipeline with hybrid retrieval, reranking and cited streaming, the stable instructions are the cacheable part. What are prompt caching best practices? Put stable content first and variable content last, keep cached prefixes byte-for-byte identical, meet the minimum cacheable length, and monitor cache hit rates from usage fields. Small changes such as a timestamp at the top silently disable caching. Keep tool definitions in a fixed order and avoid editing system prompts mid-session. Put dates, user names and retrieved passages after the cached block. For explicit caching, place breakpoints where content changes rate, such as after tools and after a document. Choose cache lifetimes that match traffic, since a short lifetime with sparse requests means paying to write caches that expire unused. Track cached tokens, time to first token and cost per request, and alert when hit rates drop after a deploy. Treat prompt layout as part of your API contract.

# Prompt engineering for students: bias, ambiguity, techniques, GenAI, scope and clubs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-engineering-bias-students-techniques/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt engineering shapes how AI models respond, from reducing biased outputs to handling vague questions, and it is one of the most practical AI skills for students. I founded the TechVerse Enclave community, which has grown past 500 members, mentor students and use prompt design in products such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page covers bias, students and extracurriculars, ambiguous inputs, how many techniques exist, improving responses, generative AI, why it matters, jobs and scope, and what prompt engineering means. How does prompt engineering help with AI bias? Prompts can reduce biased outputs by instructing models to avoid stereotypes, use neutral language, consider diverse perspectives and base judgements only on relevant criteria. Anthropic researchers found in 2023 that such instructions reduced bias in large models on benchmarks. Prompting cannot remove bias embedded in training data, so combine it with evaluation and design choices. Test with counterfactual examples, swapping names, genders or regions while keeping everything else equal, and compare outputs. For high-stakes uses, such as hiring or lending, avoid letting models make final decisions, and audit results regularly. Diverse example sets in few-shot prompts also help, and diverse reviewers should judge outputs. Document known limitations so users understand residual risks. How can prompt engineering help you as a student? Good prompting turns AI into a tutor: ask for explanations at your level, step-by-step solutions after you try first, practice questions, feedback on essays and code reviews, while following your institution's rules on AI use. Effective student prompts include context, such as your course level and what you already understand, and ask the AI to check your reasoning rather than just give answers. Verify facts and citations, since models can be wrong. Use AI to plan study schedules, summarise readings you have actually read, and generate flashcards. Keep a prompt notebook for subjects you study often. The skill also helps in internships and projects, where clear instructions to AI tools save hours. Can you make prompt engineering an extracurricular activity? Yes. You can start or join an AI club, run workshops on prompting and AI tools, organise prompt challenges, build projects that use AI well, write about what you learn, and teach juniors, all of which strengthen your profile. Also asked as: can i make ai prompt engineering an extracurricular Make it concrete: a club that builds a campus assistant with RAG, a workshop series for non-technical students, or a blog comparing prompts on real tasks with measured results. Hackathons with AI themes give deadlines and visibility. Community building counts too; I founded TechVerse Enclave, which grew past 500 members, and that experience showed how much students gain from learning together. Record outcomes for your resume and portfolio. How does prompt engineering handle ambiguous inputs? Instruct the model to ask clarifying questions when a request is ambiguous, or to state its assumptions and offer options. Examples showing good clarifying behaviour help, and routing steps can detect vague requests before answering. In products, decide upfront which ambiguities justify a question and which can use sensible defaults, since too many questions frustrate users. For retrieval systems, rewriting vague queries into clearer search terms improves results. When evidence is insufficient, declining is better than guessing; RAG.NextUpgrad's confidence gate declines when retrieved evidence is weak. Test prompts with deliberately ambiguous inputs to see how the model behaves, and refine instructions until responses are consistently sensible. How many prompt engineering techniques are there? There is no fixed number. The Prompt Report, a 2024 survey by Schulhoff and colleagues, catalogued 58 text-based prompting techniques, plus others for multimodal and agent settings, and new techniques continue to appear. In practice, a handful cover most needs: clear instructions, role or system prompts, few-shot examples, step-by-step reasoning, structured outputs, prompt chaining, retrieval grounding and self-checking. Many named techniques are variations of these. Learn the core set deeply and test variants on your own tasks rather than memorising lists. Modern reasoning models handle some techniques internally, such as thinking step by step, which reduces the need for manual tricks. How does prompt engineering improve AI responses? It improves responses by giving models clear goals, relevant context, examples of desired output, explicit formats and constraints, which reduces guessing and makes answers more accurate, consistent and useful. Breaking complex tasks into steps, asking the model to cite sources from provided documents, and adding a self-check step further improve quality. Specifying audience and tone makes outputs fit their purpose. Structured outputs, such as JSON, make responses usable by software, especially when validated in code, as DocuLens AI does. Small wording changes can matter, so test them. The improvement should be measured: compare outputs on a test set before and after changes, keeping only changes that help. What is the difference between generative AI and prompt engineering? Generative AI is the technology: models that create text, images, audio or code. Prompt engineering is the skill of instructing those models effectively. One is the tool; the other is how you get good results from it. Also asked as: difference between genai and prompt engineering Generative AI includes the models, their training and the products built on them, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and image generators. Prompt engineering applies across all of them, adapting to each model's strengths. Better models reduce the need for elaborate prompts, but clear communication of goals, context and quality standards remains essential. Practising with several tools builds flexible skills. Learning prompt engineering is one of the fastest ways to get practical value from generative AI. Why does prompt engineering matter in the AI era? As AI becomes part of everyday work, the ability to communicate goals, context and standards to AI systems determines how much value people get from them. Clear prompts produce reliable results; vague prompts waste time and introduce errors. Organisations depend on prompts inside products, from support assistants to document extraction, so prompt quality affects customers directly. Prompting also matters for safety, reducing harmful outputs and resisting prompt injection. The skill is evolving into context engineering and evaluation, but its core, precise thinking about what you want, transfers to every AI tool. Students who master it early gain an advantage in studies, internships and careers. What is prompt engineering, and what are its jobs and scope? Prompt engineering is the practice of designing instructions and context for AI models. Its job scope now sits mostly inside broader roles, such as AI engineer, content strategist, product manager, educator and analyst, rather than standalone prompt engineer titles. Also asked as: what is prompt engineering (jobs, scope and salary The scope is wide: anyone using AI at work benefits from prompting skills, and technical roles combine them with retrieval, evaluation and software engineering. Demand is strongest for people who can build reliable AI features and measure their quality. Writing, teaching and domain expertise pair especially well with prompting. Compensation varies widely by role, company and location, so focus on building demonstrable skills and portfolio projects rather than chasing a job title that may be short-lived. What is prompt engineering in the context of AI? In AI, prompt engineering is the process of crafting the inputs given to models, including instructions, context, examples and formatting, to obtain accurate, relevant and safe outputs without changing the model itself. It applies to language models, image generators and multimodal systems. Prompts can be single questions, detailed system instructions, templates filled with retrieved documents, or tool descriptions for agents. Unlike training or fine-tuning, which change model weights, prompting changes behaviour instantly and cheaply, making it the first tool to try. Effective prompt engineering is iterative and evidence-based, testing prompts on realistic inputs and refining them based on observed failures. In production, prompts should be versioned like code.

# Prompt engineering careers: degrees, jobs, earning, AI replacement, getting started
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-engineering-careers-degree-jobs/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt engineering is the skill of instructing AI models to produce reliable, useful results, and it has become a core part of building with AI rather than a standalone career for most people. You do not need a degree to learn it. I use prompt design daily in products such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI and mentor students learning AI, so this page covers degrees, jobs, earning, whether AI will replace prompting, getting started, what it entails, its purpose and how it relates to LLMs. Does prompt engineering require a degree? No. Prompt engineering is learned through practice, not formal qualifications. Anyone who writes clearly, understands a domain and tests systematically can become good at it, whether they studied computer science, literature or business. A degree helps for roles that combine prompting with software engineering, such as AI engineer, where you also need programming, APIs and evaluation skills. For content, research, operations or product roles, domain expertise plus strong prompting skills often matter more than a specific degree. Many skilled prompt engineers are self-taught. Build proof instead: a portfolio of prompts with test cases, before-and-after results and a small application where prompts power a real feature. Can you get a degree in prompt engineering? Standalone degrees in prompt engineering are rare. Universities instead teach it within AI, computer science or digital skills programmes, while online courses and certificates from institutions such as Vanderbilt on Coursera, DeepLearning.AI and AI labs cover it directly. Because the field changes quickly, short courses and hands-on practice often teach more current techniques than long degree programmes. A broader degree in computer science, data science or a domain such as law or healthcare, combined with prompting skills, offers more lasting value. Be cautious of expensive programmes promising prompt engineering careers; check their curriculum, instructors and graduate outcomes against free official resources first. How many prompt engineering jobs are there? Dedicated prompt engineer job titles are relatively few and peaked in popularity around 2023. Far more jobs list prompting as a required skill within roles such as AI engineer, ML engineer, content strategist, product manager and data analyst. As models improved at understanding plain instructions, standalone prompt roles merged into broader positions that combine prompting with evaluation, software engineering, domain expertise or product thinking. Job boards show steady demand for AI engineers who can design prompts, build retrieval systems and measure quality. Read job descriptions closely to see which skills employers actually want. Treat prompt engineering as a skill that multiplies your value in a role, not as a complete career by itself. How can you make money with prompt engineering? The most reliable ways combine prompting with other skills: building AI-powered features or products, automating workflows for businesses as a freelancer or consultant, creating educational content, and helping teams improve AI quality through evaluation. Also asked as: how to make money with prompt engineering Small businesses pay for practical results, such as automating customer replies, drafting product descriptions or summarising documents, more than for prompts themselves. Selling individual prompts on marketplaces rarely earns much, since good prompts are easy to replicate. Avoid schemes promising passive income from prompts. Build a portfolio showing measurable outcomes, such as time saved or accuracy improved, and pair prompting with tools such as n8n, APIs or no-code builders. Will prompt engineering be replaced by AI? Partly. Models increasingly understand plain requests, and tools such as DSPy and built-in prompt improvers optimise prompts automatically. But the core skill, clearly specifying goals, context and quality standards, and testing results, remains essential and is evolving into context engineering. Tricks such as magic phrases matter less with each model generation, while system design matters more: what information the model receives, which tools it can use, how outputs are validated and how quality is measured. In RAG.NextUpgrad, for example, retrieval quality and the confidence gate shape answers as much as prompt wording. People who communicate precisely and evaluate rigorously will stay valuable as tools automate the mechanical parts. How do you get started with prompt engineering? Read the official prompting guides from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, then practise on real tasks from your studies or work. Write clear instructions with context, examples and output formats, and compare results as you change one thing at a time. Also asked as: how to get started with prompt engineering Next, build a small test set of ten to twenty inputs with expected outputs, so you can measure improvements rather than judging by feel. Try structured outputs, prompt chaining and retrieval grounding. Then use an API to build a simple application, which teaches system prompts, parameters and error handling. Keep a prompt library documenting what worked and why. Free courses from DeepLearning.AI and Anthropic's GitHub tutorials provide guided exercises. What does prompt engineering entail in AI? Prompt engineering entails designing instructions, providing context and examples, specifying output formats, testing prompts against representative inputs, analysing failures, iterating, and guarding against misuse such as prompt injection. In products, it also involves managing system prompts, tool descriptions and retrieved context, versioning prompts like code, and monitoring quality after deployment as models change. For example, DocuLens AI combines prompts that request structured fields with schema validation in code, so failures are caught rather than trusted. The work is iterative and empirical: hypotheses about wording or structure are tested on data, and only changes that measurably improve results are kept. Collaboration with domain experts improves prompts significantly. What is the purpose of prompt engineering? The purpose is to get reliable, accurate, useful and safe outputs from AI models for a specific task, with less trial and error, lower cost and consistent behaviour across many inputs and users. Without careful prompting, models may misunderstand tasks, ignore constraints, produce inconsistent formats or invent information. Good prompting aligns model behaviour with goals: answering only from provided sources, following a brand voice, producing valid JSON or refusing out-of-scope requests. It also reduces costs by enabling smaller models to perform well, and makes outputs easier to review and audit. Ultimately, prompt engineering translates human intent into instructions a model can follow dependably. What should you know about prompt engineering? Know that models are probabilistic, so the same prompt can produce different outputs; that specificity, context and examples matter most; that different models respond differently; and that only testing on real inputs reveals whether a prompt works. Also asked as: what should i know about prompt engineering Also know the limits: prompts cannot reliably add knowledge a model lacks, so use retrieval for facts; they cannot guarantee formats, so validate outputs in code; and they can be undermined by prompt injection from untrusted content. Keep prompts versioned, documented and retested after model updates. Prompting skills transfer across tools, so investing in clear thinking and evaluation pays off regardless of which AI provider dominates next year. What is the difference between prompt engineering and an LLM? An LLM is a large language model, the AI system that generates text. Prompt engineering is the practice of writing instructions and context that guide an LLM to produce the outputs you want. One is the tool; the other is the skill of using it. Also asked as: difference between prompt engineering and llm Changing the prompt changes behaviour without changing the model, while training or fine-tuning changes the model itself. The same LLM can act as a tutor, coder or analyst depending on its prompts. Prompt engineering applies to image and audio models too, not just LLMs. Understanding how LLMs work, such as tokens, context windows and sampling, makes prompt engineering more effective, since you know why certain instructions help.

# Prompt engineering: certificates, courses, roadmap, techniques, tools and image prompts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-engineering-courses-techniques/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and testing instructions so language and image models produce reliable results. Courses and certificates help you start, but skill comes from building test sets and iterating on real tasks. I build AI products such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, where prompts drive grounded answers and schema-validated extraction, so this page covers certifications, Udemy and YouTube courses, a beginner roadmap, techniques and examples, blind prompting, RAG and fine-tuning, toolkits and image prompting. What is the best prompt engineering certification? Well-regarded options include Vanderbilt University's Prompt Engineering for ChatGPT and Google's Prompting Essentials on Coursera, DeepLearning.AI's ChatGPT Prompt Engineering for Developers, and free courses from Anthropic and Microsoft Learn. Also asked as: example of prompt engineering toolkit or library Certificates show initiative, but employers rarely hire for prompt engineering alone; they value it as part of building AI products. Choose a certification that includes hands-on exercises with APIs, structured outputs and evaluation, not only chat tips. Complement it with a portfolio: a set of prompts with test cases and measured improvements, or an application where prompts power a real feature. Check each provider's current course list, since offerings change frequently. What is the best prompt engineering course on Udemy? Udemy offers many prompt engineering courses; the best are recently updated, cover current models from several providers, include API exercises and evaluation, and come from instructors with real product experience. Check previews, update dates and recent reviews. Also asked as: best prompt engineering course in udemy Avoid courses built around prompt templates that promise passive income or guaranteed results, and courses tied to a single outdated model version. Look for coverage of system prompts, few-shot examples, structured outputs, tool use, RAG and testing prompts systematically. Since free official guides from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google cover much of the same ground, use paid courses mainly for structure, projects and a teaching style you like. Courses frequently go on sale, so compare before enrolling. What is the best prompt engineering course on YouTube? Strong free options include DeepLearning.AI's videos and short course recordings, Anthropic's talks and prompt engineering sessions, Google's prompting tutorials, and conference talks on building with LLMs. Andrej Karpathy's videos explain how LLMs work, which improves prompting intuition. Choose videos that show prompts being tested and improved on real tasks rather than lists of magic phrases. Model behaviour changes with each release, so prefer recent content and verify techniques on the model you use. Pair videos with official documentation and the interactive prompt engineering tutorial Anthropic publishes on GitHub. Practise immediately after each video by applying the technique to a task from your own work or studies. What is a prompt engineering roadmap for beginners? Start by understanding how LLMs work: tokens, context windows and sampling. Then learn clear instructions, roles, examples, structured outputs and step-by-step reasoning, followed by prompt chaining, retrieval grounding, tool use and systematic evaluation. A four-week plan: week one, read the official prompting guides from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google and practise clear instructions; week two, few-shot examples, XML or JSON structure and output validation; week three, chaining prompts and grounding answers in documents; week four, build a test set of twenty or more cases and measure improvements. Then build a small application through an API, since production prompting involves code, logging and error handling. What are examples of prompt engineering techniques? Core techniques include zero-shot instructions, few-shot examples, role or system prompts, chain-of-thought reasoning, structured output with XML tags or JSON schemas, prompt chaining, retrieval-augmented prompting, self-consistency and ReAct-style tool use. Each solves a specific problem. Few-shot examples teach format and tone. Chain-of-thought improves multi-step reasoning, though modern reasoning models often think internally. XML tags separate instructions from documents, reducing confusion and injection risk. Prompt chaining splits complex tasks into reliable steps. Retrieval grounding supplies facts and citations, as in RAG.NextUpgrad. Schema-constrained outputs make responses machine-readable, as in DocuLens AI's validated extraction. Choose techniques based on the failure you observe. What are examples of effective prompt engineering? Effective prompts state the goal, audience, context, constraints and output format. For example: You are reviewing a pull request for security issues. Read the diff inside the diff tags. List each issue with file, line, severity and fix, or say none found. Other effective patterns: giving the model permission to say it does not know, which reduces hallucination; providing two or three diverse examples of desired output; asking for a plan before a long piece of writing; and splitting extraction from summarisation into separate steps. In RAG.NextUpgrad, instructions to answer only from retrieved passages, cite them and decline when evidence is weak, combined with a confidence gate, keep answers grounded. Effectiveness is proven by tests, not by how clever a prompt looks. Prompt engineering vs blind prompting: what is the difference? Blind prompting is trial and error: tweaking prompts until one output looks right, without systematic testing. Prompt engineering defines the task, builds a test set of inputs with expected outputs, measures accuracy, and iterates based on evidence. The distinction was popularised by Mitchell Hashimoto's essay Prompt Engineering vs. Blind Prompting, which argued that prompts deserve the same rigour as code. Blind prompting fails silently: a prompt that works on three examples may fail on the fourth in production. Engineering prompts means versioning them, measuring results across many cases, comparing alternatives and checking cost and latency. Tools such as promptfoo and evaluation datasets make this practical even for small teams. Prompt engineering vs fine-tuning vs RAG: which should you use? Use prompt engineering first for behaviour and format, RAG when answers need private or changing knowledge, and fine-tuning when you need consistent style, a narrow skill or a smaller, cheaper model. Many systems combine all three. Also asked as: prompt engineering vs. finetuning vs. rag Prompting is fastest to change and cheap to try. RAG supplies facts at query time with citations, keeping knowledge current without retraining, which is why RAG.NextUpgrad retrieves before answering. Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour permanently and suits stable, high-volume tasks, as FineTune Studio's QLoRA workflow demonstrates. Fine-tuning does not reliably teach new facts, so avoid it for knowledge that changes. Evaluate each option on the same test set before investing time and compute. What are examples of prompt engineering toolkits or libraries? Examples include DSPy, which optimises prompts programmatically; LangChain prompt templates; Microsoft's Guidance for constrained generation; promptfoo for testing and comparing prompts; and prompt tools in the Anthropic Console and OpenAI Playground for drafting and improving prompts. Evaluation and tracking tools, such as LangSmith, Langfuse and OpenAI Evals, store prompt versions and measure results over datasets. Structured output libraries such as Instructor and Pydantic validate responses against schemas. Templating with Jinja keeps prompts readable and reusable in code. For most projects, start simply: store prompts in version control, write tests with expected outputs, and add a framework only when it clearly saves time. What is a good prompt engineering guide for DALL-E 2? For DALL-E 2, effective prompts described the subject, setting, style, medium, lighting, colour palette, composition and camera details, such as a watercolour painting of a lighthouse at sunset, wide angle, soft pastel colours. The DALL-E 2 Prompt Book compiled many examples. Also asked as: a prompt engineering guide for dalle-2 DALL-E 2 has since been replaced by newer OpenAI image models in ChatGPT, which understand longer, conversational prompts and render text more accurately. The same principles still apply across image generators such as Midjourney, Imagen and Stable Diffusion: be specific about subject and style, reference art movements or photography terms, iterate on one element at a time, and use editing tools for details. Avoid prompts depicting real people without consent or closely copying living artists' styles.

# Does prompt engineering have a future? Is it dead, a real job, hard or worth learning?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-engineering-future/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Prompt engineering has a future, but not mainly as a standalone job title: it is becoming a core skill inside AI engineering, product and everyday knowledge work, and it is evolving into context engineering, designing everything a model sees, not just the wording. I write prompts, retrieval context and evaluations for products such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, so this page covers whether it is dead, a real job, in demand, hard or easy, worth learning, its history, IBM's definition and how to master it.

## Does prompt engineering have a future?

Yes, as a skill rather than a job title. Models follow instructions better every year, so tricks matter less, but clear task design, context selection, examples, output formats and evaluation still decide whether an AI feature works.

The work is shifting from clever phrasing to systems: choosing what context to retrieve, how to structure tool definitions, how to make outputs machine-checkable, and how to test prompts against real cases. That is why many people now call it context engineering. Developers, product managers, analysts, teachers and writers all benefit from it. Anyone building AI products will keep writing and refining prompts, just with better tooling, version control and evaluation around them, so the skill compounds rather than expires.

## Is prompt engineering dead?

Headlines saying prompt engineering is dead usually mean that magic phrases and long trick prompts matter less, because newer models understand plain instructions and can even improve prompts themselves. That part is true.

What is not dead is the underlying discipline: specifying tasks precisely, giving the right context, defining output schemas, handling edge cases and measuring results. Poor prompts still produce vague, inconsistent or unsafe outputs, and automated prompt optimisers such as DSPy still need a clear objective and test data from humans. The standalone prompt engineer role has mostly merged into AI engineer and applied AI roles, but the skill itself is used more widely than ever, by far more people than in 2023.

## Is prompt engineering a real job?

It was briefly a distinct job title during the 2023 boom, and some companies still hire for it, especially in AI labs, content and evaluation teams. Today most of this work sits inside broader roles.

Common titles that include prompt work are AI engineer, applied AI engineer, LLM engineer, AI product manager, conversation designer and AI trainer or evaluator. These roles combine prompting with coding, retrieval, evaluation, data work or domain expertise. If you want a career, treat prompt engineering as one strong skill on top of a foundation such as software engineering, data analysis, writing or a domain like law or healthcare, rather than as a complete profession on its own.

## Is prompt engineering in demand?

The skill is in high demand; the standalone title is less so. Job descriptions for AI engineers, analysts, marketers and product roles increasingly list prompt design, LLM evaluation or experience with AI tools as requirements.

Employers want people who can turn a business problem into a reliable AI workflow: write instructions, build retrieval, test outputs and catch failures. Pure prompt writing without technical or domain depth is easy to replace, because tools and models keep improving. The strongest demand is in applied AI roles, where prompting combines with Python, APIs, RAG and evaluation. Show this skill with portfolio projects that include before-and-after results, not just certificates, so employers can see the improvement you produced.

## Is prompt engineering hard?

Basic prompting is easy: anyone can learn to give clear instructions, context and examples in an afternoon. Doing it reliably for production systems is hard, because you must handle edge cases, inconsistent outputs and changing models.

The hard parts are measurable quality and robustness: a prompt that works on five examples may fail on the fiftieth. Production prompting means building test sets, defining success criteria, checking structured outputs, defending against prompt injection, and re-testing when you switch models. It also requires understanding the domain well enough to spot wrong answers. So it is easy to start and hard to master, like writing or programming, and the gap is closed by systematic testing rather than intuition alone.

## Is prompt engineering a skill?

Yes. It is the skill of communicating tasks to AI models clearly enough that they produce useful, consistent results, combining writing, logical thinking, domain knowledge and testing.

Like any skill, it improves with deliberate practice: you learn which instructions models follow, how examples shape output, when to break tasks into steps, and how to give models a way to say they are unsure. Good prompt engineers think like teachers writing an exam brief: specify the goal, the audience, constraints, format and what to avoid. For most beginners, the biggest jump comes from giving context and examples instead of one-line requests, and from reading outputs critically instead of accepting the first answer.

## Is prompt engineering worth it?

Learning it is worth it for almost everyone who uses AI, because a few hours of practice make AI tools far more useful. Building a career only on prompting is riskier than combining it with technical or domain skills.

For students, I recommend learning prompting alongside programming: build a small app that calls a model API, add structured output, retrieval and evaluation, and you will learn prompting in its real context. For professionals, apply it to your daily work, such as drafting, analysis or code review, and keep a library of prompts that work. Skip expensive courses that promise jobs from prompting alone; free official guides from model providers cover the essentials.

## When did prompt engineering start?

Prompt engineering became a recognised practice around 2020 and 2021, after OpenAI's GPT-3 paper showed that large models could perform new tasks from instructions and a few examples in the prompt, known as few-shot learning.

Earlier work on templates for language models and question answering existed, but GPT-3 made prompting the main way to use a model. Research then added techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting in 2022, which asks models to reason step by step. ChatGPT's launch in late 2022 brought prompting to the public, and the 2023 boom created prompt engineer job titles. Since then, practice has moved toward system prompts, tool use, structured outputs and context engineering.

## What is prompt engineering according to IBM?

IBM describes prompt engineering as the process of designing and refining inputs to guide generative AI models toward desired outputs. Its explainers cover techniques such as zero-shot and few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought and role prompting.

IBM's material also places prompting within enterprise AI practice, alongside governance, model choice and evaluation, which reflects how companies actually use it: prompts are assets to be versioned, tested and reviewed. The definition matches those from model providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, whose prompting guides go deeper into practical techniques. Use IBM's explainer for a clear conceptual overview, then move to provider guides and hands-on practice for the details that change with each model.

## How do you master prompt engineering?

Learn the fundamentals from official provider guides, then practise on real tasks with measurement: write a prompt, test it on a set of examples, analyse failures, and revise. Mastery comes from this loop, not from memorising templates.

A practical path:

- **Fundamentals**: clear instructions, context, examples and output formats.
- **Structure**: system prompts, delimiters, step-by-step tasks and structured outputs.
- **Systems**: retrieval, tool calling, agents and prompt injection defences.
- **Evaluation**: test sets, rubrics, automated checks and model comparisons.
- **Practice**: build two projects and document what changed between prompt versions.

Read prompts from open-source projects and compare how different models respond to the same instructions, since that teaches you which habits transfer.

# Prompt engineering vs fine-tuning: differences, why prompts matter, MCP, and courses
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-engineering-vs-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Prompt engineering and fine-tuning both shape what a language model produces, at different levels. Prompt engineering changes what you send the model, instructions, examples and context, without altering the model. Fine-tuning changes the model itself by training its weights on examples. Prompting is fast and cheap to iterate; fine-tuning gives consistent behaviour at scale. I do both: production prompts in RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, and QLoRA fine-tuning in FineTune Studio, so this page covers the differences, developer practice, MCP and learning resources.

## How is prompt engineering different from fine-tuning?

Prompt engineering designs the input: role, instructions, examples, retrieved context and output format. Fine-tuning trains the model on many input and output examples so the behaviour is built in. Prompting changes in minutes; fine-tuning needs data, training runs and evaluation.

Rules of thumb:

- **Knowledge that changes**: use retrieval with prompts, not fine-tuning.
- **Format, tone or narrow task behaviour at scale**: fine-tuning helps.
- **Quick experiments and broad tasks**: prompting first.
- **Cost at high volume**: a fine-tuned small model can replace a large prompted one.

In FineTune Studio, comparing the base model with a good prompt against the tuned model is the first test, since a strong prompt sometimes makes fine-tuning unnecessary.

## What is the difference between generative AI and prompt engineering?

Generative AI is the technology: models that create text, images, audio, video and code. Prompt engineering is a skill for using those models well: writing inputs that produce accurate, useful outputs.

Prompt engineering applies to all generative models, including image models, where prompts describe subject, style, composition and lighting. It is one part of building with generative AI, alongside retrieval, tool integration, evaluation, safety and deployment. Knowing prompt engineering without understanding these other parts limits what you can build; understanding generative AI without prompting skill limits how well it works.

## How should a developer understand LLM prompt engineering?

Treat prompts as code: they are specifications that the model executes probabilistically. Version them in git, test them against a fixed set of inputs, review changes, and measure quality before deploying, just like any code change.

Developer practices: separate the stable system prompt from per-request data; use clear structure, such as XML tags or headings, to delimit instructions and documents; ask for structured output and validate it with a schema; give examples of edge cases; and explain the reasons behind rules, which models follow better than bare commands. Log prompts and outputs in production so you can debug failures. Small wording changes can have large effects, so automated evaluation is essential.

## How does prompt engineering make LLMs more effective?

Good prompts give the model the context and constraints it needs: who the audience is, what success looks like, which sources to use, what format to return and what to do when information is missing. This reduces vague, wrong or inconsistent answers.

Techniques that help: specifying a role and goal; providing examples; asking the model to reason before answering on complex tasks; breaking large tasks into steps or chained prompts; grounding answers in retrieved documents with citation rules; and allowing "I don't know". In RAG.NextUpgrad, the prompt's rule to answer only from retrieved passages and cite them, combined with a confidence gate, is a major reason answers stay grounded.

## Why is prompt engineering critical in AI development?

Because the same model can be excellent or useless depending on how it is instructed. Prompts define product behaviour, safety boundaries and output formats, and changing them is the fastest lever for improving quality before considering model changes or fine-tuning.

Prompts also encode business rules: what an assistant may discuss, how it handles personal data, when it escalates to humans. Poor prompts cause hallucinations, inconsistent formats that break downstream code, and policy violations. Because prompts are cheap to change, teams that test them systematically improve quickly. In model development itself, prompts drive evaluation, synthetic data generation and red-teaming.

## Is prompt engineering being replaced in software?

The narrow idea of clever prompt tricks is fading, because newer models follow plain instructions well and tools optimise prompts automatically. But the underlying skill, giving models the right context, instructions and tools, is growing into context engineering and agent design.

Developers now spend less time on wording hacks and more on: what information to retrieve and include, how to structure tools, how to evaluate outputs, and how to manage memory in long-running agents. Prompt optimisation frameworks automate some tuning against metrics. So job titles like "prompt engineer" are less common, while prompting skill has become a standard part of software engineering with AI.

## What is the difference between MCP and prompt engineering?

The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is a standard for connecting AI models to tools and data sources, such as files, databases and business apps. Prompt engineering is writing the instructions and context that guide the model's behaviour. They complement each other.

MCP gives the model capabilities: a server exposes tools like "search tickets" or "read file" with descriptions and schemas. Prompt engineering, including well-written tool descriptions, tells the model when and how to use those tools, how to combine results and what to return. Good tool descriptions are themselves a form of prompt engineering, and they strongly affect how reliably agents choose the right tool.

## Is there an Anthropic prompt engineering tutorial?

Yes. Anthropic publishes a free interactive prompt engineering tutorial on GitHub, with chapters and exercises covering clear instructions, roles, separating data from instructions, output formatting, step-by-step thinking, examples, avoiding hallucinations and building complex prompts.

Anthropic's documentation also has a prompt engineering guide with techniques such as using XML tags, giving Claude a role, chaining prompts and long-context tips, plus a prompt generator and improver in its developer console. Work through the exercises with real tasks from your projects. The principles apply to other models too, though details such as formatting preferences differ slightly between providers.

## What is a free prompt engineering course for beginners?

Good free options include DeepLearning.AI's short course on prompt engineering for developers, Anthropic's interactive tutorial, OpenAI's and Google's prompt engineering guides, and Microsoft Learn's generative AI modules. Each takes a few hours.

A beginner plan:

- Learn the basics: clear instructions, examples, roles and formats.
- Practise on everyday tasks: summarising, rewriting, extracting data.
- Learn structured output and validation for developer use.
- Build a small app, such as an email classifier, with a test set.
- Compare prompts systematically rather than by feel.

Practice on real tasks teaches more than collecting prompt templates.

## Is there a prompt engineering guide PDF?

Yes. Google published a widely shared prompt engineering whitepaper in 2025 as a PDF, and providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic maintain detailed web guides that you can save as PDFs. Many university and company guides are also available.

Web guides are usually more current than PDFs, since model behaviour and recommended techniques change. Save the guide for the model you actually use, because each provider documents its own best practices, such as Anthropic's emphasis on XML structure or OpenAI's on developer messages. Pair any guide with experiments: run the same task with different prompts and compare results on a fixed set of examples.

# Prompt injection explained: attacks, examples, origin, prevention, resistance, resumes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/prompt-injection-attacks-prevention/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Prompt injection is an attack where text in a model's input tricks it into ignoring its instructions, and it is the top security risk for applications built on language models, especially agents that read untrusted content and take actions. I build AI products where untrusted documents meet models, such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, so this page covers what prompt injection means, how attacks work, types and examples, who coined the term, vulnerability status, prevention, resistance, why it persists and resume tricks. What does prompt injection mean in AI? Prompt injection is when attacker-controlled text in a model's input overrides or subverts the developer's instructions, making the model ignore rules, leak information or take unintended actions. The name echoes SQL injection, where data is mistaken for commands. It happens because language models read instructions and data in the same stream of text and cannot reliably tell them apart. Direct injection comes from a user typing malicious instructions; indirect injection hides instructions in content the model processes, such as web pages, emails or documents. Risk grows with capability: a chatbot can only say wrong things, while an agent with tools can send emails or change data. Every LLM application that reads untrusted text should consider it. How does a prompt injection attack work? The attacker places instructions where the model will read them, such as in a message, a web page, a PDF or an email, phrased to look authoritative, for example claiming to be a system update or urging the model to ignore earlier instructions. Also asked as: how does prompt injection attack work When the application feeds this content to the model alongside its own instructions, the model may follow the injected text. In agents, the injected instructions might direct the model to call tools, such as sending data to an attacker's address or approving a transaction. Hidden text, such as white text on white backgrounds or content in metadata, makes injections invisible to human reviewers while remaining visible to the model. What are the main types of AI prompt injection attacks? Main types are direct injection, where users type override instructions; indirect injection, hidden in external content the model reads; jailbreaks, which aim to bypass safety rules; and data exfiltration attacks, which trick models into leaking secrets or private data. Also asked as: what are ai prompt injection attacks Indirect injection is especially dangerous for agents and RAG systems, since attackers do not need access to the conversation; planting text in a web page or shared document is enough. Other variants include multi-step attacks that gradually shift behaviour, injections in images or audio for multimodal models, and attacks on tool descriptions in connected servers. Research by Greshake and colleagues in 2023 highlighted indirect injection risks in integrated applications. What does prompt injection look like? Examples include a web page with hidden text telling an assistant to praise a product, an email instructing an AI to forward the inbox to an outside address, or a document saying to ignore previous instructions and reveal the system prompt. Other examples: a support chat user claiming to be an administrator who needs refunds approved, a calendar invite containing instructions for an assistant, or code comments telling a coding agent to add a hidden backdoor. Injections often use urgency, fake authority or formatting that mimics system messages. Recognising these patterns helps developers design tests and helps users spot when an AI's behaviour has been hijacked. Who coined the term prompt injection? Simon Willison coined the term prompt injection in September 2022, comparing it to SQL injection, after Riley Goodside publicly demonstrated that instructions in user input could override a GPT-3 application's original instructions. Researchers at Preamble had privately reported a similar issue to OpenAI earlier in 2022. Willison has since written extensively about the problem, arguing that it is hard to solve and proposing design patterns to limit damage, such as separating privileged and quarantined models. The term stuck because the analogy captures the core problem: untrusted data being interpreted as instructions, though unlike SQL injection, there is no simple escaping fix. Is prompt injection a vulnerability? Yes. Prompt injection is recognised as a security vulnerability, ranked first in the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, and it appears in government and industry guidance on securing AI systems. Its severity depends on what the application can do: a chatbot without tools may only produce misleading text, while an agent with email, payment or code execution access can cause real harm. Security teams treat it like other injection classes, assessing impact, adding defences and testing regularly. Bug bounty programmes increasingly include prompt injection findings. Any application processing untrusted content with an LLM should include it in threat modelling and document accepted risks and mitigations clearly. How do you prevent prompt injection in LLM applications? No single method prevents it fully, so combine defences: treat external content as data, separate it from instructions with clear delimiters, give models least-privilege tools, require human approval for sensitive actions, and never place secrets in prompts. Also asked as: how to prevent prompt injection in llm Add input and output filtering with classifiers that detect injection attempts, validate outputs against schemas, as DocuLens AI does for extracted fields, and restrict where data can be sent. Design patterns such as separating a privileged model from one that reads untrusted content, or Google DeepMind's CaMeL approach separating control flow from data, limit damage. Red-team regularly with injected documents and web pages, and monitor agent actions for anomalies. What is prompt injection resistance? Prompt injection resistance is a model's or system's ability to keep following legitimate instructions despite injected text. Providers improve it through training, such as teaching models an instruction hierarchy that prioritises system and developer instructions over content in data. OpenAI's instruction hierarchy research and similar work at other labs train models to ignore instructions found in tool results and documents. Classifiers screen inputs and outputs, and benchmarks such as AgentDojo measure how often agents resist attacks while completing tasks. Resistance improves but never reaches perfection, so system design must assume some attacks succeed. Measure resistance on your own scenarios, since results vary by model, prompt and tools. Why won't prompt injection be fully fixed? Language models process instructions and data as the same kind of text, so there is no reliable boundary between them, unlike SQL where parameters can be escaped. Defences are probabilistic, and attackers keep finding new phrasings that slip through. Also asked as: why prompt injection won&#x27;t be &quot;fixed Training and filters reduce success rates but cannot guarantee zero, and a single successful attack can be enough when agents have powerful tools. That is why experts emphasise architecture over prompts: limit permissions, isolate untrusted content, require confirmations and design systems so that a hijacked model cannot cause serious harm. Progress continues, but builders should plan for prompt injection as a permanent risk to manage rather than a bug awaiting a patch. Does prompt injection work on resumes? Some candidates hide instructions in resumes, such as white text telling AI screeners to rank them highly. It may fool naive screening tools, but many systems detect it, recruiters may disqualify candidates for it, and it undermines trust. Hidden instructions have also appeared in academic papers aimed at AI reviewers, drawing public criticism in 2025. For job seekers, the better strategy is a clear, honest resume with relevant keywords and measurable achievements, which works for both AI tools and human reviewers. Honesty also protects your reputation in small professional circles. For employers, AI screening should keep humans in the loop, sanitise inputs by extracting visible text, and never rely solely on model rankings for hiring decisions.

# What is Qdrant Cloud? Qdrant URL, who built it, and Qdrant vs Pinecone and OpenSearch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/qdrant-cloud-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Qdrant is an open-source vector database, written in Rust, for storing embeddings with metadata and running fast similarity search with filtering; Qdrant Cloud is the company's managed service that runs Qdrant clusters for you. It is a popular choice for RAG, semantic search and recommendations. This page explains Qdrant Cloud and how to use it, finding the Qdrant URL, who builds and uses Qdrant, and how it compares with OpenSearch, Pinecone, Chroma and PostgreSQL with pgvector.

## What is Qdrant Cloud?

Qdrant Cloud is the managed, hosted version of the Qdrant vector database. It creates and runs clusters on major cloud providers, handling setup, scaling, backups and upgrades, and offers a free tier for small projects alongside paid plans.

You create a cluster in the Qdrant Cloud console, get a URL and API key, and connect from your application with Qdrant's client libraries, exactly as you would to a self-hosted instance. This suits teams who want Qdrant's features without operating infrastructure. Because the core database is open source, you can also self-host the same software with Docker if you need full control or data residency on your own servers.

## How do I use Qdrant Cloud?

Sign up, create a cluster, copy its URL and create an API key, then connect with a Qdrant client, create a collection with the right vector size and distance metric, upsert points with payloads, and query.

```python
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.models import VectorParams, Distance, PointStruct

client = QdrantClient(url="https://YOUR-CLUSTER-URL", api_key="YOUR_KEY")
client.create_collection("notes", vectors_config=VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE))
client.upsert("notes", points=[PointStruct(id=1, vector=[0.1] * 384, payload={"subject": "os", "page": 3})])
hits = client.query_points("notes", query=[0.1] * 384, limit=3).points
```

Keep the API key in environment variables, match the vector size to your embedding model, and add payload indexes for fields you filter on.

## What is the Qdrant URL?

For a local Qdrant instance, the default URL is `http://localhost:6333` for the REST API, with gRPC on port 6334. For Qdrant Cloud, each cluster has its own HTTPS URL shown in the console, used together with an API key.

The REST URL also serves a web dashboard at `/dashboard` on local instances, useful for inspecting collections. In Docker, map the ports with `-p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334` and mount a volume for storage so data persists. When your app runs in another container, use the Qdrant service name as the host, such as `http://qdrant:6333`, rather than localhost.

## Where do I find my Qdrant URL?

For Qdrant Cloud, open the cloud console, select your cluster, and copy its endpoint URL from the cluster details; create or copy an API key from the same area. For self-hosted Qdrant, the URL is your server's address with port 6333.

Common mistakes: using `localhost` from inside a different container, forgetting the port, using HTTP instead of HTTPS for cloud clusters, and missing the API key. If connection fails, test the URL with a simple request in the browser or with curl, check firewall rules, and confirm the cluster is running. Never expose a self-hosted Qdrant to the internet without authentication.

## Who developed Qdrant?

Qdrant is developed by Qdrant, a company founded in 2021 that maintains the open-source database under the Apache 2.0 licence and runs Qdrant Cloud. The core is written in Rust for performance and memory safety.

The open-source project has an active community on GitHub, with client libraries for Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, Rust, Go, Java and .NET. Because it is open source, you can inspect the code, self-host freely, and contribute. The company funds development through its cloud and enterprise offerings, a common model for open-source infrastructure.

## Who uses Qdrant?

Qdrant is used by startups, enterprises and developers building RAG systems, semantic search, recommendation engines, anomaly detection and AI agents' memory. The company publishes case studies and the open-source project has a large community of users.

Typical users choose it for fast filtered search, where vector similarity is combined with conditions on metadata, such as user, language or date, and for the option to self-host. It integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex and other frameworks, so it appears in many tutorials. For your own decision, what matters is how it performs on your data and operational needs, not who else uses it.

## What is the difference between Qdrant and OpenSearch?

Qdrant is a dedicated vector database focused on similarity search with rich filtering. OpenSearch is a search and analytics engine that combines strong keyword search, aggregations and logs with vector search.

Choose Qdrant when vectors are the core workload and you want a lean, fast, specialised engine with excellent filtering. Choose OpenSearch when you need full-text search, BM25 relevance tuning, analytics and vectors in one system, or already run OpenSearch for logs or search. Hybrid search is possible in both: Qdrant supports sparse and dense vectors together, and OpenSearch combines BM25 with vector queries. Test retrieval quality on your own queries.

## Qdrant vs Pinecone: how do they compare?

Both are vector databases with fast similarity search and metadata filtering. Qdrant is open source and can be self-hosted or used through Qdrant Cloud; Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed service with no self-hosting option.

Feature-wise, both support namespaces or collections, filtering and hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors. Differences show in deployment control, data residency options, pricing models and operational responsibility. Qdrant lets you run the same software locally for development and in production on your own infrastructure; Pinecone minimises operations by being serverless. Benchmark both on your data, latency targets and expected scale.

## Which is better, Pinecone or Qdrant?

Neither is better universally. Choose Pinecone if you want zero infrastructure work and a fully managed serverless service. Choose Qdrant if you want open source, self-hosting options, strong filtering and the flexibility to move between local, self-hosted and cloud.

Decision factors:

- **Control and residency**: Qdrant can run on your own servers.
- **Operations**: Pinecone requires none; self-hosted Qdrant requires some.
- **Lock-in**: open-source Qdrant reduces it.
- **Cost**: compare on your expected data size and query volume.
- **Developer experience**: try both SDKs on a small prototype.

For most RAG projects, retrieval quality depends more on chunking, hybrid search and reranking than on this choice.

## Which is better: Qdrant, Chroma or Postgres?

For small projects and prototypes, Chroma is the simplest. If you already use PostgreSQL, pgvector keeps vectors with your data and is often enough. Qdrant is the strongest of the three as a dedicated vector database for larger workloads with heavy filtering.

A rough guide:

- **Chroma**: notebooks, prototypes, small local apps.
- **Postgres with pgvector**: apps already on Postgres; joins, transactions, row-level security.
- **Qdrant**: larger vector workloads, high query volume, complex payload filters, multi-tenant setups.

RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval in about 220 MB on a free tier, a reminder that the simplest store that meets your needs is usually the right one. Measure recall and latency on your data before switching.

# Qdrant explained: uses, how it works, client, best practices, vs pgvector and Chroma
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/qdrant-explained-best-practices/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Qdrant is an open-source vector database, written in Rust, for storing embeddings with metadata and searching them by similarity with fast filtering, which makes it a common choice for RAG, semantic search and recommendations. I build RAG systems, including RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval, so this page covers what Qdrant is used for, how it works, its client, best practices, comparisons with pgvector and Chroma, examples, where the company is based and what to do if it seems down.

## What is Qdrant used for?

Qdrant is used for semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, image and audio similarity search, anomaly detection and deduplication: any task where you find items whose embeddings are close to a query embedding, often with metadata filters.

In RAG, Qdrant stores chunk embeddings with payloads such as document ID, page and access permissions, and returns the most relevant chunks for each question, filtered to what the user may see. Its support for sparse vectors and hybrid queries lets one collection serve both keyword-like and semantic retrieval. It runs locally in Docker, in your own cluster, or as the managed Qdrant Cloud, so the same code moves from prototype to production.

## How does Qdrant work?

Qdrant stores points in collections. Each point has an ID, one or more vectors and a JSON payload. It builds an HNSW graph index over vectors for fast approximate nearest neighbour search and payload indexes for filtering, combining both during queries.

When you search, Qdrant traverses the HNSW graph to find vectors closest to the query by cosine, dot product, Euclidean or Manhattan distance, while applying filters during traversal rather than after, which keeps filtered results accurate. Data is stored in segments that are optimised in the background. Quantization, scalar, product or binary, compresses vectors to save memory. Distributed mode shards and replicates collections across nodes, and snapshots support backups and migration.

## What is the Qdrant client?

The Qdrant client is the official library for talking to a Qdrant server from your code. The Python package `qdrant-client` is the most used, with official clients also for JavaScript and TypeScript, Rust, Go, Java and .NET.

With the Python client, you create a `QdrantClient` pointing at a URL or local path, create a collection with a vector size and distance, upsert points with vectors and payloads, and call query methods with optional filters. It supports both REST and gRPC, async usage, and a local mode that runs in memory or on disk without a server, useful for tests. It also integrates with FastEmbed to generate embeddings directly, and with LangChain and LlamaIndex.

## What are Qdrant best practices?

Match the distance metric to your embedding model, create payload indexes on fields you filter by, batch uploads, use quantization to reduce memory for large collections, and tune HNSW parameters only after measuring recall and latency on real queries.

More practices: use named vectors when storing several embeddings per item, such as dense and sparse; for multitenant apps, partition by a tenant ID payload with a tenant index rather than creating thousands of collections; keep original vectors on disk with quantized copies in memory, then rescore for accuracy; schedule snapshots; set API keys and TLS in production; pin server and client versions together; and monitor memory, latency and indexing status through metrics.

## Qdrant vs pgvector: which should you use?

Use pgvector when you already run PostgreSQL, have up to a few million vectors, and want transactions, joins and one database to operate. Use Qdrant when vector search is central, collections are large, or you need advanced filtering, quantization and hybrid queries at scale.

pgvector keeps vectors next to relational data, which simplifies permissions and consistency; with HNSW indexes it performs well for many applications, and PostgreSQL full-text search enables hybrid retrieval with SQL. Qdrant is purpose-built, with filtering integrated into graph search, rich quantization, sparse vectors and horizontal scaling. Benchmarks vary by version and configuration, so measure recall, latency and memory on your own data. Many teams start with pgvector and move to Qdrant when scale demands.

## What is the difference between Qdrant and Chroma?

Chroma is a lightweight, developer-friendly vector store, popular for prototypes and notebooks, that can run embedded in a Python process. Qdrant is a production-oriented vector database with stronger filtering, quantization, distributed deployment and performance tooling.

Chroma's strength is simplicity: a few lines create a collection and query it, with built-in embedding functions. It also offers a client-server mode and a hosted cloud. Qdrant offers more control over indexing, memory, payload indexes, multitenancy and replication, which matters as data and traffic grow. For a hackathon or a small internal tool, Chroma is quick; for a multi-user production RAG system with permissions and millions of chunks, Qdrant is usually the safer choice.

## What is the difference between Chroma and pgvector?

Chroma is a dedicated vector store focused on easy embedding storage and retrieval, often embedded in Python apps. pgvector is an extension that adds vector types and similarity indexes to PostgreSQL, so vectors live alongside your relational tables.

Choose Chroma for quick prototypes and local experiments where you want minimal setup. Choose pgvector when your application already uses PostgreSQL, since you get SQL filters, joins, transactions, backups and access control without another system to run. pgvector suits production apps with moderate vector counts; Chroma suits learning and small projects. Both integrate with LangChain and LlamaIndex, so switching later is manageable if you keep retrieval behind a small interface in your code.

## What are some Qdrant examples?

Qdrant's documentation and GitHub include examples for semantic search, RAG with LangChain and LlamaIndex, hybrid search with sparse vectors, recommendation systems, image similarity search and multitenant setups, many with runnable notebooks.

A minimal Python example: start Qdrant with Docker, create a collection with a vector size of 384 and cosine distance, embed a few sentences with FastEmbed or Sentence Transformers, upsert them with payloads such as category, then query with a sentence and a filter on category. From there, extend to RAG by chunking documents, storing page metadata, and passing the top results to a language model with citations. The qdrant/examples repository collects many such projects.

## Where is Qdrant based?

Qdrant, the company, was founded in 2021 and is headquartered in Germany, with a distributed team working across countries. It develops the open-source Qdrant engine under the Apache 2.0 licence and offers Qdrant Cloud and enterprise deployment options.

For developers, location matters mostly for data residency: Qdrant Cloud lets you choose cloud providers and regions, so data can stay in specific geographies, and the hybrid and private cloud options run Qdrant inside your own infrastructure. The open-source engine itself runs anywhere you can run a container or binary. Check the company's website for current details on offices, compliance certifications and support plans, which change as it grows.

## Is Qdrant down?

For Qdrant Cloud, check the official status page for incidents first. For a self-hosted server, check whether the container or process is running, read its logs, and call a health endpoint, such as `/healthz` or `/readyz`, on port 6333.

Common self-hosted problems: the container restarted after running out of memory, a full disk stopped writes, a port is not exposed, TLS or API key settings mismatch the client, or the client and server versions are incompatible. Check `docker ps` and `docker logs`, memory and disk usage, and collection status, which shows whether indexing is still running. For production, add monitoring and alerts on these metrics so you hear about issues before users do.
