# RAG vs fine-tuning: when to use each for LLMs, with examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning solve different problems. RAG gives a model the right information at question time by retrieving passages from your documents; fine-tuning changes the model's weights so it behaves differently, such as following a format, a tone or a narrow task. Most products need RAG for knowledge and only sometimes fine-tuning for behaviour. I have built both: RAG.NextUpgrad for grounded answers and FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning, so this page answers the common questions with practical examples.

## Is it "fine tuning" or "fine-tuning"?

Both spellings appear, and they mean the same thing. "Fine-tuning", with a hyphen, is the more standard form in technical writing as a noun and adjective, as in "fine-tuning a model" or "a fine-tuned model".

You will see "finetuning" as one word in some papers and code, such as library names, and "fine tuning" in casual writing and search queries. In documentation and reports, pick one form and use it consistently; "fine-tuning" is the safe choice. The concept is the same in every spelling: continuing to train a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so it adapts to your use case.

## Fine-tuning LLMs vs RAG: what is the difference?

RAG keeps the model as it is and supplies relevant documents with each question. Fine-tuning trains the model further on examples, changing its weights so it behaves differently without needing those examples in the prompt.

Compare them on what matters:

- **Knowledge**: RAG handles private and changing facts; fine-tuning bakes in knowledge poorly.
- **Updates**: RAG updates by editing documents; fine-tuning needs retraining.
- **Citations**: RAG can cite sources; fine-tuned models cannot.
- **Behaviour and format**: fine-tuning is strong; RAG does not change style.
- **Cost**: RAG costs more per query because of longer prompts; fine-tuning costs up front.

They also combine well: a fine-tuned model that follows your format, with RAG for the facts.

## When should I use fine-tuning vs RAG?

Use RAG when answers depend on documents, especially private, large or frequently changing ones. Use fine-tuning when you need consistent behaviour that prompts cannot achieve: a strict output format, a specific tone, a narrow classification task, or a smaller, cheaper model that matches a larger one on one job.

Decision rules I use:

- Answer must cite a source or reflect today's documents: RAG.
- Output must always follow a complex structure: try structured outputs first, then fine-tune.
- High-volume narrow task where cost and latency matter: fine-tune a small model.
- Domain jargon the model misreads: RAG with good examples, then consider fine-tuning.
- Both knowledge and behaviour: RAG plus a fine-tuned model.

Measure on a test set either way.

## Why does fine-tuning not work as well as RAG for knowledge?

Fine-tuning teaches patterns more readily than facts. A model trained on your documents may pick up their style without reliably recalling specific details, may mix them with what it already knew, and cannot show where an answer came from.

There are practical problems too. Every document change needs a new training run. Verifying which facts the model has learned is hard. Fine-tuning on new facts can increase hallucination, because the model learns to answer confidently about things it only partly absorbed. RAG avoids these: the exact passage is in the prompt, the answer can quote it, and updating knowledge means updating the index. That is why RAG.NextUpgrad grounds answers in retrieved passages with citations and refuses when evidence is weak, rather than relying on a model's memory.

## What is the difference between prompt engineering, RAG and fine-tuning?

Prompt engineering changes the instructions and examples you send; RAG adds retrieved information to the prompt; fine-tuning changes the model itself. They form a ladder from cheapest and fastest to most involved.

Start at the bottom:

- **Prompt engineering**: clear instructions, examples, output format. Minutes to try, no infrastructure.
- **RAG**: an index of your documents and a retrieval step. Days to build well, easy to update.
- **Fine-tuning**: a dataset of examples and a training run. Days to weeks, needs evaluation and re-training for changes.

Move up a rung only when the one below demonstrably fails on your test set. Many teams fine-tune when better prompts or retrieval would have solved the problem faster.

## What are some examples of fine-tuning?

Good fine-tuning targets are behaviours: classifying support tickets into your categories, extracting fields into a strict schema, writing in a brand's voice, generating SQL for your database schema, or making a small model match a larger one on one task.

Concrete examples:

- A sentiment or intent classifier trained on a few thousand labelled messages.
- A model that turns invoice text into a fixed JSON format every time.
- A customer-support model that answers in your company's tone and structure.
- A small open model distilled from a larger model's outputs for cheaper inference.
- A model adapted to Indian-English phrasing for a specific domain.

FineTune Studio runs this loop from the browser: upload a dataset, train a QLoRA adapter, watch the loss curve live, and compare base and tuned outputs side by side.

## How long does fine-tuning take?

With parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA or QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model on a few thousand examples takes from minutes to a few hours on a single GPU. Full fine-tuning of large models takes far longer and needs many GPUs.

Time depends on model size, dataset size, sequence length, number of epochs and hardware. A 7B or 8B model with QLoRA on a few thousand short examples commonly trains within an hour or two on one modern GPU, including free or low-cost cloud options for small runs. Hosted fine-tuning services queue and run jobs for you, typically finishing within minutes to hours. Preparing a clean dataset and an evaluation set usually takes longer than training itself, and matters more for the result.

## What type of fine-tuning does the OpenAI API use?

OpenAI's API offers supervised fine-tuning on example conversations, preference fine-tuning with Direct Preference Optimization using preferred and rejected answers, and reinforcement fine-tuning for reasoning models using graders. Vision fine-tuning with images is also supported on some models.

Supervised fine-tuning is the common starting point: you upload JSONL examples of input messages and ideal assistant replies. Preference fine-tuning helps when you can say which of two answers is better more easily than writing the perfect one. Reinforcement fine-tuning suits tasks with checkable answers. OpenAI hosts the training and serves the resulting model through the same API; you do not get the weights. Which models can be fine-tuned changes, so check the fine-tuning guide.

## Why is a vector database required for fine-tuning or RAG?

A vector database is required for RAG, not for fine-tuning. RAG stores document embeddings in a vector index so it can find relevant passages by meaning; fine-tuning trains on a dataset file and never needs a vector store.

The confusion comes from both being ways to "teach a model about your documents". For RAG, the vector store, or PostgreSQL with pgvector, or a library such as FAISS, holds embeddings and returns the nearest chunks. Many production systems also add keyword search such as BM25, because embeddings miss exact terms. For fine-tuning, you need training examples in a format such as JSONL, a training framework or hosted service, and an evaluation set. If someone says you need a vector database to fine-tune, they are describing RAG.

## How does fine-tuning work for question answering on custom documents?

You create question-and-answer pairs from your documents and train the model on them, so it learns to answer in that domain and format. It works for consistent style and common questions, but it is unreliable for exact facts, so it is usually combined with RAG.

A better recipe for document Q&A is RAG first: index the documents, retrieve passages for each question, and answer with citations. If answers are correct but the style or format is wrong, fine-tune on examples where the input includes retrieved passages and the output is the ideal grounded answer, which teaches the model to use context well. Evaluate on held-out questions, including ones the documents cannot answer, and check that the model declines rather than inventing.


---

# RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering: which one your problem actually needs, with a decision tree and real costs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## RAG vs fine-tuning: what is the difference?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, changes what the model reads: at answer time it retrieves passages from your documents and answers from them, with citations. Fine-tuning changes what the model is: it trains the weights on your examples so the model's behaviour, style, format or skill shifts permanently. RAG is for knowledge the model lacks or that changes. Fine-tuning is for behaviour no prompt can produce. They solve different problems, and the most common mistake is using one for the other's job.**


I built both kinds of system in the same six months of 2026: RAG.NextUpgrad, a production retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate [9], and FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry and base-versus-tuned evaluation [10]. Clients asked me the same question about both, and this page is the answer I now give before writing any code.

> Knowledge or behaviour? Answer that in one word and you have chosen your architecture. Everything after is engineering.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## When should I use RAG?

**When the answer depends on information the model does not have: your documents, your database, anything after its training cutoff, anything private. When answers must cite their source. When content changes often, because re-indexing a document takes seconds while retraining takes hours. When different users may see different documents, because retrieval can filter by permission and a model's weights cannot. When you need to ship this week, because a RAG prototype is an afternoon.**


Lewis et al. introduced the pattern for knowledge-intensive tasks precisely because a model's parameters are a poor place to store facts that must be exact and current [1]. Ovadia et al. compared knowledge injection by fine-tuning against retrieval directly and found retrieval consistently better at giving models new factual knowledge [3].

## When should I use fine-tuning?

**When the problem is how the model behaves, not what it knows: a consistent voice, a strict output format, a domain's phrasing, a classification or extraction skill the base model does poorly, or a narrow task you want a small, cheap, fast model to do well. When you have hundreds to thousands of clean examples of the right output. When the requirement is stable enough that retraining every month would not be needed. When prompting with examples has been tried and still falls short.**


LoRA made this affordable by training small adapters instead of all weights [2], and LIMA showed how few examples alignment needs when they are clean: a thousand, not a hundred thousand [4]. Both papers point the same way: fine-tuning is a scalpel for behaviour, not a container for facts.

## Where does prompt engineering fit?

**First. A prompt is free to change, takes effect instantly and often solves the problem: a clear task, an output format, a few examples, a rule for the not-enough-information case. Few-shot examples in the prompt were the original demonstration that models can learn a task without training [7]. Every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that says "answer only from these passages and cite them", and every fine-tuning project should start by proving that prompting was insufficient.**



The official prompting guides are free and current; read one before spending on anything else [8].

## RAG vs fine-tuning: side by side

**The comparison, on the dimensions that decide real projects.**



## Can I combine RAG and fine-tuning?

**Yes, and mature systems usually do. RAG supplies the facts; a fine-tune supplies the behaviour: the house voice, a strict answer format, better use of retrieved passages, or a smaller model that follows citation rules reliably. You can also fine-tune the embedding model or the reranker on your own query-passage pairs to improve retrieval itself. Add the fine-tune after the RAG system works and is measured, never before, so you can see what the training actually changed.**



## Can fine-tuning add knowledge to a model?

**Weakly, unreliably and expensively. A model fine-tuned on facts may repeat some of them, but it cannot cite them, it does not know when they changed, and it blends them with prior beliefs. Ovadia et al. found retrieval outperformed fine-tuning for injecting new knowledge, and that repeated exposure to facts was needed for fine-tuning to teach them at all [3]. Luo et al. document the forgetting that aggressive fine-tuning causes [5]. If the fact must be right and traceable, retrieve it.**


This is the expensive mistake I see most: a team fine-tunes a model on their product manual, the manual changes, and the model confidently describes the old version with no way to show where it got it.


## What does each approach cost?

**RAG costs are in retrieval engineering up front, chunking, embeddings, indexing, evaluation, and then per query, because every answer sends retrieved passages as tokens. Fine-tuning costs are up front in the dataset, weeks of a person's time to write and clean examples, plus a few GPU hours that are cheap or free, and then again with every requirement change. Per-query, a fine-tuned small model is cheaper than a large model with a long RAG prompt. Total cost depends on volume and how often things change.**



## What are the failure modes of each?

**RAG fails when retrieval returns the wrong passage, when chunks lose context, when the prompt lets the model ignore the documents, or when passages conflict. Fine-tuning fails when the dataset is inconsistent, when the model overfits and memorises, when it forgets general ability, when the chat template is wrong, or when facts in the training data go stale. Prompting fails when phrasing breaks across model versions and when a task genuinely exceeds the model's ability. Each failure has a specific fix, and none of the fixes is "switch approaches" without measuring first.**



## Which is easier for a beginner or a student project?

**RAG. A retrieval system over documents you know is an afternoon to prototype, runs on a laptop with a free model API or a local model, and teaches chunking, embeddings, prompting, evaluation and hallucination in one project. Fine-tuning is a strong second project once you have a dataset you understand; QLoRA on a small model fits a free GPU. Doing both, and being able to say which problem each solved, is what interviewers want to hear.**



## RAG vs fine-tuning interview questions

**Define both and state the one-line rule. Give an example that needs RAG, one that needs fine-tuning and one that needs both. Explain why fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts, citing forgetting and the inability to cite. Explain how you would prove prompting was insufficient before training. Estimate the cost shape of each. Describe a system you built and which approach it used, and why.**



## Where to go from here

**Build the RAG version first, measure recall on twenty questions, and write down what it cannot do. That list is your fine-tuning specification, if you need one at all.** My longer decision write-up with client examples is on the portfolio [11]. For a session at your college on choosing and building these systems, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# RAG vs MCP, vector search, context windows, agentic RAG, chatbots and GraphRAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-mcp-agentic-rag-graphrag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, gives a language model relevant information at question time so it answers from evidence. Many related terms, from MCP to agentic RAG and GraphRAG, describe different layers or variations. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, reranking, cited streaming and a confidence gate, so this page untangles RAG versus MCP, pipelines, vector search, long context, agentic search and RAG, chatbots, GraphRAG and knowledge graphs, and RAG-Sequence versus RAG-Token. What is the difference between RAG and MCP? RAG is a technique: retrieve relevant information and give it to a model so it answers from evidence. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources through servers. They operate at different layers and work well together. An MCP server can expose a search tool over your documents, which an assistant calls to perform RAG. MCP also connects models to actions, such as creating tickets or querying databases, which go beyond retrieval. Anthropic introduced MCP in 2024, and it has since been adopted across many AI tools. Think of RAG as what you do with information, and MCP as how tools plug in. What is the difference between RAG and a RAG pipeline? RAG is the general idea of augmenting generation with retrieved information. A RAG pipeline is a concrete implementation: the sequence of steps and components that ingest documents, retrieve passages and produce grounded answers. Also asked as: difference between rag and rag pipeline A typical pipeline includes document loading, cleaning, chunking, embedding, indexing, query processing, hybrid retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, generation with citations and evaluation. Each step involves design choices that strongly affect quality. RAG.NextUpgrad's pipeline combines dense retrieval with BM25 through reciprocal rank fusion, reranks the results, streams cited answers and declines through a confidence gate when evidence is weak. Two systems both called RAG can perform very differently because their pipelines differ. What is the difference between vector search and RAG? Vector search finds items whose embeddings are closest to a query's embedding. RAG uses retrieval, often including vector search, to supply context that a language model then uses to generate an answer. Vector search alone returns a ranked list of passages or items, like a search engine. RAG adds generation: it turns those passages into a synthesised answer with citations. RAG's retrieval step need not be vector-based; keyword search, SQL or hybrid methods often work better for exact terms. Semantic search and vector databases are building blocks, while RAG is the full question-answering system that combines retrieval with a model's language abilities. What is the difference between RAG and a large context window? A large context window lets you place whole documents directly in the prompt. RAG retrieves only the most relevant passages. Long context is simpler for small collections, while RAG scales to large, changing knowledge bases at lower cost. Also asked as: difference between rag and context window Long-context prompts cost more per question, increase latency and can suffer from models overlooking information in the middle, as the lost-in-the-middle study by Liu and colleagues found. RAG keeps prompts small and focused, supports access control per document and updates instantly when content changes. Combined approaches work well: retrieve relevant documents, then include larger sections thanks to long context. Test both on your questions, comparing accuracy, latency and cost. What is the difference between RAG and agentic search? Classic RAG retrieves once from a fixed index using the user's question. Agentic search lets a model decide what to search, run multiple queries with tools such as web search, file search or grep, read results and search again until satisfied. Agentic search handles complex, multi-step questions and sources that are not pre-indexed, such as codebases or the live web, which is why coding agents often search files directly. It costs more tokens and time, and can wander without good limits. Classic RAG is faster, cheaper and more predictable for well-defined knowledge bases. Many systems combine them: a fast retrieval first, with agentic follow-up searches when the first pass is insufficient. What is the difference between naive RAG and agentic RAG? Naive RAG embeds the question, retrieves the top chunks once and generates an answer. Agentic RAG lets the model plan retrieval: rewrite queries, choose sources, retrieve multiple times, check whether evidence suffices and verify its answer. Naive RAG fails on multi-hop questions, vague queries and questions spanning several sources. Agentic RAG handles these by decomposing questions, routing to the right index or tool, and iterating, using patterns such as self-reflection and corrective retrieval. The cost is higher latency, more tokens and harder evaluation. A middle ground adds query rewriting, hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, before reaching for full agentic loops. What is the difference between RAG and a chatbot? A chatbot is a conversational interface. RAG is a technique that can power a chatbot by retrieving relevant information before each answer. Many chatbots use RAG; others rely only on the model's training or scripted responses. Also asked as: what is the difference between rag and chatbot A chatbot without RAG answers from what the model learned during training, risking outdated or invented information about your specific organisation. A RAG chatbot grounds answers in your documents, citing sources and staying current as content changes. RAG can also power non-chat interfaces, such as search results with generated summaries or document question answering. When evaluating a chatbot product, ask whether it retrieves from your data, how it cites sources and what it does when evidence is missing. What is the difference between GraphRAG and a knowledge graph? A knowledge graph is a data structure storing entities and their relationships. GraphRAG is a retrieval technique that uses a graph, often built automatically from documents by an LLM, to retrieve connected information for answering questions. Also asked as: difference between graph rag and knowledge graph Microsoft's GraphRAG approach extracts entities and relationships from documents, clusters them into communities, and generates summaries that help answer broad questions about a whole collection, which plain vector RAG handles poorly. Traditional knowledge graphs are often curated, with defined schemas, and queried directly. GraphRAG uses graphs as an index for language models. Building and updating graphs costs more than vector indexing, so use GraphRAG when questions depend on relationships or global summaries. What is the difference between the RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token models? Both come from the original 2020 RAG paper by Lewis and colleagues. RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to generate the entire answer, while RAG-Token can draw on different retrieved documents for each generated token. Also asked as: what is the difference between rag-sequence model and rag-token model In RAG-Sequence, the model generates a full answer for each top document and combines them by their retrieval probabilities. RAG-Token combines documents at every token step, allowing answers that blend facts from several sources. The paper found each variant performed better on different tasks. Modern RAG systems rarely use these exact formulations; instead, they place several retrieved passages in a large language model's prompt, letting the model attend to all of them. MCP vs agentic RAG: how do they relate? They are complementary. Agentic RAG is a strategy where a model plans and performs retrieval across steps. MCP is a protocol that standardises how the model connects to tools, including retrieval tools, databases and APIs. An agentic RAG system might use MCP servers for a document search, a SQL database and a web search, choosing among them per question. MCP reduces the custom integration work, since one server can serve many AI applications. Security still matters: MCP servers can expose sensitive data or actions, so apply permissions, authentication and logging. Design the retrieval strategy first, then use MCP to connect the sources it needs.

# RAG without a vector database, plus Postgres, SQLite, ClickHouse, Databricks and OpenAI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-without-vector-database-options/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

RAG does not strictly need a vector database: keyword search, SQL, graphs or plain in-memory indexes can retrieve context too. Vector databases help when you need semantic search at scale with filtering. In RAG.NextUpgrad I combine dense vector retrieval with BM25 through reciprocal rank fusion and reranking, so this page covers RAG without vector databases, what they are, how search and indexing work, choosing one, and options in Postgres, SQLite, ClickHouse, OpenAI and Databricks. Can RAG work without a vector database? Yes. RAG only needs a way to retrieve relevant context. Keyword search with BM25, SQL queries over structured data, knowledge graphs, file search with grep, or embeddings held in memory all work, depending on the data. Also asked as: can rag work without vector database For small collections of a few thousand chunks, store embeddings in a NumPy array or a FAISS index file and search in memory. For exact terms, codes and names, BM25 often beats vectors. Coding agents retrieve context by searching files directly. Long-context models can sometimes take whole documents without retrieval. A vector database becomes worthwhile when you need semantic search over large, changing collections with filters, concurrency and persistence. Hybrid retrieval, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, combines keyword and vector signals. What is a vector database in simple terms? A vector database stores items as lists of numbers, called embeddings, that capture their meaning, and quickly finds the items whose numbers are closest to a query's. It searches by meaning rather than exact words. Also asked as: what is vector database in simple terms For example, an embedding model turns the sentence how do I reset my password into a vector, and the database finds help articles with similar vectors, even if they say account recovery instead. Vector databases add features around this core: metadata filters, updates, scaling across machines, access control and backups. Examples include Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone and Chroma, while general databases such as PostgreSQL add vector support through extensions. How does vector database search work? The query is converted into an embedding with the same model used for documents. The database then finds the nearest stored vectors by a similarity measure, such as cosine similarity, using an index that avoids comparing every vector. Approximate nearest neighbour indexes, such as HNSW, explore a small part of the collection to find likely nearest neighbours quickly, trading a little accuracy for large speed gains. Metadata filters, such as document type or date, narrow results before or during search. The top results, with scores and stored text, return to the application, which often reranks them with a cross-encoder before sending them to the LLM. Search quality depends heavily on chunking and the embedding model. How does vector database indexing work? Indexing organises vectors so similar ones can be found without scanning everything. HNSW builds a layered graph linking each vector to its neighbours; IVF clusters vectors and searches only nearby clusters; quantization compresses vectors to save memory. When you insert a vector into an HNSW index, the database connects it to nearby vectors at several layers, so searches can hop quickly from distant regions to the closest matches. Parameters control the trade-offs: more connections and wider search improve recall but use more memory and time. IVF indexes need training on sample data to define clusters. Updates and deletions affect index quality over time, so some systems rebuild or compact indexes periodically. How do you choose a vector database for RAG? Choose based on scale, existing stack, filtering needs, hybrid search support, operations effort and cost. For many projects, pgvector in an existing PostgreSQL database is enough, while dedicated databases suit large or demanding workloads. Also asked as: how to choose vector database for rag Questions to ask: how many vectors now and in a year; do you need fast filtering by tenant, date or permissions; do you need keyword and vector hybrid search; should it be managed or self-hosted; and what latency is acceptable. Benchmark candidates on your own data, measuring recall and latency with realistic filters. Remember that chunking, embeddings and reranking usually matter more for answer quality than the database choice itself. Avoid premature complexity. Can you use Postgres as a vector database? Yes. The pgvector extension adds a vector data type, distance operators and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes to PostgreSQL, letting you store embeddings beside relational data and query them with SQL. Also asked as: can i use postgres as vector database This suits many RAG applications: keep documents, users, permissions and embeddings in one database, filter with ordinary WHERE clauses, and combine vector similarity with PostgreSQL full-text search for hybrid retrieval in a single query. Managed services such as Supabase, Neon and major clouds support pgvector. Performance is strong up to millions of vectors with proper indexes and memory, and extensions such as pgvectorscale extend it further. Very large or high-throughput workloads may still benefit from dedicated vector databases. Can you use SQLite as a vector database? Yes, with extensions. sqlite-vec adds vector storage and similarity search to SQLite, making it practical for local apps, desktop tools, mobile devices and prototypes that need RAG without running a separate server. Also asked as: can i use sqlite as a vector database SQLite keeps everything in one file, which simplifies deployment and backups, and combines well with SQLite's FTS5 full-text search for hybrid retrieval. It suits collections from thousands to a few million vectors on a single machine, depending on hardware and query patterns. It is less suited to many concurrent writers or distributed scaling. For offline or privacy-sensitive applications, such as personal document assistants, SQLite with local embeddings keeps all data on the user's device. Can ClickHouse replace a vector database? For many workloads, yes. ClickHouse supports vector distance functions and approximate vector similarity indexes, so it can store embeddings alongside large analytical datasets and run similarity searches with SQL filters. It fits teams already using ClickHouse for analytics, logs or events who want semantic search without another system, such as finding similar support tickets across millions of records with time and category filters. Dedicated vector databases may still offer better tooling for frequent updates, low-latency serving, hybrid search features and RAG integrations. Evaluate recall, latency and update patterns on your data. Choosing a database your team already operates well often beats adopting a specialised one. What vector database does OpenAI use for ChatGPT? OpenAI does not publicly detail the internal retrieval stack behind ChatGPT. It acquired Rockset, a real-time search and analytics database company, in 2024 to strengthen its retrieval infrastructure, and its API offers managed vector stores for file search. Also asked as: what vector database does chatgpt use For developers, the File Search tool lets you upload files to an OpenAI-managed vector store, which handles chunking, embedding and retrieval automatically, with configurable options. This is convenient but less flexible than running your own retrieval, where you control chunking, hybrid search, reranking and citations. Many teams use OpenAI embeddings with their own database, such as pgvector or Qdrant, to keep control over data and ranking, and to switch providers more easily. Does Databricks have a vector database? Yes. Databricks offers Mosaic AI Vector Search, a managed vector search service integrated with Unity Catalog and Delta tables, which can automatically sync embeddings when source data changes. Also asked as: does databricks have vector database It suits organisations whose data already lives in Databricks, since indexes stay governed by the same permissions and lineage as other data. You can compute embeddings with Databricks-hosted models or supply your own, and query indexes from RAG applications built with Databricks tools or external frameworks. Features include filtering and hybrid keyword and vector search. As with any managed option, compare cost, latency and flexibility against pgvector or dedicated databases for your workload.

# Redis and caching strategies for LLM apps: exact-match caching, semantic caching, and what to cache when every model call costs money and time
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/redis-and-caching-strategies-for-llm-apps/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why does caching matter so much for LLM applications?

**Because an LLM call is both slow, often one to several seconds, and billed by the token, unlike a typical database query that is usually fast and free at the margin. A cache hit for a repeated or near-duplicate question skips both costs entirely: no tokens billed, no round trip to the provider, an answer in milliseconds instead of seconds. For any application with real traffic, a meaningful fraction of questions repeat or nearly repeat, which makes caching one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk optimisations available.**


Every production system I run treats caching as part of the architecture from day one, not a later optimisation, because the cost and latency gap between a cache hit and a fresh model call is too large to leave on the table.

> The fastest, cheapest LLM call is the one you don't make. Caching is how you make fewer of them without answering fewer questions.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is exact-match caching, and how do I set it up with Redis?

**Exact-match caching stores the response for a specific input, and returns it instantly if the exact same input is seen again, typically keyed by a hash of the normalised prompt plus relevant parameters, model name, temperature, system prompt version [1]. Redis fits this well because it is a fast in-memory key-value store with built-in expiry, so a cache entry can be set to expire after a sensible time-to-live. This catches genuinely repeated questions, the same FAQ asked verbatim, but misses near-duplicates that are worded differently.**



## What is semantic caching, and when does it help?

**Semantic caching catches near-duplicate questions that are not worded identically: "what is RAG" and "can you explain retrieval augmented generation" mean the same thing but would miss an exact-match cache entirely. It works by embedding the incoming query, searching a small vector index of previously cached queries, and returning the cached response if a past query is similar enough, above a chosen similarity threshold [2][3]. This catches far more repeats than exact matching, at the cost of needing an embedding call per request and careful threshold tuning to avoid returning a cached answer to a subtly different question.**




## What should I never cache, and what needs careful scoping?

**Never cache anything containing per-user private data under a key shared across users; a cache is a way to leak one user's private answer to another user if scoped incorrectly. Never cache a response that depends on real-time information, current stock levels, today's date-sensitive content, without a very short TTL matched to how fast that information actually changes. Scope any cache key that includes personalised context, a user's name, their account data, their specific documents, to that user or session specifically, never globally.**



## How does caching interact with RAG, and how do I invalidate it correctly?

**A RAG answer's correctness depends on the documents it was generated from, so a cache entry must be invalidated the moment a source document changes, not just after a fixed TTL expires. The reliable pattern is to tie the cache key, or a cache-validity check, to a version identifier of the underlying document set, a hash or a last-updated timestamp, so a document update naturally invalidates every cache entry that depended on the old version, rather than serving a stale answer until an arbitrary timer runs out.**



## What is provider-side prompt caching, and how is it different?

**Some providers offer their own prompt caching, where a long, repeated prefix of a prompt, a large system prompt or a big block of retrieved context, is cached on the provider's side across calls, so you are billed less and served faster for the repeated portion even though the full request still goes to the model [4][5]. This is different from application-side caching like Redis: it does not skip the model call entirely, it makes the unavoidable model call cheaper and faster when large parts of the prompt repeat across requests, which stacks well alongside your own exact-match and semantic caching layers.**


## How do I know if my caching setup is actually worth it?

**Measure the real cache hit rate in production, not an assumption. A cache with a ten percent hit rate is complexity added for a small saving; a cache with a fifty percent hit rate on a high-traffic FAQ-style application is a major cost and latency win. Track hit rate, cost saved, and latency saved separately, and revisit the caching strategy, exact-match only, add semantic, adjust the similarity threshold, if the measured hit rate does not match what the traffic pattern suggested it should be.**



## Caching interview questions for AI applications

**Explain the difference between exact-match and semantic caching. Describe how you would scope cache keys to avoid leaking one user's data to another. Explain how you would invalidate a RAG cache when source documents change. Describe provider-side prompt caching and how it differs from an application cache. Explain how you would measure whether a caching layer is actually worth its complexity. The strongest answer includes a real hit-rate number you measured.**



## Where should I start?

**Add a simple exact-match Redis cache in front of your most repeated LLM call this week, measure the hit rate for a few days, and only add semantic caching if the traffic pattern shows enough near-duplicate questions to justify it.** For a hands-on session on cost and latency optimisation for LLM applications, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is residual vector quantization? VQ, AWQ, and quantization's effect on models
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/residual-vector-quantization-awq/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Residual vector quantization (RVQ) compresses a vector in stages: a first codebook approximates it, a second codebook encodes what the first missed, and so on, so a few small codebooks represent it precisely. It powers neural audio codecs and compressed vector search. Model quantization applies a related idea to weights. I use 4-bit quantization in FineTune Studio for QLoRA training, so this page covers RVQ and vector quantization, why quantization is needed, sampling and non-uniform levels, its effect on accuracy and multilingual models, and AWQ.

## What is residual vector quantization?

Residual vector quantization encodes a vector with a sequence of codebooks: the first picks the nearest codeword, the next encodes the residual error left over, and each later stage refines what remains. The final vector is the sum of the chosen codewords.

With eight stages of 1,024 codewords each, every vector is stored as eight small integers, yet the combinations can represent an enormous number of distinct vectors. RVQ is used in neural audio codecs such as SoundStream and EnCodec, where audio frames become tokens that language models can generate, and in vector search to compress embeddings. Its coarse-to-fine structure is useful: dropping later stages gives a lower bitrate at lower quality, which lets one model serve several bandwidths.

## What is vector quantization?

Vector quantization maps each vector to the nearest entry in a fixed codebook of representative vectors, so you store a short index instead of the full vector. The codebook is usually learned with k-means clustering on sample data.

It is lossy compression: the error is the distance between a vector and its codeword. Classic uses include image and speech compression. In vector search, product quantization splits each embedding into sub-vectors and quantises each separately, shrinking memory many times over so very large collections fit in RAM; FAISS implements this. In deep learning, VQ-VAE models learn discrete codes for images and audio, which made token-based generation of non-text media practical.

## What does quantization do to a model?

Quantization stores a model's weights, and sometimes activations, in fewer bits, for example 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. The model becomes smaller, needs less memory and often runs faster, at the cost of a small loss in precision.

A 7-billion-parameter model needs about 14 GB in 16-bit precision and roughly 4 GB at 4 bits, the difference between needing a data-centre GPU and running on a laptop. Each weight is rounded to one of a few levels using a scale factor per group of weights, and good methods keep quality close to the original. In FineTune Studio, QLoRA loads the base model in 4-bit NF4 format and trains small LoRA adapters on top, which makes fine-tuning possible on a single modest GPU.

## Why is quantization required?

Quantization is required because large models are too big and slow for most hardware at full precision. Lower precision cuts memory, bandwidth and energy use, so models fit on cheaper GPUs, phones and browsers, and serve more users per machine.

Language model inference is usually limited by memory bandwidth: every generated token reads all the weights. Halving the bytes per weight roughly halves that traffic, so quantised models often generate tokens faster. Quantization also enables on-device AI where data must stay local, and lowers serving costs at scale. It is not free, so measure quality on your own tasks: summarisation might be unaffected while maths or code may degrade more.

## Why is non-uniform quantization required?

Non-uniform quantization spaces its levels unevenly, placing more levels where values are common and fewer where they are rare. It is needed because real signals and neural network weights are not spread evenly; most values cluster near zero.

In telephone speech, the mu-law and A-law companding schemes give quiet sounds finer steps than loud ones, matching how speech amplitudes are distributed and how we hear. In neural networks, weights roughly follow a bell-shaped distribution, so the NF4 format used by QLoRA places its 16 levels according to a normal distribution, giving lower error than evenly spaced 4-bit levels for the same number of bits. Uniform quantization is simpler for hardware, which is why both remain in use.

## Why are sampling and quantization required?

Sampling and quantization turn an analogue signal into digital data. Sampling measures the signal at regular time or space intervals; quantization rounds each measurement to one of a fixed set of levels so it can be stored as a number.

Both are required because computers store finite numbers. In images, sampling sets the resolution, the pixel grid, and quantization sets the bit depth, such as 256 levels per colour channel. In audio, CD quality samples 44,100 times a second at 16 bits. Too few samples cause aliasing; too few levels cause banding or noise. Every vision model, including the face pipeline in FaceVision and the document models behind DocuLens AI, starts from images that were sampled and quantised this way.

## Does quantization affect accuracy?

Yes, usually a little. 8-bit quantization typically keeps accuracy very close to the original model, while 4-bit methods such as AWQ and GPTQ lose a small amount on most benchmarks. Below 4 bits, losses grow quickly.

The impact depends on the model, the method and the task. Larger models tolerate quantization better than small ones. Reasoning, maths, code and long-context tasks tend to degrade before simple chat. Calibration-based methods that protect important weights outperform naive rounding. The practical rule: evaluate the quantised model on your own test set, compare it with the full-precision version, and choose the lowest precision that meets your quality bar. Perplexity alone can hide task-specific drops.

## How does quantization affect multilingual LLMs?

Research suggests quantization hurts non-English languages, especially those in non-Latin scripts, more than English, and that automatic metrics can understate the damage. A 2024 study found human evaluators noticed larger drops than benchmarks showed.

For products serving Indian users in Hindi, Tamil or other languages, this matters: a 4-bit model that scores well in English may give weaker answers in Hindi. Test every language you support separately, include native speakers in evaluation, and consider higher precision or a larger model when multilingual quality is critical. The same study found difficult tasks such as mathematical reasoning degrade fastest, so test those in each language too.

## What is AWQ quantization?

AWQ, activation-aware weight quantization, is a 4-bit weight quantization method published by MIT researchers in 2023. It finds the small fraction of weights that matter most, judged by activation sizes, and protects them by scaling before quantising.

The key observation is that around 1 percent of weights or fewer, those connected to large activations, carry disproportionate importance. Instead of keeping them in higher precision, which complicates hardware, AWQ scales those channels up before quantization and compensates in the activations, reducing their rounding error. It needs only a small calibration set and no backpropagation, so it generalises well across domains. AWQ models are widely shared on Hugging Face and supported by inference engines such as vLLM.

## How do I quantize a model with AWQ?

The quickest path is to download an existing AWQ model from Hugging Face. To quantise your own, use a library such as vLLM's LLM Compressor, which took over from the archived AutoAWQ project, with a calibration dataset, then load the result in vLLM or Transformers.

A short tutorial outline:

- Pick a base model and a GPU with enough memory to load it in 16-bit.
- Prepare a few hundred calibration samples similar to your real inputs.
- Run the AWQ recipe with 4-bit weights and a group size of 128.
- Save the quantised model with its configuration.
- Load it and compare outputs with the original on your own test set.

Check the library's current documentation, because quantization tooling changes quickly.

# Best resume format and templates for freshers, section by section
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/resume-format-for-freshers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The best resume format for freshers is a clean, one-page, single-column layout that puts your strongest evidence first: for tech roles, that means projects with links, then skills, education, internships and achievements. Simple templates beat designer ones because many companies screen resumes with applicant tracking systems that struggle with columns, tables and graphics. This page covers templates and format, CV versus resume, length, and what to write in the summary, profile, skills and hobbies sections, plus how to make a good resume in Canva.

## What are the best resume templates for freshers?

The best templates are simple: one column, clear headings, standard fonts, and no photos, charts or skill bars. Google Docs and Word templates, LaTeX templates on Overleaf, and clean single-column Canva templates all work.

What to look for:

- One column, so text reads in the right order for screening software.
- Section headings such as Projects, Skills, Education, Experience.
- Plenty of white space and consistent formatting.
- Room for project links and short bullet points.

Avoid templates with two columns, icons for every skill, progress bars, photos or heavy colour. They look attractive but often parse badly and waste space. Recruiters spend seconds on a first read, so clarity wins.

## What is the right resume format for freshers?

Use a reverse-chronological layout adapted for freshers: header, short summary, projects, skills, education, internships or experience, and achievements. Put the section that best proves your fit near the top.

For tech roles, a strong order is:

- **Header**: name, phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub, portfolio.
- **Summary**: two lines tailored to the role.
- **Projects**: two or three with stack, what you built, a result and a link.
- **Skills**: grouped by languages, frameworks, tools, databases.
- **Education**: degree, college, years, CGPA if strong.
- **Experience**: internships, freelance work, leadership roles.
- **Achievements**: hackathons, competitive programming, certifications that matter.

Use action verbs and real numbers where you have them.

## Where can I get a free resume template for freshers?

Free sources include the resume templates in Google Docs and Microsoft Word, LaTeX templates on Overleaf, and free templates in Canva. Pick a single-column one and keep it plain.

Google Docs is the quickest and exports clean PDFs. Overleaf templates produce neat, consistent resumes and are popular among engineering students; LaTeX takes an hour to learn. Canva is fine if you choose a minimal template and avoid graphic elements. Whatever you use, save the final version as a PDF, name it sensibly, such as "FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf", and keep an editable copy so you can tailor it for each application.

## Should a fresher use a CV or a resume?

In India, recruiters often use the words interchangeably and mean the same short document. Strictly, a resume is a one or two-page summary tailored to a job, while a CV is a longer, complete record of academic history, used for research, academia and some countries.

For freshers applying to companies, send a one-page resume, even if the application form says "CV". Use a long academic CV only for research positions, PhD or master's applications abroad, or when an institution specifically asks for full academic details such as publications, conferences and teaching. When applying internationally, check local conventions: in the UK and Europe, "CV" often means a two-page resume.

## Can a fresher's resume be two pages?

Keep it to one page. A fresher rarely has enough relevant experience to fill two pages with strong content, and recruiters reading quickly may never reach page two.

Fit it on one page by cutting weak items: school-level achievements, generic skills like "MS Office" for a developer role, long objective statements, and course lists. Keep only projects and experience that support the role, with two or three bullet points each. If you have substantial research, publications or multiple internships, a second page can be justified, but then the first page must still carry your best evidence. Consistent, readable formatting matters more than squeezing in everything.

## What is the summary in a resume for freshers?

The summary is a two to three-line introduction at the top that states your target role, your strongest skills and your best evidence. It replaces the old "objective" statement and should be tailored to each application.

Example for a GenAI role: "Final-year BCA student building GenAI applications with Python, FastAPI and LLM APIs. Built a document question-answering app with retrieval and citations, deployed and used by classmates. Looking for a GenAI engineering internship." Keep it specific and factual. Avoid clichés such as "hard-working team player seeking a challenging role". If you cannot write something specific, skip the summary and let projects speak.

## What is the profile section in a resume for freshers?

A profile section is another name for the summary: a short paragraph about who you are professionally and what you offer. Some templates also use "profile" for links such as LinkedIn, GitHub and portfolio.

Write the profile in the same way as a summary: role, key skills, best evidence, in two or three lines. If your template has a separate profile links section, include LinkedIn, GitHub and a portfolio site, and make sure each link works and shows your best work. A GitHub with clean, pinned projects and good READMEs supports every claim in your resume, so prepare it before you send applications.

## What should I write in the skills section of a fresher's resume?

List skills you can prove, grouped by type and matched to the job description: programming languages, frameworks, databases, tools and platforms. Every skill should appear in at least one project or experience entry.

An example for a developer:

- **Languages**: Python, JavaScript, SQL.
- **Frameworks**: FastAPI, React, Next.js.
- **Data and AI**: pandas, scikit-learn, LLM APIs, embeddings and vector search.
- **Tools**: Git, Docker, Linux, VS Code.
- **Cloud**: Vercel, Render, basic AWS or Azure.

Avoid rating bars and percentages, which mean nothing to a reader. Skip skills you used once in a tutorial; interviewers will ask about anything listed.

## Should I add hobbies to a fresher's resume?

Only if they add something: evidence of discipline, leadership, creativity or relevant skills, or a genuine conversation starter. If space is tight, drop hobbies before dropping projects.

Hobbies that help are specific: "run a 500-member student tech community", "competitive chess, state level", "write a weekly blog on web development", or "build robots for a school robotics club". Generic lines such as "reading, music, travelling" add little. Never list hobbies you cannot talk about, because interviewers sometimes use them to break the ice. For tech roles, community and building activities can sit under "Achievements" or "Leadership" instead.

## How do I make a fresher's resume in Canva?

Pick a single-column, minimal template, replace the content with your own, remove decorative graphics, photos and skill bars, use standard fonts, and download it as a PDF. Then check that the text can be selected and copied in order.

Steps:

- Search Canva's resume templates and filter for simple, single-column designs.
- Set the page to A4 and keep margins reasonable.
- Use clear headings and bullet points, not text boxes scattered across the page.
- Add clickable links to GitHub, LinkedIn and your portfolio.
- Download as "PDF Standard" and test by copying all text into a plain text editor.

If the copied text comes out jumbled, an applicant tracking system may read it the same way, so simplify the layout.

# RAG explained: how retrieval-augmented generation helps LLMs, privacy, tutorial, roadmap
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/retrieval-augmented-generation-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, is a technique where an AI application searches a knowledge source for relevant information and gives it to a language model along with the question, so the answer draws on current, specific and citable facts instead of the model's memory alone. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, with hybrid retrieval, fusion, reranking, cited answers, a confidence gate and multi-provider fallback, so this page covers what RAG is, how it helps LLMs, context limits, privacy, retriever training, best practices, a tutorial, an example and a roadmap.

## What is retrieval-augmented generation in AI applications?

In AI applications, RAG combines a retriever, which finds relevant passages from documents, databases or the web, with a generator, a language model that writes the answer using those passages. It turns a general model into a domain-specific assistant without retraining.

The term comes from a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, which combined a neural retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator. Today RAG describes a broad pattern used in support bots, enterprise search, legal and medical assistants, study tools and coding assistants. The application controls what knowledge the model sees, which makes answers more accurate, current and auditable, especially when each claim cites its source document.

## How does RAG enhance the capabilities of an LLM?

RAG gives an LLM knowledge it lacks: private data, recent events and specialised documents. It reduces hallucination by grounding answers in retrieved evidence, enables citations, and lets you update knowledge by changing documents rather than retraining the model.

It also improves efficiency: a smaller, cheaper model with good retrieval often matches a larger model without it on domain questions. Access control becomes possible, since retrieval can filter documents by user permissions. RAG does not improve reasoning itself, and poor retrieval can still mislead the model, so quality depends on chunking, search, reranking and prompts. A confidence gate, like the one in RAG.NextUpgrad, lets the system decline when evidence is weak.

## How does RAG work around limited context length?

Instead of putting entire documents into the prompt, RAG selects only the most relevant chunks for each question, so a corpus of millions of pages fits through a context window of a few thousand tokens.

Techniques that help: chunk documents into focused passages; retrieve broadly, then rerank and keep only the top few; compress or summarise passages before generation; deduplicate overlapping chunks; and use hierarchical retrieval, first finding relevant documents, then relevant sections. Even with long-context models, RAG stays useful, because stuffing huge contexts is slower, costlier and can bury key facts in the middle, where models attend less reliably. Selecting the right evidence beats sending everything.

## Does RAG let the LLM violate my data privacy?

RAG itself does not leak data, but it sends retrieved passages to the model, so privacy depends on where that model runs and on access controls. With a hosted API, your passages reach the provider; with a local model, they stay on your infrastructure.

Protect privacy by enforcing permission filters in retrieval so users only see documents they may access; choosing providers with data processing agreements and no training on your data; masking personal data before indexing where possible; running local models for sensitive content; logging access; and defending against prompt injection in documents, which can trick models into revealing other content. FaceVision applies a similar principle in vision: it stores embeddings only, never images.

## How is the retriever's query encoder trained end-to-end in RAG?

In the original RAG paper, the retrieved documents are treated as latent variables. The model marginalises the generator's output probability over the top retrieved documents, so gradients from the generation loss flow back into the query encoder through the document scores.

Specifically, the query encoder from DPR produces a query vector; document scores are inner products with precomputed document vectors; these scores become a probability distribution over retrieved documents; and the final loss combines the generator's likelihood for each document weighted by those probabilities. To keep training affordable, the document encoder and index stay fixed, and only the query encoder and generator are updated. Most production RAG systems skip end-to-end training and use pretrained embedding models instead.

## What are the best practices in retrieval-augmented generation?

Use structure-aware chunking with metadata, hybrid retrieval combining BM25 and embeddings, reranking, clear prompts that require citations and allow refusal, and an evaluation set that measures both retrieval and answer quality before and after every change.

More practices: clean and deduplicate source documents; keep chunk sizes appropriate to your content, often a few hundred tokens; add titles and section headings to chunks; rewrite conversational follow-ups into standalone queries; filter by permissions and freshness; stream answers; log questions with low-confidence retrieval; and monitor latency and cost. Provide fallbacks, such as a second model provider, for reliability. RAG.NextUpgrad uses multi-provider fallback for exactly this reason.

## What is a good RAG tutorial?

Build the simplest working version first: load a few documents, split them into chunks, embed them, store them in a vector store, retrieve the top matches for a question, and send them with the question to a language model. Then improve step by step.

Good tutorials include LangChain's and LlamaIndex's RAG guides, the Hugging Face cookbook, and DeepLearning.AI short courses. After the basics, add improvements one at a time and measure each: hybrid search, reranking, better chunking, citations and refusal behaviour. Use 20 to 50 real questions with known answers as your test set. Deploy with FastAPI and a simple frontend, and you have a portfolio project that demonstrates real AI engineering skills.

## How do you use RAG with ChromaDB and Mistral-7B-Instruct?

Embed your document chunks with a sentence embedding model and store them in a Chroma collection; for each question, query Chroma for the top chunks, format them into a prompt using Mistral-7B-Instruct's chat template, and generate the answer with the model.

Run Mistral-7B-Instruct locally through Ollama, llama.cpp or Hugging Face Transformers with 4-bit quantization on a consumer GPU. Chroma can compute embeddings automatically with its default embedding function, or you can pass your own. Keep the prompt explicit: instruct the model to answer only from the provided context, cite chunk sources, and say when the answer is missing. Small models follow instructions less reliably, so test carefully and keep retrieved context short and relevant.

## What is an example of retrieval-augmented generation?

A company help assistant is a classic example: a customer asks how to reset a router, the system retrieves the relevant manual section and troubleshooting article, and the model answers with steps and links to those sources.

Other examples: a university assistant answering questions about course rules from official handbooks; a legal tool retrieving relevant clauses from contracts; a doctor's reference tool citing clinical guidelines; and a coding assistant searching internal documentation. The OCR & Speech Workspace I built shows a document example: it OCRs uploaded files with Mistral and answers questions with document-scoped RAG and page citations, so users can check each answer against the exact page.

## What is a retrieval-augmented generation roadmap?

Learn Python and APIs; then embeddings and vector search; then a basic RAG app; then hybrid retrieval, reranking and chunking strategies; then evaluation; then agentic RAG, GraphRAG and multimodal retrieval; and finally production concerns such as security, monitoring and cost.

Milestones: a notebook RAG over your own notes; a deployed RAG API with citations; a measured comparison of vector, keyword and hybrid retrieval; reranking added with before-and-after metrics; an evaluation suite with faithfulness and retrieval scores; and an agent that chooses between document search and a database. Read the original RAG paper and recent surveys, and follow engineering blogs from teams running RAG in production to learn real failure modes.

# Retrieval augmented generation guide: examples, tutorials, courses, books, tools, LLMs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/retrieval-augmented-generation-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, connects a language model to your documents so it answers from evidence with citations instead of relying only on training data. It is the most common pattern for building useful AI assistants. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, reranking, cited streaming and a confidence gate, so this page explains RAG, a step-by-step guide, examples, tutorials, PDFs, courses, books, tools, the best LLMs and fine-tuning versus RAG. What is retrieval augmented generation, explained simply? RAG combines search with generation: when a user asks a question, the system retrieves relevant passages from a knowledge source, adds them to the prompt, and the language model writes an answer grounded in that evidence, ideally with citations. Also asked as: retrieval augmented generation explained The term comes from a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research. RAG solves key LLM limits: outdated knowledge, no access to private documents and confident hallucination. Because knowledge lives in an index rather than model weights, you update answers by updating documents, without retraining. Retrieval can use keyword search, embeddings or both. RAG powers support assistants, internal knowledge tools and document question answering, and its quality depends mostly on retrieval. What is a step-by-step guide to building RAG? Load and clean documents, split them into chunks, embed and index them, retrieve with hybrid dense and keyword search, rerank the top results, prompt the model to answer only from retrieved passages with citations, then evaluate and monitor. Each step has choices: chunk by headings or semantic boundaries, keep metadata for filtering and citations, and merge retrieval results with reciprocal rank fusion. Add a confidence gate so the system declines when evidence is weak, as RAG.NextUpgrad does. Evaluate retrieval recall separately from answer faithfulness using tools such as RAGAS. Stream answers for responsiveness, log retrieved passages for debugging, and refresh indexes when documents change. What are examples of retrieval augmented generation? Examples include support chatbots answering from help centre articles, internal assistants searching company policies, legal research tools citing cases, medical guideline assistants, coding assistants grounded in documentation, and study tools answering from course notes. Also asked as: guide to retrieval augmented generation · retrieval augmented generation examples · course on retrieval augmented generation The OCR &amp; Speech Workspace I built uses document-scoped RAG: users upload documents, Mistral OCR extracts text page by page, and answers cite specific pages. RAG.NextUpgrad applies hybrid retrieval and reranking to general document collections with cited streaming answers. Enterprise products such as Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google's NotebookLM use RAG over users' own content. Each example pairs retrieval with clear citations users can check, grounding answers in verifiable sources rather than model memory. What does a RAG tutorial cover? A typical RAG tutorial loads documents, splits them into chunks, creates embeddings, stores them in a vector store such as Chroma or FAISS, retrieves relevant chunks for a question, and passes them to an LLM to generate an answer. Good tutorials go further: hybrid search, reranking, citations, evaluation and handling questions without answers. LangChain's and LlamaIndex's official RAG tutorials are solid starting points, and the rag-from-scratch repository walks through advanced techniques step by step. After following one, rebuild the pipeline with your own documents and twenty real questions, measuring how often the right passage is retrieved. That exercise teaches more than reading several tutorials. Is there a retrieval augmented generation tutorial PDF? There is no single official RAG tutorial PDF, but the foundational papers are freely available as PDFs on arXiv, including the original 2020 RAG paper and comprehensive surveys of RAG techniques. Documentation pages can also be saved as PDFs. Also asked as: rag retrieval augmented generation tutorial The survey by Gao and colleagues reviews naive, advanced and modular RAG approaches, retrieval methods, augmentation and evaluation, making it a useful offline reference. Framework documentation from LangChain and LlamaIndex can be printed for study. Be cautious with unofficial PDFs circulating online, which may be outdated given how fast tools change. Pair reading with hands-on building, since retrieval quality only becomes clear when you test real questions. What are good courses on retrieval augmented generation? Strong options include DeepLearning.AI's RAG courses, including short courses on advanced RAG and knowledge graphs for RAG and a longer RAG course on Coursera, plus IBM's generative AI courses with RAG modules and LangChain Academy. Look for courses that cover chunking strategies, hybrid retrieval, reranking, evaluation and production concerns such as latency, cost and access control, not just a basic demo. Coursera courses can usually be audited for free, with certificates through paid enrolment or financial aid. Complete the projects with your own documents. Discussion forums attached to courses help when you get stuck. Combine courses with framework documentation, since libraries evolve faster than recorded lessons. What are the best books on retrieval augmented generation? Useful books include RAG-Driven Generative AI by Denis Rothman and Unlocking Data with Generative AI and RAG by Keith Bourne, while broader books such as Chip Huyen's AI Engineering and Hands-On Large Language Models include strong RAG chapters. Books are best for concepts: retrieval methods, chunking, evaluation and system design trade-offs. For current APIs and tools, rely on documentation and recent papers, since frameworks change quickly. Read sample chapters before buying, prefer books with maintained code repositories, and check publication dates, favouring recent editions. Pair each chapter with experiments on your own data. The RAG survey papers on arXiv complement books with up-to-date overviews of techniques. What are the best tools for retrieval augmented generation? Core tools include frameworks such as LangChain, LlamaIndex and Haystack; vector databases such as pgvector, Qdrant and Weaviate; embedding models such as BGE-M3 or commercial APIs; rerankers such as Cohere Rerank or BGE rerankers; and document parsers such as Docling and Unstructured. For evaluation, RAGAS, TruLens and DeepEval measure faithfulness, relevance and retrieval quality, while Langfuse and similar tools trace requests in production. OCR tools, such as Mistral OCR used in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, handle scanned documents. Choose tools your team can operate, and remember that good chunking, hybrid retrieval and reranking often matter more than any specific framework choice. Start simple and add components only when measurements justify them. What is the best LLM for retrieval augmented generation? The best RAG models follow instructions closely, use long context well, cite sources faithfully and decline when evidence is missing. Strong choices include Claude, GPT and Gemini models, Cohere's Command models designed for RAG, and open models such as Qwen, Llama and gpt-oss. Retrieval quality usually matters more than model size: a mid-size model with excellent retrieval and reranking can beat a larger model with weak retrieval. Test candidates on your own questions, measuring faithfulness, citation accuracy and refusal behaviour when answers are absent. Consider latency and cost per query at your expected volume. RAG.NextUpgrad's multi-provider fallback shows the value of keeping the model swappable as better options appear. Fine-tuning vs retrieval augmented generation: which should you use? Use RAG when answers depend on specific, changing or private knowledge that must be cited. Use fine-tuning to change behaviour, such as format, tone or a narrow skill. Many production systems combine both: RAG supplies facts, fine-tuning shapes how answers are written. Also asked as: fine tuning vs retrieval augmented generation RAG updates instantly when documents change and shows sources, while fine-tuning bakes behaviour into weights and does not reliably teach new facts. Fine-tuning can also make a smaller model follow RAG instructions better, such as citing passages consistently. Start with RAG and prompting, measure where they fall short, then fine-tune for those gaps, evaluating both on the same test set. FineTune Studio and RAG.NextUpgrad represent these two complementary approaches in practice.
