# Small language models: hallucination, size, training, fine-tuning, local use, agents
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/small-language-models-training-local-agents/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Small language models trade breadth for efficiency: they run on laptops, phones and browsers, cost little to serve and can be fine-tuned cheaply, but they know less and hallucinate more on facts. I fine-tune small models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio and run models in the browser for FaceVision, so this page covers hallucination, how small is small, training and building one, fine-tuning, running locally, retrieval, why researchers care, the hype and agents. Do small language models hallucinate? Yes, and generally more than large models on factual questions, because fewer parameters store less world knowledge. They may confidently invent names, dates or details, especially for rare topics. Reduce hallucination by giving small models the facts through retrieval, constraining outputs with schemas, fine-tuning them on domain data with examples of declining when unsure, and keeping tasks narrow, such as classification or extraction where answers come from the input. Evaluation should measure faithfulness to provided context, not just fluency. In RAG designs such as RAG.NextUpgrad, a confidence gate that declines when evidence is weak helps whichever model size you use. Always test hallucination rates on your own questions. How many parameters does a small language model have? There is no strict definition, but small language models usually range from a few hundred million to around ten or fifteen billion parameters, small enough to run on a single consumer GPU, laptop or phone. Also asked as: how many parameters in small language models The boundary keeps moving as hardware improves and large models grow. Mixture-of-experts models blur it further: a model may have thirty billion total parameters but activate only three billion per token, running nearly as fast as a small dense model. Practically, small often means a model you can run locally with acceptable speed. Examples include Qwen3 at 0.6B to 8B, Gemma 3 at 1B to 12B, Llama 3.2 at 1B and 3B, and Phi-4-mini. How are small language models trained? Small language models are pretrained on trillions of tokens of filtered text, often including high-quality synthetic data, then instruction-tuned and aligned with preference methods. Many also learn from larger models through distillation. Data quality matters more at small scale: Microsoft's Phi models showed that carefully curated, textbook-style data lets small models punch above their weight. Google's Gemma models used distillation, training on a larger teacher's predictions. Training small models longer than older scaling rules suggested improves quality per parameter. After pretraining, supervised fine-tuning teaches instruction following, and preference tuning improves helpfulness and safety. Open projects such as SmolLM document these recipes publicly. How do you create a small language model? You can train a tiny language model from scratch for learning, following Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT or nanochat repositories: build a tokenizer, prepare text data, define a small transformer, train on a GPU and evaluate. Useful models usually start from existing ones instead. Also asked as: how to create a small language model Training a capable small model from scratch needs huge datasets and substantial compute, so practitioners almost always fine-tune an existing open model for their task. Building one from scratch remains an excellent way to understand transformers, tokenization and training dynamics. Start with a character-level model on a small corpus, then scale up. Sebastian Raschka's book Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) walks through the full process in PyTorch. How do you fine-tune small language models? Collect a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality examples of your task, choose an instruction-tuned base model, and train with LoRA or QLoRA using tools such as Unsloth, TRL or Axolotl, then compare the tuned model with the base model. Also asked as: how to fine tune small language models Small models make fine-tuning cheap: a 1B to 4B model can be fine-tuned on a free Colab GPU or a consumer card in hours. Use the correct chat template, a small learning rate and few epochs, watching validation loss for overfitting. Test on held-out examples and check general skills for regressions. FineTune Studio follows this workflow, streaming live loss charts and showing base-versus-tuned outputs side by side. How do you run a small language model locally? Use Ollama or LM Studio on a laptop or desktop, llama.cpp for maximum control, MLX on Apple silicon Macs, or browser runtimes such as WebLLM and Transformers.js with WebGPU. Phones can run small models through on-device frameworks. Also asked as: how to run small language model locally Download a quantized version, such as 4-bit GGUF, to reduce memory use; a 3B to 8B model runs comfortably on most modern laptops. On phones, Google's AI Edge tools and Apple's Foundation Models framework give apps access to on-device models. Browser deployment, similar to how FaceVision runs vision models with ONNX Runtime Web, keeps data on the user's device. Measure tokens per second and memory before choosing a model size. Can small language models use what they retrieve? Yes, but less reliably than large models. Small models sometimes ignore retrieved passages, get distracted by irrelevant ones, or blend context with invented details. Careful retrieval, clear prompts and fine-tuning improve their faithfulness. Send fewer, better passages using hybrid search and reranking, so the model sees mainly relevant evidence. Instruct it to answer only from the context and cite sources. Fine-tuning methods such as RAFT train models to use relevant documents and ignore distractors, improving grounded answering. Measure faithfulness directly by checking whether answers are supported by retrieved text. Small embedding models and rerankers also run locally alongside them. With good retrieval, small models can match larger ones on domain question answering. Why do researchers care about small language models? Small models are cheaper to train and study, run on accessible hardware, protect privacy on devices, and reveal how data quality, distillation and training choices affect capability, making AI research more reproducible and inclusive. Universities and independent researchers can experiment with small models without massive compute budgets, testing ideas that later scale up. Small models also enable applications in low-resource settings, such as offline tools for regions with limited connectivity, and languages underserved by large commercial models. They lower energy use per query. Work on small models has shown that curated and synthetic data can substitute for sheer scale in many tasks. Open releases with documented recipes accelerate this work. Why are small language models called the next big thing in AI? Small models are gaining attention because they cut costs and latency, run privately on devices, can be specialised cheaply, and handle many real tasks well enough, especially combined with retrieval and larger models for hard cases. Also asked as: why small language models are the next big thing in ai As companies scale AI features to millions of users, per-request costs matter, and small models can be many times cheaper to serve. On-device AI in phones and laptops depends on them. Specialised fine-tuned small models often beat general large models on narrow tasks. The claim is partly hype, since frontier models remain essential for complex reasoning, but the trend toward mixing model sizes is real and growing. Expect hybrid architectures to become the default. How are small language models key to scalable agentic AI? Agents make many model calls per task, so cost and latency multiply quickly. Small models can handle most routine steps, such as routing, extraction and tool calls, while larger models handle the hardest reasoning, making agent systems affordable at scale. Also asked as: how small language models are key to scalable agentic ai NVIDIA researchers argued in 2025 that small language models are sufficient for many agent subtasks and more economical to deploy. Fine-tuning a small model on an agent's real tool-calling logs can improve reliability for that workflow. Heterogeneous systems route each step to the cheapest capable model, escalating when confidence is low. This design also enables on-device agents that keep data private and work offline, which matters for sensitive personal and business data.

# What is Smart India Hackathon? Who runs it, how it works, eligibility and SPOC
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/smart-india-hackathon-guide-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Smart India Hackathon (SIH) is a nationwide initiative in which student teams from colleges across India build solutions to problem statements posed by central ministries, state departments, public sector bodies and industry, with software and hardware editions and a grand finale for shortlisted teams. It is among the largest hackathons in the country. As a three-time hackathon winner who has judged and mentored teams, I have put together the essentials: who runs SIH and when it began, how it works, eligibility, the SPOC and internal hackathon, problem statements, presenting, and checking results.

## What is Smart India Hackathon?

Smart India Hackathon is a national programme that gives students the chance to solve real problems faced by government and industry, by building working prototypes and presenting them to experts. It runs in editions, typically with a software category and a hardware category.

Problem statements are published on the official portal, and teams choose one, propose a solution, and, if selected, build it during a grand finale at nodal centres. Beyond prizes, SIH offers exposure to real problems, mentoring from domain experts, and a chance for strong solutions to be taken forward. For students, it is a major line on a CV and an intense learning experience in teamwork and building under pressure.

## Who conducts Smart India Hackathon?

Smart India Hackathon is conducted by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell together with AICTE, with support from partner organisations, ministries, state governments and companies that contribute problem statements, mentors and judges.

The organisers manage registration, problem statements, evaluation and the grand finale, while participating institutions coordinate their teams through a designated SPOC. Problem statement owners, such as ministries or companies, often take part in evaluating solutions for their statements. Official announcements, rules and results are published on the SIH website and official social channels.

## When did Smart India Hackathon start?

Smart India Hackathon began in 2017 and has been held in editions since then, growing in the number of participating students, institutions and problem statements, with additional formats such as a junior edition for school students in some years.

Each edition updates its rules, timelines and categories, so information from previous years may not apply. If you are planning ahead, read past editions' problem statements to understand the style and domains, such as agriculture, health, education, smart automation, disaster management and sustainability, then check the current edition's official guidelines for dates and eligibility.

## How does Smart India Hackathon work?

The typical flow is: problem statements are published, institutions run internal hackathons to select teams, SPOCs nominate selected teams with idea presentations on the portal, experts evaluate submissions, and shortlisted teams build their solutions at the grand finale, where winners are chosen per problem statement.

Stages in brief:

- **Problem statements**: published on the official portal.
- **Internal hackathon**: each institution selects its best teams.
- **Idea submission**: teams submit a presentation in the official format through the SPOC.
- **Evaluation**: experts shortlist teams for each statement.
- **Grand finale**: teams build and present at nodal centres, often over a continuous multi-hour hackathon with mentoring rounds.

Exact steps change by edition; follow the current guidelines.

## Who is eligible for Smart India Hackathon?

Students currently enrolled in recognised higher education institutions in India are eligible, participating in teams through their institution. Rules on team size and composition, such as including at least one female member, are set for each edition.

Typical requirements cover team size, mixing members across branches or years, a mentor from the institution, and participation through the institution's SPOC rather than directly. Check the current edition's eligibility rules on the official website, since they can change. If your college has not registered, ask your faculty or innovation cell coordinator to register and appoint a SPOC.

## What is a SPOC in Smart India Hackathon?

SPOC means Single Point of Contact: a faculty member or official designated by the institution to manage SIH participation, including registration, the internal hackathon, nominating teams and communicating with organisers.

Students should contact their SPOC early to learn internal deadlines, the selection process and how to submit ideas. The SPOC uploads selected teams' details and presentations on the portal and receives official communication. If you do not know who your SPOC is, ask your department head, training and placement cell or institution's innovation council. Respect internal deadlines; they are usually earlier than the national ones.

## What is the internal Smart India Hackathon?

The internal hackathon is the college-level round where an institution evaluates its student teams and selects the best ideas to nominate for the national stage. Each institution runs it in its own format, guided by the official instructions.

It is your first filter, so treat it seriously: choose a problem statement, research it, build an early prototype if possible, and present clearly using the official template. Judges at internal rounds look for understanding of the problem, feasibility, innovation and team capability. Feedback from this round is valuable; use it to sharpen your idea before national submission.

## What are the Smart India Hackathon problem statements?

Problem statements are real challenges published by ministries, departments, public sector organisations and companies, each describing a problem, context and expected outcome, across themes such as agriculture, healthcare, education, disaster management, clean energy, transport and smart automation.

To choose well:

- Read the full statement, including organisation and category.
- Prefer statements where you understand the user and can access or simulate data.
- Check how many teams might pick it; popular statements need a sharper angle.
- Sketch a demo you could build in the finale time.

Use the official portal for the current edition's list; unofficial lists can be outdated or incomplete.

## How do I present for Smart India Hackathon?

Use the official presentation template exactly, and make every slide count: problem understanding, proposed solution, technical approach, feasibility, impact and the team. Include diagrams, mock-ups or prototype screenshots instead of long text.

Tips from judging experience:

- Open with the user and the problem in one clear slide.
- Show the solution flow as a diagram.
- Name the technologies and explain why they fit.
- Address risks: data availability, scalability, cost.
- Show impact with realistic, sourced numbers where possible.
- Rehearse answers to likely questions.

At the finale, a working demo of the core flow outweighs ambitious slides.

## How do I check Smart India Hackathon results?

Check results on the official SIH website and official social media channels, where shortlisted teams and winners are announced for each edition. Your SPOC also receives communication about your team's status.

Be cautious of unofficial websites and forwarded messages claiming results or asking for payments to "confirm selection"; SIH does not charge teams to participate. If results are delayed, follow official channels for updates. Whatever the outcome, keep your project: a well-documented SIH prototype with a clear README is a strong portfolio item and a good story for interviews.

# Smart India Hackathon guide: how SIH works, how to register through your college, choose a problem statement, clear the internal round and present to ministry judges
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/smart-india-hackathon-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is Smart India Hackathon?

**Smart India Hackathon is a nationwide competition organised by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell with AICTE and partners, in which student teams build solutions to problem statements posted by central and state government departments, public sector organisations and industry [1][2]. Teams register through their own college, go through an internal selection round, and shortlisted teams compete at the national level, where the problem statement's owners sit on the judging panels. It has software and hardware editions and runs on a months-long calendar.**


Everything specific to a year, the dates, the number of problem statements, the team size rules, the prize amounts, changes each cycle and is published on the official portal [1]. This page is about the parts that do not change: how the structure works and what wins inside it.

I have won three hackathons and lost one that taught me more, and I have judged and mentored at college events since. SIH is different from a weekend campus hackathon in two ways that decide everything: the judges own the problem, and the internal round is the real competition.

> At a campus hackathon you impress an engineer. At SIH you have to convince the person whose department will live with your solution. Build for the second person from day one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does Smart India Hackathon work, step by step?

**Problem statements are published on the portal. Your college registers as a participating institute and appoints a coordinator. Students form teams within the rules and register under the college. The college runs an internal hackathon to shortlist teams, typically a handful per problem statement it nominates. Shortlisted teams submit ideas through the portal, are evaluated, and the selected ones are invited to the grand finale, a multi-day build at a nodal centre, judged by the problem statement owners and experts.**



The rules for team size, gender composition, mentor involvement and eligibility have varied between editions; the portal's current rules override anything you read elsewhere, including here [1].

## How do I register for Smart India Hackathon?

**Registration runs through your institute, not directly as an individual. Find your college's SIH coordinator, often in the training and placement cell or the innovation cell, confirm the college is registered for the current edition, form your team within the rules, and register your team under the college on the portal by the deadline. If your college is not registered, the coordinator registers the institute first. Start this a month before the internal round, because approvals move at college speed.**


If your college has never participated, a small group of students taking the portal's institute registration page to the principal with the previous year's results usually gets it done. That is how many first-time colleges join.

## How do I choose a problem statement?

**Read the full statement, not the title, and answer four questions: who owns it and what outcome do they need; what data or systems does the solution depend on and can you get or simulate them; what is the constraint that makes it hard for the owner today; and can your team build a working prototype of the core in the time available. Prefer statements where you can reach a real user of the department's service. Avoid ones that need data you will never see.**



KrishGyan, which won Changethon at IIT Roorkee, came from exactly this reading of a problem: farmers who do not read or type, a voice-first assistant in their language over WhatsApp [4]. The same reading applies to ministry statements: find the constraint everyone else will ignore, and design for it.

## How do I clear the internal college round?

**Treat the internal presentation as the final, because for most teams it is. Bring a working prototype, even a thin one, not a slide deck. Open with the department's problem in its own words, demo the core in two minutes, show one architecture slide, then say what a pilot would look like. Practise the pitch with a timer. Ask the coordinator what the internal judges weigh and match it. Most internal panels eliminate on clarity and feasibility, not on ambition.**



## What do SIH judges look for at the grand finale?

**The same four things every hackathon judge scores, weighted toward the owner's reality: feasibility, does it work and can it run in their environment; innovation, is there an insight about their problem; practicality, would their staff and citizens adopt it; and problem solving, did you understand the constraint. Ministry judges add a fifth: fit with existing systems and policy. Show that you know what the department already runs and how your solution attaches to it.**


Those four criteria are the ones I put on screen when I brief a judging room, and the ones I have written about after sitting on panels [5][6]. At SIH the panel includes the people who wrote the statement, so the fifth criterion carries more weight than at any campus event.


## What should the SIH presentation contain?

**The portal prescribes a template for the idea submission; use it exactly. Inside it, the order that wins: the problem as the department experiences it, the proposed solution in one diagram, a working demo or a video of one, the technical approach with honest limits, feasibility and the constraints you honoured, the impact for the department and the citizen, and a pilot plan. Keep every slide readable from the back of a room.**


The general pitch deck structure I recommend, adapted to whatever template the portal requires that year, is written up separately [7].

## How do I build the prototype for SIH?

**Build the core workflow end to end first, with seeded or simulated data that looks like the department's, and make it demonstrable in three minutes. Honour the constraints in the statement, low bandwidth, regional languages, feature phones, offline use, from the first version, because that is where ministry judges look. Keep an architecture that could plausibly run inside government infrastructure. Add features only after the demo path is solid.**



## What happens after Smart India Hackathon?

**Winners receive prizes, and in many cases the problem owner explores piloting or developing the solution further with the team; several past solutions have continued as products or government pilots. Whether you win or not, the project, the repository and the write-up are the durable result. Publish them, add the finale to LinkedIn under honours with the statement and department, and use the story in interviews. The line "grand finalist, Smart India Hackathon, problem statement from [department]" is understood by every Indian recruiter.**


Prize amounts and post-event arrangements are set per edition on the portal [1]; do not rely on figures from earlier years.


## Common mistakes SIH teams make

**Choosing a statement by its title. Building for three months without ever showing a department user. Presenting the tech stack before the problem. Ignoring the constraint in the statement, offline, language, device, and getting caught in Q&A. Six people with no roles. A demo that needs the venue's Wi-Fi. Reading the previous year's rules instead of this year's. Every one of these is avoidable with the checklists above.**



## Can you mentor or judge our SIH team or internal hackathon?

**Yes. I mentor teams on statement selection, scoping and the demo, and I judge and brief judging panels at college internal rounds, on-site across India or remote. Send the statement you are considering and your date.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Speech AI guide: TTS vs AI, conversion, code, best tools, realtime, iPhone, Kindle
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/speech-ai-tts-tools-realtime-iphone/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Text-to-speech and speech-to-text are now powered by AI models that produce natural voices and accurate transcripts, often in real time. Using them well means understanding how conversion works, which tools fit, and how to fix common device problems. I built the OCR &amp; Speech Workspace with live speech-to-text, so this page covers text-to-speech versus AI, the conversion process, code, the best transcription tools, realtime transcription, iPhone fixes, Kindle, energy use and Premiere Pro. What is the difference between text to speech and AI? Text-to-speech is a task: converting written text into spoken audio. AI is the broad field of building systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence. Modern text-to-speech uses AI, specifically neural networks, to produce natural-sounding voices. Older text-to-speech systems used hand-written rules or stitched together recorded sound units, producing robotic or choppy speech without machine learning. Neural text-to-speech, from WaveNet onwards, learns pronunciation, rhythm and intonation from recordings, enabling expressive voices, many languages and voice cloning. So all modern AI voices are text-to-speech systems, but not all text-to-speech is AI. When people say AI voice, they usually mean neural text-to-speech, sometimes combined with a language model for conversation. What does text to speech conversion involve? Conversion involves normalising text, such as expanding numbers and abbreviations, converting words into phonemes, predicting prosody such as stress and pitch, generating an acoustic representation, and turning it into an audio waveform with a vocoder. For example, a sentence containing a date, a number and an abbreviation must become spoken words with correct expansions, which depend on context and locale. Grapheme-to-phoneme models handle pronunciation, including names and borrowed words. Neural acoustic models predict spectrograms, and vocoders synthesise sound. Many modern systems combine these steps end to end. SSML markup lets developers control pauses, emphasis and pronunciation. Errors usually come from normalisation, such as reading chemical formulas or abbreviations oddly. How do you convert a text string to speech in code? In Python, pyttsx3 speaks a string offline using your operating system's voices, while cloud SDKs from OpenAI, Azure or Google return natural neural audio files. In browsers, JavaScript's Web Speech API speaks text with the speechSynthesis interface. Also asked as: how to convert text string to speech sound For offline neural quality, open-source engines such as Piper run locally and are fast enough for real-time use on modest hardware. Cloud APIs offer the most natural voices and many languages, but need network access and handle data externally. Save generated audio to files and cache repeated phrases to save time. For accessibility features in web apps, test voices on different browsers and devices, since available voices vary widely between platforms. What are the best speech to text AI tools? Strong options include OpenAI's Whisper and newer transcription models, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Azure AI Speech, Amazon Transcribe and ElevenLabs Scribe. For local use, whisper.cpp and faster-whisper run Whisper efficiently on your own hardware. Choose by language support, accuracy on your audio, speaker labelling, real-time streaming, timestamps, privacy and cost. For Indian languages and code-mixed speech, test carefully, and consider models from AI4Bharat alongside commercial services. Benchmarks rarely match your recordings, so transcribe a sample of real audio, including noisy and accented speech, and compare word error rates. Live speech-to-text in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace sits alongside OCR, which suits document and meeting workflows. Why is realtime the future of speech to text? Realtime transcription powers experiences that batch transcription cannot: voice agents that respond within a second, live captions for accessibility, meeting notes as you speak, and translation during conversations. Users increasingly expect immediate, streaming results. Also asked as: why realtime is the future of speech-to-text Streaming models transcribe audio as it arrives, returning partial results that update as more context comes in, with latency of a few hundred milliseconds. Combined with fast language models and text-to-speech, they enable natural voice conversations with AI. Challenges include accuracy on partial audio, deciding when a speaker has finished, and cost at scale. For students, live captions also make lectures easier to follow and review. Live speech-to-text in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace reflects this shift toward immediate transcription. Why does speech to text not work on iPhone? Check that Dictation is enabled under Settings, General, Keyboard, that the correct dictation language is selected, and that the app has microphone permission. Screen Time restrictions, a faulty microphone or network issues can also stop dictation. Tap the microphone key on the keyboard to start; if it is missing, Dictation is disabled or restricted. Test the microphone with Voice Memos, and remove cases covering microphones. Many languages run on the device, but some features need internet. Restart the iPhone and install iOS updates. If Siri also fails, reset Siri and Dictation settings by turning them off and on. Background noise and speaking too quickly reduce accuracy rather than stopping it completely. Why won't text to speech work on your iPhone? Enable Speak Selection or Speak Screen under Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content. Then select text and tap Speak, or swipe down with two fingers from the top of the screen to hear the whole screen read aloud. Also asked as: why won&#x27;t my text to speech work on iphone If you hear nothing, raise the volume, check that audio is not routed to disconnected Bluetooth headphones, and confirm a voice is downloaded under Spoken Content, Voices. Some apps block text selection, which prevents Speak Selection; Speak Screen often still works, and you can also ask Siri to speak the screen. VoiceOver is a separate, full screen reader with different gestures, so turn it off if you enabled it accidentally. Restarting the phone fixes many temporary audio issues. Which Kindles have text to speech? Current Kindle e-readers, including recent Kindle, Paperwhite, Oasis and Scribe models, support the VoiceView screen reader through Bluetooth headphones or speakers. Fire tablets include text-to-speech, and older Kindle Keyboard models had built-in speakers with Text-to-Speech. Also asked as: which kindles have text to speech feature VoiceView is designed mainly as an accessibility screen reader, reading menus and book text aloud. Not every book supports text-to-speech, since publishers can restrict it, and the book's details page shows whether it is enabled. Kindle apps on phones can use the device's screen reader or built-in read-aloud features. For a narrated experience, Audible audiobooks with Whispersync let you switch between reading and listening. Check Amazon's current device documentation, since features change. Is text to speech AI bad for the environment? Individual text-to-speech requests use relatively little energy, especially compared with training large models or streaming video. At scale, however, data centres running AI models consume significant electricity and water, so efficiency and clean energy matter. On-device text-to-speech, such as built-in phone voices or local models like Piper, uses minimal energy and avoids network transfer. Cloud neural voices use more computing but are still modest per request. The bigger environmental question is the growth of AI overall, driven by large language and image models. Practical steps include caching generated audio, choosing efficient models and providers with renewable energy commitments, and avoiding unnecessary regeneration. Measuring energy per request helps teams compare options honestly. What is Adobe Speech to Text in Premiere Pro? Speech to Text in Adobe Premiere Pro automatically transcribes the dialogue in your video sequence, then generates captions and enables Text-Based Editing, where you edit video by deleting or rearranging words in the transcript. Also asked as: what is adobe speech to text for premiere pro After downloading language packs, transcription runs on your computer, supporting many languages. You can identify speakers, search the transcript for moments, remove pauses and filler words, and style captions for social media or accessibility. Review transcripts for errors in names and technical terms before publishing captions. For creators, it saves hours of manual captioning and makes rough cuts of interviews and talks much faster. Export transcripts as text files for blog posts or show notes.

# Speech to text explained: examples, best models and apps, ASR, accents, IPA and Tacotron
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/speech-to-text-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Speech to text converts spoken audio into written text: live captions, voice typing, meeting transcripts, voice assistants, call analytics and searchable recordings all use it. Modern systems are deep learning models trained on huge amounts of speech, and they now handle many languages and accents well. I built live speech-to-text into the OCR and Speech Workspace, so this page covers examples, choosing models and apps, ASR versus dictation, VS Code voice input, accents and phonetics, IPA in text to speech, Tacotron 2, and a tutorial.

## What are examples of speech to text?

Everyday examples include voice typing on phone keyboards, live captions in video calls and on Android and iPhone, meeting transcription in Teams, Zoom and Google Meet, voice assistants such as Google Assistant and Siri, YouTube auto-captions, and WhatsApp voice-message transcripts.

Business examples: transcribing customer support calls for quality analysis, medical dictation, court and lecture transcription, subtitles for videos, and voice search in apps. In education, students use transcription to turn lectures into searchable notes. In my OCR and Speech Workspace, live speech-to-text sits alongside OCR so spoken and written material can both be searched and questioned.

## What is the best speech-to-text model in 2026?

There is no single best model; quality depends on language, accent, audio quality, domain vocabulary and latency needs. Strong options include OpenAI's Whisper family and newer transcription models, NVIDIA's open ASR models, and commercial services from Google, Deepgram, AssemblyAI and others.

Choose by testing: record twenty to fifty clips representative of your users, including accents and background noise, transcribe them with each candidate, and compute word error rate. Public leaderboards such as Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard help shortlist. For Indian languages and code-mixed Hindi-English speech, test models specifically trained on Indian data, since general models vary widely.

## What is the best speech-to-text app for Android?

For most users, Google's built-in options are excellent: Gboard voice typing for dictation in any app, Live Transcribe for real-time captions of conversations, and the Recorder app on Pixel phones for transcribed recordings. Samsung phones have their own voice input and recorder transcription.

Choose by use: Gboard for typing messages and notes; Live Transcribe for accessibility and following conversations; recorder apps for lectures and interviews. Download offline speech packs for private, faster recognition without internet. For long recordings with speaker labels and summaries, dedicated transcription apps add features, but check their privacy policies before uploading recordings.

## What is the difference between ASR and speech to text?

There is essentially no difference: ASR, automatic speech recognition, is the technical term for the technology, and speech to text is the everyday name for what it does. Both mean converting spoken language into text automatically.

Researchers and engineers say ASR when discussing models, accuracy metrics such as word error rate, and system design. Product pages say speech to text or transcription. Related terms include speaker diarisation, identifying who spoke when, and spoken language understanding, extracting meaning and intent from speech. Text to speech, TTS, is the reverse direction, generating audio from text.

## What is the difference between dictation and speech to text?

Dictation is a specific use of speech to text: speaking to type text live, usually in a document or message, with voice commands for punctuation and editing, such as "comma", "new line" or "delete that". Speech to text is the broader technology that also transcribes recordings, meetings and calls.

Dictation prioritises low latency and accuracy for one speaker close to the microphone, and integrates with keyboards and editors. Transcription of recordings handles multiple speakers, longer audio and timestamps. Professional dictation software for medicine and law adds specialised vocabularies. For students, phone dictation is a quick way to capture ideas and draft assignments. Speaking a first draft and then editing it by keyboard is often faster than typing from scratch.

## How do I use speech to text in VS Code?

Install Microsoft's VS Code Speech extension, which adds voice input for Copilot Chat and dictation into the editor, processing speech locally on your machine. Then use the microphone button in chat or the dictation command to speak.

This helps with accessibility, describing coding tasks to AI assistants by voice, and writing comments or documentation hands-free. Configure the speech language in settings. Operating system dictation features, such as Windows voice typing, also work in VS Code. Dictating code itself is awkward, but dictating instructions to an AI coding assistant works well.

## Is machine learning a viable tool to map accent from speech onto text or syllables?

Yes. Machine learning models can transcribe speech into phonemes, the sound units of language, rather than ordinary spelling, capturing how something was actually pronounced, and other models classify accents or measure pronunciation differences. These are active research and product areas.

Phoneme recognition models, often fine-tuned from self-supervised speech models, output IPA-like sequences that reveal accent features, useful for language learning, pronunciation scoring and speech therapy. Accuracy depends on training data covering the accents involved, and phonetic labels themselves vary between annotators. Combining phoneme recognition with forced alignment tools gives syllable-level timing.

## Is there text-to-speech software that accepts IPA phonetic transcription?

Yes. Many text-to-speech systems accept IPA through SSML's phoneme tag, which specifies pronunciation using the IPA alphabet, including major cloud TTS services. Open-source engines such as eSpeak NG also support phonetic input.

SSML phoneme tags are useful for names, technical terms and words in other languages that TTS mispronounces, such as Indian names in English speech. Support for exact IPA symbols varies by engine and voice, so test the pronunciations. Some neural TTS systems also let you add custom lexicons, mapping words to phonetic spellings once and reusing them.

## How many spectrogram frames per input character does Tacotron 2 generate?

Tacotron 2 does not use a fixed ratio. Its attention mechanism learns alignments, so each character maps to a variable number of mel-spectrogram frames, typically several, depending on the sound, speaking rate and pauses.

Tacotron 2 predicts mel spectrograms with a frame hop of 12.5 milliseconds, about 80 frames per second. At a speaking rate of roughly 12 to 15 characters per second, that averages around five to seven frames per character, with vowels and pauses taking more frames than short consonants. The decoder generates frames autoregressively until a stop token predicts the end.

## What is a simple speech-to-text tutorial?

A simple tutorial uses OpenAI's open-source Whisper model in Python: install it, load a model size suited to your hardware, and transcribe an audio file, getting text and timestamps.

```python
import whisper
model = whisper.load_model("small")
result = model.transcribe("lecture.mp3", language="en")
print(result["text"])
for seg in result["segments"][:3]:
    print(seg["start"], seg["end"], seg["text"])
```

Install with `pip install openai-whisper` and have ffmpeg available. Faster implementations such as faster-whisper speed up transcription on CPUs and GPUs. For live transcription, stream audio in short chunks. Choose the model size by hardware: tiny and base run on almost any laptop, while medium and large models are far more accurate but need a GPU for reasonable speed. Always check transcripts of names, numbers and technical terms, and add a short vocabulary prompt describing the topic to improve recognition of domain words.

# Speech tools and AI: Canva, STT models, generative AI, CapCut, Mac, Outlook, Notes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/speech-tools-canva-stt-models-dictation/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Speech technology now appears in design tools, video editors, email and note apps, powered by neural models that turn text into voices and voices into text. Knowing which tools offer it and how the models work helps you use them well. I built the OCR &amp; Speech Workspace with live speech-to-text, so this page covers Canva and CapCut voices, speech-to-text models, whether they count as AI or generative AI, dictation on Mac, Outlook and Notes, uses of text-to-speech and word tracking. Does Canva have text to speech? Yes, through apps in Canva's Apps marketplace. Voice apps let you type a script, choose an AI voice and add the generated voiceover to videos and presentations directly in the editor. Features and free usage vary by app and plan. Search the Apps panel for text to speech or voiceover to see current options, such as voice generators from third-party providers. After generating audio, trim and position it on the timeline like any audio clip. Check licensing for commercial use, especially for client work or ads. For more control over pronunciation and pacing, generate voiceovers in a dedicated text-to-speech tool and upload the audio file to Canva. What are speech to text models? Speech-to-text models are neural networks that convert audio into text. Popular examples include OpenAI's Whisper, NVIDIA's Parakeet and Canary, Meta's wav2vec 2.0 family, and commercial models from Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Google and Microsoft. Architectures differ: Whisper is an encoder-decoder transformer trained on huge multilingual audio datasets, Conformer models combine convolution and attention for efficient streaming, and wav2vec 2.0 learns from unlabelled audio before fine-tuning. Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard compares open models on word error rate and speed. Choose by language support, accuracy on your audio, streaming needs and whether you need local deployment for privacy. Smaller models can run on phones and laptops for offline transcription. Is speech to text generative AI? Partly. Modern speech-to-text models such as Whisper generate text token by token, using the same transformer techniques as generative language models, so they are often grouped with generative AI. But their task is recognition, not creating new content. The distinction matters for risk: generative recognition models can occasionally hallucinate words that were never spoken, especially during silence or noise, a known issue with some Whisper deployments. Classic recognition systems made different errors, such as misheard words. When accuracy matters, as in medical or legal transcripts, review outputs, use models with timestamps and confidence scores, and keep original audio for verification. Does speech to text count as AI? Yes. Speech recognition has been an AI research area for decades. Early systems used statistical models such as hidden Markov models, and modern systems use deep neural networks trained on vast amounts of audio, making them clearly AI. The field progressed from recognising single digits in the 1950s to large-vocabulary dictation in the 1990s, then deep learning breakthroughs in the 2010s that brought accuracy close to human transcribers on clean audio. Today's voice assistants, live captions and dictation features all rely on neural speech recognition. Whether a product markets itself as AI or not, if it converts natural speech to text, it uses machine learning. Is text to speech on CapCut AI? Yes. CapCut's text-to-speech uses AI-generated neural voices that read your on-screen text or script aloud, with different voice styles and languages. It also offers AI voice effects and, in some versions, voice features that mimic speakers. Add text, select it, and choose text to speech to generate narration on the timeline. Voices vary in quality and language coverage, and available voices can differ by region and app version. Check CapCut's terms for commercial use, especially for advertising or client videos. Avoid using voice features to imitate real people without consent, which can breach platform rules and laws. Many creators record their own voice for authenticity. Can you use speech to text on a MacBook? Yes. Turn on Dictation in System Settings, Keyboard, then press the microphone key or the Globe key twice in any text field to start speaking. On Apple silicon Macs, dictation in many languages runs on the device. Also asked as: can i speech to text on macbook You can speak punctuation and commands such as new line, and edit text with the keyboard while dictating. For full hands-free control, Voice Control lets you operate the Mac and dictate with voice commands. Accuracy improves with a good microphone and quiet environment. For long recordings, such as lectures or interviews, transcription tools or apps with Whisper models produce transcripts from audio files, with timestamps for review. Can you use speech to text in Outlook? Yes. Outlook for Microsoft 365 includes Dictate, available in new Outlook for Windows, Outlook on the web and Mac versions, letting you speak emails instead of typing. On Windows, voice typing also works with Windows key plus H. Also asked as: can i speech to.text in outlook Start Dictate from the message toolbar, speak naturally and say punctuation, such as comma or full stop. Dictation needs an internet connection and supports many languages. On phones, use the keyboard's microphone in the Outlook app. Outlook's Read Aloud does the reverse, reading emails to you. Pausing briefly between sentences often improves punctuation accuracy. Review dictated emails before sending, since names, numbers and technical terms are common error points. Can you use speech to text in Notes? Yes. On iPhone and iPad, tap the microphone key on the keyboard in the Notes app to dictate. Recent iOS versions also let you record audio in Notes with a live transcript. On Android, Google Keep supports voice notes with transcription. Also asked as: can you speech to text in notes On Mac, use Dictation in Notes like any text field. On Windows, Sticky Notes and OneNote accept voice typing with Windows key plus H, and OneNote also offers its own dictation and transcription. Voice notes are useful for capturing ideas while walking or after meetings, but review transcripts for errors. For organised meeting notes, transcription tools that separate speakers and produce summaries save more time. What is text to speech used for? Text-to-speech is used for accessibility, such as screen readers for blind and low-vision users, reading support for people with dyslexia, audiobooks and article narration, video voiceovers, navigation directions, language learning, customer service phone systems and voice assistants. It also helps writers proofread by hearing their text, students review notes while commuting, and businesses produce training content in many languages. Podcasts and news apps increasingly offer narrated versions of articles. In AI agents, text-to-speech gives voice to conversational assistants. For accessibility, built-in operating system readers remain essential, while neural cloud voices suit polished narration. Disclose AI-generated voices in published content where audiences might assume a human speaker, and respect voice licensing terms. What is text to speech tracking? Text-to-speech tracking usually means highlighting each word or sentence as it is read aloud, so readers can follow along visually. Tools such as Microsoft's Immersive Reader, Speechify and many e-reader apps offer it. Tracking helps people with dyslexia, language learners and young readers connect written and spoken words, improving comprehension and focus. Technically, apps use word timing information from the speech engine, such as boundary events in the browser's Web Speech API or timestamps returned by cloud voices, to highlight the current word. Adjustable speed and colour options help readers find a comfortable setup. Developers should test synchronisation across voices and speeds, since mismatched highlighting quickly becomes distracting.

# Speech vs text: TTS history, failing speech recognition, costs, ChatGPT, Copilot, Word
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/speech-vs-text-tts-stt-word/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Speech and text are two forms of language, and AI now converts between them: speech-to-text transcribes what people say, while text-to-speech reads text aloud with natural voices. Both are built into phones, Office apps and AI assistants. I built the OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, which includes live speech-to-text, so this page covers speech versus text, TTS history, why recognition fails, TTS costs, ChatGPT and Copilot voices, Word and PowerPoint dictation, and hyphenation. What is the difference between speech and text? Speech is spoken language carried by sound, including tone, pace, emphasis and emotion. Text is written language, made of characters that can be read, searched and edited. Speech recognition converts speech into text, and speech synthesis converts text into speech. Speech carries information text loses, such as sarcasm, hesitation and speaker identity, while text is easier to skim, store, translate and search. Spoken language also tends to be less structured, with fillers and restarts. For AI, the difference matters: transcripts lose prosody unless annotated, and synthesised speech must add natural rhythm. Modern multimodal models increasingly process audio directly, preserving more of speech's information than plain transcripts. How long has text to speech existed? Mechanical speaking machines date back to the eighteenth century, Bell Labs demonstrated the electronic Voder in 1939, and computer speech synthesis arrived in 1961, when an IBM computer at Bell Labs sang Daisy Bell. Rule-based and concatenative systems followed, such as DECtalk in the 1980s, which became familiar through assistive devices. Concatenative synthesis stitched recorded speech units together, sounding clearer but less flexible. Screen readers made synthetic speech essential for blind and low-vision users. Neural text-to-speech, beginning with DeepMind's WaveNet in 2016, transformed quality, producing voices that are hard to distinguish from humans. Today's systems support many languages, emotional styles and voice cloning, raising both accessibility benefits and impersonation concerns. Why does speech to text seem to be getting worse? Speech recognition usually seems worse because of microphone problems, background noise, a changed device or app setting, network issues with cloud recognition, software updates that changed models, or speaking styles and vocabulary the system handles poorly. Also asked as: why is speech to text getting worse Check microphone permissions and input selection, clean or replace the microphone, and test in a quiet room. Updates sometimes switch between on-device and cloud recognition, which differ in accuracy. Accents, mixed languages and technical terms reduce accuracy, so use apps that support custom vocabulary or your language. Live transcription tools, including the speech-to-text in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, depend heavily on clean audio input. Modern models such as Whisper are far more accurate than older systems, so persistent problems usually have a local cause. Why doesn't your text to speech work? Common causes include muted or wrong audio output, missing voice data or language packs, disabled app permissions, an unsupported language, browser settings blocking speech, or no internet connection for cloud voices. Also asked as: why doesn&#x27;t my text to speech work Check volume and the selected output device first. On Windows, open Settings, Time and language, Speech, and install voices; on Android, check the text-to-speech engine settings and voice data; on iPhone and Mac, check Spoken Content under Accessibility. In browsers, try another browser or disable extensions that block audio. For apps using cloud voices, confirm connectivity and account limits. Restarting the app or device fixes many temporary failures, and reinstalling voices fixes corrupted voice data. Why is text to speech so expensive? High-quality neural voices require significant computing power to generate audio, licensed or recorded voice talent, and ongoing model development. Providers usually charge per character or per minute, so long content and premium voices add up quickly. Voice cloning, emotional control and commercial usage rights cost more. Cheaper options exist: built-in operating system voices are free, cloud providers offer standard voices at lower rates than premium ones, and open-source models such as Piper and Kokoro run locally at no per-use cost. For accessibility features, built-in voices are often good enough. For large projects, compare quality and licensing terms carefully, and cache generated audio rather than regenerating identical content repeatedly. Can ChatGPT generate text to speech? Yes. ChatGPT can read responses aloud and hold spoken conversations through voice mode. Developers can generate speech files with OpenAI's text-to-speech API models, choosing voices and adjusting style with instructions. In the ChatGPT apps, a read-aloud option plays any response, and voice mode allows natural back-and-forth conversation. Through the API, you send text and receive audio in formats such as MP3, useful for narration, accessibility features and voice assistants. Usage policies require disclosing that voices are AI-generated where relevant and prohibit impersonating real people. For long-form narration, compare voices from several providers, since quality varies by language and some voices suit certain content better. Can Copilot generate text to speech? Microsoft Copilot can speak responses in voice conversations, and Microsoft Edge's Read Aloud reads web pages and PDFs. For developers, Azure AI Speech provides neural text-to-speech voices in many languages through an API. Microsoft 365 apps also include Read Aloud in Word, Outlook and other tools, helpful for proofreading and accessibility. Edge's Read Aloud is free and highlights words as it reads. Azure AI Speech supports custom voices, speaking styles and SSML markup for controlling pronunciation and pauses. GitHub Copilot, by contrast, is a coding assistant and does not generate speech, though it can write code that calls speech APIs. Check language availability, since neural voice coverage differs across languages. Is speech to text available in Word? Yes. Microsoft Word for Microsoft 365 includes Dictate, found on the Home tab, which transcribes your speech into the document. On Windows, voice typing also works in Word and other apps by pressing Windows key plus H. Dictate needs an internet connection and a Microsoft 365 subscription or account, supports many languages and lets you speak punctuation, such as comma or new line. Word for the web also offers Dictate and a Transcribe feature for recorded audio. For better accuracy, use a good microphone, speak clearly and review the text afterwards. Word's Read Aloud does the reverse, reading text to you, which helps catch errors. How do you use speech to text in PowerPoint? In PowerPoint for Microsoft 365, select a text box or the notes pane and click Dictate on the Home tab, then speak. On Windows, you can also press Windows key plus H to use system voice typing in any text field. Also asked as: how to speech to text in powerpoint Dictation suits drafting speaker notes and slide text quickly. During presentations, PowerPoint can show live subtitles, transcribing your speech on screen in the same or another language, enabled through the Slide Show tab's subtitle settings. This helps audiences with hearing impairments and multilingual rooms. Test subtitles before presenting, since accuracy depends on microphone quality and room noise. Review dictated text carefully for errors in names and technical terms. Should speech to text be hyphenated? Hyphenate it when it works as a compound adjective before a noun, as in speech-to-text software. When used as a phrase describing conversion, as in convert speech to text, leave out the hyphens. Many technical writers also hyphenate speech-to-text when using it as a noun naming the technology, as in improvements in speech-to-text, and this usage is widely accepted. The same rule applies to text-to-speech. Consistency matters more than any single choice, so follow your style guide and apply it everywhere, including headings. Abbreviations such as STT and TTS are common in technical writing after the first full mention, but spell them out for general audiences.

# Synthetic data: meaning, examples, how to build it, AI generation, validation, privacy
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/synthetic-data-meaning-build-privacy/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Synthetic data is artificially generated data that mimics the patterns of real data without copying real records. Teams use it to train and test AI, protect privacy and fill gaps where real data is scarce. I built FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning, where dataset quality decides results, so this page covers what synthetic data means and looks like, why we need it, how to build it, generating it with AI and Claude, reliability, validation, privacy and testing. What is meant by synthetic data? Synthetic data is information created by algorithms, simulations or AI models rather than collected from real events or people. It is designed to keep the statistical properties and structure of real data while containing no actual records. It comes in many forms: tabular rows that resemble customer or transaction tables, text such as generated questions and answers, images rendered from 3D scenes, sensor readings from simulators and time series. The term covers fully synthetic data, generated from scratch, and partially synthetic data, where sensitive fields in real records are replaced. Synthetic data is used in machine learning, software testing, research and analytics, especially where real data is scarce, expensive, sensitive or legally restricted. What does synthetic data look like? Synthetic data looks like ordinary data. A synthetic customer table has names, ages, cities and purchase amounts in realistic formats; synthetic text reads like real questions or documents; synthetic images resemble photographs or scans. The difference lies in origin: no row corresponds to a real person. For example, a fine-tuning dataset might contain thousands of generated instruction and response pairs in JSON lines, each written by a model following a template. A vision dataset might contain rendered images of products from many angles, with labels produced automatically. Good synthetic data preserves correlations, such as the relationship between age and income, and realistic messiness, including missing values and typos, rather than looking suspiciously clean. Why do we need synthetic data? We need synthetic data when real data is scarce, sensitive, expensive to label or missing rare cases. It lets teams train models, test software and share datasets without exposing personal information. Common drivers include privacy laws that restrict sharing health or financial records, rare events such as fraud or equipment failures that appear too seldom for training, and costly human labelling. Synthetic data also balances datasets, adding examples for underrepresented groups or languages. In AI, it powers instruction tuning and evaluation: projects such as Self-Instruct showed models can generate their own training examples, and Microsoft's Phi models relied heavily on synthetic textbook-style data. It complements real data rather than fully replacing it. How do you build synthetic data? Start by defining the purpose and the schema, then choose a method: rule-based generators such as Faker for test data, statistical or deep generative models such as those in the SDV library for tabular data, or LLM prompting for text. Also asked as: how to build synthetic data For tabular data, fit a model such as a Gaussian copula or CTGAN on real data, then sample new rows and compare distributions. For text, write a prompt template with varied seeds, such as topics, personas and difficulty levels, generate examples in batches, then deduplicate and filter. For images, render scenes in simulators or game engines with randomised lighting and angles. Always validate the output against real data and the downstream task before using it. Can AI generate synthetic data? Yes. Large language models generate synthetic text, such as questions, answers, dialogues and documents; generative models create images and audio; and specialised models produce tabular data that mirrors real distributions. LLM-generated data is now common for fine-tuning: a strong model writes instruction and response pairs that train a smaller model, a technique called distillation. Diversity is the main challenge, since models repeat phrasings, so vary prompts, personas and seeds, and filter near-duplicates. Quality checks matter too: use rules, another model as a judge, or human review on samples. In FineTune Studio, base-versus-tuned evaluation shows whether a dataset actually improves the model, which applies equally to synthetic datasets. Can Claude generate synthetic data? Yes. Claude can generate synthetic text data such as question and answer pairs, customer support dialogues, classification examples, test inputs and structured JSON records, following a schema and style you specify. For larger datasets, use the API with batch processing and structured outputs, varying the prompt across topics, personas and difficulty to avoid repetitive examples. Ask Claude to include edge cases and realistic errors, then validate outputs with schema checks and sampling. Review the provider's terms before using generated data, since terms may restrict using outputs to train competing models. The same approach works with other models, so compare quality and diversity across providers on a small sample first. Is synthetic data reliable? Synthetic data can be reliable for specific purposes when it is validated, but it is only as good as the process and real data behind it. It may miss rare patterns, amplify biases or contain generator errors. Risks include oversimplified distributions, invented relationships that do not exist in reality and, for LLM-generated text, factual errors and repetitive styles. Research published in Nature in 2024 showed that models trained repeatedly on their own generated data can degrade, a problem called model collapse. Mixing synthetic with real data, validating carefully and testing final models on real data keep results trustworthy. Use synthetic data to augment and protect, and keep real-world evaluation as the final judge. What is synthetic data validation? Synthetic data validation checks whether generated data is faithful to real data, useful for its task and safe for privacy. It typically measures fidelity, utility and privacy separately. Fidelity compares distributions, correlations and summary statistics between real and synthetic data. Utility trains a model on synthetic data and tests it on real data, comparing performance with a model trained on real data. Privacy checks measure how close synthetic records are to real ones, testing for memorised or re-identifiable rows. Libraries such as SDMetrics in the SDV ecosystem automate many of these tests. For text data, also check diversity, factual accuracy and label correctness through sampling and human review. Can synthetic data protect privacy? Synthetic data can reduce privacy risk because records do not belong to real people, but it does not guarantee privacy. Generators can memorise and reproduce real records, especially outliers, so protection must be tested. Stronger guarantees come from differential privacy, which adds controlled noise during generation so no individual's data overly influences the output. Even then, check for records too similar to real ones, and treat datasets with rare combinations of attributes carefully, since they can enable re-identification. Regulators generally assess synthetic data by its actual re-identification risk rather than its label. For sensitive domains such as health or finance, combine privacy testing, access controls and legal review before sharing. What is synthetic data in testing? In software testing, synthetic data is generated test data used instead of production data, such as fake users, orders and payments, so developers can test features, performance and edge cases without exposing real customer information. Tools such as Faker generate realistic names, addresses and emails, while custom scripts create edge cases: empty fields, very long strings, unusual characters and boundary dates. Load testing uses synthetic data at scale to simulate heavy traffic. For AI systems, synthetic test sets probe behaviour on rare or adversarial inputs. Keep test data versioned and reproducible with fixed random seeds, so failures can be recreated. Never copy production databases into test environments without masking sensitive fields.

# System design for AI applications: how to answer 'design a RAG system' or 'design an AI agent' in an interview, and how to actually build one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/system-design-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I answer an AI system design question?

**With the same four-part shape as any system design answer, adapted to where AI systems actually break: clarify requirements first, latency budget, data volume, accuracy bar, and what happens when the model is wrong; sketch the full pipeline at a high level before going deep anywhere; go deep on the two or three components the interviewer is actually probing, usually retrieval quality, evaluation, or failure handling; and close with explicit failure modes and how the system degrades gracefully rather than breaking silently. The classic scaling concerns, load balancers, database sharding, still matter, but they are rarely where an AI system design question's real difficulty lives.**


I run a production RAG platform and have both sat on the interviewing side of this question and answered it as a candidate; this page is the framework I actually use, worked through twice.

> A classic system design answer worries about the database falling over. An AI system design answer has to worry about the model being confidently wrong, which a database never is.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the first thing I should do when given the question?

**Clarify requirements before drawing a single box. What is the data: how much, how messy, updated how often. What is the latency budget: is this a chat interface where two seconds feels slow, or a batch job where a minute is fine. What is the accuracy bar, and who is harmed by a wrong answer, a wrong answer in a college FAQ bot and a wrong answer in a medical triage tool need completely different amounts of caution. What happens when the system does not know: does it refuse, escalate to a human, or guess. Every one of these answers changes the design that follows.**



## How do I design a RAG system in an interview?

**Sketch the pipeline first, end to end, at a high level: ingestion and chunking, embedding and indexing, retrieval with hybrid search, reranking, generation with citations, and a confidence gate that refuses when evidence is weak. Then, based on what the interviewer probes, go deep on one or two pieces: how you would chunk a specific messy document type, how you would evaluate retrieval quality without labelled data, how you would handle a document that updates daily without re-embedding the whole corpus. Naming these trade-offs explicitly is what separates a strong answer from a recited diagram.**



My detailed breakdown of RAG evaluation specifically, which interviewers probe on more than any other RAG sub-topic, is written up separately [5].


## How do I design an AI agent in an interview?

**Start by asking whether the task actually needs an agent at all, a single well-built RAG pass often outperforms a multi-step agent on the same question, and saying so is a strong opening move [8]. If an agent is genuinely needed, describe the loop: a planner or router deciding the next action, a set of tools with strict schemas, a step limit, and a way to know when to stop. Cover reliability explicitly: what happens when a tool call fails, how you prevent an infinite loop, and how you validate the model's proposed actions before anything runs.**



## What failure modes should every AI system design answer cover?

**What happens when retrieval finds nothing relevant: refuse, do not guess. What happens when the model provider is down: a fallback provider, a cached response, or a clear error, never a silent failure. What happens when a tool call returns malformed data: validate and retry, do not pass it straight to the next step. What happens under load: rate limiting, queuing, and graceful degradation rather than the whole system falling over. Naming these unprompted, before the interviewer has to ask, is one of the clearest signals of real production experience.**



## How is this different from classic system design?

**Classic system design worries most about scale: sharding, caching, load balancing, consistency. AI system design carries all of that plus a layer classic systems do not have: the component that can be confidently, plausibly wrong, and the entire evaluation and guardrail layer that exists specifically to catch that. A classic database returns wrong data only when something has actually broken; a language model can return wrong data while functioning exactly as designed, which is why evaluation and confidence gating are first-class design concerns here, not an afterthought.**



## What mistakes do candidates make in AI system design interviews?

**Jumping straight to an architecture diagram without clarifying requirements first. Describing an agent for a task a single RAG pass would solve better and cheaper. Never mentioning evaluation, as if a system's accuracy is assumed rather than measured. Skipping failure modes entirely, describing only the happy path. Reciting a generic RAG diagram without adapting it to the specific data and constraints the interviewer just described. The fix for all of these is the same: treat the question as designing a real system for a real constraint, not reciting a diagram you memorised.**


## AI system design interview questions

**Design a RAG chatbot over a company's internal documentation. Design a document-extraction pipeline for invoices at scale. Design an agent that can answer questions using multiple internal tools. Design a system to detect when a model's confidence is too low to answer. For each, expect to be pushed on one specific component in depth after your high-level pass, so know which two or three parts of your own designs you can go deep on.**



## Where should I start?

**Take a system you have actually built, or RAG.NextUpgrad's public architecture as a worked example, and practise explaining it in the four-part shape: requirements, pipeline, depth, failure modes, out loud, in under five minutes.** For a mock interview and system design coaching session for GenAI roles, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
