# What is Tesseract OCR used for? Offline use, formats, speed, OpenCV and the 4D tesseract
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tesseract-ocr-uses-formats/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tesseract is a free, open-source OCR engine that converts images of printed text into machine-readable text in more than 100 languages. It runs offline on Windows, Mac and Linux and powers tools such as OCRmyPDF. I build document pipelines, including the OCR & Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page covers what Tesseract is used for, who makes it, offline use, formats, speed, Tesseract versus OpenCV, preserving layout, and where the word tesseract comes from.

## What is Tesseract OCR used for?

Tesseract is used to extract text from scanned documents, photos of printed pages, screenshots, receipts and book scans, and to make PDFs searchable. Developers embed it in apps through command-line calls or libraries such as pytesseract.

Common uses include digitising archives and books, automating data entry from forms and invoices, indexing scanned documents for search and RAG, reading text in screenshots for testing, and accessibility tools that read printed text aloud. It works best on clean, printed text; for handwriting, complex layouts or low-quality photos, modern deep learning OCR or cloud services usually perform better. Many teams start with Tesseract and switch engines only for the pages it handles poorly.

## Why is Tesseract used?

Tesseract is popular because it is free under the Apache 2.0 licence, runs fully offline, supports over 100 languages including Hindi and other Indic scripts, and is mature, well documented and easy to integrate.

Its LSTM-based engine, introduced in version 4, improved accuracy substantially over the original pattern-matching approach. It runs on modest CPUs without a GPU, which keeps costs low for large batch jobs, and it outputs plain text, hOCR, TSV with word boxes, and searchable PDFs. Being offline also matters for privacy, since sensitive documents never leave your machine. Its weaknesses are handwriting, complex layouts and noisy images, where newer engines often do better.

## Who makes Tesseract: is it a company?

Tesseract is not a company product today. It was developed at Hewlett-Packard between 1985 and 1994, released as open source in 2005, and then developed with Google's sponsorship for many years. It is now maintained by an open-source community.

The project lives on GitHub under the tesseract-ocr organisation, with contributors worldwide maintaining the engine, language data and documentation. Ray Smith led much of its development at HP and Google. Other unrelated businesses also use the name Tesseract, so searching for the company can return different results. For OCR purposes, you can use Tesseract freely in commercial products under the Apache 2.0 licence, keeping its licence notices.

## Does Tesseract need internet?

No. Tesseract runs entirely offline once installed with its language data files. Images and documents are processed locally on your computer, and nothing is sent to external servers.

You need internet only to download the software and any extra language packs, called traineddata files, which you can copy into the tessdata folder on offline machines. This makes Tesseract suitable for air-gapped environments, privacy-sensitive documents and edge devices. Wrappers such as pytesseract simply call the local executable. If a tool built on Tesseract requires internet, that requirement comes from the tool's own features, such as cloud storage or a hosted API, not from Tesseract itself.

## What image formats does Tesseract support?

Tesseract reads common image formats through the Leptonica library, including PNG, JPEG, TIFF, including multi-page TIFF, BMP, GIF, WebP and PNM. It does not read PDFs directly; convert PDF pages to images first or use OCRmyPDF.

For best results, use lossless formats such as PNG or TIFF at around 300 DPI, since JPEG compression artefacts can blur characters. Multi-page TIFF works well for scanned documents. In Python, pytesseract accepts PIL images and NumPy arrays, so you can load, preprocess with OpenCV and pass images directly. Output formats include plain text, hOCR HTML, TSV with bounding boxes and confidence, ALTO XML and searchable PDF, chosen with configuration options.

## How long does Tesseract OCR take?

On a modern CPU, Tesseract typically processes a clean, single page at 300 DPI in about one to a few seconds. Time grows with resolution, text density, the number of languages loaded and image noise.

To speed it up, process pages in parallel across CPU cores, but limit Tesseract's own threading with `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1` to avoid oversubscription; load only the languages you need; crop to text regions; use the faster `tessdata_fast` models when slight accuracy loss is acceptable; and avoid excessively high resolution. For thousands of pages, OCRmyPDF's parallel processing handles batching. Benchmark on your own documents, since tables, small fonts and poor scans can slow processing and reduce accuracy.

## How do you choose between Tesseract and OpenCV?

They do different jobs and are usually combined. OpenCV is an image processing library for loading, cleaning, transforming and analysing images; Tesseract is an OCR engine that recognises text. Use OpenCV to prepare images, then Tesseract to read them.

A typical pipeline: OpenCV converts to grayscale, removes noise, binarises, deskews and finds text regions or table cells; Tesseract then recognises text in each region. OpenCV also includes a text detection model, EAST, and its DNN module can run other OCR networks, but for reading printed documents Tesseract remains simpler. If you only need to detect where text is, OpenCV may suffice; if you need the words themselves, you need an OCR engine.

## How do you preserve document structure in Tesseract?

Use output formats that keep positions, such as hOCR, TSV or ALTO, which record blocks, paragraphs, lines and words with bounding boxes. Then rebuild structure from those coordinates instead of relying on plain text output.

Choose page segmentation modes carefully: `--psm 3` for automatic layout, `--psm 6` for a uniform block, and `-c preserve_interword_spaces=1` to keep spacing in tables. For columns and tables, detect regions first with OpenCV or a layout model, then OCR each region separately and reassemble. Tesseract's layout analysis is basic, so for complex documents, layout-aware tools such as Surya, docTR, LayoutParser or cloud document AI services preserve reading order and tables better.

## What does tesseract mean?

In geometry, a tesseract is a four-dimensional hypercube: the 4D analogue of a cube, just as a cube is the 3D analogue of a square. The word was coined by Charles Howard Hinton in 1888.

A tesseract has 16 vertices, 32 edges, 24 square faces and 8 cubic cells. The name has been borrowed widely: the OCR engine, the cosmic cube in Marvel films, and the folding of space in the novel A Wrinkle in Time, where tessering means travelling by folding space-time. The OCR engine shares only the name and has no connection to four-dimensional geometry, so context tells you which meaning someone intends.

## Why is a tesseract 4D?

A tesseract is 4D because it extends a cube along a fourth direction perpendicular to the other three. A point extended makes a line, a line a square, a square a cube, and a cube a tesseract.

We cannot see four spatial dimensions, so we view tesseracts through projections, just as a cube drawn on paper is a 2D projection of a 3D object. The familiar image of a small cube inside a larger cube, with corners connected, is a 3D projection of a tesseract. It is not 5D: a 5D hypercube is called a penteract. Thinking in higher dimensions is useful in AI too, since embeddings live in spaces with hundreds of dimensions.


---

# Can Tesseract read PDFs and handwriting? Confidence scores, zonal OCR, EasyOCR and fixes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tesseract-pdf-handwriting-confidence/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tesseract cannot open PDFs directly, but it can OCR PDF pages once they are converted to images, and it can output searchable PDFs. It reads printed text well and handwriting poorly. I build document pipelines such as the OCR & Speech Workspace, which uses Mistral page-batched OCR, and DocuLens AI, so this page covers PDFs with Tesseract and OpenCV, handwriting and maths, confidence scores, zonal OCR for invoices, why OCR fails, speeding up EasyOCR, and whether OCR is machine learning.

## Can Tesseract read PDFs?

Not directly. Tesseract accepts image files, so you first render each PDF page to an image, such as PNG at 300 DPI, then run Tesseract on those images. OCRmyPDF automates this for whole PDFs.

In Python, render pages with PyMuPDF or pdf2image, which uses Poppler, then pass each image to pytesseract. From the command line, `pdftoppm -r 300 -png input.pdf page` creates page images for Tesseract. Before OCR, check whether the PDF already contains text; if so, extract it directly with pdfplumber or PyMuPDF, which is faster and exact. For scanned books or forms with hundreds of pages, run OCR in parallel and cache results so failed pages can be retried.

## Does Tesseract support PDF output?

Yes, as output. Tesseract can create a searchable PDF from images with the pdf output option, such as `tesseract page.png out pdf`, embedding an invisible text layer under the page image.

For multi-page documents, list image paths in a text file and pass it as input to produce one combined PDF. OCRmyPDF builds on this with better PDF handling: it preserves the original PDF structure, skips pages that already have text, optimises file size, and produces PDF/A for archiving. For production use with real PDFs, OCRmyPDF is usually the right tool, while Tesseract's own PDF output suits simple image-to-PDF conversions, quick tests and searchable copies of photographed receipts.

## Can OpenCV read PDFs?

No. OpenCV reads images and video, not PDFs. Convert PDF pages to images first with PyMuPDF, pdf2image or Poppler's pdftoppm, then load them into OpenCV as NumPy arrays for processing.

With PyMuPDF, render a page to a pixmap at your chosen zoom, convert its samples into a NumPy array, and reshape it to height, width and channels; OpenCV can then deskew, denoise, threshold or detect tables before OCR. This combination, a PDF renderer plus OpenCV plus an OCR engine, is a standard document pipeline. Keep resolution consistent, around 300 DPI for text, and remember that OpenCV uses BGR channel order, unlike most PDF renderers.

## Can Tesseract read handwriting?

Poorly. Tesseract's models are trained mainly on printed fonts, so handwriting, especially cursive, produces many errors. Neat block capitals in separate boxes may partly work, but results are rarely reliable.

For handwriting, use models built for it: Microsoft's TrOCR for line-level handwriting, cloud services such as Google Cloud Vision, Azure AI Document Intelligence or Amazon Textract, or vision-language models that read handwritten notes in context. Fine-tuning Tesseract on handwriting samples is possible but laborious and usually inferior. Whatever you choose, scan clearly, crop to the text, and route low-confidence words to a person for review, since handwriting varies hugely between writers.

## Which OCR should you use for handwritten maths answers?

Use a tool designed for mathematical notation: Mathpix is the best-known commercial option for converting handwritten and printed maths into LaTeX, and modern vision-language models can also transcribe handwritten equations into LaTeX reasonably well.

Open-source options include models trained on handwritten maths datasets such as CROHME, and Pix2Text, which converts images with formulas into Markdown and LaTeX. Plain OCR engines such as Tesseract cannot handle fractions, superscripts and two-dimensional layout. For grading student answers, combine transcription with human review, since a single misread symbol changes the meaning. Test candidates on real student scripts, which are messier than benchmark samples, and measure symbol-level accuracy.

## How do you read OCR confidence scores in C# and trust Tesseract results?

In C#, the popular Tesseract .NET wrapper gives a page-level `GetMeanConfidence()` value and lets you iterate words with a result iterator to read each word's confidence, from 0 to 100, at the word level.

Treat confidence as a ranking signal, not a probability of correctness. Set thresholds per field using labelled samples: accept words above a chosen value, flag lower ones for review, and always validate critical fields with rules, such as checksums for IDs, date formats and totals that must add up. Mean page confidence hides single bad words, so check word-level scores for important fields. Log confidence with outcomes to tune thresholds over time.

## Zonal or template OCR for reading invoices: which is better?

Zonal or template OCR reads fixed regions defined for a known layout, such as the invoice number box, which works well when every invoice comes from the same template. It breaks when layouts vary across suppliers.

For many suppliers, use layout-independent extraction: prebuilt invoice models from Azure AI Document Intelligence, Amazon Textract's expense analysis or Google Document AI, or a vision-language model extracting fields into a JSON schema. Combine any method with validation: totals must equal line items plus tax, dates must parse, and supplier details must match your records. DocuLens AI follows this pattern, extracting fields with a language model and validating them against a schema before anyone relies on them.

## Why does OCR keep failing?

Common causes are poor image quality, low resolution, skewed or curved pages, unusual fonts, complex layouts, handwriting, wrong language settings, and using an engine unsuited to the document type.

Diagnose systematically: view the exact image the engine receives; check resolution, aiming for about 300 DPI; fix orientation and skew; improve contrast with grayscale and thresholding; set the correct language packs; and choose a page segmentation mode matching the layout. For tables and multi-column pages, detect regions first. If failures persist on handwriting or photos, switch to a deep learning OCR or cloud service. Keep a small test set of failing pages to measure each fix.

## How do you improve the performance of EasyOCR?

Run EasyOCR on a GPU if available, load only the languages you need, resize very large images, and reuse a single Reader object instead of creating one per image, since model loading is slow.

For accuracy, preprocess images: crop to text regions, improve contrast, and deskew. Tune detection parameters such as text_threshold, low_text and link_threshold for your documents, and use `paragraph=True` to merge lines when you need blocks of text. For throughput, batch images and process them in parallel workers, each with its own reader. If speed remains a problem on CPU, compare RapidOCR or PaddleOCR, which are often faster with similar accuracy.

## Is OCR a machine learning model?

OCR is a task, recognising text in images, not a single model. Early OCR used hand-crafted rules and template matching; modern OCR systems use machine learning, typically deep neural networks for detecting text regions and recognising characters.

Tesseract switched to LSTM neural networks in version 4. Engines such as PaddleOCR and EasyOCR combine a detection network with a recognition network, often a CNN with a sequence model and CTC decoding. The newest approaches use transformers, such as TrOCR, or vision-language models that read whole pages. So today, most OCR is machine learning, trained on large datasets of labelled text images, though simple rule-based OCR still exists for fixed fonts such as MICR.

# Tesseract vs EasyOCR, PaddleOCR and pytesseract, plus the 4D and Marvel tesseract
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tesseract-vs-easyocr-paddleocr/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


"Tesseract" means three different things: the open-source OCR engine that reads text from images, the four-dimensional analogue of a cube in geometry, and the glowing cube holding the Space Stone in Marvel films. This page starts with the OCR engine, because I work with document AI in DocuLens AI and the OCR and Speech Workspace, and compares it with pytesseract, EasyOCR and PaddleOCR. It then explains whether a 4D tesseract is possible and how it relates to cubes and hypercubes, and finally the Marvel Tesseract, Cosmic Cube, scepter and Infinity Stones.

## What is the difference between Tesseract and pytesseract?

Tesseract is the OCR engine itself, a C++ program and library maintained as open source. pytesseract is a small Python wrapper that calls the installed Tesseract program and returns its output to your Python code.

So you need both for Python: install Tesseract on the system, then `pip install pytesseract`. pytesseract adds no recognition ability; it passes images and options such as language and page segmentation mode to Tesseract and parses results, including text, word boxes and confidence scores. If pytesseract says Tesseract is not found, the engine is missing or not on your path. Alternatives such as tesserocr bind to the library directly and can be faster for many small images.

## What is the difference between Tesseract and EasyOCR?

Tesseract is a mature engine with an LSTM recogniser that works best on clean, scanned printed documents. EasyOCR is a Python deep-learning toolkit that detects and reads text in natural images, and usually handles photos, angled text and busy backgrounds better.

Practical differences: Tesseract runs fast on a CPU and is easy to deploy; EasyOCR uses PyTorch, is heavier, and benefits from a GPU. Tesseract expects reasonably preprocessed images, while EasyOCR includes a text detector that finds text regions anywhere. EasyOCR supports over 80 languages. For scanned forms and books, Tesseract is often sufficient; for photos of signboards, receipts or screens, test EasyOCR. Always compare both on a sample of your own images.

## What is the difference between Tesseract and PaddleOCR?

PaddleOCR is a deep-learning OCR toolkit from Baidu's PaddlePaddle ecosystem, with text detection, recognition and layout analysis. It is often more accurate than Tesseract on photographs, complex layouts and Chinese and other Asian scripts.

PaddleOCR includes tools for document structure, such as tables and layout, and offers lightweight models that run on CPUs and mobile devices. Tesseract is simpler, has decades of history and broad language support, and is easier to install on many systems. Many teams now test vision language models and dedicated document AI too: for scanned PDFs in the OCR and Speech Workspace, I use Mistral's OCR in page batches because layout and table handling matter more than raw character accuracy.

## Is a tesseract possible?

Mathematically, yes: a tesseract is a well-defined four-dimensional shape with 16 vertices, 32 edges, 24 square faces and 8 cubic cells. Physically, we cannot build one in our three-dimensional space; we can only build or draw its 3D projections or unfoldings.

The familiar picture of a small cube inside a larger cube, with corners joined, is a projection, much like a drawing of a cube on paper is a 2D projection of a 3D object. Salvador Dalí's painting "Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)" shows an unfolded tesseract, a 3D net of eight cubes. Physics does use extra dimensions in some theories, but no experiment has shown a spatial fourth dimension we could move through.

## What is the difference between a cube and a tesseract?

A cube is the three-dimensional shape made of six square faces; a tesseract is its four-dimensional analogue, made of eight cubes. You get a cube by sliding a square along a new direction, and a tesseract by sliding a cube along a fourth one.

The counts show the pattern: a square has 4 vertices, a cube 8, and a tesseract 16, doubling each time. A cube has 12 edges; a tesseract has 32. A cube is bounded by 2D squares; a tesseract by 3D cubes. Thinking by analogy, from square to cube to tesseract, is the standard way to understand higher dimensions, because we cannot visualise four spatial dimensions directly.

## What is the difference between a tesseract and a hypercube?

There is no difference in shape: the tesseract is the four-dimensional hypercube. "Hypercube" is the general term for the cube's analogue in any number of dimensions, so a square is a 2D hypercube and a cube is a 3D hypercube.

In mathematics and computer science, an n-dimensional hypercube has 2 to the power n vertices. The term also appears in computer networks, where processors are connected in a hypercube topology, and in data analysis, where an "OLAP cube" or hypercube describes multi-dimensional data. "Tesseract" specifically names the 4D case and was coined by Charles Howard Hinton in 1888.

## What is the Tesseract in Marvel?

In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the Tesseract is a glowing blue cube that contains the Space Stone, one of the six Infinity Stones. It enables teleportation and portals across space, and drives the plots of Captain America: The First Avenger, The Avengers and Captain Marvel.

The Red Skull uses it to power HYDRA's weapons in the Second World War; Loki uses it to open a portal for the Chitauri invasion; and Thanos crushes it in Avengers: Infinity War to take the Space Stone. The film borrows its name from the geometric shape, suggesting something beyond ordinary three-dimensional space, but it is fiction, unrelated to the OCR engine or real geometry.

## What is the difference between the Tesseract and the Cosmic Cube?

They are essentially the same object in different media. In Marvel comics, the Cosmic Cube is a powerful artefact that can reshape reality; the films renamed it the Tesseract and made it the container of the Space Stone.

The comics version has a different origin and history from the film version, and its powers are broader, sometimes able to fulfil a holder's wishes. The film version's power comes from the Space Stone inside. Fans often use the names interchangeably, but if you are discussing the films, "Tesseract" is the accurate term, and "Cosmic Cube" points to the comics continuity.

## What is the difference between the Tesseract and the scepter?

They hold different Infinity Stones. The Tesseract contains the Space Stone, which controls space and teleportation; Loki's scepter contains the Mind Stone, which can control minds and later gives life to Vision.

In The Avengers, Loki receives the scepter from Thanos and uses it to control people such as Hawkeye and Erik Selvig, while using the Tesseract to open a portal. After the battle, the scepter's stone is used in Avengers: Age of Ultron to create Ultron and then Vision. So the objects appear together but have separate powers and stories, and neither is the same as the other.

## What is the difference between the Tesseract and the Infinity Stones?

The Tesseract is a container; the Infinity Stones are the six sources of power: Space, Mind, Reality, Power, Time and Soul. The Tesseract houses only the Space Stone, much like the scepter houses the Mind Stone.

The other stones appear in other containers or forms: the Aether is the Reality Stone, the Orb holds the Power Stone, the Eye of Agamotto holds the Time Stone, and the Soul Stone is found on Vormir. Thanos gathers all six in his gauntlet in Avengers: Infinity War. So asking whether the Tesseract is an Infinity Stone has a precise answer: it holds one.

# Text embeddings in LLMs: how they work, ada-002, text-embedding-3 small and large, 004
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/text-embedding-models-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A text embedding turns a piece of text into a vector of numbers that captures its meaning, so software can compare texts by similarity. LLM applications use embeddings for semantic search, RAG, clustering and classification, while LLMs themselves use embedding layers internally. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense embedding retrieval with BM25, so this page explains how text embeddings work, the difference from LLM embeddings, OpenAI's ada-002 and text-embedding-3 models, how to use them, and Google's text-embedding-004.

## What is a text embedding in LLM applications?

A text embedding is a fixed-length vector representing the meaning of a sentence, paragraph or document, produced by an embedding model. LLM applications use these vectors to find relevant text, for example retrieving passages to feed an LLM in RAG.

Embedding models are usually separate from the chat model: you call an embeddings API or run a local model such as a Sentence Transformers checkpoint, store vectors in a vector database, and compare them with cosine similarity. Texts about the same topic produce nearby vectors even when the wording differs, such as how to reset my password and I forgot my login. This semantic matching is what makes modern search and retrieval far better than keyword matching alone.

## How do text embedding models work?

A transformer encoder reads the tokenized text and produces a vector for each token; the model then pools these, often by averaging or using a special token, into one vector. Training makes similar texts produce similar vectors.

Training typically uses contrastive learning: the model sees pairs that should match, such as a question and its answer passage, and pairs that should not, and it adjusts weights so matching pairs score higher in cosine similarity. Large datasets of paired text, such as search queries with clicked results, teach general semantic similarity. Some modern embedding models are built from decoder LLMs fine-tuned for this task. Benchmarks like MTEB compare models across retrieval, clustering and classification.

## What is an embedding inside an LLM?

Inside an LLM, the embedding layer is a learned table that converts each token ID into a vector, the first step of processing. Positional information is added, and every transformer layer then transforms these vectors into richer contextual representations.

These internal embeddings differ from text embeddings used for search. They represent individual tokens, change at every layer, and are not designed for comparing whole texts. You could average an LLM's hidden states to get a sentence vector, but dedicated embedding models usually perform much better for retrieval because they are trained specifically for similarity. The size of the embedding layer equals the vocabulary size times the hidden dimension, often hundreds of millions of parameters.

## What is text-embedding-ada-002?

text-embedding-ada-002 is an OpenAI embedding model released in December 2022. It produces 1,536-dimensional vectors, accepts up to 8,191 input tokens, and at the time replaced several older OpenAI embedding models with one cheaper, stronger model.

It became the default embedding model for early RAG tutorials and applications. In January 2024, OpenAI released text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large, which outperform ada-002 on benchmarks such as MTEB and the multilingual MIRACL retrieval benchmark. Existing systems built on ada-002 still work, but new projects should use the newer models. If you migrate, re-embed all documents, since vectors from different models are not comparable.

## What is text-embedding-3-small?

text-embedding-3-small is OpenAI's efficient embedding model, released in January 2024. It outputs 1,536-dimensional vectors by default, supports shortening them with a dimensions parameter, and beats ada-002 on retrieval benchmarks at much lower cost.

OpenAI reported an MTEB average of about 62.3 for text-embedding-3-small versus 61.0 for ada-002, and a large jump on the multilingual MIRACL benchmark, from about 31.4 to 44.0. It is a strong default for RAG, semantic search and classification when you want a hosted model with good quality and low latency. Like other OpenAI embeddings, its vectors are normalised, so cosine similarity and dot product give the same ranking.

## What is text-embedding-3-large?

text-embedding-3-large is OpenAI's most capable embedding model from the January 2024 release. It produces 3,072-dimensional vectors by default and scores higher than the small model on retrieval benchmarks, especially multilingual ones.

OpenAI reported an MTEB average of about 64.6 and a MIRACL score of about 54.9. Its vectors can be shortened with the dimensions parameter, for example to 256 or 1,024, trading a little accuracy for much less storage, and OpenAI noted that even shortened large embeddings can outperform full ada-002 vectors. Choose it when retrieval quality matters more than cost, such as multilingual or technical corpora, and test it against the small model on your own queries.

## How do you use text-embedding-3-small?

Call the OpenAI embeddings endpoint with the model name and a list of texts, then store the returned vectors. In Python, `client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=texts)` returns one embedding per input.

```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
texts = ["How do I reset my password?", "Steps to recover a login"]
resp = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=texts)
vectors = [item.embedding for item in resp.data]
```

Batch many texts per request, respect the token limit per input, and add `dimensions=512` if you want smaller vectors. Store vectors with their text and the model name, embed queries with the same model, and rank results by cosine similarity.

## What is text-embedding-004?

text-embedding-004 is a Google text embedding model released in 2024 for the Gemini API and Vertex AI. It produces 768-dimensional vectors and supports task types, such as retrieval query and retrieval document, to optimise embeddings for their use.

Task types matter: embedding documents with the retrieval document type and queries with the retrieval query type improves search quality. The model also supports reducing output dimensionality. It performed strongly on MTEB at release among models of its size. Google has since released gemini-embedding-001, a larger, multilingual model with 3,072-dimensional output that can be shortened, which Google positions as the successor for new projects.

## Is text-embedding-004 deprecated?

Google announced the deprecation of text-embedding-004 in the Gemini API after gemini-embedding-001 became generally available in 2025, and directed users to migrate. Check Google's model deprecation pages for the exact dates that apply to the Gemini API and Vertex AI.

If you still use it, plan a migration: choose the replacement model, re-embed your entire corpus, since old and new vectors are incompatible, update your vector index dimensions if they change, and run a retrieval evaluation comparing old and new results before switching traffic. Keep the old index until the new one is verified. This applies to any embedding model change, which is why storing the model name alongside every vector is a good habit.

## How do you use text-embedding-ada-002?

Use the same OpenAI embeddings endpoint with `model="text-embedding-ada-002"`, passing a string or list of strings, and read vectors from the response. Each vector has 1,536 numbers; compare them with cosine similarity.

Unlike the newer models, ada-002 does not support the dimensions parameter, so vectors are always 1,536 long. If you maintain an ada-002 system, keep queries and documents on the same model, since mixing models breaks similarity. For new work, text-embedding-3-small offers better quality at lower cost with the same default dimension, which makes migration simple: re-embed documents, rebuild the index and compare retrieval results on a test set before switching.

# What is text to speech and speech to text? AI voice tools compared
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/text-to-speech-and-speech-to-text/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Text to speech (TTS) converts written text into spoken audio, and speech to text (STT), also called automatic speech recognition, converts spoken audio into written text. Both now use AI: neural networks trained on large amounts of recorded speech. This page explains how they work, how to convert speech to text on any device, the best converters, how OpenAI's Whisper compares with cloud services, what Gemini can do with audio, how to create an AI voice, and how to use the Microsoft tools, including dictation in Word.

## What is text to speech (TTS)?

Text to speech is technology that reads text aloud in a synthetic voice. Modern TTS uses neural networks that generate natural-sounding speech with realistic rhythm and intonation, in many languages and voices.

A TTS system first analyses the text, expanding numbers and abbreviations and working out pronunciation, then a neural model generates the audio. Uses include screen readers for visually impaired users, voice assistants, audiobook and video narration, navigation apps and language learning. Quality is now high enough that synthetic voices can be hard to tell from real ones, which is why responsible services restrict cloning a real person's voice without consent. When you use TTS in a project, label it as synthetic where listeners might be misled.

## Does speech to text use AI?

Yes. Modern speech to text uses deep learning models, typically transformers, trained on very large amounts of transcribed audio. Older systems used statistical models with separate acoustic and language components.

Today's models map audio directly to text and handle accents, background noise and natural speech far better than earlier systems. Some, like Whisper, were trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of multilingual audio from the web. Accuracy still depends on conditions: clear microphones, one speaker at a time and common vocabulary work best, while cross-talk, heavy noise, code-switching between languages and technical jargon cause errors. In the OCR & Speech Workspace I built live speech-to-text into the same workspace as document chat, because once speech is text, search and summaries work on it too.

## Can you convert speech to text?

Yes, on almost any device for free. Phones have voice typing in the keyboard, Windows has voice typing with Windows key plus H, macOS has Dictation, and Word, Google Docs and most messaging apps support dictation.

For recordings rather than live speech, options include:

- **Transcription in apps**: Microsoft Word's Transcribe on the web, meeting tools such as Teams and Google Meet, and voice recorder apps.
- **Open-source models**: Whisper runs on your own computer, privately and free.
- **Cloud APIs**: Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Azure AI Speech, Amazon Transcribe and others for apps and large volumes.
- **AI assistants**: Gemini and ChatGPT can transcribe uploaded audio within their limits.

Always proofread names, numbers and technical terms, the most common error points.

## What is the best speech to text converter?

There is no single best one; it depends on the job. For dictation, your device's built-in voice typing is best. For recordings and privacy, Whisper. For apps, live captions and scale, a cloud API such as Google, Azure or Amazon.

How to choose:

- **Accuracy on your audio**: test three short clips in your accent, with your vocabulary and noise.
- **Live or recorded**: live captions need streaming support.
- **Languages**: check support for Indian languages and mixed Hindi-English speech if you need it.
- **Speaker labels and timestamps**: needed for meetings and interviews.
- **Privacy**: sensitive recordings are safer on a local model.

For a student transcribing lectures, Whisper on your own laptop or Word's Transcribe is usually enough.

## Whisper vs other speech to text: which is better?

Whisper is a free, open-source speech recognition model from OpenAI that is accurate across many languages and runs on your own hardware. Cloud speech services add real-time streaming, speaker separation, custom vocabularies and managed scale.

Choose Whisper when you want privacy, no per-minute cost and offline use, and you can provide a GPU or accept slower transcription on a CPU; faster community implementations make it practical on laptops. Choose a cloud service for live captions, call-centre volumes, guaranteed uptime or features like speaker diarisation built in. Accuracy differs by language and audio, so benchmark on your own samples:

```bash
pip install -U openai-whisper
whisper lecture.mp3 --model small --language en
```

That writes text and subtitle files you can compare against a cloud service's output.

## Can Gemini do speech to text?

Yes. Gemini models accept audio input, so they can transcribe recordings, and also summarise them, answer questions about them or translate them. You can do this in the Gemini app, in Google AI Studio or through the Gemini API.

Upload an audio file and ask for a transcript with timestamps, or ask directly for meeting notes and action items. Because Gemini understands the content, it can also label speakers and clean up filler words if you ask. For long recordings, the API's file upload handles large files better than pasting. For precise, verbatim transcripts at scale with live streaming, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text is the more specialised option. Check the Gemini API audio documentation for supported formats and length limits.

## How do I create an AI voice with text to speech?

Choose a TTS tool, paste your script, pick a voice, adjust speed and style, and export the audio. Most tools offer many ready-made voices; cloning a specific voice needs that person's consent and a service that supports it.

Tips for natural results:

- Write for the ear: short sentences, contractions and clear punctuation for pauses.
- Spell out tricky names phonetically or use the tool's pronunciation settings.
- Use style controls or prompts, such as "calm and friendly", where available.
- Generate one paragraph at a time and listen before continuing.
- Export WAV or high-quality MP3 for video editing.

Free options include the Gemini API's speech generation in Google AI Studio, Microsoft Edge's Read Aloud for listening, and video editors such as Clipchamp with built-in TTS.

## How do I use text to speech in Google AI Studio?

Open Google AI Studio, choose the speech generation option, select a model that supports audio output, enter your text and a style instruction, pick a voice, and run it. You can play the audio and download it, or get the code to do the same through the Gemini API.

Gemini's speech generation lets you steer delivery with natural-language instructions, such as "read this like an excited sports commentator", and supports multiple speakers for dialogue, with each speaker assigned a different voice. It is a quick way to prototype narration for a project demo or a podcast-style explainer. Usage is subject to AI Studio's free limits and the API's pricing, and models with audio output may be in preview, so check the speech generation documentation for current model names.

## Which Microsoft text to speech should I use?

For listening to documents and web pages, use Read Aloud in Microsoft Edge or the Immersive Reader in Word. For video narration, use Clipchamp's built-in text to speech. For apps and developers, use Azure AI Speech, which offers many neural voices and languages.

Windows also has Narrator, a full screen reader for accessibility. Azure AI Speech provides a text-to-speech API with standard neural voices, control over pronunciation and pauses through SSML, a markup language for speech, and options for custom voices with consent and approval. Many Indian English and Indian-language voices are available. For a student project, Edge's Read Aloud is enough to test how text sounds, and the Azure free tier is enough to build a small voice feature.

## How do I use speech to text in Microsoft Word?

Open your document, select Home, then Dictate, and start speaking. Word types what you say and supports voice commands for punctuation such as "comma", "full stop" and "new line". Select Dictate again to stop.

Dictate needs a Microsoft 365 account and an internet connection, and you can change the spoken language in its settings. To transcribe a recording instead, Word for the web has Transcribe, which uploads an audio file and produces a transcript with speakers and timestamps that you can insert into the document. On Windows you can also press Windows key plus H in any text box to use system voice typing. Proofread afterwards, especially names and numbers.

# How to use text to speech on a PDF, phones and WhatsApp, and how speech to text works
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/text-to-speech-pdf-speech-to-text/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To have a PDF read aloud, open it in Microsoft Edge and choose Read aloud, use Adobe Acrobat's Read Out Loud, or use your phone's built-in screen reader features. Speech to text works the other way, turning your voice into text through dictation on phones, keyboards and apps. I built the OCR and Speech Workspace, which includes live speech-to-text alongside OCR, so this page covers reading PDFs and text aloud, Android, iPhone, Samsung and WhatsApp, how speech recognition works, its history, ChatGPT, and AI voices.

## How do I use text to speech on a PDF?

On a computer, open the PDF in Microsoft Edge and press Ctrl+Shift+U or choose Read aloud; Edge reads the text with natural voices and highlights words. In Adobe Acrobat Reader, use View, then Read Out Loud. On phones, use Select to Speak on Android or Speak Screen on iPhone.

If nothing is read, the PDF may be a scanned image without text. Run OCR first, with Acrobat, a scanner app or a tool such as OCRmyPDF, to add a text layer. For long documents, choose a comfortable voice speed, and use headphones to focus. Students often use this to review notes while commuting or to proofread their own reports by ear.

## How do I use text to speech in general?

Most devices have built-in text to speech. On Windows, use Narrator or Edge's Read aloud; on macOS, enable Spoken Content and press the shortcut to speak selected text; on phones, use the accessibility reader features. Browser extensions and apps add more voices.

Tips for better listening:

- Choose a natural, neural voice in system settings.
- Adjust the speed; many people prefer slightly faster than normal speech.
- Use reader mode on web pages to remove clutter before reading.
- Download offline voices for reading without internet.
- For other languages, install the language's voice data.

Text to speech supports accessibility for people with visual impairments and dyslexia, and helps anyone learn while multitasking.

## How do I use text to speech on Android?

Turn on Select to Speak in Settings under Accessibility, then tap its icon and select text on screen to hear it read aloud. Android's text-to-speech settings let you choose the engine, language, voice and speed, usually with Google's speech services.

For whole pages, use the Read aloud feature in the Google app or Chrome where available, or "Reading mode" for clean, readable text with playback. TalkBack is Android's full screen reader for people with visual impairments, which reads everything as you navigate. Install additional language voices, such as Hindi, from the text-to-speech settings.

## How do I use speech to text on iPhone?

Tap the microphone key on the iPhone keyboard and start speaking; Dictation converts your speech to text in any app with a text field. Say punctuation such as "comma" or "full stop", and tap the microphone again to stop.

Enable Dictation in Settings under General, then Keyboard, if the microphone key is missing. Newer iPhones process many languages on the device, which works offline and keeps audio private. Voice Control, in Accessibility settings, lets you control the whole phone and edit text by voice. For long recordings, the Voice Memos app can also create transcripts on supported iOS versions.

## How do I use speech to text on Samsung phones?

Use the microphone key on Samsung Keyboard or Google's Gboard to dictate into any text field. Samsung phones also support Google's voice typing, and recent Galaxy models include transcription features in apps such as Voice Recorder and Notes.

If the microphone key is missing, check keyboard settings for voice input, and choose between Samsung voice input and Google voice typing. Download offline speech recognition languages in Google voice typing settings for faster, private dictation. Samsung's AI features on newer models can transcribe and summarise recordings and translate calls, depending on model and region.

## How do I use speech to text in WhatsApp?

Use your phone keyboard's microphone key in the WhatsApp message box to dictate a text message, instead of the WhatsApp microphone button, which records a voice note. WhatsApp can also transcribe received voice messages into text on supported devices.

To enable voice message transcripts, look for the transcripts option in WhatsApp's chat settings, choose your language, then long-press a voice message and select transcribe. Transcription happens on your device, so messages stay private. Availability and languages vary by device and region. Dictating messages is faster than typing for many people, but review the text before sending, especially names and numbers.

## How does speech to text software work?

Speech recognition converts audio into a sequence of acoustic features, such as spectrograms, then a neural network predicts the most likely text. Modern systems are end-to-end deep learning models trained on thousands of hours of transcribed speech.

Models such as OpenAI's Whisper use an encoder that processes audio and a decoder that generates text tokens, learning pronunciation, vocabulary and context together. Language modelling helps choose between similar-sounding words. Live transcription processes audio in small streaming chunks to show text as you speak, which is how the OCR and Speech Workspace displays live speech-to-text. Accuracy depends on audio quality, accents, background noise and vocabulary.

## How long has speech to text been around?

Speech recognition research began in the 1950s: Bell Labs' "Audrey" system in 1952 recognised spoken digits, and IBM's Shoebox in 1962 understood a few words. Consumer dictation arrived in the 1990s with products like Dragon NaturallySpeaking.

Statistical models dominated the 1980s to 2000s; deep learning brought dramatic accuracy gains from around 2010, enabling voice assistants such as Siri, Google Assistant and Alexa. Large models trained on huge multilingual datasets, such as Whisper in 2022, made accurate transcription in many languages widely available, including free open-source options you can run locally.

## Can ChatGPT do speech to text?

Yes. The ChatGPT apps include voice features: you can dictate messages with the microphone, and voice conversations transcribe your speech and respond aloud. For developers, OpenAI offers speech-to-text models through its API, and its open-source Whisper model runs locally.

For transcribing recordings, upload audio to tools built on these models, or use the API with your own app. Accuracy is high for clear speech in common languages; check names, numbers and technical terms. For private recordings, consider running Whisper locally so audio never leaves your device. Always get consent before recording or transcribing other people.

## Is AI text to speech bad?

AI text to speech is mostly beneficial: it gives people with visual impairments, dyslexia or reading difficulties access to text, helps language learners, and makes content available in audio. Modern neural voices sound natural and support many languages.

The concerns are real but specific: voice cloning can be misused for scams and impersonation, synthetic voices can spread misinformation, and voice actors raise concerns about consent and compensation. Responsible use means cloning only voices with explicit permission, labelling synthetic audio, and verifying unexpected voice requests for money or information through another channel.

# Tool calling explained: function calling, internals, MCP, RAG, LangChain, Ollama, Llama
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tool-calling-function-calling-mcp-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Tool calling lets a language model request actions, such as searching, querying a database or calling an API, by returning structured arguments that your code executes. It is the foundation of agents. I build AI systems with retrieval, validation and fallbacks, such as RAG.NextUpgrad and DocuLens AI, so this page covers tool versus function calling, how it works inside models, MCP and RAG comparisons, LangChain, Ollama, Llama 3.1, benchmarks and a minimal JavaScript loop. Is tool calling the same as function calling? Yes, essentially. Function calling was OpenAI's original name for letting models return structured requests to call developer-defined functions. Tool calling or tool use is the broader term now used by most providers, including Anthropic. Also asked as: is tool calling and function calling the same Tools can include your own functions plus built-in capabilities offered by providers, such as web search, code execution or computer use, which run on the provider's side. In both cases, the model does not execute anything itself; it outputs a tool name and arguments, and an application runs the tool and returns the result. Documentation and frameworks use the terms interchangeably, so treat them as synonyms. Learning one provider's format makes others easy to pick up. How does tool calling work under the hood? The API inserts your tool definitions, names, descriptions and JSON schemas, into the model's context using special formatting. Models are trained to emit a structured tool call when useful, which the API parses and returns to your application. Your code executes the tool, sends the result back as a tool result message, and the model continues, either calling more tools or answering. Some providers use constrained decoding to guarantee arguments match the schema. Parallel tool calls let models request several tools in one turn. Training on many examples of tool use teaches models when to call tools and how to fill parameters. Tool descriptions act as prompts, so clear names, purposes and parameter explanations directly improve reliability. What is the difference between tool calling and MCP? Tool calling is the model's ability to request a tool with structured arguments. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way for applications to discover and run tools hosted on servers, which are then presented to the model through tool calling. Without MCP, developers define each tool in their application code. With MCP, a server exposes tools, resources and prompts that any compatible client, such as Claude Desktop or coding agents, can connect to and use. The client converts MCP tools into tool definitions for the model, executes calls through the server, and returns results. MCP standardises integration; tool calling remains the underlying model mechanism. Secure MCP servers with authentication and least-privilege access. What is the difference between tool calling and RAG? RAG retrieves relevant information before generation and adds it to the prompt, following fixed steps. Tool calling lets the model decide during generation to request actions, including retrieval, calculations or external API calls. Classic RAG always retrieves, whether needed or not, and suits question answering over documents, as in RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval and citations. Tool calling enables dynamic behaviour: the model might search only when needed, refine queries, or call other tools, such as a calendar or database. Agentic RAG combines them by exposing retrieval as a tool. Fixed RAG is more predictable; tool-driven retrieval is more flexible but harder to evaluate. How does LangChain tool calling work? In LangChain, you define tools as Python functions with the tool decorator or Pydantic schemas, attach them to a chat model with bind_tools, and the model returns messages containing tool_calls with names and arguments. You then execute the calls, either manually or with prebuilt components such as ToolNode in LangGraph or LangChain's agent helpers, and pass results back as tool messages. LangChain standardises tool calling across providers, so the same tools work with Claude, OpenAI, Gemini and Ollama models. Write clear docstrings, since they become tool descriptions. For production, add validation, error handling and limits on how many tool calls an agent may make. How do you enable tool calling in Ollama? Use a model that supports tools, then pass a tools array with JSON schemas in requests to Ollama's chat API or its OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model returns tool calls, which your code executes before sending results back. Also asked as: how to enable tool calling in ollama Ollama's Python and JavaScript libraries accept Python functions or schemas as tools and return structured tool calls. Streaming responses can include tool calls in recent versions. Reliability depends on the model, its size and the chat template; small models may skip tools or produce invalid arguments. Increase context length for agent workflows, validate arguments, and test with realistic prompts. Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex wrap Ollama tool calling for agents. Which Ollama models support tool calling? Ollama marks tool-capable models with a tools tag in its library. Common choices include Llama 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, Mistral and Mistral Nemo, gpt-oss, Devstral, Granite and Command R models. Filter the Ollama library by the tools category to see the current list, since new models are added frequently. Larger models handle multi-step tool use more reliably, while small ones suit single, well-defined tools. Models trained specifically for agents, such as Qwen3 and gpt-oss, tend to follow tool formats more consistently. Test your exact tools and prompts, because performance varies widely between tasks even among models that support tools. Does Llama 3.1 support tool calling? Yes. Llama 3.1 was trained for tool use, supporting custom tools defined with JSON schemas and built-in tool formats for search, a code interpreter and Wolfram Alpha. It works through Ollama, vLLM, Groq and other providers. The 70B and 405B models handle tools more reliably than the 8B model, which works for simple single calls but can struggle with complex sequences. Use the correct chat template, which serving engines usually apply automatically. Newer models, such as Llama 3.3, Qwen3 and gpt-oss, often perform better on tool benchmarks, so compare options. Validate arguments and handle cases where the model answers directly instead of calling a needed tool. Which LLM benchmark measures tool calling? The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard is the best-known benchmark for tool calling, testing simple, multiple, parallel and multi-turn calls. Tau-bench measures agents completing realistic customer service tasks with tools and policies. Also asked as: which llm benchmark mesures tool calling Other benchmarks include ToolBench, API-Bank and newer evaluations focused on MCP servers and agentic workflows. Benchmarks measure different skills: correct arguments, choosing between tools, knowing when not to call any, and completing multi-step tasks reliably over repeated attempts. Repeated runs reveal reliability, which single scores hide. Leaderboard ranks may not match your tools, so build a small evaluation set from your real use cases, measuring success rate, argument accuracy and how often the model needs retries. How does AI tool calling work in plain JavaScript? In about forty lines: define a tools array with names, descriptions and JSON schemas; call a model API with fetch; if the response contains a tool call, run the matching JavaScript function; append the result; and call the API again until the model answers. Also asked as: how ai tool calling works (40 lines of vanilla javascript Keep a map from tool names to functions, parse arguments with JSON.parse inside a try block, and return errors to the model as tool results so it can recover. Add a maximum loop count to prevent endless cycles. Never expose API keys in browser code; run this loop on a server, such as Node.js, or behind your own API. Log every call and result to debug unexpected behaviour. Writing it by hand clarifies what agent frameworks automate.

# Traditional vs agentic RAG: diagrams, agentic search, GraphRAG, LangGraph tutorial, tools
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/traditional-vs-agentic-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Traditional RAG runs one fixed pipeline: retrieve passages once, then generate an answer. Agentic RAG puts a language model agent in control: it decides whether to retrieve, which source or tool to use, rewrites queries, checks results and retrieves again until it has enough evidence. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, fusion, reranking and a confidence gate, so this page compares traditional and agentic RAG, agentic search, GraphRAG, a LangGraph tutorial, examples, frameworks, models, courses and code.

## Traditional vs agentic RAG: what is the difference?

Traditional RAG is a fixed sequence: embed the question, retrieve top passages, generate. Agentic RAG makes retrieval a tool the model chooses to use in a loop, planning queries, selecting sources, evaluating results and iterating before answering.

Traditional RAG is fast, cheap, predictable and easy to evaluate, which suits single-hop questions over one knowledge base. Agentic RAG handles multi-step questions, such as comparing policies across years, combining documents with database queries, or recovering when the first search returns nothing useful. The costs are latency, more model calls, harder debugging and new failure modes, like loops or irrelevant tool use. Start traditional, measure failures, and add agentic steps only where they fix real problems.

## What does a RAG vs agentic RAG diagram look like?

A traditional RAG diagram is a straight line: question, retriever, top passages, prompt, language model, answer. An agentic RAG diagram is a loop: question, agent, decision, tool calls to retrievers or APIs, observation, decision again, and finally an answer.

In the agentic version, the agent box connects to several tools, such as a vector search over documents, a web search, a SQL database and a calculator, with arrows back to the agent after each call. Many diagrams also show a grader step that checks whether retrieved documents are relevant, and a rewrite step that reformulates the question if not. Drawing your own diagram before building helps decide where loops are truly needed and where a straight pipeline is enough.

## RAG vs agentic search: how do they differ?

RAG retrieves from a prepared index of your documents to answer one question. Agentic search uses an agent that issues many searches, often on the web or across several sources, reads results, follows leads and synthesises a report, like a research assistant.

Agentic search powers deep research features in assistants, which may run dozens of searches and browse many pages for one request. RAG is better for fast, cited answers from known, trusted content; agentic search is better for open-ended research where the right sources are unknown. They converge in agentic RAG, where an agent searches internal indexes iteratively. Both need source quality checks, since agents can collect unreliable pages, and both should cite sources so users can verify.

## Agentic RAG vs GraphRAG: what is the difference?

GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from documents, extracting entities and relationships and often summarising communities of related entities, then retrieves over that structure. Agentic RAG adds an agent that decides how and where to retrieve. They address different problems and can be combined.

GraphRAG, popularised by Microsoft Research, helps with global questions such as the main themes across a large corpus, and with multi-hop relationships between entities, which chunk search handles poorly. Building the graph costs significant indexing compute and needs updating as documents change. Agentic RAG improves flexibility at query time instead. An agent can use a graph as one of its tools, querying relationships when needed and falling back to vector search for detailed passages.

## How do you build agentic RAG with LangGraph?

In LangGraph, define a state with the question, messages and retrieved documents; add nodes for an agent that decides to call a retriever tool, a grader that checks relevance, a rewriter that reformulates queries, and a generator; then connect them with conditional edges.

The flow: the agent node receives the question and either answers directly or calls the retriever tool; the grader node scores retrieved documents; if relevant, the generate node writes a cited answer; if not, the rewrite node improves the query and loops back, with a maximum iteration count to prevent endless loops. Compile the graph, run it with streaming to watch each step, and trace runs in LangSmith. LangGraph's documentation includes an agentic RAG tutorial with this structure.

## What are some examples of agentic RAG?

Examples include a support agent that searches documentation, checks order data and opens a ticket; a research assistant that runs multiple searches and compares findings; a legal assistant that retrieves clauses across contracts and compares them; and a coding agent searching a codebase.

Other examples: a financial analyst agent that pulls figures from reports with retrieval and computes ratios with a calculator tool; an HR assistant that routes questions to the right policy collection; and a study assistant that searches course notes, then quizzes the student. In each, the agent decides which source to query and whether results are sufficient. The common thread is multi-step reasoning where a single retrieval pass would miss evidence or tools.

## What is the best agentic RAG framework?

Popular choices are LangGraph for explicit, stateful control flows, LlamaIndex for data-centric agents with strong retrieval components, Haystack for production pipelines with agents, and lighter options such as smolagents, PydanticAI or provider agent SDKs.

Choose by control and team skills. LangGraph suits complex flows with branching, retries and human approval. LlamaIndex offers many retrievers, query engines and agent workflows out of the box. Haystack provides modular pipelines with clear components. Provider SDKs, such as OpenAI's Agents SDK or Google's ADK, are simple for tool-calling agents. For many teams, plain Python with a tool-calling model and a well-built retriever is enough, and easier to debug than a heavy framework.

## What is the best LLM for agentic RAG?

Agentic RAG needs models that call tools reliably, follow instructions over many steps and judge relevance well. Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google lead on these abilities, while strong open models such as the Llama, Qwen and Mistral families work well for self-hosting.

Benchmark on your own tasks: measure tool-call accuracy, answer faithfulness, number of steps and latency. A practical pattern is model routing: a fast, cheap model for query rewriting and relevance grading, and a stronger model for planning and final answers. Models with long context windows help when many passages are retrieved, but good reranking keeps context small. For hosted open models, providers such as Groq offer fast inference, which matters when agents make many sequential calls.

## What is the best agentic RAG course?

Good options include DeepLearning.AI short courses on agentic RAG with LlamaIndex and on LangGraph agents, LangChain Academy's free LangGraph course, Hugging Face's Agents Course, and the official tutorials in the LlamaIndex and LangGraph documentation.

Before agentic RAG, make sure you understand basic RAG well: chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking and evaluation, since agents amplify retrieval problems rather than hiding them. Then follow a course that builds a working agent with a retriever tool, a relevance grader and query rewriting. Finish by adding evaluation: compare agentic and traditional pipelines on the same questions, measuring accuracy, latency and cost, to learn when agents actually help.

## What are the best agentic RAG GitHub repositories?

Useful repositories include the LangGraph examples with agentic RAG notebooks, LlamaIndex's agent and workflow examples, Microsoft's GraphRAG, Haystack's tutorials, and curated awesome-RAG lists that link to many implementations.

When evaluating a repository, check recent activity, issues, licence, and whether it includes evaluation, not just a demo. Prefer examples that log every tool call and show failure handling, such as retries and iteration limits. Clone one, run it on your own documents, and break it deliberately: ask multi-hop questions, questions with no answer in the data, and ambiguous follow-ups. Studying how the agent fails teaches more than reading code that works on curated examples.

# Training loss explained: what it should look like, spikes, overfitting and Hugging Face
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/training-loss-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Training loss measures how wrong a model's predictions are on the training data, computed after each batch or step. A healthy curve drops quickly at first, then flattens with some noise; what matters most is how it compares with validation loss and real task metrics. FineTune Studio streams loss live over WebSockets during QLoRA fine-tuning, because watching the curve catches problems early. This page covers healthy loss curves, targets, direction, negative values, overfitting, spikes, accuracy versus loss, Hugging Face Trainer, and loss in FCNs.

## What should training loss look like?

A typical healthy training loss curve falls steeply in the first steps, then decreases more slowly and flattens, with small up-and-down noise between batches. Smoothed curves make the trend easier to read.

Warning signs: loss that does not decrease at all suggests a bug, a learning rate far too low, or labels not matching inputs; loss that explodes or becomes NaN suggests a learning rate too high or numerical instability; and loss that drops to almost zero very quickly on a small dataset often means memorisation. Always plot validation loss alongside training loss, ideally evaluated at regular intervals, to judge generalisation.

## How low should training loss be?

There is no universal target. The right level depends on the loss function, task difficulty, label noise and data. Cross-entropy loss for language model fine-tuning might settle around 1 or lower, while other tasks have completely different scales.

Judge by comparison instead: does validation loss track training loss, and do task metrics such as accuracy, F1 or human ratings improve? Pushing training loss extremely low usually means overfitting, especially on small datasets. For fine-tuning language models, a modest drop from the starting loss, with improving outputs on held-out prompts, is often what you want. In FineTune Studio, I compare base and tuned outputs side by side rather than chasing a number.

## Why does training loss always decrease?

Training loss usually decreases because the optimiser adjusts weights specifically to reduce it on the training data. With enough capacity, a model can keep reducing training loss by fitting the training examples ever more closely, even memorising them.

It does not always decrease smoothly: batch noise, learning rate schedules, regularisation and data augmentation cause fluctuations. That steady fall is why training loss alone is misleading: it measures fit to data the model has already seen. Validation loss on unseen data tells you whether learning generalises. When training loss falls but validation loss rises, the model is overfitting.

## Should training loss increase or decrease?

Training loss should generally decrease over time. Short-term increases are normal noise, and learning rate warm-up or restarts can cause temporary rises. A sustained increase signals a problem, such as an unstable learning rate, corrupted data or a bug.

If loss increases steadily, lower the learning rate, check for exploding gradients and enable gradient clipping, inspect recent batches for bad data, and verify mixed precision settings. If loss plateaus early at a high value, the learning rate may be too low, the model too small, or the data or labels flawed. Change one thing at a time so you know what fixed it.

## Can training loss be negative?

Most standard losses, such as cross-entropy and mean squared error, cannot be negative, so a negative value usually indicates a bug: probabilities outside 0 to 1, a wrong sign, or an incorrect custom loss. Some losses legitimately go negative, such as certain log-likelihood formulations and some contrastive or reward-based objectives.

If you see unexpected negative loss, check that model outputs are passed in the form the loss expects, such as logits versus probabilities, that labels are correctly encoded, and that custom loss code has the right sign. For losses that can be negative by design, judge progress by trends and validation metrics, not by the value crossing zero.

## How do training and validation loss show overfitting?

Overfitting appears when training loss keeps falling while validation loss stops improving and starts rising. The model is learning patterns specific to the training data that do not generalise to new examples.

Remedies:

- Stop training at the best validation checkpoint, known as early stopping.
- Add more or more varied training data.
- Use regularisation, such as dropout or weight decay.
- Reduce model size or trainable parameters, as LoRA does.
- Use data augmentation where appropriate.
- Train for fewer epochs with a lower learning rate.

For language model fine-tuning, one to three epochs on good data is often enough; more frequently causes overfitting.

## Why do I get spikes in loss during training?

Spikes usually come from a learning rate that is too high, a batch containing unusual or corrupted examples, very small batch sizes, numerical issues in mixed precision, or exploding gradients. Occasional small spikes that recover are normal.

Fixes:

- Lower the learning rate or add warm-up.
- Enable gradient clipping to cap update sizes.
- Inspect data around spike steps for bad examples.
- Increase batch size or use gradient accumulation.
- Use bfloat16 instead of float16 if supported, or enable loss scaling.
- Shuffle data properly so batches are representative.

Log which samples were in spiking batches; the cause is often in the data.

## What is the difference between training accuracy and training loss?

Training loss measures how wrong predictions are in a continuous, differentiable way, including how confident the model is. Training accuracy measures the fraction of correct predictions, ignoring confidence. The optimiser minimises loss; accuracy is what humans usually care about.

They can move differently: loss can fall while accuracy stays flat, when the model becomes more confident in already-correct answers, or accuracy can rise while loss rises, when a few predictions become very confidently wrong. Track both, plus validation versions of each. For imbalanced data, also track precision, recall and F1, since accuracy can be misleading.

## What loss function does the Hugging Face Trainer use?

The Hugging Face Trainer uses the loss returned by the model's forward pass when labels are provided. For classification and language modelling models, that is usually cross-entropy loss, computed inside the model class.

To use a different loss, such as weighted cross-entropy for imbalanced classes, subclass Trainer and override `compute_loss`, returning your custom loss. TRL's trainers, such as the SFT trainer used for instruction tuning, build on the same idea, with options such as computing loss only on assistant responses. Check the model's documentation to see exactly which loss its forward pass computes.

## What is training loss in an FCN?

In a fully convolutional network for semantic segmentation, training loss is usually pixel-wise cross-entropy: each pixel is classified, and the loss averages errors across all pixels and images. FCNs, introduced in 2014, made dense pixel prediction efficient.

Because some classes cover far fewer pixels, such as thin roads or small lesions, plain cross-entropy can favour large classes. Common fixes include class-weighted cross-entropy, Dice loss, focal loss or combinations. Monitor validation metrics such as mean intersection over union alongside loss, since a falling loss may not reflect better segmentation of small but important classes.
