# Training loss explained: minimising it, loss functions, validation curves, overfitting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/training-loss-validation-overfitting/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Loss measures how wrong a model's predictions are, and training is the process of reducing it. But low training loss alone is not the goal; the model must generalise to new data, which validation loss reveals. FineTune Studio streams live loss charts over WebSockets during QLoRA fine-tuning and compares base and tuned models, so this page covers minimising loss, loss functions, training versus validation loss and curves, flat losses, Keras stopping, overfitting, soft labels and distillation temperature. How do you minimise loss when training a model? Use a suitable optimiser such as AdamW, tune the learning rate with warmup and a decay schedule, normalise inputs, choose a sensible batch size, and make sure data and labels are clean. Monitor validation loss, not just training loss. Also asked as: how to minimize loss when training a model If loss falls slowly, try a higher learning rate or check that gradients flow through all layers. If loss is unstable or explodes, lower the learning rate or use gradient clipping. Better data often reduces loss more than architecture changes. For fine-tuning, LoRA ranks and learning rates matter most. Remember that minimising training loss to near zero usually means memorising; the goal is the lowest validation loss on unseen data. What functions can you use for training loss? Common loss functions include mean squared error and Huber loss for regression, cross-entropy for classification, focal loss for imbalanced classes, contrastive and InfoNCE losses for embeddings, CTC loss for speech and handwriting, and next-token cross-entropy for language models. Choose the loss that matches your task and output: probabilities need cross-entropy, ranking tasks use pairwise or listwise losses, and face recognition uses margin losses such as ArcFace. KL divergence compares probability distributions, useful in distillation. Custom losses can encode business priorities, such as penalising false negatives more. Frameworks such as PyTorch and Keras provide most standard losses. Plot loss alongside task metrics, since they can disagree, and test custom losses carefully. What is the difference between training loss and validation loss? Training loss is measured on the data the model learns from; validation loss is measured on held-out data it never trains on. Validation loss estimates how well the model generalises to new examples. Also asked as: difference between training and validation loss Training loss usually keeps falling as the model fits the data, while validation loss falls at first, then may rise once the model starts memorising. The gap between them indicates overfitting. Use validation loss to choose checkpoints, tune hyperparameters and decide when to stop. Keep a separate test set, untouched until the end, for a final honest evaluation, since repeated tuning on validation data can make it optimistic. Report both numbers when sharing results. How do you read a training vs validation loss curve? If both curves fall and stay close, training is healthy. If training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises, the model is overfitting. If both stay high, it is underfitting. Large spikes suggest learning rate or data problems. Validation loss below training loss can occur when dropout or augmentation apply only during training, or when validation data is easier, so check for leakage too. Noisy curves often come from small batches or high learning rates; smoothing helps reading trends. FineTune Studio streams these curves live during fine-tuning, so problems can be caught early rather than after hours of wasted training. Save checkpoints near the validation minimum. Why are training and validation loss not changing? Flat losses usually mean the model is not learning: the learning rate is too low or extremely high, layers are frozen, gradients are zero because of a bug, labels are wrong or constant, or the optimiser step is missing in the training loop. Also asked as: why my training and validation loss is not changing Check basics: confirm the backward pass and optimiser step run each batch, gradients are non-zero, trainable parameters exist, and inputs are normalised and shuffled. Try overfitting a tiny batch, which a working setup should achieve quickly; if it cannot, there is a bug. Verify the loss function matches the output, such as cross-entropy with raw logits. Dead activations and poor initialisation can also stall learning. Logging gradient norms makes these problems visible. How do you tell Keras to stop training based on loss? Use the EarlyStopping callback, monitoring validation loss with a patience value and restore_best_weights set to true, so training stops when validation loss stops improving and keeps the best weights. Also asked as: how to tell keras stop training based on loss value To stop at a specific loss threshold, write a custom callback whose on_epoch_end method checks the logged loss and sets the model's stop_training attribute to true when the threshold is reached. Combine early stopping with ModelCheckpoint to save the best model to disk. Choose patience carefully: too small stops before noisy curves recover, while too large wastes time and risks overfitting. Log metrics to TensorBoard for easy comparison across runs. What is overfitting in machine learning? Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely, including noise and quirks, so it performs well on training data but poorly on new data. A widening gap between training and validation performance reveals it. Causes include too little data, overly complex models, too many training epochs and data leakage. In LLM fine-tuning, overfitting shows up as the model repeating training phrases, losing general abilities or answering only in the training format. Detect it by monitoring validation loss and testing on realistic held-out examples. FineTune Studio's base-versus-tuned comparison helps reveal when a fine-tuned model has lost useful general behaviour. Simple models trained on enough data often generalise surprisingly well. How do you overcome overfitting in ML? Add more or more varied data, use data augmentation, apply regularisation such as dropout and weight decay, stop training early based on validation loss, simplify the model, and use cross-validation to tune choices reliably. Also asked as: what is overfitting in ml · how to overcome overfitting in ml For fine-tuning language models, use fewer epochs, lower learning rates, smaller LoRA ranks and more diverse examples, and mix in general data to preserve broad skills. Remove duplicates and near-duplicates between training and validation sets, which hide overfitting. Ensembles and pretrained backbones also improve generalisation. Track experiments so you know which change helped. Always confirm improvements on a final test set, since repeated tuning against validation data can itself lead to overfitting the validation set. What loss function should you use when labels are probabilities? Use cross-entropy with soft targets, which accepts probability distributions as labels, or KL divergence between the predicted and target distributions. For independent per-label probabilities in multi-label tasks, use binary cross-entropy on each label. Also asked as: what loss function to use when labels are probabilities Soft labels appear in knowledge distillation, label smoothing, crowd-sourced annotations with disagreement, and mixup augmentation. Make sure predictions pass through softmax or sigmoid consistently with the loss, and avoid applying them twice. Check that target rows sum to one. PyTorch's cross-entropy loss supports probability targets directly, and Keras's categorical cross-entropy accepts them as well. Mean squared error on probabilities works but usually trains less effectively than cross-entropy for classification. Why is temperature necessary in distillation loss? Temperature softens the teacher's output probabilities, revealing how similar it considers different classes, information that hard labels and sharp probabilities hide. The student learns from these softer distributions, often generalising better than from labels alone. Also asked as: why is temperature necessary in the loss function for model distillation In Hinton and colleagues' 2015 formulation, both teacher and student logits are divided by a temperature greater than one before softmax, and the distillation loss compares them with KL divergence. Because softening shrinks gradients, the loss is multiplied by the temperature squared to keep its scale. Usually, distillation loss is combined with standard cross-entropy on true labels. Tune temperature on validation data, since values that are too high flatten useful distinctions.

# Training vs validation loss: oscillation, overfitting, schedulers and eval_loss errors
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/training-vs-validation-loss/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Loss curves are the main window into training: training loss shows how well a model fits its training data, and validation loss shows how well it generalises to data it has not seen. Their shapes reveal learning-rate problems, overfitting and bugs. FineTune Studio, which I built, streams live training loss over WebSockets during QLoRA runs for exactly this reason, so this page explains oscillation, the training and validation gap, overfitting in LLMs, stuck runs, schedulers and common logging errors.

## What could an oscillating training loss curve represent?

Oscillation usually means the learning rate is too high, the batch size is too small, or the data is noisy or poorly shuffled. Some oscillation is normal with mini-batches; large, growing swings signal instability.

Diagnose step by step: plot a smoothed moving average to see the trend under the noise; lower the learning rate or add warmup; increase the effective batch size with gradient accumulation; check that data is shuffled, since batches ordered by class or length create periodic patterns; and look for bad examples that spike the loss. Gradient clipping helps with occasional explosions. If loss oscillates and rises, stop and fix the setup before wasting compute on a run that will not recover.

## Validation loss vs training loss: what is the difference?

Training loss is computed on the data the model learns from, usually averaged during each epoch. Validation loss is computed on held-out data the model never trains on, measuring generalisation. The gap between them is your main overfitting signal.

Healthy training shows both decreasing, with validation slightly above training. Validation lower than training can happen when dropout or augmentation is active only during training, or when training loss is averaged over an epoch while the model improves. A widening gap with rising validation loss means overfitting. Both high and flat means underfitting: the model is too small, the learning rate is wrong, or the features carry little signal. Always choose checkpoints by validation, not training, loss.

## How do you read a training vs validation loss plot?

Plot both losses against steps or epochs on the same axes, often with a log scale for loss. Look at three things: whether both decrease, the gap between them, and the point where validation loss stops improving.

Common shapes: both falling together means keep training; validation flattening while training keeps falling means you are near the best checkpoint; validation rising means overfitting, so stop or regularise; both flat and high means underfitting or a bug; sudden spikes mean instability or bad data. In code, log both to TensorBoard or Weights & Biases, or plot the trainer's log history with matplotlib. Mark the best validation checkpoint on the plot for clarity.

## What should you do if training loss decreases but validation loss does not?

That is overfitting or a mismatch between training and validation data. The model is memorising training examples instead of learning patterns that transfer. Stop at the best validation checkpoint and then improve data or regularisation.

Fixes, roughly in order: use early stopping; add more or more diverse training data; apply data augmentation; increase dropout or weight decay; reduce model capacity or, for LoRA, lower the rank; lower the learning rate or train fewer epochs. Also check the split itself: if validation comes from a different distribution, or labels differ in style, the gap reflects the data, not the model. Leakage checks matter too, since duplicates make training look better than it is.

## How do LLMs avoid overfitting?

During pre-training, LLMs see enormous, diverse datasets, often for about one pass, so they rarely overfit in the classic sense. Overfitting becomes a real risk during fine-tuning on small datasets, where a model can memorise examples within a few epochs.

Fine-tuning defences: parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA that update few weights; small learning rates with warmup; one to three epochs; dropout on LoRA layers; held-out evaluation with early stopping; and diverse, deduplicated data. Mixing in general instruction data helps prevent forgetting of broad skills. Evaluate on fresh prompts, not just validation loss, since a model can keep a low loss while copying phrasing from training data. FineTune Studio compares base and tuned outputs for this reason.

## Why is training loss not decreasing when fine-tuning Qwen with Unsloth?

Common causes are a learning rate that is too low or too high, a wrong chat template, labels masked incorrectly so the model trains on nothing useful, LoRA targeting too few modules, or a dataset that is already easy for the model.

Check the formatted training examples: apply the Qwen chat template your model expects and print a sample to confirm roles and special tokens are correct. If you train only on responses, verify that response masking actually leaves response tokens unmasked. Try a learning rate around 2e-4 for LoRA, target all linear layers, and confirm the count of trainable parameters is non-zero. Also check whether loss is already low at step one, which means the model already knows the task.

## Should a learning rate scheduler step per batch or per epoch?

For modern training, especially transformers, step the scheduler per optimisation step, so warmup and decay are smooth. Per-epoch stepping suits older schedules such as step decay every few epochs, mostly in classic vision training.

Hugging Face schedulers like linear or cosine with warmup are defined in optimisation steps and called after each optimizer step. With gradient accumulation, count optimizer updates, not micro-batches, when computing total steps. PyTorch's ReduceLROnPlateau, by contrast, steps on a validation metric, typically once per epoch. Whatever you choose, log the learning rate alongside loss, since many confusing loss curves turn out to be scheduler mistakes, such as decay finishing far too early.

## What is the difference between training error and training loss?

Training loss is the value of the differentiable objective the optimiser minimises, such as cross-entropy. Training error is a task metric on the same data, such as the fraction of misclassified examples. They usually move together but are not the same.

Loss captures confidence: a classifier can predict the right class with low confidence, giving zero error but non-zero loss, or become more confident without changing any predictions, lowering loss while error stays the same. That is why you track both: loss to guide optimisation and spot instability, and error or accuracy to judge usefulness. For language models, perplexity, the exponential of the average loss, is often reported alongside task metrics.

## Do we need zero training loss after achieving zero training error?

No. Zero training error means every training example is classified correctly; pushing loss to zero after that only makes predictions more confident on training data, which often harms generalisation and calibration.

Continuing to train can still help in some regimes, since margins grow and validation may improve for a while, but watch validation metrics rather than training loss. Techniques such as label smoothing deliberately keep training loss above zero to improve calibration. A 2020 method called flooding even keeps training loss near a small floor instead of driving it to zero. In practice, stop when validation performance peaks, regardless of what training loss is doing at that point.

## Why is there no training log and a KeyError for eval_loss?

In the Hugging Face Trainer, eval_loss only exists when evaluation runs. A KeyError appears when settings such as load_best_model_at_end or metric_for_best_model reference eval_loss but no evaluation dataset or evaluation strategy is configured.

Fix it by passing an `eval_dataset`, setting `eval_strategy` (older versions call it `evaluation_strategy`) to steps or epoch, and matching `save_strategy` to it. Missing training logs usually mean `logging_steps` is larger than the total number of steps, or `report_to` is set to none without a console callback. Also confirm the model returns a loss: labels must be present in each batch, otherwise the trainer cannot compute it, and evaluation will silently report nothing useful.

# What does tuning mean in machine learning? Fine-tuning, GPUs and GPU tuning
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/tuning-fine-tuning-gpus/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tuning means adjusting something to make it work better. In machine learning it has two common meanings: hyperparameter tuning, choosing settings such as learning rate before or during training, and fine-tuning, continuing to train a pretrained model on your own data. "GPU tuning" is different again: adjusting a graphics card's clocks, power and fans. This page explains each meaning, whether fine-tuning retrains the whole model, which GPUs and clouds suit LLM fine-tuning, whether and how to tune an NVIDIA GPU, and vLLM on AMD, drawing on building FineTune Studio, a browser-based QLoRA fine-tuning tool.

## What is the meaning of tuning?

Tuning means making small adjustments to improve performance or fit a purpose, like tuning a guitar, an engine or a radio. In computing, it means adjusting settings of software or hardware to run faster, more accurately or more efficiently.

In AI, you will meet several kinds: hyperparameter tuning, fine-tuning a model, prompt tuning, performance tuning of databases and inference servers, and GPU tuning. They share the idea of adjusting a system against a measurable goal. The key habit in all of them is measurement: change one thing, measure the effect, keep what helps.

## What is the meaning of fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning means taking a model that has already been trained on a large general dataset and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset, so it adapts to a particular task, domain, format or style.

For example, a general language model can be fine-tuned on support tickets to classify them into your categories, or on examples of your reports to follow your format. Fine-tuning is much cheaper than training from scratch because the model already knows language; you only teach the specifics. It changes behaviour well, but is weaker for adding facts, where retrieval-augmented generation is usually better.

## What is tuning in machine learning?

In machine learning, tuning usually means hyperparameter tuning: finding the best values for settings that are not learned from data, such as learning rate, batch size, number of trees, regularisation strength or model depth, by testing combinations on validation data.

Methods include grid search, which tries every combination; random search, which samples combinations and is often more efficient; and Bayesian optimisation, which uses past results to choose promising settings. Always tune on a validation set and report final results on a separate test set, or you overfit to your evaluation. Libraries such as scikit-learn and Optuna make this straightforward. For LLM fine-tuning, the important hyperparameters are learning rate, number of epochs, LoRA rank and batch size.

## Does fine-tuning require retraining the entire model?

No. Full fine-tuning updates all weights, but parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA freeze the original model and train only small added matrices, often well under one per cent of the parameters. QLoRA also loads the frozen model in 4-bit precision to save memory.

The benefits: far less GPU memory, faster training, tiny adapter files that can be swapped on one base model, and less risk of damaging the model's general abilities. Quality is close to full fine-tuning for many tasks. Full fine-tuning still makes sense for large changes in behaviour or domain when you have lots of data and compute. FineTune Studio uses QLoRA through Transformers, PEFT and TRL so fine-tuning fits on modest GPUs.

## What is the best GPU for fine-tuning LLMs?

The most important factor is GPU memory. With QLoRA, 7B to 8B models fit on GPUs with 16 to 24 GB; larger models need 40 to 80 GB data-centre GPUs or several GPUs. NVIDIA GPUs have the broadest software support.

Rough guidance:

- **Learning and small models**: free cloud GPUs in Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks.
- **7B to 8B models with QLoRA**: consumer GPUs with 24 GB, or cloud GPUs such as the L4.
- **13B to 34B models**: 40 to 80 GB GPUs such as A100 or H100 class, or multi-GPU setups.
- **Very large models**: multiple data-centre GPUs and distributed training.

Memory also depends on sequence length and batch size; long contexts need much more. Measure peak memory on a short run before a long one.

## Big vs small GPU clouds for fine-tuning LLMs: which is better?

Large cloud providers offer reliability, enterprise security, many regions and integration with other services, at higher prices and with quota hurdles for GPUs. Smaller GPU clouds often offer cheaper, easier access to GPUs by the hour, with fewer extra services.

For students and individual experiments, smaller GPU clouds and notebook platforms are usually the most practical: quick to start, pay only for training time. For companies with compliance needs or data already in a major cloud, the big providers simplify security and data transfer. Whichever you use, save checkpoints to persistent storage, shut instances down when finished, set budget alerts, and keep training scripts reproducible so you can move between providers.

## What is GPU tuning?

GPU tuning means adjusting a graphics card's operating settings, such as core and memory clock speeds, voltage, power limit and fan curve, to get more performance, lower temperatures, less noise or better efficiency.

There are two directions. Overclocking raises clocks for more performance, at the cost of heat, power and possible instability. Undervolting or power limiting lowers voltage or power for nearly the same performance with less heat and noise, which is often ideal for long machine learning runs. Tools include vendor utilities and third-party apps. Changes should be small and tested for stability, because an unstable GPU can crash a training run after hours.

## Should I tune my GPU?

For machine learning, modest power limiting or undervolting is often worth it: it reduces temperature, noise and power draw, usually with little loss of speed, which helps on long training runs. Aggressive overclocking is rarely worth the instability risk for training.

Before tuning, make sure drivers are up to date, cooling and airflow are good, and dust is cleared, since these often matter more. Change one setting at a time and run a stress test or a short training job to check stability. On laptops, manufacturer power modes are safer than manual tuning. If you are not comfortable, leave defaults; modern GPUs already manage boost clocks and thermals automatically.

## How do I tune an NVIDIA GPU?

Use NVIDIA's own app or a third-party tool to adjust power limit, clocks and fan curve, or `nvidia-smi` on the command line to set a power limit, then test stability with a real workload.

A cautious approach for machine learning:

- Check current power, temperature and clocks with `nvidia-smi`.
- Lower the power limit step by step, for example in small percentages, and measure training speed.
- Keep the setting where speed barely drops but temperature and noise fall clearly.
- Adjust the fan curve if temperatures stay high.
- Run a full training epoch to confirm stability.

Setting power limits may need administrator rights and resets after reboot unless made persistent.

## Does vLLM support AMD GPUs?

Yes. vLLM supports AMD GPUs through AMD's ROCm software platform, in addition to NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA, and it also has support for other accelerators. Check the documentation for supported AMD models, ROCm versions and installation steps.

On AMD, installation typically uses ROCm-specific Docker images or builds, and some features may arrive later than on NVIDIA. Before committing, verify that your exact GPU and ROCm version are supported, and benchmark throughput with your model and settings. vLLM's strengths, efficient memory management and continuous batching, apply on both platforms, which makes it a good choice for serving open models to many users.

# Turning a student project into a startup: the real signal to look for, what changes, and what most student founders get wrong first
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/turning-a-student-project-into-a-startup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## When does a student project actually deserve to become a startup?

**When strangers use it without being asked to, repeatedly, for a problem that costs them real time or money. Not when you are proud of the code, not when it won a hackathon, not when friends say it's a good idea. The signal that separates a project worth pursuing from one that should stay a project is unprompted, repeated use by people who owe you nothing, because that is the only signal that is hard to fake and hard to talk yourself into.**


Annapurna, a food-sharing platform I built for a hackathon, won first prize and then kept running as a real tool afterward, and the difference between it and other hackathon projects that stopped the day after judging was exactly this signal, not the idea's cleverness or the demo's polish [7].

> A hackathon prize measures whether judges liked your demo in three minutes. A startup measures whether a stranger comes back on their own, for weeks, with nobody grading them for it.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why do most student projects, including good ones, not deserve this?

**Because most student projects are built to demonstrate a skill or win a specific evaluation, a grade, a hackathon prize, an interview portfolio piece, and that goal is fully achieved the moment the evaluation ends. A project built to impress a judge for three minutes was never tested against the much harder question of whether a stranger would choose to keep using it a month later with no one watching. Most good projects are good demonstrations, not good businesses, and there is nothing wrong with that; the mistake is assuming every good demonstration is secretly a startup waiting to happen.**



## What actually changes when you move from project to startup attempt?

**You need users who did not choose you out of friendship, loyalty, or a grading relationship, which means finding and convincing strangers, the hardest part most student founders underestimate [2]. You need a reason to keep working without a deadline, grade or judging panel forcing progress, which most people discover they do not actually have once the artificial deadline disappears. You need to survive being told no, or being ignored, repeatedly, by people who have no obligation to engage with you at all. None of this is about the code getting harder; the code is often the easy part.**




## Is a hackathon win a signal that a project should become a startup?

**A hackathon win is a strong signal of judged execution: you built something that worked, demoed well, and impressed a panel in a short, high-pressure window. It is not a signal of market demand, which is measured over weeks by whether people choose to keep using the thing without a judge, a prize, or a room full of attention pushing them toward it. Some hackathon-winning projects do have real demand underneath, Annapurna did, but the win itself is not the evidence; what happens in the weeks after, with no one watching, is the evidence [7].**



## What is the honest test before committing real time?

**Would you keep working on this for a stranger who owes you nothing, with no deadline, no grade, and no one watching, for the next month? Not "is the idea good" or "do I believe in it", both of which are easy to answer yes to for almost anything you built. The honest test is behavioural: are you actually still doing the unglamorous work, talking to users, fixing the boring bug, following up on a lead, once the applause from the demo has faded. Most ideas fail this test quietly, and that is useful information, not failure.**


## What mistakes do student founders make first?

**Pursuing every reasonably good project as a potential startup, diluting effort across ideas instead of concentrating it on the one with a real signal. Confusing a hackathon prize or a good grade with market validation. Building for months in isolation before showing it to a single stranger outside their circle [3]. Assuming the hard part is the code, when for most consumer and small-business ideas the hard part is finding and keeping the first real users. Quitting a real signal too early because the early weeks of any real attempt are slow and unglamorous, indistinguishable from the early weeks of one that will fail.**



## Interview and pitch questions this topic prepares you for

**"Why did you stop working on that project" or "why did you keep going" comes up naturally once you have a project with real signal or a clear decision to move on from one without it. The strongest answer names the specific evidence, user behaviour, not vibes, that drove the decision either way, which reads as founder judgement whether or not you ultimately built a company.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your best finished project and show it to five strangers outside your immediate circle this week. Watch what they actually do, not what they politely say. That is the whole test.** For a session on evaluating student projects for real founder potential, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Types of embeddings, embeddings vs vectors, LLM and vector DB types, and tutorials
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/types-of-embeddings-tutorials/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Embeddings come in several types, word, sentence, document, image, multimodal, graph and user or item embeddings, and they can be dense or sparse. All are vectors, lists of numbers, learned so that similar things sit close together. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense embeddings with BM25 sparse retrieval, so this page covers types of embeddings, embeddings versus vectors, embedding sizes in GPT models, types of LLMs and vector databases, tutorials for LangChain and Hugging Face, and recommender systems.

## How many types of embeddings are there?

There is no fixed number, but common types are word embeddings, sentence and document embeddings, image embeddings, audio embeddings, multimodal embeddings, graph or node embeddings, and user and item embeddings in recommenders. Each can be dense or sparse.

By form, dense embeddings are short vectors of real numbers from neural models, while sparse embeddings, such as SPLADE or BM25-style term weights, have mostly zero values tied to vocabulary terms. Multi-vector embeddings, as in ColBERT, keep one vector per token for fine-grained matching. Embeddings also differ by training: static ones like word2vec give one vector per word, while contextual ones from transformers change with the surrounding text.

## What are embeddings and vectors?

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as (0.2, -1.3, 0.8). An embedding is a vector produced by a model to represent something, such as a word, image or user, so that meaningful relationships become distances between vectors.

Vectors are the mathematical container; embeddings are vectors with learned meaning. A colour as RGB values is a vector but not usually called an embedding, because the numbers were not learned to capture similarity. Embeddings typically have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and their individual numbers are not interpretable; meaning lies in the overall pattern. In AI applications, embeddings are stored in vector databases and compared with cosine similarity or dot product.

## Are embeddings and vectors the same thing?

Every embedding is a vector, but not every vector is an embedding. The word embedding implies the vector was learned to represent an object's meaning or properties, so that similar objects have similar vectors.

In conversation, people use the terms loosely: vector database, vector search and embeddings often refer to the same workflow. The precise distinction helps when debugging: a feature vector of hand-crafted values, such as price and size, behaves differently from a learned embedding, because distances may not reflect similarity unless features are scaled and weighted. Embeddings from different models also live in different spaces, so their vectors cannot be compared directly, even with equal dimensions.

## How many embeddings does ChatGPT have?

OpenAI has not published full architecture details for current ChatGPT models. For reference, GPT-3's largest version used an embedding dimension of 12,288, with a vocabulary of about 50,000 tokens, meaning one 12,288-number vector per token.

Inside the model, every token is converted to an embedding vector, then transformed through many layers. Newer GPT models use larger vocabularies, such as the roughly 200,000-token o200k tokenizer used by GPT-4o, but exact embedding sizes are not disclosed. Separately, OpenAI offers embedding API models for developers: text-embedding-3-small outputs 1,536 dimensions and text-embedding-3-large 3,072. Those are the embeddings you can actually use in your own applications.

## How many types of LLMs are there?

LLMs can be grouped by architecture, training and access: decoder-only models like GPT and Llama, encoder models like BERT, and encoder-decoder models like T5; base, instruction-tuned and reasoning models; and open-weight versus proprietary models.

Other useful categories: by size, from small models of one to a few billion parameters to frontier models; by modality, text-only versus multimodal models that handle images, audio and video; by architecture variant, dense versus mixture-of-experts; and by purpose, general assistants, coding models, embedding models and domain models for medicine or law. Embedding models are technically language models too, but they output vectors rather than text, which is why RAG systems use both kinds together.

## How many types of vector databases are there?

Broadly three types: purpose-built vector databases such as Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus; general databases with vector extensions such as PostgreSQL with pgvector, MongoDB Atlas and Redis; and search engines with vector support such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch.

Libraries such as FAISS, Annoy and hnswlib form a fourth category: vector indexes without database features like persistence, filtering and replication. Deployment options add another dimension: managed cloud services, self-hosted open source, and embedded databases such as Chroma or LanceDB that run inside your application. Choose based on scale, hosting preferences, filtering and hybrid search needs, and whether you want vectors stored alongside existing relational or document data.

## What is a good vector embeddings tutorial?

Start by generating embeddings for a few sentences with Sentence Transformers, computing cosine similarities between them, and seeing which pairs score highest. Then build a tiny semantic search over a list of documents, and visualise embeddings in two dimensions.

Step by step: install sentence-transformers, load a small model such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2, call `model.encode(sentences)`, and compare with `util.cos_sim`. Next, embed 100 short documents, embed a query, and print the top five matches. Plot embeddings with UMAP or PCA to see clusters. Finally, store them in FAISS or Chroma and add metadata. This sequence teaches the core ideas behind semantic search and RAG in an afternoon.

## How do you use embeddings in LangChain?

LangChain provides embedding classes with a common interface: `embed_documents` for lists of texts and `embed_query` for a single query. Choose a provider class, such as OpenAIEmbeddings, HuggingFaceEmbeddings or OllamaEmbeddings, then pass it to a vector store.

A typical flow: load documents, split them with a text splitter, create an embeddings object, and build a vector store with `FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)` or a Chroma equivalent. Then create a retriever with `as_retriever()` and use it in a chain. Use the same embedding class for indexing and querying. Add caching with a cache-backed embeddings wrapper to avoid recomputing vectors for unchanged documents, which saves time and API costs during development.

## How do you use Hugging Face embeddings?

The simplest route is Sentence Transformers: `SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2").encode(texts)` returns embeddings for a list of texts. You can also call models through Hugging Face's Inference API or a Text Embeddings Inference server for production.

Choose a model from the MTEB leaderboard suited to your language and task, such as the BGE, E5 or GTE families, and read its model card, since some require prefixes like query: and passage: for best retrieval. Normalise embeddings for cosine similarity. For speed, batch inputs and use a GPU, or deploy Text Embeddings Inference, which serves models efficiently. LangChain and LlamaIndex wrap these models, so you can plug them into RAG pipelines directly.

## Can you use embeddings for a recommender system?

Yes, embeddings are central to modern recommenders. Collaborative filtering learns latent vectors for users and items from interactions, and recommends items whose vectors score highly with a user's vector. Content embeddings from text or images handle new items.

Common architectures include matrix factorisation, two-tower models that embed users and items separately for fast retrieval, and sequence models that embed browsing history. At scale, item embeddings go into a vector index, the system retrieves hundreds of candidates by similarity, and a ranking model orders them using more features. Text embeddings of product descriptions help with cold start, when items have no interaction history yet. Evaluate with offline metrics and online A/B tests.

# Types of mentorship: mentor vs advisor, sponsorship, internship, apprenticeship, plans
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/types-of-mentorship/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Mentorship comes in several forms, one-to-one, group, peer, reverse, virtual and situational, and it is easily confused with advising, sponsorship, supervision, internships and apprenticeships, which overlap but serve different purposes. Knowing the difference helps you ask for the right kind of help. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023 and built TechVerse Enclave, a student community of over 500 members, so this page covers the types of mentorship, how it compares with related roles, a sample plan, startup mentorship and its wider impact.

## What are the different types of mentorship?

The main types are one-to-one mentoring, group mentoring with one mentor and several mentees, peer mentoring between people at similar stages, reverse mentoring where juniors teach seniors, virtual or e-mentoring online, and situational mentoring focused on a specific short-term need.

Other forms include formal programme-based mentoring with structured matching, informal mentoring that grows naturally, and team mentoring with several mentors for one group. Each fits different needs: peer mentoring suits first-year students adjusting to college; reverse mentoring helps senior leaders learn new tools like AI; situational mentoring helps before a specific event, such as an interview or hackathon pitch.

## What is the difference between a mentor and an advisor?

An advisor gives expert advice on specific decisions or problems, often within a formal role, such as an academic advisor choosing courses or a startup advisor guiding strategy. A mentor invests in your overall long-term development, beyond any single decision.

Advisors are often consulted as needed and may be paid or formally appointed; mentors usually build an ongoing relationship based on trust and shared goals. An advisor might say what to do about your fundraising terms; a mentor helps you grow into a founder who handles such decisions. Many people need both, and one person can play both roles at different times.

## What is the difference between mentorship and sponsorship?

A mentor talks with you, sharing advice and feedback. A sponsor talks about you, using their influence to recommend you for opportunities, promotions and projects when you are not in the room.

Sponsorship requires the sponsor to trust your work, since their reputation is at stake. Research on careers, especially for women and underrepresented groups, shows that mentoring without sponsorship often fails to translate into advancement. To move from mentorship to sponsorship, deliver strong results, make your goals clear, and give your mentor evidence they can share. Good mentors become sponsors when they see consistent excellence.

## What is the difference between mentorship and an internship?

An internship is a temporary work arrangement where you gain experience at an organisation, usually with defined tasks and sometimes a stipend. Mentorship is a guidance relationship. Good internships include mentorship, but they are not the same thing.

During an internship, your mentor or buddy helps you learn the codebase, understand the culture and grow; your manager assigns and evaluates work. Mentorship can exist without any job, through communities, alumni or professionals you contact. To get the most from an internship, ask early who your mentor is, set learning goals, and request regular feedback.

## What is the difference between mentorship and an apprenticeship?

An apprenticeship is a structured training arrangement where you learn a trade or profession by working under skilled practitioners, often combined with formal instruction and leading to a recognised qualification. Mentorship is the guidance relationship within or outside such programmes.

Apprenticeships are formal, time-bound and usually paid, with defined skills to master, common in trades and increasingly in technology. Mentorship is more flexible, covering career direction, confidence and networks, not only skills. An apprentice typically has a mentor, but mentorship does not require an apprenticeship. India's apprenticeship schemes and many companies' tech apprenticeship programmes combine both.

## What is the difference between mentorship and supervision?

A supervisor manages your work: assigning tasks, setting standards, evaluating performance and holding authority over your role. A mentor supports your development without formal authority, offering guidance in a confidential, often voluntary relationship.

Because supervisors evaluate you, you may hesitate to share struggles with them; mentors outside your reporting line provide a safer space. In research, a supervisor guides a thesis, while a mentor might advise on careers and wellbeing. In healthcare and social work, "clinical supervision" has a specific professional meaning. Ideally you have both: a supportive supervisor and mentors who broaden your perspective.

## What does an example mentorship plan look like?

A simple six-month plan: agree on two or three goals in the first meeting, meet every two weeks for 45 minutes, set a milestone for each month, review progress at the midpoint, and close with a reflection on what worked and next steps.

Example for a student aiming for an AI internship:

- **Month 1**: skills audit, learning plan, first small project.
- **Month 2**: build a RAG project with evaluation.
- **Month 3**: portfolio and resume review.
- **Month 4**: hackathon participation and pitch practice.
- **Month 5**: applications and mock interviews.
- **Month 6**: review outcomes and set next goals.

Write the plan down and share it with your mentor.

## How do I get startup mentorship?

Seek mentorship through startup incubators and accelerators, college entrepreneurship cells, government programmes such as Startup India, founder communities, pitch events and hackathons, and by reaching out directly to founders a few years ahead of you.

Make it easy for mentors to help: share a short summary of your startup, traction, the specific question and what you have tried. Founders respond better to focused asks than to "can you mentor me?" Show progress between conversations. Many incubators provide structured mentor networks, and hackathon judges and mentors are often experienced founders worth following up with after the event.

## How can mentorship benefit future generations?

Mentorship passes knowledge, values and opportunities forward: each mentee who benefits often becomes a mentor, creating a chain that spreads skills and access far beyond the original relationship. It shortens learning curves for each new generation.

In education and technology, this matters especially for first-generation students, who lack family networks in their chosen fields. Communities where seniors guide juniors build lasting cultures of helping. In TechVerse Enclave, students who were mentored as juniors now run sessions for new members. That compounding effect is why mentoring is one of the highest-leverage things experienced people can do.

## How can community and mentorship improve diversity in engineering?

Open communities and deliberate mentorship widen who enters engineering and who stays, by giving people without existing networks access to guidance, role models, opportunities and a sense of belonging.

Practical steps: run beginner-friendly events and hackathons, pair newcomers with mentors, invite speakers from varied backgrounds, make resources free and accessible, combine mentoring with sponsorship for opportunities, and measure who participates and who progresses. Students from smaller colleges and towns often lack exposure rather than ability; community and mentorship close that gap, as I have seen at campus sessions and in TechVerse Enclave.

# Vector database basics: AWS, SQL or NoSQL, LlamaIndex, storage, setup, learning, hype
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vector-database-aws-sql-nosql-setup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

A vector database stores embeddings with their metadata and finds the most similar ones quickly, but the term covers dedicated systems, cloud services and features inside ordinary databases. I build retrieval systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad, which combines dense vectors with BM25 and reranking, so this page covers AWS options, whether vector databases are relational, SQL or NoSQL, LlamaIndex, what they store and where, setting one up, building one, learning the topic and whether we are at peak vector database. Does AWS have a vector database? Yes, several options. Amazon OpenSearch Service offers vector search, including a serverless vector engine; Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS support pgvector; MemoryDB and DocumentDB add vector search; and Amazon S3 Vectors stores vectors cheaply in S3. Also asked as: does aws has vector database Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides managed RAG on top of these stores, handling chunking, embedding and retrieval. Choose by existing stack and scale: teams on PostgreSQL often use Aurora with pgvector, search-heavy applications suit OpenSearch, low-latency in-memory needs suit MemoryDB, and very large, cost-sensitive archives suit S3 Vectors. Third-party databases such as Pinecone, Qdrant and Milvus also run on AWS through marketplaces or self-hosting. Check each service's current regions and features before designing. Is a vector database relational? Dedicated vector databases are generally not relational. They store vectors with metadata in collections and focus on similarity search rather than tables, joins and foreign keys. However, relational databases can add vector features, such as PostgreSQL with pgvector. Also asked as: is vector database relational · how to setup vector database · how to learn vector database This gives two styles. A dedicated vector database keeps embeddings separate from business data, syncing through pipelines. A relational database with vector support keeps everything together, so one query can join users, permissions and document vectors. For many applications, the relational approach simplifies architecture and consistency. Dedicated systems can perform better at very large scale or with heavy filtering, so test your workload before splitting data. Is a vector database SQL or NoSQL? Most dedicated vector databases are NoSQL systems with their own APIs and query languages, such as Qdrant, Pinecone, Milvus and Weaviate. Some systems offer SQL access, including PostgreSQL with pgvector, ClickHouse and several cloud data warehouses. Also asked as: is vector database sql or nosql Vector search is better seen as a capability than a database category. Document databases such as MongoDB Atlas, search engines such as Elasticsearch, key-value stores such as Redis, and SQL databases all now provide it. Choose based on how the rest of your data is stored and queried. If your team knows SQL and data is relational, SQL with vectors is often simplest; dedicated NoSQL vector databases suit specialised, large-scale retrieval. Is LlamaIndex a vector database? No. LlamaIndex is a data framework for building LLM applications, handling document loading, parsing, chunking, indexing, retrieval and agents. It connects to vector databases rather than being one, though it includes a simple in-memory vector store for prototypes. LlamaIndex supports dozens of vector store integrations, such as Qdrant, Chroma, pgvector and Pinecone, letting you switch backends with little code change. It also offers advanced retrieval patterns, such as hierarchical and recursive retrieval, and document parsing tools. LlamaCloud, its commercial service, adds managed parsing and indexing. Use LlamaIndex to organise the RAG pipeline and a vector database to store and search embeddings at scale. What does a vector database store? A vector database stores embeddings, which are lists of numbers representing meaning, along with an ID for each item and metadata, such as document title, source, date or permissions. Many also store the original text chunk. Also asked as: what does vector database store It also stores index structures, such as HNSW graphs, that make similarity search fast, and sometimes compressed or quantized copies of vectors to save memory. Metadata enables filtering, such as searching only a user's documents. Storing the text alongside vectors lets the application return passages directly for RAG, with sources for citations. Some systems store multiple vectors per item, such as dense and sparse vectors for hybrid search. Where is a vector database stored? It depends on the system: in memory for speed, on local disk for persistence, in cloud object storage for low-cost scale, or on a managed provider's infrastructure. Many combine memory caching with disk or object storage. Also asked as: where is vector database stored Local tools such as Chroma and LanceDB store files in a folder on your machine. Self-hosted servers such as Qdrant or Milvus store data on the server's disks, often in containers with mounted volumes. Managed services, such as Pinecone or cloud provider offerings, store data in their data centres in regions you choose. For sensitive data, check where data is physically stored, how it is encrypted and how backups work. How do you set up a vector database? For a quick start, run Qdrant with one Docker command, install Chroma with pip for local Python use, or enable pgvector in PostgreSQL with CREATE EXTENSION vector. Then create a collection or table with your embedding dimension and distance metric. Next, embed documents with your chosen model, insert vectors with IDs, text and metadata, and run a similarity query to confirm results. Create an index such as HNSW for speed as data grows. Test with a few hundred documents before loading everything. For production, configure persistence, backups, authentication, monitoring and resource limits, or use a managed service. Keep the embedding model name and version recorded with your data, since changing models requires re-embedding everything. How do you build a vector database? To learn the idea, store vectors in an array, compute cosine similarity between a query and every vector, and return the top results. Then add an approximate index, such as HNSW through hnswlib or FAISS, persistence to disk and metadata filtering. Also asked as: how to build a vector database Building a toy vector database teaches why indexes matter: brute-force search becomes slow as vectors grow, while HNSW finds neighbours in a fraction of the time with small accuracy loss. Add an API with FastAPI for inserting and searching, and save index files so data survives restarts. Production databases add replication, sharding, concurrent updates and crash recovery, so use an existing database for real applications. How do you learn vector databases? Learn embeddings and similarity metrics first, then approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as HNSW, metadata filtering, hybrid search and evaluation. Free resources include DeepLearning.AI's short course on vector databases, Qdrant and Weaviate documentation, and Pinecone's learning articles. Practise by building a semantic search over your own notes: embed documents, store them in Chroma or pgvector, and query by meaning. Then build a small RAG app that answers questions with citations. Compare two databases on the same data, measuring recall and latency. Reading the HNSW paper deepens understanding. Combine database knowledge with chunking, embeddings and reranking, since retrieval quality depends on all of them. Write a short post about what you learned to consolidate it. Are we at peak vector database? Possibly for standalone hype, not for vector search itself. Vector search is becoming a standard feature of general databases, which reduces the need for separate systems in many projects, while retrieval remains essential for AI applications. Long context windows let some applications skip retrieval, and many teams use pgvector or existing search engines instead of new databases. Dedicated vector databases are responding with stronger hybrid search, filtering, scale and cost efficiency, and some consolidation through acquisitions is likely. For builders, the lesson is to treat vector search as one component, choose the simplest option that meets requirements, and keep retrieval design portable. Retrieval quality, not the database brand, decides answer quality.

# Vector database guide: vs embeddings, SQL, Elasticsearch, MCP, and Chroma in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vector-database-guide-chroma/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector database stores embeddings with their metadata and finds the most similar ones to a query quickly, which is how RAG systems fetch relevant passages for a language model. It complements, rather than replaces, embedding models, SQL databases and search engines. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense vector retrieval with BM25, so this page explains vector databases, how they compare with embeddings, SQL, Elasticsearch and MCP, best practices, deploying Chroma in production, a Python tutorial, RAG examples and courses.

## What is a vector database?

A vector database is a system designed to store vectors, such as text or image embeddings, along with metadata, and to answer nearest neighbour queries: given a query vector, return the most similar stored vectors quickly.

It combines an approximate nearest neighbour index, often HNSW, with database features: inserts, updates, deletes, metadata filters, persistence, replication and access control. In RAG, each chunk of a document becomes a vector with fields such as source, page and permissions; a question is embedded and the database returns relevant chunks in milliseconds. Many also support hybrid search, combining vector similarity with keyword scoring, which improves results for exact terms and names.

## Embeddings vs vector database: what is the difference?

Embeddings are the vectors themselves, produced by an embedding model from text, images or other data. A vector database is where you store and search those embeddings. You need both: one creates representations, the other makes them searchable.

The embedding model determines quality: if it places similar meanings close together, search works well. The vector database determines speed, scale, filtering and reliability. Changing the embedding model requires re-embedding everything, while changing the database only requires migrating stored vectors and metadata. Some databases can call embedding models for you during insert and query, which blurs the line, but conceptually they remain separate components to choose and evaluate independently.

## SQL vs vector database: which should you use?

SQL databases excel at exact queries, joins, transactions and structured data such as users, orders and permissions. Vector databases excel at similarity search over embeddings. Many applications need both, and PostgreSQL with pgvector can provide both in one system.

Use SQL for anything requiring exact matching or aggregation, such as finding orders by date or counting users. Use vector search for meaning-based retrieval, such as finding passages similar to a question. With pgvector, you can combine them in one query, filtering by tenant and date while ranking by similarity. Dedicated vector databases make sense at large scale or when you need advanced vector features, with your relational data remaining in SQL.

## Elasticsearch vs vector database: how do they compare?

Elasticsearch is a search engine built on Lucene for full-text search, analytics and logs, and it now supports dense vector search with HNSW. Dedicated vector databases focus on vector workloads with simpler APIs and vector-specific features.

Elasticsearch shines when you need strong keyword search, aggregations, existing log or document pipelines, and hybrid retrieval in one engine, including reciprocal rank fusion. Dedicated vector databases can offer leaner operations, more vector-focused tuning and lower memory use for large embedding collections. OpenSearch, the open-source fork, offers similar capabilities. If your team already runs Elasticsearch for search, adding vectors there is often simplest; otherwise compare both on your data and filters.

## MCP vs vector database: what is the difference?

They are different layers. A vector database stores and searches embeddings. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. An MCP server can expose a vector database search as a tool.

For example, you might build a retrieval service over your company documents in Qdrant or pgvector, then wrap it in an MCP server with a search tool. Assistants such as Claude Desktop or Cursor can then call that tool to fetch relevant passages during conversations. Several vector database vendors publish MCP servers for this purpose. Choose a vector database for retrieval performance, and use MCP to make that retrieval available to many AI clients.

## What are vector database best practices?

Store source text, document IDs, model version and metadata with every vector; index fields you filter on; choose the distance metric your embedding model expects; batch writes; and evaluate recall on real queries before tuning indexes.

More practices: separate tenants with metadata partitions rather than thousands of collections; use quantization to reduce memory for large collections, with rescoring for accuracy; keep vectors in sync when documents change by tracking content hashes; back up regularly and test restores; secure access with authentication and network rules; and monitor latency, memory and index build status. Combine vector search with keyword search and reranking for the best RAG quality.

## How do you deploy Chroma in production?

Run Chroma in client-server mode rather than embedded in your app: deploy the official Chroma server Docker image with a persistent volume, enable authentication, and connect from your application with the HTTP client. Chroma Cloud is a managed alternative.

Production checklist: mount durable storage for the data directory; put the server behind HTTPS and restrict network access; configure token-based authentication; set resource limits and monitor memory, since indexes live in memory; back up the persistent directory regularly; and pin the Chroma version, upgrading deliberately after reading migration notes. For large multi-tenant workloads or strict high-availability needs, compare Chroma with Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus or pgvector before committing.

## What is a good vector database tutorial in Python?

Start with Chroma or Qdrant's local mode: create a client, create a collection, add a few documents with metadata, then query with text and a metadata filter. Both run in a Python process without extra infrastructure.

Example flow with Chroma: `client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="db")`, then `col = client.create_collection("notes")`, `col.add(ids=[...], documents=[...], metadatas=[...])`, and `col.query(query_texts=["your question"], n_results=3)`. Next, swap in your own embedding model, load real documents with chunking, and measure whether the right chunks come back for test questions. Then try the same with Qdrant or pgvector to compare. Each vendor's GitHub organisation provides complete notebooks for RAG, hybrid search and filtering.

## What are vector database examples for RAG?

Common RAG setups include Chroma for prototypes, pgvector for apps already on PostgreSQL, Qdrant or Weaviate for self-hosted production with filtering and hybrid search, Pinecone for fully managed scale, and Elasticsearch or OpenSearch where keyword search already runs.

Example: a university handbook assistant stores chunks in pgvector with metadata for faculty and year, retrieves with hybrid search and reranking, and cites pages. Another: a support assistant uses Qdrant with tenant filters so each customer sees only their documents. A third: a legal tool uses Weaviate hybrid search to match exact clause numbers plus meaning. The database choice matters less than chunking, retrieval quality and evaluation, which decide answer accuracy.

## What is a good vector database course?

Good options include DeepLearning.AI short courses on vector databases and semantic search, vendor learning hubs from Pinecone, Weaviate and Qdrant, and Hugging Face material on embeddings. Most are free and hands-on.

Look for courses that cover embeddings, ANN indexes such as HNSW, metadata filtering, hybrid search, reranking and evaluation, not just inserting and querying vectors. Vendor courses teach their own APIs, so learn concepts that transfer between systems. After a course, build a small benchmark: index the same documents in two databases and compare recall, latency and memory. That exercise teaches more about trade-offs than any lecture and makes a strong portfolio piece.

# Vector databases compared: how many, examples, storage, LLMs, SQL, evaluation, 2026
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vector-databases-compared-evaluation/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Vector databases store embeddings and find the most similar ones quickly, which makes them central to RAG, semantic search and agent memory. Dozens now exist, and general databases keep adding vector features. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense vector retrieval with BM25 and reranking, so this page covers how vector databases differ, how many exist, examples, how they store vectors, use with LLMs and LangChain, comparisons with SQL and LLMs, how to evaluate them and what is changing in 2026. How do vector databases differ from each other? Vector databases differ in index types, filtering performance, hybrid keyword and vector search, scaling and distribution, managed versus self-hosted options, multi-tenancy, consistency guarantees, quantization support, APIs and licensing. For example, Qdrant emphasises fast filtered search and a Rust core, Milvus targets very large distributed deployments, Weaviate offers built-in modules and hybrid search, Pinecone is fully managed and serverless, Chroma prioritises simplicity for local development, and pgvector keeps vectors inside PostgreSQL. Some store data in memory, others on disk or object storage, affecting cost and latency. These differences matter more as data and traffic grow, so match the database to your workload rather than popularity. Read each database's documented limits before committing. How many vector databases are there? There are dozens. Database rankings list many systems with vector support, spanning dedicated vector databases, general databases with vector extensions, and libraries for vector search, and new options appear every year. Dedicated databases include Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Chroma, LanceDB, Vespa and turbopuffer. General databases with vector features include PostgreSQL through pgvector, MongoDB Atlas, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Redis, Cassandra-based services, ClickHouse, Oracle and SQL Server. Libraries such as FAISS, hnswlib and ScaNN provide search without database features. Because the field is crowded, many projects succeed with whatever database the team already runs, adding a specialised one only when requirements demand it. What are some examples of vector databases? Popular examples include Pinecone, a managed service; Qdrant, Milvus and Weaviate, open-source databases with managed clouds; Chroma and LanceDB for local and embedded use; and pgvector, which adds vector search to PostgreSQL. Also asked as: what are vector databases give few examples Each suits different needs. A student project might use Chroma for simplicity. A startup already on PostgreSQL might use pgvector to avoid another service. A company with billions of vectors might choose Milvus or a managed option. Teams wanting strong filtering and hybrid search often try Qdrant or Weaviate. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch users can add vectors to existing search clusters. Try two candidates on a sample of your data before deciding. How do vector databases store vectors? Vector databases store each vector as an array of numbers, usually 32-bit floats, alongside an ID and metadata, then build an index such as an HNSW graph over them so similar vectors can be found quickly without scanning everything. To save memory, many compress vectors with quantization, storing 8-bit integers, binary codes or product-quantized codes, sometimes keeping full vectors on disk for re-scoring. Data is organised into segments, with write-ahead logs for durability and memory-mapped files for fast access. Newer serverless designs keep data in cheap object storage with caching. Metadata, called payloads in some systems, is indexed separately to support fast filtering. Higher dimensions increase storage and slow search, so choose dimensions deliberately. How are vector databases used with LLMs? Vector databases give LLMs relevant knowledge and memory. The most common use is retrieval-augmented generation, where similar document chunks are retrieved and added to the prompt. Others include semantic caching, agent memory and selecting few-shot examples. In RAG, documents are embedded and stored; each question is embedded and matched, and the top passages, often reranked, ground the answer with citations. Semantic caching returns stored answers for similar repeated questions, saving cost. Agents store memories and retrieve relevant past interactions. Vector search also deduplicates data and powers recommendations around LLM features. RAG.NextUpgrad shows that combining vector results with keyword search improves retrieval for mixed queries. What is LangChain's role with vector databases? LangChain provides a standard VectorStore interface with integrations for most vector databases, so you can add documents, run similarity searches and turn any store into a retriever for RAG chains and agents with consistent code. Also asked as: what is langchain and vector databases You pair a vector store with an embeddings object, call methods to add documents and search, and use as_retriever to plug it into a chain. This makes switching databases easier, such as moving from Chroma in development to Qdrant or pgvector in production. LangChain also offers loaders, splitters and retrievers for hybrid and multi-query retrieval. Advanced features of specific databases may need their native clients, so check the integration's documentation. What is the difference between a vector database and SQL? SQL databases store structured data in tables and answer exact queries, such as filtering orders by date. Vector databases store embeddings and answer similarity queries, such as finding documents related to a question by meaning. Also asked as: difference between vector databases · difference between vector database and sql SQL excels at transactions, joins, aggregations and precise filters; vector databases excel at approximate nearest neighbour search over high-dimensional vectors. The boundary is fading: PostgreSQL with pgvector, Oracle, SQL Server and others now support vector types, letting one SQL query combine similarity search with relational filters. Many applications keep business data in SQL and add vectors there, avoiding synchronisation between two systems until scale demands a specialised vector database. What is the difference between a vector database and an LLM? A vector database stores and searches embeddings; it does not generate text. An LLM generates text from prompts; it does not store your documents in a searchable way. RAG systems combine them: the database retrieves, and the LLM answers. Also asked as: difference between vector database and llm LLMs hold general knowledge in their weights, fixed at training time, and cannot cite your private documents reliably. Vector databases hold your current data, updated instantly, and return exact passages. An embedding model connects them by converting text into vectors. Thinking of the database as long-term searchable memory and the LLM as the reasoning and writing engine clarifies their roles. Neither replaces the other in production knowledge applications. How do you evaluate vector databases in 2026? Measure recall against exact search, latency at p95 and p99 with realistic filters, throughput, ingestion and update speed, memory and storage cost, hybrid search support, multi-tenancy, operational effort and security features, using your own data. Also asked as: how to evaluate vector databases in 2026 Public benchmarks such as ANN-Benchmarks and VectorDBBench help shortlist, but filtered queries, concurrent updates and your vector dimensions change results significantly. Build a test with production-like data volumes, query patterns and filters, and run it on each candidate's recommended configuration. Include failure and recovery tests, backups and upgrade paths. Consider total cost of ownership, including engineering time. The best database is the one that meets requirements with the least operational burden. What is changing in vector databases in 2026? Key trends include general databases adding strong vector support, hybrid dense and sparse search becoming standard, aggressive quantization and disk-based indexes cutting costs, serverless designs built on object storage, and growing use as memory for AI agents. Also asked as: what&#x27;s changing in vector databases in 2026 Multi-vector retrieval, such as ColBERT-style late interaction, is gaining support, improving accuracy for complex documents. GPU-accelerated indexing speeds up building large indexes. Many teams now question whether they need a separate vector database at all, choosing pgvector or their existing search engine. Meanwhile, dedicated databases compete on filtering, scale and developer experience. Expect continued consolidation through acquisitions and feature overlap, which favours flexible designs that let you switch databases.
