# Vector databases explained: history, how they work with LLMs, SQL vs NoSQL, AWS options
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vector-databases-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector database stores embeddings, numerical vectors that represent meaning, and finds the most similar ones to a query vector quickly, even among billions, using approximate nearest neighbour indexes. Vector databases became central to AI applications with RAG and semantic search. RAG.NextUpgrad pairs dense vector retrieval with BM25, so this page covers their history, how they work with LLMs, why they matter, whether they are dead, NoSQL or SQL, whether they are trained, examples and AWS options.

## When were vector databases invented?

The underlying ideas are decades old: nearest neighbour search research dates to the 1970s, locality-sensitive hashing to 1998, product quantization to 2011, and the HNSW graph index to 2016. Dedicated vector databases emerged around 2017 to 2019.

Facebook released the FAISS library in 2017, Milvus was open-sourced in 2019, and companies such as Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant and Chroma launched between 2019 and 2022. The category exploded in 2023, when RAG made vector search essential for LLM applications. At the same time, established databases added vector support, such as PostgreSQL's pgvector, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, MongoDB and Redis, so today vector search is both a product category and a common database feature.

## How do vector databases work with LLMs?

In a RAG system, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings and stored in a vector database. When a user asks a question, the question is embedded, the database returns the most similar chunks, and the LLM answers using them.

The database handles the heavy lifting: indexing millions of vectors with structures such as HNSW, filtering results by metadata such as user permissions or dates, and returning results in milliseconds. Many also support hybrid search, combining keyword scores with vector similarity. Vector databases also give LLM applications memory, storing past conversations or facts as embeddings to retrieve later. The LLM itself never reads the whole database; it only sees the retrieved passages.

## Why are vector databases important for AI?

AI models represent meaning as vectors, and vector databases make those representations searchable at scale. They power semantic search, RAG, recommendations, image and audio search, deduplication and anomaly detection, where finding similar items quickly is the core operation.

Without an index, finding the nearest neighbours means comparing a query with every stored vector, which is too slow for millions of items. Approximate nearest neighbour indexes trade a tiny loss in recall for searches thousands of times faster. Vector databases add production features around this: persistence, updates, filtering, replication, access control and monitoring. That combination lets AI applications ground answers in private, current data rather than relying only on what a model memorised.

## Why use a vector database?

Use a vector database when you need fast similarity search over many embeddings with filters, updates and reliability. For small collections, a simple in-memory array or a library like FAISS may be enough.

Signs you need one: more than a few hundred thousand vectors, frequent inserts and deletes, metadata filtering by user, tenant or date, multiple concurrent users, or requirements for backups and high availability. If you already run PostgreSQL, pgvector may cover your needs without a new system. Choose a dedicated vector database for very large collections, heavy filtering or advanced features such as quantization and multi-tenancy. Let measured scale and operational needs, not hype, drive the decision.

## Are vector databases dead?

No, but the market has changed. Vector search is now a feature in many general databases, long context windows reduce some retrieval needs, and some coding agents rely on keyword and file search instead of embeddings, which led to dead-or-alive debates.

For large knowledge bases, retrieval remains essential: even million-token contexts are slower and costlier than retrieving relevant passages, and models can miss details in very long inputs. What changed is that vector search is often one component of hybrid retrieval, alongside keyword search, reranking and structured queries, and it frequently lives inside an existing database. Dedicated vector databases remain relevant for scale and advanced features, while many teams use pgvector or search engines instead.

## Are vector databases NoSQL?

Dedicated vector databases are usually classed as NoSQL, since they are non-relational systems built around collections of vectors with JSON-like metadata, queried through APIs rather than SQL. But vector search also exists inside relational databases.

Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Chroma use their own APIs and data models, resembling document stores with vector indexes. Document databases such as MongoDB and key-value stores such as Redis add vector search to NoSQL foundations. Relational databases, including PostgreSQL with pgvector, Oracle and SQL Server, add vector types to SQL tables. So the label depends on the product; what matters is how you query, filter and scale your data.

## Do vector databases use SQL?

Some do. PostgreSQL with pgvector, SingleStore, ClickHouse, DuckDB with vector extensions, Oracle and SQL Server support vector search through SQL. Most dedicated vector databases use their own APIs with filter expressions instead of SQL.

With pgvector, a similarity query is ordinary SQL: order rows by the distance operator between the embedding column and a query vector, add WHERE clauses for filters, and limit the results. That lets you join vectors with users, permissions and other tables in one query. Dedicated databases offer client libraries where you pass a vector and a filter object. SQL support is valuable when vectors must live alongside relational data and transactions.

## Are vector databases trained?

Generally no. The embedding models that create vectors are trained; the database stores and indexes those vectors. However, some index types do require a training step on sample data, such as clustering for IVF indexes or codebooks for product quantization.

For example, a FAISS IVF index first runs k-means on a sample of vectors to create clusters, then assigns all vectors to them; product quantization learns compression codebooks the same way. HNSW indexes need no training: they build a graph as vectors are inserted. If your data distribution changes greatly, retraining or rebuilding such indexes can restore accuracy. None of this changes the embeddings themselves, which come from your embedding model.

## What are some examples of vector databases?

Dedicated examples include Pinecone, Milvus and Zilliz Cloud, Weaviate, Qdrant, Chroma, LanceDB and Vespa. Databases with vector support include PostgreSQL with pgvector, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, MongoDB Atlas, Redis, DataStax Astra DB and SQLite with sqlite-vec.

Libraries such as FAISS, Annoy, ScaNN and hnswlib provide vector indexes without database features, useful inside applications or for research. Choose based on hosting, managed or self-hosted; scale; filtering and hybrid search needs; ecosystem integrations; and your team's existing infrastructure. For a first RAG project, Chroma or pgvector is easy; for large production systems, compare Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Pinecone or your search engine of choice on your own data.

## What are vector databases in AWS?

AWS offers vector search in several services: Amazon OpenSearch Service and OpenSearch Serverless with k-NN search, Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector, Amazon MemoryDB, DocumentDB, Neptune Analytics, and Amazon S3 Vectors for low-cost storage of large vector sets.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases builds managed RAG on top of these, handling chunking, embedding and retrieval with a choice of vector stores, including some third-party databases such as Pinecone. Choose OpenSearch for hybrid search at scale, Aurora with pgvector when data is relational, MemoryDB for very low latency, and S3 Vectors for large, infrequently queried collections. Third-party vector databases are also available through AWS Marketplace or self-hosted on EC2 and EKS.

# Vector search explained: IVF, HNSW, semantic vs keyword, pgvector, MongoDB, Databricks
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vector-search-ivf-hnsw-pgvector-mongodb-databricks/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24

Vector search finds items whose embeddings are closest to a query embedding, letting applications search by meaning rather than exact words. It powers semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for LLM apps. RAG.NextUpgrad combines dense vector search with BM25 keyword search using reciprocal rank fusion, and FaceVision stores face embeddings, never images, in PostgreSQL, so this page covers IVF and HNSW, current algorithms, semantic search, full-text and keyword comparisons, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Databricks and troubleshooting. How does vector search actually work with IVF and HNSW? Exact search compares the query with every vector, which is too slow at scale, so approximate nearest neighbour indexes trade a little accuracy for speed. IVF partitions vectors into clusters, while HNSW builds a layered graph of neighbours. Also asked as: how vector search actually works: ivf and hnsw IVF, the inverted file index, runs k-means to create clusters and assigns each vector to its nearest centroid. At query time it searches only the closest few clusters, controlled by a parameter often called nprobe, and it can be combined with product quantization to compress vectors. HNSW, from Malkov and Yashunin, links each vector to nearby vectors across several layers; searches start at a sparse top layer and greedily descend toward the closest neighbours. HNSW usually gives higher recall at low latency but uses more memory, while IVF builds faster and compresses better. Which algorithm is the current state of the art for vector search? There is no single winner. Graph-based methods such as HNSW are the common default for in-memory search, DiskANN-style graphs handle billion-scale data on SSDs, and quantization methods, such as product and binary quantization, cut memory. Google's ScaNN uses anisotropic quantization for strong speed and recall trade-offs, and GPU libraries such as NVIDIA's CAGRA accelerate graph search for very large workloads. Benchmarks such as ANN-Benchmarks compare recall against queries per second across libraries and datasets, and rankings shift with data size, dimensions and hardware. For most applications under tens of millions of vectors, HNSW in a mature database works well. Choose based on your scale, memory budget, update frequency and filtering needs, and measure recall on your own data rather than trusting headline numbers. What is semantic search in a vector database? Semantic search in a vector database converts documents and queries into embeddings with the same model, stores the document vectors, and returns the nearest vectors to the query, so results match meaning even when words differ. Also asked as: what is semantic search in vector database For example, a query about resetting a password can find a passage titled recovering account access. The pipeline involves chunking documents, embedding chunks, indexing them with metadata, embedding each query, retrieving top matches, and often reranking them with a cross-encoder for precision. Filters on metadata, such as date, language or permissions, narrow results. Quality depends mostly on the embedding model and chunking, not the database. For LLM applications, retrieved chunks are then passed to the model as context, which is the core of retrieval-augmented generation. Is semantic search the same as querying a vector database? Not quite. Semantic search is the goal of finding results by meaning; querying a vector database is one common way to implement it. A complete semantic search system also needs an embedding model, chunking, ranking and evaluation. Vector databases store any embeddings, including image, audio and recommendation vectors, so not every vector query is semantic text search. Conversely, semantic search can run without a dedicated vector database, using libraries such as Faiss, extensions such as pgvector, or search engines with vector support. Good semantic search often combines vector similarity with keyword matching and rerankers, since vectors alone miss exact terms. Think of the vector database as storage and retrieval infrastructure, and semantic search as the end-to-end experience you design around it. What is the difference between a vector database and full-text search? Full-text search uses an inverted index of words and ranks documents with formulas such as BM25, matching exact terms and their variants. A vector database indexes embeddings and ranks by similarity of meaning using approximate nearest neighbour search. Also asked as: what&#x27;s the difference between a vector database and full-text search Full-text search excels at exact names, codes, phrases and Boolean queries, is explainable, and needs no model. Vector search excels at paraphrases, synonyms, natural-language questions and cross-language matching, but depends on embedding quality and can return confidently irrelevant results. The line has blurred: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, PostgreSQL and many vector databases now support both. Most production systems use hybrid search, running both and fusing results with methods such as reciprocal rank fusion, as RAG.NextUpgrad does before reranking. Where do keyword search and vector search each fail? Keyword search fails when users and documents use different words, such as synonyms, paraphrases or other languages. Vector search fails on exact identifiers, product codes, rare names, numbers and negations, where similar-looking meaning is not enough. Also asked as: where keyword search and vector search each fail A query for car insurance claim may miss a document about vehicle policy reimbursement with keyword search alone. A query for error code E1047 may return documents about other errors with vector search, because embeddings blur exact tokens. Vector search also struggles with very short queries, domain jargon outside the embedding model's training, and constraints such as dates or numeric ranges. Hybrid search covers both weaknesses, and a reranker then orders the combined candidates by true relevance. Evaluate both failure types with real queries from your users. How do you create a vector database in PostgreSQL? Install the pgvector extension, run CREATE EXTENSION vector, add a column of type vector with your embedding dimensions, insert embeddings from your model, and query nearest neighbours by ordering on a distance operator such as cosine distance. Also asked as: how to create vector database in postgresql For speed at scale, create an HNSW or IVFFlat index on the vector column with the operator class matching your distance metric, such as vector_cosine_ops. Combine vector similarity with normal SQL filters and joins, which is a major advantage over separate vector stores. PostgreSQL's built-in full-text search can sit alongside it for hybrid retrieval. Managed services such as Supabase, Neon and most cloud PostgreSQL offerings support pgvector. FaceVision keeps face embeddings, never images, in PostgreSQL, which keeps identity data and application data in one familiar database. How do you create a vector search index in MongoDB? In MongoDB Atlas, store embeddings in a document field, then create a Vector Search index specifying the field path, number of dimensions and similarity function, such as cosine, euclidean or dot product, through the Atlas UI, CLI or drivers. Also asked as: how to create vector search index in mongodb Query with the $vectorSearch aggregation stage, passing the index name, field path, query vector, the number of candidates to consider and the limit of results. Add filter fields to the index definition if you want to pre-filter by metadata such as category or tenant. Larger candidate numbers improve recall at some latency cost. Vector search runs alongside regular MongoDB queries, so you can combine it with lookups and projections. Generate embeddings with any model, or use the Voyage AI embedding models that MongoDB now offers. How do you create a vector search index in Databricks? Create a vector search endpoint in Mosaic AI Vector Search, then create an index on a Delta table, either a Delta Sync index that updates automatically from the table or a Direct Vector Access index you write to through the API. Also asked as: how to create vector search index in databricks For a Delta Sync index, enable Change Data Feed on the source table, choose a primary key, and either let Databricks compute embeddings from a text column using a model serving endpoint or supply your own embedding column. You can create indexes in Catalog Explorer or with the Python SDK. Query with similarity search, passing query text or a vector, the columns to return and the number of results, optionally with filters or hybrid keyword matching. Indexes are governed through Unity Catalog, which keeps permissions consistent with your data. How do you troubleshoot vector search in an AI application? Start by inspecting what is retrieved for failing queries. Most problems come from mismatched embedding models, wrong distance metrics, poor chunking, overly strict filters, stale indexes or approximate index settings that sacrifice too much recall. Also asked as: how to troubleshoot vector search in an ai application Confirm queries and documents use the same embedding model, version and any required prefixes, and that normalisation matches the metric. Compare approximate results with exact search on a sample to measure recall, and raise parameters such as efSearch or nprobe if needed. Check that new documents were indexed and that filters are not excluding answers. Review chunk sizes, since chunks that are too large dilute meaning and too small lose context. Build a labelled test set and track recall at k. Add hybrid search and a reranker when exact terms keep failing.

# Vercel AI SDK explained: how it works, install, open source, Python, vs LangChain, Genkit
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vercel-ai-sdk-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Vercel AI SDK is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building AI features: one API to call many model providers, stream responses, generate structured objects, use tools, and connect everything to React and other frontends with hooks such as useChat. I build AI products with Next.js and FastAPI, so this page explains how it works, installation, licence and history, Python support, comparisons with LangChain, Genkit and AG-UI, streaming from custom endpoints, and a short tutorial.

## How does the Vercel AI SDK work?

AI SDK Core gives you provider-agnostic functions, such as generateText, streamText and generateObject, that call any supported model through provider packages. AI SDK UI adds framework hooks, such as useChat, that consume streamed responses in the browser.

On the server, you call streamText with a model from a provider package, such as OpenAI or Anthropic, plus messages and optional tools, and return the result as a streaming response. On the client, useChat sends messages to that route, renders tokens as they arrive, and manages chat state. Tools are defined with Zod schemas, and structured outputs are validated automatically. Switching providers means changing one import, which makes model comparisons and fallbacks easy.

## How do you install the Vercel AI SDK?

Install the core package and a provider: `npm install ai @ai-sdk/openai`, or use the Anthropic or Google provider packages instead. For React hooks, add `@ai-sdk/react`. Set your provider API key in an environment variable.

In a Next.js app, create an API route that imports streamText and your provider, reads messages from the request, and returns a streaming response; then build a client component using useChat. The SDK works with Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt, Node.js servers and edge runtimes. Keep API keys on the server only. Check the documentation for your installed major version, since APIs changed between versions, for example in how streaming responses are returned. Pin versions in package.json to avoid surprises.

## Is the Vercel AI SDK open source?

Yes. The AI SDK is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, developed in the vercel/ai repository on GitHub. You can use it in any project and deploy anywhere, not only on Vercel's platform.

Its providers cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq, Amazon Bedrock, Azure and many more, plus community providers for others, including OpenAI-compatible endpoints and local models through Ollama community packages. Open source means you can inspect how streaming and tool calls work, contribute fixes, or fork if needed. Vercel offers related paid hosting products, such as an AI gateway, but the SDK itself does not require them. Licence terms of the models you call still apply separately.

## When was the Vercel AI SDK released?

Vercel released the AI SDK in June 2023, initially focused on streaming chat responses into React and other frameworks. It has since gone through several major versions adding tools, structured outputs and agents.

Notable milestones include version 3 in 2024, which introduced generative UI ideas with React Server Components, version 4 with improved provider support, and version 5 in 2025, which redesigned the UI message format and transport layer for more flexible streaming and agent workflows. Because APIs evolve, tutorials from 2023 or early 2024 may use outdated functions, such as older stream helpers. Always check the documentation matching your installed major version before copying examples.

## Does the Vercel AI SDK support Python?

No. The AI SDK is a TypeScript and JavaScript library. There is no official Python version, but a Python backend can still serve a frontend that uses the AI SDK's React hooks by streaming in a compatible protocol.

For example, a FastAPI backend can call models with Python SDKs and stream responses in the AI SDK's stream protocol, and a Next.js frontend can use useChat pointed at that endpoint. Vercel has published templates combining Next.js with a Python backend in this way. If your stack is fully Python, use Python libraries instead, such as provider SDKs, LangChain, LlamaIndex or PydanticAI, and a Python web framework for streaming.

## LangChain vs Vercel AI SDK: which should you use?

Use the AI SDK for TypeScript apps that need clean model calls, streaming, tools and chat UIs with minimal abstraction. Use LangChain or LangGraph when you need many integrations, such as document loaders and vector stores, or complex agent graphs.

The AI SDK is lighter and closer to the provider APIs, with excellent frontend integration, which suits product teams shipping chat and generative UI features in Next.js. LangChain.js offers a broader ecosystem for RAG pipelines and agent orchestration, plus LangSmith tracing. They can be combined: use LangChain for retrieval and the AI SDK for streaming responses to the UI. For Python backends, LangChain is the more natural choice, since the AI SDK is TypeScript only.

## Genkit vs Vercel AI SDK: what is the difference?

Genkit is Google's open-source framework for building AI features, with flows, a local developer UI for testing and tracing, and strong Firebase and Google Cloud integration. The AI SDK focuses on provider-agnostic model calls and frontend streaming hooks.

Genkit supports TypeScript and Go, with Python support emerging, and offers plugins for many models, including Gemini, plus evaluation and observability tooling. The AI SDK excels in React and Next.js user interfaces, with useChat and structured streaming. Choose Genkit if you build on Firebase or Google Cloud and want built-in flow tooling; choose the AI SDK for frontend-heavy web apps with many providers. Both are open source, so trying each on a small feature is easy.

## AG-UI vs Vercel AI SDK: how do they differ?

AG-UI, the Agent-User Interaction protocol introduced by CopilotKit in 2025, is an open protocol standardising the events streamed between agent backends and user interfaces. The AI SDK is a library with its own streaming protocol and UI hooks.

AG-UI defines event types such as text messages, tool calls, state updates and lifecycle events, so frontends can work with agents built in different frameworks, including LangGraph, CrewAI and others. The AI SDK provides a complete toolkit, from model calls to UI hooks, within its own ecosystem. If you connect a frontend to several agent frameworks, a shared protocol like AG-UI helps; if you build the whole stack in TypeScript, the AI SDK alone is simpler.

## Can you use Vercel AI SDK streaming with a custom endpoint?

Yes. Point useChat at your own API route, through its endpoint or transport option, and return a response in the SDK's stream protocol, or a plain text stream. Any backend language can produce this format.

For a model server with an OpenAI-compatible API, such as a self-hosted model or proxy, create a provider with a custom baseURL using the OpenAI-compatible provider package, then use streamText as usual. For a fully custom backend, implement the documented stream protocol events for text, tool calls and finish signals. Test with network tools to check that chunks arrive incrementally, and disable proxy buffering, since some servers buffer responses and break streaming.

## What is a good Vercel AI SDK tutorial?

Start with the official getting-started guides on the AI SDK website for your framework, such as the Next.js App Router, which walk through a streaming chatbot in a few files. Then follow guides on tools, structured outputs and RAG.

A practical path: build a chat route with streamText and a page with useChat; add a weather or calculator tool to learn tool calling; use generateObject with a Zod schema to extract structured data; then add retrieval over your documents with embeddings and a vector store. Vercel's templates and examples repository provide complete starter apps. Deploy early, add rate limiting and logging, and test providers side by side by swapping one import.

# Vibe coding guide: tutorial, roadmap, examples, and vibe coding vs spec-driven development
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vibe-coding-guide-roadmap/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI coding tool and steering by results rather than reading every line. Done well, it turns ideas into working prototypes in hours; done carelessly, it produces fragile code nobody understands. I use AI coding tools daily on production products, so this guide covers how to vibe code well, a tutorial, roadmap and examples, why the term has a negative edge, how it compares with AI-assisted coding, vibe engineering and spec-driven development, why sessions fall apart, and its future.

## What is a good guide to vibe coding?

Start with a clear goal, a small scope and a short written spec, then build in small steps: ask for one feature, run it, test it, and commit to git before the next. Read the parts that matter, especially security and data handling.

Principles:

- Choose one tool and learn it well, such as Cursor, Claude Code or a browser builder.
- Keep a rules or instructions file describing your stack and conventions.
- Give precise requests with examples and expected behaviour.
- Paste exact errors and describe what you expected instead.
- Ask the AI to write tests, and run them.
- Commit working states so you can roll back.

## What is a simple vibe coding tutorial?

Build a small web app, such as a study planner, in one session: describe it, let the AI scaffold the project, run it locally, then add features one by one with testing after each.

Tutorial steps:

- Write a five-line spec: users, core feature, data, pages, stack.
- Ask the AI to create the project structure and a minimal working page.
- Run it and fix any errors by pasting them back.
- Add one feature, such as adding and listing tasks with a database.
- Ask for tests for that feature and run them.
- Commit, then add the next feature.
- Deploy to a free host once the core works.

## What is a roadmap for learning vibe coding?

Learn basic programming concepts alongside AI tools, so you can judge output: start with simple apps, then add databases, authentication and deployment, then learn testing, security and code review. The goal is moving from vibe coding to confident AI-assisted development.

A roadmap:

- **Weeks 1 to 2**: build static sites and small scripts with AI; learn Git.
- **Weeks 3 to 4**: a CRUD app with a database; read the generated code.
- **Month 2**: authentication, deployment and environment variables.
- **Month 3**: tests, debugging without AI, and security basics.
- **Ongoing**: hackathons and real users, which expose what prototypes miss.

## What are some vibe coding examples?

Common examples include personal tools such as habit trackers and expense splitters, event or portfolio websites, internal dashboards that read spreadsheets, browser games, small Chrome extensions, Discord bots, and quick prototypes to test startup ideas.

People also vibe code automations, such as scripts that rename files, scrape public data or generate reports, and teaching tools, such as quiz apps for a class. These work well because they are small, low-risk and easy to test by using them. Vibe coding works less well for systems handling payments, health data, many users or complex business rules, which need engineering discipline.

## Does vibe coding have a negative connotation?

In professional software circles, often yes. The original meaning, accepting AI code without really reading it, suggests carelessness, and critics associate it with insecure apps, unmaintainable code and inflated claims about replacing engineers.

In other contexts it is neutral or positive, describing how non-programmers and creators can now build useful tools. The connotation depends on what is being built: vibe coding a personal prototype is reasonable; vibe coding a banking backend is not. Many developers now describe their careful AI-assisted work with different terms to avoid the implication that they skip review.

## What is the difference between vibe coding and AI-assisted coding?

Vibe coding hands most control to the AI and judges results by whether the app seems to work. AI-assisted coding keeps the developer in control: the AI suggests, drafts and explains, while the developer designs, reviews, tests and takes responsibility for every change.

The tools can be identical, such as Cursor, Copilot or Claude Code; the difference is the workflow. AI-assisted developers read diffs, write or require tests, enforce architecture and security, and understand the code they ship. For production software, AI-assisted coding is the professional norm; vibe coding fits prototypes and personal tools.

## What is the difference between vibe coding and vibe engineering?

"Vibe engineering" was proposed by developer Simon Willison in 2025 to describe experienced engineers using AI agents responsibly at full speed, with tests, planning, code review, documentation and version control, in contrast to vibe coding's hands-off approach.

Vibe engineering leans on engineering practices that make AI output trustworthy: comprehensive test suites, clear specifications, good project documentation, and the judgement to recognise poor solutions. It treats AI agents like capable but fallible collaborators. The term highlights that AI amplifies existing skills: strong engineers get dramatically more productive, while fundamentals still matter.

## What is the difference between vibe coding and spec-driven development?

Spec-driven development writes a clear specification first, covering requirements, design decisions and acceptance criteria, then has AI agents implement tasks against that spec, checking work against it. Vibe coding improvises through prompts without a durable specification.

Tools such as GitHub's Spec Kit and spec-focused AI IDEs formalise this: generate a spec, review it, break it into tasks, then implement and verify. Specs give agents stable context, reduce drift over long sessions and make reviews easier. For anything beyond a small prototype, a lightweight spec pays for itself quickly, which is why many teams combine AI speed with spec discipline.

## Why does a vibe coding session fall apart after a couple of hours?

As sessions grow, the conversation context fills with old attempts and errors, the codebase accumulates inconsistent patches, there are no tests to catch regressions, and the AI loses track of earlier decisions, so fixes start breaking other features.

Prevent it by keeping a written spec and rules file the AI always reads, committing working states often, writing tests as you go, starting fresh sessions with a short summary instead of one endless chat, and refactoring when code gets messy. When stuck in loops, stop, read the relevant code yourself, and give the AI precise guidance or revert to the last working commit.

## Will vibe coding end like the maker movement?

Some compare vibe coding's hype to the maker movement, which promised everyone would manufacture products with 3D printers but settled into a valuable niche. Vibe coding may follow a similar path as a term, while AI-assisted software creation keeps growing.

The difference is that software is cheap to distribute and AI tools keep improving, so many people will continue building personal tools and prototypes. Professional development will absorb AI deeply but with engineering discipline. Likely outcome: the label fades, the capability becomes normal, and the skills that matter shift towards specifying, verifying and owning quality.


---

# Vision language models explained: vs LLMs, examples, open-source picks, Ollama, CLIP, VLA
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vision-language-models-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vision language model, VLM, is an AI model that takes images and text as input and produces text, so it can describe photos, read documents, answer questions about charts and reason about what it sees. Most combine a vision encoder with a large language model. I build vision and document systems, including FaceVision and DocuLens AI, so this page explains VLMs, how they differ from LLMs and multimodal models, examples, open-source and Ollama choices, where they look, CLIP's design and courses.

## What are vision language models?

A VLM pairs a vision encoder, often a Vision Transformer trained like CLIP or SigLIP, with a language model. The encoder turns an image into visual tokens, a small projector maps them into the language model's space, and the LLM reads them with your text.

Training usually has stages: first align vision features with language using image-caption pairs, then instruction-tune on question-answer data about images, documents and charts, sometimes followed by preference tuning. The result can caption images, answer visual questions, extract fields from forms, read handwriting and explain diagrams. Limitations include hallucinating objects not present, struggling with counting and fine spatial details, and sensitivity to image resolution, so validate outputs for important uses.

## Vision language model vs LLM: what is the difference?

An LLM processes only text. A VLM adds visual input, so it can answer questions about images, screenshots and documents. Many VLMs are built by attaching a vision encoder to an existing LLM, so their text abilities are similar.

The visual pathway adds costs: images consume many tokens, raising latency and cost, and the model may be slightly weaker on pure text tasks than its text-only base if training traded off capabilities. VLMs can do things LLMs cannot, such as reading a chart or checking a UI screenshot. For document work, a VLM can sometimes replace OCR plus an LLM, though validation remains important, which is how DocuLens AI treats extracted fields.

## Vision language model vs multimodal model: what is the difference?

A VLM is a type of multimodal model focused on vision and language. Multimodal models more broadly can handle any combination of text, images, audio, video and sometimes actions, as input or output.

Some frontier models are natively multimodal, trained on several modalities together and able to accept audio and video, and sometimes generate images or speech. Classic VLMs accept images and output text only. Image generators such as diffusion models are also multimodal, text in and images out, but are not VLMs. When choosing a model, check exactly which inputs and outputs it supports, since marketing terms vary between providers and versions.

## What are some examples of vision language models?

Proprietary examples include GPT-4o and later OpenAI models, Claude and Gemini, all of which accept images. Open examples include LLaVA, the Qwen-VL family, InternVL, Llama 3.2 Vision, Gemma 3, Pixtral, Molmo, PaliGemma, SmolVLM and MiniCPM-V.

They serve different needs: large proprietary models lead on difficult reasoning and document understanding; Qwen-VL and InternVL are strong open models for documents and charts; SmolVLM and Moondream are tiny models for edge devices; PaliGemma is designed for fine-tuning on specific tasks; and Florence-2 handles captioning, detection and OCR-style tasks with a small footprint. Specialised document models also exist for converting pages into structured text or Markdown.

## What are the best open-source vision language models?

Strong open choices include the latest Qwen-VL models, InternVL, Gemma 3, Llama 3.2 Vision, Molmo and Pixtral for general use, plus SmolVLM and Moondream for small devices. Rankings change quickly, so check current leaderboards.

Hugging Face's Open VLM Leaderboard and benchmarks such as MMMU, DocVQA, ChartQA and OCRBench compare models, but test on your own images, since benchmark strengths differ from real tasks. Consider licence terms, which vary, model size versus your GPU memory, and support in serving tools such as vLLM, llama.cpp and Ollama. For document extraction, prioritise models strong on OCR benchmarks; for chat about photos, general reasoning benchmarks matter more.

## What is the best vision language model on Ollama?

Good Ollama options include Gemma 3, Qwen2.5-VL, Llama 3.2 Vision, MiniCPM-V, LLaVA and Moondream. Pick by hardware: small models such as Moondream or 4-billion-parameter Gemma 3 run on laptops, while larger ones need more memory.

Run one with a command such as `ollama run gemma3`, then pass an image path in the prompt, or send images as base64 through Ollama's API from Python or JavaScript. For document reading, Qwen2.5-VL is often strong; for general chat about photos, Gemma 3 and Llama 3.2 Vision perform well. Test several on your own images, comparing accuracy and speed, and keep image resolution reasonable, since very large images slow inference.

## Where do large vision language models look when answering questions?

Researchers study this with heatmaps from attention weights or gradient-based attribution, showing which image regions most influence an answer. A 2025 paper with this exact title proposed a method for visualising these regions across many models.

Such interpretability studies find that models do not always focus on the evidence a human would use; sometimes they answer from language priors, guessing from the question, with little reliance on the image. Higher input resolution and better vision encoders tend to improve grounding on small details. For practitioners, the lesson is to test with images where the correct answer differs from common expectations, and to ask models for bounding boxes or quotes as evidence.

## Why doesn't CLIP use a pretrained LLM as its text encoder?

CLIP, released by OpenAI in 2021, trained a modest transformer text encoder from scratch jointly with the image encoder, because contrastive learning needed text and image embeddings shaped together, and captions are short.

Large decoder LLMs are optimised to predict the next token, not to produce one compact embedding for a sentence, and running a huge model for every caption in hundreds of millions of training pairs would have been very expensive. Later work explored the idea: LiT locked a pretrained image encoder and trained the text side, and LLM2CLIP used an LLM to strengthen CLIP's text understanding for long, detailed captions, showing benefits once methods matured.

## What is a good course on vision language models?

Good starting points include Hugging Face's community computer vision course, which covers multimodal models, DeepLearning.AI short courses on multimodal RAG and prompting vision models, and university lectures such as Stanford's CS231n on vision and language.

Hands-on practice matters most: run an open VLM with Transformers or Ollama, compare models on your own images, and fine-tune a small one such as SmolVLM or PaliGemma on a narrow task with LoRA. Read the LLaVA and CLIP papers to understand the architecture. Hugging Face's blog posts on VLMs explain training stages and evaluation clearly. Build a project, such as extracting fields from receipts, and measure accuracy against labelled examples.

## What are vision language action models, and where can you learn them?

Vision language action models, VLAs, extend VLMs to robotics: they take camera images and instructions and output robot actions. Examples include Google DeepMind's RT-2, the open OpenVLA, Physical Intelligence's pi-zero and Gemini Robotics.

To learn VLAs, start with Hugging Face's LeRobot library and tutorials, which provide datasets, pretrained policies and simulation environments, and read the RT-2 and OpenVLA papers. University robotics and deep reinforcement learning courses cover the control foundations. Practise in simulation first, then on affordable robot arms supported by LeRobot. VLAs face challenges VLMs do not, including safety, real-time control and the cost of collecting demonstration data, so expect slower, more hardware-dependent progress.

# How to serve models with vLLM: setup, vs LLMs, llama.cpp, Triton, LiteLLM and TensorRT-LLM
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vllm-serve-setup-comparisons/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


To serve a model with vLLM, install it on a machine with a supported GPU and run `vllm serve` followed by a Hugging Face model name; vLLM downloads the model and starts an OpenAI-compatible API server that any OpenAI client can call by changing the base URL. vLLM is an inference engine, not a model. After fine-tuning models in FineTune Studio, choosing how to serve them is the next step, so this page covers setup and how serving works, and compares vLLM with LLMs, llama.cpp, Triton, LiteLLM and TensorRT-LLM, GGUF support, and VLMs.

## How do I use vllm serve?

After installing vLLM, run `vllm serve <model>` with a Hugging Face model ID. It starts an HTTP server, by default on port 8000, exposing OpenAI-style endpoints for chat completions, completions and models.

```bash
pip install vllm
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9
```

Then call it with the OpenAI Python client by setting `base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1"`. Useful options include `--tensor-parallel-size` for multiple GPUs, `--quantization` for supported formats, `--api-key` to require authentication, and `--enable-lora` to serve fine-tuned adapters. Check the documentation for options in your version. If the server fails to start with an out-of-memory error, reduce `--max-model-len` or choose a smaller or quantised model before buying bigger hardware.

## How does vllm serve work?

`vllm serve` loads the model weights onto the GPU, allocates memory for the key-value cache using PagedAttention, and runs a scheduler that continuously batches incoming requests, so new requests join as others finish and the GPU stays busy.

Each request's tokens are processed in prefill, reading the prompt, and decode, generating tokens one by one, with responses streamed back over HTTP. Prefix caching reuses computation for shared prompt beginnings, such as system prompts. The OpenAI-compatible layer translates API requests into engine calls, which is why existing applications can switch to self-hosted models with minimal code changes.

## How do I set up vLLM?

Use a Linux machine or container with a supported NVIDIA or AMD GPU and matching drivers, create a Python environment, install vLLM with pip or use the official Docker image, then start a server with a model that fits your GPU memory.

Setup checklist:

- Check GPU memory against model size and context length.
- Install drivers and the CUDA or ROCm version vLLM requires.
- Use the official Docker image to avoid dependency conflicts.
- Log in to Hugging Face for gated models.
- Start with a small model to verify the setup.
- Add authentication and a reverse proxy before exposing it.

Monitor GPU memory and throughput with vLLM's metrics endpoint.

## What is the difference between vLLM and an LLM?

An LLM, large language model, is the trained neural network, such as Llama, Qwen or Mistral, defined by its architecture and weights. vLLM is software that runs LLMs efficiently, serving their predictions to applications.

Think of the LLM as the engine design and vLLM as the factory machinery that runs it at scale. The same LLM can be run with different inference engines, such as Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or TensorRT-LLM, with different speed and memory trade-offs. The extra "v" in vLLM is part of the project name, not a type of model.

## What is the difference between vLLM and llama.cpp?

vLLM targets GPU servers handling many concurrent users, using batching and memory management for high total throughput. llama.cpp targets efficient local inference of quantised GGUF models on CPUs, Macs and consumer GPUs, typically for one or a few users.

Use llama.cpp, or Ollama built on it, for laptops, desktops, edge devices and offline apps. Use vLLM for production APIs on GPU servers. llama.cpp's aggressive quantisation lets large models run on modest hardware; vLLM's strengths are throughput, OpenAI-compatible serving and multi-GPU scaling. Many teams prototype locally with Ollama and deploy with vLLM. Because both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs, application code can stay the same while the serving layer changes.

## What is the difference between vLLM and Triton?

NVIDIA Triton Inference Server is a general-purpose model server supporting many frameworks, including TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX and Python backends, with features for model versioning, ensembles and metrics. vLLM is specialised for LLM inference. Triton can even use vLLM as a backend.

Choose Triton when you serve many model types, such as vision, speech and language, under one platform with enterprise features. Choose vLLM directly for simpler, LLM-focused deployments. Triton adds configuration complexity but standardises operations across models; vLLM gives fast results for LLM serving with minimal setup.

## What is the difference between vLLM and LiteLLM?

vLLM runs models on your hardware. LiteLLM is a Python SDK and proxy that provides one OpenAI-style interface to many providers and servers, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock and self-hosted vLLM, adding routing, fallbacks, budgets and logging.

They work together: deploy models with vLLM, then put LiteLLM in front to route traffic between your vLLM servers and external APIs, enforce rate limits and track costs per team. Multi-provider fallback, like the one in RAG.NextUpgrad, follows the same idea: if one provider fails, route to another, keeping the application running.

## vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM: which is faster?

TensorRT-LLM, from NVIDIA, compiles models into optimised engines for NVIDIA GPUs and can deliver top performance, especially with FP8 and specific hardware. vLLM is easier to set up, supports more models quickly, and runs on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs with strong performance.

Benchmarks vary by model, batch size, sequence lengths and hardware, and both projects improve rapidly. TensorRT-LLM suits teams willing to invest in build pipelines for maximum NVIDIA efficiency at scale; vLLM suits most teams wanting fast deployment and flexibility. Benchmark both on your workload before committing, measuring latency and throughput. Also count engineering time: a slightly slower engine your team can operate confidently may beat a faster one that is hard to maintain.

## Can vLLM serve GGUF models?

vLLM has experimental support for loading GGUF files for some model architectures, but GGUF is designed for llama.cpp, and vLLM performs best with Hugging Face weights in safetensors format or GPU-oriented quantisation such as AWQ, GPTQ and FP8.

If you have a GGUF model, check vLLM's documentation for current support and limitations, such as needing the original tokenizer. For production GPU serving, prefer the original weights or GPU quantisation formats. For local use of GGUF files, llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio are more straightforward choices.

## What is the difference between a VLM and an LLM?

An LLM, large language model, processes and generates text. A VLM, vision language model, also accepts images, and sometimes video, as input, combining a vision encoder with a language model to describe images, answer questions about them and read documents.

Examples of VLMs include multimodal versions of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Qwen-VL and LLaVA. They power document understanding, chart reading, visual question answering and UI agents. vLLM can serve many open VLMs too. For document AI, VLMs can read layouts that text-only pipelines miss, though dedicated OCR plus validation, as in DocuLens AI, remains important for exact extraction.

# What are vLLM and SGLang? Open source status, why vLLM is fast, Unsloth, and builds
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/vllm-sglang-unsloth-open-source/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


vLLM and SGLang are open-source inference engines that serve large language models efficiently on GPUs, handling many users at once with high throughput and exposing OpenAI-compatible APIs. vLLM is known for PagedAttention memory management; SGLang for fast prefix caching and structured generation. Both suit production serving of open models. I fine-tune models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio, where serving choices follow training, so this page covers vLLM and SGLang, their origins and speed, llama.cpp, build times, Unsloth's licensing, and open versus closed models.

## What are vLLM and SGLang?

vLLM is a high-throughput serving engine for LLMs that manages GPU memory efficiently and batches requests continuously, letting one GPU serve many concurrent users. SGLang is a serving framework and language for structured LLM programs, with a fast runtime that reuses shared prompt prefixes.

Both load models from Hugging Face, support quantised formats such as AWQ, GPTQ and FP8, run across multiple GPUs, and offer OpenAI-compatible servers, so existing client code works by changing the base URL. Teams use them to self-host open models for chatbots, RAG systems and agents, reducing per-request cost at scale compared with simpler serving. Both projects move quickly, adding support for new model architectures within days of release, so check their supported-models lists before choosing.

## What is the difference between vLLM and SGLang?

vLLM pioneered PagedAttention and has the broadest model and hardware support with a very large community. SGLang emphasises RadixAttention, which caches and reuses shared prompt prefixes across requests, plus a frontend language for structured generation, making it very fast for agents and multi-turn workloads.

In practice, performance differences depend on model, hardware, batch size and workload: SGLang often excels when many requests share long prefixes, such as system prompts or few-shot examples; vLLM is a safe, well-supported default. Benchmark both with your model and traffic pattern, measuring throughput, latency and memory, before choosing.

## Is vLLM open source?

Yes. vLLM is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, developed on GitHub with contributions from many companies and individuals. You can use it freely, including commercially, under the licence terms.

The project is community-governed and has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a hosted project, which supports long-term neutral stewardship. Commercial companies offer managed services and support built on vLLM, but the engine itself is free. Remember that the models you serve have their own licences, which may restrict commercial use separately from vLLM's licence.

## Who built vLLM?

vLLM was created by researchers at UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab, led by Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li and colleagues, with professors including Ion Stoica. Their 2023 paper introduced PagedAttention, the memory management technique at vLLM's core.

After release in 2023, vLLM grew rapidly into one of the most widely used open-source LLM serving engines, with contributors from major technology companies, cloud providers and hardware vendors. Its development is now a large community effort, with regular releases adding new models, hardware backends and optimisations.

## Why is vLLM faster?

vLLM is fast mainly because PagedAttention stores the attention key-value cache in small blocks, like virtual memory pages, eliminating wasted GPU memory, so far more requests fit in a batch. Continuous batching adds new requests as others finish, keeping the GPU busy.

Other optimisations include fused and optimised CUDA kernels, CUDA graphs to cut overhead, prefix caching to reuse shared prompt computations, speculative decoding, chunked prefill and efficient quantised kernels. Together these give much higher throughput than naive serving with Hugging Face Transformers, especially under many concurrent users. For a single user, the speed difference is smaller. Measure tokens per second per user and total throughput separately, since optimising one can hurt the other.

## Why is vLLM faster than llama.cpp?

They target different situations. vLLM is optimised for GPU servers handling many concurrent requests, where batching and memory management multiply throughput. llama.cpp is optimised for running quantised models efficiently on CPUs, Macs and consumer GPUs, typically for one or a few users.

For a single local user, llama.cpp can be very fast and uses far less memory thanks to aggressive quantisation. For an API serving hundreds of users, vLLM's batching delivers far higher total throughput per GPU. Choose llama.cpp or Ollama for local and edge use, and vLLM or SGLang for production serving on GPUs.

## How long does vLLM take to build?

Installing vLLM from prebuilt pip wheels takes a few minutes. Building from source can take much longer, from tens of minutes to over an hour, because it compiles many CUDA kernels; build time depends on CPU cores, memory and which GPU architectures you target.

To speed up source builds, limit target GPU architectures, increase parallel compile jobs if you have enough memory, and use the project's documented build caching. Most users never need to build from source: use the official wheels or Docker images matched to your CUDA version. Build from source only for development or unsupported platforms. Version mismatches between vLLM, PyTorch and CUDA cause most installation problems, so follow the compatibility table in the documentation.

## Is Unsloth open source?

Yes, the core Unsloth library is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence. It speeds up fine-tuning of language models with LoRA and QLoRA through optimised kernels, reducing memory use and training time, and works with Hugging Face's TRL.

Unsloth also offers paid tiers for teams needing extra features such as multi-GPU support and enterprise help. For students and individuals, the free library with its notebooks for Google Colab and Kaggle is enough to fine-tune popular open models on a single GPU and export them to formats such as GGUF for Ollama.

## Is Unsloth Studio open source?

Unsloth's core library is open source, but licensing can differ for newer tools, interfaces or enterprise products a company releases. Check the specific project's repository and licence file, or Unsloth's official documentation, before assuming any new tool is open source.

As a rule, look for a LICENSE file in the repository, read whether it is a standard open-source licence such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, and check whether some features require a paid key. For production or client work, record the licence of each tool you use. If a tool's licence is unclear, ask the maintainers or choose an alternative with clear terms.

## Open-source vs closed-source LLMs for fine-tuning: which is better?

Open-weight models, such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral releases, let you download weights and fine-tune freely with LoRA or QLoRA, run them anywhere and keep data private. Closed models offer fine-tuning only through provider APIs, with less control but often stronger base capability.

Choose open models for data privacy, offline deployment, cost control at scale and full customisation, as in FineTune Studio's QLoRA workflow. Choose closed-model fine-tuning when you need the strongest base model and accept provider hosting. Either way, compare the tuned model against a well-prompted base model, since prompting or retrieval sometimes makes fine-tuning unnecessary.

# What is Weaviate? Uses, querying, bulk import, client, examples, vs Pinecone and Qdrant
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/weaviate-explained-examples/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Weaviate is an open-source vector database that stores data objects with their embeddings and supports semantic, keyword and hybrid search, with built-in modules that can create embeddings and run generative RAG queries. It is used for semantic search, RAG and recommendations. I build retrieval systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page explains what Weaviate is, why to use it, whether it is a graph database, how to query it, bulk operations, its client, examples, and how it compares with Pinecone and Qdrant.

## What is the Weaviate database?

Weaviate is an open-source vector database written in Go. It stores objects, such as documents or products, with properties and vectors in collections, and searches them by meaning using approximate nearest neighbour indexes, alongside keyword and filtered search.

Its distinctive features include vectorizer modules that call embedding models automatically during import and queries, hybrid search that blends BM25 and vector scores, generative search that sends results to a language model, multi-tenancy for SaaS apps, and named vectors for storing several embeddings per object. You can self-host it with Docker or Kubernetes, or use the managed Weaviate Cloud. The company behind it is based in the Netherlands, and the core is open source.

## What is Weaviate used for?

Weaviate is used for semantic search over documents and products, retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation systems, question answering, image and multimodal search, and classification, anywhere similarity between embeddings matters.

In a RAG application, you import document chunks into a collection, let a vectorizer module or your own code create embeddings, then run hybrid queries with filters such as source or date to fetch context for a language model. E-commerce teams use it to search products by meaning, such as a query for comfortable shoes for long walks. Multimodal modules let text queries find images. Its generative search can even run the RAG step inside the query itself.

## Why use Weaviate?

Choose Weaviate when you want an open-source vector database with strong built-in features: integrated vectorization, native hybrid search, generative modules, multi-tenancy and flexible deployment from local Docker to managed cloud, with clients in several languages.

Its modules reduce glue code: you can insert raw text and let Weaviate call your chosen embedding provider, including local models through Ollama. Hybrid search with a tunable alpha makes it easy to balance keyword and semantic matching. The trade-offs are higher memory use than some alternatives and more configuration to learn. For a simple prototype, Chroma may be quicker; for very large filtered workloads, compare against Qdrant or Milvus on your own data before deciding.

## Is Weaviate a graph database?

No, not in the usual sense. Weaviate is a vector database. Its name and early design included a GraphQL API and cross-references between objects, which gave it graph-like links, but it does not offer graph traversal queries like Neo4j.

Cross-references let an object point to others, such as an article referencing its author, and queries can return referenced properties. That is useful for modelling simple relationships, but deep multi-hop traversals and graph algorithms belong in a dedicated graph database. If your RAG system needs entity relationships, consider pairing Weaviate with a graph database or a GraphRAG index. Newer Weaviate clients use gRPC and REST, with GraphQL still available for some queries.

## How do you query Weaviate?

With the v4 Python client, get a collection and call a query method: `near_text` for semantic search, `bm25` for keyword search, `hybrid` for both, `near_vector` with your own vector, or `fetch_objects` for filtered retrieval without similarity.

For example, `articles.query.hybrid(query="solar subsidies", alpha=0.5, limit=5)` returns the five best matches blending keyword and vector scores. Add `filters=Filter.by_property("year").greater_than(2022)` to restrict results, and `return_metadata=MetadataQuery(score=True)` to inspect scores. For generative RAG, use the `generate` namespace with a prompt that includes the retrieved objects. Use `near_text` only if the collection has a vectorizer configured; otherwise pass vectors yourself. Results come back as objects with properties and metadata you can loop over.

## What property or field is used when querying in Weaviate?

Semantic queries search the object's vector, which was created from the properties the vectorizer was configured to include. Keyword and hybrid queries search text properties, and you can restrict them with `query_properties`, optionally boosting fields like `title^2`.

Filters use `Filter.by_property("name")` with operators such as equal, greater_than or contains_any, and need the property to be indexed for filtering, which is on by default for most types. Use `return_properties` to choose which fields come back, which reduces payload size. If semantic results seem off, check which properties were vectorized: including irrelevant fields, such as IDs or long boilerplate, can blur embeddings. Configure this per property in the collection's schema when you create it.

## Does Weaviate support bulk queries?

Yes, in several forms. Batch import inserts many objects efficiently, the iterator reads every object in a collection, `fetch_objects` with filters returns many objects at once, and multiple searches can run concurrently from the async client.

For imports, use `with collection.batch.dynamic() as batch:` and call `batch.add_object()` in a loop; the client groups requests and handles retries, and you should check `collection.batch.failed_objects` afterwards. For exporting or processing everything, use `collection.iterator()`, which pages through results with a cursor. Batch deletes accept a filter, such as deleting all objects from one source. For many independent searches, send them concurrently with the async client rather than one by one.

## What is the Weaviate client?

The Weaviate client is the official library for connecting to a Weaviate instance from code. Official clients exist for Python, TypeScript and JavaScript, Go and Java, with the Python v4 client using gRPC for faster operations.

Connect with helpers such as `weaviate.connect_to_local()`, `connect_to_weaviate_cloud()` with a URL and API key, or `connect_to_embedded()`, which downloads and runs Weaviate inside your Python process for experiments. With the embedded client, the server starts when you connect and stops when your script ends, so keep the script running while you query. Always close the client with `client.close()` or a context manager, and keep client and server versions compatible.

## What are some Weaviate examples?

Weaviate's recipes repository on GitHub has many runnable notebooks: semantic and hybrid search, RAG with various model providers, multi-tenancy, multimodal search, reranking and integrations with LangChain and LlamaIndex. The OpenAI Cookbook also includes Weaviate examples.

A simple example: run Weaviate in Docker with an Ollama vectorizer, create a collection called Notes with title and body properties, batch import your notes, then run hybrid queries. Next, add generative search so Weaviate passes the top notes to a language model and returns an answer. From there, explore filters by date, named vectors for titles and bodies, and evaluating retrieval quality with a small labelled question set.

## Pinecone vs Weaviate vs Qdrant: how do you choose?

Pinecone is fully managed and serverless, ideal when you want no infrastructure work. Weaviate is open source with built-in vectorization, hybrid and generative modules. Qdrant is open source, written in Rust, with strong filtering, quantization and efficient resource use.

Decide on hosting first: if you must self-host or keep data in your own environment, choose Weaviate or Qdrant; if you prefer a managed service, all three offer cloud options, with Pinecone being cloud only. Then compare the features you need, such as hybrid search, multi-tenancy and filtering, and test recall, latency, memory and cost on your own data with realistic filters. Keep retrieval behind a small interface in your code, so switching later is a contained change.

# Weaviate tutorial: how it works, setup, Weaviate Cloud, pricing, and vs Elasticsearch
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/weaviate-tutorial-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Weaviate is an open-source vector database that stores data objects together with their vector embeddings, and lets you search by meaning, by keywords, or both together in hybrid search, with filters on properties. It can generate embeddings through integrated model modules, which makes building RAG systems quick. I design hybrid retrieval in RAG.NextUpgrad, so this page gives a Weaviate tutorial, how it works and is set up, Weaviate Cloud, cost, a comparison with Elasticsearch, ownership and history, its business model, and outages.

## What is a quick Weaviate tutorial?

Run Weaviate locally with Docker, install the Python client, create a collection with a vectoriser or your own vectors, import objects, then query with near-text, BM25 keyword or hybrid search.

```python
import weaviate
client = weaviate.connect_to_local()
docs = client.collections.get("Doc")
docs.data.insert({"title": "Refund policy", "body": "Refunds within 30 days..."})
res = docs.query.hybrid(query="how do refunds work", limit=3, alpha=0.5)
for o in res.objects:
    print(o.properties["title"])
client.close()
```

Create the collection first with a vectoriser configuration, or supply vectors yourself when inserting. The official quickstart walks through both local and cloud setups step by step. Once the basics work, try filters on properties, compare pure vector search with hybrid search on the same questions, and check which returns the passages you expected.

## How does Weaviate work?

Weaviate stores objects in collections, each with properties and one or more vectors. It builds an HNSW index for vector search and an inverted index for keyword search and filtering, then combines them for hybrid queries using a weighting parameter called alpha.

Optional modules call embedding models, from providers or local containers, so Weaviate can vectorise data on import and queries at search time. Generative modules can send retrieved results to a language model, giving RAG in one query. It supports multi-tenancy for SaaS apps, replication and sharding for scale, and quantisation to reduce memory. Clients exist for Python, JavaScript, Go and Java. Its GraphQL and REST APIs also let you query without a client library.

## How do I set up Weaviate?

The simplest local setup is Docker Compose: generate or copy the compose file from Weaviate's documentation, choose modules, start it, and connect from your client. For production, use Kubernetes with Helm charts or Weaviate Cloud.

Setup checklist:

- Install Docker and create a compose file with the Weaviate image.
- Enable the modules you need, such as a text vectoriser.
- Mount a volume so data persists across restarts.
- Set authentication with API keys before exposing it.
- Configure backups to a storage bucket.
- Monitor memory, since HNSW indexes live largely in RAM.

An embedded option also exists for some clients, useful for quick experiments.

## What is Weaviate Cloud?

Weaviate Cloud is the managed version of Weaviate, run by Weaviate the company, offering serverless clusters, dedicated deployments and options to run inside your own cloud account. It handles hosting, scaling, upgrades, backups and monitoring.

It suits teams that want Weaviate's features without operating infrastructure. Typically there is a free sandbox for experiments that expires after a period, and paid tiers for production. Choose a region close to your users and data, check compliance options for sensitive data, and keep your embedding model and source data reproducible so you can migrate if needs change. Test performance from your application's region before going live, since network latency adds to every query.

## Is Weaviate paid?

The core Weaviate database is open source under the BSD-3-Clause licence, so self-hosting is free apart from your infrastructure costs. Weaviate Cloud and enterprise support are paid, with a free sandbox for trying it out.

Self-hosting costs include servers with enough memory for your vectors, storage, backups and engineering time for operations. Managed hosting trades those costs for a subscription. Embedding models used through modules may also have their own API costs. Compare total cost of ownership, including your team's time, before deciding between self-hosting and the cloud service. For students and prototypes, a local Docker instance costs nothing beyond your laptop.

## Weaviate vs Elasticsearch: which should I use?

Choose Elasticsearch when mature full-text search, aggregations, analytics and logs are central, with vector search as an addition. Choose Weaviate when semantic and hybrid retrieval are the core, and you want built-in vectorisation and RAG-friendly features.

Elasticsearch has deep text analysis, language analysers and a huge ecosystem, and supports dense vector kNN search, but is heavier to operate. Weaviate is vector-first, simpler for embedding workflows, and offers hybrid search with BM25 out of the box. For RAG over documents, both can work; test retrieval quality on your own queries, including exact terms like product codes and paraphrased questions. Also weigh your team's existing skills: an organisation already running Elasticsearch for logs may prefer adding vectors there rather than operating a new system.

## Who owns Weaviate?

Weaviate is developed by Weaviate B.V., a venture-backed company based in the Netherlands, co-founded by Bob van Luijt, its chief executive, and Etienne Dilocker. The open-source project is maintained by the company with community contributions.

The company was originally known as SeMI Technologies before adopting the Weaviate name. Its open-source licence means you can use and modify the database freely, while the company offers the managed cloud and enterprise services.  As with any vendor, keep your data and embeddings reproducible so you are not locked in if circumstances change.

## When was Weaviate founded?

The open-source Weaviate project began around 2016, and the company behind it, originally SeMI Technologies, was founded in 2019. It grew rapidly as vector search became central to AI applications after 2022.

Since then, Weaviate has added hybrid search, generative modules for RAG, multi-tenancy, multiple named vectors, vector quantisation and a serverless cloud. The vector database market is young and changes fast, so check release notes for current features and avoid relying on comparisons written a few years ago, which may describe very different versions.

## How does Weaviate make money?

Weaviate earns revenue mainly from Weaviate Cloud, its managed hosting with serverless and dedicated options, from enterprise deployments in customers' own cloud environments, and from support and services for organisations running Weaviate in production.

This open-core model is common for infrastructure companies: the free open-source database drives adoption and community, while businesses pay for convenience, reliability, security features and expert support. For users, it means the open-source version remains usable on its own, while paid options exist if you prefer not to operate it yourself.

## Is Weaviate down?

If Weaviate Cloud seems unavailable, check Weaviate's status page for incidents. If you self-host, the problem is in your deployment: check container logs, memory usage, disk space and network access.

Common self-hosted issues include running out of memory as HNSW indexes grow, disk full errors, misconfigured authentication, and modules failing to reach embedding providers. Client errors can also come from version mismatches between client and server. Add health checks, monitoring and alerts, and keep backups so you can restore quickly. For critical applications, consider replication across nodes.
