# What is a context window? Tokens, max tokens, context length, full windows, memory, MCP
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-context-window/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can consider at once, including your prompt, conversation history, documents and the model's own response. When it fills up, older content must be dropped or summarised. I build RAG systems that exist largely because of context limits, so this page covers context windows, tokens, max tokens, input and output, context length, full windows in Claude Code, agent memory, masking, MCP and very large windows.

## What is a context window?

A context window is the model's working memory: the total number of tokens it can process in a single request, covering system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results and the generated answer.

Models cannot see anything outside the window, so long conversations or documents must be trimmed, summarised or retrieved selectively. Window sizes have grown from a few thousand tokens in early models to hundreds of thousands or millions today. Larger windows allow whole documents or codebases, but cost and latency grow with input size, and models may attend less reliably to details buried in the middle. Good systems choose what to include rather than filling the window by default.

## Token vs context window: what is the difference?

A token is a unit of text, often a word or part of a word, that models read and write. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can handle at once. Tokens are the units; the window is the capacity.

In English, one token averages about three to four characters, or roughly three quarters of a word, though other languages, including many Indic scripts, can use more tokens per word. Tokenizers differ between models, so the same text can count differently. Use the provider's tokenizer or token-counting API to measure prompts accurately. Pricing and limits are counted in tokens, so understanding tokenisation helps estimate cost and avoid hitting window limits unexpectedly.

## What is the difference between max tokens and the context window?

The context window is the model's total capacity for input plus output. Max tokens, or max output tokens, is a request parameter that caps how many tokens the model may generate in its response.

Your input tokens plus the max output setting must fit within the context window, and many models also have a separate fixed limit on output length, smaller than the window. Setting max tokens too low truncates answers mid-sentence; setting it high does not force long answers but reserves room. For reasoning models, internal reasoning tokens may also count toward output limits, so allow generous values. Check each model's documented context and output limits.

## Does the context window include input and output tokens?

Yes. The context window covers both: everything you send, including the system prompt, history, documents and tool results, plus the tokens the model generates. Together they must fit within the window.

In multi-turn conversations, previous outputs become part of later inputs, so windows fill faster than people expect. Reasoning models may generate hidden thinking tokens that also occupy space during the request. Applications manage this by trimming old turns, summarising history, or retrieving only relevant past messages. Watch the usage fields returned by APIs, which report input and output tokens per request, to understand consumption and cost precisely and to catch prompts that are growing too large.

## What is the difference between context window and context length?

Usually they mean the same thing: the maximum number of tokens a model can process at once. Some people use context length for the actual length of a given prompt and context window for the maximum capacity.

In model specifications, context length often refers to the maximum sequence length the model was trained or configured to handle, such as 128,000 tokens. In local inference tools like llama.cpp or Ollama, you set a context length parameter that may be smaller than the model's maximum, to save memory, since the KV cache grows with it. Window size can also refer to sliding window attention, where each token attends only to nearby tokens, a different concept.

## What happens when the context window is full in Claude Code?

Claude Code automatically compacts the conversation when the context approaches its limit, summarising earlier messages so work can continue. You can also run /compact yourself with optional instructions about what to keep, or /clear to start fresh.

To avoid losing important details, keep durable instructions in a CLAUDE.md file, which Claude Code loads into every session, and break large tasks into focused sessions. Ask Claude to write plans or progress notes to files, so state survives compaction. Use subagents for broad searches so their large outputs stay out of the main context. Monitor context usage indicators, and compact at natural breakpoints, such as after finishing a feature, rather than mid-task.

## How do you architect AI agent memory that survives context window limits?

Separate memory into layers: the current context for the active task, a running summary of the session, and long-term memory stored outside the model, such as files, databases or vector stores, retrieved when relevant.

Practical patterns: write structured notes and decisions to files the agent rereads; summarise completed steps and drop raw details; store facts and preferences with embeddings and retrieve them by similarity; keep task state, such as a to-do list, in a durable store; and use subagents with their own contexts for large explorations, returning only conclusions. Test memory by restarting sessions and checking whether the agent recovers its goals correctly.

## Why do LLMs need masking and a context window during inference?

Causal masking ensures each token attends only to earlier tokens, matching how the model was trained to predict the next token. The context window bounds how many tokens attention covers, because memory and compute grow with sequence length.

During inference, the model generates one token at a time, and the KV cache stores keys and values for previous tokens so they are not recomputed; masking keeps attention causal within this cache. Padding masks also tell the model to ignore padding when batching sequences of different lengths. The window limit exists because positional encodings were trained for certain lengths and because attention cost and KV cache memory grow with every token.

## MCP vs context window: how do they relate?

They are different things. The context window is the model's token capacity per request. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. MCP results consume context window space when returned to the model.

Each connected MCP server adds tool descriptions to the prompt, and every tool result, such as a file's contents or a database query, adds tokens. Many servers with verbose tools can fill the window quickly, leaving less room for reasoning. Good practice: enable only the servers you need, design tools that return concise, filtered results, paginate large outputs, and summarise before passing data on. MCP extends what a model can access, not how much it can hold.

## Do huge context windows, such as 2 million tokens, change everything?

Very large windows, such as the 2-million-token contexts offered by some models, make it possible to load whole codebases, books or long histories at once, which simplifies some applications. They do not remove the need for retrieval and context design.

Long inputs cost more, increase latency and can reduce accuracy, as models may miss details buried in vast contexts. Benchmarks that hide facts in long documents show that performance varies by model and position. Retrieval still wins for large, changing knowledge bases, access control and citations. Large windows work best for tasks needing broad context at once, such as analysing a full contract or repository, combined with careful prompting and verification of key details.

# What is a fine-tuned model? LLMs, BERT, Llama, Gemma, and loading or merging LoRA
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-fine-tuned-model/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Fine-tuned means a pretrained model has been trained further on a smaller, specific dataset so it performs better at a task, follows a style or knows a domain. Most useful AI models today are fine-tuned versions of larger base models. I built FineTune Studio, which runs QLoRA fine-tuning with Transformers, PEFT and TRL and compares base and tuned outputs, so this page covers fine-tuned models, LLMs and BERT, examples, Llama and Gemma, instruct models as autocomplete, and loading and merging LoRA adapters.

## What does fine-tuned mean?

In AI, fine-tuned describes a model that started from pretrained weights and was trained further on task-specific data. In everyday English, fine-tuned means precisely adjusted for best performance, like a fine-tuned engine or argument.

The AI meaning follows from the everyday one: pretraining gives broad ability, and fine-tuning makes small, targeted adjustments rather than training from scratch. It is far cheaper than pretraining because the model already understands language or images. Fine-tuning can update all weights or only small added modules, as with LoRA. The term also appears in physics, where the fine-tuned universe argument discusses why physical constants seem precisely set, which is unrelated to machine learning.

## What is a fine-tuned model?

A fine-tuned model is a pretrained model adapted to a specific purpose by training on a focused dataset, such as customer support conversations, medical notes or labelled product reviews. It keeps general knowledge while gaining specialised behaviour.

Fine-tuned models appear everywhere: image classifiers trained on a company's product photos, sentiment classifiers for reviews, speech models adapted to accents, and chat assistants trained to follow instructions. They are typically smaller and cheaper to run than general giant models for the same task. A fine-tuned model should be evaluated against its base model on held-out examples, since fine-tuning can also introduce errors or forget skills if the data is narrow or noisy.

## What is a fine-tuned LLM?

A fine-tuned LLM is a large language model trained further after pretraining. The most common types are instruction-tuned models that follow requests, and task- or domain-tuned models that specialise in areas such as code, medicine, law or a company's format.

Methods include supervised fine-tuning on prompt and response pairs, preference tuning such as RLHF or DPO, and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA and QLoRA that train small adapters instead of all weights. Typical goals are consistent output formats, a brand voice, domain terminology, tool-calling reliability or smaller, faster models that match a larger model on one task. For changing factual knowledge, retrieval is usually better than fine-tuning, so many systems combine both.

## What are some examples of fine-tuned LLMs?

ChatGPT itself began as a GPT model fine-tuned with instruction data and human feedback. Other examples include Code Llama, fine-tuned from Llama 2 for programming, Google's Med-PaLM 2 for medical questions, and early open models such as Alpaca and Vicuna.

More recent examples include the distilled DeepSeek-R1 models, which fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models on reasoning outputs, and countless community fine-tunes on Hugging Face for roleplay, coding, languages and function calling. Companies fine-tune open models for structured extraction, classification and support replies to cut costs and latency. FineTune Studio, which I built, follows the same pattern at small scale: QLoRA training with live loss charts and a side-by-side base-versus-tuned comparison.

## What is a fine-tuned BERT model?

A fine-tuned BERT is Google's BERT encoder, pretrained on large text, with a small task head added and trained on labelled data for tasks such as sentiment classification, named entity recognition, question answering or semantic similarity.

Fine-tuning BERT typically takes a few epochs with a small learning rate, around 2e-5 to 5e-5, using the Hugging Face Trainer and a model class such as `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`. Well-known variants include DistilBERT fine-tuned for sentiment, BERT fine-tuned on SQuAD for extractive question answering, and domain models like BioBERT and FinBERT. Encoder models like BERT remain efficient choices for classification and extraction, often cheaper than prompting a large LLM.

## Can Llama be fine-tuned?

Yes. Meta's Llama models are released with weights you can fine-tune under the Llama community licence, which permits derivative models subject to conditions, such as attribution and naming rules and a large-user threshold requiring a separate licence.

Practical options: QLoRA with Hugging Face TRL and PEFT on a single consumer GPU for 8-billion-parameter models, Unsloth for faster, memory-efficient training, and Axolotl or torchtune for configurable pipelines. Start from the instruct version for chat-style tasks, format data with the official chat template, and train an adapter for one to three epochs. Read the licence version that applies to your model, since terms differ between Llama releases.

## Can Gemma be fine-tuned?

Yes. Google's Gemma models are open-weight and can be fine-tuned under the Gemma terms of use, which allow modification and commercial use with restrictions on prohibited uses. Sizes range from about 1 to 27 billion parameters in Gemma 3.

You can fine-tune Gemma with Hugging Face Transformers and TRL, Keras with LoRA support, Unsloth, or Google's Vertex AI. Small sizes, such as Gemma 3 1B or 4B, fine-tune quickly on modest GPUs or free notebook tiers, making them good for learning. Use the instruction-tuned checkpoint as the starting point for chat tasks and apply its specific chat template. Evaluate against the base model, since gains on narrow tasks can come with losses elsewhere.

## Can instruct fine-tuned LLMs still autocomplete text?

Yes, partly. An instruct model is still a next-token predictor, so if you send raw text without the chat template, it will continue it. But instruction tuning shifts its behaviour toward answering, so completions may be less natural than from a base model.

Instruct models may add commentary, end early, or treat the text as a request. For pure continuation, such as autocomplete, story continuation or code completion in an editor, base models or models trained for fill-in-the-middle usually work better. With an instruct model, you can prompt explicitly, for example asking it to continue the passage exactly in the same style, or use the API's completion mode where available. Test both approaches on your own examples.

## How do you load a fine-tuned PEFT or LoRA Llama model?

Load the base model with `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(base_id)`, then attach the adapter with `PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, adapter_path)`. Alternatively, `AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(adapter_path)` reads the base model name from the adapter config and loads both.

Load the tokenizer from the adapter folder if you saved one, since special tokens or chat templates may have changed during training. Use the same dtype and quantization settings as training where possible, for example 4-bit loading for QLoRA adapters when memory is tight. Call `model.eval()` and generate with the same chat template used in training. If outputs look like the base model, check that the adapter actually loaded and targets the right modules.

## How do you merge a fine-tuned adapter into the base model and push to the Hub?

Load the base model in full or half precision, attach the adapter with PeftModel, call `merge_and_unload()` to fold the LoRA weights into the base weights, then save with `save_pretrained` or upload with `push_to_hub`.

Do not merge into a 4-bit quantized base: load the base in float16 or bfloat16 instead, merge, then quantize the merged model later if needed. Save the tokenizer alongside the model, and push both with `model.push_to_hub("your-name/model-name")` and `tokenizer.push_to_hub(...)` after logging in with a Hugging Face token. Write a model card describing the base model, data, training settings, evaluation and licence, which the base model's terms may require.

# What is a mentor, and how do you find one? Mentor vs coach, and mentoring platforms
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-mentor-how-to-find-one/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A mentor is a more experienced person who guides you over time by sharing knowledge, perspective and connections, helping you avoid mistakes and see opportunities you would miss alone. Mentors appear in schools, colleges, workplaces and communities. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023 and founded TechVerse Enclave, a student tech community of over 500 members, so this page covers what mentors are, how to find the right one, mentors versus coaches, and how to check mentor-matching services.

## What is a mentor in school?

In school, a mentor is a teacher, senior student or adult volunteer who supports a student's learning, confidence and choices beyond regular classes. They listen, advise on studies and careers, and act as a trusted person to talk to.

Schools run mentoring programmes where older students guide younger ones through transitions, teachers mentor small groups, or professionals volunteer to share career insights. Good school mentoring builds study habits, confidence and awareness of options. In college, seniors often play this role informally, which is why induction sessions matter: at the VSICS induction in July 2025, I walked over 100 first-year students through a three-year roadmap so they knew what to focus on each year.

## What exactly is a mentor, and how do I find the right one?

A mentor is someone further along a path you want to follow, who shares experience and honest feedback because they want you to succeed. The right one has relevant experience, time for you, and a style that challenges you without discouraging you.

To find one, identify what you need help with, such as getting into AI engineering or speaking confidently, then look for people a few steps ahead in that area. Engage with their work first, ask a specific question, and show what you have tried. Mentorship often grows from a few good conversations rather than a formal request. You can have several mentors for different areas.

## What does "professional mentor" mean?

A professional mentor is an experienced person in your field or workplace who guides your career development: skills, decisions, workplace navigation, networking and growth opportunities. The relationship may be formal, through a company programme, or informal.

Some people also use "professional mentor" for paid mentoring services, where experienced practitioners offer sessions for a fee. Both can be valuable, but distinguish them from coaching and consulting. A good professional mentor gives honest feedback, shares lessons from their mistakes, opens doors when appropriate, and respects your goals rather than shaping you into a copy of themselves.

## How do I find a professional mentor?

Look within your workplace's mentoring programme, professional associations, alumni networks, industry communities, conferences and meetups, and platforms such as LinkedIn and free mentorship communities like ADPList.

Practical steps:

- Ask your manager or HR whether the organisation has a mentoring programme.
- Attend events and talk to speakers afterwards with a thoughtful question.
- Contact alumni from your college working in roles you want.
- Join active online communities and contribute before asking for help.
- Send short, specific messages that show you have done your homework.

Start with one conversation; do not ask a stranger "Will you be my mentor?" in the first message.

## How do I find a mentor for career growth?

Look for someone two to five years ahead of you on the path you want, because their advice is recent and relevant, plus occasionally a senior leader for broader perspective. Approach them with a specific goal and evidence of your effort.

For example: "I'm building RAG projects and aiming for a GenAI engineering role. Could I share my portfolio and ask what would make it stronger?" Specific asks are easy to say yes to. Follow up with what you did with their advice; mentors invest more in people who act. Students I mentor who return with progress get far more time and help than those who only ask questions.

## How do I find a mentor who can accelerate my career?

Choose a mentor whose experience matches your next step, make each conversation count, and turn advice into visible progress. Acceleration comes from focused feedback and opportunities, so prepare questions and share work they can react to.

Habits that accelerate mentorship:

- Set a clear goal, such as a role, skill or project, and share it.
- Bring specific work: a resume, a demo, a talk draft.
- Ask what they would do in your place, and what to stop doing.
- Act quickly and report results.
- Help them back: share useful resources, volunteer, give credit publicly.

Over time, good mentors may recommend you for opportunities, which is when mentorship becomes sponsorship.

## What is the difference between a mentor and a coach?

A mentor shares their own experience and advice, usually over a longer, informal relationship. A coach uses structured conversations and questions to help you find your own answers and reach specific goals, often over a defined period and usually as a paid service.

Mentors say, "Here is what worked for me." Coaches ask, "What options do you see, and what will you do?" Mentors typically come from your field; coaches may not, because their skill is the coaching process. Both are valuable: mentors for industry insight and networks, coaches for behaviour change, confidence and decision-making. Some people combine both skills.

## When should I coach and when should I mentor?

Mentor when the person needs knowledge or experience you have: how to navigate a field, avoid common mistakes or make industry-specific decisions. Coach when they already have the knowledge but need clarity, confidence or accountability to act.

As someone who mentors students, I switch often. A first-year asking which skills to learn needs mentoring with a direct roadmap. A final-year student choosing between two offers usually benefits more from coaching questions about their own priorities, because the decision depends on their values, not mine. A good rule: tell when they lack information; ask when they lack clarity.

## What is the difference between a mentor and a career coach?

A career coach is usually a paid professional trained in coaching methods who helps with career decisions, job searches, interviews and transitions. A mentor is usually an unpaid, experienced person in your field who shares their own journey and advice.

Career coaches offer structure, accountability and techniques for resumes, interviews and decision-making, and work with people across many industries. Mentors offer insider knowledge, industry context and sometimes connections. If you need help with a career change or job search process, a coach can help; if you need industry-specific guidance, find a mentor. Check coaches' credentials, such as International Coaching Federation accreditation, and reviews.

## Is Mentor Match legit?

Several programmes and platforms use names like "Mentor Match", so check the specific one: who runs it, whether mentors are verified, what it costs, and what real users say. Legitimate services are transparent about all of these.

Checks before joining a mentor-matching platform:

- Clear ownership, contact details and privacy policy.
- Verified mentor profiles with real, checkable experience.
- Reviews on independent sites, not just testimonials on its own page.
- Transparent terms with no pressure to pay upfront for vague promises.
- No requests for unnecessary personal or financial information.

Free communities, alumni networks and school or employer programmes are reliable alternatives.

# What is a public speaker? The job, how to become one, getting paid, and speaking classes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-public-speaker/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A public speaker is someone who presents ideas live to an audience, at conferences, colleges, companies, community events or online, to inform, persuade, teach or inspire. Some speak occasionally alongside their main work; others build careers around speaking. I have given more than 20 campus sessions, including the VSICS induction seminar for over 100 first-year students in July 2025, so this page covers what public speakers are and do, how to become one and get paid, how to be great and effective, public speaking classes, and a short guide.

## What is a public speaker?

A public speaker is a person who delivers prepared talks or presentations to groups of people. The role ranges from a student presenting at a seminar to a professional keynote speaker at large conferences.

Public speakers usually share expertise or experience: engineers explain technology, founders share startup lessons, scientists present research, and advocates promote causes. What makes someone a public speaker is not fame but the practice of communicating clearly to audiences. Many professionals become public speakers naturally as their expertise grows, because organisers seek people who have done the work they want audiences to learn about. In technology, a student who has shipped a real project can already be a valuable speaker for juniors.

## What is a public speaker called?

Depending on context, a public speaker may be called an orator, speaker, keynote speaker, presenter, lecturer, guest speaker, panellist, trainer, facilitator or motivational speaker. "Orator" suggests formal, persuasive speaking; "keynote speaker" means the main speaker at an event.

In education, invited speakers are often called guest speakers or resource persons; in companies, trainers or facilitators; at conferences, speakers, panellists or keynotes. The art of persuasive speaking is called rhetoric, and a skilled practitioner can be called a rhetorician. On event materials, use the title organisers expect, such as "speaker" or "resource person" for Indian colleges.

## What is a public speaker's job?

A professional speaker's job includes researching audiences, preparing and rehearsing talks, delivering keynotes, workshops or training, answering questions, and marketing themselves to event organisers. Many combine speaking with consulting, writing, coaching or a main profession.

Behind each talk is significant work: understanding what organisers want, tailoring content, preparing slides and demos, travel and logistics, and follow-up with attendees. Full-time speakers are relatively rare; most speakers are experts whose talks support their main work, such as engineers, founders, academics and authors. Speaking builds visibility that feeds their other work. Even a few talks a year can open doors to collaborations, hiring conversations and new clients.

## How do I become a public speaker?

Build expertise in a topic, start speaking at small events such as college clubs, meetups and webinars, record your talks, gather feedback, and steadily seek bigger stages. Make it easy for organisers to find and invite you.

Steps:

- Choose two or three topics where you have real experience.
- Prepare one strong talk and refine it through repetition.
- Speak free at communities, colleges and online events.
- Collect recordings, photos and organiser feedback.
- Create a speaker page with topics, bio, past talks and contact.
- Write or post about your topics to build visibility.

My path started with sessions for juniors and grew into college seminars and campus visits.

## How do I become a paid public speaker?

Paid speaking usually follows a track record: proven expertise, strong recordings, testimonials and visibility. Start with free talks to build these, then approach events, companies and colleges that have budgets, clearly stating your topics, formats and terms.

Ways to get paid opportunities: corporate workshops and training, which often pay better than conferences; college programmes with funding for expert sessions; industry conferences after you are known in a niche; and referrals from organisers who liked your previous talks. A clear invite or booking page with topics and terms helps. Many speakers also earn indirectly, through clients, jobs or courses that talks generate.

## How do I become a great public speaker?

Great speakers know their audience, have one clear message, tell specific stories with evidence, structure talks simply, and rehearse until delivery feels natural. They speak with energy and authenticity rather than performance.

Habits of great speakers: they open with a hook, such as a question or story; use slides as support, not scripts; show real examples and demos; vary pace and pause for emphasis; make eye contact; handle questions honestly; and end with a clear takeaway or action. They also seek feedback after every talk and keep improving. Watching recordings of yourself is uncomfortable but the fastest way to improve.

## How do I become an effective public speaker?

Effectiveness means the audience understands, remembers and acts on your message. Focus on clarity, relevance and actionability: one main idea, concrete examples, and specific next steps the audience can take.

Tips:

- Define what the audience should know or do after your talk.
- Cut content that does not serve that goal.
- Use stories and data together.
- Check understanding with questions or quick polls.
- Give a resource or roadmap they can use later.
- Follow up with slides or links.

At my campus sessions, a concrete three-year roadmap students could photograph did more than any inspirational speech.

## What is a public speaking class?

A public speaking class teaches how to prepare and deliver presentations: choosing topics, structuring talks, writing openings and closings, using voice and body language, managing nerves, using visual aids and handling questions, with lots of practice and feedback.

Classes may be in schools, colleges, community centres, online platforms or clubs such as Toastmasters, which uses structured speeches and peer evaluation. The value comes from repeated practice in a supportive setting, plus feedback you cannot get alone. Look for classes with small groups, recorded practice and individual feedback. Online courses can teach techniques, but nothing replaces speaking to real people regularly.

## What is a public speaking class in college?

In college, a public speaking class, often called communication skills or speech communication, is a course where students learn and practise presentations, speeches, group discussions and sometimes debates, with assessments based on actual speaking.

Many Indian colleges include communication skills in their curriculum, and placement training often covers group discussions and interviews. Take these classes seriously: speaking skills affect interviews, project vivas, hackathon pitches and leadership roles. Supplement them with club activities, tech talks and competitions to practise beyond the classroom.

## What is a quick public speaking guide?

Prepare, practise and connect. Know your audience and message, structure the talk, rehearse out loud, and focus on helping the audience rather than on yourself.

A compact guide:

- **Audience**: who they are and what they need.
- **Message**: one sentence summarising your talk.
- **Structure**: hook, three key points, takeaway.
- **Evidence**: stories, examples, demos, data.
- **Slides**: minimal text, large visuals.
- **Practice**: three full rehearsals, timed.
- **Delivery**: slow down, pause, make eye contact.
- **Questions**: listen fully, answer honestly.

After the talk, ask for feedback and note one thing to improve next time. Keep a simple log of each talk, audience and lesson, and you will see steady progress within a year.

# What is a system prompt? In AI, Claude and Claude Code, and how to write one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-a-system-prompt/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A system prompt is the set of instructions given to an AI model before the conversation that defines its role, rules, context and output style, such as "You are a tutor for first-year BCA students; explain with examples; never write assignments". User prompts are the individual messages that follow. This page explains system and user prompts, how system prompts work, how they apply in Claude and Claude Code, how to write and use one, whether they can be cached, whether you need one, and whether you can see an app's hidden system prompt.

## What is a system prompt in AI?

A system prompt is a special instruction message that sets up how an AI model should behave for an entire conversation or application: who it is, what it should and should not do, what context it has, and how to format answers.

Applications use system prompts to turn a general model into a specific assistant: a support bot that only answers from the help centre, a code reviewer that lists issues by severity, or a tutor that asks questions instead of giving answers. Chat apps such as ChatGPT and Claude have their own system prompts written by the companies, and your custom instructions or project instructions add to them. In APIs, developers write system prompts themselves.

## What is the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt?

The system prompt sets the rules and context for the whole interaction; the user prompt is the specific request in each turn. Models are trained to give system instructions higher priority and to apply them across all user messages.

For example, the system prompt says "Answer only from the provided handbook and cite section numbers; if the answer is not there, say so", and the user prompt asks "How many leaves can I take in a semester?". Put stable rules and context in the system prompt and task-specific details in user messages. Avoid repeating the same instructions in every user message; it wastes tokens and can confuse priorities.

## How does a system prompt work?

The system prompt is placed at the start of the model's input, marked as system-level by the chat format. The model reads it with every turn, so its instructions shape each response, and training teaches models to follow system instructions over conflicting user requests.

It is not a separate program or hard rule; it is text the model conditions on. That is why clear, specific instructions work better than vague ones, why contradictory instructions cause inconsistent behaviour, and why applications still need code-level safeguards, such as validating outputs and restricting tools, for anything critical. Long conversations can dilute instructions, so important rules should be concise and prominent.

## What is the system prompt in Claude?

In the Claude API, the system prompt is passed in a separate `system` parameter, not as a message, and Claude uses it to set role, tone, rules and context. In the Claude apps, Anthropic writes a system prompt and publishes it in its documentation's release notes.

Anthropic recommends using the system prompt to give Claude a role, such as "You are a senior data analyst", which improves performance in that domain, and putting task details in the user turn. With the API, you control the whole system prompt; in claude.ai you shape behaviour with profile preferences, project instructions and styles, which add to Anthropic's own prompt.

## What is the system prompt in Claude Code?

Claude Code has its own built-in system prompt that sets it up as a coding agent with tools for reading files, editing and running commands. You customise its behaviour mainly through `CLAUDE.md` files in your project and home directory, plus settings and options that append instructions.

A `CLAUDE.md` file holds project knowledge: build and test commands, coding conventions, architecture notes and rules such as "never commit directly to main". Claude Code reads it at the start of each session, so it works like a project-specific addition to the system prompt. For scripted use, command-line options let you append extra system instructions. Keep `CLAUDE.md` concise and current; outdated instructions mislead the agent.

## How do I write a system prompt?

State the role, the goal, the rules, the context and the output format clearly, in that order, and keep it as short as possible while being complete. Then test it against real inputs and refine.

A template:

```
Role: You are a support assistant for a college's admissions office.
Goal: Answer applicants' questions accurately and briefly.
Rules: Use only the provided handbook passages. Cite section numbers.
If the answer is not in the passages, say so and suggest emailing admissions.
Never collect personal data such as phone numbers or ID numbers.
Format: 2 to 4 sentences, then "Source: section X".
```

Test with normal, tricky and adversarial questions, and change one instruction at a time.

## How do I use a system prompt?

In APIs, pass it in the system field or as the first system or developer message; in chat apps, use custom instructions, project instructions or a custom assistant's instructions. Keep it in version control for applications.

Examples:

- **Claude API**: `client.messages.create(model=..., system="...", messages=[...])`.
- **OpenAI API**: instructions or a system or developer message, depending on the endpoint.
- **ChatGPT and Claude apps**: custom instructions, Projects, custom GPTs or styles.
- **Agents**: system prompt plus tool descriptions, which act as instructions too.

Pair the system prompt with retrieval for facts, so the prompt holds rules while documents hold knowledge.

## Can a system prompt be cached?

Yes. Prompt caching lets providers reuse the processed form of a long, unchanging prompt prefix, such as a system prompt with reference material, which cuts cost and latency on later requests. Anthropic's API supports explicit cache markers, and OpenAI applies automatic caching for long repeated prefixes.

Caching works only for an identical prefix, so put stable content, such as system instructions, tool definitions and reference documents, at the start, and variable content, such as the user's question, at the end. Cached content expires after a period of inactivity. For applications that send the same long instructions with every request, caching can substantially reduce costs; check each provider's documentation for current rules and pricing.

## Is a system prompt necessary?

Not strictly: models respond without one. But any real application benefits from a short system prompt that sets role, boundaries and format, because it makes behaviour more consistent and safer across users.

For quick personal chats, the app's default plus clear user prompts is enough. For products, a tested system prompt is essential, along with code-level checks, because users will ask things you did not expect. Keep it focused: long, unfocused system prompts can make behaviour worse. If you find yourself writing pages of facts into it, move those facts into retrieval instead.

## How do I get a system prompt?

For your own applications, the system prompt is whatever you write. For commercial chat apps, the companies decide whether to publish them; Anthropic publishes its Claude app system prompts in its documentation, which is the legitimate way to read them.

Attempts to trick an app into revealing hidden system prompts, known as prompt extraction, may break its terms of use, and the output may be partial or fabricated anyway. If you are building an app, assume your system prompt could be extracted: do not put secrets, API keys or private data in it, and enforce important rules in code, not only in text.

# What is agentic RAG and Graph RAG? Query rewriting, multi-step retrieval, knowledge graphs, and when a plain RAG pipeline is not enough
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-agentic-rag-and-graph-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is agentic RAG?

**Agentic RAG wraps the retrieval pipeline in a decision loop run by the model: decide whether retrieval is needed at all, rewrite or decompose the query, choose which index or tool to search, inspect what came back, and retrieve again or differently if the evidence is weak, before generating. A plain RAG pipeline does one fixed retrieve-then-generate pass [1]; an agentic one lets the model steer, using patterns from ReAct and its descendants [9]. It answers harder, multi-step questions at the cost of more model calls, more latency and more ways to fail.**


RAG.NextUpgrad, the production platform I built, is deliberately not agentic in the full sense: it has one pass with hybrid retrieval, reranking and a confidence gate, and that pass scores above ninety percent recall on the labelled set [15]. This page is about what the agentic and graph layers add, what they cost, and the test I use to decide whether a system needs them. My notes on multi-hop questions and query rewriting are on the portfolio [13][14].

> Every agentic RAG system I have audited that was struggling had a chunking or ranking problem underneath. Fix the pipeline first. Add planning when the pipeline is good and the questions still fail.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does agentic RAG differ from a plain RAG pipeline?

**A plain pipeline is a fixed sequence: embed, retrieve, rerank, generate, once. An agentic system inserts model decisions between the stages: a router that picks the retriever, a rewriter that improves the query, a grader that checks whether retrieved passages actually answer the question, and a loop that retries with a different query or source. The decisions are prompts or small classifiers; the loop is a graph with a step limit. Every decision is a place for the model to be right or wrong, and a place to measure.**



## What is query rewriting, and what is HyDE?

**Query rewriting has the model turn the user's question into a better retrieval query: expanding abbreviations, adding likely terms, splitting a compound question into sub-questions, or removing conversational noise. HyDE, hypothetical document embeddings, goes further: the model writes a short hypothetical answer, and that text is embedded and used to search, because an answer-shaped passage is closer in vector space to real answer passages than a short question is [5]. Both are one extra model call and often the biggest agentic-style gain available.**



Query rewriting is the one agentic element I add to almost every system, because conversational follow-ups such as "and for the other plan?" are unretrievable as written [14].

## What are Self-RAG and corrective RAG?

**Self-RAG trains a model to emit reflection tokens that decide whether to retrieve, whether a passage is relevant, whether the generation is supported, and whether it is useful, so retrieval and self-critique happen inside generation [3]. Corrective RAG adds a lightweight evaluator that grades retrieved documents as correct, incorrect or ambiguous and triggers web search or query refinement when retrieval looks wrong [4]. Both formalise the same idea a confidence gate implements more simply: check the evidence before you trust it.**


The confidence gate in RAG.NextUpgrad is the minimal version of this family: it inspects reranker scores and passage agreement and refuses when support is weak, with no extra model call [15]. Start there; graduate to graded loops when the refusal rate on answerable questions is measurably too high.

## What is Graph RAG?

**Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph from the corpus, extracting entities and the relationships between them with a model, clusters the graph into communities, writes a summary for each community, and then retrieves through the graph: by entity for specific questions, by community summary for global ones. Microsoft's Graph RAG paper showed gains on query-focused summarisation, questions such as "what are the main themes across these documents", where chunk retrieval has nothing to retrieve because the answer is not in any single chunk [6][7].**



RAPTOR reaches a similar goal, multi-level retrieval, by recursively clustering and summarising chunks into a tree, without extracting an explicit graph [8]. Both trade index-time cost for the ability to answer questions about the whole.

## When do I actually need agentic RAG or Graph RAG?

**When the plain pipeline is measurably good and specific question types still fail. Multi-hop questions that need two retrievals, "who leads the team that built the tool mentioned in the June report", need interleaved retrieval and reasoning, which IRCoT and agentic loops provide [10]. Global questions about a corpus need Graph RAG or RAPTOR. Questions spanning several systems need a router. Everything else, which is most questions in most products, needs chunking, hybrid search and reranking done well.**




## How do I build an agentic RAG system?

**Model it as a graph with explicit state: nodes for rewrite, retrieve, grade, generate and refuse, edges chosen by the grader's output, a step limit and a token budget. LangGraph is the common framework for this shape [11]; the same loop is a couple of hundred lines without one. Log every decision. Evaluate the agentic system against the plain pipeline on the same labelled set and keep it only where it measurably wins. Anthropic's guidance applies: the simplest architecture that works, and the model's judgement only where it is actually needed [12].**



## What does agentic RAG cost?

**Several model calls per question instead of one, plus latency that users notice, plus a larger failure surface: a rewriter that drifts, a grader that is too strict, a loop that runs to its limit. A rewriter and a grader roughly double cost; a full multi-agent design can multiply it several times. Graph RAG shifts cost to index time, with many model calls to extract entities and write summaries, which repeats when documents change. Budget both before building, and measure whether the gain in recall or answer quality pays for it.**



## What are common mistakes with agentic and Graph RAG?

**Adding an agent loop to a pipeline with bad chunking. No step limit, so a hard question loops until the budget dies. A grader that rejects good passages and triggers endless retries. Graph RAG for a corpus of precise procedures where chunk citations were the requirement. Not logging decisions, so failures cannot be traced. Evaluating the agentic system alone instead of against the plain baseline. Every one of these is avoided by measuring first and adding layers only where the measurement demands them.**



## Agentic RAG interview questions

**Define agentic RAG and Graph RAG and say what each fixes. Explain query rewriting and HyDE. Describe Self-RAG or corrective RAG in a sentence. Give a question a plain pipeline cannot answer and say which layer fixes it. Explain how you would decide whether to add an agentic layer, and how you would measure the result. Describe the cost trade-offs. The strongest answer includes a pipeline you measured and a layer you chose not to add.**




## Where should I start?

**Measure your plain pipeline's recall on twenty labelled questions. Read the misses. If they are conversational follow-ups, add query rewriting. If they are multi-hop, add a retrieval check and one retry. If they are global questions about the corpus, prototype RAPTOR or Graph RAG on a subset and compare. Add nothing you cannot measure.** For a hands-on session on retrieval systems from the notebook to the operator level, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is an AI product manager? Role, skills, coding, demand and a roadmap
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-ai-product-manager/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An AI product manager is a product manager who leads products or features powered by AI: deciding which problems AI should solve, defining what good output looks like, working with engineers and data scientists to build and evaluate it, and owning its quality, safety and business impact. The role combines classic product skills with fluency in data, models and their limits. This page covers the role, how it differs from regular PM and data science, whether it needs coding or is technical, demand and career prospects, a roadmap, certifications and pay.

## What is an AI product manager?

An AI product manager owns AI-powered products or features end to end: identifying user problems where AI helps, defining success metrics and quality bars, prioritising work, coordinating engineering, data and design, and making launch decisions based on evaluations and risks.

Typical responsibilities include writing specifications that describe desired model behaviour with examples, deciding between approaches such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning with engineers, planning evaluation sets, setting guardrails and human review for risky outputs, tracking cost per request, and communicating limitations honestly to users and stakeholders. They also handle feedback loops, so the product improves from real usage.

## How is an AI product manager different from a product manager?

All product managers decide what to build and why. AI product managers additionally manage probabilistic behaviour: outputs that can be wrong, data dependencies, evaluation, model costs and AI-specific risks such as hallucination, bias and prompt injection.

Practical differences:

- **Specs**: describe quality with examples and evaluation sets, not only features.
- **Uncertainty**: plan for wrong answers with fallbacks, citations and human review.
- **Data**: understand what data the model sees and how it is protected.
- **Costs**: track cost per request and latency as product metrics.
- **Iteration**: improve through evaluation and prompt or retrieval changes, not only new screens.

A regular PM building a checkout flow can test deterministic behaviour; an AI PM must manage a system that is right most of the time.

## Does an AI product manager need to code?

Usually not as a job requirement, but basic technical skills make AI PMs much more effective. Being able to call an LLM API, build a quick prototype, read evaluation results and understand system design lets you make better decisions and earn engineers' trust.

Useful technical skills for AI PMs:

- Prompting and writing clear model specifications.
- Basic Python or a no-code tool to prototype ideas.
- Understanding of RAG, embeddings, fine-tuning and agents at a conceptual level.
- Reading metrics: accuracy, recall, latency, cost.
- SQL for analysing usage data.

With AI coding tools, PMs can now prototype far more than before; use that to test ideas before asking engineers to build them.

## Is AI product manager a technical role?

It is a technical-leaning product role. AI PMs are not expected to train models, but they must understand how AI systems work well enough to define behaviour, judge feasibility, interpret evaluations and weigh trade-offs with engineers.

Some AI PM roles are deeply technical, such as product managers for AI platforms, developer tools or model APIs, where customers are engineers. Others are closer to traditional product work, adding AI features to consumer apps. Read job descriptions closely: phrases like "experience with LLM evaluation" or "familiarity with RAG architectures" signal a more technical role.

## Is AI product manager in demand?

Demand is growing as companies add AI features to products and build new AI-first products, and employers increasingly ask product managers for AI experience. Competition is also strong, because many PMs are moving into AI.

What stands out to employers: evidence that you have shipped or prototyped AI features, can define quality and evaluation, understand costs and risks, and communicate clearly with technical teams. Experience in a domain, such as education, health, finance or developer tools, combined with AI fluency, is especially valuable. For students, entry usually goes through associate product manager programmes, product analyst roles, or engineering roles followed by a move into product.

## Is AI product manager a good career?

It can be an excellent career for people who enjoy understanding users, making decisions under uncertainty and working across disciplines, and who are curious about technology. It offers high impact and visibility, but also responsibility for products that can fail in unusual ways.

Consider the trade-offs: PMs spend much of their time communicating, prioritising and resolving conflicts, with less hands-on building. AI products bring extra ethical and quality responsibilities. If you love building, engineering roles with product ownership may suit you better; if you love deciding what to build and why, AI product management is a strong fit. Many successful AI PMs started as engineers, designers or analysts.

## Data scientist vs AI product manager: which should I choose?

Choose data science if you enjoy analysis, statistics, modelling and experiments; choose AI product management if you enjoy defining problems, prioritising, coordinating teams and owning outcomes. The roles work closely together.

Data scientists explore data, build and evaluate models and run experiments, going deep on technical questions. AI product managers decide which problems matter, define success, and make trade-offs across users, business and technology. Data scientists often move into product roles later, bringing strong analytical skills. Try both through projects: build a model and analyse results, then write a product specification for an AI feature, and notice which you enjoy more.

## What is a roadmap to become an AI product manager?

Build product fundamentals, AI fluency and evidence. Learn how products are discovered, prioritised and measured, learn how modern AI systems work and fail, and ship at least one AI prototype with an evaluation plan and a product write-up.

A practical roadmap:

- **Product basics**: user research, problem framing, prioritisation, metrics, writing specifications.
- **AI fluency**: LLMs, prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, evaluation, costs and risks.
- **Hands-on**: build a small AI feature, such as a document Q&A assistant with citations.
- **Evaluation**: create a test set, measure quality, and iterate.
- **Portfolio**: a case study covering the problem, decisions, results and what you would change.
- **Experience**: associate PM roles, product internships, or leading AI features in your current role.

## What is the best AI product manager certification?

There is no single standard certification. Some universities, online platforms and companies offer AI product management courses with certificates, and broader product management certifications cover fundamentals. Choose programmes with hands-on projects and practitioner instructors.

Certificates help a little for career switchers, but hiring managers look for evidence: a shipped or prototyped AI feature, an evaluation approach, and clear product thinking. Free resources, such as Google's People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, teach valuable principles for designing AI products. Pair any course with a real project and a written case study.

## What is the salary of an AI product manager?

Pay varies widely with company, location, seniority and how technical the role is, so there is no single figure. AI product roles are generally paid in line with or above comparable product management roles at the same company.

To understand current pay for roles you target, compare listings and verified reports on job platforms for your country and level, and talk to people in those roles. For students, focus on getting the first product role, often through associate PM programmes, internships or a move from engineering or analytics, since early experience drives later earnings more than any certificate.

# What is an AI agent? Definition, examples, tools, and how to build one free
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


An AI agent is a system in which a language model works towards a goal in a loop: it decides the next step, calls a tool such as search, a database query or code execution, reads the result, and continues until the task is done or it needs a person. That loop is what separates an agent from a chatbot that only replies. This page defines agents with examples, separates agents from agentic AI, explains tools, skills and harnesses, and shows how to build one for free and which frameworks and builders to consider.

## What is an AI agent?

An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to choose and take actions towards a goal, observing the results of each action before deciding the next. It typically has a model, instructions, a set of tools, memory of what it has done, and a loop that runs until the goal is reached.

The key word is decide. In a fixed workflow, the developer writes every step. In an agent, the model chooses which tool to call and with what inputs, based on the situation. That flexibility handles messy, varied tasks, such as researching a question or fixing a failing test, but it also makes agents less predictable. Good agents limit that freedom with clear instructions, a small set of well-described tools, step limits and approval for risky actions.

## What is an AI agent, explained with an example?

Take a support agent for a college's admissions office. A student asks "has my application fee been received, and when is the counselling date?". The agent looks up the application in the database, checks the payment status, searches the admissions notice for dates, and replies with both answers and links.

Step by step:

- The model reads the question and decides it needs two lookups.
- It calls `get_application(student_id)` and reads the payment status.
- It calls `search_notices("counselling date")` and reads the passage.
- It writes the answer, citing the notice.
- If the record is missing, it hands over to a staff member instead of guessing.

A chatbot would answer from general knowledge; the agent acts on real systems.

## What is the difference between an AI agent and agentic AI?

Agentic AI is the broad approach of giving AI systems autonomy to plan and act towards goals. An AI agent is a specific system built that way. Agentic describes the quality; an agent is the thing.

In practice, "agentic" also describes a spectrum. A chatbot with search that decides when to search is slightly agentic. A coding agent that plans a change, edits ten files, runs tests and fixes failures is highly agentic. Many production systems sit in between: mostly fixed workflows with a few agentic steps where judgement helps. That middle ground is often the best design, because each added degree of autonomy adds failure modes. Choose the least autonomy that solves the problem.

## What are AI agent tools?

Tools are functions an agent can call: search the web, query a database, read a file, run code, send an email, call an API. Each tool has a name, a description and an input schema, and the model chooses tools based on those descriptions.

A tool definition looks like a function signature with documentation: `search_orders(customer_email: string)`, "Find a customer's recent orders; use when the user asks about an order". The quality of descriptions decides how well the agent picks tools, so write them as you would for a new teammate. Tools should validate inputs, return compact results and fail with clear error messages the model can act on. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for packaging tools so many agents and apps can use them.

## What are AI agent skills?

Skills are packaged know-how an agent loads when a task needs it: instructions, examples, templates and sometimes scripts for a specific job, such as creating a report in your company format or following your testing procedure.

The agent first sees only a short description of each skill and loads the full contents when relevant, which keeps its context small even with many skills available. That differs from tools, which are actions it can take, and from the system prompt, which is always loaded. Skills are supported in Claude's apps and API, Claude Code and other agent environments. Write a skill like a good checklist for a colleague: when to use it, the exact steps, and an example of the expected output.

## What is an AI agent harness?

The harness is the code around the model that turns it into an agent: it runs the loop, sends the model its instructions and context, executes the tools it asks for, enforces limits and permissions, manages memory and logs everything.

The model only produces text, including tool requests; the harness does the actual work. A good harness handles errors and retries, caps the number of steps and cost, asks a person before risky actions, trims or summarises context as it grows, and records every step for debugging. Claude Code and other coding agents are harnesses around models; frameworks such as LangGraph and agent SDKs help you build your own. Much of an agent's reliability comes from its harness, not the model.

## Can I build an AI agent?

Yes. If you can write basic Python and call an API, you can build a simple agent in an afternoon: a model API, two or three tools as Python functions, and a loop that runs the model's tool calls until it gives a final answer.

A sensible first project is an agent that answers questions about your own documents and can look up one live data source, such as a timetable or an API. Log every step so you can see how it decides. Then add evaluation: twenty test questions with expected answers, run after every change. Agents look impressive in demos and fail in subtle ways in real use; the evaluation set is how you find and fix those failures.

## How do I make an AI agent for free?

Use a free-tier model API, such as Google's Gemini API through AI Studio, or a local model with Ollama, and write a small agent loop in Python with an open-source framework or none at all.

A minimal agent with free tools:

- **Model**: Gemini's free tier, or a local model such as a Llama or Qwen model in Ollama.
- **Tools**: plain Python functions, such as a calculator, a search over your notes, a weather API with a free key.
- **Loop**: send the conversation and tool definitions, run any tool calls, append results, repeat with a step limit.
- **Interface**: a terminal, or Streamlit for a quick web page.
- **Hosting**: run locally, or a free tier on Hugging Face Spaces.

Keep API keys in environment variables and never let a free agent take irreversible actions without confirmation.

## What is the best AI agent framework?

There is no single best one. LangGraph suits complex, stateful workflows with explicit control; the OpenAI Agents SDK and the Claude Agent SDK are lightweight and close to their providers' models; CrewAI and AutoGen focus on multi-agent setups; LlamaIndex suits document-heavy agents.

Choose by your needs: control and observability for production, provider flexibility if you may switch models, and a community large enough to find answers. Many experienced builders start with no framework at all, a plain loop over the model's tool-calling API, because it is easier to debug and understand. Add a framework when you need what it offers, such as persistence, branching or human-in-the-loop steps, not before.

## What is the best AI agent builder?

For no-code and low-code agents, Microsoft Copilot Studio suits Microsoft 365 organisations, OpenAI's agent tools and custom GPTs suit ChatGPT users, and workflow tools such as n8n and Zapier offer agent steps for automations. For developers, code frameworks give more control.

Pick by where the agent will live and what it must reach: Teams and SharePoint point to Copilot Studio; Google Workspace points to Google's agent tools; many SaaS integrations point to n8n or Zapier; custom products point to code. Whatever you choose, judge it on how well you can test, monitor and limit the agent, not on how quickly the demo appears. The builder that makes failures visible is the better one.

# What is an AI agent? Agentic AI explained: tools, function calling, MCP, frameworks, and why most agents fail
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is an AI agent?

**An AI agent is a language model running in a loop with tools. Given a goal, the model decides on an action, your code executes it, a search, a database query, an API call, a file edit, the result is fed back, and the model decides the next action, until it judges the goal met or a stopping rule fires. The model supplies judgement; the tools supply reach; the loop supplies persistence. Without the loop it is a chatbot; without tools it is a planner that cannot act.**


The pattern was named ReAct by Yao et al., reasoning and acting interleaved, with the model writing a thought, an action and reading an observation on each turn [1]. Toolformer showed models could learn when to call tools [2], Reflexion added self-critique between attempts [3], and the survey by Wang et al. maps the many variants that followed [4]. Anthropic's practitioner guide distinguishes fixed workflows, where code decides the steps, from true agents, where the model does, and argues for the simplest design that works [5].

I ship both kinds. My publishing pipeline is a workflow: code decides the order, models write the text. The coding assistant that helped build it is an agent: it reads, edits and runs tests until the tests pass. The distinction is the first thing to get right, because a workflow is cheaper, more predictable and easier to test, and most "agent" products are workflows that would be better admitted as such.

> Every agent I have built started as a workflow that needed one decision I could not write as an if-statement. That decision is where the model belongs. Everywhere else, write code.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is agentic AI, and how is it different from generative AI?

**Generative AI produces content on request: text, images, code, audio. Agentic AI uses a generative model to pursue a goal through actions over multiple steps, using tools and reacting to results. The same model can do both; the difference is the harness around it. A chat window is generative. A system that reads your inbox, drafts replies, checks your calendar and books the meeting is agentic.**



## How do AI agents work?

**Each turn, the agent's context holds the goal, the tool definitions, the history of previous actions and their results. The model reads it and outputs either a final answer or a tool call: the tool's name and arguments as structured data. Your code validates the call, runs the tool, appends the result to the context, and calls the model again. Guardrails sit around the loop: a maximum number of steps, a budget, permissions per tool, and confirmation for irreversible actions.**



The whole loop is under a hundred lines in any language. The frameworks add memory management, retries, streaming, tracing and multi-agent orchestration on top; none of that changes the loop.

## What is tool calling or function calling?

**Tool calling, also called function calling, is the API feature that lets a model request an action in a machine-readable form instead of free text. You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model decides a tool is needed it returns a call object with the tool name and arguments; your code runs the function and returns the result as a tool message. It is what makes agents reliable enough to build on, because you never parse prose to find the action.**


The shape, in the form both major providers use [7][8]:

```json
{
  "name": "search_docs",
  "description": "Search the company knowledge base. Use for any question about policies or products.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {"type": "string", "description": "What to search for, in the user's words"},
      "top_k": {"type": "integer", "default": 5}
    },
    "required": ["query"]
  }
}
```

Two rules that decide whether the model picks the right tool: the description says when to use it, not just what it does, and the tools do not overlap. Ten tools with fuzzy boundaries produce worse agents than three tools with sharp ones.

## What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol?

**The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing tools, data sources and prompt templates to AI applications through a common interface, so that a tool server written once can be used by any client that speaks the protocol, a coding assistant, a chat app, an agent framework, without a custom integration each time [6]. An MCP server declares its tools with schemas; the client lists them, the model calls them, the server executes. It turns "integrate this API with this agent" into "run this server".**


I run a public MCP server at tools.scult.in that exposes the same free tools and prompt library the website offers, so an agent can call the schema generator or pull a stamped prompt with one line of configuration and no signup [12]. Building it taught me the practical value of the protocol: the client side is finished by other people, so a server is the whole product.


## How do I build an AI agent from scratch?

**Pick one task with a verifiable outcome, define one to three tools with tight descriptions and schemas, write the loop with a step limit and a budget, log every call, and run it on twenty real cases before adding anything. Only then decide whether it needs memory, more tools, a planner or a second agent. Most successful agents in production have fewer than five tools and a very clear stopping condition.**


The loop, in plain Python against a tool-calling API:

```python
def run_agent(goal: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 12) -> str:
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(max_steps):
        reply = llm(history, tools=[t.schema for t in tools.values()])
        if reply.tool_calls is None:
            return reply.text                      # final answer
        for call in reply.tool_calls:
            tool = tools[call.name]
            if tool.needs_confirmation and not confirm(call):
                return "Stopped: action needs approval"
            result = tool.run(**call.arguments)    # validated by the schema
            history.append(tool_result(call.id, result))
            log(step, call, result)
    return "Stopped: step limit reached"
```

Everything a framework gives you is a refinement of those lines. Write them once yourself; you will debug every framework faster afterwards.


### Which AI agent framework should I use?

**For a first agent, none: the loop above and your provider's SDK. When you need branching, retries, persistence and human-in-the-loop steps, LangGraph models the agent as a graph with explicit state and is the most widely used [9]. Provider SDKs from Anthropic and OpenAI now include agent loops and tool handling. For non-developers, n8n and similar automation tools wire models and APIs visually [11]. Choose by how much control you need over state and failure, not by popularity.**


## What are multi-agent systems?

**A multi-agent system splits a task across several agents with different tools or roles, a researcher, a writer, a reviewer, coordinated by a planner or a fixed handoff. It helps when the task decomposes cleanly and each part needs a different context, and it hurts when the coordination overhead, cost and failure surface outgrow the benefit. Start with one agent; move to several only when one agent's context or tool set becomes unmanageable.**


Anthropic's guide makes the same recommendation from a larger sample of deployments than I have: composable patterns first, prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, and autonomous agents only for open-ended problems where the model's judgement is needed at every step [5].

## Why do AI agents fail?

**Agents fail for predictable reasons: the goal was vague, so the model optimised the wrong thing; too many overlapping tools, so it picked badly; no stopping rule, so it looped; a tool returned an error the model could not interpret; the context filled with history and it forgot the goal; it took an irreversible action nobody confirmed; or a document it read contained instructions and it followed them. Almost all of these are design failures, fixed in the harness rather than the model.**



OWASP lists excessive agency and prompt injection among the top risks for LLM applications, and agents are where both bite hardest, because an injected instruction can now cause an action, not just a bad sentence [10].

## What is agent memory?

**Agent memory is whatever the agent can consult beyond the current context: the conversation so far, a scratchpad of notes it writes to itself, a vector store of past interactions or documents it can retrieve from, and structured facts in a database. Short-term memory is the context window; long-term memory is retrieval. Most agents need less memory than their builders assume and more discipline about what to forget.**


## Are AI agents worth learning, and what jobs use them?

**Yes. Agents are how language models get connected to real systems, and every AI engineering role I see in 2026 expects familiarity with tool calling, at least one orchestration pattern and the safety basics. Learn them by building one that does a job you actually have, connect it to a real API, and measure how often it finishes the task. That measured number, on a public repository, is worth more than any course certificate.**


I will not quote an "agentic AI engineer salary" because I have no measured source for one; job posts in India in 2026 mostly list it under AI engineer or GenAI engineer roles, and pay tracks those roles in the same city and company tier.



## What are common AI agent interview questions?

**Explain the agent loop and where the model's judgement is actually needed. Compare a workflow with an agent and say when you would choose each. Describe how tool calling works and how you write a tool description. Explain how you would stop an agent from taking a harmful action, and how you would measure whether it works. Describe a failure you debugged. If you have built even one agent with a real tool, you can answer all five.**



## Where can I try an agent for free?

**Point any MCP-capable client at the server at tools.scult.in and you have an agent with a working tool set in a minute, no signup [12].** Then build your own with one tool. If your college or hackathon wants a hands-on session on agents, tool calling and MCP, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
