# What is edge AI and on-device AI? Running models in the browser and on phones with ONNX Runtime, WebGPU and quantization, from building a browser-only face recognition system
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-edge-ai-and-on-device-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is edge AI?

**Edge AI is running machine learning inference on the device that has the data, a phone, a laptop, a browser tab, a camera, a sensor board, instead of sending the data to a server. The model is downloaded once and runs locally, so predictions arrive in milliseconds, work offline, cost nothing per call, and the raw input, a face, a voice, a document, never leaves the device. On-device AI, browser AI and TinyML are the same idea at different scales.**


I built FaceVision in 2026 as a browser-only face detection, recognition and liveness system: the camera frames are processed in the user's browser with ONNX Runtime Web, only a numeric embedding is sent to the server, and no image is ever stored [11]. That architecture is the concrete version of every argument on this page.

> The most effective privacy feature I have ever shipped was not encryption or a policy. It was never having the data in the first place.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FaceVision</cite>

## Why run AI on the device instead of the cloud?

**Four reasons, and each alone can justify it. Privacy: raw data stays with the user, which simplifies compliance and trust. Latency: no network round trip, so camera and audio features feel instant. Cost: no per-inference server bill, which matters when usage grows. Availability: it works offline and on bad connections, which in India is not an edge case. The trade-offs are model size, device variability and the work of exporting and testing.**



## What is ONNX, and what is ONNX Runtime?

**ONNX is an open file format for trained models that most frameworks can export to, so a model trained in PyTorch can run in a different runtime [1]. ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's inference engine for that format, with builds for servers, mobile and the web; ONNX Runtime Web runs models in the browser using WebAssembly on the CPU or WebGPU on the graphics card [2]. Together they are the most portable path from a training notebook to a device.**



My step-by-step guide to ONNX Runtime Web, with the preprocessing pitfalls, is on the portfolio [13].

## What is WebGPU, and does browser AI need it?

**WebGPU is the web standard that gives browser code access to the graphics card for general computation, not just rendering [3]. For AI in the browser it means models run several times faster than on WebAssembly alone, which turns real-time camera and audio models from a demo into a product. It does not replace WebAssembly: you ship both and fall back to the CPU path on browsers or devices without WebGPU support. Small models run acceptably on WebAssembly; larger ones need WebGPU.**


## What models can run on a device or in a browser?

**Comfortably: face detection and recognition, object detection with MobileNet-class or small YOLO models, image classification, OCR for clean text, speech recognition with small Whisper variants, text embeddings, and classifiers. Possibly: small language models of one to three billion parameters, quantized, on a laptop or a recent phone, with llama.cpp or a browser runtime. Not yet: large language models, high-resolution generative image models, or anything that needs tens of gigabytes.**



MobileNets set the pattern for models designed for devices [8]; Transformers.js brings Hugging Face models to the browser [4]; MediaPipe ships ready-made vision and audio pipelines for web and mobile [7].

## How do I make a model small enough for a device?

**Quantize to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, which cuts size and speeds inference on most hardware with a small accuracy loss [9]. Prune or distil into a smaller architecture when quantization is not enough. Fix input sizes and remove training-only operations at export. Then measure accuracy and latency on the actual target devices, because a model that passes in a notebook can fail on a low-end phone's memory or a browser's WebAssembly limits.**




## How does FaceVision keep faces on the device?

**The browser captures camera frames and runs three ONNX models locally: a face detector, a liveness check, and a recognition network that produces a 512-number embedding. Only that embedding is posted to a FastAPI backend, which stores it in PostgreSQL per user and compares it on verification. No image is transmitted or stored anywhere. If the server is breached, the attacker has vectors that cannot be turned back into faces. The design is on GitHub [11], and the reasoning about privacy is written up separately [12].**



## What are the platform options beyond the browser?

**On Android, LiteRT, formerly TensorFlow Lite, and ONNX Runtime Mobile [5][2]. On iOS, Core ML, with converters from PyTorch and ONNX [6]. On laptops and small servers, ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp for language models [10]. For ready-made vision and audio, MediaPipe on all of them [7]. The browser is the widest reach with the least installation; native platforms give more performance and background execution.**


## What are common edge AI use cases?

**Face and document capture for onboarding, attendance and KYC with privacy by design. Real-time translation and captions. Offline speech recognition for field workers and farmers. Quality inspection on factory cameras. Health and fitness sensing on wearables. Smart-camera detection without a cloud subscription. Browser tools that process a user's data without ever seeing it, which is how 13 of the 15 free tools at tools.scult.in work.**



## Edge AI interview questions

**Explain the trade-offs between on-device and cloud inference. Explain what ONNX and ONNX Runtime are for. Describe how you would take a PyTorch model to a browser and what could go wrong in preprocessing. Explain quantization's effect on size and accuracy. Design a privacy-preserving face verification system. Each answer is above, and a browser demo you built is the strongest evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Export a small image classifier to ONNX, load it with ONNX Runtime Web in a plain HTML page, and classify a webcam frame without a server. Then quantize it and measure the speed difference. That afternoon is the whole field in miniature.** For a hands-on session on privacy-first vision systems at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is face detection? How it works, landmarks, liveness, MTCNN and Python
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-face-detection/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Face detection is the computer vision task of finding where faces are in an image or video, usually returning a bounding box and confidence score for each face. It answers "is there a face, and where?", not "whose face is this?", which is face recognition. It is the first step for camera autofocus, filters, face recognition and liveness checks. I built browser-based detection, recognition and liveness in FaceVision, so this page covers how detection works, in AI and cameras, the main technologies including MTCNN, landmarks, liveness, mask detection and a Python example.

## What is face detection?

Face detection is identifying the presence and location of human faces in images or video frames. A detector outputs, for each face, a box, a confidence score and sometimes a few key points such as eye centres.

It is different from related tasks: face recognition identifies or verifies a person by comparing faces; landmark detection finds detailed points on the face; and attribute analysis estimates things like expression. Detection comes first in all of them. It must handle different sizes, angles, lighting, skin tones, occlusions such as glasses or hands, and many faces at once, which is why modern detectors are trained on large, diverse datasets.

## How does face detection work?

Modern face detection uses a neural network that scans an image at multiple scales and predicts, for many candidate regions, whether a face is present and the exact box around it. Overlapping predictions are merged with non-maximum suppression.

The network learns visual patterns of faces, from edges and textures to eyes and mouth arrangements, from thousands of labelled images. Lightweight architectures make it fast enough for phones and browsers. The output boxes are then used to crop faces for further steps. Quality depends on training data diversity: detectors trained on narrow datasets perform worse on under-represented groups, which is an important fairness consideration.

## What is face detection in AI?

In AI, face detection is a computer vision task solved with machine learning, specifically deep learning object detection models trained to find faces. It is one of the most widely deployed applications of AI, in phones, cameras, social apps and security systems.

It belongs to the broader field of object detection, with face-specific models designed for speed and accuracy on faces. In AI pipelines, detection is often followed by alignment, which rotates and crops faces using landmarks, and then embedding models for recognition, or classifiers for emotion and attributes. Because it involves personal data, responsible use includes consent, minimal data retention and clear purpose.

## What is face detection technology?

Face detection technology has evolved from hand-crafted methods to deep learning. The landmark early method, the Viola-Jones detector from 2001, used Haar-like features and a cascade of classifiers and made real-time detection possible on ordinary computers.

Since the 2010s, convolutional neural networks have replaced hand-crafted features, with detectors such as MTCNN, RetinaFace, BlazeFace and YOLO-based face models offering much better accuracy on difficult images. Today the technology runs on phone chips, in browsers with WebAssembly and WebGL, and on edge devices in cameras. Haar cascades are still used for simple, low-power tasks but fail on tilted faces and poor lighting.

## What is face detection in a camera?

In cameras, face detection finds faces in the live view so the camera can focus on them, set exposure for skin tones, track people as they move, and sometimes trigger the shutter on smiles. Security cameras use it to flag frames with people.

Phone cameras and many digital cameras run detection on dedicated image processors or neural engines, continuously and with very low delay. Modern cameras extend this to eye detection, keeping focus on the nearest eye for sharp portraits, and to body and animal detection. In CCTV systems, face detection can trigger recording or alerts, and some systems add recognition, which raises legal and privacy obligations depending on where it is used.

## What is MTCNN face detection?

MTCNN, the Multi-task Cascaded Convolutional Network, is a face detector introduced in 2016 that uses three small neural networks in sequence to propose face regions, refine them and output final boxes with five facial landmarks: eyes, nose and mouth corners.

Its cascade design was efficient for its time and its landmarks made face alignment easy, so it became a popular first stage for face recognition systems. It is still easy to use through Python packages, but newer detectors, such as RetinaFace or MediaPipe's BlazeFace, are generally faster or more accurate today. MTCNN remains a good teaching example of cascaded detection.

## What is face landmark detection?

Face landmark detection finds specific points on a face, such as eye corners, eyebrows, nose tip, lips and jawline. Simple models output five points; dense models output hundreds, enough to describe the face's 3D shape.

Landmarks are used to align faces before recognition, apply AR filters and makeup, track eye blinks and gaze, measure head pose, animate avatars from expressions, and support liveness checks. Google's MediaPipe Face Landmarker, for example, outputs 478 3D landmarks with expression scores. Accuracy drops with extreme angles, heavy occlusion and poor lighting, so test on conditions like your users'.

## What is face liveness detection?

Face liveness detection checks that a real, live person is in front of the camera, not a printed photo, a screen replay, a mask or a deepfake. It protects face-based login and identity verification from spoofing.

Methods include active checks, asking users to blink, turn their head or smile, and passive checks, which analyse texture, depth, reflections and subtle motion in a single image or short clip. Stronger systems combine several signals and, where available, depth sensors. FaceVision runs detection, recognition and liveness in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, and its server stores face embeddings only, never images, which reduces the damage if data leaks. Liveness is an arms race, so systems need regular testing against new attacks.

## What is face mask detection?

Face mask detection is a classification task that detects faces and then decides whether each person is wearing a mask, and sometimes whether it is worn correctly over nose and mouth. It became common in 2020 for public health compliance.

A typical pipeline detects faces with a face detector, crops each face, and runs a small image classifier trained on masked and unmasked faces. Challenges include masks hiding features that detectors rely on, varied mask types, and angles. It is a popular student project because it combines detection and classification, uses public datasets, and runs in real time on a laptop webcam.

## How do I make face detection in Python?

Use OpenCV or MediaPipe. OpenCV's deep learning face detector or MediaPipe's face detection find faces in a few lines; then draw boxes on the image or process each face further.

```python
# pip install mediapipe opencv-python  (download blaze_face_short_range.tflite from the MediaPipe guide)
import cv2, mediapipe as mp
from mediapipe.tasks.python import vision, BaseOptions

det = vision.FaceDetector.create_from_options(
    vision.FaceDetectorOptions(base_options=BaseOptions(model_asset_path="blaze_face_short_range.tflite")))
img = cv2.imread("group.jpg")
res = det.detect(mp.Image(image_format=mp.ImageFormat.SRGB, data=cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)))
for d in res.detections:
    b = d.bounding_box
    cv2.rectangle(img, (b.origin_x, b.origin_y), (b.origin_x + b.width, b.origin_y + b.height), (0, 255, 0), 2)
cv2.imwrite("faces.jpg", img)
```

Get consent before processing people's images, and avoid storing faces you do not need.

# What is function calling (tool use) in LLMs? How models call your code, structured outputs, and building a reliable tool-using agent
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-function-calling-and-tool-use-in-llms/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is function calling in an LLM?

**Function calling, also called tool use, is a mechanism where you describe a set of functions to a model, name, description, and a JSON schema of its arguments, and the model, instead of only returning prose, can return a structured request to call one of those functions with specific argument values. Your application code receives that request, validates it, actually runs the function, and optionally feeds the result back to the model to continue. The model never executes code itself; it only ever proposes what to call and with what [1][2].**


Every agentic system I have built, and every document-extraction pipeline, depends on this mechanism in one of its two disguises: as a way to let a model act, or as a way to force a model's output into a shape your code can trust.

> A model that calls a function has not done anything yet. It has asked you to do something, in a format your code can check before it runs.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Is tool calling the same thing as function calling?

**Yes, in current usage they are the same mechanism under two names: OpenAI and Google call it function calling [1][3], Anthropic calls the equivalent capability tool use [2], and both describe the same shape, a schema-described capability the model can request to invoke. Some documentation reserves "tool" for a slightly broader idea that includes non-function capabilities such as web search or code execution provided by the platform itself, with "function calling" specifically meaning your own custom functions, but in practice the terms are used interchangeably almost everywhere.**


## How does function calling actually work, step by step?

**You send the model a prompt plus a list of function definitions, each with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters. The model, based on the conversation, decides whether calling one of those functions would help, and if so, returns a structured object naming the function and its argument values instead of, or alongside, ordinary text. Your code parses that object, validates the arguments against your own rules, executes the real function, and sends the result back to the model as a new message so it can continue the conversation or produce a final answer.**



## What is structured output, and how does it relate to function calling?

**Structured output is function calling used for a single purpose: forcing the model's response into a schema you define, rather than letting it call an arbitrary tool. You define one "function" that represents the shape of the answer you want, a set of extracted fields, a classification, a form, and the model is constrained to fill it in rather than write free text [8]. This is the same JSON-Schema-and-validation mechanism as tool use; it is simply used to make model output reliably parseable rather than to trigger an action.**




## How does multi-step tool use turn a chatbot into an agent?

**A single function call answers one question. An agent repeats the loop: call a tool, read the result, decide whether the goal is met or another tool call is needed, and continue until it is, or until a step limit is hit. This pattern, reason then act then observe, was formalised as ReAct [5] and is what separates a simple assistant from something that can, say, search documentation, run a calculation, and check its own answer before replying. The Model Context Protocol standardises how tools are described and connected across different agent implementations [6].**


My longer explanation of agent architectures generally is on the AI agent page [9], and how tool descriptions get standardised across systems is on the MCP page [10].

## How do I make function calling reliable in production?

**Validate every proposed function call against a strict schema and your own business rules before running anything; never assume the model's arguments are safe just because they parsed. Set timeouts and retries around the actual function execution, not just the model call. Give the model a clear error message back when a call fails or arguments are invalid, so it can retry sensibly rather than looping blindly. Log every call, its arguments, and its result, so a bad outcome can be traced to exactly what was requested and what ran. Never let a model-proposed call touch anything destructive, a delete, a payment, a send, without an explicit confirmation boundary outside the model's control.**



My notes on project structure put the provider, the tool definitions, and the execution layer in separate modules for exactly this reason: validation and logging belong at the boundary, not scattered through the code [11].

## What goes wrong with function calling in practice?

**The model hallucinates a plausible-looking call with arguments that do not correspond to anything real, an order ID that does not exist, a date outside range; this is caught only by validation, never by the model itself. A tool description is ambiguous, and the model picks the wrong function among several similar ones. A multi-step loop runs without a step limit and burns cost on an unproductive path. Errors from a failed call are not surfaced back to the model in a useful form, so it repeats the same failing call. Every one of these is a process failure, not a fundamental limitation, and every one has a known fix.**



## Function calling interview questions

**Explain what happens, step by step, when a model calls a function. Explain the difference between the model proposing a call and your code executing it. Describe how you would validate a proposed function call before running it. Explain how structured outputs reuse the same mechanism as tool use. Describe how a multi-step agent loop terminates. The strongest answer names a specific validation rule you added after something went wrong.**



## Where should I start?

**Define one simple function, a calculator or a lookup against a small local list, give it to a model with a strict schema, and make it call the function for a question that needs it. Log the full call and result. That one afternoon teaches the whole mechanism.** For a hands-on session on building reliable tool-using agents, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is function calling in AI? How it works in OpenAI, Gemini and Mistral
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-function-calling/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Function calling, also called tool use, lets a language model ask your application to run a function: instead of only replying with text, the model returns a structured request such as `get_order_status(order_id="4521")` with arguments in JSON, your code runs the function, and the result goes back to the model to finish its answer. It is how chatbots check orders, book slots, query databases and act as agents. This page explains what it is, how it works, OpenAI's version and its history, which models support it including Gemini and Mistral, how it relates to RAG, and how to test it.

## What is function calling?

Function calling is a feature of LLM APIs where you describe functions your application can perform, and the model can choose to call one by returning its name and arguments in a structured format, rather than answering in free text.

The model never runs code itself. It decides that a function would help, produces the call with arguments that match your schema, and your application executes it, then sends back the result. This turns a model into an interface to real systems: databases, APIs, calculators, search and internal tools. It is the foundation of AI agents, which call functions repeatedly in a loop to complete multi-step tasks.

## What is function calling in AI?

In AI, function calling is the mechanism that connects language models to external capabilities, letting them retrieve live data, perform calculations precisely and take actions, which models cannot do from their training alone.

For example, a college assistant can answer "Is lab 3 free at 2 pm?" only if it can call a `check_room(room, time)` function that queries the booking system. Without function calling, it would guess. With it, the answer is accurate and current. It also helps with structured extraction: asking the model to "call" a function whose arguments are the fields you want is a reliable way to get structured data.

## How does function calling work in an LLM?

You send the model the user's message plus a list of function definitions. The model either replies normally or returns a function call with arguments. Your code runs the function, adds the result to the conversation, and calls the model again so it can respond using the result.

A function definition looks like this:

```json
{"name": "check_room", "description": "Check if a campus room is free at a given time",
 "parameters": {"type": "object",
   "properties": {"room": {"type": "string"}, "time": {"type": "string", "description": "24h time, e.g. 14:00"}},
   "required": ["room", "time"]}}
```

Good names and descriptions matter most: the model chooses functions by reading them. Validate arguments before executing, and never let a model call destructive functions without checks.

## What is function calling in OpenAI?

In OpenAI's API, function calling lets you pass tool definitions with JSON schemas, and the model responds with tool calls containing the function name and JSON arguments. You execute them and return outputs; a strict mode makes arguments conform exactly to your schema.

OpenAI's models can call several functions in one turn and choose between your functions and built-in tools such as web search or file search, depending on the API. Use strict schemas for reliability, keep the number of functions manageable, and write descriptions that say when to use each one. The official function calling guide shows the request and response format for the current API.

## When was function calling introduced?

OpenAI introduced function calling in its API in June 2023, which made tool use mainstream for developers. Other providers, including Anthropic, Google and Mistral, added their own tool use or function calling features soon after.

Earlier, developers used prompt tricks, asking the model to output JSON and parsing it, which was fragile. Native function calling made outputs reliable and models better at choosing tools, which led directly to the growth of AI agents. Research such as ReAct and Toolformer had already explored models using tools. Today, standards such as the Model Context Protocol build on function calling to connect models with many tools consistently.

## Which LLMs support function calling?

Most current major models support it: OpenAI's GPT models, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, Mistral's models, and many open-weight models such as Llama, Qwen and others, often through serving tools like Ollama and vLLM.

Quality varies. Frontier hosted models are generally most reliable at choosing the right function and producing valid arguments, especially with many tools. Smaller open models work well for a few simple functions but make more mistakes as tasks get complex. Benchmarks such as the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard compare models; still, test with your own functions, because results depend heavily on your schemas and descriptions.

## Does Gemini support function calling?

Yes. The Gemini API supports function calling: you declare functions with names, descriptions and parameter schemas, and Gemini returns function calls for your code to execute, including parallel calls and modes that control whether calling is automatic, required or disabled.

Gemini also offers built-in tools, such as grounding with Google Search and code execution, alongside your custom functions. The Python SDK can automatically call Python functions you pass in, which is convenient for prototypes. For production, handle calls explicitly so you can validate arguments, log actions and require confirmation for anything risky.

## Does Mistral support function calling?

Yes. Mistral's API supports function calling with tool definitions in JSON schema form, and several of Mistral's models, including open-weight ones, are trained for tool use.

The workflow is similar to other providers: define tools, send them with the messages, handle tool calls in the response, return results, and let the model produce the final answer. Because Mistral offers both hosted and open models, you can prototype with the API and later self-host an open model with tool support. Check Mistral's documentation for which current models support function calling and any limits.

## Is function calling RAG?

No, but they work well together. RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt. Function calling lets the model request actions or data from your code. Retrieval is often exposed to the model as a function, such as `search_documents(query)`.

When retrieval is a function, the model decides when to search and what to search for, which is useful in agents and multi-turn conversations. Fixed RAG pipelines, which always retrieve before answering, are simpler and more predictable for document Q&A. RAG.NextUpgrad uses a fixed pipeline with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, because predictable retrieval made answers easier to test and trust.

## How do you test function calling?

Build a test set of user requests with the expected function, arguments and behaviour, then check that the model picks the right function, fills arguments correctly, asks for missing information, and does not call functions when none fit.

What to test:

- **Selection**: correct function chosen among similar ones.
- **Arguments**: valid types and values, correct formats such as dates.
- **Missing information**: the model asks instead of inventing.
- **No-call cases**: small talk or out-of-scope requests do not trigger calls.
- **Multi-step**: correct sequence of calls for complex tasks.
- **Safety**: prompt injection in tool results does not trigger unwanted actions.

Run tests after every change to prompts, functions or models, and log real usage to find new failure cases.

# What is generative AI, and where can you actually learn it for free? A clear definition and a vetted list of free courses and certificates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-generative-ai-and-where-to-learn-it-free/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is generative AI?

**Generative AI is the category of AI systems trained to create new content, text, images, audio, video, code, rather than only classify, predict a number, or recommend from a fixed set of options. A generative model learns the statistical shape of its training data well enough to produce plausible new examples of it: a language model generates the next word, a diffusion model generates pixels, a codec model generates audio. Classic machine learning mostly answers "which category" or "what number"; generative AI answers "produce a new thing like this."**


Every system I have built professionally sits inside this category somewhere: a RAG platform that generates answers, a fine-tuning studio that trains generative language models, a document extractor that generates structured fields from images. This page is the plain definition, and underneath it, the free courses that are actually worth the hours, filtered from the ones that are mostly a certificate PDF.

> Generative AI is not a separate technology from machine learning. It is machine learning pointed at "produce a new artefact" instead of "predict a label."
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How is generative AI different from classic machine learning?

**Classic machine learning, and classic AI more broadly, is mostly discriminative: given an input, predict a category, a score, or a ranking, spam or not spam, this customer will churn, this image contains a cat. Generative AI is trained to model the full distribution of the data well enough to sample new examples from it. The training objective and the mathematics overlap heavily, the same neural network architectures show up on both sides, but the task the model is optimised for is different, and that difference is what makes an LLM able to write an essay while a classic classifier can only ever pick from options you gave it.**



## Is an LLM the same as generative AI?

**An LLM, a large language model, is one specific kind of generative model: one trained to generate text (and, in multimodal versions, respond to images too) [10]. Generative AI is the broader category that also includes image generators such as diffusion models, audio and speech generators, video generators, and code generators. Every LLM is a generative AI system; not every generative AI system is an LLM. When people say "generative AI" and mean ChatGPT specifically, they usually mean the LLM case, but the term covers much more.**


## Where is generative AI actually used?

**Writing and editing assistance, code generation and completion, customer support and internal knowledge assistants built with RAG, image and video generation for marketing and design, voice cloning and text-to-speech, data augmentation for training other models, drug and material discovery through generated molecular structures, and increasingly agentic systems that use generation as one step inside a larger workflow. The common thread is a task where "produce a plausible new thing" is more valuable than "pick from a fixed menu."**




## Which free courses on generative AI are actually worth it?

**Very few. The market is full of half-hour "courses" that end in a shareable certificate and teach almost nothing, and a handful of providers that genuinely teach the material for free. Google's Introduction to Generative AI is a solid, short, accurate primer [2]. Microsoft's Generative AI for Beginners is a free multi-lesson curriculum with real code [3]. DeepLearning.AI's short courses are consistently well made and free, though the certificates from some of their paid specializations are not [4][5]. Hugging Face's NLP and Agents courses are free, technical, and hands-on [6][7]. Anthropic Academy teaches building with Claude specifically [8]. fast.ai remains one of the best free deep learning courses that exist, code-first [9].**



## What should I actually do with these courses?

**Pick one short course for vocabulary, one hands-on course that has you write code, and stop collecting courses after that. The certificate is not the goal. Within a week of finishing, build something small using what you learned, a script, a tiny app, a notebook, and measure whether it works. Post it. That sequence, one primer, one hands-on course, one shipped thing, teaches more than ten certificates with nothing behind them, and it is what a resume or an interviewer can actually verify.**



## What mistakes do people make chasing generative AI courses?

**Collecting certificates from courses that are mostly marketing for a paid upsell. Treating a certificate as equivalent to a shipped project on a resume, when interviewers weight them very differently. Starting with the most advanced course available instead of the one that matches where you actually are. Never building anything between courses, so the vocabulary never turns into a skill. Ignoring that the field moves fast enough that a two-year-old course on a specific tool may already be stale, even if the fundamentals it teaches are not.**



## Generative AI interview questions

**Define generative AI and contrast it with discriminative machine learning. Explain where an LLM sits inside the broader category. Give three applications beyond chatbots. Explain, honestly, what you built after your last course and what it measured. The question behind the question is always the same: did the course change what you can do, or only what your certificate says.**



## Where should I start?

**Take Google's short primer this week, then Microsoft's Generative AI for Beginners for the code, then build one small thing with what you learned and share it.** For a hands-on session that takes students from definition to a shipped generative AI project in one workshop, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What does GGUF stand for? GGUF models, quant levels, safety, LM Studio and GGUF vs MLX
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-gguf-vs-mlx/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


GGUF is a single-file format for storing language models, especially quantized ones, so they run efficiently on CPUs, laptops and consumer GPUs through llama.cpp and apps built on it, such as Ollama and LM Studio. I fine-tune models with QLoRA in FineTune Studio and run models locally, so this page explains what GGUF stands for, GGUF and quantized models, quant types, picking a level for your VRAM, safety and malware, LM Studio, and GGUF versus Apple's MLX.

## What does GGUF stand for?

GGUF is commonly expanded as GPT-Generated Unified Format. The GG is widely credited to Georgi Gerganov, who created the ggml library and llama.cpp. GGUF replaced the older GGML file format in August 2023.

In AI, GGUF names a binary file format, usually with a `.gguf` extension, that stores a model's weights and everything needed to run it: architecture details, tokenizer, special tokens and often a chat template, in one file. Its design goals were extensibility, so new model types and metadata can be added without breaking old files, fast memory-mapped loading, and support for many quantization schemes. Today it is the standard format for local LLM inference.

## What are GGUF models?

GGUF models are language models converted into the GGUF format for local inference, usually from Hugging Face checkpoints. They run with llama.cpp and tools built on it, including Ollama, LM Studio, GPT4All, KoboldCpp and llama-cpp-python.

Hugging Face hosts thousands of GGUF versions of popular open models, such as Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma and Phi, often published by the model makers or community quantizers. You download one file matching your hardware and run it without Python dependencies or large frameworks. GGUF models work on Windows, Mac and Linux, on CPUs alone or with partial or full GPU offload, which makes them the easiest way to run capable models on ordinary computers.

## What are GGUF quantized models?

Quantized GGUF models store weights at lower precision, such as 4, 5 or 8 bits instead of 16, shrinking file size and memory use by two to four times with modest quality loss. Most GGUF downloads are quantized.

llama.cpp's k-quants group weights into blocks with shared scales, and some layers can keep higher precision than others. Importance matrices, computed from calibration text, help quantization preserve the weights that matter most, especially at very low bit widths. The result is that an 8-billion-parameter model, about 16 GB at 16-bit precision, fits in about 5 GB at a 4-bit quant and runs on a laptop. Quantization trades some accuracy for this efficiency, so test quality on your tasks.

## What is the difference between GGUF quant types?

GGUF files of the same model differ mainly by quant type, shown in the filename: Q8_0 is nearly lossless, Q6_K and Q5_K_M are high quality, Q4_K_M is the popular balance of size and quality, and Q3 and Q2 levels save memory with noticeable degradation.

The K means k-quant block quantization; S, M and L suffixes indicate small, medium and large variants that keep different layers at higher precision. IQ types, such as IQ4_XS or IQ2_M, use importance-matrix techniques to perform better at very low bit rates. Files also differ by base model, instruction tuning, context length and who converted them, so prefer reputable uploaders whose model cards explain the conversion and quantization method.

## How do you pick a GGUF quant level for your VRAM?

Estimate file size as parameters times bits per weight divided by eight, then add room for the KV cache, which grows with context length. Choose the highest-quality quant whose file fits in VRAM with one to two gigabytes to spare.

Rough guide: a 7 to 8 billion parameter model at Q4_K_M needs about 5 GB, so 8 GB of VRAM runs it with moderate context; 12 GB allows Q6_K or Q8_0; 24 GB fits larger 14 to 32 billion parameter models at 4 to 5 bits. If a model does not fit, offload only some layers to the GPU with llama.cpp's `--n-gpu-layers`, accepting slower speed. A bigger model at Q4 often beats a smaller model at Q8.

## Are GGUF files safe?

GGUF is safer than pickle-based formats because loading it reads data rather than executing code. Still, risk exists: bugs in GGUF parsers have allowed crafted files to trigger memory corruption, and chat templates in metadata have been abused in vulnerable tools.

In 2024, security researchers reported memory-safety vulnerabilities in GGUF parsing code and a template injection issue in llama-cpp-python, both fixed in updated versions. To stay safe: download from trusted, well-known publishers; keep llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio and libraries updated; check file hashes when provided; and run unfamiliar models in a sandbox or container. Also remember that a safe file format does not guarantee safe behaviour, since a model can be fine-tuned to produce harmful outputs.

## Can GGUF files contain malware?

A GGUF file is not an executable, so it cannot run code by itself. However, a maliciously crafted file can target vulnerabilities in outdated software that reads it, and its embedded metadata, such as templates, can carry injection attempts.

The practical risk is low with updated software and reputable sources, but it is not zero. Treat model files like any downloaded file: prefer official or well-known community uploaders on Hugging Face, which scans repositories for some threats, avoid random links, and update your inference tools regularly. For sensitive environments, run local models in isolated containers without network access or access to secrets, so even a successful exploit cannot reach important data.

## How do you open a GGUF file in LM Studio?

The easiest way is to search for the model in LM Studio's Discover tab and download a GGUF version. For a file you already have, import it with the `lms import` command or place it in LM Studio's models folder in a publisher and model subfolder structure.

After importing, the model appears in My Models; select it in the chat view or load it in the developer tab to serve an OpenAI-compatible local API. When loading, adjust GPU offload, context length and other settings to fit your hardware. If LM Studio does not recognise the file, update the app, since new architectures need newer llama.cpp versions, and check that the download completed by comparing file size or hash.

## GGUF vs MLX: which is better on a Mac?

GGUF is a cross-platform model format used by llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio. MLX is Apple's machine learning framework for Apple silicon, with its own model format and quantization. On Macs, both run well; MLX is often faster for generation.

MLX is designed around Apple's unified memory and Metal, and mlx-lm supports running and fine-tuning models natively, so it often achieves higher tokens per second on M-series chips. GGUF offers more quantization choices, broader tool support and portability across Windows, Linux and Mac. LM Studio supports both engines on Mac, which makes comparison easy. Benchmark the same model at a similar bit width on your machine, measuring speed and output quality, before choosing.

## Why do MLX quantized models sometimes underperform Unsloth GGUF quants?

At the same nominal bit width, quantization method matters. Unsloth's dynamic GGUF quants keep sensitive layers at higher precision and use calibration data, while basic MLX quantization applies uniform low-bit quantization to most layers, which can lose more quality.

So a 4-bit MLX model and a 4-bit Unsloth GGUF are not equivalent: the GGUF may spend more bits per weight in important places and preserve accuracy better on hard tasks. MLX has added improved methods, such as distillation-based quantization, which narrow the gap. Compare like for like by checking average bits per weight and evaluating on your own prompts, since benchmark differences depend heavily on the model and task.

# What is GPT in ChatGPT? What it stands for, actions, and embeddings
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-gpt-in-chatgpt/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


GPT in ChatGPT is the large language model underneath the chat app. GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer: a neural network that generates text, was first pre-trained on a huge amount of text, and uses the transformer architecture. ChatGPT is the product built around those models, adding a chat interface, memory, tools such as search and code execution, and safety systems. This page explains each word in GPT, which GPT powers Copilot, what GPT actions are, whether GPT-2 embeddings work for classification, how GPT uses water, and what GPT can do with video.

## What is GPT in ChatGPT?

GPT is the family of large language models made by OpenAI, and ChatGPT is the chat application that runs on them. When you type a message, ChatGPT sends it, with your conversation and instructions, to a GPT model, which generates the reply.

The distinction matters when you build things. ChatGPT has features the bare model does not: conversation history, memory across chats, web search, file uploads, image generation and a code tool. Developers who use the OpenAI API get the model and must add those pieces themselves. ChatGPT also chooses which model handles a request in some modes, routing simple questions to fast models and hard ones to reasoning models. So "ChatGPT said X" really means a GPT model, plus ChatGPT's tools and settings, produced X.

## What does GPT stand for?

GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. OpenAI introduced the name with its first GPT model in 2018, and every later generation, from GPT-2 and GPT-3 to the current models, keeps it.

The 2018 paper showed that a transformer pre-trained on a large body of unlabelled text, then fine-tuned for specific tasks, beat models designed for each task separately. GPT-2 in 2019 showed that a larger model could do many tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. GPT-3 in 2020 scaled this further and made prompting, simply describing the task in text, a practical way to use a model. ChatGPT, launched in late 2022, added instruction tuning and human feedback so the model follows requests conversationally.

## What does GPT stand for in the context of AI?

Each word describes a design choice. Generative: the model produces new text one token at a time. Pre-trained: it first learns general language patterns from a massive dataset before any specific use. Transformer: the neural network architecture it is built on.

In more detail:

- **Generative**: it predicts the next token given everything before it, and repeating that prediction produces sentences, code and answers.
- **Pre-trained**: the expensive learning happens once, on a large corpus; later steps such as instruction tuning and fine-tuning adapt it cheaply.
- **Transformer**: an architecture from 2017 built on attention, which lets every token weigh every earlier token, so the model can use context across long passages.

GPT models are decoder-only transformers: each token attends only to earlier tokens, which suits generation.

## Which GPT does Copilot use?

Microsoft Copilot runs mainly on OpenAI's GPT models, and Microsoft has moved it to newer GPT generations as they launch, including the GPT-5 family. It chooses the model for each request automatically and also uses Microsoft's own models for some features.

Microsoft 365 Copilot similarly uses GPT models hosted in Microsoft's cloud, and Microsoft has added models from other providers in some features. GitHub Copilot is different: it has a model picker with options from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and new models are announced on GitHub's changelog. Microsoft rarely promises a fixed model for a feature, because it updates the service continuously. For most users the model name matters less than the grounding: whether Copilot is answering from the web, your files or your code.

## What are GPT actions?

GPT actions let a custom GPT in ChatGPT call an external API. You describe the API with an OpenAPI schema, and the GPT decides when to call it, fills in the parameters from the conversation, and uses the response in its answer.

For example, a college events GPT could have an action `get_events(date)` that calls your events API, so a student can ask "what is happening on campus on Friday?" and get live data instead of a guess. Actions support authentication with an API key or OAuth, so a GPT can act for a signed-in user. They are the no-code end of tool use. For richer apps with their own interface inside ChatGPT, OpenAI's newer Apps SDK, built on the Model Context Protocol, is the more capable route.

## How do GPT actions work?

When you build a custom GPT, you paste an OpenAPI schema describing your endpoints, set authentication, and write instructions about when to use them. During a chat, the model decides to call an endpoint, ChatGPT makes the HTTP request, and the model reads the JSON response.

Steps to build one:

- Create a GPT in the GPT editor and write clear instructions.
- Under Actions, add your OpenAPI schema with clear `operationId`s and descriptions for each endpoint.
- Configure authentication: none, API key or OAuth.
- Add a privacy policy URL if you plan to share it.
- Test in the preview pane and inspect each call and response.

Most failures come from vague endpoint descriptions; the model chooses tools from the text you write, so describe each one as you would to a new teammate.

## Can we use GPT-2 sentence embeddings for classification tasks?

Yes. You can take GPT-2's hidden states, pool them into one vector per sentence, and train a simple classifier such as logistic regression on top. It works, but sentence-embedding models trained for this purpose usually give better results.

GPT-2 is a decoder-only model, so each token only sees the tokens before it. Mean pooling over all tokens or using the last token's state are the usual choices:

```python
from transformers import GPT2Tokenizer, GPT2Model
import torch

tok = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2"); tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
model = GPT2Model.from_pretrained("gpt2")
batch = tok(["great product", "terrible support"], return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    h = model(**batch).last_hidden_state
mask = batch["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1)
emb = (h * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1)   # one 768-d vector per sentence
```

Compare against a Sentence-BERT style model on the same data before choosing.

## How does GPT use water?

GPT models do not use water directly; the data centres that train and run them do, mainly for cooling servers and indirectly through the water used to generate their electricity. The amount depends heavily on location, season and cooling technology.

A 2023 study from researchers at the University of California estimated that training GPT-3 in Microsoft's US data centres directly evaporated hundreds of thousands of litres of fresh water, and that running models adds more over time. Such figures are estimates with wide ranges, because companies do not publish per-model water use. Data centres in hot, dry regions use more water for evaporative cooling; others use air cooling or recycled water and use more electricity instead. Major cloud providers publish annual sustainability reports with their overall water use.

## Can GPT watch videos?

Not in the way people do. GPT models in ChatGPT can analyse images, so they can examine frames taken from a video, and transcripts from its audio, but they do not reliably watch a full-length video from start to finish.

The practical approach is to extract a transcript with a speech-to-text tool and a set of key frames, for example one every few seconds or at scene changes, and give those to the model with a precise question. In ChatGPT's mobile app, voice mode can use the live camera, which helps for quick questions about what is in front of you. Some other models, such as Google's Gemini, accept video files directly through their API and are a better fit when you need to analyse long footage.

## Can GPT make videos?

GPT models themselves generate text and, in ChatGPT, images. Video generation comes from a separate OpenAI model, Sora, available through its own app and website for eligible users.

You can still use GPT for most of video production: scripts, storyboards, shot lists, captions, titles and thumbnail ideas. With its code tool, ChatGPT can sometimes assemble a simple slideshow video from images by writing Python, but that is a workaround. For generated footage, write a detailed prompt in Sora describing the subject, setting, camera movement and style, generate several takes, and edit the best clips in a normal video editor. Label AI-generated footage when you publish it.

# What is handwriting recognition? How it works, OneNote, Goodnotes, Notability, and HMMs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-handwriting-recognition/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Handwriting recognition is the technology that converts handwritten text into machine-readable text, either from pen strokes as you write on a tablet, called online recognition, or from photos and scans of handwritten pages, called offline recognition. Note apps use it to make handwriting searchable and convertible, and businesses use it to digitise forms. I work with OCR and document AI in the OCR and Speech Workspace and DocuLens AI, so this page covers how it works, AI, software, OneNote, Goodnotes, Notability, HMMs, and building your own.

## What is handwriting recognition?

Handwriting recognition, also called handwritten text recognition, is the automatic conversion of handwriting into digital text. It powers searchable notes, form digitisation, postal address reading, cheque processing, and historical archive transcription.

Two settings differ greatly. Online recognition uses the sequence, timing and pressure of pen strokes on a tablet or phone, which gives rich information and high accuracy. Offline recognition only sees a static image of finished writing, as in a scanned exam paper, which is harder because stroke order is lost and image quality varies. Printed-text OCR is easier still, because characters are uniform. In India, handwriting recognition also has to cope with many scripts, such as Devanagari, and with notes that mix Hindi and English on the same line.

## Is handwriting recognition AI?

Yes. Modern handwriting recognition uses machine learning, mostly deep neural networks trained on large collections of handwriting samples. Older systems used hand-designed features and statistical models such as hidden Markov models, which are also forms of AI.

Today's best systems use CNN and recurrent networks with connectionist temporal classification, or transformer models that read whole lines, and vision language models can read handwriting in context. These learn to handle the huge variety of handwriting styles. Accuracy still varies with writing neatness, language, script and image quality, so critical documents benefit from human review.

## How does handwriting recognition work?

The system first finds where the writing is, splits pages into lines or words, normalises them for slant and size, then a neural network converts each line image or stroke sequence into a probability over characters, decoded into text, often with a language model to pick likely words.

For online ink, the input is a sequence of pen coordinates over time, which recurrent or transformer models process directly. For offline images, convolutional layers extract visual features first. CTC training lets models learn without marking where each character starts. Language models correct ambiguous characters, for example choosing "clear" over "cIear". Post-processing restores layout and punctuation.

## What makes automatic handwriting recognition work, and what makes it hard?

It works because neural networks learn patterns from many writers' samples, generalising to new handwriting, and because context from language models resolves ambiguous letters. It is hard because handwriting varies enormously between people, letters connect in cursive, and scans add noise.

Specific challenges: segmentation of connected letters, inconsistent spacing, slanted and overlapping lines, crossings-out, mixed scripts such as Hindi and English together, rare words and names, and poor image quality. Systems improve with more varied training data, line-level rather than character-level recognition, and domain-specific vocabularies, such as medical terms. Doctors' handwriting remains a famously hard case.

## What is the best handwriting recognition software?

For notes, Microsoft OneNote, Goodnotes, Notability, Apple Notes with Apple Pencil, Samsung Notes and Nebo have strong built-in recognition. For documents and images, Google Lens, Microsoft's and Google's cloud vision services, and vision language models handle handwriting well.

Choose by task: for converting your own tablet notes, the note app's built-in recognition is easiest; for digitising scanned forms at scale, cloud document AI services with handwriting support; for developers, Apple's Vision framework, Google ML Kit's digital ink recognition, or open models such as TrOCR. Test with samples of the actual handwriting you need to read. Measure accuracy on twenty or thirty real pages before choosing, since vendor demos usually show neat writing.

## Does OneNote have handwriting recognition?

Yes. OneNote recognises handwriting so it can be searched, and its Ink to Text feature converts handwritten notes into typed text. Ink to Math converts handwritten equations into typed mathematical notation and can help solve them.

To convert, use the Draw tab's Ink to Text option after selecting your handwriting, or use the lasso selection tool and choose the conversion. Accuracy depends on neatness and language settings, so set the proofing language correctly for your notes. Search for words in handwritten notes works in many versions, making OneNote useful for students who write by hand on tablets.

## What is handwriting recognition in Goodnotes?

In Goodnotes, handwriting recognition makes your handwritten notes searchable and lets you convert selected handwriting into typed text using the lasso tool. Recognition happens in the background for supported languages.

Set your handwriting recognition language in Goodnotes settings for best results. To convert, select handwriting with the lasso tool, tap the selection, and choose the convert option, then copy or insert the text. Search finds words in your handwriting across notebooks. Recognition quality improves with clear, consistent writing and correct language settings.

## What is handwriting recognition in Notability?

Notability recognises handwriting so you can search your notes and convert handwriting to typed text. Handwritten words are indexed for search, and you can select writing and convert it to text to copy into other apps or documents.

Like other note apps, Notability works best with clear writing and the correct language set. Students often combine handwritten lecture notes with typed text, audio recordings and search. If conversion struggles with technical terms or mixed languages, correct the text manually after converting, or keep the handwriting and rely on search instead.

## How can HMMs be used for handwriting recognition?

Hidden Markov models were the leading approach before deep learning. Each character is modelled as a sequence of hidden states emitting observed features from small slices of the image or pen trajectory, and words are recognised by finding the most likely sequence of character models with the Viterbi algorithm.

HMMs handle variable-length writing naturally and allow segmentation-free recognition of cursive text. Combined with language models, they powered many systems in the 1990s and 2000s. Their limitation is reliance on hand-crafted features and simplifying assumptions. Modern recognisers replaced them with neural networks trained with CTC, which learn features directly and achieve far lower error rates.

## How do I make handwriting recognition software?

Start from a pretrained model and fine-tune it on your handwriting style rather than training from scratch. Collect line images with accurate transcriptions, fine-tune a model such as TrOCR or a CRNN, and evaluate with character error rate on held-out samples.

Steps:

- Gather samples, including public datasets like IAM for English.
- Segment pages into lines and label them carefully.
- Fine-tune a pretrained recogniser with augmentation for slant and noise.
- Add a language model or vocabulary constraints for your domain.
- Evaluate character and word error rates.
- Deploy with on-device options such as Apple's Vision framework or Google ML Kit for ink.

Always plan human review for important documents.

# What is hybrid search? How it works, and support in FAISS, Qdrant, Chroma, pgvector
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-hybrid-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Hybrid search combines two kinds of retrieval: keyword search, usually BM25, which matches exact words, and vector search, which matches meaning through embeddings. Running both and merging the results gives better retrieval than either alone, which is why it is standard in serious RAG systems; RAG.NextUpgrad uses dense plus BM25 retrieval merged with reciprocal-rank fusion before re-ranking. This page explains how hybrid search works, why it helps, BM25's role, support in FAISS, Qdrant, Chroma, pgvector and Pinecone, and the unrelated meaning of hybrid in job search.

## What is hybrid search?

Hybrid search is a retrieval approach that runs a keyword search and a semantic vector search for the same query and combines their results into one ranked list.

Each method catches what the other misses. Keyword search finds exact terms such as product codes, error messages, names and acronyms, but misses paraphrases. Vector search understands meaning and paraphrases, but often blurs specific identifiers and rare terms. Combining them gives robust retrieval across question styles, which matters in real systems where users mix natural questions with exact codes, such as "why does ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR appear on login?".

## How does hybrid search work?

The query goes to a keyword index and a vector index in parallel; each returns its top candidates; a fusion method merges the two lists; optionally a reranker reorders the merged candidates; the top results are returned or passed to an LLM.

Reciprocal-rank fusion is the most common merge: each document's fused score is the sum over lists of 1 divided by a constant plus its rank, so documents ranked well in either list rise to the top. It needs no score calibration, since BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on different scales. Weighted score fusion is an alternative, but requires normalising scores and tuning weights. Retrieve generously from each list, such as the top 20 to 50, before fusing.

## Why use hybrid search?

Because real queries need both exact matching and semantic understanding, and hybrid search consistently improves recall over either method alone, especially on technical, product and enterprise content full of codes and names.

Benefits:

- **Fewer misses**: exact identifiers found by keywords, paraphrases by vectors.
- **Robustness**: works across short keyword queries and long natural questions.
- **Better RAG answers**: the right passage reaches the prompt more often.
- **Low cost**: BM25 is cheap; fusion is simple arithmetic.

Measure recall at 5 on your own test questions with vector-only, keyword-only and hybrid retrieval; the gain is usually clear, and it tells you where to invest next, such as reranking or chunking.

## Is BM25 hybrid search?

No. BM25 is a keyword ranking function, one half of hybrid search. Hybrid search combines BM25, or another keyword method, with vector search based on embeddings.

BM25 scores documents by matching query terms, weighted by how rare they are and normalised for document length. On its own, it is lexical search. Some systems implement the keyword half with learned sparse vectors instead of BM25, which can capture some synonyms while keeping exact matching. Either way, the "hybrid" part comes from combining a lexical or sparse method with dense vectors.

## Does FAISS support hybrid search?

Not natively. FAISS is a library for dense vector similarity search and has no built-in keyword or BM25 search. You implement hybrid search by pairing FAISS with a separate keyword index, such as BM25 in Python or a search engine, and fusing the results in your code.

A simple setup: index embeddings in FAISS, index the same chunks with a BM25 library, query both with the same question, and merge with reciprocal-rank fusion. Frameworks such as LangChain provide ensemble retrievers that combine a FAISS retriever with a BM25 retriever. For larger systems, a database with native hybrid support reduces the glue code you maintain.

## Does Qdrant support hybrid search?

Yes. Qdrant supports hybrid search by storing dense and sparse vectors for each point and combining results in a single query with fusion methods such as reciprocal-rank fusion, plus payload filters.

You generate sparse vectors with a keyword method or a learned sparse model and dense vectors with an embedding model, store both under named vectors, then use Qdrant's query API to prefetch candidates from each and fuse them. Reranking can follow in your application. This keeps hybrid retrieval inside one database, which simplifies operations compared with running a separate search engine.

## Does ChromaDB support hybrid search?

Chroma's core strength is vector search with metadata filters, and it supports filtering by document text content. For full BM25-style hybrid ranking, many projects combine Chroma with a separate keyword index and fuse results; check current Chroma documentation, as search features have been expanding.

A practical pattern: store chunks and embeddings in Chroma, keep a BM25 index of the same chunk IDs, query both, and merge with reciprocal-rank fusion in a small function. Because both indexes share IDs, merging is straightforward. For prototypes this works well; for production at scale, consider a store with native hybrid support.

## Does pgvector support hybrid search?

pgvector provides vector search, and PostgreSQL provides full-text search with `tsvector` and ranking functions, so you can build hybrid search entirely in PostgreSQL by running both queries and fusing their rankings in SQL or in your application.

A typical approach: add a `tsvector` column with a GIN index alongside the embedding column with an HNSW index; run a full-text query and a vector query, each returning the top candidates with ranks; then combine with reciprocal-rank fusion. This keeps everything in one database with transactions and row-level security, which suits many applications. PostgreSQL's built-in ranking is not identical to BM25, but works well, and extensions offer BM25 if you need it.

## Does Pinecone support hybrid search?

Yes. Pinecone supports hybrid search with sparse-dense vectors: you store a dense embedding and a sparse vector, such as BM25-style weights, for each record, and query with both, weighting their influence.

You can tune the balance between semantic and keyword matching by scaling the dense and sparse query vectors with an alpha parameter. Pinecone also offers integrated features for reranking in some setups. As with any approach, evaluate the weighting on your own queries: technical content with many identifiers often benefits from more keyword weight, while conversational questions benefit from more semantic weight.

## What does hybrid mean in job search?

In job search, hybrid refers to a work arrangement that mixes working from the office and working remotely, such as three days in the office and two at home. It is unrelated to hybrid search in information retrieval.

On job portals, you can filter listings by on-site, remote or hybrid. Hybrid roles are common in tech companies, offering collaboration days in the office and focus days at home. Check the specific expectations in each offer: required office days, location, and flexibility. If you came here for hybrid search in AI and databases, the sections above cover it.


---

# What is image classification? How it works, CNNs, YOLO, LLMs, and GIS classification
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-image-classification/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Image classification is the computer vision task of assigning a label, or several labels, to an entire image: this photo shows a dog, this leaf is diseased, this X-ray looks normal. A trained model looks at the image and outputs probabilities for each class. It is the foundation of visual AI, and I work with related vision tasks in FaceVision and DocuLens AI. This page covers how classification works, models, why CNNs suit it, YOLO and LLMs, whether it is NLP, and classification in GIS and QGIS.

## What is image classification?

Image classification is predicting which category an image belongs to from a fixed set of classes. Single-label classification picks one class; multi-label classification can assign several, such as "beach" and "sunset" together.

It differs from object detection, which finds and boxes each object, and segmentation, which labels every pixel. Applications include sorting products in e-commerce, detecting crop diseases from leaf photos, flagging defects in manufacturing, medical image screening, content moderation and organising photo libraries. It is usually the first computer vision task students learn, with datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

## How does image classification work?

A model converts the image into numbers, extracts visual features through many layers, and ends with a layer that outputs a probability for each class. It learns by training on labelled images, adjusting its weights to reduce prediction errors.

Steps in a typical project:

- Collect and label images for each class.
- Resize and normalise images; apply augmentations like flips and crops.
- Start from a pretrained model and fine-tune it on your data.
- Validate on held-out images and inspect mistakes.
- Deploy, and monitor accuracy on real inputs.

Transfer learning from models pretrained on large datasets lets you get strong results with a few hundred images per class.

## What are image classification models?

Common models include convolutional networks such as ResNet, EfficientNet and MobileNet, vision transformers such as ViT and its variants, and hybrid designs such as ConvNeXt. Libraries like PyTorch, timm and Hugging Face provide pretrained versions.

Choose by deployment target and accuracy needs: MobileNet and EfficientNet-Lite suit phones and browsers; ResNet-50 is a reliable baseline; vision transformers excel with large data and pretraining. Foundation models such as CLIP classify images by comparing them to text labels without task-specific training. For small datasets, fine-tuning a pretrained model almost always beats training from scratch.

## Why are CNNs good for image classification?

CNNs suit images because convolution layers detect local patterns, such as edges and textures, with small filters that slide across the image, sharing weights so the same pattern is recognised anywhere. This makes them efficient and data-friendly.

Stacking layers builds a hierarchy: early layers find edges, middle layers find shapes and parts, and deep layers find objects. Pooling adds tolerance to small shifts. ResNet's residual connections, introduced in 2015, made very deep CNNs trainable. Vision transformers now match or beat CNNs at large scale, but CNNs remain excellent for small datasets, edge devices and real-time applications, so "best" depends on context.

## How do CNNs work for image classification?

A CNN passes the image through convolution layers that apply learned filters, activation functions that add non-linearity, and pooling layers that reduce size. The resulting feature maps are flattened or pooled and fed to a final layer that outputs class probabilities.

During training, the network compares predictions to correct labels with a loss function such as cross-entropy, and backpropagation adjusts filter weights to reduce the loss. Over many examples, filters specialise in useful patterns. Techniques such as batch normalisation, dropout and data augmentation improve training and reduce overfitting. Visualisation tools like Grad-CAM show which image regions influenced a prediction, helping you debug.

## Can YOLO do image classification?

Yes. Although YOLO is best known for object detection, Ultralytics YOLO releases include classification models that label whole images, trained and used with the same simple interface as detection.

Use YOLO classification when you want fast training, easy deployment and a consistent toolkit across detection and classification. If you need to know where objects are, or count them, use detection instead. For example, classify whether a factory image contains a defect at all, then run detection only on flagged images to locate the defects. Compare accuracy and speed with other classifiers on your own data.

## Can an LLM do image classification?

Multimodal LLMs, which accept images, can classify images from a prompt such as "Is this leaf healthy or diseased? Answer with one word", without training. Text-only LLMs cannot see images, though they can classify image descriptions.

Zero-shot classification with multimodal models or CLIP is great for prototypes, many categories and changing labels. Trade-offs: higher cost per image, slower responses and less consistent outputs than a fine-tuned classifier. For high-volume, fixed-category tasks, a small fine-tuned model is cheaper and more reliable. A practical pattern is labelling an initial dataset with a multimodal model, reviewing labels by hand, then training a compact classifier.

## Is image classification NLP?

No. Image classification belongs to computer vision; NLP, natural language processing, deals with text and speech. Both are branches of machine learning and share techniques, especially transformers.

The boundary has blurred with multimodal models, which process images and text together. CLIP learns to match images with captions, enabling classification by text prompts, and vision language models answer questions about images in natural language. Document AI also combines both: OCR reads text from images, then NLP understands it. Still, classifying an image's content is a vision task.

## What is image classification in GIS?

In GIS and remote sensing, image classification labels pixels or objects in satellite or aerial imagery into land cover classes, such as water, forest, farmland, urban and bare soil, creating thematic maps from raw imagery.

Supervised classification uses training samples drawn by an analyst for each class, with algorithms such as random forest, support vector machines, maximum likelihood or deep learning. Unsupervised classification groups pixels by spectral similarity, and the analyst names the clusters afterwards. Uses include monitoring deforestation, urban growth, crop mapping and flood extent. Accuracy is checked against ground truth with a confusion matrix.

## How do I do image classification in QGIS?

The common route is the Semi-Automatic Classification Plugin: install it, load satellite imagery such as Sentinel-2 or Landsat bands, create training samples for each land cover class, run a classifier, then assess accuracy.

Steps:

- Install the plugin from QGIS's plugin manager.
- Download and preprocess imagery, including atmospheric correction.
- Build a band set from the relevant bands.
- Draw training polygons for each class.
- Run a classification algorithm such as random forest.
- Validate with separate reference samples and refine.

QGIS also offers tools through the Orfeo Toolbox and processing algorithms. ArcGIS Pro provides a similar workflow with its Image Classification Wizard.
