# What is RAG in AI? Retrieval-augmented generation, explained from a production system
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RAG in AI?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of building AI answers in two moves: first search a store of your own documents for the passages most relevant to the question, then hand those passages to a large language model and have it write the answer from them, with citations.** The model no longer answers from memory alone. It answers from evidence you chose, which is why RAG is the default architecture for chatbots over company documents, support desks, legal and medical search, and any product where "I'm not sure" beats a confident guess.


The term comes from a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, which combined a dense retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator and showed the pair beat purely parametric models on knowledge-intensive tasks while producing more specific, factual language [1]. The idea has since grown into an entire engineering discipline, catalogued in surveys such as Gao et al. [2].

The one-sentence version I give students: a plain LLM is a very well-read person answering with the library door locked. RAG unlocks the door, walks them to the right shelf, and asks them to quote the page.

> A RAG demo works on the one document you tested it with. A RAG product works on the document a stranger uploads at 2 a.m. Everything in this guide is about closing that gap.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## How does RAG work?

**RAG runs in two phases. Offline, you split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding vector and store it in an index. Online, you embed the user's question, pull the closest chunks, optionally rerank them, and prompt the model with the question plus those chunks so it answers from them.**



The offline phase is where most quality is won or lost, because everything downstream can only choose among the chunks you created. The online phase is where latency and cost live, since each question costs an embedding call, a search, possibly a reranker pass and a generation.

In RAG.NextUpgrad, the platform I built at NextUpgrad in 2026, the online path looks like this: the query is embedded and also tokenised for BM25, both retrievers return candidates, reciprocal rank fusion merges them, a cross-encoder reranks the top set, a confidence gate checks whether the evidence actually supports an answer, and only then does the model stream a response with inline citations [17].

### What is a RAG pipeline?

**A RAG pipeline is the chain of components that turns a raw document collection and a user question into a cited answer: loaders, a chunker, an embedding model, a vector index, usually a keyword index, a retriever, a reranker, a prompt template, the LLM and an evaluation harness.** Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex give you each piece; the engineering is in choosing and tuning them for your documents.


### What is a RAG model?

**There is no separate "RAG model". RAG is a system pattern that wraps an ordinary language model, open or closed, with a retriever.** The original paper trained the retriever and generator jointly [1], but almost every production system today uses an off-the-shelf embedding model for retrieval and an off-the-shelf LLM for generation, connected by code.


## Why do we need RAG? Why is it important?

**RAG solves three problems a plain LLM cannot: it knows nothing after its training cutoff, it knows nothing about your private data, and when it lacks facts it invents plausible text. Retrieval supplies current, private, checkable facts at answer time, so the model can quote instead of guess.**


The practical benefits, in the order clients care about them:

- **Grounding and citations.** Every sentence can point at the passage it came from, which makes answers auditable. This matters more than raw accuracy in regulated work.
- **Freshness without retraining.** Add a document to the index and it is answerable a minute later. Retraining or fine-tuning a model for new facts takes hours and still does not cite.
- **Access control.** Retrieval can filter by user, tenant or clearance before the model ever sees the text. A fine-tuned model has no such boundary.
- **Cost.** Retrieval is cheap compared with training, and with a small model plus good retrieval you often match a much larger model answering from memory.

The limit is just as important: RAG helps with what the model knows, not how it reasons or writes. If your problem is tone, format or a specialised skill, retrieval will not fix it. That is where fine-tuning belongs.

## What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

**RAG changes what the model can see at answer time; fine-tuning changes the model's weights, so it changes how the model behaves. Use RAG when the answer depends on facts, documents or anything that changes. Use fine-tuning when you need a consistent style, a strict output format, a niche skill, or lower latency and cost on a narrow task. Many production systems do both.**




I have built both kinds of platform in the same year, RAG.NextUpgrad and FineTune Studio, and the question I ask clients is one word: is the problem *knowledge* or *behaviour*? Knowledge is retrieval. Behaviour is training. A support bot that must know your refund policy is a knowledge problem. A model that must write incident reports in your house format is a behaviour problem. A bot that must do both is RAG for the policy and a small fine-tune for the voice.

### What is the difference between RAG and prompt engineering?

**Prompt engineering writes better instructions for the model; RAG adds a retrieval system that supplies evidence to those instructions. Prompt engineering alone cannot give the model facts it never saw, but every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that tells the model to answer only from the passages and to say so when they are insufficient.**


## What is chunking in RAG, and what is the best chunking strategy?

**Chunking is splitting documents into passages that can be embedded and retrieved on their own. The best strategy respects the document's structure, headings, paragraphs, table rows and code blocks, keeps chunks small enough to be precise and large enough to be understood alone, and prepends the section heading to each chunk so a passage carries its context.**


There is no universal chunk size, and anyone quoting one without asking about your documents is guessing. What holds across the projects I have shipped:

1. **Chunk for the question, not the document.** A chunk should be able to answer a realistic user question by itself. For policy documents that is often a few hundred tokens; for API references it can be one function signature plus its description.
2. **Overlap is insurance, not a strategy.** A small overlap catches sentences that straddle a boundary. Large overlaps duplicate what the reranker sees and inflate the index.
3. **Never split inside a structure.** Tables, code blocks, numbered procedures, and a heading with its first paragraph belong together. Splitting them yields chunks that are individually meaningless.
4. **Carry the heading.** Prepending "Section 4.2, Rate limits" to a chunk that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" did more for answer accuracy in RAG.NextUpgrad than any embedding model change.


Barnett et al. list missing content and wrongly ranked chunks among the seven failure points of RAG systems, and both usually trace back to chunking decisions [10].

## What are embeddings, and which embedding model is best for RAG?

**An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a piece of text so that texts about the same thing end up close together. RAG uses embeddings to find chunks that are semantically similar to the question even when they share no keywords. The best model is the one that scores well on retrieval for your language and domain on the MTEB benchmark and fits your latency and cost budget; test two or three on your own questions before committing.**


Dense retrieval with learned embeddings was shown to beat traditional keyword retrieval for open-domain question answering by Karpukhin et al. in 2020 [3], and that result is why almost every RAG system starts with a vector index. Three practical notes:

- **Dimensions are a trade-off, not a score.** A 1,536-dimension vector costs more storage and search time than a 384-dimension one. Whether it retrieves better for you is an empirical question.
- **Embeddings are not tokens.** Tokens are the pieces a model reads; an embedding is a single vector summarising a whole chunk. People search for the difference often enough that it deserves saying plainly.
- **Switching models means re-embedding everything.** Vectors from two models are not comparable. Budget for a full re-index when you upgrade.

The MTEB leaderboard on Hugging Face ranks open and commercial embedding models on retrieval and other tasks [14]. Use it to shortlist, then evaluate on your own documents, because leaderboard corpora are not your corpus.

## What is a vector database, and do I need one?

**A vector database stores embeddings and answers "which stored vectors are closest to this one" quickly, usually with an approximate nearest-neighbour index. You need one when your index outgrows memory, needs filtering by metadata, or must serve many concurrent users. For a prototype or a few hundred thousand chunks, a library such as FAISS or the pgvector extension inside the Postgres you already run is enough.**



FAISS is described in Johnson, Douze and Jégou's 2017 paper and remains the reference implementation for in-process search [7]. pgvector adds vector columns and indexes to PostgreSQL [15]. Qdrant is documented at qdrant.tech [16]. My default for a new client project is pgvector, because the vectors then live next to the metadata, the permissions and the audit log, and "one more database to operate" is a real cost for a small team.

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every question, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, then merges their ranked lists. Keywords catch exact terms, product codes, names and rare words that embeddings blur; embeddings catch paraphrases and meaning that keywords miss. Fusing them, most simply with reciprocal rank fusion, gives better recall than either alone.**


BM25 is the classic probabilistic ranking function, described in full by Robertson and Zaragoza [4]. Reciprocal rank fusion, from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher, scores each document by the sum of 1 divided by (a constant plus its rank) in every list, which needs no score normalisation and was shown to outperform more complex fusion methods [5]. It is a dozen lines of code and it is in RAG.NextUpgrad exactly because of that paper.

The pattern I see in support corpora: users ask with the product's own words ("error E-4021", "Form 16"), and dense retrieval alone often returns something semantically nearby but wrong. BM25 nails the exact token. The reverse happens for how-do-I questions phrased in plain language, where BM25 misses and embeddings win. Hybrid is not a luxury; it is the fix for both.

## What is reranking in RAG?

**Reranking is a second scoring pass over the top retrieved candidates using a model that reads the question and the passage together, a cross-encoder, and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare vectors computed separately for speed; a reranker looks at the pair, which is far more accurate, so you retrieve, say, 30 candidates and rerank to the best 5 before generation.**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho in 2019 and remains the standard recipe [6]. It also addresses a known weakness of long prompts: Liu et al. showed that models use information at the start and end of a long context far better than information in the middle [8], so sending five well-ordered passages beats sending thirty in a heap.

## How do I build a RAG chatbot?

**Start with one document type and ten real questions. Load and chunk the documents with structure-aware splitting, embed with a model you shortlisted from MTEB, index in pgvector or FAISS, add BM25, retrieve with both and fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, rerank with a cross-encoder, and prompt the model to answer only from the passages and to cite them. Measure retrieval recall on your ten questions before touching the prompt. Then add streaming, a confidence gate and logging.**


The skeleton of the query side, without any framework, is short enough to read:

```python
def answer(question: str) -> dict:
    q_vec = embed(question)                       # same model used at index time
    dense = vector_index.search(q_vec, k=30)      # pgvector / FAISS / Qdrant
    sparse = bm25_index.search(question, k=30)    # keyword retriever
    fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense, sparse], k=60)
    top = rerank(question, fused[:30])[:5]        # cross-encoder scores the pairs
    if confidence(question, top) < THRESHOLD:     # evidence too weak
        return {"answer": None, "reason": "no supporting passages", "sources": []}
    prompt = build_prompt(question, top)          # "answer only from these passages, cite [n]"
    return {"answer": llm(prompt), "sources": [c.source for c in top]}
```

Everything else, ingestion jobs, a UI, authentication, tenant filters, is ordinary software engineering. In RAG.NextUpgrad that engineering includes Docker, CI/CD, structured logging, and a test suite of 196 tests, and the whole service runs in about 220 MB of RAM on a free tier, which is a useful reminder that RAG is not inherently heavy [17].


### Which framework should I use, LangChain or LlamaIndex, or none?

**Use a framework to prototype and to borrow loaders, then own the retrieval code yourself once you know what your system needs.** Both LangChain and LlamaIndex are excellent for getting to a first answer in an afternoon. The trouble comes later, when a bug sits under three layers of abstraction. The query path above is a few hundred lines; you can read all of it.


## How do I evaluate a RAG pipeline?

**Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For retrieval, build a set of real questions with the passages that should be returned and measure recall at k, the share of questions where a correct passage is in the top k. For generation, measure faithfulness, whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages, and answer relevance. Frameworks such as RAGAS automate the generation metrics with an LLM judge, but the retrieval set you must build by hand.**


RAGAS, from Es et al., defines faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance as reference-free metrics scored by a model [9]. They are useful, and they are not a substitute for a human-labelled retrieval set, because a system can be perfectly faithful to the wrong passage.


The metric that changed my own systems most was the simplest: for each question, was the right chunk anywhere in the top 30? When it was not, no prompt or model could help, and the fix was always upstream, in chunking or in adding keyword retrieval.

## Why does RAG fail, and how do I fix it?

**RAG fails for a small number of repeatable reasons: the answer was never in the index, it was in the index but chunked so it lost its meaning, retrieval ranked the right chunk too low, the model ignored the passages and answered from memory, or the passages contradicted each other and the model picked wrong. Each has a specific fix, and the fix is almost never "a bigger model".**



Barnett et al. catalogue seven failure points from three case studies, from missing content to incomplete answers, and their central observation matches my experience: you only discover most failures in operation, so logging every retrieval and every answer is part of the architecture, not an add-on [10].

## What is a confidence gate, and why did I build one?

**A confidence gate is a check between retrieval and generation that measures how strongly the retrieved passages support an answer, and refuses to generate when support is weak. Instead of a fluent hallucination the user sees "I could not find this in the documents", with the option to rephrase or upload more. It turns the most dangerous RAG failure, a confident wrong answer, into an honest non-answer.**


In RAG.NextUpgrad the gate looks at reranker scores and the agreement between passages before any tokens are generated. The threshold is tuned on the evaluation set so that it rarely blocks answerable questions. This is the single feature clients noticed most, and I wrote up the reasoning in a separate article [18]. Research is moving the same way: Self-RAG trains a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own output with reflection tokens [12].

> The model is never allowed to guess. If the evidence is not there, the honest answer is that the evidence is not there, and the product says so out loud.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, RAG.NextUpgrad design note</cite>

## What is agentic RAG, and what is Graph RAG?

**Agentic RAG puts a planning loop around retrieval: the model decides whether to retrieve, rewrites the query, calls several retrievers or tools, checks the results, and retrieves again if needed, instead of doing one fixed search. Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the documents and retrieves over that graph, which helps with questions that need connections across many documents, such as "what are the main themes in this corpus".**



Microsoft's Graph RAG paper describes building an entity graph with community summaries and shows gains on global, sense-making questions over a corpus [13]. HyDE, another retrieval upgrade, has the model write a hypothetical answer first and embeds that to search, which helps when questions are short and vague [11]. My advice to students is to climb the levels above in order. Agentic loops and graphs are level-eight problems; most systems I audit are stuck at level two.

## Is RAG still relevant with long context windows?

**Yes. Long context windows let you paste more into a prompt, but they do not tell you which of a million documents to paste, they cost per token on every question, and models still attend unevenly across long inputs. Retrieval is how you choose what deserves the context window. Longer windows make RAG easier, because you can send more and better passages, not unnecessary.**


Liu et al.'s finding that accuracy drops when relevant information sits in the middle of a long context is the empirical reason retrieval and reranking still matter [8]. The economics are the practical reason: a 200-page manual is hundreds of thousands of tokens; five reranked passages are a few thousand.

## What are common RAG interview questions?

**Expect to explain the two phases, to compare RAG with fine-tuning, to describe chunking trade-offs, to justify hybrid search and reranking, to define recall and faithfulness, and to walk through a failure you debugged. Interviewers are testing whether you have operated a RAG system, not whether you can recite the paper.**


The questions that separate candidates, from the interviewing I have done for SCULT INDIA and from the sessions I run for students:

1. How do you know your retrieval is working before you look at the answers?
2. A user says the bot gave a wrong answer. Walk me through your debugging, in order.
3. Why would you add BM25 to a system that already has embeddings?
4. What happens when two retrieved passages disagree?
5. How do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer?

If you can answer those five from experience, you can build the system. The rest of this guide is the experience, compressed.


## Where can I learn RAG properly?

**Read the original paper and the 2023 survey for the map, build one pipeline by hand without a framework so you understand every stage, then evaluate it on your own questions. That order, paper, build, measure, teaches more than any course, and it is exactly what I ask of students who want to work on retrieval systems with me.**


A good first project is a RAG system over your own college's notes, syllabus and previous-year papers, because you can judge the answers yourself and the documents are messy in exactly the ways real client documents are. I mentor students through TechVerse Enclave on projects like this, and the ones who finish have something no certificate gives them: a system they can explain failure by failure. If you want to talk RAG at your college or hackathon, my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com and the invite page is at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is RAG in LLMs? How RAG works, building it, and fixing bad results
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-llm/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of using a large language model where the system first retrieves relevant passages from your own documents and then has the LLM answer from them. It gives LLMs knowledge they were not trained on, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets every answer cite its source. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, a production RAG platform with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, so this page explains RAG in LLMs from practice: how it works, how to build and update it, how to evaluate it on a budget, and why results go wrong.

## What is RAG in LLMs?

RAG in LLMs means retrieval-augmented generation: before the model answers, a retriever searches a document collection for passages relevant to the question, and those passages are added to the prompt so the LLM answers from them.

The term comes from a 2020 research paper that combined a neural retriever with a generator. Today it describes a broad pattern used in company knowledge bots, customer support, document Q&A and research assistants. The LLM provides language understanding and fluent answers; retrieval provides the facts. Done well, users get specific answers with citations they can check, instead of the model's general and possibly outdated memory.

## What is a RAG system?

A RAG system is the full application that implements retrieval-augmented generation: document ingestion and chunking, an index such as a vector store with keyword search, a retrieval and reranking step, a prompt that grounds the LLM, and evaluation and monitoring.

Components in a production system:

- **Ingestion**: load PDFs, web pages and databases; clean text; keep metadata.
- **Chunking**: split into passages that keep meaning together.
- **Indexing**: embeddings in a vector index plus a keyword index.
- **Retrieval**: hybrid search, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- **Reranking**: a cross-encoder reorders the top candidates.
- **Generation**: grounded prompt, citations, refusal on weak evidence.
- **Operations**: updates, logging, evaluation, cost control.

## How does RAG work with an LLM?

The user's question is turned into a search, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and ranked, and the top few are placed into the LLM's prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite them. The LLM writes the answer.

Step by step: embed the question; search the vector index and the keyword index; merge and rerank results; select the top passages within the context budget; build a prompt with the passages labelled by ID; generate the answer with citations; check that citations point to real passages; and decline if the evidence was weak. Streaming the answer keeps the experience fast. Logging the retrieved passages for every query is what lets you debug wrong answers later.

## How does RAG enhance an LLM?

RAG gives an LLM access to private, recent and specific information, reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in sources, enables citations, and lets you update knowledge by updating documents instead of retraining the model.

It also lowers cost and risk compared with fine-tuning for knowledge: smaller models can answer well when given the right passages, and access control can be applied at retrieval time so users only get answers from documents they are allowed to see. The limits are equally important: RAG cannot fix bad source documents, and if retrieval misses the right passage, the model has nothing correct to work with. That is why retrieval quality is the main lever.

## What is the difference between RAG and an LLM?

An LLM is a trained model that generates text from its input. RAG is a system design that adds a retrieval step before the LLM, so the model's input includes relevant documents. RAG uses an LLM; it is not an alternative to one.

Without RAG, the LLM answers from what it learned in training, with no access to your files and no sources. With RAG, it answers from passages your system chose. That changes accuracy, freshness and trust. RAG is also different from fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights; RAG changes only what the model reads at question time, which makes it far easier to update and audit.

## How do I build a RAG-based LLM application?

Start with a small, real document set and a list of real questions, build a simple pipeline end to end, measure retrieval and answer quality, then improve the weakest part. Resist adding complexity before you can measure it.

A build order that works:

- Collect 50 real questions with known answers in your documents.
- Ingest and chunk documents by structure, such as headings, with page numbers in metadata.
- Index with embeddings and BM25; merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- Add a cross-encoder reranker on the top candidates.
- Prompt the LLM to answer only from passages, with citations.
- Add a confidence gate that declines on weak evidence.
- Evaluate after every change.

RAG.NextUpgrad follows this design and runs in about 220 MB on a free tier.

## How do I keep information updated in a RAG system?

Re-index incrementally: detect new, changed and deleted documents, re-chunk and re-embed only what changed, and delete outdated chunks so old versions never reach the model. Store document versions and timestamps in metadata.

Practical habits:

- Give every chunk an ID derived from its document and position, so updates replace rather than duplicate.
- Track a hash of each document to detect changes cheaply.
- Schedule syncs from source systems, or trigger them on changes.
- Filter or boost by date for time-sensitive questions.
- Show the source date in citations so users see how current an answer is.

If you change the embedding model, re-embed everything; vectors from different models are not comparable.

## How do I evaluate a RAG system with a local or free-tier model?

Build a test set, measure retrieval with simple metrics that need no model, and use a local model through Ollama or a free API tier as a judge for answer faithfulness, checking a sample by hand to confirm the judge agrees with you.

Steps:

- Write 50 questions with the passage that answers each.
- Compute recall at 5 and 10 for retrieval: free, fast and deterministic.
- Generate answers and ask a judge model: is every claim supported by the passages?
- Include unanswerable questions and measure how often the system declines.
- Hand-check 20 judged answers to calibrate.

Small local judges are less reliable than large ones, so keep the rubric simple, binary where possible, and trust retrieval metrics most.

## Why do RAG hallucinations often start at ingestion?

Because bad ingestion corrupts what the model reads: broken PDF extraction, tables flattened into nonsense, headers repeated in every chunk, lost page structure, or chunks that split a fact from its context. The LLM then faithfully answers from garbled or misleading text.

Fixes at ingestion:

- Use layout-aware extraction or OCR for scanned and complex PDFs.
- Keep tables as tables, or convert them to clear text rows.
- Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation.
- Chunk by headings and paragraphs, with overlap where meaning spans boundaries.
- Carry titles and section names into each chunk.

Inspect random chunks by eye before indexing; many "model" problems disappear once the text is clean.

## Why does a large FAISS RAG system return irrelevant results?

With many chunks, pure semantic search tends to surface passages that are topically similar but not relevant, especially when chunks are noisy, embeddings are mismatched, or the index uses approximate settings that trade recall for speed.

Common causes and fixes:

- **Mixed or mismatched embeddings**: use one model for indexing and queries, and normalise vectors for cosine similarity.
- **Noisy chunks**: remove boilerplate and duplicates.
- **Approximate index settings**: raise `nprobe` for IVF or `efSearch` for HNSW and measure recall.
- **No keyword search**: add BM25 and fuse results.
- **No reranking**: rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder.
- **Wrong scope**: filter by metadata such as document type or date.

Measure recall at 10 before and after each change.

# What is RLHF, instruction tuning and DPO? How base models become assistants, what alignment training actually does, and when a small team should use it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rlhf-instruction-tuning-and-dpo/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RLHF?

**Reinforcement learning from human feedback is the training stage that turns an instruction-following model into one whose answers people prefer. Humans compare pairs of model answers to the same prompt and pick the better one; a reward model is trained to predict those preferences; the language model is then optimised with reinforcement learning, classically PPO, to produce answers the reward model scores highly, with a penalty for drifting too far from the starting model [1][2]. It is how InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT were trained, and it is why assistants sound the way they do [1][3].**


Fine-tune Studio, the training platform I built, stops at supervised fine-tuning for a reason that this page explains: for most teams, the preference stage costs more in data than it returns in quality, and knowing where it does pay off is the useful part [14].

> Every alignment method is a way to spend human judgement efficiently. The algorithm is a detail; the comparisons are the product.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a base model, and what is instruction tuning?

**A base model is trained only to predict the next token over a huge corpus, so given "What is the capital of France?" it may continue with another question rather than an answer, because that is what documents look like. Instruction tuning, also called supervised fine-tuning or SFT, trains the base model on demonstrations: prompts paired with good responses, in a chat format, so it learns to answer rather than continue [1][9]. FLAN showed instruction-tuned models generalise to unseen tasks [9]; LIMA showed a thousand very good demonstrations can be enough for the format [10].**



## How does RLHF work step by step?

**Start from an instruction-tuned model. Sample several answers per prompt. Have humans rank or compare them. Train a reward model, usually a copy of the language model with a scalar head, to predict which answer wins. Then run reinforcement learning: the policy generates an answer, the reward model scores it, and the policy is updated to increase the score while a KL penalty keeps it close to the SFT model so it does not collapse into reward-gaming gibberish [1]. Iterate with fresh comparisons as the policy changes.**



## What is DPO, and why did it replace much of RLHF?

**Direct preference optimisation skips the reward model and the reinforcement learning. It takes the same comparison data, preferred and rejected answer per prompt, and trains the language model directly with a loss that raises the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one, measured against a frozen reference model [4]. The paper shows this is mathematically equivalent to optimising the RLHF objective under the usual reward model assumptions, with none of the instability or infrastructure of PPO. It became the default for open models because a fine-tuning script can run it.**



## What are ORPO, KTO and GRPO?

**Variants that change what data or memory the preference stage needs. ORPO folds preference learning into the SFT stage with an odds-ratio term, so no reference model is needed and one training run does both [6]. KTO works from single answers labelled good or bad instead of pairs, which is much cheaper to collect from real users, who give thumbs up or down rather than comparing two answers [7]. GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that estimates the baseline from a group of sampled answers rather than a value model, used to train reasoning models on verifiable rewards such as maths answers [8].**



## What is RLAIF and Constitutional AI?

**Reinforcement learning from AI feedback replaces some or all of the human comparisons with judgements from a model, guided by written principles. Constitutional AI is the best-known form: the model critiques and revises its own answers against a set of principles, the revisions become SFT data, and a model-generated preference set trains the reward model [5]. It makes preference data cheap and scalable, at the cost of inheriting the judging model's biases. Most current open preference datasets are at least partly model-judged.**



## What does preference data look like, and how much do I need?

**A prompt, a chosen answer and a rejected answer, in the model's chat format, with the difference between them being the behaviour you want to teach: more accurate, better formatted, more concise, safer, more on-brand. Quality dominates quantity; a few thousand clean pairs where the preference is unambiguous beat fifty thousand noisy ones. The cheapest real source is your own product: two generations, a user choice, or thumbs up and down for KTO. The most common mistake is pairs where the rejected answer is obviously broken, which teaches the model nothing about the hard cases.**



## What goes wrong in RLHF and DPO?

**Reward hacking: the policy finds outputs the reward model over-scores, such as longer answers, confident tone or particular phrases, without being better. Sycophancy: models learn that agreeing with the user is preferred, and start agreeing when the user is wrong [11]. Over-refusal: safety preferences push the model to decline reasonable requests. Mode collapse: the model's answers become samey. Length bias is the most common of all, because raters prefer longer answers slightly and the optimiser amplifies it. Each is a data or reward problem and shows up in evals before users notice, if you have evals.**



## Should a student or small team do RLHF or DPO?

**Usually not yet. Supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on a few thousand good examples captures most of what a small team needs: format, tone, domain vocabulary, task behaviour. Preference tuning pays off when you have real comparisons from users, a measured quality gap that SFT could not close, and an eval set to prove the gap closed. If you have those, DPO or KTO with the TRL library on a LoRA adapter is a weekend of work on a rented GPU [12][13]. If you do not, the time is better spent on data and evals.**



## How do I run DPO in practice?

**Start from your SFT model. Build the preference set in the chosen and rejected format. Use the TRL DPO trainer with a LoRA adapter, a small learning rate, one to three epochs, and the SFT model as the frozen reference [13]. Evaluate against the SFT model on a held-out set with a model judge and with your task metrics. Check for length inflation explicitly. Keep the adapter that wins the eval, and log everything so the run can be reproduced.**



## RLHF and DPO interview questions

**Explain the three training stages. Describe how a reward model is trained and why the KL penalty exists. Derive or sketch why DPO needs no reward model. Compare DPO, KTO and ORPO by the data each needs. Name three failure modes and their causes. Explain what GRPO changes and where verifiable rewards apply. Say when you would not do preference tuning. The strongest answer includes an SFT run you evaluated and a reason you did or did not go further.**



## Where should I start?

**Read the DPO paper's first four pages, then run the TRL DPO example on a small model with a public preference set for one epoch and compare outputs against the starting model. An evening, and the abstractions become concrete.** For a workshop on fine-tuning and alignment for students, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is semantic search? Meaning, engines, vs RAG, Python, testing and tuning
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-semantic-search/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Semantic search means searching by meaning rather than exact words: a query like "laptop gets hot when gaming" finds an article titled "managing thermal throttling on notebooks" even though they share no keywords. It works by converting queries and documents into embeddings and finding the closest matches. It is the retrieval step in RAG systems such as RAG.NextUpgrad, where I pair it with keyword search. This page covers the meaning, semantic search engines, similarity search, whether it is NLP or uses LLMs, how it relates to RAG, building it in Python, testing and improving it, and the Semantic Scholar academic search engine.

## What is semantic search?

Semantic search is a search technique that tries to understand the intent and meaning of a query and return results that are relevant in meaning, not just results that contain the same words.

Traditional keyword search matches terms, so synonyms, paraphrases and natural-language questions often fail. Semantic search uses language models to represent text as vectors in which similar meanings are close together, so it handles "how do I fix a slow laptop" and "speed up my computer" as related. Its weakness is exact details: specific codes, names and numbers are better handled by keyword search, which is why production systems combine both.

## What is a semantic search engine?

A semantic search engine is a search system that ranks results by meaning, typically using embedding models to encode documents and queries and a vector index to find nearest matches, often combined with keyword search, filters and reranking.

Examples range from web search engines, which use semantic understanding heavily, to site search, e-commerce product search, documentation search and enterprise knowledge search. Building blocks include an embedding model, a vector database or library, a keyword index for hybrid search, a reranker for precision, and an interface that may show snippets or generated answers. Many search platforms now offer semantic features built in.

## What is the difference between semantic search and similarity search?

Similarity search is the technical operation: finding vectors nearest to a query vector by cosine similarity or distance. Semantic search is the application: using similarity search over meaning-based embeddings to return relevant results to people.

Similarity search can be used for many things beyond text meaning, such as finding similar images, songs, products or fraud patterns. Semantic search specifically aims at relevance to a user's intent, which often requires more than raw similarity: query understanding, hybrid keyword matching, filters such as language or date, and reranking. In short, similarity search is a tool; semantic search is a product built with it.

## Is semantic search NLP?

Yes. Semantic search is an application of natural language processing: it uses NLP models, especially transformer-based embedding models, to understand the meaning of queries and documents.

It sits at the intersection of NLP and information retrieval. NLP provides the models that represent meaning; information retrieval provides indexing, ranking and evaluation methods. Related NLP techniques often support it, such as query expansion, named entity recognition for filters, and language detection. Semantic search also extends beyond text: multimodal models can match text queries to images, which uses the same principles.

## Does semantic search use LLMs?

Not necessarily. Semantic search usually uses embedding models, which are smaller transformer encoders, not large generative LLMs. LLMs can be added to rewrite queries, generate hypothetical answers to search with, rerank results or produce a summarised answer.

A basic semantic search system needs only an embedding model and a vector index, which is fast and cheap. Adding an LLM increases cost and latency, so use it where it helps: rephrasing vague questions, generating answers with citations in RAG, or reranking a small set of candidates. Many embedding models are themselves derived from language models, which is why the line can seem blurry.

## Is semantic search the same as RAG?

No. Semantic search finds and returns relevant documents. RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, uses retrieval, often semantic search, to find passages and then has an LLM generate an answer from them.

So semantic search is a component of most RAG systems. Search results alone let users read sources directly; RAG adds a synthesised answer, ideally with citations. RAG quality depends heavily on search quality: if the right passage is not retrieved, the answer cannot be right. That is why improving semantic search, through hybrid retrieval and reranking, is the most effective way to improve a RAG system.

## How do I do semantic search in Python?

Use the sentence-transformers library to embed documents and queries, then compute cosine similarity and return the top matches. For larger collections, store embeddings in a vector index such as FAISS, Chroma or pgvector.

```python
# pip install sentence-transformers
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
docs = ["Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages.",
        "A deadlock occurs when processes wait on each other forever.",
        "Thermal throttling slows a laptop when it gets too hot."]
doc_emb = model.encode(docs, convert_to_tensor=True)
q = model.encode("why does my laptop slow down when gaming", convert_to_tensor=True)
best = util.semantic_search(q, doc_emb, top_k=1)[0][0]
print(docs[best["corpus_id"]], round(best["score"], 2))
```

Swap in a stronger or multilingual embedding model for production.

## How do I test semantic search?

Create a set of real queries with known relevant documents, run your search, and measure metrics such as recall at k, precision at k and mean reciprocal rank. Also review results by hand for a sample of queries.

A simple process:

- Collect 50 to 100 real queries from users or logs.
- Label the relevant documents for each.
- Compute recall at 5 and 10: how often a relevant document appears in the top results.
- Include hard cases: exact codes, synonyms, misspellings and multi-part questions.
- Re-run after every change to embeddings, chunking or ranking.

Track failures by type, such as exact-term misses or wrong-topic matches, to choose the right fix.

## How do I improve semantic search?

The biggest improvements usually come from hybrid search, adding keyword ranking such as BM25 to vector search, better chunking of documents, a stronger or domain-suited embedding model, metadata filters, and a reranker on the top results.

Checklist:

- **Hybrid retrieval** merged with reciprocal-rank fusion.
- **Chunking** by structure, with titles and headings included in each chunk.
- **Embedding model** chosen by tests on your own queries.
- **Query handling**: rewrite vague queries, expand acronyms.
- **Reranking** with a cross-encoder on the top 20 to 50.
- **Feedback**: log clicks or ratings to find weak queries.

Measure each change; some ideas that sound good do not help on a given dataset.

## How do I search on Semantic Scholar?

Semantic Scholar is a free academic search engine from the Allen Institute for AI. Enter keywords, a paper title or an author's name in the search box, then filter by year, field of study, publication type and venue.

Useful features: paper pages show abstracts, citations, references and AI-generated short summaries; "highly influential citations" highlight important follow-up work; you can create a library and set alerts for new papers; and an API supports programmatic access. For literature reviews, start with a few key papers, follow their citations and references, and save relevant ones to your library. Always open and read the actual paper before citing it.

# What is the Supabase database? Postgres, connection URL, backups, reset and security
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-supabase-database/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


The Supabase database is a full PostgreSQL database that Supabase hosts and manages for you, with auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs, a dashboard, extensions such as pgvector, and built-in backups. Supabase wraps it with authentication, file storage, realtime updates and edge functions, making it a complete backend. PostgreSQL is central to my stack for products like FaceVision's embedding store, so this page covers what Supabase's database is, how it works, connection URLs, backups and exports, resets and security.

## What is the Supabase database?

Every Supabase project includes a dedicated PostgreSQL database. You can create tables with the dashboard's table editor or SQL, and Supabase instantly exposes them through APIs your front end can call with client libraries.

Because it is real Postgres, you get SQL, joins, transactions, views, functions, triggers and extensions, including pgvector for embeddings and PostGIS for location data. Supabase adds conveniences: a visual editor, SQL editor, database migrations through its CLI, connection pooling, logs and performance advisors. It is used for SaaS apps, mobile back ends, internal tools and AI applications that need structured data and vectors together.

## Which database does Supabase use?

Supabase uses PostgreSQL, the open-source relational database. It is not a custom database; your data lives in standard Postgres, so any Postgres tool, driver or ORM can connect to it.

This is a key difference from Firebase, which uses NoSQL document databases. Using Postgres means your data model is relational, with tables, foreign keys and SQL queries, and your data is portable: you can export it with standard tools and move it to any Postgres host. Supabase keeps its Postgres versions reasonably current and supports a wide range of extensions, which you enable from the dashboard.

## Is Supabase a database or a backend?

Both. At its core is a Postgres database, and around it Supabase provides backend services: authentication, file storage, realtime subscriptions, edge functions and auto-generated APIs, so many apps need no separate server.

Developers often describe Supabase as a backend-as-a-service or an open-source Firebase alternative. You can use just the database, connecting from your own server like any Postgres host, or use the full platform from front-end code with Row Level Security protecting data. For complex business logic, many teams pair Supabase with their own API, such as a FastAPI service, using Supabase for data, auth and storage.

## Is Supabase a relational database?

Yes. Supabase's database is PostgreSQL, a relational database, so data lives in tables with columns and types, related through keys, and queried with SQL. It also supports JSON columns for flexible, document-style data when needed.

Relational structure suits most applications: users, orders, posts and comments relate naturally through foreign keys, and constraints keep data consistent. Postgres's JSONB type lets you store semi-structured data, such as settings or metadata, without giving up relational features. Design your schema thoughtfully, with indexes on columns you filter by, because a well-designed relational schema scales far better than one that stores everything as JSON.

## How does the Supabase database work?

Your app talks to Postgres either through Supabase's auto-generated APIs, using client libraries with a project key and user session, or directly with a Postgres connection string from servers. Row Level Security policies decide what each user can access.

When a logged-in user queries through the API, Supabase passes their identity to Postgres, and policies such as "users can read only their own rows" are enforced inside the database. Realtime streams changes to subscribed clients. Database functions can be called as remote procedures, and triggers can run logic on inserts or updates. Migrations, managed with the Supabase CLI, version your schema changes like code.

## How do I get the Supabase database URL?

Open your project in the Supabase dashboard and click Connect, or look under the project's database settings, to find connection strings for direct connections and for the connection pooler. Replace the password placeholder with your database password.

Which string to use:

- **Direct connection**: for long-running servers and migrations.
- **Pooler in transaction mode**: for serverless functions and many short connections.
- **Pooler in session mode**: for clients that need session features over IPv4.

The project URL and API keys used by client libraries are different from the database connection string; find them in the API settings. Keep the database password and service keys in environment variables, never in front-end code or public repositories.

## How do I back up a Supabase database?

Supabase runs automatic daily backups on paid plans, with point-in-time recovery available as an add-on. For your own copies, use the Supabase CLI's `supabase db dump` or standard `pg_dump` with your connection string, and store dumps securely off-platform.

A practical routine:

- Rely on managed backups for quick restores.
- Schedule your own dumps, for example nightly through a CI job.
- Back up files in storage separately; database dumps do not include them.
- Test restoring a backup into a new project occasionally.
- Encrypt and restrict access to backup files.

Free plan projects have limited backup options, so take your own dumps if your data matters.

## Can I export a Supabase database?

Yes. Because it is PostgreSQL, you can export the whole database with `pg_dump` or the Supabase CLI, export individual tables as CSV from the dashboard's table editor, or copy data with any Postgres-compatible tool.

Exports include schema, data, functions and policies when using full dumps; choose schema-only or data-only options as needed. To migrate elsewhere, restore the dump into another Postgres server, then reconfigure auth and storage, which are separate services. Supabase's documentation includes migration guides to and from other platforms. This portability is a major advantage over proprietary databases that lock data into one vendor.

## How do I reset a Supabase database?

For local development, run `supabase db reset`, which recreates your local database and reapplies all migrations and seed data. For a hosted project, there is no single button to wipe data; drop and recreate schemas or tables carefully, restore a backup, or create a fresh project.

Before any reset of a hosted project, take a backup, because deletions are permanent. If you only need a clean database password, use the dashboard option to reset the database password, which does not touch data. Managing schema through migrations makes resets safe and repeatable: your database can always be rebuilt from versioned files.

## Is the Supabase database secure?

Supabase encrypts data at rest and in transit, runs on major cloud infrastructure, and offers compliance options for organisations. Real-world security, though, depends mostly on configuration: Row Level Security, key handling and access policies you set.

Essential practices:

- Enable Row Level Security on every table exposed to clients, with tested policies.
- Never expose the service role or secret key in front-end code.
- Use strong database passwords and restrict network access where possible.
- Review the dashboard's security and performance advisors.
- Keep auth settings strict, such as email confirmation and rate limits.

Most Supabase data leaks come from tables without RLS, not from platform breaches.

# What is system design? Interviews, examples, AI system design, and preparation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-system-design/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


System design is the process of deciding how a software system is built to meet its requirements: which components it has, how data flows between them, where data is stored, how it scales, and what happens when parts fail. It is also a standard interview round for software engineers. This page explains system design and how it differs from architecture, what interviews test and how to prepare, works through an example, covers AI and agentic system design, asks whether it is AI-proof, and clears up two other meanings: VLSI system design and UI design systems.

## What is system design?

System design is planning the structure of a software system: its components, such as services, databases, caches and queues, the interfaces between them, and the trade-offs that let it meet functional needs and goals such as scale, latency, reliability and cost.

A system design starts from requirements: what users must be able to do, and how many users, how fast, how reliable. Then you choose components and data models, estimate load, plan for failure, and decide on trade-offs, such as consistency versus availability, or cost versus speed. Good designs are as simple as the requirements allow and evolve as the product grows. The skill combines knowledge of building blocks with judgement about which ones fit.

## What is a system design interview?

A system design interview asks you to design a system, such as a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed, in about 45 to 60 minutes, explaining your reasoning aloud. Interviewers assess how you clarify requirements, structure the problem and reason about trade-offs.

A typical flow: clarify functional and non-functional requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, define APIs and data models, then go deep on one or two parts, such as storage or caching, and discuss bottlenecks, failures and improvements. There is no single correct answer. Interviewers look for structured thinking, sensible choices with reasons, awareness of trade-offs and good communication. For junior roles, expect simpler problems and more focus on fundamentals; for senior roles, more depth on scale and reliability.

## How do I prepare for system design?

Learn the building blocks, practise a set of classic designs out loud with a fixed structure, and connect it all to your own projects. Six to eight weeks of steady practice is enough for most junior and mid-level interviews.

A preparation plan:

- **Concepts**: load balancers, caching, databases and indexing, replication and sharding, queues, CDNs, consistency, rate limiting.
- **Estimation**: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth.
- **Classic problems**: URL shortener, chat, news feed, file storage, rate limiter, notification system.
- **Structure**: requirements, estimates, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs.
- **Mock interviews**: practise with a friend or record yourself.

Read The System Design Primer and Designing Data-Intensive Applications for depth.

## What is an example of system design?

A URL shortener is the classic example: users submit a long URL and get a short code; visiting the short link redirects to the original. It is simple to describe but raises real design questions about IDs, storage, caching and scale.

A sketch:

- **API**: `POST /shorten` returns a code; `GET /{code}` redirects.
- **ID generation**: base62-encode a unique counter or a random ID, checking for collisions.
- **Storage**: a key-value store or database table mapping code to URL.
- **Caching**: popular codes in an in-memory cache, since reads vastly outnumber writes.
- **Scale**: stateless app servers behind a load balancer; replicate the database for reads.
- **Extras**: analytics through an asynchronous queue, expiry, abuse checks.

Practise explaining each choice and its alternatives.

## What is the difference between system design and software architecture?

They overlap heavily. Software architecture usually refers to the high-level structure and principles of a system and the decisions that are expensive to change; system design is the broader activity of designing a specific system, from architecture down to data models, APIs and capacity planning.

In practice, architecture answers questions like "monolith or services, synchronous or event-driven, which data stores", and system design also covers "this table, this index, this cache policy, this API contract, this number of servers". Architects focus on long-term structure across many systems and teams; system design interviews test whether you can design one system end to end. Both depend on understanding requirements and trade-offs.

## What is system design in AI?

AI system design adds machine learning concerns to classic design: data pipelines, feature or document processing, model training or selection, serving and scaling inference, retrieval for LLM apps, evaluation, monitoring for quality drift, and cost per request.

For an LLM application, a design might include document ingestion and chunking, an embedding model and vector index, hybrid retrieval and reranking, an LLM call with a grounded prompt, guardrails, caching, fallbacks across providers, and evaluation and logging. RAG.NextUpgrad is a compact example: hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, cited streaming answers, a confidence gate that refuses weak evidence, multi-provider fallback, and a small enough footprint, about 220 MB, to run on a free tier. Interviews for AI roles increasingly include designs like this.

## What is agentic AI system design?

Agentic AI system design is designing systems where a model plans and takes actions with tools. Beyond normal design, it covers the agent loop, tool definitions and permissions, state and memory, limits on steps and cost, human approval for risky actions, evaluation and observability.

Key decisions include how much autonomy to grant, since workflows with a few agentic steps are often more reliable than fully autonomous agents; how tools authenticate and what they may change; how to persist state so long tasks can resume; how to defend against prompt injection from content the agent reads; and how to trace every step for debugging. Designs should define failure behaviour clearly: when unsure, the agent asks or stops rather than guessing.

## Is system design AI-proof?

No skill is entirely AI-proof, but system design is among the most durable. AI tools can suggest components and draw diagrams, but deciding trade-offs for a specific business, team, budget and risk tolerance requires judgement and accountability that remain human responsibilities.

AI actually raises the value of design skills. As coding becomes faster with AI assistance, the bottleneck shifts to deciding what to build and how pieces fit together, and to reviewing AI-generated code against that design. Engineers who can design systems, including AI systems, evaluate trade-offs and explain decisions clearly are well placed. Use AI tools to explore alternatives faster, but own the decisions.

## What is system design in VLSI?

In VLSI, very large-scale integration, system design means designing electronic chips: defining the architecture of a chip or system-on-chip, then implementing it in hardware description languages, verifying it, and taking it through synthesis, layout and fabrication.

The flow typically goes from specification and architecture, to register-transfer level design in Verilog or VHDL, functional verification, logic synthesis, physical design including placement and routing, timing analysis and sign-off checks. It is a different field from software system design, though both involve architecture, trade-offs and verification. Electronics students interested in it should learn digital design, HDLs and verification, and get familiar with EDA tools from vendors such as Cadence, Synopsys and Siemens.

## How do I use a design system?

A design system, in UI and product design, is a shared library of components, styles and guidelines, such as buttons, colours, typography and spacing, used to build consistent interfaces. Use it by building screens from its components instead of styling from scratch.

To use one well: learn its tokens for colours, spacing and type; use existing components before creating new ones; follow its accessibility and usage guidelines; and contribute improvements back rather than making one-off variations. Popular examples include Google's Material Design and many open-source React component libraries. Despite the similar name, it is unrelated to system design interviews, which are about software architecture and scale.

# What is a tech fest? Event, project, poster and decoration ideas, and Best Buy Tech Fest
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-tech-fest/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A tech fest is a festival of technology events, usually organised by college students, featuring hackathons, coding contests, robotics, workshops, expert talks, project exhibitions and gaming, often over two or three days. Indian college tech fests range from department events to large national festivals that attract thousands of participants. I have spoken at campus events and won hackathons at college fests such as Vividhotsava 2025, so this page covers what tech fests are, event and project ideas, posters, decoration, Black Tech Fest, and Best Buy's Tech Fest deals.

## What is a tech fest?

A tech fest is an event, usually at a college, that celebrates technology through competitions, learning sessions and showcases. Students compete in coding, hackathons, robotics and quizzes, attend workshops and talks, and display projects, while companies sponsor events and scout talent.

Tech fests build skills and communities: participants learn by doing, meet peers from other colleges, and connect with mentors and recruiters. Organising one teaches leadership, budgeting, sponsorship and event management. Large fests also feature startup expos, panel discussions and cultural events alongside technical ones, making them some of the most energetic events on the college calendar. For first-year students, attending a tech fest is often the first exposure to hackathons, open source and industry speakers, which can shape the rest of their college journey.

## What is a technical fest?

A technical fest is the same idea, with emphasis on engineering and science competitions: coding, hackathons, robotics, circuit design, technical paper presentations, model exhibitions, CAD and quizzes, organised by colleges or technical societies.

Many colleges run an annual technical fest alongside a cultural fest. Events are often divided by department, so computer science, electronics, mechanical and civil students each find relevant competitions, plus interdisciplinary events such as hackathons. Participation certificates and prizes add to resumes, and the experience of competing under time pressure is valuable preparation for placements.

## What are good tech fest event ideas?

Mix competitions, learning and fun so beginners and experts both participate. Popular events include hackathons, competitive coding, AI and data challenges, robotics races, web design contests, debugging challenges, tech quizzes, project expos, workshops and expert talks.

More ideas:

- A prompt engineering or AI app challenge.
- A capture-the-flag cybersecurity contest.
- A startup pitch competition with mentor feedback.
- A UI/UX design sprint.
- An open-source contribution day.
- A "build with AI in two hours" mini-hackathon for first-years.

Include at least one beginner-friendly event so first-year students do not feel excluded. Publish rules, judging criteria and schedules early, and run a short orientation for participants so events start on time.

## What are good tech festival ideas beyond competitions?

Add experiences that create learning and connection: hands-on workshops, talks by alumni and engineers, panel discussions on careers, project showcases, startup stalls, gaming zones, VR and robotics demos, and networking sessions with sponsors.

Workshops on in-demand skills, such as building RAG chatbots, deploying web apps or using Git, often attract more students than competitions. Talks work best when speakers share real projects and practical roadmaps; in my campus sessions, live demos and concrete plans get the strongest response. A themed fest, such as "AI for Bharat" or "Tech for Sustainability", gives coherence to events, posters and decoration.

## What are good tech fest project ideas?

Good projects solve real problems with working demos: an AI assistant that answers questions from college documents, a local-language voice assistant, an accessibility tool, a smart attendance system with privacy protection, an agriculture advisory bot, or a surplus-food coordination app.

Judges at fest exhibitions value clear problems, live demos, technical depth and impact. Projects like KrishGyan, which gives farmers advice in their own voice and language over WhatsApp, and Annapurna, which coordinates surplus food, show how simple ideas with real users stand out. Prepare a short explanation, a demo flow that works reliably, and answers about your design choices. Bring a backup video of the demo in case the venue Wi-Fi fails, which happens at almost every fest.

## What are good tech fest poster ideas?

Effective posters have one bold visual theme, a clear fest name, dates, venue, key events and a registration QR code, readable from a distance. Futuristic, circuit, space, cyberpunk and minimalist styles are popular for tech fests.

Design tips:

- Make the fest name and dates the largest text.
- Use two or three colours that match your theme.
- Add a QR code linking to registration.
- List highlight events, not every event.
- Keep text minimal and fonts readable.
- Create versions for social media, print and stories.

Tools such as Canva and Figma offer templates; customise them so your fest has a distinct identity.

## What are good tech fest decoration ideas?

Use the fest's theme consistently: LED strips and neon colours for futuristic looks, circuit-board patterns, cardboard robots, space or cyberpunk installations, projection mapping, and photo booths with tech props. Direct visitors with clear signage to event venues.

Budget-friendly ideas: recycled electronics as art, paper-craft geometric shapes, QR code walls linking to projects, and student-made LED displays. Interactive decoration, such as a gesture-controlled light display built by students, doubles as a showcase. Make sure decorations are safe, with secure wiring and clear pathways, and plan clean-up and recycling afterwards.

## What is Black Tech Fest?

Black Tech Fest is an annual festival in the United Kingdom that celebrates and connects Black professionals and talent in technology, featuring talks, panels, workshops and networking, with the aim of improving representation and inclusion in the tech industry.

Events like it, along with communities supporting women, LGBTQ+ people and first-generation students in tech, address barriers to entering and progressing in the industry. Their approach, role models, mentorship, networking and accessible learning, applies to inclusion efforts everywhere, including college tech fests that want to welcome students from all backgrounds.

## What is Tech Fest at Best Buy?

At Best Buy, the US electronics retailer, "Tech Fest" is the name used for promotional sales events offering discounts on laptops, TVs, phones, appliances and other electronics for a limited period.

These events are unrelated to college tech fests. If you shop during such sales, compare prices across retailers, check that discounted models are current, read return policies and avoid buying unneeded items because of time-limited offers. Similar sales happen in India through online marketplaces and electronics chains during festive seasons.

## What is a Tech Fest deal?

A Tech Fest deal is a discounted offer during a retailer's Tech Fest sale, such as reduced prices on laptops, headphones or smart devices, sometimes with bundles, gift cards or limited-time pricing.

To judge a deal, check the product's price history with price trackers, compare specifications with newer models, and read reviews. For students buying laptops for coding or AI work, prioritise RAM, storage and processor over flashy features, and consider whether a GPU is needed. A genuinely good deal is on something you already planned to buy. Check warranty terms and whether the seller is authorised, since grey-market products may lack local service support.

# What is tool calling in AI? Tool vs function calling, LangChain, MCP and Gemma
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-tool-calling/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Tool calling is how a language model uses external tools: you describe tools to the model, it decides when one is needed and returns a structured request with arguments, your application runs the tool, and the result goes back to the model so it can continue. Tools can be anything code can do: search, calculators, databases, APIs, file operations or other agents. This page explains tool calling in AI and how it works, how it relates to function calling, tool-calling models, LangChain, agentic AI, MCP, and whether Gemma supports it.

## What is tool calling?

Tool calling is a capability of language models to request the use of external tools by producing a structured call, usually a tool name and JSON arguments, instead of plain text. The application executes the tool and returns the result to the model.

This bridges the gap between language and action. A model cannot check today's train timings or query your database by itself, but with a `search_trains(from, to, date)` tool it can request exactly that, then answer from real data. Tool calling also makes structured output reliable, because arguments must match a schema. It is the foundation of AI agents and of integrations such as coding assistants that edit files and run tests.

## What is tool calling in AI?

In AI, tool calling extends a model's abilities beyond its training data and text generation, letting it retrieve live information, compute precisely and take actions in other systems, under the control of the application.

Examples include chatbots that look up orders, assistants that schedule meetings, coding agents that read files and run commands, research agents that search the web, and data assistants that run SQL queries. In each, the model decides what to call and with what arguments, and the application decides what is allowed. Good systems keep sensitive actions behind confirmations and log every call for review.

## How does tool calling work?

You send the model the conversation plus tool definitions with names, descriptions and input schemas. The model either answers or returns one or more tool calls. Your code validates and runs them, adds the results to the conversation, and calls the model again.

The loop in steps:

- Define tools clearly: what each does and when to use it.
- Send the user message and tool list to the model.
- If the model returns tool calls, validate arguments and execute.
- Return results to the model, marked as tool results.
- Repeat until the model gives a final answer, with a step limit.

Tool descriptions are the most important prompt in this process: models choose tools by reading them.

## What is the difference between tool calling and function calling?

They mean essentially the same thing. "Function calling" was the name OpenAI used when it launched the feature in 2023; "tool calling" or "tool use" is the broader term now used by most providers, since tools also include built-in capabilities such as web search and code execution.

In practice, a "function" is one kind of tool: a custom operation you define with a JSON schema. Providers also offer server-side tools they run themselves, such as search or code interpreters, alongside your functions. APIs and frameworks use both terms, sometimes interchangeably, so do not let naming confuse you: the concept is the model requesting a structured action that the system performs.

## What are tool-calling models?

Tool-calling models are language models trained to decide when to use tools and to produce correctly formatted tool calls. Most current major models support it, including models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Mistral, and many open-weight models.

Quality differs in choosing the right tool, producing valid arguments, handling many tools, and calling tools in sequence for multi-step tasks. Frontier models are generally most reliable; smaller open models work for simple tool sets. Leaderboards for function calling compare models, but testing with your own tools and tasks is essential. When running open models locally, check that the model and serving tool, such as Ollama or vLLM, support tool calling.

## What is tool calling in LangChain?

In LangChain, tool calling means defining tools, often with the `@tool` decorator on a Python function, binding them to a chat model with `bind_tools`, and handling the tool calls the model returns, either manually or through an agent that runs the loop.

```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers."""
    return a + b

llm = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5").bind_tools([add])
msg = llm.invoke("What is 19 + 23?")
print(msg.tool_calls)     # [{'name': 'add', 'args': {'a': 19, 'b': 23}, ...}]
```

LangChain standardises tool calls across providers, so the same code works with different models. Check the docs for current model names.

## What is tool calling in agentic AI?

In agentic AI, tool calling is the mechanism through which agents act: the agent repeatedly reasons about the goal, calls tools, observes results and decides the next step, until the task is complete or it needs a person.

The quality of an agent depends heavily on its tools: a small set of well-designed, clearly described tools with good error messages works far better than many overlapping ones. Agents also need guardrails around tool calls: permission checks, confirmation for destructive actions, limits on steps and cost, and defences against prompt injection from tool results. Logging every call makes debugging and auditing possible.

## Is tool calling agentic?

A single tool call is not agentic by itself; it is one structured request. A system becomes agentic when the model uses tool calls in a loop, choosing which tools to use and when, to pursue a goal across multiple steps.

For example, a chatbot that always calls a weather API for weather questions is tool use, not an agent. A system that plans a trip by searching trains, checking hotels, comparing options and asking you to confirm bookings is agentic. Many useful products sit in between: mostly fixed workflows with one or two model-chosen tool calls, which are easier to test and more reliable than fully autonomous agents.

## Is MCP tool calling?

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is not tool calling itself; it is a standard way to provide tools, resources and prompts to AI applications. The model still uses tool calling to invoke MCP tools, while the MCP client handles talking to MCP servers.

In practice: an MCP server exposes tools such as `query_database`; the AI application, as an MCP client, lists them to the model as available tools; the model returns a tool call; the client forwards it to the server and returns the result. MCP's value is reuse: build a tool once as an MCP server and use it from many assistants and agents, instead of writing separate integrations for each.

## Can Gemma do tool calling?

Gemma models can be used for function calling: Google's newer Gemma releases support it through prompting and structured outputs, and serving tools that run Gemma, such as Ollama or Hugging Face libraries, can expose tool calling depending on the model version and template.

Results are best with clear function descriptions, few tools and strict JSON schemas, and with validation in your code. Smaller Gemma sizes make more mistakes on complex tool use than larger hosted models. For production agents needing many tools, test carefully or use a larger model; for simple local tasks, such as routing requests or extracting fields, Gemma can work well. Check Google's Gemma documentation for the current function-calling guidance.
