# What is vector data? GIS vector data, vector database data, storage, and why vector DBs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vector-data/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


"Vector data" means two different things. In geography and GIS, vector data represents real-world features as points, lines and polygons with attributes, such as wells, roads and district boundaries. In AI, vector data means embeddings: lists of numbers that represent the meaning of text, images or audio so software can search by similarity. I work with the AI kind in RAG.NextUpgrad and FaceVision, so this page covers both meanings, examples, how vector databases store data, why and how to use one, LangChain, and initialisation vectors in encryption.

## What is vector data?

In GIS, vector data stores geographic features as geometry, coordinates forming points, lines or polygons, plus attribute tables describing them. In machine learning, vector data is numerical arrays, embeddings, representing items in a high-dimensional space.

The two share the mathematical idea of vectors but serve different purposes. GIS vector data answers "where is it and what is it?", such as the boundary of a farm and its crop type. AI vector data answers "what is similar to this?", such as finding documents related to a question. Context usually makes the meaning clear: shapefiles and GeoJSON are GIS; embeddings and vector databases are AI.

## What is the vector data model?

In GIS, the vector data model represents the world as discrete features: points for single locations, lines for linear features such as rivers and roads, and polygons for areas such as lakes and administrative boundaries. Each feature links to attributes in a table.

It contrasts with the raster model, which represents the world as a grid of cells, suited to continuous data such as elevation, rainfall or satellite imagery. Vector data is precise, compact for discrete features and good for network analysis and maps with sharp boundaries. Common formats include shapefiles, GeoJSON, GeoPackage and spatial databases such as PostGIS.

## What are some vector data examples?

GIS examples: schools and hospitals as points, roads, railways and rivers as lines, and state boundaries, land parcels and lakes as polygons. AI examples: sentence embeddings for search, image embeddings for visual similarity, and face embeddings for recognition.

Concretely, a GeoJSON file of bus stops is GIS vector data, each stop a point with a name and route attributes. A 384-number embedding of the sentence "How do I apply for a scholarship?" is AI vector data. In FaceVision, each enrolled face becomes an embedding vector, stored without the original image, and recognition compares a new face's vector against stored ones.

## What does data in a vector database look like?

Each record typically has an ID, a vector of numbers, metadata such as source, title, page and date, and often the original text chunk. For example: ID "handbook-p12-c3", a 768-number embedding, metadata about the hostel rules section, and the chunk text.

```json
{"id": "handbook-p12-c3",
 "vector": [0.021, -0.113, 0.087, "..."],
 "metadata": {"source": "student-handbook.pdf", "page": 12, "section": "Hostel rules"},
 "text": "Students must return to the hostel by 10 pm..."}
```

Queries send a vector, plus optional metadata filters, and receive the most similar records with scores.

## How do vector databases store data?

Vector databases store vectors with IDs and metadata in segments on disk or in memory, and build approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, commonly HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, so searches check only promising candidates instead of every vector.

Many also compress vectors with quantisation to save memory, keep payload or metadata indexes for filtering, and use write-ahead logs for durability. Database extensions such as pgvector store vectors in ordinary table columns, with indexes managed by PostgreSQL. Storage design trades off memory, speed and accuracy, so most systems let you tune index parameters and choose in-memory or disk-based storage.

## Does a vector database keep the original chunked text for RAG?

It can, and for RAG it usually should. Most vector databases let you store the chunk text and metadata alongside each vector, so retrieval returns the text needed for the prompt. Alternatively, store only IDs and fetch text from another database.

Storing text with vectors is simpler; keeping text in a separate store suits large documents, strict access control or existing databases. Either way, keep the original documents and chunk text somewhere durable, because you will need to re-embed everything when you change embedding models. Vectors alone cannot be reliably turned back into exact text, and you need the text for citations.

## Why do we need a vector database?

We need vector databases to search large collections by meaning quickly, with filtering, updates and persistence. Comparing a query against millions of vectors one by one is too slow; vector indexes make it fast.

You may not need a dedicated one: for small collections, an in-memory library or a few thousand vectors in a NumPy array works; for apps already on PostgreSQL, pgvector is often enough. Dedicated vector databases help with very large scale, heavy filtering, multi-tenancy and high query volumes. Choose based on data size, latency needs and what your team already operates.

## How do I use a vector database?

Choose an embedding model, embed your data in chunks, insert vectors with IDs, metadata and text, create an index, then embed each query with the same model and search for the nearest vectors, optionally with filters.

Steps for a RAG app:

- Chunk documents and embed each chunk.
- Upsert vectors with metadata such as source and page.
- Create an HNSW or similar index.
- At query time, embed the question and retrieve the top 5 to 20.
- Optionally combine with keyword search and rerank.
- Pass the best chunks to a language model with citation instructions.

Record the embedding model name with your index so you never mix models.

## Does LangChain have a vector database?

LangChain is not a vector database, but it provides a common vector store interface with integrations for many databases, including pgvector, Chroma, FAISS, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate and Milvus, plus a simple in-memory store for testing.

This lets you write retrieval code once and switch backends with minimal changes. For production, choose the underlying database deliberately for scale, filtering and operations, and consider writing direct queries when you need features the abstraction does not expose, such as hybrid search tuned in SQL. LangChain's retriever interface then connects the store to chains and agents.

## What is the difference between an initialisation vector and a key in encryption?

The key is the secret that encrypts and decrypts data and must be protected. The initialisation vector, or IV, is a random or unique value used with the key so the same plaintext encrypts differently each time; it is not secret but must not be reused improperly.

For example, with AES in GCM mode, each message needs a unique nonce or IV with the same key; reusing one can break security badly. The IV is usually stored or sent alongside the ciphertext. This "vector" is simply a block of bytes and has nothing to do with embeddings or GIS vector data. Use well-tested libraries rather than implementing encryption yourself.

# What is a vector embedding? Embedding models, search, and long texts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vector-embedding/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A vector embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of data, such as a word, sentence, image or document, so that similar things have vectors close together. Embedding models produce these vectors, and vector search uses them to find the most similar items to a query, which is the retrieval step in RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains embeddings and embedding models, how search works, terminology, building an embedding layer from scratch, long texts, embeddings versus TF-IDF, rerankers, and choosing a model.

## What is a vector embedding?

A vector embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers, often hundreds or thousands long, that encodes the meaning or features of an input. Inputs with similar meaning map to vectors that are close in that space, measured by cosine similarity or distance.

For example, "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login" have different words but similar embeddings, so a search using embeddings matches them. Embeddings exist for text, images, audio and code, and multimodal models can place images and text in the same space. They power semantic search, recommendations, clustering, duplicate detection and classification, and they are the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation.

## What is an embedding model?

An embedding model is a neural network that converts input, such as text, into an embedding vector. Text embedding models are trained so that related sentences or passages produce nearby vectors and unrelated ones produce distant vectors.

You can use hosted embedding models through APIs from providers such as OpenAI, Google and others, or open models from Hugging Face, such as sentence-transformers and newer open embedding families, run locally or through Ollama. Important properties are the vector dimension, maximum input length, supported languages and quality on retrieval benchmarks. The rule that matters most in practice: use the same embedding model for indexing documents and for embedding queries, or the vectors will not be comparable.

## How does an embedding model work?

Modern text embedding models are transformer encoders. They tokenise the text, process tokens with attention so each token's representation reflects its context, and pool the token vectors, for example by averaging, into one vector for the whole text.

They learn useful vectors through contrastive training: pairs of related texts, such as a question and its answer passage, are pulled together, while unrelated texts are pushed apart. Training on millions of such pairs teaches the model which meanings are similar. Sentence-BERT popularised this approach for sentence embeddings. Some models also accept instructions, such as "represent this query for retrieval", which improves search quality, so follow each model's usage notes on its model card.

## How does vector embedding search work?

You embed every document chunk once and store the vectors in an index. At query time, you embed the query with the same model and find the stored vectors nearest to it, returning their chunks as results.

Comparing a query with every vector works for small collections but becomes slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, that return nearly the best matches in milliseconds. Normalise vectors and use cosine similarity or inner product as the model recommends. In production, combine vector search with keyword search, merge the lists with reciprocal-rank fusion, and add metadata filters, because embeddings alone often miss exact terms such as IDs and error codes.

## Are "vector embedding" and "embedding vector" interchangeable?

Yes, in practice they mean the same thing: the vector produced by an embedding model. "Embedding" alone is also common. Strictly, "embedding" can mean the mapping itself, while "embedding vector" is one output of it.

You will also see "dense vector" or "dense representation", in contrast to sparse vectors from keyword methods such as BM25 or TF-IDF, where most values are zero. In vector database documentation, "vectors" usually refers to embeddings. When writing documentation or reports, pick one term and use it consistently, and say which model produced the vectors, because embeddings from different models are not interchangeable.

## How can I create an embedding layer from scratch?

An embedding layer is a lookup table: a matrix with one row per word in your vocabulary, initialised randomly and learned during training. In PyTorch, `nn.Embedding` provides it; training the network on a task updates the rows so useful word relationships emerge.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
vocab = {"<pad>": 0, "ai": 1, "model": 2, "data": 3}
emb = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=len(vocab), embedding_dim=8, padding_idx=0)
ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3]])
vectors = emb(ids)          # shape (1, 3, 8)
```

To learn word vectors without a downstream task, train word2vec-style: predict surrounding words from a word, or the reverse, which makes words in similar contexts get similar vectors. For real projects, pre-trained sentence embedding models are far better than training from scratch.

## How do you create embeddings for long texts?

Split long texts into chunks, embed each chunk, and store them separately with a reference to the source document. A single vector for a 32,000-character document averages away detail, and many embedding models cannot accept that much text anyway.

Chunking guidelines:

- Split by structure, such as headings and paragraphs, to keep ideas together.
- Use chunks of a few hundred tokens, with small overlap where meaning spans boundaries.
- Include the document title and section heading in each chunk's text.
- Keep page numbers and IDs in metadata for citations.

If you need one vector per document, for example for clustering, average the chunk embeddings or use a long-context embedding model, but retrieve at chunk level for question answering.

## Vector embeddings vs TF-IDF: which is better for document similarity?

Embeddings usually perform better when meaning matters and wording differs, such as paraphrases and questions versus answers. TF-IDF and BM25 perform better for exact terms, rare names, codes and specialised jargon. Combining both usually beats either alone.

TF-IDF and bag-of-words count words, so "car" and "automobile" do not match, but "error 0x80070005" matches exactly. Embeddings capture semantics but can blur specific identifiers. TF-IDF is also cheap, transparent and needs no model. A sound approach is to evaluate both on your own data with labelled similar pairs or search queries, then use hybrid retrieval: run both, and merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with dense retrieval and BM25.

## What is the difference between an embedding model and a reranking model?

An embedding model encodes the query and each document separately into vectors, which makes search over millions of documents fast. A reranking model, usually a cross-encoder, reads the query and one document together and outputs a relevance score, which is more accurate but too slow to run over everything.

So they work in two stages: embeddings, often with keyword search, retrieve the top 50 to 100 candidates quickly, and the reranker reorders those candidates by true relevance. Adding a reranker is one of the most effective ways to improve RAG answers, because the right passage is often retrieved but ranked too low to reach the prompt. Measure retrieval recall at 5 before and after adding one.

## What is the best embedding model for semantic search?

There is no universal best. Check the MTEB leaderboard for retrieval scores, then test two or three candidates on your own queries, considering language support, maximum input length, vector size, speed and cost.

Practical guidance:

- **Hosted and easy**: embedding APIs from major providers.
- **Open and local**: strong sentence-transformers and newer open embedding models, runnable with Ollama or Hugging Face.
- **Indian languages or mixed Hindi-English**: choose a multilingual model and test on your own data.
- **Large scale**: smaller dimensions reduce storage and speed up search.

Build a test set of 50 real queries with known relevant passages, and pick the model with the best recall at 5 for your data, not the best leaderboard score.

# What is vibe coding? Origin, best platforms, Claude and GitHub, and jobs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vibe-coding-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI tool in plain language, running what it produces, and steering by results rather than writing or reading every line yourself. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025, and it spread quickly with app builders and coding agents. It is a fast way to prototype and a risky way to ship. This page covers its origin, the main apps and platforms, how to do it with Claude and GitHub Copilot, Power Apps, when to use it, whether it helps you get a job, and its future.

## What is vibe coding in AI?

Vibe coding is a style of AI-assisted programming where you describe the app or feature you want, let an AI generate the code, test it by using it, and keep asking for changes until it works, focusing on the result rather than the code itself.

It differs from traditional AI-assisted coding, where a developer reads and owns every line the assistant suggests. In vibe coding the human acts more like a product owner: "add a login page", "make the button blue", "fix this error". It lowers the barrier to building, letting non-programmers create working tools. The trade-off is hidden problems: security holes, duplicated logic, fragile code and dependencies nobody understands, which surface later.

## When was vibe coding coined?

Andrej Karpathy, an AI researcher who co-founded OpenAI and led AI at Tesla, coined "vibe coding" in a post in February 2025, describing coding where you "give in to the vibes" and let the AI handle the code.

The term caught on quickly because it named something many people were already doing with tools such as Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT and app builders. Within months, it was used in product marketing, job posts and debates about software quality. It describes a practice made possible by much stronger coding models and agentic tools in 2024 and 2025, which could write and fix whole features rather than single lines.

## What are vibe coding apps?

Vibe coding apps let you build software from natural language. Browser-based app builders such as Lovable, Bolt, v0 by Vercel and Replit generate and host full apps from prompts; coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent mode and Codex work inside real codebases.

The two groups suit different people. App builders give the fastest path from idea to a running web app with hosting included, ideal for non-developers and prototypes. Coding agents work with your own repository, tools and tests, ideal for developers who want speed with control. Many builders start a prototype in an app builder, export the code, and continue in a coding agent when the project becomes serious.

## Which vibe coding platform is best?

For non-developers building a web app prototype, Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Replit are the easiest. For developers working on real projects, Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot's agent mode give more control and better results on existing codebases.

How to choose:

- **Speed to a hosted demo**: an app builder.
- **Your own stack and repository**: a coding agent.
- **Team on GitHub with enterprise controls**: GitHub Copilot.
- **Long, multi-file changes**: Claude Code or Cursor's agent.
- **Free start**: free tiers of several tools, which change often.

Try two on the same small project, such as a hackathon registration app, and compare how much you had to fix.

## How do I vibe code with Claude?

Use Claude Code in your terminal or IDE for real projects, or artifacts on claude.ai for quick prototypes. Describe the feature, let Claude build it, run it, and ask for fixes with exact error messages.

A workflow with Claude Code:

- Start a project folder with Git, and add a `CLAUDE.md` describing the stack and rules.
- Ask for a plan first: "Plan a Next.js app for hackathon registrations with a form and admin list."
- Build feature by feature, running the app after each step.
- Ask for tests alongside features.
- Commit after every working step so you can roll back.
- Ask Claude to review the code for security issues before sharing.

Keep API keys in `.env` files and never paste secrets into prompts.

## How do I vibe code with GitHub?

Use GitHub Copilot's agent mode in VS Code to build features from natural language, and the Copilot coding agent on GitHub to hand off issues and review the pull requests it opens. GitHub then gives you version history, reviews and continuous integration.

Steps:

- Create a repository and open it in VS Code with Copilot.
- Add `.github/copilot-instructions.md` with your stack and conventions.
- In agent mode, describe a feature and review each change before accepting.
- Set up GitHub Actions to run tests on every push.
- For small tasks, write an issue with clear acceptance criteria and assign it to Copilot.

Version control is what makes vibe coding safe: every change is reviewable and reversible.

## What is vibe coding in Power Apps?

In Power Apps, Microsoft's low-code platform, vibe coding refers to building business apps by describing them in natural language with Copilot, which generates the app's screens, data tables and logic for you to refine.

You describe something like "an app for tracking lab equipment loans with a form, a list and an approval step", and Copilot proposes the data structure and screens, which you then adjust conversationally or in the editor. Because it runs on the Power Platform, the result inherits Microsoft 365 sign-in, Dataverse data storage and admin governance, which suits organisations. Microsoft's natural-language app-building features have been changing quickly, so check current Power Apps documentation for what is available.

## When should I use vibe coding?

Use vibe coding for prototypes, hackathon builds, internal tools, personal scripts and exploring ideas, where speed matters more than long-term maintainability. Avoid pure vibe coding for production systems that handle money, personal data or security-sensitive operations.

Signs it fits: a short-lived project, a demo, a tool only you use, or a first version to test with users. Signs it does not: payments, authentication, health or legal data, or code that a team must maintain for years. For those, use AI as a pair programmer instead: generate code, but read it, test it and understand it. Security basics, such as input validation and access control, are where vibe-coded apps fail most often.

## Can vibe coding get you a job?

Not on its own. Employers hire people who can build reliable software and explain how it works. Vibe coding can help you ship more projects faster, which helps, but only if you understand and can defend what you built.

How to make it count: use AI tools to build real projects, then study the code, refactor it, add tests and write a README explaining design decisions. In interviews, you will be asked why you chose an approach, how you handled errors and what you would change. Hackathon judges ask the same, and I have seen teams lose points for polished demos they could not explain. Skill with AI coding tools is now expected; understanding is what sets you apart.

## Why is vibe coding the future?

Because building software through natural language makes creation accessible to far more people and makes developers much faster. The future is likely a mix: vibe coding for exploration and simple apps, and engineering discipline for systems people depend on.

As models improve, more of the code will be written by AI, and the human role shifts to defining requirements, designing systems, reviewing changes, testing and taking responsibility for quality and security. That favours people who combine product sense with engineering judgement. Students should learn to use AI coding tools fluently while building strong fundamentals, because when the vibes fail, someone has to debug the system.

# What is vibe coding? How it works, doing it well with Cursor or Copilot, and its future
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vibe-coding-3/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI coding tool in plain language, running what it produces, and steering by results rather than reading every line. It makes prototypes possible in hours, even for non-programmers, but it can hide bugs and security holes when used carelessly. I build production AI products and use AI coding tools daily, so this page covers what vibe coding is, its name, doing it well with Cursor or Copilot, tools, whether it is easy or a skill, the criticism, and its future.

## What is vibe coding and how does it work?

Vibe coding is a style of programming where you prompt an AI to write code, run the result, describe what to change, and repeat, often accepting changes without studying them closely. The AI acts as the programmer; you act as the product owner and tester.

A typical loop: describe the app, let an agent create files, run it, paste error messages back, ask for features, and keep going. Tools such as Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot's agent mode, Replit and Lovable support this. It works surprisingly well for small apps, scripts and prototypes. It works poorly when the codebase grows and nobody understands it, because problems compound and become hard to fix.

## Why is it called vibe coding?

The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy, a co-founder of OpenAI and former head of AI at Tesla, in a post in February 2025. He described "fully giving in to the vibes" and forgetting the code even exists, accepting AI suggestions and steering by feel.

The phrase spread quickly because it captured a real shift: people building working software by conversation. Its popularity led dictionaries to recognise it, with Collins naming it a word of the year for 2025. Over time, "vibe coding" has also been used loosely for any AI-assisted coding, though its original meaning is specifically about not reviewing the code closely.

## How do I vibe code effectively?

Work in small, testable steps, keep the AI focused with clear instructions, run and test after every change, commit to git often so you can roll back, and read the parts that matter: security, data handling and anything that touches money or users.

Practices that work:

- Start with a short spec: features, stack, data model and constraints.
- Ask for one feature at a time, then test it.
- Keep a project rules file describing conventions for the AI.
- Paste exact error messages and expected behaviour when fixing bugs.
- Ask the AI to write tests, and run them.
- Review authentication, database queries and secrets handling yourself.

## How do I vibe code with Cursor?

Open your project in Cursor, use the agent or chat panel to describe what to build, let it edit files across the project, and review the diffs before accepting. Add project rules so it follows your conventions, and run your app after each change.

Tips specific to Cursor: reference files or folders with the @ symbol to give precise context; use a rules file to describe your stack and style; break big requests into steps; check diffs rather than accepting everything blindly; and use checkpoints or git to revert bad changes. Choose the model per task, using stronger models for complex changes. Run tests in Cursor's terminal and let the agent fix failures.

## Can I vibe code with GitHub Copilot?

Yes. GitHub Copilot's chat and agent mode in VS Code and other editors can create and edit files, run commands and iterate on errors, which supports a vibe coding workflow. Copilot's coding agent can also work on GitHub issues and open pull requests.

Use Copilot's agent mode for multi-file changes, custom instructions files for project conventions, and pull request reviews to check AI changes before merging. As with any tool, quality depends on clear instructions and testing. Copilot integrates tightly with GitHub, which makes reviewing AI-generated changes through pull requests natural for teams.

## Which vibe coding tool is best?

It depends on your skill and goal. Cursor and Claude Code suit developers working on real codebases; GitHub Copilot suits teams on GitHub; Replit, Lovable and Bolt suit non-developers building web apps quickly in the browser with hosting included.

Compare on: how well the tool understands your whole project, model quality, ability to run and test code, deployment options, cost and data privacy. For learning, a tool that shows diffs and explains changes helps you understand the code. For production, choose tools that fit code review, testing and version control. Try two tools on the same small project and keep the one whose output needs the least fixing.

## Is vibe coding easy?

Starting is easy: you can build a simple working app in an afternoon without deep programming knowledge. Keeping it working as it grows is hard, because without understanding the code you cannot easily diagnose bugs, performance issues or security problems.

Beginners often hit a wall when the AI keeps "fixing" one bug and creating another, or when deployment, databases and authentication get involved. Learning programming basics, reading error messages, understanding project structure and using git, makes vibe coding dramatically more effective. The people who get the most from AI tools are those who can judge whether the output is right.

## Is vibe coding a skill?

Yes, partly: writing clear specifications, breaking problems into steps, testing thoroughly and steering an AI efficiently are real skills. But it is not a substitute for software engineering skills like design, debugging, security and maintainability.

Employers increasingly expect developers to use AI tools productively, so the skill is valuable when combined with fundamentals. A developer who understands architecture and reviews AI output ships faster and safer than one who either avoids AI or accepts everything blindly. For students, use AI to learn faster, asking it to explain code, while making sure you can build and debug without it.

## Why is vibe coding frowned upon?

Critics point to real risks: code nobody understands, security vulnerabilities such as exposed keys and injection flaws, poor performance, duplicated logic, and apps that break unpredictably. Shipping such code to real users can cause data leaks and outages.

There have been public examples of vibe-coded apps leaking user data through misconfigured databases or exposed secrets. Experienced engineers also worry that beginners skip learning fundamentals. The criticism is mainly about using vibe coding for production systems without review. For prototypes, demos, learning and personal tools, most engineers consider it a useful and legitimate approach.

## Will vibe coding die?

The label may fade, but AI-assisted software development will not. Tools are improving at understanding codebases, testing and reviewing their own work, so building by describing intent will become more common and more reliable.

What will likely change is the balance: professional work will blend AI generation with strong review, testing and architecture, sometimes called agentic engineering, while pure "never read the code" vibe coding stays mostly in prototyping and personal projects. The durable skills are knowing what to build, specifying it clearly, verifying results and owning quality, which matter more as AI writes more code.

# What is vLLM? vLLM vs Ollama vs llama.cpp vs SGLang, and how to actually serve an LLM in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vllm-ollama-and-llm-inference-serving/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is vLLM?

**vLLM is an open-source inference server for large language models built around PagedAttention, a memory-management technique that lets many concurrent requests share a GPU's memory efficiently by managing the attention key-value cache the way an operating system manages virtual memory, in pages, rather than reserving one large contiguous block per request [1][2]. The practical result is much higher throughput on the same hardware compared with naively calling a model's `generate()` method for each request, which is why vLLM is the default choice for serving open-weight models at real request volume.**


Every production system I run that serves an open model sits on some form of batched serving; the difference between "it works in a notebook" and "it serves five hundred requests a minute without falling over" is almost entirely this layer.

> A model that answers one request beautifully and a service that answers a thousand requests a minute are different engineering problems. vLLM, SGLang and friends are the answer to the second one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why can't I just call `model.generate()` for production traffic?

**Because it processes one request, or a small fixed batch, at a time, and each request occupies GPU memory for its full duration even while it is producing tokens slowly one at a time. Real traffic arrives as many concurrent requests of different lengths, and naive batching either wastes memory reserving worst-case space for every request or wastes GPU time waiting for a batch to fill before starting. Continuous batching solves the second problem, starting and finishing requests within a batch as they arrive and complete rather than waiting for a fixed batch to fill [8]. PagedAttention solves the first, sharing memory pages between requests instead of reserving a contiguous block per request [1].**



## What is Ollama, and how is it different from vLLM?

**Ollama is a tool for running open-weight models easily on a laptop or a single machine, wrapping llama.cpp with a simple CLI, a model library, and an API that feels like calling a hosted service [3]. It optimises for ease of local use, quantized models that fit on consumer hardware, and a good single-user experience, not maximum concurrent throughput. Running Ollama to serve many simultaneous users at scale is possible but is not what it is built or tuned for; vLLM is built specifically for that case.**


## What is llama.cpp, and where does it fit?

**llama.cpp is a C++ inference engine for running LLMs efficiently on CPUs and consumer GPUs, using quantized model formats such as GGUF to shrink memory use [4]. It underlies Ollama and many other local-inference tools. Its strength is portability and running well on hardware without a data-centre GPU, phones, laptops, Raspberry Pi-class devices; it is not designed around maximising throughput for many concurrent server requests the way vLLM is.**



## What is SGLang, and how does it compare to vLLM?

**SGLang is an inference framework that combines fast serving, similar in spirit to vLLM's continuous batching and paged memory, with a structured-generation front end that lets you express constrained outputs, branching, and reused prompt prefixes efficiently [5][6]. Its RadixAttention technique caches shared prompt prefixes across requests, which is particularly effective for workloads with repeated system prompts or few-shot examples, agents calling the same tools repeatedly. Benchmarks between vLLM and SGLang shift with every release of both; the honest answer is to benchmark your own workload rather than trust either project's numbers alone.**



## How do I decide what I actually need?

**Count your expected concurrent requests per second and your latency budget, then pick backward from that. A weekend project or an internal tool with a handful of users rarely needs more than Ollama on a single GPU or even a good CPU. A product with real concurrent traffic needs vLLM or SGLang on dedicated GPU serving from day one, because retrofitting proper batching after launch under load is a much worse day than provisioning for it up front.**



## What does this cost, and how does quantization fit in?

**Serving throughput and quantization are separate levers that stack: a quantized model uses less memory and can run on smaller GPUs, while a serving engine like vLLM uses that freed memory to run more concurrent requests rather than only fitting a bigger model [9]. The cheapest production setup is usually a quantized model served through vLLM or SGLang on the smallest GPU that hits your latency target, re-benchmarked whenever a new quantization method or a smaller strong model appears, since the frontier moves every few months.**



## LLM serving interview questions

**Explain what problem continuous batching solves. Describe PagedAttention in your own words. Compare vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp and say when you would choose each. Explain how quantization and serving throughput interact. Describe how you would capacity-plan a serving setup for a given requests-per-second target. The strongest answer includes a real throughput number you measured, not a number you read.**


## Where should I start?

**Stand up vLLM on a rented GPU with a small open model and hit it with a simple load-testing script, then repeat with Ollama on the same hardware and compare throughput yourself. The gap will be obvious within the first ten minutes.** For a hands-on session on serving LLMs in production, from a notebook to real concurrent traffic, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is workflow automation? How it works, with AI, and versus RPA
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-workflow-automation/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Workflow automation is using software to run a repeatable sequence of business steps, such as approving a leave request, onboarding a customer or processing an invoice, automatically instead of by hand. A trigger starts the workflow, and the software moves data between apps, applies rules and takes actions. With AI, workflows can also read documents, classify messages and draft replies. This page explains how it works, which tools to use, examples, how it differs from RPA, how to add AI safely, and how to learn it.

## What is workflow automation?

Workflow automation is the use of software to carry out a series of tasks, decisions and hand-offs that people used to do manually, following defined rules, so that work moves from start to finish with little human effort.

Typical candidates are tasks that are frequent, rule-based and boring: copying form responses into a spreadsheet, sending welcome emails, routing support tickets, creating invoices from orders, or posting alerts to a team chat. Automating them saves time, removes copy-paste errors and makes the process consistent and auditable. People stay in the loop for exceptions and decisions that need judgement. The aim is not to remove people but to stop them doing work a machine does better.

## How does workflow automation work?

A workflow starts with a trigger, then runs a series of steps: fetch or transform data, check conditions, and take actions in other systems through their APIs. Each run is logged so failures can be seen and retried.

A simple example: a trigger fires when a new row is added to a Google Sheet; a step formats the data; a condition checks whether the amount is above a threshold; an action creates a record in the CRM and another sends a message to the sales channel. Under the hood, the tool calls each app's API with stored credentials. Good workflows also handle errors: retries with back-off, alerts when a step fails, and idempotency so that a retry does not create duplicates. That last point is where most homemade automations break.

## What is a workflow automation tool?

A workflow automation tool is software that lets you build, run and monitor automated workflows, usually with a visual editor of triggers and steps and ready-made connectors to common apps. Zapier, Make, n8n and Microsoft Power Automate are popular examples.

They suit different people. Zapier is the easiest for non-developers connecting popular SaaS apps. Make offers more complex visual logic. n8n is popular with developers because it can be self-hosted, runs custom JavaScript or Python steps and has strong AI nodes. Power Automate fits organisations on Microsoft 365. For data and engineering pipelines, developers use code-first orchestrators such as Apache Airflow or Temporal instead, because they need versioning, testing and scale.

## What are some workflow automation examples?

Common examples include lead capture into a CRM, employee onboarding, invoice processing, support ticket routing, social media scheduling, report generation and alerts when a metric crosses a threshold.

Examples a student or small team can build this week:

- A contact form that saves to a sheet, emails a confirmation and notifies you on Telegram or Slack.
- A daily job that pulls yesterday's sales or website visits and emails a summary.
- An inbox rule that labels invoices, extracts amounts and adds them to a spreadsheet.
- A GitHub workflow that runs tests and deploys on every push.
- A hackathon registration flow that checks team sizes and sends welcome kits.

Pick one you do by hand every week; that is the best first automation.

## What is the difference between workflow automation and RPA?

Workflow automation connects systems through their APIs and data. Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software robots that operate an application's user interface like a person, clicking buttons and typing into fields.

Use RPA when a system has no API, such as an old desktop application or a government portal, because it is the only way in. Its weakness is fragility: a moved button or a changed page layout can break the robot. API-based workflow automation is faster, more reliable and easier to maintain. In practice, mature teams combine them: workflow tools orchestrate the process and call an RPA bot only for the one legacy step that needs it. UiPath and Power Automate Desktop are common RPA tools.

## What is workflow automation using AI?

AI workflow automation adds steps that need judgement, such as reading an email, extracting fields from a document, classifying a request or drafting a reply, to workflows that used to handle only fixed rules.

A classic workflow can route an email if the subject contains "invoice". An AI workflow can read any email, decide whether it is an invoice, a complaint or a meeting request, extract the amount and due date, and draft a response. AI agents go further, choosing which tools to call to reach a goal. This is powerful but less predictable than rules, so the AI step must be constrained: structured output, validation, confidence thresholds, and a human review queue for uncertain cases. Deterministic rules should still make the final decision on anything with money or legal effect.

## How do I use AI for workflow automation?

Put the model where judgement is needed and keep everything else deterministic. Give it a narrow job, require structured JSON output, validate it against a schema, and route low-confidence results to a person.

That is the design I used in DocuLens AI: a Groq-hosted Llama model extracts fields from invoices and contracts, the output is validated against a schema, and compliance scoring is deterministic code, not the model's opinion. A practical starting pattern in n8n or Make: trigger on a new email, send the text to an LLM with a prompt that returns `{"type", "amount", "due_date", "confidence"}`, check the JSON, then branch: high confidence goes to the spreadsheet, low confidence goes to a review list. Log every input and output so you can measure accuracy.

## What is the best AI workflow automation platform?

There is no single best one. n8n is a strong choice for developers who want AI agents, custom code and self-hosting; Zapier for the fastest setup with popular apps; Make for complex visual flows; Power Automate for Microsoft 365 organisations.

Choose by four questions. Where does your data live: Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or your own database? Who will maintain it: a developer or a non-technical team? Do you need self-hosting for data control? How many runs a month will you need, since pricing usually scales with runs or tasks? For custom AI products, a code-first approach with Python, a queue and an orchestrator gives the most control. Prototype the same flow on two platforms before committing.

## Is there an AI workflow automation tutorial?

Yes. The official documentation of n8n, Zapier, Make and Power Automate includes step-by-step tutorials, including AI steps. The fastest way to learn is to build one real automation end to end.

A one-evening tutorial with n8n:

- Run n8n locally or use its cloud trial, and create a workflow with a Gmail or IMAP trigger.
- Add an AI step that classifies each email and returns JSON.
- Add an IF node that checks the class and confidence.
- Send high-confidence results to a Google Sheet and the rest to a Slack or Telegram message for review.
- Add an error workflow that alerts you when a step fails.

Then run it for a week and read the logs.

## What is the best AI workflow automation course?

The best course is the official learning material of the tool you choose, plus a project you build yourself. n8n, Zapier and Microsoft Learn for Power Automate all have free tutorials and learning paths.

Look for courses that cover more than the visual editor: APIs and webhooks, JSON, authentication with OAuth and API keys, error handling, and how to evaluate AI steps. Those skills transfer between tools, while button-by-button lessons date quickly. If you know some Python, learning to call an LLM API and validate its output teaches more than a no-code course alone. A finished automation on your GitHub or in a short demo video is worth more to an employer or client than a certificate.

# What is YOLO in machine learning? Uses, versions and commercial licensing
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-yolo-machine-learning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


YOLO, short for You Only Look Once, is a family of deep learning models for real-time object detection: given an image, it predicts boxes around objects and labels them, such as person, car or helmet, in a single pass of the network. That speed made it the default choice for video, robotics and edge devices. This page explains why YOLO is used, how the versions differ, whether it can classify, segment and work on video, the commercial licensing question, how it relates to vision-language models, how it compares with MediaPipe, and how to train one in Colab.

## What is YOLO in machine learning?

YOLO is an object detection model that divides an image into a grid and predicts, in one forward pass, bounding boxes, confidence scores and class labels for objects. It was introduced by Joseph Redmon and colleagues in 2016.

Earlier detectors first proposed many candidate regions and then classified each one, which was slow. YOLO framed detection as a single regression problem from image pixels to boxes and classes, trading a little accuracy for a large gain in speed. Later versions improved accuracy with better backbones, multi-scale features, anchor-free heads and training tricks, while keeping real-time performance. The output is a list of boxes with class and confidence, usually cleaned up with non-maximum suppression to remove duplicates.

## Why is YOLO used?

YOLO is used because it is fast, accurate enough for most practical tasks, easy to train on custom data and easy to deploy, from GPUs to phones and edge devices.

Typical uses:

- Traffic and vehicle counting from CCTV.
- Safety compliance, such as helmet and vest detection on construction sites.
- Retail shelf monitoring and product counting.
- Crop, pest and fruit detection in agriculture.
- Robotics and drones that must see in real time.

Its ecosystem matters too: tools such as Ultralytics provide training, evaluation and export in a few lines of code, and models export to formats such as ONNX and TensorRT. In FaceVision I ran vision models in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, and the same export path lets YOLO run client-side.

## What is the difference between YOLO versions?

Versions differ in architecture, accuracy, speed and tooling, and they come from different authors. The original author released v1 to v3; later versions came from other researchers and from Ultralytics, which maintains the most widely used library.

A rough map:

- **v1 to v3** (2016 to 2018): the original design, adding anchors and multi-scale prediction.
- **v4** (2020): many training and architecture improvements.
- **v5 and v8**: Ultralytics' popular, easy-to-use releases; v8 added an anchor-free head and multiple tasks.
- **v6, v7, v9, v10**: research and industry releases with their own trade-offs.
- **YOLO11 and later**: newer Ultralytics models with better accuracy per computation.

For a new project, start with the latest stable Ultralytics model and compare two sizes on your own data.

## Can YOLO be used for image classification?

Yes. Ultralytics YOLO models include classification variants that predict a single label for a whole image, alongside detection, segmentation and pose models. Use classification when you only need "what is in this image", not where.

For example, classifying leaf images as healthy or diseased is a classification task; finding every diseased leaf in a field photo is detection. Classification models are smaller and faster, and need simpler labels: just a folder per class. If you might later need locations or counts, label boxes from the start, because converting a classification dataset into a detection dataset means relabelling everything. For pure classification, other architectures, such as EfficientNet or vision transformers, are also strong options.

## Can YOLO be used for segmentation?

Yes. YOLO segmentation models predict a pixel mask for each detected object as well as its box, which is instance segmentation. Ultralytics provides segmentation versions of its models.

Segmentation helps when the shape matters: measuring the area of a crack, counting overlapping fruits, separating people from background, or cutting out products. It needs polygon or mask labels, which take longer to create than boxes, though annotation tools with AI assistance speed this up. Segmentation models are a bit slower than detection models of the same size. If boxes are enough for your decision, use detection; add segmentation only when you need precise outlines.

## Can YOLO detect objects in video?

Yes. YOLO processes each video frame as an image, fast enough for real-time video on a GPU and often on edge devices with smaller models. Tracking links detections across frames so each object keeps an ID.

With Ultralytics, running on a video is one line, and tracking is another:

```python
from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")
model.predict(source="traffic.mp4", save=True)          # boxes on every frame
model.track(source="traffic.mp4", save=True)            # adds persistent IDs
```

For counting objects crossing a line, use tracking IDs rather than raw detections, or you will count the same car many times. Lower resolution and smaller models increase frame rate.

## Can YOLO be used commercially?

It depends on the model's licence. Ultralytics YOLO models are released under AGPL-3.0, which requires releasing your source code if you distribute or offer the software as a service; closed-source commercial use needs an Ultralytics enterprise licence.

Other YOLO implementations have different licences, some more permissive, so check the licence of the exact repository and weights you use, including any pretrained weights and datasets. For college projects, research and open-source work, AGPL is usually fine. For a startup product or client work, decide on licensing before you build, because switching models late means retraining and re-validating. When unsure, ask the licensor or a lawyer; this page is not legal advice.

## Can YOLO be used with vision-language models?

YOLO itself is not a vision-language model; it predicts boxes for a fixed set of classes. But open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World accept text prompts for classes, and YOLO is often combined with vision-language models in pipelines.

Two common patterns: use YOLO to find and crop objects quickly, then ask a vision-language model to describe or reason about each crop; or use a vision-language model to label images automatically, then train a fast YOLO model on those labels for real-time deployment. Open-vocabulary models let you detect "red helmet" or "fire extinguisher" without training a new model, at some cost in speed and accuracy compared with a custom-trained detector.

## MediaPipe vs YOLOv8: which should I use?

Use MediaPipe for ready-made, highly optimised on-device solutions such as face detection, face mesh, hand tracking and pose estimation. Use YOLOv8 or newer when you need to detect your own custom objects or want to train and tune the model yourself.

MediaPipe, from Google, provides pipelines that run in real time on phones and in browsers with little setup, and it offers some customisation through model training tools. YOLO gives you more control: custom classes, model sizes, training options and export targets. For a fitness app that counts squats, MediaPipe's pose solution is the quick path. For detecting helmets on a site or pests on leaves, train a YOLO model. Some projects use both.

## How do I train YOLOv8 in Google Colab?

Open a Colab notebook with a GPU, install Ultralytics, upload a labelled dataset in YOLO format with a `data.yaml` file, train a small model, then evaluate and export it.

```python
!pip install ultralytics
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")                       # small pretrained model
model.train(data="data.yaml", epochs=50, imgsz=640)
metrics = model.val()                            # mAP on the validation set
model.export(format="onnx")                      # for deployment
```

Label a few hundred images per class with an annotation tool, keep a separate test set, and check predictions visually, not only the mAP number. Save weights to Google Drive, because Colab sessions reset.

# What does mentorship look like? Finding mentors, what it provides, and good programmes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-mentorship-looks-like/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Yes, you can gain mentorship: most mentoring relationships start when someone shows initiative, asks a specific question and acts on the advice, prompting the mentor to invest more. Mentorship looks like regular conversations about goals, honest feedback on real work, and help with decisions and opportunities. I have mentored more than 200 students since 2023, so this page covers how to gain mentorship and who provides it, what it provides and looks like, successful and professional mentoring, good programmes, speaker bios, and what "ICT mentorship" means.

## Can you gain mentorship?

Yes. Mentorship can be gained through formal programmes at school, college or work, or informally by building relationships with people further along your path. Initiative is the key: mentors invest in people who show effort and follow through.

How to start: join communities and events, ask thoughtful, specific questions, share your work, and report back on what you did with advice. Avoid asking strangers "Will you be my mentor?"; instead ask for one short conversation on a specific topic. Over time, repeated helpful exchanges become mentorship naturally. Students who return with progress get far more of my time than those who only ask questions.

## Which people provide mentorship?

Mentors can be senior students, teachers and professors, alumni, managers and senior colleagues, community and club leaders, professionals in your target field, startup founders, and peers slightly ahead of you. Formal mentors come through programmes; informal ones through relationships.

The best mentor depends on your goal: for choosing college electives, a senior student; for entering an industry, someone two to five years into that career; for leadership, an experienced manager. Diverse mentors give diverse perspectives, so many people have several. Online communities and mentorship platforms connect you with professionals beyond your local network.

## What does mentorship provide?

Mentorship provides guidance from experience, honest feedback, perspective on decisions, accountability for goals, encouragement through setbacks, and connections to people and opportunities. It shortens your learning curve by sharing lessons others learned the hard way.

For mentees, benefits include clearer direction, faster skill growth, better decisions and access to networks. Mentors gain leadership skills, fresh perspectives and satisfaction. Organisations gain retention, knowledge transfer and stronger cultures. The value depends on the relationship's quality: a good mentor helps you think and act, not just listen. For students from smaller towns or first-generation families, mentorship often provides the career information that others get at home.

## What does mentorship look like in practice?

In practice, mentorship looks like regular conversations, perhaps every two to four weeks, where the mentee brings goals, questions and work, and the mentor asks questions, shares experience, gives feedback and suggests next steps. Between meetings, the mentee acts and reports progress.

A typical session: a quick update on progress, one or two specific challenges, discussion and advice, and agreed actions. Mentors may review a resume, a project or a talk, introduce someone useful, or suggest resources. Communication can happen in person, on calls or by messages. Over time, the relationship grows more collaborative. Keeping a shared document of goals, notes and actions makes progress visible to both people.

## What does a successful mentorship look like?

A successful mentorship has clear goals, consistent contact, mutual respect and trust, honest two-way feedback, and visible progress for the mentee. Both people find it worthwhile and look forward to conversations.

Signs of success: the mentee achieves milestones, such as a first internship, a shipped project or a new role; they make better decisions independently over time; and the relationship evolves, sometimes into friendship or sponsorship. Unsuccessful mentorships drift without goals, rely on the mentor to drive everything, or feel transactional. Periodic check-ins on how the relationship is working help keep it healthy.

## What does professional mentorship look like?

Professional mentorship focuses on career growth: skills, workplace navigation, decisions such as role changes or promotions, leadership development and networking, often through company programmes or industry relationships. Meetings are structured around career goals.

A professional mentor might help you prepare for a promotion conversation, review your technical design, explain how decisions are made in your organisation, or introduce you to leaders. Confidentiality and trust are important, especially when discussing challenges at work. Professional mentorship often complements, rather than replaces, guidance from your manager.

## What does a good mentorship programme look like?

A good programme has clear purpose, careful matching on goals and interests, mentor training, agreed expectations, a meeting schedule, resources for sessions, check-ins from coordinators, and evaluation at the end. It supports relationships without over-controlling them.

Key features: an orientation explaining roles; goal-setting templates; flexibility to rematch if pairs do not work; recognition for mentors' time; and measurement of outcomes such as retention, skill growth or placements. Programmes for students benefit from pairing mentoring with real opportunities, such as hackathons, internships and projects.

## How does mentorship actually work, and what is having a mentor like?

Having a mentor feels like having an experienced ally: someone you can ask honest questions, who gives you feedback you might not hear elsewhere, and who cares about your progress. It works through regular, purposeful conversations and your action between them.

The mentee drives the relationship: setting goals, scheduling meetings, preparing questions and following through. The mentor contributes experience, perspective and sometimes connections. Expect challenge as well as support; good mentors point out blind spots. Respect their time, say thank you, share wins, and look for ways to help them back.

## What does a speaker bio look like?

A speaker bio is a short, third-person paragraph of about 50 to 200 words introducing a speaker's current role, credibility and topics. Organisers use it in programmes, posters and introductions on stage.

Example: "Pranjul Rathour leads engineering at SCULT INDIA and shipped five production AI applications in 2026. He has mentored more than 200 students since 2023 and won first prizes at Changethon 2025 and Vividhotsava 2025. He speaks on building and shipping AI products." Keep short, medium and long versions, use specifics rather than adjectives, and update them regularly.

## Which ICT mentorship is the best?

It depends what "ICT" means. In education and careers, ICT means information and communication technology, and good mentorship comes from industry professionals, alumni, communities and structured programmes. In trading, ICT refers to the Inner Circle Trader education brand, a different topic altogether.

For ICT careers, look for mentors working in roles you want, communities with active members, and programmes with clear goals and real project feedback. For trading education of any kind, be very cautious: verify claims independently, avoid paying for promises of profits, learn about risks from regulators' investor education resources, and remember that studies by India's market regulator SEBI found most individual traders in futures and options lost money. Neither is a substitute for professional financial advice.

# What problems does RAG solve? How it works, implementing it, and is it dead
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-problems-does-rag-solve/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Retrieval-augmented generation primarily solves four problems with language models: their knowledge is frozen at training time, they do not know your private data, they can make up confident answers, and they cannot show where an answer came from. RAG retrieves relevant documents at question time and makes the model answer from them, with citations. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate, so this page covers RAG's purpose and name, how it works, implementing and improving it, SQL, ChatGPT, NVIDIA and its future.

## What problems does RAG primarily solve?

RAG solves stale knowledge, missing private or specialised data, hallucination and lack of traceability. Instead of relying on what the model memorised, it grounds answers in documents you supply and update.

Concretely: a college chatbot can answer from this year's fee and exam rules; a support assistant can use the latest product manuals; a legal research tool can cite exact clauses. Updating knowledge means updating documents, not retraining models. RAG also supports access control, since retrieval can respect who may see which documents. It does not eliminate errors, but evidence plus citations lets users verify, and a refusal rule can stop answers when evidence is weak.

## Why is it called retrieval-augmented generation?

The name describes the method: the generation of text by a language model is augmented with information obtained by retrieval from an external source. It comes from the 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues that introduced the approach.

Lewis has said in interviews that the team would have chosen a more appealing name had they known how widely it would be used. The acronym stuck anyway, and "RAG" now names a whole family of techniques. It is unrelated to "RAG" in project management, which means Red, Amber, Green status.

## How does retrieval-augmented generation work?

Documents are split into chunks, embedded and indexed. When a question arrives, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks, inserts them into the prompt with instructions to answer only from them, and the model generates an answer citing those chunks.

Production systems add steps: query rewriting for follow-up questions, hybrid retrieval combining keyword and vector search, fusion of result lists, reranking with a cross-encoder, a confidence threshold, streaming output, and logging for evaluation. In RAG.NextUpgrad, dense and BM25 results are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, reranked, and answered with streamed citations, with multi-provider fallback if a model provider fails.

## Is retrieval-augmented generation a model?

No. RAG is a technique and system architecture that combines a retriever, such as a search index, with a generator, a language model. You can build RAG with many different models and search engines.

The original 2020 paper trained a retriever and generator together as one model, which is why some people still describe RAG as a model. Today's systems usually combine separately chosen components: an embedding model, a vector or hybrid search index, a reranker and a chat model. Changing any component keeps the system "RAG". This modularity is a strength: you can upgrade the model or search without rebuilding everything.

## How do I implement retrieval-augmented generation?

Start simple: parse your documents, chunk them by structure, embed and index them, retrieve the top chunks for each question, and prompt a model to answer with citations. Then evaluate and improve retrieval before anything else.

Implementation checklist:

- Parse documents, using OCR for scans.
- Chunk by headings with metadata such as title and page.
- Index for both vector and keyword search.
- Retrieve, fuse and rerank.
- Prompt with rules: answer only from context, cite, refuse if unsure.
- Build 30 to 100 test questions with expected answers.
- Serve through an API with streaming and logging.

Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex speed this up, but understand each step.

## How do I improve retrieval in RAG?

Fix chunking first, then add hybrid search, reranking and query rewriting, measuring each change on a fixed evaluation set. Retrieval quality, not the language model, causes most RAG failures.

Proven improvements:

- Chunk along document structure and prepend section titles.
- Add BM25 keyword search alongside vectors, fused with reciprocal rank fusion.
- Rerank the top 20 to 50 candidates with a cross-encoder.
- Rewrite follow-up questions into standalone queries.
- Use metadata filters for date, product or department.
- Add short contextual descriptions to chunks.
- Try a better or domain-tuned embedding model.

Track recall at k: whether the right chunk appears in the retrieved set.

## Why use SQL for retrieval-augmented generation?

SQL databases such as PostgreSQL can store chunks, embeddings, full-text indexes, metadata and permissions together, so one query can combine vector similarity, keyword matching, filters and access control. Much business knowledge also already lives in SQL tables.

With pgvector and Postgres full-text search, hybrid retrieval runs in a single database with transactions, backups and row-level security. For structured questions, such as "How many orders were delayed last week?", text-to-SQL retrieval queries the data directly instead of searching documents. Many strong RAG systems combine both: document retrieval for policies and explanations, SQL for numbers and records.

## Does ChatGPT use retrieval-augmented generation?

Yes, in several features. ChatGPT's search retrieves web pages and answers with cited sources, uploaded files and custom GPT knowledge use retrieval over your documents, and connectors retrieve from linked apps. Plain chat without these relies on the model's trained knowledge.

When ChatGPT shows citations to web pages, it is using a form of RAG. Answer quality then depends on which sources were retrieved. For your own organisation's data, a dedicated RAG system gives you control over sources, permissions, evaluation and refusal behaviour that general assistants cannot fully provide.

## What is retrieval-augmented generation according to NVIDIA?

NVIDIA describes RAG as a technique for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of generative AI models with facts fetched from external sources, and offers tools to build it: NeMo Retriever for embedding and reranking, NIM microservices for deploying models, and reference blueprints for RAG pipelines.

Its widely read explainer compares RAG to a court clerk fetching precedents for a judge. NVIDIA's focus is enterprise RAG on GPU infrastructure, with fast embedding, retrieval and inference at scale. The underlying concepts are the same as any RAG system; NVIDIA's offerings are one implementation option, alongside open-source frameworks and cloud services.

## Is retrieval-augmented generation dead?

No. Claims that long-context models or agents make RAG obsolete misread the problem. Even very long context windows cannot hold an organisation's entire knowledge base, and stuffing huge contexts is slow, costly and less accurate than retrieving relevant parts.

What is changing is the form: agentic RAG lets models decide when and where to search, long context lets them read more retrieved material, and tools like file search and grep complement vectors. All of these are still retrieval feeding generation. As long as models need current, private and verifiable information, retrieval will remain central.

# When to use Ollama: vs vLLM, production, VS Code, Copilot, n8n and LlamaIndex
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/when-to-use-ollama/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Use Ollama when you want to run open language models on your own machine with minimal setup: local development, prototypes, privacy-sensitive documents, offline work and small internal tools. For serving many users at high throughput on GPU servers, a dedicated serving engine such as vLLM is the better fit. This page covers when Ollama fits, Ollama versus vLLM, production use, choosing a model, and using Ollama with VS Code, GitHub Copilot, n8n and LlamaIndex, plus Gemini and NPU questions.

## When should I use Ollama?

Use Ollama when data must stay on your machine, when you want free, unlimited local experimentation, when you work offline, or when you need a quick local model for a prototype, internal tool or learning.

Good fits:

- Building and testing RAG pipelines without API costs.
- Processing private documents that cannot go to cloud services.
- Coding help in your editor with a local model.
- Automations with simple language tasks, such as classification or extraction.
- Teaching and learning how LLMs behave.

Poor fits: hard reasoning and complex coding, where frontier hosted models are much stronger, and high-traffic production APIs, where serving engines and managed services scale better.

## Should I use Ollama or vLLM?

Use Ollama for simplicity on a single machine: easy installs, model management and a friendly API. Use vLLM when serving a model to many concurrent users on GPUs, where its continuous batching and memory management give far higher throughput.

A common pattern is Ollama during development and vLLM, or a managed provider, in production. vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so code written against OpenAI-style endpoints moves between them easily. vLLM needs more setup, a capable GPU and attention to model formats, while Ollama runs on laptops and CPUs. Benchmark your real workload: requests per second, latency at your concurrency, and memory use.

## Can I use Ollama in production?

Yes, for modest workloads such as internal tools, small teams or low-traffic features, if you add authentication, monitoring and fixed model versions. For high concurrency or strict latency targets, a serving engine or managed API is usually better.

Production checklist for Ollama:

- Put an authenticated proxy in front; the API has no login.
- Pin model versions and test before updating.
- Set concurrency and queue limits for your hardware.
- Keep models loaded to avoid cold starts.
- Log requests, latency and errors; alert on failures.
- Have a fallback provider for outages.

Multi-provider fallback, which RAG.NextUpgrad uses, keeps users served when one model server struggles.

## Which Ollama model should I use?

Choose by task and hardware: a 7B to 8B instruction model for general chat on a 16 GB laptop, a coding-tuned model for programming, a small 1B to 4B model for fast simple tasks or weak hardware, and an embedding model for search and RAG.

How to decide:

- **List your task**: chat, coding, extraction, classification, embeddings.
- **Check memory**: model file size plus room for context.
- **Shortlist two or three** from recent, reputable families in the Ollama library.
- **Test** on ten real prompts and compare quality and speed.

Re-check every few months; open models improve quickly, and a newer small model often beats an older larger one.

## Can I use Ollama in VS Code?

Yes. Several VS Code extensions connect to Ollama's local API for chat, code explanation and autocomplete, and VS Code's own AI chat can use Ollama models through its language model settings. Configure the extension with the Ollama URL and model name.

For coding, choose a coding-tuned model that fits your GPU, and a small fast model for inline completions, since completions need low latency. Expect local models to be weaker than frontier hosted models on complex refactors, but useful for explanations, boilerplate and private codebases. Keep Ollama running in the background, and check `ollama ps` if responses are slow.

## How can I use Ollama models in GitHub Copilot?

In VS Code, Copilot Chat lets you add models from other providers, including local models served by Ollama, through its model management settings, so you can chat with a local model in the Copilot interface. Availability depends on your Copilot plan, VS Code version and organisation policies.

Steps generally involve opening the model picker in Copilot Chat, choosing to manage models, selecting Ollama as a provider, and picking an installed model. Local models will not match the hosted premium models on hard tasks, but they keep code on your machine and do not use premium request allowances. Organisations may disable bring-your-own-model options, so check policies at work.

## How do I use Ollama in n8n?

Add n8n's Ollama chat model or embeddings node, set the credentials to your Ollama base URL, usually `http://localhost:11434`, or `http://host.docker.internal:11434` if n8n runs in Docker, and connect it to an AI Agent or chain node.

Typical uses: classify incoming emails, extract fields from form submissions into JSON, summarise documents, or answer questions over a vector store, all without sending data to external APIs. Keep prompts strict and outputs structured, validate them with an IF or Code node, and route uncertain results to a person. If n8n and Ollama run on different machines, secure the connection; never expose Ollama's port publicly.

## How do I use Ollama with LlamaIndex?

Install LlamaIndex's Ollama integrations for the LLM and embeddings, set them as the defaults in LlamaIndex settings, then build an index and query engine as usual.

```python
# pip install llama-index llama-index-llms-ollama llama-index-embeddings-ollama
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader, Settings
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding

Settings.llm = Ollama(model="llama3.2", request_timeout=120)
Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="nomic-embed-text")
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(SimpleDirectoryReader("notes").load_data())
print(index.as_query_engine().query("What is paging?"))
```

Raise timeouts for slower hardware, and evaluate retrieval with a few known questions before trusting answers.

## Can you use Gemini with Ollama?

No. Gemini models are proprietary and only available through Google's apps and APIs, so they cannot run in Ollama. Google's open-weight Gemma models, which share research with Gemini, are available in Ollama.

If you want Gemini, call the Gemini API, which has a free tier through Google AI Studio. If you want a local Google model, run Gemma with Ollama, choosing a size that fits your hardware. Many applications combine both: Gemma locally for private or high-volume simple tasks, and Gemini or another hosted model for harder ones, behind a common interface so switching is a configuration change.

## Will Ollama use my NPU?

Generally not. Mainline Ollama runs models on CPUs and on supported GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple Silicon; neural processing units in recent laptops are not its main target. Some vendors provide their own tools or builds for running models on their NPUs.

Copilot+ PCs and other laptops with NPUs use them mainly for Windows AI features and vendor-optimised runtimes. If NPU acceleration matters to you, look at the chip vendor's AI toolkits and check whether they support the models you want. For most users, a GPU or a strong CPU with enough RAM is what determines Ollama performance, so check `ollama ps` to see where your model runs.
