# Where do Copilot files go? Uploads, downloads, chat history and limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/where-do-copilot-files-go/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Where Copilot files go depends on the account. With a work or school account, files you upload to Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and documents it creates are usually stored in your OneDrive. With a personal account, files stay attached to the conversation and generated files are offered as a download link. This page explains Copilot versus Copilot Chat, where uploads, downloads and exports end up, what to do when Copilot will not produce a file, whether it reads Excel, how long it keeps history, why it has limits, and how it compares with ChatGPT.

## Copilot vs Copilot Chat: what is the difference?

Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat is the chat assistant included for work and school accounts, grounded in the web and the files you give it. Microsoft 365 Copilot is the paid add-on that also reads your organisation's emails, files and meetings and works inside the Office apps.

The practical difference is reach. Copilot Chat answers from public web content and from documents you upload or open, under enterprise data protection. The full Microsoft 365 Copilot can answer "what did my manager say about the launch?" by searching your mailbox, Teams chats and SharePoint, within your permissions, and it adds features such as meeting recaps in Teams and analysis in Excel. Consumer Copilot, for personal Microsoft accounts, is a third product with its own app and limits. Check the Copilot icon and the account shown in the corner to know which one you are using.

## Where do Copilot files go?

On work and school accounts, files that Copilot Chat receives or creates are generally saved to your OneDrive, in a folder created for Copilot. On personal accounts, they stay with the conversation and you download what you need.

The quickest way to find a file is the link in Copilot's reply: open it, then use "open file location" or check the file's path in OneDrive. Documents created inside Word, Excel or PowerPoint with Copilot are ordinary files and save wherever you save them, usually OneDrive or SharePoint. Copilot Pages, the shareable canvas for Copilot responses, are stored in Microsoft's cloud and appear in your Microsoft 365 app. Exact folder names and behaviour have changed over time, so search OneDrive for the file name if the link does not show it.

## Where does Copilot save files?

Copilot saves files where the surrounding app saves them. In Word, Excel and PowerPoint it is your chosen location, usually OneDrive or SharePoint. In Copilot Chat on a work account it is your OneDrive. In consumer Copilot it is your browser's download folder once you download.

This matters for two reasons. First, Copilot in Excel and Word works best on files saved to OneDrive or SharePoint, because it relies on the cloud copy; local files can limit features. Second, saved files follow normal sharing rules: a file in your OneDrive is private until you share it, and a file in a team SharePoint site is visible to that team. Rename generated files straight away, because default names such as "Document 3" are hard to find later.

## Where do files uploaded to Copilot go?

On a work or school account, a file you upload to Copilot Chat is generally stored in your OneDrive so Copilot can read it, and it stays covered by your organisation's security and compliance policies. On a personal account, it is kept with that conversation.

Uploading a file does not make it public or share it with colleagues. For work accounts, Microsoft states that prompts, responses and uploaded content are not used to train the foundation models and remain inside the Microsoft 365 service boundary. Even so, follow your college or company's data policy: do not upload documents you are not allowed to process with AI tools, such as other people's personal data. If you upload sensitive drafts often, clean up the OneDrive folder now and then.

## Where do Copilot files export to?

Exports go to the app or folder you choose. Copilot responses can be copied, exported to Word or turned into a Copilot Page; downloaded files go to your browser's downloads folder; and Office documents save to OneDrive or SharePoint by default.

If you want a response as a document, ask Copilot to create a Word document or use the export option under the response, then open it and save it under a proper name. For tables, ask for an Excel file or copy the table into Excel directly; formatting usually survives the paste. On phones, downloads go to the system's download location or the Files app. If an export link expires, which can happen with generated files, ask Copilot to regenerate the file in the same conversation.

## Why is Copilot not giving downloadable files?

Usually because the product or plan you are using cannot create that file type in chat, the request did not trigger file creation, or the download link expired. Asking explicitly for a named file type often fixes it.

Try these in order:

- Ask clearly: "Create a Word document named report.docx with this content."
- Ask for the content as text or a table in the chat, then paste it into Word or Excel yourself.
- Use Copilot inside the target app instead: Copilot in Word for documents, in Excel for spreadsheets, in PowerPoint for decks.
- Start a new conversation if the old one is long; long chats behave less reliably.
- Check whether your organisation has disabled file generation.

Copying the content is always the fallback, and it is often faster than fighting the download.

## Can Copilot read Excel files?

Yes. You can upload an Excel file to Copilot Chat and ask questions about it, and Copilot inside Excel analyses the open workbook directly: summaries, formulas, charts, PivotTables and trends.

For the best results inside Excel, format the data as a table with Ctrl+T, give each column a clear header, remove merged cells and blank rows, and save the file to OneDrive or SharePoint. Then ask specific questions, such as "which product had the largest month-on-month drop?". In chat, very large workbooks may be summarised rather than read in full, so share a focused sheet. Check any formula Copilot writes on a few rows by hand before trusting the totals.

## How long does Copilot keep chat history?

Consumer Copilot keeps your conversations until you delete them, either one by one or all at once in privacy settings. Work and school accounts keep Copilot interactions according to your organisation's retention policies, which admins set.

On work accounts, Copilot interactions are stored within the organisation's Microsoft 365 environment so they can be covered by compliance features such as retention and eDiscovery, the same way email is. Deleting a conversation from your view may not remove the organisation's record if a retention policy applies. On personal accounts you control the history yourself. Either way, assume anything you type may be kept and read later, and keep passwords, keys and personal identity numbers out of every chat.

## Why does Copilot have a chat limit?

Limits keep the service affordable and reliable. Every reply costs computing time, very long conversations exceed what the model can hold in context, and long chats tend to drift and give worse answers.

A model can only consider a fixed amount of text at once, its context window. In a long chat, older messages are dropped or summarised, so Copilot can forget instructions you gave at the start. Limits on turns per conversation or requests per day also protect the service at busy times and differ by account type. Work with the limits rather than against them: one conversation per task, a short summary of the important facts when you start a new chat, and the key instructions repeated in your first message.

## How does Copilot compare to ChatGPT?

Both are capable assistants, and Copilot uses OpenAI's GPT models for much of its work. The difference is integration: Copilot is built into Windows, Edge and Microsoft 365, while ChatGPT is a standalone app with its own tools.

Choose Copilot if your work happens in Outlook, Word, Excel and Teams, or your organisation provides it with enterprise data protection, because it can see the documents you are working on. Choose ChatGPT if you want one broad assistant with strong voice mode, image generation, custom GPTs and many third-party apps. Many people use both: Copilot for work documents, ChatGPT for learning and side projects. Test both on the same real task before deciding, because model updates change the balance every few months.

# Where to vibe code an app or website: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, iOS, games and time
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/where-to-vibe-code-an-app/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


You can vibe code an app in an AI code editor such as Cursor, in a terminal agent such as Claude Code, or in a browser builder such as Replit, Lovable or Bolt that also hosts the result. Chat assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot can write code too, but tools that edit files, run code and fix errors in a loop work far better for complete apps. I build products with AI coding tools daily, so this page covers where to vibe code apps and websites, specific assistants, iOS apps, games, time, portfolios, and Claude Code.

## Where can I vibe code an app?

For beginners without a coding setup, browser builders such as Replit, Lovable and Bolt let you describe an app, see it running, and deploy it with one click. For developers, Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot's agent mode and similar tools work inside real projects on your computer.

Choose by goal: browser builders for quick prototypes and demos; AI editors and terminal agents for apps you will maintain, extend and deploy properly. Whichever you choose, keep the code in a git repository, so you own it and can move it elsewhere. Check data handling: anything with user accounts or payments needs careful review of authentication and database security.

## Where can I vibe code a website?

For simple websites, use a browser builder or ask an AI editor to create a static site, then host it free on GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages. For sites with logins and data, use a full-stack builder or a framework project with a managed database.

A good workflow: describe the pages, sections, style and audience; generate the site; review it on mobile; then iterate section by section. Ask for accessibility and performance checks, and fix SEO basics such as titles, descriptions and headings. A personal or event website is an ideal first vibe coding project, because it is low risk and quick to see results.

## Can I vibe code with ChatGPT?

Yes, partly. ChatGPT can write complete code files, explain errors and suggest fixes, and its coding agent features can work on repositories. For full apps, copying code between chat and your editor gets tedious, so agentic tools that edit files directly work better.

Practical use: describe the app, ask for a project structure and files, run the code locally, and paste errors back. ChatGPT's Canvas helps for editing single files. OpenAI's Codex tools offer more agent-like coding on repositories. Keep projects small at first, and ask ChatGPT to explain any part you do not understand, so you can maintain the code later.

## Can I vibe code with Gemini?

Yes. Gemini can generate code in chat and Canvas, and Google AI Studio can build and preview small web apps from prompts. Google also offers Gemini-powered coding agents and command-line tools for working on projects.

Gemini's long context helps when pasting large files or documentation. As with any assistant, test everything it produces, keep code in git and review security-sensitive parts. For full applications, use tools that run the code and iterate on errors automatically. Compare Gemini with other assistants on your own project, since quality varies by task and language.

## Can I vibe code with Microsoft Copilot?

Microsoft Copilot, the general assistant, can write and explain code in chat, which supports small scripts and learning. For real vibe coding in projects, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft's developer tool, is the better fit, with agent mode that edits files and runs commands in VS Code.

The names cause confusion: Microsoft 365 Copilot helps with documents and email; GitHub Copilot helps with code. Students can often get GitHub Copilot free through GitHub's education programme. Use custom instruction files to tell it your project's conventions, review diffs before accepting, and run tests after changes.

## Can I vibe code an iOS app?

Yes, especially with SwiftUI, which AI tools write fairly well. You need a Mac with Xcode to build and test iOS apps, and an Apple Developer Program membership to publish on the App Store. Cross-platform frameworks such as React Native or Flutter are alternatives.

Expect friction beyond the code: signing, provisioning profiles, device permissions, App Store review guidelines, and privacy disclosures. AI tools help with these, but you must follow Apple's rules. Start with a simple app, such as a habit tracker, test on a real device, and keep the scope tight. Review how the app stores user data, especially if it uses accounts or the camera.

## Can you vibe code a video game?

Yes, simple games such as puzzles, platformers and arcade games are very achievable, often as browser games with HTML5 and JavaScript or in engines like Godot. Complex 3D games with polished art and balance still need substantial human work.

Tips: start with a small, clear game loop, such as "dodge falling objects and score points"; ask for one mechanic at a time; playtest after every change; and keep assets simple. AI can also help with level design ideas and dialogue. Performance, controls and fun come from iteration, so expect many rounds of tweaking. Game jams are a great way to practise this under time limits.

## How long does it take to vibe code an app?

A simple app or website can take a few hours to a weekend. A multi-feature app with accounts, a database and deployment usually takes days to weeks. Turning it into a reliable product with tests, security and real users takes much longer.

Time grows non-linearly: the first 80 percent appears quickly, and the last 20 percent, edge cases, bugs, performance and polish, takes most of the effort. Developers who understand the code move faster through that stage. Plan small releases, test each one, and avoid adding features before the core works. Track time spent fixing AI-introduced bugs; it shows when to slow down and review more carefully.

## Should I vibe code my portfolio?

You can vibe code your portfolio website, as long as you understand and can explain it, and it is fast, accessible and accurate. The content, your projects and results, matters more than how the site was built.

For portfolio projects themselves, be careful: employers want evidence of your skills. Vibe coded projects are fine if you can explain the architecture, decisions and code in an interview, and if you contributed meaningfully beyond prompting. Be honest about AI use if asked. Projects where you designed the system, debugged real problems and measured results make far stronger portfolio pieces than generated demos.

## What is the difference between vibe coding and Claude Code?

Vibe coding is a way of working: building software by prompting AI and steering by results, with little manual code review. Claude Code is a specific tool: Anthropic's agentic coding assistant that runs in your terminal and editors, reading code, editing files and running commands.

You can vibe code with Claude Code, but you can also use it as a careful engineer: planning changes, reviewing diffs, running tests and enforcing project rules. Its permission prompts, project memory files and git integration support disciplined development. In short, vibe coding describes how much you supervise the AI; Claude Code is one of the tools you can use either way.

# Whisper in Python: install, audio arrays, timestamps, speakers, and self-hosting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/whisper-ai-python-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Whisper in Python usually means `openai-whisper`, the open-source package for OpenAI's speech recognition model: install it, load a model and call `transcribe` on an audio file to get text with timestamps. This page is a developer's guide: setup and Python versions, feeding audio as NumPy arrays, word-level timestamps, adding speaker labels, choosing between self-hosted Whisper and a hosted API, apps built on Whisper, and safety. Speech-to-text is part of my OCR & Speech Workspace, so the advice comes from building with it.

## What is Whisper in Python?

In Python, Whisper is the `openai-whisper` library, which runs OpenAI's open-source Whisper speech recognition models locally. It transcribes audio in many languages, can translate speech into English, and returns segments with start and end times.

It depends on PyTorch for the model and ffmpeg for reading audio files. Model sizes range from tiny to large, trading speed for accuracy. Faster community implementations, such as faster-whisper and whisper.cpp, run the same models more efficiently and are popular in production. The Hugging Face Transformers library also provides Whisper models through its speech recognition pipeline, which is convenient if you already use Transformers.

## How do I use Whisper AI in Python?

Install ffmpeg on your system, install the package, load a model and transcribe.

```bash
pip install -U openai-whisper
```

```python
import whisper
model = whisper.load_model("small")             # tiny, base, small, medium, large
result = model.transcribe("lecture.mp3", language="en")
print(result["text"])
for seg in result["segments"][:3]:
    print(f'{seg["start"]:.1f}-{seg["end"]:.1f}s: {seg["text"]}')
```

Set the language when you know it, to avoid misdetection on short clips. Use a GPU if available; on CPU, start with `small` or try faster-whisper. For translation into English, pass `task="translate"`. The result also includes the detected language and segment timings, which you can turn into SRT subtitles with a few lines of code. For very long recordings on limited memory, split the audio into parts of a few minutes, transcribe each, and keep the offsets so every line still points to the right moment in the original file.

## Does Whisper AI work with Python 3.13?

It depends on whether PyTorch and Whisper's other dependencies provide packages for your Python version on your platform. If installation fails on a very new Python, create a virtual environment with a Python version that PyTorch officially supports and install there.

Check PyTorch's installation page for the supported Python versions and your operating system and GPU combination, then install the matching PyTorch build before installing Whisper. Most problems on new Python releases come from compiled dependencies not yet published as wheels, which makes pip try to build from source and fail. Using tools such as `pyenv` or `uv` to manage several Python versions side by side avoids breaking your system Python.

## How do I convert any audio file to a NumPy array for Whisper?

Whisper expects mono audio sampled at 16 kHz as a float32 NumPy array with values between -1 and 1. Use `whisper.load_audio`, which calls ffmpeg, or a library such as librosa, then pass the array to `transcribe`.

```python
import whisper, librosa
audio = whisper.load_audio("call.m4a")                       # float32, 16 kHz mono via ffmpeg
# or: audio, _ = librosa.load("call.m4a", sr=16000, mono=True)
result = whisper.load_model("base").transcribe(audio)
```

If your audio arrives as raw bytes from a microphone or stream, convert integer samples to float32 by dividing by 32768 for 16-bit audio, and resample to 16 kHz. Wrong sample rates produce garbled or sped-up transcripts, a common bug.

## How do I use whisper_timestamped in Python?

`whisper_timestamped` is an open-source extension of Whisper that adds word-level timestamps and confidence scores. Install it, load a model through it, and call its `transcribe` function; each segment then includes a list of words with start and end times.

```python
import whisper_timestamped as wt
audio = wt.load_audio("talk.mp3")
model = wt.load_model("small")
out = wt.transcribe(model, audio, language="en")
for w in out["segments"][0]["words"][:5]:
    print(w["text"], w["start"], w["end"], w["confidence"])
```

Word timestamps help with subtitles, karaoke-style highlighting and aligning transcripts with slides. Alternatives include WhisperX, which aligns words with a separate model, and the word timestamp option in faster-whisper. Check each project's README for current usage.

## Does Whisper do speaker diarisation, and how do I add it?

No. Whisper transcribes what was said but does not label who said it. To add speakers, run a diarisation model, such as pyannote.audio, to find speaker turns, then assign each transcript segment or word to the speaker active at that time. WhisperX combines these steps.

The pipeline: transcribe with Whisper and get timestamps; run diarisation to get segments like "Speaker 1 from 0.0 to 12.3 seconds"; align by overlapping times; merge consecutive segments from the same speaker. Diarisation works best with clear audio and distinct voices, and struggles with overlapping speech. Some diarisation models require accepting terms and a Hugging Face token. For meetings, many cloud speech services provide diarisation built in.

## AssemblyAI vs Whisper large-v3: which should you ship?

Ship self-hosted Whisper large-v3 when you need privacy, control and low cost at high volume, and can run GPUs. Ship a hosted speech API such as AssemblyAI when you need fast integration, streaming, diarisation and other features out of the box, and accept per-minute pricing and sending audio to a provider.

Decide with a test: transcribe 20 to 50 of your real recordings with both, compute word error rate against reference transcripts, and check names, numbers and speaker labels. Also compare latency, uptime commitments, data retention terms and total cost, including your engineering time for GPUs, scaling and monitoring. Accuracy differences vary by accent, domain and audio quality, so public benchmarks are only a starting point.

## When should I stop self-hosting Whisper?

Consider moving to a hosted API when GPU costs and maintenance time exceed API costs, when you need real-time streaming at scale, when reliability requirements outgrow your setup, or when you need features such as diarisation and custom vocabulary without building them.

Keep self-hosting when privacy or data residency rules require audio to stay on your infrastructure, when volume is high enough that GPUs are cheaper per minute, or when you need full control over models and versions. A useful middle path is a hybrid: self-host batch transcription of sensitive recordings and use an API for live features. Track cost per audio hour and engineer hours monthly to make the decision with numbers.

## Does Whisper AI have an app?

OpenAI does not ship Whisper as a standalone consumer app; Whisper is a model and open-source library. Many third-party apps use Whisper for transcription on desktop and mobile, and OpenAI's own products use speech recognition in features such as voice input.

If you want an app, look for transcription apps that state they run Whisper on the device, which keeps audio private, or that use a cloud API, which is faster on weak hardware. Check reviews, privacy policies and whether recordings are uploaded. For developers, a simple personal app is easy to build: a small web page that uploads audio to your own Whisper backend and returns a transcript.

## Is Whisper AI safe?

Whisper itself is safe to use: it is open-source software from OpenAI, and running it locally keeps audio on your machine. Safety concerns come from how you use it and which apps or services wrap it.

Points to watch: third-party apps may upload your recordings, so read their privacy policies; Whisper can occasionally produce text that was never spoken, especially during silence or music, which matters for medical, legal or accessibility uses; and recording people requires their consent. Download Whisper and models from official sources, keep dependencies updated, and review transcripts for important decisions.

# Who are web developers? The job, who hires them, demand, remote work and how to start
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/who-are-web-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Web developers are the people who build and maintain websites and web applications: front-end developers create what users see and interact with, back-end developers build servers, databases and APIs, and full-stack developers do both. They work at tech companies, agencies, startups and enterprises, or as freelancers. I build web products with Next.js, FastAPI and PostgreSQL and lead engineering at SCULT INDIA, so this page covers who web developers are, their work, who hires them, self-taught and remote developers, demand, courses, becoming one and freelancing.

## Who are web developers?

Web developers are programmers who specialise in the web: they write HTML, CSS and JavaScript for interfaces, and languages such as JavaScript, Python, PHP, Java or Go for servers, working with databases, APIs and cloud hosting to make websites and web apps work.

They come from varied backgrounds: computer science graduates, BCA and MCA students, bootcamp graduates and self-taught programmers. Many specialise, for example in front-end frameworks like React, back-end APIs, e-commerce, performance or accessibility. Increasingly, web developers also integrate AI features, such as chat assistants and document processing, into web applications. Their work powers everything from college websites and online shops to banking portals and SaaS dashboards.

## What does web developer work involve?

Daily work includes building features from designs and requirements, writing and reviewing code, fixing bugs, connecting front ends to APIs, designing databases, testing, deploying, improving performance and security, and collaborating with designers, product managers and other developers.

A typical feature flows from planning to implementation, code review, testing and release. Developers also maintain existing code, update dependencies and respond to incidents. Communication matters as much as coding: understanding requirements, explaining trade-offs and documenting work. Tools include code editors, Git, browser developer tools, package managers, CI pipelines and, increasingly, AI coding assistants.

## What is the web developer job like?

The job combines problem solving, building and continuous learning. Roles include front-end, back-end, full-stack, WordPress or e-commerce developers, and titles range from junior and associate to senior, lead and architect.

Work settings vary: product companies focus on one product deeply; agencies build many client projects quickly; startups need generalists who do everything; and enterprises have larger teams and processes. Day to day, expect a mix of focused coding, meetings, code reviews and debugging. Technologies change fast, so ongoing learning is part of the job. Many developers find the work rewarding because they see their creations used by real people. Pay and growth depend heavily on skills, the type of employer and the quality of your portfolio.

## Who hires web developers?

Web developers are hired by software product companies, IT services and consulting firms, digital and marketing agencies, startups, e-commerce businesses, banks and fintechs, media companies, educational institutions, governments, and freelance clients such as small businesses.

In India, large IT services companies hire many freshers, while product companies and startups often hire through skills tests and portfolios. Agencies value speed and versatility; startups value ownership. Freelance platforms and direct client relationships provide independent work. Networking, hackathons and open source often lead to opportunities that never appear on job boards. Referrals from people who have seen your work remain one of the strongest ways in.

## How many web developers are self-taught?

Developer surveys such as Stack Overflow's consistently find that most developers learned at least partly through online resources like documentation, videos and tutorials, and a significant share report being largely self-taught, even many who also hold degrees.

Self-teaching works in web development because resources are abundant and free, and portfolios can prove skill. Degrees still help with some employers, structured fundamentals and campus placements. The best approach combines both: formal education where available, plus self-directed projects that show you can build real things. Employers increasingly assess skills directly through projects and coding tests. That shift rewards anyone willing to build consistently, regardless of where they studied.

## How many web developers work remotely?

Remote and hybrid work are common in web development, more than in most professions, since the work needs only a computer and internet. Developer surveys show a large share of developers working fully remote or hybrid, though many companies have shifted towards office or hybrid policies.

Remote roles are competitive, so they often favour experienced developers with strong communication and proven independent work. Freelancers usually work remotely by default. To be remote-ready, practise written communication, documentation and self-management, and build a public portfolio. For freshers, in-person or hybrid roles often provide faster learning through mentorship. Many developers start in office roles and move to remote work once they have experience and references.

## How in demand are web developers?

Web developers remain in steady demand because nearly every organisation needs websites, web apps and internal tools. Competition is strongest at entry level, while experienced developers with modern frameworks, cloud and AI integration skills are especially sought after.

AI tools are changing the work, automating routine coding and increasing productivity, but they raise the value of developers who understand architecture, security, performance and user needs. Developers who can build AI-powered features, such as RAG assistants or document processing in web apps, have an advantage. Specialising while keeping broad fundamentals is a strong strategy. Accessibility, performance and security skills are also increasingly valued as regulations and user expectations rise.

## What is a web developer course?

A web developer course teaches the skills to build websites and web apps: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, a front-end framework, a back-end language, databases, version control and deployment. Options include free curricula, paid bootcamps, university courses and certifications.

Strong free choices are MDN's learning area, freeCodeCamp and The Odin Project, which emphasise building projects. Choose courses with real projects, current technologies and community support. Avoid courses that promise jobs without serious practice. Whatever course you take, build your own projects alongside it, because portfolios get interviews.

## How do I become a web developer step by step?

Learn the fundamentals, build projects of increasing complexity, learn a back end and databases, deploy everything, build a portfolio, and apply for internships and jobs while contributing to communities.

Steps:

- HTML and CSS: build static pages and responsive layouts.
- JavaScript: interactivity, the DOM, fetching APIs.
- A framework such as React or Next.js.
- A back end with Node.js or Python and FastAPI, plus SQL databases.
- Git, testing and deployment to Vercel or a cloud.
- Three portfolio projects solving real problems.
- Internships, hackathons and open-source contributions.

## How do I become a freelance web developer?

Build a portfolio of real projects, define a niche and services, set up a professional profile, find first clients through your network, local businesses or freelance platforms, and deliver excellent work that earns referrals and reviews.

Tips: start with small, well-defined projects; use written agreements covering scope, timelines, payments and ownership; communicate clearly and often; handle hosting, domains and maintenance as optional services; and keep learning. Specialising, for example in e-commerce or business websites with booking systems, helps you stand out. Manage taxes and invoicing properly from the start.

# Who can build an app? From scratch, with AI and Claude, Flutter, Canva, Wix or Excel
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/who-can-build-an-app/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Anyone can build an app today: professional developers write code, students learn by building, and non-programmers use no-code builders and AI assistants that generate code from descriptions. What matters is a clear problem, a simple first version, and the willingness to test and improve. I have shipped five production AI apps and many hackathon projects, so this page covers who builds apps and why, building from scratch or with AI and Claude, where to build web apps, Flutter, and what Canva, Wix and Excel can really do.

## Who can build an app?

Anyone with a problem to solve and time to learn can build an app. Developers build with code; designers and founders use no-code tools such as Bubble, Glide or FlutterFlow; and AI coding assistants now let beginners create working prototypes by describing what they want.

The difference between a prototype and a reliable app is engineering: handling errors, security, data, performance and updates. Non-coders can build useful personal and small-business apps; complex apps with many users still need developers. Students are in a great position: free tools, cloud credits and hackathons let you build and launch real apps while studying. My first projects started exactly that way.

## Why build a mobile app?

Build a mobile app when users need features phones do best: notifications, the camera, location, offline use, quick daily access, or device sensors. For many ideas, a mobile-friendly website is enough and cheaper to build and maintain.

Good reasons include frequent use, such as habit trackers, messaging or delivery apps; hardware access, such as scanning documents or recording audio; and offline needs in areas with weak connectivity. Consider the costs: app store reviews, separate platforms, updates and higher development effort. A progressive web app, which installs from the browser, is a middle path for many startups.

## How do I build an app from scratch?

Define one problem and one user, sketch the core screens, choose a simple stack, build the smallest version that solves the problem, test it with real users, and improve based on feedback. Launch early instead of perfecting features nobody uses.

Steps:

- Write a one-sentence problem statement and a user story.
- Sketch three to five screens on paper or Figma.
- Pick a stack: for web, Next.js and a database; for mobile, Flutter or React Native.
- Build the core flow end to end first.
- Add authentication, data storage and error handling.
- Deploy, share with ten users, collect feedback and iterate.

## How do I build an app using AI?

Use AI at every stage: brainstorm and refine the idea, generate designs or screen descriptions, write code with AI coding assistants, debug errors by pasting them in, write tests, and draft documentation. Tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Replit and Lovable support this.

Work in small steps: ask for one feature, run it, test it, then continue. Keep the code in git so you can undo mistakes. Review anything involving logins, payments and data storage yourself, since AI-generated code can contain security flaws. To build an app that uses AI, such as a chatbot or document assistant, call model APIs from your back end and keep keys secret.

## Can I build an app with Claude AI?

Yes. Claude can plan an app, write front-end and back-end code, explain and fix errors, and create interactive prototypes as artifacts in the Claude apps. Claude Code goes further, editing project files, running commands and tests in your terminal.

A practical workflow: describe the app and ask for a plan and file structure; build features one by one with Claude Code or in chat; run the app locally and share errors; ask for tests; and deploy to a host such as Vercel or Railway. You still need to review, test and understand the code, especially for user data and security, before real users rely on it.

## Where can I build a web app?

You can build locally on your computer with a code editor and deploy to hosts such as Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Render or cloud providers, or build entirely in the browser with platforms such as Replit, CodeSandbox and AI app builders that include hosting.

For learning and serious projects, local development with git gives the most control. Popular stacks: Next.js with a hosted Postgres database; Python FastAPI with a React front end; or a backend-as-a-service like Supabase. Browser builders are great for quick prototypes and demos. Choose a host with a free tier for early projects and move to paid plans only when you have users.

## How do I build an app in Flutter?

Install the Flutter SDK and an editor such as VS Code, create a project with `flutter create my_app`, run it on an emulator or your phone, then build screens with Flutter's widgets in the Dart language. One codebase targets Android, iOS, web and desktop.

Learning path: Dart basics, widgets and layouts, navigation, state management with a solution such as Provider or Riverpod, calling APIs, and storing data locally or in a backend such as Firebase or Supabase. Building iOS apps requires a Mac for final builds. Flutter's hot reload makes iterating on designs fast, which suits hackathons and student projects.

## Can I build an app in Canva?

Canva is mainly a design tool, but it can build simple websites with Canva Sites and, in newer features, small interactive experiences generated with AI. It is not suited to full apps with user accounts, databases and complex logic.

Use Canva to design app mockups, screens, icons, presentations and marketing materials, then build the real app with code or a no-code app builder. For a simple event page or portfolio, Canva's website feature can be enough. For anything that stores user data or needs reliable functionality, use proper development tools.

## Can I build an app with Wix?

Wix is primarily a website builder, and it can create websites with app-like features: bookings, online stores, member logins, forms and databases through its developer tools. Wix also offers ways for businesses to give customers a mobile app experience connected to their Wix site.

It suits small businesses that need a website with bookings or sales quickly, without code. For custom apps with unique logic, heavy data processing or AI features, a coded solution gives more flexibility. Consider lock-in: moving away from Wix later can be difficult, so think about long-term needs before investing heavily.

## Can you build an app in Excel?

You can build useful tools in Excel, such as calculators, trackers and dashboards with formulas, forms and VBA macros, but not real standalone apps. For app-like tools based on spreadsheet data, Microsoft Power Apps can turn Excel or SharePoint data into simple apps.

Excel tools work well for personal use and small teams, but struggle with many users, data integrity, security and mobile access. When a spreadsheet becomes business-critical, consider moving it to a database with a simple web app or Power Apps. Many successful apps started as spreadsheets that proved a need, so Excel is a fine place to prototype logic.

# Who is a prompt engineer? Role, job description, and is it a real job?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/who-is-a-prompt-engineer/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


A prompt engineer is someone who designs, tests and refines the instructions, examples and context given to AI models so that they produce accurate, consistent and useful output for a specific product or task. The skill is real and valuable, but most people who do it hold broader titles, such as AI engineer, GenAI developer or conversation designer. This page covers the role and a typical job description, whether it is a real, lasting and technical job, certifications and pay, and how to prompt-engineer LLMs and AI systems well.

## Who is a prompt engineer?

A prompt engineer is a specialist in getting reliable behaviour from AI models through prompts: system instructions, task instructions, examples, output formats and the context supplied, often inside a software product.

They typically sit between product, engineering and domain experts: understanding what users need, translating it into precise instructions, and proving with tests that the model behaves correctly across many inputs. In practice, many are software engineers, data scientists, writers or domain experts who developed strong prompting and evaluation skills. The job title is less common than the skill, which has become part of everyday AI engineering.

## What is the role of a prompt engineer?

The role is to make AI features reliable: write and maintain system prompts, design structured outputs, write tool descriptions for agents, build test sets, measure quality, analyse failures and improve prompts and context until results meet the bar.

Day-to-day tasks:

- Turning product requirements into clear model instructions.
- Creating evaluation sets of real and adversarial examples.
- Comparing models and prompt versions with metrics.
- Working with retrieval to supply the right context.
- Guarding against prompt injection and unsafe outputs.
- Documenting prompts and versioning them like code.

The role overlaps heavily with AI engineering, which adds building the surrounding software.

## What is a prompt engineer job description?

A typical job description asks for designing and optimising prompts for LLM-powered features, building evaluation frameworks, collaborating with engineers and product teams, and staying current with model capabilities, along with experience using LLM APIs and often Python.

Common requirements in listings:

- Experience with LLM APIs from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic or Google.
- Python for scripting evaluations and integrations.
- Understanding of retrieval-augmented generation and structured outputs.
- Strong writing and analytical thinking.
- Ability to design tests and interpret metrics.
- Domain knowledge for specialised roles, such as legal, health or education.

When you read a listing, check whether it is really an AI engineering role in disguise; most are.

## Is prompt engineer a real job?

Yes, the work is real: companies building AI products need people who can make models behave reliably. But dedicated "prompt engineer" titles are relatively uncommon, and most of this work is done by AI engineers, ML engineers, product specialists and domain experts.

Early hype suggested prompt engineering would be a large standalone profession. In practice, as models became better at following plain instructions, the work shifted from clever wording to specification, context design and evaluation, which fit naturally into engineering and product roles. For students, the safest path is to learn prompting as part of a broader skill set rather than betting on the title alone.

## Is prompt engineer still a job?

The skill is more important than ever, but it is increasingly part of other roles. Job listings now more often ask for "experience with prompt engineering" within AI engineer, GenAI developer, solutions engineer or content roles than for standalone prompt engineers.

What has grown is the surrounding work: building agents, writing tool descriptions, designing retrieval, evaluating outputs and handling safety. Those are prompt engineering in a wider sense. If you enjoy the work, aim for roles such as AI engineer or applied AI specialist, where prompting is a daily tool and you also build the systems around it.

## Is prompt engineer a technical job?

It can be either, but the most valuable version is technical. Strong prompt engineers use APIs, write Python to run evaluations, design JSON schemas, work with retrieval systems and understand model behaviour, tokens, context limits and costs.

Less technical versions exist in content, marketing and education, where the focus is writing prompts for tools such as ChatGPT to produce material. Those roles value writing skill and domain knowledge. For long-term career growth in tech, build the technical side: being able to build and measure an AI feature end to end is far more valuable than writing good prompts in a chat window.

## What is a certified prompt engineer?

A "certified prompt engineer" usually means someone who completed a prompt engineering course that issues a certificate. There is no widely recognised industry licence or official certification body for prompt engineering.

Certificates from reputable course providers show you studied the topic, which may help a little on a CV. Employers care more about evidence: a project with measurable improvements, such as raising extraction accuracy on a test set by redesigning prompts and adding validation. Be cautious of expensive certifications that promise jobs. Free official guides from model providers, plus a portfolio project, are a better investment.

## What is the salary of a prompt engineer?

Pay depends on the actual role, company, location and experience rather than the title, and listings vary widely. Because standalone prompt engineer roles are uncommon, there is no reliable single figure, especially in India.

To understand current pay for the roles you target, compare listings on job portals and company career pages for AI engineer and GenAI developer positions, and talk to people in those roles. Technical roles that combine prompting with software engineering, retrieval and evaluation are generally valued more than prompt-writing alone. Focus on building the skills those higher-value roles require.

## How do I prompt-engineer an LLM?

Treat prompts like code: define the task precisely, write a clear system prompt, specify the output format, add examples where format matters, supply the right context, then test against a set of real inputs and iterate based on failures.

A practical loop:

- Write a test set of 30 to 50 real inputs with expected outputs.
- Draft the prompt with role, rules, context and output schema.
- Run all tests, score results and read failures.
- Fix one thing at a time: instruction, example, context or schema.
- Re-run and keep the version only if scores improve.

Use structured outputs for anything parsed by code, and keep prompts in version control.

## How do I prompt-engineer AI systems beyond a single model?

For AI systems, prompt engineering extends to context design and tools: deciding what information to retrieve, how to describe tools so agents use them correctly, when the model should ask for help, and how to evaluate the whole pipeline, not just one prompt.

In a RAG system, most quality comes from retrieval: good chunks, hybrid search and reranking, then a prompt that requires citations and permits "I don't know". In agents, tool names and descriptions are the most influential prompts. Evaluate end to end with task success rates and faithfulness scores. That system-level view is what separates prompt engineering in production from prompting in a chat window, and it is how I approach systems like RAG.NextUpgrad.

# Why attend hackathons? How to participate, how long they last, AI rules, and platforms
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-attend-hackathons/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Attend hackathons to learn faster than any course allows, build portfolio projects under real constraints, meet mentors, teammates and recruiters, and sometimes win prizes or opportunities. Even without winning, you leave with new skills and a demo. I have won first prizes at Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats, and mentored at more than ten hackathons, so this page covers why to attend, how to participate, what they are like, duration, AI hackathons and rules, honest criticisms, and where to find events.

## Why should I attend hackathons?

Hackathons compress months of learning into a weekend: you pick a problem, learn whatever tools you need, build, debug under pressure and present. You also meet people who share your interests, get feedback from experienced mentors, and gain projects to discuss in interviews.

Other benefits: exposure to sponsor technologies and recruiters, confidence presenting to judges, teamwork experience, and sometimes internships, funding or incubation offers for strong teams. Hackathons also reveal what you enjoy, whether front end, AI, design or pitching, which helps choose a career direction. For students, they are among the best investments of a weekend. My own first prizes came from projects that started as hackathon ideas, and the experience of building under pressure shaped how I ship products today.

## How do I participate in hackathons?

Find events on platforms such as Devfolio, Unstop, Devpost and Major League Hacking or your college fest pages, register before deadlines, form a team or join one through the event's matching channels, prepare your tools, then build and submit by the deadline.

Steps:

- Choose an event matching your interests and level.
- Register and read rules on team size, eligibility and AI use.
- Form a balanced team: front end, back end, design, domain knowledge.
- Prepare a starter template and accounts for APIs and hosting.
- At the event, pick a narrow problem and build one complete flow.
- Submit code, a demo video and slides on time.

## What are hackathons like?

Hackathons are intense, energetic and social: an opening ceremony with themes and rules, hours of building with teammates, mentor visits, workshops, food and snacks, late-night debugging, and final presentations where judges ask questions.

Offline events feel like a mix of a workplace and a festival, with teams spread across halls, music, games and sponsor booths. Online events happen through chat channels, video calls and submission portals. Expect moments of panic when something breaks, and satisfaction when the demo finally works. Most participants remember the people and the learning more than the results.

## How long do hackathons last?

Most in-person hackathons last 24 to 48 hours, often over a weekend, with 36 hours common. Shorter formats of 6 to 12 hours exist for beginners or college events, while online hackathons may run for several days or weeks.

Multi-stage events, such as Smart India Hackathon, include idea submission and shortlisting rounds over weeks, followed by a final hackathon lasting 24 to 36 hours. Check each event's schedule: some include workshops and mentoring sessions before building starts. Plan travel and rest accordingly, especially for overnight events.

## Why are hackathons so long?

Hackathons last a day or two because building a working prototype, from idea to demo, takes real time: understanding the problem, designing, coding, integrating, testing and preparing a pitch. The length also creates an immersive, focused environment.

The continuous format encourages teams to push through problems, collaborate intensely and learn quickly. However, long events can lead to exhaustion, so good participants pace themselves: plan sleep in shifts, take breaks and eat properly. Many organisers now encourage rest and offer quiet spaces. Shorter formats exist for those who prefer not to stay overnight.

## What are AI hackathons?

AI hackathons are events focused on building with artificial intelligence: language models, computer vision, speech, agents, RAG systems and machine learning, often sponsored by AI companies providing API credits, models and mentors.

Typical projects include chatbots grounded in documents, AI tools for education, healthcare or agriculture, voice assistants in local languages, and agents automating workflows. Judges look for meaningful use of AI, not just a chatbot wrapper: real data, evaluation, safety considerations and a clear problem. KrishGyan, which gives farmers advice in their own voice and language, is the kind of AI project that stands out.

## Are AI tools allowed in hackathons?

Usually yes, but rules vary. Many hackathons allow AI coding assistants and AI APIs, sometimes requiring disclosure; some restrict pre-built code or certain tools to keep competition fair. Always read the rules and ask organisers if unsure.

Even where allowed, judges evaluate your understanding: you should explain the architecture, choices and code. Using AI to write boilerplate is common; submitting a project you cannot explain is risky. If your project uses AI as a feature, mention which models and services you used, and how you handled accuracy, privacy and costs.

## How can I use AI during hackathons effectively?

Use AI coding assistants to scaffold projects, generate boilerplate, debug errors and write documentation quickly, and use AI APIs to add capabilities such as summarisation, search or vision that would otherwise take weeks to build.

Tips:

- Prepare prompts and starter code before the event, if rules allow.
- Use AI for repetitive code; focus your time on the core idea.
- Test AI-generated code immediately; integration bugs are common.
- Keep API keys secure and monitor usage limits.
- Have a fallback if an AI API slows down during the demo.

Rehearse the demo with real AI responses so there are no surprises.

## Why do some people not like hackathons?

Common criticisms include exhaustion from overnight coding, projects that are shallow and abandoned afterwards, judging that favours polished pitches over technical depth, exclusion of people with caregiving responsibilities, and companies using hackathons for cheap ideas.

These concerns are valid, and good events address them with reasonable hours, beginner tracks, clear judging criteria and fair intellectual property terms. As a participant, choose well-organised events, rest properly, and continue promising projects afterwards. Hackathons are not for everyone; open source, personal projects and internships offer similar learning without the intensity.

## What sites list online hackathons and startup challenges, like Agorize?

Platforms listing hackathons and innovation challenges include Agorize, Devpost, Devfolio, Unstop, HackerEarth, Major League Hacking, Kaggle for data competitions, and college or company event pages. Some focus on student events; others on corporate open innovation challenges.

Agorize and similar platforms host corporate and startup challenges where students and professionals solve business problems, sometimes with prizes, internships or pilot contracts. Devpost lists many online hackathons globally, while Devfolio and Unstop cover many Indian events. Follow these platforms and set alerts for themes you care about. Check each listing's organiser, rules and prize terms, and prefer events with mentors and transparent judging.

# Why does Copilot not work? Fixes, offline use, saved chats and credits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-copilot-not-working/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot usually stops working because of a sign-in or licence problem, an outdated app, a network or firewall block, a policy set by your organisation, or an outage at Microsoft. It also needs an internet connection, since its models run in the cloud. This page walks through fixes for constant and intermittent failures, what works offline, how long Copilot and Claude keep your chats, and how Copilot credits and Copilot Studio work.

## Why does Copilot not work?

The most common causes are being signed in with the wrong account, a missing licence for the feature you want, an outdated Windows, Edge or Office version, a network that blocks Copilot, or a policy that disables it on work devices.

A checklist that fixes most cases:

- Confirm which account is signed in, personal or work, and that it has the feature.
- Update Windows, Edge and the Microsoft 365 apps.
- Sign out completely and sign back in.
- Try copilot.microsoft.com in a browser to isolate app problems.
- Switch networks, for example to mobile data, to rule out a firewall or VPN.
- Ask IT whether Copilot is enabled for your account and device.

If nothing works, check Microsoft's service status for an incident.

## Why does Copilot sometimes not work?

Intermittent failures usually come from temporary service load, an expiring sign-in session, unstable network connections, very long conversations, or hitting a usage limit for a feature such as image creation.

Patterns and fixes:

- **Fails at busy times**: wait a few minutes or retry; heavy load causes timeouts.
- **Fails after a long chat**: start a new conversation with a short summary.
- **Fails on one feature only**: you may have reached that feature's limit.
- **Fails on campus or office Wi-Fi only**: the network may filter some endpoints.
- **Fails after waking the laptop**: sign-in tokens may need refreshing; restart the app.

Note the time and what you were doing when it fails; patterns point to the cause quickly.

## Does Copilot work offline?

No. Copilot's chat runs on large models in Microsoft's cloud, so it needs an internet connection. Without one, the app cannot send your prompt or receive an answer.

Some AI features on Copilot+ PCs run locally on the laptop's neural processing unit, such as certain camera effects, live captions and some image tools, and those can work offline. They are Windows features, not the Copilot chat assistant. If you need an assistant without internet, for example while travelling, you can run a small open-weight model locally with a tool such as Ollama, accepting much lower capability than Copilot or other cloud assistants.

## Does Copilot work without internet?

The Copilot assistant does not work without internet, but you can prepare for offline time: export or copy answers you need, save documents locally, and use on-device Windows features that do not need the cloud.

Practical tips for poor connectivity, common on trains and in hostels: draft prompts offline and send them when connected; keep conversations short so they load quickly on slow networks; use the mobile app on mobile data if Wi-Fi is unreliable; and save important outputs as files rather than relying on chat history. GitHub Copilot in your code editor also needs a connection for suggestions, so download documentation you will need for offline coding.

## Do Copilot chats save?

Yes. Consumer Copilot saves your conversations in your account so you can return to them, until you delete them. Work and school accounts store Copilot interactions within the organisation's Microsoft 365 environment.

On a personal account, open your conversation history in the Copilot app or website to revisit, rename or delete chats, and use your Microsoft privacy settings to manage stored data. On a work account, your history may be visible to you in Copilot Chat, and the organisation can retain and search interactions for compliance, like email. If you do not want something stored, do not type it into any assistant. GitHub Copilot keeps chat history in your editor session.

## How long are Copilot chats saved?

On personal accounts, chats are kept until you delete them or clear your history. On work and school accounts, the organisation's retention policies decide how long Copilot interactions are kept, which can range from short periods to several years.

Deleting a chat on a work account removes it from your view, but a retention policy may keep a copy for compliance. Admins configure these policies in Microsoft Purview, often matching the rules for Teams chats and email. If you need to know your organisation's rules, ask IT or check your company's data policy. For personal accounts, review the privacy dashboard periodically and delete conversations you no longer need.

## Do Copilot chats expire?

Generally no, on personal accounts: conversations stay in your history until you delete them. On work accounts, an organisation's retention policy can delete them automatically after a set time.

Some temporary content does expire: generated download links for files can stop working after a while, and very old features or conversation formats can change when Microsoft updates the app. If a chat contains something you will need later, such as code, a plan or an important explanation, copy it into a document or notes app. Chat history is a convenience, not a reliable archive.

## Does Claude AI save chats?

Yes. Claude saves your conversations in your Anthropic account so they sync across the web, desktop and mobile apps, until you delete them. Projects keep their files and instructions as well.

You can delete individual chats, and your privacy settings control whether your conversations may be used to improve Anthropic's models; review that setting and choose deliberately. Deleted conversations are removed from your history and deleted from Anthropic's systems after a period described in its privacy policy. Incognito-style chats that are not saved to history are available too. As with any assistant, keep passwords, keys and identity documents out of your chats.

## How do Copilot credits work?

In Copilot Studio, agent usage is measured in Copilot Credits: each interaction or action an agent performs consumes credits from your organisation's capacity, with more complex actions, such as generative answers or autonomous runs, costing more. Consumer Microsoft 365 plans use a separate allowance of AI credits for Copilot in apps.

For organisations, admins buy capacity and assign it to environments, then monitor consumption in the Power Platform admin centre. Agents used by licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot users inside Microsoft 365 may be billed differently from public website agents. Because Microsoft adjusts rates and names, check the current Copilot Studio licensing guide before estimating costs. Designing agents with focused knowledge and fewer unnecessary actions reduces consumption.

## How does Copilot Studio work?

Copilot Studio is a low-code tool where you build an agent from instructions, knowledge sources and actions, test it in a chat pane, then publish it to channels such as Teams, websites and Microsoft 365 Copilot. A language model orchestrates which knowledge and actions to use for each message.

The building blocks are knowledge such as websites, SharePoint and uploaded files; actions such as connectors, Power Automate flows and APIs; topics for fixed conversation paths; and triggers for agents that run on events or schedules. Analytics show conversations, success rates and where users get stuck. Agents live in Power Platform environments, so development, testing and production can be separated and governed. Start with one narrow use case and expand after reviewing real conversations.

# Why does Copilot take so long? Deep research times, rate limits, trials and meeting notes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-copilot-takes-so-long/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


Copilot takes longer when it is reasoning in depth, researching the web, reading large files or long conversations, generating images, or facing high demand, and network or browser problems add delay. The same causes slow Claude, ChatGPT and other assistants. Deep research modes are slow by design, taking several minutes to read many sources. I build AI products where latency matters, using streaming and fallbacks, so this page covers slowness, research timings, Copilot's history, rate limits, trials, meeting notes and AI agent timing.

## Why does Copilot take so long?

Copilot slows down when it uses deeper reasoning modes, searches the web, reads large documents or long chat histories, works across Microsoft 365 data, or generates images. Peak demand and network issues add further delay, and some features wait for tool results before answering.

Ways to speed it up:

- Use quick or standard modes for simple questions.
- Start a new chat when conversations get long.
- Attach or reference only the files you need.
- Check your connection and disable heavy browser extensions.
- Try the desktop or mobile app if the browser is slow.

If Copilot is consistently slow for an organisation, admins can check Microsoft's service health dashboard for incidents.

## Why does Claude AI take so long?

Claude takes longer with extended thinking on complex tasks, long conversations that it rereads each turn, large file uploads, web search, generating long documents or code, and during high demand. Capacity limits can also slow responses or trigger usage limit messages.

Start a new conversation for new topics, use projects to share context instead of repeating files, choose a faster model for simple tasks, and turn off extended thinking when you do not need it. For developers using the API, stream responses so users see text immediately, and implement retries with backoff for overload errors. Anthropic's status page shows incidents.

## How long has Copilot been around?

GitHub Copilot launched as a technical preview in June 2021 and became generally available in June 2022. Microsoft's chat assistant began as Bing Chat in February 2023 and was renamed Copilot later that year, when Microsoft 365 Copilot also became available to businesses.

Since then, Microsoft has expanded Copilot across Windows, Edge, Office apps, Teams and Copilot Studio for building agents. The name now covers several products: GitHub Copilot for coding, Microsoft Copilot for general use, and Microsoft 365 Copilot for work data. Knowing which one you use helps when searching for help or limits.

## How long does Copilot Researcher take?

Microsoft 365 Copilot's Researcher agent typically takes several minutes, because it plans the research, searches your work data and the web, reads many sources, and writes a structured report with citations. Broad questions take longer than focused ones.

To get faster, better results, give a clear scope: the question, audience, time period, sources to prioritise and desired format. You can usually continue other work while it runs. Review citations before sharing the report, since research agents can misread or overgeneralise sources. Availability depends on your Microsoft 365 Copilot licence and admin settings.

## How long does Copilot deep research take?

Copilot's deep research or "think deeper" style features generally take from under a minute to several minutes, depending on how many sources they consult and how complex the question is. They trade speed for thoroughness.

Use them for questions that need multiple sources, comparisons or analysis, not quick facts. Write a specific prompt with the scope and the output you want, such as a comparison table with sources. If a response takes unusually long or stalls, refresh and retry, or break the question into smaller parts. As with any AI research, open the cited sources for key claims.

## How long does ChatGPT deep research take?

ChatGPT's deep research usually takes around five to thirty minutes, as it browses, reads and analyses many sources before writing a report with citations. OpenAI designed it for multi-step research rather than quick answers.

You can leave the chat while it works and come back to the finished report. It may first ask clarifying questions; answering them precisely improves results. Usage is limited per month depending on your plan. Treat reports as strong starting points: verify the most important claims in the original sources, especially numbers, dates and quotations.

## How long does a Copilot rate limit last?

Rate limits in Copilot products usually reset within minutes to hours, depending on the product, feature and plan. GitHub Copilot may limit premium model requests per period, while chat assistants may limit messages or long-running features per day.

When you hit a limit, the product usually shows when it resets or suggests switching to a different model. To avoid limits, use standard models for simple tasks, avoid repeatedly regenerating long responses, and space out heavy usage. For organisations, admins can review licences and policies. Check the specific product's documentation, since limits change as Microsoft and GitHub update plans.

## How long is the Copilot Studio free trial?

Microsoft has offered Copilot Studio trials, typically around a month, letting you build and test agents before buying, sometimes with options to extend. Terms change, so check the Copilot Studio website or Microsoft Learn for the current trial length and conditions.

Use the trial efficiently: plan one narrow agent, such as an internal FAQ assistant, prepare real knowledge sources and test questions beforehand, build and test it, then measure whether it answers correctly. Developer environments and Microsoft 365 developer programmes may also give access for learning. Note what will happen to your agents when the trial ends.

## Can I use Copilot to take meeting notes?

Yes. In Microsoft Teams, Copilot can summarise meetings, list action items with owners, answer questions about what was said, and draft follow-up messages, when transcription or recording is enabled and your organisation has the required licence.

Ask Copilot during the meeting, "What did I miss?", or afterwards, "Summarise decisions and action items." Some versions also offer AI meeting notes that are generated automatically and shared. Inform participants when meetings are transcribed, follow your organisation's policies, and review notes before sharing, since summaries can miss nuance or attribute points incorrectly.

## How long does an AI agent take to complete a task?

It ranges from seconds to hours. Simple tool-using agents finish in seconds; research agents take minutes; coding agents on large tasks or background agents can run for an hour or more. Time depends on steps, tool speed, model choice and how often the agent must retry.

To manage it: cap steps and runtime, stream progress so users see what is happening, use faster models for simple steps, run independent tool calls in parallel, and cache repeated work. For long tasks, run agents in the background and notify users when results are ready. Measure both duration and success rate; a fast agent that fails often costs more in review time.

# Why use pgvector? Is it a vector database, GPUs, FAISS, dimensions, alternatives, Supabase
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/why-use-pgvector-supabase/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-24


pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector data type, distance operators and approximate nearest neighbour indexes, so you can store embeddings next to your relational data and run semantic search with SQL. I build RAG systems with Python, FastAPI and PostgreSQL, so this page covers why to use pgvector, whether it is a vector database, when you need a dedicated one, GPUs and FAISS, semantic search, mixed dimensions, alternatives inside PostgreSQL, and setting it up on Supabase.

## Why use pgvector?

Use pgvector when your application already runs on PostgreSQL: embeddings live beside users, documents and permissions, so you get transactions, joins, backups and access control without operating a second database or syncing data between systems.

It supports HNSW and IVFFlat indexes; cosine, Euclidean, inner product and other distances; half-precision and binary vectors; and filtering with ordinary WHERE clauses. Most managed PostgreSQL services include it, such as Supabase, Neon, Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL and Azure. For many RAG applications with up to several million vectors, its performance is more than enough, and the operational simplicity of one database is a major advantage for small teams.

## What is the pgvector database?

pgvector is not a separate database; it is an extension you enable inside PostgreSQL with `CREATE EXTENSION vector`. It adds a `vector(n)` column type for embeddings of n dimensions and operators to compare them.

Distance operators include `<->` for Euclidean distance, `<=>` for cosine distance and `<#>` for negative inner product. A similarity search orders rows by distance to a query vector and limits the results. Indexes accelerate this: HNSW gives strong speed and recall with more memory and slower builds, while IVFFlat builds faster but needs data present before indexing and tuning of lists and probes. It is open source under the PostgreSQL licence.

## Is pgvector a vector database?

Functionally, PostgreSQL with pgvector acts as a vector database: it stores embeddings, indexes them and answers similarity queries. Strictly, it is a general relational database with a vector extension, not a purpose-built vector database.

The distinction matters for features and scale. Purpose-built vector databases offer things like advanced quantization, built-in hybrid fusion, multi-tenant vector partitioning and horizontal sharding designed for billions of vectors. pgvector offers the full power of SQL and PostgreSQL's maturity, plus vector search good enough for most applications. Many teams describe their PostgreSQL with pgvector as their vector store, which is accurate for practical purposes, especially in RAG systems of moderate size.

## Do you really need a vector database, or is pgvector enough?

For many applications, pgvector is enough, especially when you already use PostgreSQL and have up to a few million vectors. Choose a dedicated vector database when scale, latency targets, heavy filtering or advanced features exceed what PostgreSQL handles comfortably.

Signs you may need a dedicated system: hundreds of millions of vectors, very high query rates, strict low-latency requirements under heavy filtering, many tenants with separate indexes, or a need for features such as built-in sparse vectors and rescoring. Before switching, tune pgvector: use HNSW, raise ef_search, add B-tree indexes for filters, use iterative index scans in newer versions, and size memory so indexes fit. Measure with your real queries before deciding.

## Does pgvector use a GPU?

No. pgvector runs on the CPU inside PostgreSQL. Index building and searches use CPU and memory, with SIMD instructions to speed up distance calculations, and newer versions can build HNSW indexes in parallel across CPU cores.

GPUs matter elsewhere in your pipeline: generating embeddings with an embedding model is the GPU-heavy step, and some dedicated vector systems, such as FAISS on GPU, accelerate search with GPUs at very large scale. For typical pgvector workloads, more RAM so the index fits in memory, fast storage and enough CPU cores have a bigger effect than any GPU. Raise `maintenance_work_mem` and use parallel workers to speed up index builds.

## Does pgvector use FAISS?

No. pgvector has its own implementations of HNSW and IVFFlat written in C inside PostgreSQL. It does not depend on FAISS, although the algorithms are similar in concept to those found in FAISS and hnswlib.

This independence means indexes are stored as normal PostgreSQL index structures, benefit from write-ahead logging, crash recovery and replication, and stay consistent with your table data through transactions. FAISS, in contrast, is a library that keeps indexes in application memory or files you manage yourself. If you prototype with FAISS and later move to pgvector, recall and latency may differ slightly, so re-run your retrieval evaluation after migrating.

## Does pgvector support semantic search?

Yes. Store embeddings from any embedding model in a vector column, embed the user's query with the same model, and order rows by cosine distance to find passages with similar meaning. That is semantic search.

pgvector does not create embeddings itself; your application or a database extension calls an embedding model. Combine semantic search with PostgreSQL's full-text search using tsvector and ts_rank, then merge results with reciprocal rank fusion in SQL or application code to get hybrid retrieval, which handles exact terms better. Add filters for permissions, language or document type in the same query. This makes PostgreSQL a capable foundation for RAG systems built with FastAPI or Next.js.

## How do you handle different vector dimensions in pgvector?

A vector column has a fixed dimension, and vectors from different embedding models cannot be compared anyway. Use a separate column or table per model and dimension, and always search with a query embedded by the same model.

Common patterns: an embeddings table with model name, dimension and a separate column per model; or one table per model, each with its own HNSW index. An unconstrained `vector` column can hold mixed dimensions, but indexes require a fixed size, so you can use expression or partial indexes filtered by model. When migrating models, add the new column, backfill embeddings, build its index, compare retrieval quality, then switch queries and drop the old column.

## Are there more efficient ways to do vector search in PostgreSQL than pgvector?

Yes, several extensions build on or compete with pgvector. pgvectorscale from Timescale adds a StreamingDiskANN index and statistical binary quantization for large datasets, and VectorChord offers fast indexing with quantization, aimed at very large collections.

Other options have included Lantern and Neon's pg_embedding, the latter now deprecated in favour of pgvector. Before adding extensions, tune pgvector itself: use HNSW with suitable m and ef_construction, half-precision vectors to cut memory, binary quantization with re-ranking, and iterative scans for filtered queries. Check that your managed PostgreSQL provider supports the extension you choose, since many only allow a fixed list. Benchmark with your data, filters and hardware before committing.

## How do you use pgvector in Supabase?

Enable it in the Supabase dashboard under Database, Extensions, by turning on vector, or run `create extension vector;` in the SQL editor. Then create a table with a vector column sized for your embedding model.

Next, write a SQL function that takes a query embedding and returns the closest rows, for example ordered by cosine distance with a match threshold and count, and call it from your app through Supabase's RPC interface. Add an HNSW index for speed. Generate embeddings in an Edge Function or your backend, and store them with the text and metadata. Use row level security so users only retrieve documents they may access, which matters for multi-user RAG.
